The reaction conditions for the catalytic upgrading of acetic acid are as follows: catalyst amount, 0.325 g; space-time, 0.325 (g of catalyst) h (g of acetic acid)-1; pressure, atmospheric; partial pressure of acetic acid, 9 kPa; temperature, 450 °C; water content, 50% by volume; diluted with nitrogen.

According to the predicted conversions and yields of olefins and byproducts, valuable results are obtained with the reactor-regenerator system in the DTO process using HZSM-5 catalysts and assumable mean residence time values. The catalyst acidity plays a key role in the selection of the optimum operation conditions: temperature, space time, water concentration in the feed, and mean residence time in the reactor. Overall, increasing the temperature to 400 °C requires a decrease in the mean residence time of the catalyst (1 h) and space time (2 g h molC -1) in order to maximize the olefin yields ( > 50%) with the more selective catalyst.

In conclusion, direct synthesis of aromatics from syngas conversion with very low CH4 selectivity was achieved using a tandem reactor system composed of CoMnAl composite oxides and HZSM-5 zeolites. The CoMnAl composite oxides enabled the formation of olefins via FTS over the Co2C phase with high selectivity, and the HZSM-5 zeolites with appropriate acidity were responsible for the further aromatization of olefins. The two-stage tandem reactor showed better performance compared with other catalyst configurations, where the CoMnAl catalyst in the upstream reactor can maintain unique outstanding FTO catalytic performance and zeolites in the downstream can work at its own optimum reaction temperature. The total aromatics selectivity reached 55.5 C % at CO conversion of 34.9 C % while CH4 selectivity was as low as 2.7 C %. The optimization of zeolites acidity suppressed the hydrogenation of C2-4 - and favored the formation of aromatics. Tuning the mass ratio of the CMA catalyst to HZSM-5 can balance the rates of formation and consumption of olefins. The space velocity also affected the distribution of aromatic products, and a high space velocity was favorable for the production of light aromatics (especially for p-xylene). Further catalyst optimization is still needed to improve aromatic distribution and catalytic stability.

To investigate the simultaneous resistance of the V2O5/HWO against alkali and sulfur poisoning, the catalysts are first impregnated by K2SO4 at a high loading (350 μmol gcat -1), and after drying at 100 °C, directly tested in the SCR reactions in the presence of high-concentration SO2 (1300 mg m-3). The SCR reactions are initially conducted by a temperature-programmed procedure from 25 to 350 °C, and then the reaction temperature is kept at 350 °C for stable tests. Figure shows the NO conversions (X NO) of the catalysts under isothermal reaction conditions. Obviously, the V2O5/HWO catalyst shows excellent resistance simultaneously against alkali and sulfur poisoning, and under a GHSV of 200 000 h-1, the catalytic activity of the K2SO4-impregnated V2O5/HWO quickly increases and arrives at a steady state with a X NO of 92%. Similarly, at a higher GHSV of 400 000 h-1, the V2O5/HWO catalyst shows such a strong resistance against alkali and sulfur poisoning that alkali and sulfur have almost no influence on its catalytic activity. As expected, the conventional V2O5/WO3-TiO2 catalyst even with a low K+ loading (115 μmol gcat -1) exhibits rather poor alkali resistance and undergoes severe and continuous deactivation with time on stream until complete loss of activity is observed after 4 h. Likewise, the V2O5/HWO catalyst shows the excellent resistance against alkaline earth metals' poisoning such as Ca2+, as shown in Figure S1 in the Supporting Information.

In 2011, an organocatalyzed asymmetric cascade fluorination-heterocyclization to prepare enantiopure fluorinated heterocycles, hexahydropyrrolo [2,3-b] indole or the tetrahydro-2H-furo-[2,3-b] indole skeleton bearing a C-F quaternary benzylic carbon center 93, has been reported by the Gouverneur group. A prochiral indole 92 with a pendant heteronucleophile tethered at the C3 position enables asymmetric fluorocyclization in moderate to good enantioselectivity (52% ee to 84% ee) by the combination of bis-cinchona alkaloid (DHQ)2PHAL (C4, 20 mol %)/NFSI (1.2 equiv)/K2CO3(6.0 equiv) in acetone at -78 °C (Scheme ). The presence of a substituent at C5 position (R1 ≠ H) led to a markedly improved enantioselective control in this irreversible fluoroquaternization at C3 followed by the intramolecular capture of the transient iminium intermediate by the pendant oxygen or protected nitrogen nucleophile. Under catalytic reaction conditions, only slight decrease of enantiomeric excess and similar yields were observed by comparing with the use of stoichiometric amount of alkaloid and the level of enantioselectivity was found to be dependent on the nature of the nuecleophile (X = O, 66% ee; X = NTs, 64% ee; X = NOMe 80% ee; X = NBoc 78% ee). Additionally, for probing the reaction mechanism, only less than 2% (DHQ)2PHAL+-F can be detected by 19F-NMR at low temperature -78 °C with or without K2CO3. Thus, they proposed that the enantioselectivity may not be induced by in situ generated transient chiral N-F cinchona species because fluorine transfer from NFSI to (DHQ)2PHAL was proved to be ineffective at low temperature and the associative complexation seemed to take place through the effect of hydrogen bonding between the alkaloid catalysts and the indole substrates and/or NFSI.

dataset_item.question: How does the dual role of organically modified montmorillonite contribute to flame retardance in thermoplastic vulcanizate composites containing magnesium hydroxide?
dataset_item.answer: Organically modified montmorillonite (o-MMT) enhances flame retardance in thermoplastic vulcanizate (TPV) composites containing magnesium hydroxide (MH) through two synergistic mechanisms. First, o-MMT increases the composite's viscosity, effectively suppressing bubbling during polymer pyrolysis and reducing the release of combustible volatiles. Second, well-dispersed o-MMT forms a rigid network within the composite, stabilizing its structure by preventing excessive shrinkage of the TPV matrix and MH during combustion. This network, in conjunction with MgO, promotes the formation of a compact, continuous char layer that acts as a robust barrier to heat, oxygen, and smoke. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirms that o-MMT platelets accumulate on the burning surface, creating a netlike structure with MgO that further reinforces flame retardance. Additionally, increasing o-MMT content beyond 6 phr has been shown to yield the lowest peak heat release rate (pHRR) and smoke production rate (SPR), improving overall thermal stability and fire safety performance.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. Summary of the Purpose:
The paper investigates the combined effects of organically modified montmorillonite (o-MMT) and magnesium hydroxide (MH) on improving both the flame retardance and mechanical properties of thermoplastic vulcanizate (TPV) composites. It specifically explores how o-MMT enhances flame retardance by suppressing bubbling during polymer pyrolysis and forming a rigid network to stabilize the composite structure during burning, thereby improving the material's performance in fire safety and mechanical applications.

---

### 2. Classification of Purpose:
The purpose emphasizes **"<result>"**, as the study focuses on the outcomes of incorporating o-MMT and MH into TPV composites, particularly their influence on flame retardance and mechanical properties.

---

### 3. Relevant Research Questions:
1. How does the concentration of o-MMT (e.g., >6 phr) influence the peak heat release rate and smoke production rate of TPV/MH composites?
2. What mechanisms contribute to the improved mechanical properties of TPV/MH composites when o-MMT is added?
3. How does the dual role of o-MMT (increasing viscosity and forming a rigid network) contribute to flame retardance in TPV/MH composites?
4. What is the role of the interaction between o-MMT, MH, and the TPV matrix in forming a protective char structure during combustion?
5. How does the dispersion quality of o-MMT within the composite matrix affect the overall performance (flame retardance and mechanical properties)?
6. Can the findings regarding the synergistic effects of o-MMT and MH be generalized to other polymeric systems or vulcanizates?
dataset_item.true_false_question: Does organically modified montmorillonite enhance flame retardance in thermoplastic vulcanizate composites containing magnesium hydroxide by both suppressing bubbling during pyrolysis and stabilizing the char layer through a rigid network?

inference_contexts: Flame retardant thermoplastic vulcanizate (TPV) composites with magnesium hydroxide (MH) and organically modified montmorillonite (o-MMT) were prepared. The incorporation of a small amount of o-MMT into the TPV/MH composites enhances both the flame retardance and the mechanical properties. A compact and continuous char layer is generated in the ternary TPV/MH/o-MMT composites during burning. Such compact and continuous char residue acts as an effective barrier layer to prohibit transfer of heat, oxygen, and combustible volatiles. Specifically, the incorporation of more than 6 phr o-MMT leads to the lowest pHRR and lowest SPR among all of the samples. TGA showed that the thermal stabilities of TPV/MH systems are enhanced by adding the layer-structured nanoparticles (o-MMT). TEM images of the char residue after cone calorimetry tests confirmed that initially well-dispersed clay platelets accumulate on the burning surface and form a continuous netlike structure together with MgO. The simultaneous improvements in both flame retardance and mechanical performance have been attributed to the double roles of o-MMT. On the one hand, o-MMT increases the viscosity of the composite and suppresses the vigorous bubbling caused by polymer pyrolysis during burning. On the other hand, well-dispersed o-MMT serves as a rigid network in the sample that prohibits the massive shrinkage of both MH and the TPV matrix during burning.

An efficient and environment-friendly flame-retardant TNTP containing phosphonate and triazine units were synthesized and characterized. A triazine-based compound TN, and a phosphonate-based compound TP were also synthesized as controls. To study the charring effect and flame retardancy of TNTP on epoxy thermosets, TNTP, TN, and TP were applied to DGEBA with controlling phosphorus or nitrogen content. The char yield of TN/DGEBA/DDS was in the range of 13.1-14.9 wt % at 700 °C, which was lower than that of neat DGEBA/DDS thermoset (16.4 wt %). Whereas, TP/DGEBA/DDS showed a char yield in the range of 24.4-28.0 wt %, which was similar to that of TNTP/DGEBA/DDS (25.1-29.2 wt %). It was found that the charring effect of TNTP on DGEBA epoxy resin might be caused by phosphonate units rather than triazine moiety, and there was a synergistic effect on charring between phosphonate and triazine groups. TNTP modified thermosets exhibited not only the enhancement effect on char formation but also excellent flame retardancy compared with its TN and TP counterparts. The LOI value of TNTP-3/DGEBA/DDS was 32.4%, while that of TN-3/DGEBA/DDS was 29.0%, and TP-3/DGEBA/DDS was 31.8%. The flammability rating of TNTP/DGEBA/DDS could reach UL-94 V-0 rating with only 1.0 wt % phosphorus content, while that of TP/DGEBA/DDS could just reach UL-94 V-1 rating with 1.5 wt % phosphorus content, and TN/DGEBA/DDS was no rating. Moreover, the incorporation of phosphonate-containing TP and TNTP could decrease the peak heat release rate (PHRR), total heat release (THR), and average mass loss rate (AMLR). TNTP-3/DGEBA/DDS produced a thicker and tougher char layer than that of TP-3/DGEBA/DDS after cone calorimeter test. The phenomenon of intumescent and phosphorus-containing char layer showed there was a comprehensive flame-retardant mechanism, including the gas phase mechanism, the condensed phase mechanism, and the phosphorus-nitrogen synergistic mechanism during the combustion of TNTP/DGEBA/DDS. Especially TNTP could result in a decrease of the total smoke release (TSR), average CO yield (ACOY), and average CO2 yield (ACO2Y) of modified thermosets. These indicated that TNTP as a potential environmental friendly flame retardant could be applied in epoxy resins.

In this work, fire-safe EP with excellent mechanical properties was obtained through the ring-opening reaction with phosphorinane aminotriazole (P-ATA). As expected, EP/P-ATA materials had the higher char yield compared with pure EP in the results of TGA and CCT, and EP-7.5 wt % P-ATA reached the highest LOI value of 32.5%, almost 30% increase than the pure EP. In addition, P-ATA presented a positive effect on inhibiting the heat release and suppressing the production of CO and CO2 of epoxy thermosets. According to the investigation of char layers after combustion and volatile gases during the pyrolysis, the fire-retardant activity of P-ATA was deduced to exist in biphase effects, including the quenching effect of phosphorus-containing free radicals and dilution effect of nonflammable gas in the gaseous phase, and the formation of compact self-intumescent char layer to inhibit the transfer of heat, oxygen, and fuels in the condensed phase. Besides, EP/P-ATA materials achieved excellent mechanical properties due to more hydrogen bonding. Furthermore, the EP-2.5% and EP-5.0% thermosets can still maintain the transmittance more than 90% of neat EP. As a consequence, the P-ATA exhibited a great prospect in fire-safe EP with high mechanical properties and transparency.

In this work, we have successfully designed and synthesized lignin-based multifunctional additives (TP-g-lignin) with tunable chemical compositions by graft polymerization of a phosphorus-/nitrogen-containing compound (TP). The PLA composites with 5 wt % of TL4 or TP-g-lignin (1:4) achieve a satisfactory UL-94 V-0 rating, meeting the industry requirements for flame retardancy, despite the low LOI of only 22.5%. A balanced charring capability is primarily responsible for this excellent flame retardancy. The addition of TP-g-lignin makes PLA possess a superior UV-shielding property regardless of the chemical composition, and all PLA composites show a high UPF value above 60 due to abundant aromatic rings in the lignin backbone. More importantly, the presence of 5.0 wt % of TL4 increases the elastic modulus of PLA by ~26%, while fully preserving the mechanical strength due to tailored interfacial compatibility. This work not only provides a novel approach to synthesize lignin-derived multifunctional additives, significantly promoting the high-value-added utilization of lignin waste, but also significantly expands the practical applications of PLA in the field of packaging, electronics, automobiles, and so forth by improving its flame retardancy and UV-blocking performances, ultimately contributing to creating a sustainable society.

The bisphenol containing carboxyl unit monomer BHPBA was prepared using a facile hydrolysis reaction. It was conducted to prepare a kind of modified SAPs [BHPBA-(10-100)] with the nucleophilic polymerization method. The initial thermal degradation temperature was found to decrease with increasing the copolymerization ratio of BHPBA, while the glass transition temperature and complex viscosity of these SAPs gradully increased. These resultant copolymers were found to have good processability (including melt and solution processing except for BHPBA-(40-100)), thermal properties, and mechanical properties. Using this procedure, a series of SAPs exhibiting pronounced performance can be fabricated. Additionally, it was found that a part of the resultant copolymers BHPBA-20 can be applied to the compatibilizer for the composites of PA6T/CF, and played a notable role in improving the mechanics of the composites that the traditional SAPs could not match. Therefore, these SAPs containing carboxyl units can be potential candidates as coupling agents for special engineering plastics.

dataset_item.question: How does destruction of Mn4CaO5 cluster affect conformational flexibility of CP43 lumenal domain?
dataset_item.answer: Destruction of the Mn<sub>4</sub>CaO<sub>5</sub> cluster induces conformational fluctuations in the lumenal domain of the CP43 protein, as observed via HS-AFM. These fluctuations enhance the conformational flexibility of the CP43 lumenal domain, which directly interacts with the Mn<sub>4</sub>CaO<sub>5</sub> cluster through residues CP43-Glu354 and CP43-Arg357. The increased flexibility plays a critical role in stabilizing premature photosystem II (PSII) complexes containing the C-terminal extension of the pD1 protein. This facilitates the processing of the pD1 extension during PSII biogenesis and improves accessibility for Mn<sup>2+</sup> and Ca<sup>2+</sup>/Cl<sup>-</sup> ions, promoting the photoassembly of the Mn<sub>4</sub>CaO<sub>5</sub> cluster and the formation of the water-oxidizing complex (WOC). Thus, the integrity of the Mn<sub>4</sub>CaO<sub>5</sub> cluster directly modulates the conformational dynamics of the CP43 lumenal domain, influencing PSII biogenesis and WOC assembly.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. Summary of the Purpose:
The purpose of this paper is to investigate the structural dynamics of the lumenal region of the Photosystem II (PSII) core complex, particularly focusing on the role of the Mn4CaO5 cluster and its surrounding proteins, during the dissociation and conformational changes. High-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM) was used to visualize these dynamics for the first time, revealing the structural flexibility of the CP43 lumenal domain and its potential role in PSII biogenesis and the photoassembly of the Mn4CaO5 cluster.

---

### 2. Classification of Purpose:
The purpose of this paper emphasizes "<result>" because it focuses on the findings related to the structural dynamics of PSII and the roles of its components, rather than the development of a novel method.

---

### 3. Relevant Research Questions:
1. What structural changes occur in the lumenal region of PSII during the dissociation of extrinsic proteins like PsbP and PsbO?
2. How does the destruction of the Mn4CaO5 cluster influence the conformational flexibility of the CP43 lumenal domain?
3. What roles do the observed structural dynamics play in the biogenesis of PSII and the assembly of the Mn4CaO5 cluster?
4. Can high-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM) provide further insights into the dynamic processes of other multiprotein complexes in photosynthesis?
5. What are the implications of CP43's structural flexibility for the functional stability and efficiency of PSII under physiological conditions?
dataset_item.true_false_question: Does the destruction of the Mn4CaO5 cluster increase the conformational flexibility of the CP43 lumenal domain through interactions with CP43-Glu354 and CP43-Arg357?

inference_contexts: HS-AFM was successfully applied to visualize the protein dynamics of the lumenal region of the PSII core complexes. We first observed the stepwise release of the PsbP and PsbO extrinsic proteins from the PSII complex. Subsequently, upon the destruction of the Mn4CaO5 cluster, the lumenal domain of the CP43 protein, which directly interacts with the Mn4CaO5 cluster via CP43-Glu354 and CP43-Arg357, was observed to undergo conformational fluctuations. The flexible conformation of the CP43 lumenal domain has a significant function in stabilizing a premature PSII complex with a C-terminus extension of pD1 and facilitating the processing of this extension. In addition, the conformational fluctuation of this CP43 domain promotes the photoassembly of the Mn4CaO5 cluster by increasing the accessibility of Mn2+ and Ca2+/Cl- ions as constituents of the WOC. Thus, the dynamic nature of the CP43 lumenal domain plays key roles in the biogenesis of PSII complexes and the formation of WOC.

Because of the novel applications of ILs in biochemistry and biomedical technology, the search for biocompatible ILs has recently gained increasing attention. In this study, we present two novel biocompatible ILs, TMGAla and TMGAsp, and characterize their effects in dilute aqueous solutions on the structure and stability of the widely used RFP mCherry. Our temperature-dependent spectroscopy data show that while TMGAsp have effects similar to previously studied conventional ILs (BMIBF4, EMIAc, and TMGAc), TMGAla has a much stronger destabilization effect and lower the mCherry unfolding temperature from 80 to 60 °C. At 25 °C, the chromophore is modulated by TMGAla but not TMGAsp or the other conventional ILs, leading to a blueshift in absorbance and fluorescence peaks and an increased Stokes shift. Whereas the blueshift in absorbance and fluorescence indicates an increase of the viscosity of the chromophore local environment, the redshift to the Stokes shift implies an increase of polarity of the chromophore environment. Our MD data at 25 °C show that the chromophore conformation and its interaction with the protein are slightly changed relative to the conformation exhibited in the absence of ILs or TMGAsp. While the key interactions with Lys70, Arg95, and Trp93 are maintained, a hydrogen bond between the chromophore and Gln163 present more pronouncedly in mCherry with TMGAla than TMGAsp or no ILs. These changes might explain the increase of the local polarity and viscosity of the chromophore that cause the spectra shifts. In addition, the conversion of a short fragment 142-144 of the β-strand 7 into coiled conformation was observed in mCherry with TMGAla and TMGAsp. This loss of an interstrand hydrogen bond might partially explain the destabilization effects of ILs. Ala by itself has minimal effect on mCherry at the same concentration. The MD simulations predict that the mCherry-Asp interactions are hydrophilic and the mCherry-Ala interactions are more hydrophobic. Therefore, we speculate that the hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity of the amino acid anion modulates the destabilizing TMG-mCherry interaction, and with TMGAla causes a slight conformational change in the β-strand structure and destabilizes the protein structure.

Our results together with the recent discoveries in the field of SPCs bring us to the challenges that must be addressed when interested in the targeted design of SPCs. Inspired by the reticular chemistry approach, synthetic guidelines towards SPCs that make use of available topological databases seem the natural approach. The reticular chemistry approach, as a successful rigid body approach, intrinsically neglects topologic, symmetric, and thermodynamic parameters related to dynamic processes that render structural flexibility, and modifications must be applied. For instance, once a topology (from a database) has been tested for potential flexibility by applying classical counting rules or group theoretical considerations, , the next step would be the combination of the given topology with available linkers and metal nodes. The existence of a flexibility of a topology-metal-node-linker combination could then be tested by searching for the occurrence of RUMs, as open-pore to closed-pore phase transitions are typically of displacive nature. RUMs are an appealingly simple concept and their existence can be predicted by using relatively cheap algorithms, for which different available codes exist. The arguably most challenging step is then the assessment of the free energy landscape of both phases, where a free energy landscape is required that exhibits distinct energy minima, but at the same time is shallow enough to facilitate responsivity of the material as function of an external stimulus. It currently seems as a good approximation that the vibrational entropy is larger in a less-dense (potentially open-pore) structure and is therefore predetermined. Therefore, dispersion interactions might be the tool of choice for experimentalists to access the free energy landscape synthetically. The manipulation of dispersion interactions has already proved to be a useful lever to move the entropy-dispersion balance towards the one or the other direction. For instance, side-chain functionalization of the bdc2- linker within the materials series of Zn2(fu-bdc)2(dabco) can render the materials thermoresponsive. Looking at ZIF-4 (Zn), dispersion interactions thus could be accessed by linker functionalization, that is, the partial incorporation of functionalized imidazolate linkers into the structures. It is important to mention that the above-given outline neglects structural flexibility when linker deformation or metal-node deformation is involved; , here however, ideas to extend the RUM model to so-called "quasi-RUMs" have already been proposed , and potentially offers exciting opportunities for SPCs in the future. Therefore, it currently seems that the combination of topological control of vibrational entropy and the tunability of dispersion interactions offers great promise for the formulation of design guidelines of SPCs, with many challenging aspects out there that remain to be addressed by computation and experimentation.

Residues of the THP L and T strands from the NMR-derived structure showed a significant number of interactions with the CAT domain, while the THP M strand had very few interactions with the CAT domain. Interactions of the THP L and T strands with the CAT domain strained these two strands and allowed for opening near the scissile bond. The scissile bond in the NMR-derived structure was properly positioned in the catalytic site of the CAT domain in contrast to its position in the X-ray crystallographic structure, supporting the proposal that the NMR-derived structure represents a catalytically productive form of the complex.

In summary, the bidirectional tuning of thermal conductivity of the ferroelectric material PTO is investigated under an electric field through first-principles calculations. Due to the hysteresis characteristic, the structure response under the E-field is opposite depending on the direction of E-field, causing the opposite change of thermal conductivity. Moreover, the E-field can also induce the change of domain wall density, i.e.. the domain wall response, which can be combined with structure response to increase the tuning range. The tuning range due to the structure response has a weak dependence on temperature, while it increases significantly with the decreasing temperature due to the domain wall response. In addition, the dimensionality effects on the tuning range are investigated. The calculation results show that bulk PTO and the cross-plane direction of the PTO thin film have a larger tuning range, while the in-plane directions of the thin film and nanowire have a smaller value. In addition, for all dimensionalities and directions, the tuning range increases with decreasing temperature due to the domain wall response.

dataset_item.question: How do the molecular self-assembly behaviors of native silkworm fibroin and reconstituted silkworm fibroin differ under shear and at high concentrations?
dataset_item.answer: Native silkworm fibroin (NSF) and reconstituted silkworm fibroin (RSF) exhibit distinct molecular self-assembly behaviors under shear and at high concentrations. Without shear, neither NSF nor RSF self-assembles, remaining as globular proteins. However, under shear at a concentration of 1000 mg/L, NSF forms long, straight nanofibrils that resemble the structures found in natural silk fibers, whereas RSF fails to self-assemble. Quantitative analysis further reveals that even at lower concentrations (e.g., 10 mg/L), NSF consistently forms significantly larger assemblies compared to RSF under shear. These findings highlight that the reconstitution process disrupts the inherent self-assembly capability of silkworm fibroin, rendering RSF functionally inferior to NSF for applications requiring silk-like structures.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. Purpose Summary:
The paper aims to compare the molecular-scale self-assembly behavior of native silkworm fibroin (NSF) and reconstituted silkworm fibroin (RSF) using atomic force microscopy. The study highlights the dependence of self-assembly on shear and identifies significant differences between NSF and RSF, with NSF showing superior self-assembly capabilities, particularly at high concentrations. The findings suggest that the reconstitution process disrupts RSF's inherent self-assembly properties.

---

### 2. Classification of Purpose:
**<result>**  
The emphasis of the paper is on presenting results, specifically the differences in self-assembly behavior between NSF and RSF and the implications of these findings.

---

### 3. Research Questions:
1. How does the molecular self-assembly behavior of native silkworm fibroin (NSF) compare to that of reconstituted silkworm fibroin (RSF)?
2. What role does shear play in the self-assembly process of NSF and RSF?
3. How does the concentration of fibroin solutions influence the formation and properties of self-assembled fibrils in NSF and RSF?
4. To what extent does the reconstitution process affect the inherent self-assembly capabilities of silkworm fibroin?
5. What structural differences exist between the nanofibrils formed by NSF and RSF under identical experimental conditions?
6. Can atomic force microscopy and image analysis provide quantitative insights into the self-assembly mechanisms of silk dopes?
dataset_item.true_false_question: Does reconstituted silkworm fibroin self-assemble into long nanofibrils under shear at high concentrations around 1000 mg/L?

inference_contexts: Our study represents the first molecular-scale comparison of native and reconstituted silkworm protein. In particular, we used AFM to visualize the molecular structures from aqueous NSF and RSF solutions at different concentrations deposited on mica, with and without shear. Several significant qualitative observations were made. First, we found that in the absence of shear, neither NSF nor RSF showed any tendency to self-assemble whatsoever. Instead, we only observed globular protein molecules in varying densities, according to the solution concentrations. Second, we found that at the highest concentration we studied, 1000 mg/L, NSF and RSF exhibited dramatically different behaviors under shear: NSF showed long, straight, nanofibrillar assemblies, closely resembling the structures observed on the surface of natural silk fibers. RSF, in contrast, showed no self-assembly under the same conditions. From this, we concluded that the reconstitution process significantly diminished silk's inherent natural self-assembly capabilities. Furthermore, the quality, consistency, and quantity of our AFM data allowed us to employ quantitative image analysis, which provided us with additional insights. Qualitatively, both NSF and RSF protein solutions at lower concentrations exhibited self-assembly. However, our quantitative analysis of AFM images revealed that NSF assemblies at the same concentration of 10 mg/L were significantly larger than RSF assemblies, further supporting our conclusion of disrupted self-assembly in RSF. Hence, on the basis of our results, we suggest that RSF may not be considered a fully functional silk-both for silk studies and applications. We suggest that an AFM-based morphological characterization of silk assembly, which becomes ever more valuable with the emergence of increasingly powerful quantitative tools, be employed for the comparison of different silks to one another and/or a native standard in future studies of artificial silks.

In this study, we constructed gentamicin-loaded silk fibroin coatings on 3D-printed porous CoCrMo bone substitutes by using EPD technique. Through optimization, relatively intact, continuous, homogeneous, and conformal coatings with average thickness of 2.30 ± 0.58 μm were deposited around the struts with few pores blocked. The porous metal substitutes showed no obvious loss in mechanical properties after the EPD process. The initial osteoblastic response on coated substrates was better than that on metal surface, and the SFGM coatings had significant antibacterial effect within 1 week. This work would be beneficial for exploiting the beneficial properties of silk fibroin EPD coatings to improve the biological functionality of porous structures made of medical metals.

In summary, we find a silicon-based highly efficient thermoelectric material Si2Te3, having figure of merit ZT = 1.86 under n-type doping. We resolve for the first time the ground state structure of this very important silicon-based chalcogenide. We predicted the most probable 8 lattice sites for silicon out of 28 possible octahedral voids in a unit cell of Si2Te3 containing 12 Te and 8 Si atoms. With the help of of Wyckoff positions corresponding to the space group P31c, out of total C (28,8) combinations of structures, the search was narrowed down to only 15 configurations. The ground state structure of Si2Te3, thus, obtained is a layered structure with excellent electronic and transport properties. Favorable electronic properties include combination of light and heavy bands, steep nature of DOS near the Fermi level, and large number of charge carrier pockets. These give rise to high electrical conductivity, low conductivity effective mass, and large thermopower, leading to high power factor in n-doped Si2Te3. Furthermore, low-lying optical branches in phonon spectra, low phonon group velocities and large negative Gruneisen parameters result in low lattice thermal conductivity. By integrating the effect of all these features, n-doped Si2Te3 exhibits high figure of merit ZT of 1.86 at 1000 K, which is comparable to some of the best known state-of-the-art thermoelectric materials. Hence, Si2Te3, with high ZT over wide range of temperature, can be a long sought silicon-based highly efficient thermoelectrics with strong possibility of integration into the existing electronic devices.

For polymers, natural or otherwise, to produce carbon fiber of a similar quality as PAN, they cannot rely on hydrogen bonding for structural stability or contain a high mass fraction of oxygen, lest they shrink to an unusable extent. A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. Polyalanine-like domains could be incorporated into block copolymers for biomimetic graphite precursors. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

Therefore, the impact of these results goes beyond the simple question of nonspecific protein adsorption on a certain blend film system but may be a starting point for developing suitable models for the further understanding of the interaction of proteins with lignocellulosics under environmental conditions, particularly at the interfaces of the cell walls. These interfaces are the key point for all types of transport mechanisms in cells, and determine the interaction capacity with other biomolecules and even microorganisms. dataset_item.question: How are polarizability tensor components of atomic basins calculated using quantum theory of atoms in molecules?
dataset_item.answer:
The polarizability tensor components of atomic basins are calculated using the Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM) by partitioning the molecular electron density into atomic basins and analyzing their response to an applied static electric field. A uniform electric field (typically 0.001 atomic units) is applied along each Cartesian direction, inducing changes in the electron density and generating perturbed states. The dipole moment of each atomic basin is computed for both the unperturbed (ground state) and perturbed states. 

The polarizability tensor component \( \alpha_{ij}(\Omega) \) is then obtained by numerically differentiating the induced dipole moment component in direction \( i \) with respect to the applied electric field in direction \( j \), ensuring the perturbation is small enough to preserve linear response behavior. This finite-difference approach yields a symmetric polarizability tensor, whose eigenvalues define the principal polarizabilities. The isotropic polarizability (average over all directions) and anisotropic contributions (directional dependence) can be derived from these eigenvalues.

This method provides origin-independent and transferable polarizability predictions for atomic basins, making it suitable for studying molecular systems with well-defined atomic partitioning.

dataset_item.question: How do coarse granules of strontium oxide compare to fine granules in terms of CO2 carrying capacity and reaction kinetics during repeated carbonation-calcination cycles?
dataset_item.answer:
Coarse granules of strontium oxide (SrO) outperform fine granules in terms of CO₂ carrying capacity and reaction kinetics during repeated carbonation-calcination cycles. Initially, coarse SrO granules exhibit significantly higher CO₂ carrying capacities compared to fine granules, achieving a final carrying capacity of 9.4% after multiple cycles, whereas fine granules demonstrate lower and declining capacities. The enhanced performance of coarse granules is attributed to their bimodal pore structure, which facilitates efficient gas diffusion and mitigates sintering and microstructural degradation. This pore structure also helps maintain durability by reducing the transition to an inert surface and limiting capacity decay.

Reaction kinetics differ between granule sizes. Coarse granules exhibit slower carbonation kinetics initially due to the formation of a carbonated layer that hinders CO₂ diffusion. However, this effect is counterbalanced by the wider pore size distribution, enabling gas diffusion through multiple pathways and maintaining consistent reaction rates over cycles. In contrast, fine granules suffer from rapid capacity decay and incomplete calcination at high temperatures (e.g., 1200°C) due to sintering-induced microstructural rearrangements.

Composite materials such as SrO/Al₂O₃ coarse granules further enhance performance by stabilizing CO₂ uptake over repeated cycles, whereas SrO/hydroxyapatite mixtures perform poorly. Thus, granule size and microstructural stability are critical factors in optimizing high-temperature CO₂ capture systems.

dataset_item.question: How does boron-nitrogen doping affect excited-state lifetimes and photochemical product stability in hexaphenyl borazine compared to hexaphenyl benzene?
dataset_item.answer:
Boron-nitrogen (BN) doping in hexaphenyl borazine significantly reduces excited-state lifetimes and destabilizes photochemical products compared to hexaphenyl benzene. The excited-state lifetime of hexaphenyl borazine is approximately 3 ps, drastically shorter than hexaphenyl benzene's 428 ps. This reduction is attributed to BN doping, which induces electron localization and disrupts conjugation, increasing diradical character and accelerating nonadiabatic decay processes.

Photochemically, hexaphenyl benzene undergoes cyclization with a moderate yield of 25%, forming stable cyclized products with distinct spectroscopic signatures. In contrast, hexaphenyl borazine does not yield a stable cyclized product. Computational analyses reveal that BN doping lowers the activation energy for ring opening and destabilizes cyclized intermediates, suppressing photochemical cyclization altogether. These findings demonstrate how isoelectronic BN substitution fundamentally alters excited-state dynamics and thermodynamic stability, reshaping photochemical pathways despite similarities in electronic structure.

This study highlights the profound impact of BN doping on photophysical and photochemical behavior, offering insights into tailoring properties of polyaromatic compounds for advanced applications.

dataset_item.question: How does the use of 1-chloronaphthalene as a cosolvent affect the morphology of polymer films and photovoltaic performance?
dataset_item.answer: The use of 1-chloronaphthalene as a cosolvent significantly enhances the morphology and photovoltaic performance of polymer films. It promotes favorable face-on polymer chain orientation and optimized phase separation between donor and acceptor materials, which are critical for efficient charge transfer. Specifically, for PQP-based solar cells, processing with 1-chloronaphthalene achieves a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 3.52%. Furthermore, the cosolvent's ability to fine-tune the morphology enables superior device performance compared to structurally similar polymers like PFP.

dataset_item.question: How does the second-order multireference perturbative model IVO-SSMRPT compare to other MRPT methods in predicting electronic properties of tetraradicals?
dataset_item.answer:
The second-order multireference perturbative model IVO-SSMRPT demonstrates comparable accuracy to established MRPT methods such as CASPT2 and NEVPT2 in predicting electronic properties of tetraradicals. It offers distinct advantages, including strict size-extensivity, intruder-state-free calculations, and flexibility in handling both relaxed and unrelaxed model spaces. These features make it particularly robust for systems exhibiting quasidegeneracy and complex electronic structures involving both static and dynamic correlation.

For tetraradicals like 2,4,6-tridehydropyridine radical cation and tetradehydrobenzene isomers, IVO-SSMRPT reliably predicts singlet ground states, violating Hund’s rule due to weak exchange interactions, dynamic correlation effects, and through-bond coupling stabilization. Additionally, it accurately reproduces energy splittings, optimized geometries, and state orderings consistent with high-level ab initio benchmarks. In cases involving nitrogen substitution, resonance delocalization further stabilizes electronic structures without significantly altering state ordering.

While limited by its second-order treatment and basis set size, IVO-SSMRPT proves computationally efficient and reliable for studying quasidegenerate polyradicals. Its ability to capture intricate electronic effects validates it as a robust and versatile alternative to traditional MRPT approaches for systems with challenging multireference characteristics.

dataset_item.question: How does the substitution of copper ions with nickel, iron, or manganese affect the structural properties and catalytic efficiency of lithium cuprate for carbon oxide reactions?
dataset_item.answer:
The substitution of copper ions with nickel, iron, or manganese in lithium cuprate (Li₂CuO₂) induces structural changes, such as crystalline cell contraction or distortion, due to the smaller ionic radii of Ni²⁺ (63 pm), Fe³⁺ (63 pm), and Mn⁴⁺ (53 pm) compared to Cu²⁺ (71 pm). XRD analysis confirms solid solution formation, and the higher oxidation states of iron and manganese create cation vacancies, which enhance ion mobility and catalytic stability. These vacancies, combined with the redox activity of Mn⁴⁺, facilitate CO oxidation through the Mars-van Krevelen mechanism.

The catalytic efficiency varies with the substituent: manganese substitution results in superior CO oxidation due to its redox behavior and vacancy-driven sorption, while nickel substitution exhibits the highest CO₂ chemisorption efficiency (28.5 wt%) in CO/O₂ environments, aided by its ability to promote homolytic oxygen dissociation. Iron substitution contributes to catalytic stability and improved oxygen mobility.

During CO₂ capture and catalytic oxidation, the material forms Li₂CO₃ and CuO, with minor Cu⁺ phases detected. Oxygen in the reaction environment prevents structural reduction and promotes chemisorption, enabling bifunctional performance by combining efficient CO₂ capture and CO oxidation. At 700 °C, 5Ni-Li₂CuO₂ achieves the highest CO₂ capture efficiency (91.1%), while 5Mn-Li₂CuO₂ excels in CO oxidation. Overall, metal substitution enhances both structural properties and catalytic performance for carbon oxide reactions.

dataset_item.question: How can the design of metal-based ionic liquids be optimized to minimize equipment corrosion and reduce emulsification during the regeneration process in oxidative desulfurization?
dataset_item.answer:
To optimize the design of metal-based ionic liquids (MILs) for minimizing equipment corrosion and reducing emulsification during the regeneration process in oxidative desulfurization (ODS), the following strategies can be implemented:

1. **Hydrophobicity and Ligand Design**: Develop hydrophobic MILs with biodegradable ligands such as amino acids, choline, or deep eutectic solvents to enhance environmental compatibility, reduce corrosion risks, and mitigate secondary pollution. Prioritizing halogen-free formulations further reduces equipment degradation and enhances eco-compatibility.

2. **Cationic/Anionic Composition Tuning**: Optimize the ionic composition to enhance hydrophobicity, thermal stability, and selective absorption properties, which help address emulsification issues during regeneration. For example, MILs like [Bmim]FeCl4 exhibit high stability and low corrosion potential.

3. **Viscosity Reduction**: Use aprotic organic solvents with low viscosity and high boiling points to improve industrial scalability without compromising the MILs’ eco-compatibility. This mitigates challenges related to high viscosity during large-scale ODS applications.

4. **Efficient Recovery Methods**: Leverage phase-transfer characteristics of MILs to facilitate separation and recovery processes, reducing oil contamination and improving recyclability. Hydrolyzed byproducts such as Fe(OH)₃ can be repurposed to minimize secondary pollution.

5. **Emulsification Control**: Focus on creating MILs with high stability and selective absorption properties to address emulsification issues during regeneration. This ensures efficient separation and prevents contamination of oil during the process.

By integrating these strategies, MILs can be optimized for reduced corrosion, minimized emulsification, and enhanced environmental sustainability, making them more suitable for large-scale industrial applications.

dataset_item.question: How does the electrogenerated molecularly imprinted polymer film contribute to enantiospecific recognition and oxidation peak differentiation for β-blocker enantiomers?
dataset_item.answer: The electrogenerated molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP) film contributes to enantiospecific recognition and oxidation peak differentiation for β-blocker enantiomers through its chiral selectivity and unique electrochemical properties. During fabrication, the MIP film is imprinted with the R(+)-enantiomer template, forming chiral cavities that selectively bind the imprinted enantiomer. This selective interaction facilitates enantiospecific recognition of β-blockers. Additionally, the MIP-modified electrode enables differentiation of oxidation peaks by exhibiting two distinct electrochemical responses: enantiospecific oxidation peaks for the imprinted enantiomer and nonspecific oxidation peaks shared by both enantiomers. These peaks arise from the electrooxidation of the secondary amine in the β-blockers' backbone and reflect inherent electrochemical differences between the enantiomers. The combined selectivity from molecular imprinting and the electrochemical behavior of β-blockers underscores the MIP film's potential for pharmaceutical and clinical applications, though further investigation into the exact enantiospecific interactions may enhance its utility.

dataset_item.question: What factors contribute to the faster hole transfer compared to electron transfer in MoS2 and WS2 heterojunctions?
dataset_item.answer: The faster hole transfer in MoS₂/WS₂ heterojunctions is primarily attributed to a combination of factors that enhance hole mobility across the interface. These include stronger donor-acceptor interactions, larger nonadiabatic coupling, longer-lived quantum coherence (10–30 fs), and a higher density of acceptor states for holes compared to electrons. Additionally, charge separation couples to out-of-plane phonon modes (~400 cm⁻¹), which further facilitates efficient hole transfer. The asymmetry in electronic and vibrational interactions between holes and electrons leads to ultrafast hole dynamics, making MoS₂/WS₂ heterostructures highly promising for optoelectronic and energy applications.

dataset_item.question: What structural and electronic factors contribute to the formation of the Mg3TeO6-type structure in Mn3WO6, and how do they compare with other M3M'O6 phases?
dataset_item.answer:
The formation of the Mg₃TeO₆-type structure in Mn₃WO₆ is governed by a combination of structural and electronic factors that distinguish it from corundum-derived phases and other M₃M′O₆ frameworks. A key structural feature is the absence of face-sharing MnO₆ octahedra, which contrasts with polar double corundum structures. The large size of Mn²⁺ (0.83 Å) plays a significant role in stabilizing the trigonal symmetry of this structure, while the isotropic d⁵ electronic configuration of Mn²⁺ further contributes to its stability. These electronic factors, particularly the isotropy of the d⁵ configuration, are also observed in Mg²⁺ (d⁰ configuration), suggesting that orbital filling, in addition to cation size, is crucial for stabilizing the Mg₃TeO₆ structure.

While the size and charge differences between Mn²⁺ and W⁶⁺ do influence the framework, they alone do not fully explain the formation of this structure, as smaller cations like Mg²⁺ can also adopt the Mg₃TeO₆-type structure. Furthermore, Mn₃WO₆ and Cu₃WO₆ exhibit distinct coordination geometries (MnO₆ octahedra vs. CuO₅ bipyramids), highlighting the role of cation size and d-orbital filling in driving structural diversity within the M₃M′O₆ family. Overall, the interplay between cation size, isotropic electronic configurations (d⁵ or d⁰), and the absence of face-sharing octahedra distinguishes Mn₃WO₆ and expands the structural possibilities for multiferroic and magnetoelectric materials. Further investigation into the electronic and geometric factors influencing these phases is necessary to clarify broader trends within the M₃M′O₆ family.

The main advantages of commercial microdilution systems include automated reading and rapidity; on the other hand, compared with the disk diffusion method, they have still lower sensitivities in the detection of resistance mechanisms. Since Bauer, Kirby et al. described disk diffusion in 1960s, this technique has been the point of reference for antimicrobial susceptibility testing in many clinical microbiological laboratories and still remains one of the most widely used methods in routine clinical microbiology laboratories. The method is versatile for testing the majority of bacterial pathogens and it does not require any special equipment. , Moreover, it is simple and practical and well-standardized. The method involves the application of antibiotic solutions of different concentrations to cups, wells, or paper discs, placed on the surface of or punched into agar plates seeded with the test bacterial strain. dataset_item.question: How does the rotational angle between tetracene units affect the formation rate of correlated triplet pair states in para-dimers?
dataset_item.answer:
The rotational angle between tetracene units in para-dimers plays a critical role in determining the formation rate of correlated triplet pair states (1(T1T1)). Twisted configurations of tetracene units in para-bis(ethynyltetracenyl)benzene (p-BETB) exhibit the fastest 1(T1T1) formation rate among ortho-, meta-, and para-dimers due to strong vibronic couplings (VCs) and enhanced spatial overlap of electronic wave functions. This increased vibronic coupling compensates for the larger singlet fission energy gap (ΔE SF) in para-dimers, facilitating rapid triplet pair formation.  

Conversely, a coplanar alignment of tetracene units in para-dimers significantly reduces the formation rate, making it ten times slower compared to ortho-dimers. This structural dependence underscores the importance of tetracene unit rotation in optimizing electronic interactions and vibronic couplings, which are key factors driving the efficient formation of correlated triplet pair states.  

Overall, the twisting of tetracene units in para-dimers enhances the formation rate by maximizing vibronic coupling and spatial overlap, while coplanar alignment diminishes these effects, leading to slower formation rates. This explains the experimentally observed fast triplet pair formation in p-BETB.

Steady-state and time-resolved optical studies revealed that most of the photogenerated singlet excitons in the BPET thin film undergo ultrafast ( < 200 fs) relaxation to the correlated triplet pair state followed by triplet separation in a picosecond time scale. The phenylethynyl group substituted in the 5- and 12-positions of tetracene modifies the singlet-triplet energy levels and intermolecular electronic coupling favorably to induce ultrafast and efficient singlet fission. A small fraction of the singlet population, observed to undergo slow SF in tens of picoseconds, is attributed to the presence of the noncrystalline phase in the thin-film sample. Overall, the BPET thin film exhibits efficient SF with long-lived triplet transients. Low cost, commercial availability, broad UV-vis absorption covering a significant part of the solar spectrum, singlet fission with high yield, and long triplet lifetime make BPET a potential candidate for singlet-fission-based solar cell materials.

However, the iSF dynamics are slowed (1.09 ns) in the dimer having the bridge with extended conjugation showing an efficiency of 185.1%. These experimental results reveal that the pentacene dimers having a rigidity planar bridge exhibited an efficient iSF process and a higher triplet quantum yield compared to the dimer with a twisted bridge. Thus, it is inferred that while designing the new materials for high-efficiency organic photovoltaic cells, the planarity of the bridges should be maintained and bridges with twisting in nature should be avoided in the pentacene dimers.

Accounting for perturbation theory, phosphorescence gains intensity from spin-allowed S-S and T-T electronic transitions via the spin-orbit coupling mixing of the singlet excited states manifold (Sn) with the first triplet (T1) excited state and of the triplet excited states manifold (Tn) with the ground singlet (S0) electronic state. A proper account of spin-orbit coupling makes it possible to estimate the main parameters of phosphorescence, like the transition dipole moment, radiative lifetime, and rate constant for each of the spin sublevels of the triplet state. The best equipment for the theoretical study of phosphorescence of today is, in our opinion, the quadratic-response theory formalism implemented in the DALTON program package, where this method is accessible at the HF, MCSCF, or DFT levels and where the spin-orbit operator can be accounted for exactly or by various effective approximations. The quadratic-response theory rests on an implicit sum-overstate principle, which allows one to describe correctly and largely clarify the phosphorescence mechanism for a number of difficult cases such as dioxygen (magnetic phosphorescence), benzene (vibronically induced phosphorescence), porphyrins (external and internal heavy atom effects), and cyclometalated iridium complexes (spin-sublevel selectivity and tuning of transition dipole moment orientation).

dataset_item.question: What are the advantages and challenges of using moving crude adiabatic representation in quantum nonadiabatic dynamics simulations?
dataset_item.answer:
The moving crude adiabatic (MCA) representation in quantum nonadiabatic dynamics simulations offers a unique blend of advantages and challenges. On the positive side, it combines the smooth potential energy surfaces characteristic of diabatic representations with the direct accessibility of adiabatic states from electronic structure calculations. This hybrid approach allows for more accurate treatment of quantum nonadiabatic processes, especially in systems with complex electronic couplings.

However, the MCA representation comes with significant challenges due to its nonanalytic parametrization of the wave function. This nonanalyticity can result in energy nonconservation during simulations. To address this, the stationary action version of the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) is often employed, which ensures system energy conservation. A notable difficulty arises when Gaussian basis functions are propagated classically, as the basis set incompleteness and interference between Gaussian wave packets exacerbate energy nonconservation issues. Fully quantum TDVP propagation of Gaussian parameters resolves this problem but increases computational complexity due to the coupling between equations of motion.

Additional strategies are required to manage wave function complexity during simulations. Systematic basis set extensions, such as spawning and cloning, are crucial for capturing the growing complexity of the wave function. Spawning relies on estimating population flow, while cloning utilizes decoherence strain to adaptively refine the basis set. Extending MCA methods to open quantum systems introduces further challenges in maintaining energy and population conservation. The Nonstochastic Open System Schrödinger Equation (NOSSE) has been proposed as a promising solution for addressing these issues in open quantum systems.

In summary, while the MCA representation offers significant advantages in combining the strengths of diabatic and adiabatic approaches, its challenges related to energy conservation, computational complexity, and basis set management must be carefully addressed through advanced variational principles and adaptive basis set techniques.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. **Summary of the Purpose**  
The paper aims to review and analyze techniques for simulating fully quantum nonadiabatic dynamics, focusing on the use of frozen-width moving Gaussian basis functions to represent the nuclear wave function. The study explores various challenges and methodologies associated with this approach, including (1) the choice of electronic-state representation (adiabatic, diabatic, or moving crude adiabatic), (2) protocols for dynamically extending the number of Gaussians (spawning and cloning), (3) energy conservation implications of different equations of motion for Gaussians, and (4) the potential application of these methods to open quantum systems using the Nonstochastic Open System Schrödinger Equation (NOSSE).

---

### 2. **Classification of Purpose**  
The purpose of the paper emphasizes **"<method>"**, as it focuses on the development, evaluation, and comparison of computational techniques and methodologies for simulating quantum nonadiabatic dynamics.

---

### 3. **Relevant Research Questions**  
Based on the abstract, the following research questions are relevant to the themes and materials science interests:

1. **Representation of Electronic States**:
   - What are the advantages and disadvantages of adiabatic, diabatic, and moving crude adiabatic (MCA) representations in the context of quantum nonadiabatic dynamics simulations?
   - How do different electronic-state representations influence the formulation of equations of motion?

2. **Gaussian Basis Function Dynamics**:
   - What are the criteria for determining the optimal number of Gaussians required to accurately represent the nuclear wave function during quantum dynamics?
   - How do spawning and cloning protocols compare in terms of efficiency and accuracy for extending the number of Gaussians?

3. **Energy Conservation in Gaussian Dynamics**:
   - What are the implications of different equations of motion for individual Gaussians on energy conservation in quantum dynamics simulations?

4. **Open Quantum Systems**:
   - How can the Nonstochastic Open System Schrödinger Equation (NOSSE) be effectively integrated into moving Gaussian basis approaches for simulating open quantum systems?
   - What challenges arise when extending moving basis techniques to open quantum systems, and how can they be addressed?

5. **Computational Efficiency**:
   - How does the use of frozen-width moving Gaussian basis functions mitigate the "curse of dimensionality" in large systems, and what are the associated trade-offs in terms of accuracy or computational cost?

---

These questions can guide further research in improving simulation techniques for quantum dynamics, particularly in systems involving nonadiabatic transitions and open quantum systems.

inference_contexts: Wave function ansatzes based on linear combinations of moving FWGs guided by the TDVP provide powerful techniques for modeling nonadiabatic dynamics of both isolated and open molecular systems from first principles. We highlighted several features crucial for performance of this set of techniques. First, among possible electronic-state representations, the MCA representation is particularly attractive. It has all the advantages of the diabatic representation and can be directly obtained from electronic structure calculations as the regular adiabatic representation. The only caveat of the MCA use is the nonanalytic parametrization of the wave function. To avoid problems with the system energy conservation, this feature requires using the stationary action version of the TDVP. Second, if individual nuclear Gaussians are propagated classically (or generally independently) the TDVP application to the FWGs' amplitudes does not conserve the system energy. This nonconservation is especially pronounced when several Gaussians interfere in the process of dynamics, and it can be related to basis set incompleteness, which is unavoidable in practice. The only obvious way to conserve the energy is to propagate parameters of individual Gaussians quantum mechanically according to the TDVP in the action formulation. Unfortunately, this makes equations of motion for Gaussian parameters coupled and increases the computational complexity of the overall scheme. An interesting question to address is whether there exists a scheme for decoupled Gaussian parameters EOM that conserves the system energy? Third, to address the increase of the wave function complexity with time, a systematic extension of the number of nuclear FWGs is needed. Rigorous generalizations of two intuitive schemes for nuclear basis set extension (spawning and cloning) have been discussed. The spawning technique can be rooted in perturbative estimates of population flow between electronic states, while the cloning approach uses estimates of the "decoherence strain" acting on FWGs moving on different PESs. Both schemes can be successfully used for either classically propagated FWGs (e.g.. AIMS and MCE) or fully quantum TDVP schemes (e.g.. vMCG). Finally, a straightforward generalization of the TDVP to the Liouville equation in order to use FWGs to simulate a reduced density of an open system encounters two fundamental problems: (1) the total energy of the subsystem in a mixed state is not conserved in the limit of vanishing coupling to the environment, and (2) the subsystem population is not conserved even in the situations when only the energy exchange is allowed. The discussed NOSSE formalism allows us to resolve both problems and can be used among other applications for first-principle dynamics of molecules driven by incoherent light.

In summary, we have introduced two new schemes for nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations under rt-TDDFT formalism. One is the Boltzmann factor scheme which uses the decoherence time and restores the detailed balance in the simulation. It thus can be used to describe the hot carrier cooling with electron-phonon interaction and backreaction from electron dynamics to nuclear movements. However, in terms of nuclear dynamics, it uses a mean field approach, much like the original rt-TDDFT. It thus cannot be used to describe the nuclear trajectory branching, and different paths and products of an chemical reaction. The second method is a natural orbital branching (NOB) scheme based on the stochastic WFC approach. This is close to the DISH method, but with a critical difference in the collapsed wave function selection and the time evolution of the wave function. We use a density matrix formalism for time propagation, and natural orbital basis to collapse the wave function upon. Thus, unlike most many-body based methods, here we do not collapse the wave function into an many-body adiabatic state, or a SD consisted with single particle adiabatic states. Instead, we collapse the wave function into a set of natural orbital. The selection process is simple, and do not need to deal with the exponentially increasing (with system size) number of possible adiabatic state SDs. We feel this is a more natural way to collapse the wave function. We have tested our methods on the molecule radiolysis problem. We found they can efficiently study such problems delivering what the algorithms are designed to do. For the Boltzmann method, the computational time increases by a factor or 2-3 due to the solution of a linear equation, although this could be improved by further code optimizations. For the NOB method, the computational time is about the same as the plain rt-TDDFT method. These two methods make the rt-TDDFT integration more stable than the original plain TDDFT calculation. We expect them to find a wide range of applications in different nonadiabatic problems.

We have simulated ultrafast nonadiabatic population relaxation from S2 to S1 using A-FSSH simulations of the dual fluorescent molecule DMABN. Our results are largely consistent with previous theoretical calculations, , though we have gained several new pieces of insight. First, decoherence is found to not play an important role in propagating these dynamics due to the rapid excited-state relaxation and subsequent energetic separation of the first two excited states. Second, we ran simulations of DMABN in the presence of a MECN molecule and found that the ultrafast relaxation was largely unaffected by the solvent, in agreement with time-resolved fluorescence measurements of DMABN in MeCN. Third, we introduced a physically motivated diabatization procedure that is capable of converting the TDDFT excited (adiabatic) states into excited (diabatic) states of La and Lb character (which are diagonal with respect to the rotationally averaged transition dipole operator). Transforming the mixed quantum-classical density matrix into this diabatic representation, the population relaxation from La to Lb was found to be somewhat slower than the adiabatic states and consistent with the decay of the ensemble-averaged transition moment; specifically, our calculations predict a decay in the emission on the order of 15 fs (rather than 11 fs). Fourth and finally, we investigated the dynamics of the diabatization angle for all relaxation events through the CI. We found that 16% of the trajectories that we simulated fully circled the CI clockwise, 18% circled counterclockwise, and the remainder did not circle the CI at all. From these numbers and the fact that the majority of the electronic relaxation occurs within 30 fs according to our TDDFT functional, we hypothesize that if geometric phase effects are important in larger molecules, the 21 atom molecule DMABN will be an ideal test case for higher-level calculations, both for the electronic structure and the nuclear dynamics. It remains an open question as to whether or not we can predict an observable to prove such effects with nonlinear spectroscopy.

A related issue is that the TATR is not invariant to changes in the phase of molecular orbitals. In other words, even for canonical orbitals, the representation may differ when generated from different initial guess orbitals, or with different codes. For the current study, this is not problematic since training and prediction steps were performed jointly. However, in general, there is no guarantee that the phase convention is consistent throughout training and prediction, particularly if different codes or SCF solvers are used. There are two possible solutions to this issue, namely, enforcing some phase convention (which may be difficult in practice) or modifying the TATR to ensure invariance with respect to the phase of molecular orbitals.

A number of water molecules are shown to be located near a methanediol in the molecular dynamical simulation. We include additional water molecules during the water-cluster-catalyzed decomposition of a methanediol. The additional water molecules do not serve as catalyst, instead they support the structure of the methanediol with the hydrogen bonds. The smallest activation energy of 19 kcal/mol is obtained when a methanediol is supported by two additional water molecules with the hydrogen bonds and is decomposed with the catalytic effect of a water cluster with three water molecules. Water molecules play an important role in the strong molecular support during the water-cluster-catalyzed decomposition of a methanediol in aqueous solution.

dataset_item.question: How does the stacking sequence of tetracene and copper phthalocyanine affect energy level alignment in a heterojunction?
dataset_item.answer:
The stacking sequence of tetracene (Tc) and copper phthalocyanine (CuPc) significantly affects the energy level alignment (ELA) in a heterojunction. When Tc is stacked on top of CuPc on Ag(111) (Tc/CuPc/Ag(111)), constant vacuum level alignment is observed, suggesting minimal interaction at the interface. Conversely, when CuPc is stacked on top of Tc on Ag(111) (CuPc/Tc/Ag(111)), Fermi level pinning occurs, resulting in the formation of an interface dipole. This dipole enhances charge separation, which is critical for efficient exciton dissociation and charge transport. Additionally, the CuPc/Tc/Ag(111) configuration yields a higher energy difference of 0.4 eV between the HOMO of Tc and the LUMO of CuPc, which could lead to an increased open-circuit voltage in photovoltaic applications.

Dynamic studies using time-resolved XPS reveal transient charge carrier accumulation within 1.5 μs after excitation, demonstrating that exciton splitting modifies energy levels dynamically. These findings indicate that the CuPc/Tc/Ag(111) stacking sequence is more favorable for device applications due to its optimized electronic structure, enhanced charge separation, and improved energy level alignment, making it a promising candidate for photovoltaic and optoelectronic devices.

inference_contexts: We have demonstrated that Cu2-δSe has the potential to be a high-performance thermoelectric material at room temperature if the intrinsic heavily doped character can be altered. Using bromine as an electron donor, we have successfully shown that it is possible to reduce the hole concentration in copper selenide. Exploring the different possible scattering mechanisms for holes in this material showed that doping on the chemical site, which mostly contributes to the valence band, leads to enhanced alloy scattering and a reduced mobility when doping with bromine. While it shows that Br is not an ideal dopant to achieve the predicted thermoelectric performance in Cu2-δSe, different strategies for further improvement should indeed be possible because ionized impurity scattering does not play a role here. Furthermore, we have shown the reduced doping efficiency of Br by increasing amounts of copper vacancies due to Br substitution on the Se site. The interesting defect chemistry of Cu2-δSe shows, for the first time, that compensating defects and an effective pinning of the Fermi level can be achieved when shifting the chemical potential toward the valence band edge as opposed to deeper into the conduction band. This work shows the need to fully understand the underlying scattering mechanisms and the crystal and defect chemistry of a material in order to achieve high figure of merit thermoelectrics.

We have studied the energy level alignment in a model heterojunction for singlet fission photovoltaics consisting of Tc and CuPc films grown on Ag(111). By analyzing the CuPc/Tc/Ag(111) and Tc/CuPc/Ag(111) interfaces, we show how the inversion of the deposition sequence determines a different orientation of the two molecular films with respect to the substrate plane, which results in different ELAs in the two cases. In particular, a constant vacuum level alignment is found at the Tc/CuPc/Ag(111) hetero-organic junction, while Fermi level pinning introduces an interface dipole in CuPc/Tc/Ag(111) that may favor the charge separation. Moreover, in the latter a higher (0.4 eV) energy difference between the HOMO of the donor (Tc) and the LUMO of the acceptor (CuPc) potentially translates in a higher V OC in a photovoltaic cell. Both these aspects suggest that CuPc/Tc/Ag(111) may be a better choice for a prototypical device and demonstrate the importance of having the control over the heterojunction morphology for applicative purposes.

We have carried out a study of how the insertion of a SAM (ODT and MHA) between Co and Alq3 influences the electronic structure hybridization, the energetics and band offset, and the spin-dependent characteristics at the interface by using XPS, UPS, and XMCD. Our experimental results show that both ODT and MHA decrease the work function of Co, thus producing a small injection barrier for electron spins. However, our data revealed that the Fermi level pinning between Co and Alq3 can prevent further decrease in the surface work function even after the SAM deposition. In addition, we found that the orbital magnetic moment (μL) of Co became smaller when either ODT or MHA was inserted between Co and Alq3, implying that SAMs prevent hybridization between Co and Alq3. The spin magnetic moment (μS) of Co, a main contributor to the spin polarization at the interface, can be enhanced by inserting a SAM between Co and Alq3. SAMs can be used to engineer critical interface properties between metallic surfaces and organic materials. Altering the details of the self-assembled molecule such as the headgroup and tail group can change band energetics, morphology, and spin-dependent properties at the interface of a ferromagnetic metal and an organic semiconductor. Thus, the use of SAMs for interlayer engineering can be a versatile way of tuning spin injection characteristics into an organic semiconductor.

A clear epitaxial relationship with the CA network that forms on Ag(111) was also found, which helps rationalize the differences between the Au(111)- and Ag(111)-mediated CA networks. With the computational models, the epitaxial relationship matches naturally with the optimal CA-CA spacings that would occur in the absence of substrate-molecule interactions. The epitaxy is best characterized by the apparent energetic preference to place four of the five oxygen CA atoms near Ag surface sites, particularly the carbonyl oxygen atom that is not participating in a hydrogen bond. Such Ag O interactions, which have been previously discussed for other hydrogen-bonded networks on Ag(111), are consistent with the notion of maximizing the overlap between the adsorbate and surface wave functions over noble metal surfaces. The computed binding energies with the models described in this work would not predict that the network which was identified experimentally on Ag(111) has the lowest ground-state DFT energy. But the interactions between the CA network and the substrate are stronger, and the Ag(111) model allows each CA molecule to be placed in a chemically equivalent environment. Since our computations also suggest that different binding sites of CA on Ag(111) can have different effects on the nature of the electron density around the molecule, we suggest that the high-symmetry network could be influenced, and ultimately stabilized, by entropy and/or finite temperature effects.

We investigated the roles of interstate VCs in the 1(T1T1) formation rate of o-, m-, and p-BETB. We found that m-BETB showed significantly weak VCs compared with those of o- and p-BETB, leading to the slow 1(T1T1) formation rate of m-BETB. In addition, we found that the weak VCs of m-BETB resulted from the small spatial overlap ρ (x) between the electronic wave functions of 1(T1T1) and 1(S0S1). In contrast, p-BETB shows a fast 1(T1T1) formation rate, although it has a 5 times larger ΔE SF than m-BETB. This is because p-BETB shows a large ρ (x) distribution and strong VCs. We found that the 1(T1T1) formation rate of p-BETB was strongly structure dependent. When the tetracene units were twisted, p-BETB showed the fastest 1(T1T1) formation rate among o-, m-, and p-BETB. Meanwhile, when the tetracene units were coplanar, the 1(T1T1) formation rate of p-BETB was 10 times smaller than that of o-BETB. The structure dependence of the 1(T1T1) formation rate of p-BETB suggests that the rotation of the tetracene units is responsible for the experimentally observed fast 1(T1T1) formation rate of p-BETB.

dataset_item.question: How does the variation in cation radius influence the p-doping effect and work function of p-doped conjugated polymers used as interlayer materials?
dataset_item.answer: The variation in cation radius significantly influences the p-doping effect and work function of p-doped conjugated polymers (e.g., PCP-x) used as interlayer materials. Smaller cations enhance polarization effects, resulting in stronger p-doping, which enables tunable work functions in the range of 4.78–5.11 eV for modified ITO anodes. This tunability is critical for optimizing energy level alignment between the anode and the donor material in the photoactive layer, minimizing the energetic offset (<0.1 eV) and reducing performance losses. A higher work function (e.g., 5.11 eV) facilitates improved photovoltaic performance, achieving power conversion efficiencies (PCE) of up to 12.8% in non-fullerene organic solar cells (NF-OSCs). This underscores the importance of developing high-work-function interlayer materials, particularly for next-generation NF-OSCs utilizing donors with increasingly high ionization potentials.
