inference_contexts: In conclusion, we demonstrate an effective method to modulate p-doping effect and synthesize a series of p-doped conjugated polymers, PCP-x, for the application in OSCs as the anode interlayer materials. As these polymers are self-doped due to the polarization effect of the cations, we are able to easily tune the p-doping effect by changing the radius of the cations, that is, smaller ion can induce stronger p-doping effect. When these polymers are employed as interlayer materials, WF of the ITO anodes can be tuned in the range from 4.78 to 5.11 eV. Based on the PCP-H-modified ITO anodes, the one with the highest WF, a highly efficient NF-OSC with a PCE of 12.8% can be fabricated. Furthermore, based on these anodes with the gradually changed WFs, we are able to investigate the correlation between the photovoltaic performance of the NF-OSCs and the energetic offsets at the ITO anode/photoactive layer interfaces, and find that the energetic offset between WF of the anodes and IP of the donors is a critical parameter for the device, and a dE below 0.1 eV is needed to minimize the loss in photovoltaic performance.

This study also provides a new possibility of using AgQC@BSA as probes for multiple labeling or detection using the ratiometric fluorescence technique. Further probing of this system with advanced techniques and other methodologies may be required to answer questions such as reasons behind the increased tunability of AgQCs by Ova as compared to BSA, larger red-shift in the excitation wavelength of QCs compared to red-shift in the emission, etc. We believe that this study will be helpful for further improvements in the synthetic methodology and applications of protein protected AgQCs.

According to the developing trend in the field, the IPs of the donors used in the highly efficient NF-OSCs are quite high and will be further elevated for pursuing high V OC. Although PEDOT:PSS seems a quite good material for ITO anode modification in NF-OSCs, the WF of the PEDOT:PSS-modified ITO will be not sufficiently high to match the IP of new donors. Overall, in this contribution, we not only report a method to prepare a series of p-type interlayer materials with tunable WFs, but also demonstrate the critical importance of developing the anode interlayer materials with high WFs.

Combining an accurate treatment of the divalent ion-phosphate interactions based on RISM theory and simulations of RNA based on the transferable coarse-grained TIS force field, we have shown that the majority of divalent ions binds to RNA using either inner or outer shell coordination to phosphate groups. There is a negligible number of diffuse ions, which means binding is highly specific. This is in sharp contrast with the conventional view from counterion condensation theory, in which most of the ions are predicted to bind in a diffusive manner. Most importantly, the charge density of the cation is the driving factor in determining the ion chelation modes. Mg2+, which has a small radius and therefore a high charge density, has a relatively balanced distribution between the two binding modes. On the other hand, larger ions, such as Ca2+, predominantly bind using the inner sphere coordination. In addition, we also argue that, as the RNA becomes larger, there is a shift to the inner shell binding. These predictions provide an interesting new outlook of the interplay between ion-RNA interactions in the context of RNA folding. Our predictions await new experiments.

Although MD simulations suggest that entropic pushing alone could be enough to cause the observed uncompetitive inhibition effect, it should be observed that the concurrent action of weak binding of the crowders to the enzyme could not be ruled out in principle, although it is not clear in what direction that would affect the kinetics. There is some experimental evidence that long PEG polymers indeed may display weak interactions with small proteins, challenging the commonly accepted wisdom that PEG polymers are essentially inert crowders. It is not clear how PEG would interact with larger complexes such as LDH. Moreover, we found that Ficoll 70, which is to the best of our knowledge still considered a rather inert crowder, causes the same exact effect as PEG, suggesting that excluded-volume effect is key to rationalize the observed changes in enzyme kinetics. Interestingly, it has been reported that zwitterionic poly (sulfobetaine methacrylate) (pSBMA) polymers are more inert than PEG. Therefore, it would be informative to perform kinetics measurements with pSBMA polymers of the same size and compare with PEG. In principle, this could help tell entropic from enthalpic effects on enzyme kinetics.

dataset_item.question: What role does acetate anion play in the conversion of CS2 and OCS in solutions of N-butyl-N-methylpyrrolidinium acetate and 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium acetate?
dataset_item.answer:
The acetate anion plays a crucial role in the conversion of CS₂ into OCS and OCS into CO₂ in solutions of N-butyl-N-methylpyrrolidinium acetate ([BmPyrr][Ac]) and 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium acetate ([Bmim][Ac]). It primarily facilitates these reductions through mechanisms involving interatomic S-O exchange, which have lower energy barriers compared to secondary pathways involving thioacetate derivatives. 

In [BmPyrr][Ac], only these primary conversions occur, as secondary thioacetate-mediated pathways are inoperative due to higher activation energies. In [Bmim][Ac], the primary conversions coexist with selective insertion of OCS or CO₂ into the imidazolium ring, enabled by proton exchange between acetate and the cation. This unique interaction in [Bmim][Ac] differentiates its reactivity from [BmPyrr][Ac].

The absence of dithioacetate and imidazolium dithiocarboxylate species in both solutions is attributed to the lower reactivity of thioacetate compared to acetate, as confirmed by calculated energy barriers and basicity scales ([CH₃CS₂]⁻ < [CH₃COS]⁻ < [CH₃COO]⁻). Computational predictions, including ¹³C NMR chemical shifts, align with experimental observations, validating the dominant role of acetate anion in facilitating solute reduction and interatomic S-O exchange in these ionic liquids.

inference_contexts: In [Bmim] [Ac] solutions, the conversion processes of CS2 into OCS and of OCS into CO2 coexist with the selective insertion of OCS or CO2 adducts in the imidazolium ring. The existence of a proton exchange between acetate and the cation allows a specific interaction of the solute with a "transient" neutral IYC species to form a solute-IYC complex in the presence of acetic acid (primary mechanism). A >40 times increase in the time constant for oxygen exchange kinetics during ~5 days of aging was found in PCO thin films using the oxygen transmission relaxation method (OTR). The degradation in kinetics was identified to arise from accumulation of a siliceous phase on the PCO film surface. From a systematic examination of impurity sources, Si is likely introduced primarily during the OTR measurement (e.g.. from the quartz tube or furnace insulation) rather than through target purity, processing, or substrate (though these other sources may still have impurities present). Deposition of La oxide or Sm oxide on the aged film surface was found to fully recover oxygen exchange kinetics in aged films and a film intentionally coated with siliceous phase. La oxide was also deposited on aged SrTi0.65Fe0.35O3-δ, prone to degradation via Sr segregation (as opposed to siliceous phases), and no improvement was found, further indicating that La reacts with Si and is not leading to a significant catalytic effect. Finally, La was added to PCO in solid solution, and initial measurements found suppressed aging of redox kinetics.

dataset_item.question: What precautions should be taken when handling arsenic-containing compounds during high-temperature synthesis?
dataset_item.answer:
When handling arsenic-containing compounds during high-temperature synthesis, several precautions must be taken to mitigate the risks associated with toxic arsenic vapor release and potential ampule rupture. Arsenic has a high vapor pressure at elevated temperatures, which can lead to dangerous conditions. To minimize these hazards:

1. **Limit Arsenic Concentration**: Use the smallest quantity of arsenic necessary for the synthesis to reduce the risk of vapor buildup and ampule damage.
2. **Ensure Reaction Vessel Integrity**: Utilize reaction vessels specifically designed to withstand the high vapor pressures of arsenic at the target synthesis temperature, reducing the likelihood of rupture or explosion.
3. **Containment and Ventilation**: Conduct the synthesis in a well-ventilated environment, preferably under a fume hood, to safely manage any accidental release of arsenic vapors.
4. **Safety Protocols**: Employ proper protective equipment and safety protocols, including monitoring for leaks and having emergency measures in place.

These measures collectively address the risks posed by arsenic during high-temperature synthesis, ensuring both the safety of the procedure and the personnel involved.

inference_contexts: Understanding how design parameters of targeted drug carriers influence interaction with cells and the subsequent signaling leading to endocytosis is key to inform optimization of drug delivery systems. , Both the size and targeting valency of drug carriers impact cell binding and endocytic uptake. - ,,, However, how these parameters influence receptor-mediated signaling linking binding with internalization is rather obscure. For instance: Is the uptake efficiency correlative with the signaling level? Is this regulated similarly for carriers of different sizes and valencies? Are signaling and uptake events induced independently for each individual carrier or do they depend on cumulative carrier binding to cells? Is the number of receptors engaged by a carrier the factor ruling signaling and uptake, or does this depend on the density of engagement per surface area? Using model submicrometer, micrometer, and supramicrometer carriers targeted to ICAM-1 at varying valencies, we have examined these questions. Our results revealed an intricate interplay between these parameters, where the density of the targeting antibody per carrier surface area (which would determine the density of the receptor cluster on the cell surface) is the main parameter controlling the signaling conducive to endocytosis (Figure ). Larger carriers posed a requirement for stronger signaling, since carrier size impacts the ability of the plasmalemma to efficiently engulf a carrier. It is likely that for endocytic pathways lacking signals that enable sufficient plasmalemma deformability (e.g.. ceramide enrichment shown here for the CAM pathway), size will become restrictive regardless of the targeting density. Each carrier bound on a cell induced signaling based on its antibody-coat density (the density of the clustered receptors, not the absolute number of receptors engaged or the size of the cluster), and rendered endocytosis based on its size and enough buildup of the inducing signal. Each signaling-uptake event was independent for each single carrier bound on a cell, where the total number of carriers bound to the cell, the total surface area occupied by those carriers, and the total number of cell receptors engaged did not exert a major influence. It will be important to examine this regulation for other receptors and pathways in order to extract generic conclusions, and to evaluate how other carrier design parameters (e.g.. smaller sizes, different shape, curvature, carrier type, surface chemistry, etc.) and biological environments (different cell types, presence of flow, pathological alterations, etc.) impact these outcomes. - ,,, Nevertheless, other natural routes associate to signaling common to the CAM pathway, and it is expected that the findings obtained here would broadly apply to the use of said routes for drug delivery applications. For instance, ceramide and/or PKC are key for the formation of lipid domains, vesiculation, cytoskeletal rearrangements, and formation of membrane protrusions observed for phagocytic and macropinocytic pathways, intracellular invasion by certain viral and bacterial pathogens, leukocyte endothelial adhesion and extravasation, and certain events of transcytosis across cellular barriers. - Therefore, these results have shed light on key factors modulating the efficacy of uptake of targeted drug carriers, which shall inform future design of vehicles for intracellular delivery.

From direct observations, it is possible to link the shift in selectivity from nitrogen to nitrogen oxide with the transition from metallic to oxidized surfaces. Once this transition is completed, the metal-oxide interface becomes sharp and it is likely that the topmost metal layer is enriched in platinum; because the oxide layer contains only rhodium, in order to preserve the mass balance, the underlining metal must be platinum enriched. With the advent of the surface oxide, the disappearance of adsorbed nitrogen species also occurs, therefore suggesting either that there was a change in the reaction mechanism or that the oxygen dissociation was likely the limiting step of the reaction and the oxide can also act as a source of oxygen. The observations also advocate for a metal-mediated recombination of atomic nitrogen for the formation of the N2 molecule. The transition from a nitrogen-rich to an oxygen-rich mixture coincides with the topmost metallic layer changing its relaxation: moving from outward to inward at 650 K, which also links this relaxation change to product selectivity, from N2 to NO. Surface species can also be associated to the changes in relaxation: nitrogen species to outward relaxed surface and oxygen species to inward relaxed surfaces. However the 1:1 ratio is a transition area where the surface is inwardly relaxed but the presence/absence of the surface oxide is related to the position in the hysteresys cycle. It nevertheless indicates that such a change in relaxation is a preliminary step toward oxide formation. Upon speculation, one could say that the important surface rearrangements allow rhodium to emerge and form a protective and catalytically active oxide layer. The formation of volatile PtO has previously been attributed to be responsible for the loss of Pt from Pt gauzes. According to the results in the present contribution, the formation of a Rh oxide inhibits the formation of PtO. Since the rhodium oxide has a lower vapor pressure than the platinum oxide, it ultimately counteracts the platinum depletion from the gauze catalysts.

DFT calculations were performed using the B3LYP , hybrid GGA functional together with the standard 6-31+G* basis set for carbon, nitrogen, and hydrogen and 6-311+G* Se and S atoms with full-geometry optimization. The solvent effects on the mechanism have been considered using a self-consistent reaction field method based on Tomasi's polarizable continuum model (PCM). As the solvent used in the experimental work was DMSO, we have selected its dielectric constant ε = 46.7. All calculations were carried out with the Gaussian 09 suite of programs and include the zero-point energy correction. The characterization of stationary points was done by Hessian matrix calculations, with all positive eigenvalues for a minimum and one negative value for a transition state (TS); in all cases, zero-point energy corrections were included. From a methodological point of view, to calculate the reaction coordinate, we began optimizing the structure of the radical anion intermediate in solution. Intrinsic reaction coordinates were not calculated, and the following procedure was carried out. Once the minimum energy structure was obtained, the bond between the heteroatom (Z = Se or S) and the carbon of the aromatic ring (CA) of the radical anion was stretched toward reactants to obtain the structure of the transition state (TS1). Furthermore, the maximum nature of the structure was confirmed by TS and force calculations. In the same way, the bond between the heteroatom and the carbon B (CB) of the radical anion intermediate was stretched toward products to obtain the structure of the second transition state (TS2). The structures obtained for TS2 also corresponded to a maximum (see below, Scheme ). In both cases, the imaginary frequency corresponded to the stretching of the CA-Z and CB-Z bonds for TS1 and TS2, respectively, which confirms the connectivity of the stationary points along the potential energy surface (PES) reaction. Finally, the energies of the reactants and the products were obtained by calculating each of the compounds separately, considering their energy at an infinite distance.

This work demonstrates, for the first time, that designed repeat protein scaffolds can be used to synthesize and stabilize gold nanoclusters. It has been shown that neither the number of repeats in the protein, nor the presence of a single cysteine residue interfered with the formation of small blue-emitting AuNCs. A possible explanation is the presence of tyrosine residues in the repeat sequence that could adsorb gold ions and therefore stabilize the gold nanoclusters. The synthesis method using NaOH to generate a reducing environment proved to be the most efficient. However, highly basic conditions denature the protein and thus destroy its structure and function. This fact can hamper its use in further applications in which structural and functional properties of the proteins are exploited. Therefore, we developed a new synthesis protocol using milder reducing agents such as ascorbic acid and sodium citrate, increasing the efficiency to obtain the AuNCs when ascorbic acid was employed. Whenever reactions did not include the protein scaffold, the AuNCs generation did not occur, highlighting the key role of the CTPR proteins as stabilizing agents. The optimized conditions for the AuNCs formation include a metal:protein ratio of 5:1 compared to the conditions previously reported for the CTPR stabilization of AuNPs in which larger ratios were used (1000:1 to 20:1) and smaller the ratios yielded smaller nanoparticles, which is in agreement with this report, where nanoclusters are obtained with smaller metal:protein ratios. Most importantly, this method was mild enough to preserve the structure of the protein and thus permitted to take advantage of the specific function of the protein scaffold. Indeed, we demonstrate that neither the synthesis of the nanoclusters, nor the nanoclusters themselves interfered with the protein binding activity. Thus, we obtained a novel bifunctional designed unit that combines the function of the designed CTPR protein scaffold on one hand and the fluorescence emission of AuNCs on the other. Finally, we demonstrate that the fluorescence signal of the protein-stabilized AuNCs is sensitive to the ligand recognition of the specific binding module. This result confirms the potential of this system to develop new sensors. The use of repeat protein scaffolds as biomolecular templates in which stability, size, and function can be tuned at will, ,, that also comprise rational methods for the synthesis of fluorescent nanoclusters preserving the protein functions, leaves a door open for further applications in the field of molecular imaging and sensing.

For polymers, natural or otherwise, to produce carbon fiber of a similar quality as PAN, they cannot rely on hydrogen bonding for structural stability or contain a high mass fraction of oxygen, lest they shrink to an unusable extent. A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. Polyalanine-like domains could be incorporated into block copolymers for biomimetic graphite precursors. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

dataset_item.question: How does nanoscale confinement affect the adsorption selectivity of methane-ethane mixtures in shale pores?
dataset_item.answer:
Nanoscale confinement within shale pores significantly influences the adsorption selectivity of methane-ethane mixtures, with ethane being preferentially adsorbed over methane due to stronger fluid-wall interactions. This selectivity is highly dependent on factors such as temperature, pore size, reservoir pressure, and bulk fluid composition. As temperature increases, adsorption selectivity diminishes, while increasing pore size reduces confinement effects, causing the selectivity to approach unity as the confined mixture composition aligns with the bulk system. 

Confinement also alters the phase behavior of the fluids, reducing critical pressure and temperature compared to bulk mixtures and shifting dew and bubble point pressures. Smaller pores intensify these effects, further lowering critical properties and modifying phase envelopes. This preferential adsorption of heavier hydrocarbons (ethane) can result in compositional variations during production, with methane-rich initial outputs and gradual ethane release over time. Understanding these nanoscale confinement effects is crucial for optimizing hydrocarbon extraction and reservoir management, while future advancements in kerogen modeling may provide deeper insights into the adsorption dynamics and confinement-induced phase behavior.

Inkbottle-shaped and slit-like kerogen nanopores were developed to represent different nanopores in the realistic kerogen matrix. Thus, a proper CO2 injection pressure should be determined according to the geological conditions of shale reservoirs. The effect of confinement on proton transport can be counterintuitive because of two possible effects. The dynamics of water and ions slow down with increasing confinement, ,,, and in the absence of the Grotthuss transport mechanism, one would expect similar trends to hold for proton transport. In addition, slower water dynamics can diminish Grotthuss transport rates because this mechanism depends on reorganization of water solvation structures. ,, It is also possible for confinement to alter the hydrogen bond networks in a manner that is advantageous for proton hopping. Previous studies of proton transport in carbon nanotubes and other hydrophobic pores - , have shown that single water wire networks in small-diameter pores may exhibit very high Grotthuss proton transport rates. Thus, both the confinement-mediated structure and dynamics of water networks near hydronium ions can affect proton transport in different ways, and the resulting quantitative enhancement/reduction in dynamics may be specific to the microscopic properties of the system.

dataset_item.question: What are the structural and phase transformations of CuS deposited on Sn-doped In2O3 nanowires and SnO2 nanowires when processed under H2S at varying temperatures?
dataset_item.answer:
When CuS is deposited on Sn-doped In₂O₃ nanowires and processed under H₂S at temperatures between 100°C and 200°C, hexagonal CuS and cubic In₂O₃ are formed. At higher temperatures, structural transformation occurs, leading to the formation of Cu₀.₂₃In₂.₅₉S₄ nanowires. For CuS deposited on SnO₂ nanowires, processing under H₂S at 400–500°C results in the formation of tetragonal Cu₂SnS₃ nanowires embedded with SnO₂ quantum dots. These quantum dots exhibit ultraviolet emission at 3.65 eV, breaking the dipole forbidden rule. 

CuS/Sn:In₂O₃ nanowires demonstrate rectifying current-voltage behavior due to a higher built-in potential barrier and electron density, though negative differential resistance (NDR) is absent in solid-state junctions. NDR appears in weak-contact configurations or when TiO₂ barriers are introduced, attributed to oxygen vacancy trapping. Solar cells utilizing CuS/Sn:In₂O₃ nanowires achieve a conversion efficiency of 0.4% with an open-circuit voltage of 0.5 V.

dataset_item.question: What is the role of PVDF-HFP layers in improving liquid electrolyte retention and compatibility with lithium anodes?
dataset_item.answer: Polyvinylidene fluoride-hexafluoropropylene (PVDF-HFP) layers play a critical role in improving liquid electrolyte retention and compatibility with lithium anodes in lithium metal batteries. These layers, integrated within a "gel-liquid-gel" electrolyte structure, reduce side reactions between the liquid electrolyte and lithium metal, thereby mitigating dendrite formation and enhancing safety. The PVDF-HFP layers also promote uniform lithium-ion flux at the polymer/lithium interface due to their rich 3D ion transmission pathways, which contribute to stable cycling performance and improved Coulombic efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate their effectiveness: LiCu cells achieved 98% Coulombic efficiency over 400 cycles, LiLi cells maintained stable plating/stripping for 1200 hours, and LiLiFePO4 full cells retained 98.5% capacity after 200 cycles. Furthermore, the PVDF-HFP coating strategy is scalable and compatible with existing battery manufacturing processes, making it a promising solution for developing safer, longer-lasting lithium metal batteries.

dataset_item.question: What is the critical molecular weight range for conjugated copolymers that leads to significant changes in thermal, mechanical, and viscoelastic properties?
dataset_item.answer: The critical molecular weight range for conjugated copolymers, specifically P(NDI2OD-T2), is between **48 and 103 kg mol⁻¹**, where significant changes in thermal, mechanical, and viscoelastic properties are observed. Within this range, a two-fold increase in number-average molecular weight (Mn) leads to a remarkable 26-fold increase in strain at fracture and a 160-fold increase in toughness, while maintaining electrical performance. These enhancements are attributed to the presence of tie molecules and polymer chain entanglements, which enable plastic deformation and improve strain energy release during mechanical deformation. Furthermore, thermal annealing preserves mechanical robustness without compromising electronic properties, making this molecular weight range optimal for flexible and stretchable electronics.

dataset_item.question: How can the quasi-steady-state assumption be applied to identify dominating and negligible surface intermediates during ammonia decomposition?
dataset_item.answer:
The quasi-steady-state (QSS) assumption is applied to ammonia decomposition by analyzing the relative rates of production and consumption of surface intermediates, where the net production rate of intermediates approaches zero. This assumption helps identify negligible intermediates as those involved in fast reactions, which results in their low surface concentrations, while slower-reacting intermediates dominate due to their sustained accumulation on the surface.

To determine the dominating and negligible intermediates, dynamic pulse response or transient experiments can be used to observe the H/N ratio during the later stages. A high H/N ratio (close to 3) suggests that intermediates like ZNH3 and ZNH2 dominate, whereas a low H/N ratio (below 1) indicates the dominance of ZNH and ZN. This analysis simplifies kinetic modeling by distinguishing fast (negligible) and slow (dominant) intermediates, providing critical insights into the reaction mechanism and the role of specific surface species in ammonia decomposition.

inference_contexts: In our analysis, the quasi-steady-state (QSS) assumption will be widely used for understanding the mechanistic details of complex kinetic behavior. This simplification has been described as the most applied but least understood, despite the fact that it has been in use since the 1910s. The assumption is generally thought of as an approximate equality in the rate of production and consumption of intermediates, which renders the net rate of intermediate production near zero. This generates the incorrect notion that QSS is an "approximate" steady state. Rather, it is a special case of non-steady-state behavior where the rate of change of a reaction intermediate follows the time evolution of the concentrations of other species (refer to discussion in refs and ). In other words, it is a phenomenon of the relative-time behavior of processes that results in negligible surface intermediate concentrations. QSS behavior can arise from a number of factors (e.g.. a large difference in the relative amounts of gas and surface species or a large difference in the magnitudes of kinetic parameters); the slow production of an intermediate offset by fast consumption is a typical situation. In some temporal domain, an invariance is observed in the concentration ratio of the intermediate and gas-phase species.

This is a dynamic pulse response experiment, and rates decrease primarily because the gas concentrations decrease. However, with a system consisting of multiple steps, certain steps may react much faster than others, and the overall behavior is governed by the bottleneck. In QSS relationships, the concentrations of surface intermediates participating in fast reactions are negligible. At the same time, it is reasonable that one or two intermediates, those that participate in slow reactions, dominate the surface. These are the surface intermediates that constitute the observed H/N ratio in the plateau region of dynamic accumulation. On the basis of the experimental value of accumulation dynamics, it is possible to draw conclusions regarding the dominating surface species. For example, a H/N ratio near 3 indicates the likelihood of ZNH3 and ZNH2 as dominating species, whereas an H/N ratio less than 1 indicates ZNH3 is more likely a quasi-steady-state species, and ZNH and ZN dominate the surface.

In a typical QSS situation, which can arise from a significant difference of reaction kinetic parameters, some intermediates are negligible on the surface and some are dominant. Consequently, working with the given set of intermediates of the single-route catalytic reaction (ZNH3, ZNH2, ZNH, ZN, ZH, and Z), we can speculate on quasi-steady-state ("fast") intermediates, identifying them as negligible surface species.

Although alkoxy radical isomerization leads to the addition of multiple functional groups, thus enhancing the tendency of products to partition into SOA, decomposition cleaves C-C bonds to form more volatile products. The branching between decomposition and isomerization is influenced by neighboring functional groups and by the length of the alkyl chain on which isomerization occurs. In general, functional groups located on the same (α-) or an adjacent (β-) carbon relative to the alkoxy group will enhance rates of decomposition, whereas longer alkyl chains (up to a point) enhance rates of isomerization. dataset_item.question: At what alcohol concentration does the liquid crystalline phase of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine membrane undergo disintegration?
dataset_item.answer: The liquid crystalline phase of a dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) membrane undergoes disintegration at an alcohol concentration of 15 mol% in the surrounding aqueous solution. Molecular dynamics simulations indicate that both ethanol and n-propanol disrupt the membrane's structure by dissolving at the hydrophilic-hydrophobic interface. This interaction leads to lateral swelling, reduced membrane thickness, and decreased lipid tail order, ultimately compromising the structural integrity of the membrane. While lower alcohol concentrations (5–10 mol%) weaken the membrane, 15 mol% reliably induces disintegration by significantly lowering the free-energy barrier for permeation. The gel phase (298 K) exhibits lower alcohol permeability due to tighter lipid packing, whereas the liquid crystalline phase (323 K) is more vulnerable and dominates under physiological conditions. Notably, n-propanol exerts a stronger destabilizing effect than ethanol.

Such an alcohol-induced weakening of the membrane has important consequences for the functioning of the membrane and, hence, the inactivation of the virus.

dataset_item.question: How does thermal treatment at 200 °C influence structural, magnetic, and mechanical properties of micrometer-sized Fe3O4@Fe-Ti composite granules?
dataset_item.answer: Thermal treatment at 200 °C enhances the mechanical strength and crystallinity of micrometer-sized Fe₃O₄@Fe-Ti composite granules, optimizing their structural stability and durability. This treatment reduces saturation magnetization and adsorption capacity due to increased crystallinity but facilitates rapid fluoride adsorption (completed within 2 minutes) and effective magnetic separation in fluidized bed systems. Granules sized around 10 μm exhibit optimal performance, balancing reduced intraparticle diffusion resistance with high adsorption rates and magnetic recovery efficiency. While higher temperatures further impact saturation magnetization and separation efficiency negatively, 200 °C represents an ideal balance for achieving safe drinking water through ultrafiltration after fluoride removal. This process ensures mechanical stability while maintaining functional performance for water purification applications.

The minimum number of columns required for a continuous process was 4 for the single-stage Skarstrom and 8 for the single-stage 6-step cycle with PE and HPP. This value was 8 (i.e.. 4 + 4) for a dual-stage process with the Skarstrom cycle for the N2 removal stage plus the 6-step cycle with PE and LPP for the O2 purification stage. Can DCPs elevate the performance of BLYP to that of B3LYP? This is a question that was posed in the Introduction. As computational chemistry methods are applied to increasingly larger systems, the question of their efficiency-in particular, with respect to run time-becomes critical. Formally, GGA functionals like BLYP scale as N 3 with system size (with N being the number of electrons), whereas hybrid functionals scale with N 4. Therefore, low-cost corrections such as D3 and DCP that may elevate the performance of BLYP to that of B3LYP or better may be of value. To examine this possibility, we present in Table a summary of some of the performance statistics for BLYP-D3-DCP/6-31+G (2d,2p) for the benchmark sets described above and compare these to statistics obtained using B3LYP-D3/6-31+G (2d,2p). We also conducted additional performance assessments of the two methods on the BHPERI, DARC, BSR36, and the RSE43 databases. We use D3 corrections with B3LYP for our comparison because D3 has a computational cost that is negligible relative to that of the underlying DFT method and because D3 corrections (or similar) are required to predict noncovalent interactions that are reasonable. It is worthwhile restating that D3 corrections that were designed for use with B3LYP were also designed for use with nearly complete basis sets. The corrections nevertheless improve the performance of "small basis set" B3LYP, as has been shown in the past, in particular for the treatment of noncovalent interactions.

dataset_item.question: What evidence supports alternative nonlinear pathways such as inverse Raman gain scattering or vertical FSRS in time-resolved FSRS spectra of the charge transfer excited complex?
dataset_item.answer: Time-resolved femtosecond stimulated Raman spectroscopy (FSRS) of the charge transfer excited TCNE:ClN complex reveals evidence supporting alternative nonlinear scattering pathways, such as inverse Raman gain scattering (IRGS) and vertical FSRS (VFSRS). Key observations include unusual intensity and frequency behavior in the difference bands, as well as the presence of combination bands and overtones. These spectral features arise due to strong resonance of the Raman pump with localized electronic transitions within the charge transfer excited radicals. The coupling between high-symmetry charge transfer transitions and vibrational modes further contributes to nonlinear scattering mechanisms beyond conventional FSRS. Additionally, frequency shifts observed in combination bands correlate with shifts in fundamental modes, reinforcing the involvement of IRGS and VFSRS pathways in the excited-state dynamics of the system.

### 1. **Summary of the Purpose of the Paper**  
The paper investigates the molecular dynamics and vibrational features of a charge transfer (CT) excited noncovalent complex (TCNE:ClN) in dichloromethane (DCM) using femtosecond stimulated Raman spectroscopy (FSRS) with ultrafast time resolution (40 fs). The study aims to uncover time-resolved vibrational behaviors, nonlinear scattering pathways, and solvent effects that influence charge localization and recombination in the complex. By analyzing the FSRS spectra, the researchers reveal unique molecular details about intermolecular interactions, solvent reorganization, and charge transfer dynamics.

### 2. **Classification of Purpose**

### 3. **Research Questions Relevant to the Abstract**  
1. How do vibrational modes in the CT complex (TCNE:ClN) influence charge transfer and recombination dynamics?  
2. What role does solvent reorganization (e.g., dichloromethane librational motion) play in modulating vibrational frequencies and intermolecular interactions?  
3. What evidence supports alternative nonlinear pathways such as inverse Raman gain scattering (IRGS) or vertical-FSRS (VFSRS) in the time-resolved FSRS spectra?  
4. How do coherent oscillations of stimulated emission contribute to the understanding of molecular dynamics in CT complexes?

inference_contexts: In the photoexcited TCNE:ClN complex, three low frequency coordinates were indicated to induce a localization of the electron. These coordinates have frequencies of ~30, 153, and 278 cm-1 corresponding to the librational frequency of the DCM solvent shell, a b1u out-of-plane bending mode of TCNE and the symmetric Cl bending mode of DCM, respectively. After the vibrational wavepacket has mostly dephased, the excited state distortion still has a marked effect on the rate of the charge recombination by altering the intermolecular orbital overlap. The time-resolved FSRS spectra display two important reporter modes. The central C-C stretching frequency of TCNE -ClN + at 1392 cm-1 is red-shifted from that of free TCNE - due to the proximity of the contact ion pair. Difference bands, combination bands and overtones are observed in FSRS spectra when the Raman pump is strongly resonant with localized high symmetry electronic transitions such as those afforded by charge transfer excited radicals. By accounting for the fundamental time-frequency trade off, the frequency shift of the combination band can be related to the frequency shift the fundamentals. The unusual intensity and frequency behavior of the difference band is interpreted in the context of alternative FSRS pathways including IRGS and VFSRS.

The mode-specific excitation profiles in the experimental FSRS spectrum may be explained by homogeneous broadening of the T N ← T1 transitions. A Lorentzian deconvolution of the triplet absorption spectrum indicates several overlapping transitions, each with significant homogeneous broadening. Estimates of an upper limit to the Γ n values, based on the experimental TA spectrum, show that these values are roughly an order of magnitude larger than what is typically observed in resonance Raman measurements. The reasonably large Γ n values increase the relative importance of the mode-specific resonance enhancement contributions from nearby transitions, which may explain the broad excitation profiles observed for the Raman bands. The significant homogeneous broadening is possibly a result of increased vibronic coupling between the electronic states of the triplet manifold. Thus, the good agreement between the off-resonance Raman calculations and the experimental spectrum may indicate that the contributions from multiple transitions and vibronic coupling effects have an influence on the FSRS spectrum that is comparable to or even larger than the electronic resonance condition. In summary, this work highlights the necessity of considering multiple contributions when extracting information about resonant electronic states in FSRS and helps explain the good agreement of off-resonant calculations with the resonance-enhanced FSRS spectra of the triplet states of PT.

We report the excitation wavelength dependence of the FSRS spectrum for the T1 state of PT and compare the trends we observe to simulated on- and off-resonance Raman spectra using several theoretical approaches. The experimental results provide a rigorous benchmark for the accuracy of the computational techniques, whereas the computational results highlight the difficulties of interpreting FSRS spectra involving more than one resonant or nearly resonant electronic transition. These results also point to important limitations of the FC and FCHT approaches for the calculation of resonance Raman spectra in the presence of broad, overlapping transitions. The more densely packed manifold of the high-lying electronic states makes it difficult to extrapolate the PES from the excited-state minimum to the Franck-Condon geometry using the harmonic approximation.

To fully account for the absorption spectral line shapes of DPrSQ (OH)2 and DBSQ (OH)2 in solution and in the solid phase, we employed the essential state model pioneered by Painelli and co-workers to model a monomeric squaraine and subsequently added ICT and Coulomb coupling in order to model aggregates. We found that through-space Coulombic interactions alone, as exist in conventional Frenkel exciton theory, cannot satisfactorily reproduce the aggregate spectra. We subsequently confirmed that ICT plays a major role in determining the distinct absorption spectral signatures of DPrSQ (OH)2 and DBSQ (OH)2 aggregates. We point out that not all squaraines exhibit evidence of ICT; in particular, the monoclinic phase of DESQ (OH), which, unlike the triclinic phase hosts two molecules per unit cell, shows clear evidence of Davydov splitting but no ICT. Not only do we remedy any confusion regarding the origin of the panchromatic solid-state features in certain squaraines, which is critical for a substantial overlap of the solar spectrum, but with a full understanding of the excited-state assignment, we also provide a foundation for understanding the impact of aggregation on OPV device efficiency.

We have developed a new type of time-resolved phase microscope, and the basic principle of this technique has been described in a previous paper. An arbitrary light pattern is illuminated on a particulate film substrate for the photoexcitation of charge carriers, and the charge carriers decay or diffuse in time due to the recombination, charge trapping, and transport, and the pattern of the charge carrier distribution varies with time. The distribution of the photo-excited charge carriers is observed via the refractive index change by phase-contrast imaging. The refractive index was imaged by the Talbot self-imaging technique. By observation of the pattern change, the decay time and the diffusion coefficient can be estimated. Pattern illumination is preferable for applying various image recovery algorithms, as described in a different paper. In this study, only the overall background correction was processed before the analyses, which ensures prevention of the loss of small features in images.

dataset_item.question: What role do interlayer hydrogenous species such as nickel hydroxide and water play in CO2 adsorption in Ni-exchanged fluorohectorite clay?
dataset_item.answer: Interlayer hydrogenous species, such as nickel hydroxide and water, play a crucial role in CO₂ adsorption within Ni-exchanged fluorohectorite clay by facilitating its incorporation into the clay interlayers. CO₂ specifically binds to the intercalated [Ni(OH)₀.₈₃(H₂O)₁.₁₇]⁰.³⁷⁺ species, driving crystalline swelling in both dried and hydrated samples. In dried samples, CO₂ adsorption occurs predominantly in the chlorite-like layers, which contain nickel hydroxide, while smectite-like layers show negligible adsorption. In hydrated samples, CO₂ has limited impact on the water coordinated around interlayer cations, indicating that the hydration state influences the adsorption mechanism. Experimental techniques such as diffraction, spectroscopy, and neutron scattering confirm these findings, underscoring the critical role of interlayer hydrogenous species in enhancing CO₂ uptake. This insight suggests that optimizing interlayer chemistry could improve the performance of clay-based materials for carbon capture applications.

inference_contexts: Developing new sorbent materials for CO2 is of key importance to solve issues related to greenhouse gas emissions. By PXRD, Raman spectroscopy, and INS, we identified a hitherto overlooked mechanism for CO2 adsorption in hectorite clay. With these techniques, we took a new approach, where we study the mechanism for CO2 adsorption from the perspective of interlayer hydrogeneous species, that is hydroxides and water. Phase pure and charge homogeneous synthetic fluorohectorite provides a unique template for studying such interactions as it has no structural hydrogen incorporated in the 2:1 clay layer structure. For Ni-exchanged hectorite, an ordered interstratification of chlorite-like layers and smectite-like layers, we found that the intercalated nickel hydroxide promotes incorporation of CO2 in the clay interlayers. Our results suggest that the CO2 binds to the [Ni (OH)0.83(H2O)1.17]0.37 1.17+ species, both in the dried and the hydrated case, and is responsible for swelling in response to CO2. No incorporation of CO2 was found in the smectite-like layers for the dried case. Furthermore, CO2 has limited impact on the water coordinated to the interlayer cations for the hydrated case.

Flame retardant thermoplastic vulcanizate (TPV) composites with magnesium hydroxide (MH) and organically modified montmorillonite (o-MMT) were prepared. The incorporation of a small amount of o-MMT into the TPV/MH composites enhances both the flame retardance and the mechanical properties. A compact and continuous char layer is generated in the ternary TPV/MH/o-MMT composites during burning. Such compact and continuous char residue acts as an effective barrier layer to prohibit transfer of heat, oxygen, and combustible volatiles. Specifically, the incorporation of more than 6 phr o-MMT leads to the lowest pHRR and lowest SPR among all of the samples. TGA showed that the thermal stabilities of TPV/MH systems are enhanced by adding the layer-structured nanoparticles (o-MMT). TEM images of the char residue after cone calorimetry tests confirmed that initially well-dispersed clay platelets accumulate on the burning surface and form a continuous netlike structure together with MgO. The simultaneous improvements in both flame retardance and mechanical performance have been attributed to the double roles of o-MMT. On the one hand, o-MMT increases the viscosity of the composite and suppresses the vigorous bubbling caused by polymer pyrolysis during burning. On the other hand, well-dispersed o-MMT serves as a rigid network in the sample that prohibits the massive shrinkage of both MH and the TPV matrix during burning.

The experiments were conducted using a photolysis installation similar to that described in our previous study. A 200 mL solution containing 0.3 g homoionic-clay, 0.015 mM tetracycline, and 5 mM phosphate buffer was adjusted to pH 4, 5, 6, or 7. The suspension was magnetically stirred at 200 rpm in a 200 mL cylindrical cell equipped with a water jacket. During the photolysis experiment, the suspension was irradiated by a 50 W xenon lamp (CEL-HXF300, AULTT, China) at a distance of 0.2 m from the top of the suspension. The lamp spectrum was recorded using a spectrometer USB2000+ (Ocean Optics, FL, U.S.A.). dataset_item.question: How does the carbonyl substituent influence the stabilization of the barrier and twisted region on the S2 potential surface in peridinin compared to carotenoids without carbonyl substitution?
dataset_item.answer: The carbonyl substituent in peridinin significantly influences the stabilization of the barrier and twisted region on the S2 potential surface compared to carotenoids lacking this substitution, such as β-carotene. The electron-withdrawing nature of the carbonyl group redistributes π-electron density within the molecule, leading to enhanced stabilization of both the activation-energy barrier and the twisted region. This redistribution also introduces an intramolecular charge transfer (ICT) character to the excited-state dynamics, which is absent in carotenoids without carbonyl substitution. The ICT character increases solvent friction, thereby slowing the decay of the intermediate Sx state and extending its lifetime. This prolonged intermediate state facilitates more efficient excitation energy transfer from peridinin to chlorophyll a in biological systems, highlighting the functional significance of the carbonyl group in light-harvesting processes.

### 1. **Summary of the Purpose of the Paper**  
The paper investigates the ultrafast nonradiative decay pathway from the S2 (11Bu+) state to the S1 (21Ag−) state in peridinin, a carotenoid molecule, in methanol solution using femtosecond heterodyne transient grating spectroscopy. The research focuses on identifying and characterizing an intermediate state, Sx, formed during this decay process. The study compares the behavior of peridinin to β-carotene and attributes the unique features of the Sx state in peridinin to its distorted conjugated polyene backbone and the influence of its carbonyl substituent. Additionally, the findings suggest that the Sx state and subsequent distorted structures may play a critical role in excitation energy transfer to chlorophyll a in the peridinin-chlorophyll a protein of dinoflagellates.

---

### 2. **Classification of Purpose**  
The purpose emphasizes **"<result>"**, as the study aims to uncover the mechanisms underlying the decay pathway, characterize the intermediate Sx state, and highlight its potential biological implications in excitation energy transfer.

---

### 3. **Research Questions**  
Based on the abstract, the following research questions are relevant to the themes and materials science interests of the study:

1. **Mechanistic Understanding**  
   - What are the ultrafast dynamics and mechanisms involved in the nonradiative decay pathway from the S2 state to the S1 state in peridinin?  
   - How does the Sx intermediate state form, and what is its structural and electronic nature?

2. **Comparative Analysis**  
   - How do the decay dynamics and intermediate states of peridinin differ from those of other carotenoids, such as β-carotene?  
   - What role does the carbonyl substituent in peridinin play in altering the dynamics of the Sx state and its interactions with the solvent?

3. **Solvent and Environment Effects**  
   - How does solvent friction influence the lifetime and torsional motions of the Sx state in peridinin?  
   - How does the system-bath coupling differ between peridinin and other carotenoids?

4. **Biological Implications**  
   - How does the Sx state in peridinin contribute to excitation energy transfer to chlorophyll a in the peridinin-chlorophyll a protein?  
   - What are the structural and energetic features of the Sx state that make it an effective energy donor in photosynthetic systems?

5. **Spectroscopic Analysis**  
   - How can nonlinear response functions and the multimode Brownian oscillator model be used to simulate and interpret the transient grating spectroscopy data?  
   - What spectral signatures differentiate the Sx state in peridinin from similar states in other carotenoids?

These questions drive the exploration of molecular dynamics, structure-property relationships, and the role of molecular design in energy transfer processes in carotenoids.
dataset_item.true_false_question: Does the S2 potential surface in peridinin lack stabilization from intramolecular charge transfer mechanisms caused by the carbonyl substituent?

inference_contexts: The observation that the excited state absorption spectrum from the S x state of peridinin is significantly blue-shifted from that of β-carotene supports the radiationless decay model we proposed recently for carotenoids; the S x state in peridinin is assigned to a transition-state-like structure near an activation-energy barrier between planar and twisted structures on the S2 potential surface. The short lifetime for the S2 state is associated with a nonrecurrent vibrational displacement from the Franck-Condon geometry along the C-C and C-C bond-length alternation coordinates of the conjugated polyene backbone to the region of the barrier, where a gradient along torsional coordinates is encountered. Because of the intrinsic redistribution of π-electron density obtained from the electron withdrawing character of the carbonyl substituent of peridinin, the barrier and the twisted region of the S2 potential surface are substantially stabilized compared to β-carotene and other carotenoids lacking carbonyl substitution. The ICT character that results upon further relaxation on the torsional gradient on the S2 potential surface after the barrier is passed accounts for the lengthening of the lifetime of the S x state of peridinin over that observed in β-carotene; the resulting increase in the solvent friction would slow the passage from the S2 surface through a seam to the S1 surface.

The finding that the lifetime of the S2 state is much shorter than previously estimated and the suggestion that the decay of the resulting S x state is significantly slowed by solvent friction have significant implications in understanding the mechanism of excitation energy transfer from peridinin to Chl a in PCP. On the basis of fluorescence excitation experiments, the overall energy transfer efficiency from peridinin to Chl a after optical preparation of the S2 state is found to be ~90%, of which 25% is thought to occur nearly instantaneously between the peridinin S2 state to the Chl a Q x state; the remaining 75% of the energy transfer yield is currently thought to involve energy transfer from the S1/ICT state to Q y with a 3 ps time constant. , The present results suggest, in contrast, that it may actually be the S x state that serves as the excitation energy donor to either of the Chl a excited states. The average structure of peridinin in PCP is somewhat compressed along the conjugated polyene and bent prior to the allene moiety. The result is a partial inversion of the bond-length alternation pattern compared to that in the planar, all-trans ground state, as obtained as a energy minimum in electronic structure calculations. It is proposed that this distortion results in a strong mixing of the S2 and S1 states and a large enhancement of the energy transfer yield to the Chl a acceptor. , We suggest that the ground-state conformation favored in PCP results in an S x -like conformation immediately upon optical preparation of the S2 state. This conformation would be expected to relax further along torsional or out-of-plane coordinates in the protein to assume an even larger ICT character and a larger Forster transition-dipole-transition-dipole coupling to the Chl a acceptor. The result is a distorted donor state that should have some correspondence to that of the X intermediate (Figure ) reported by Ostroumov et al. , in two-dimensional electronic spectra recorded from the LH2 complex from purple bacteria.

The overlapping of steric (or electrosteric) and depletion mechanisms for colloidal stabilization of oxidized carbon nanotubes (plasma-oxidized SWCNTs and MWCNTs and chemically oxidized MWCNTs) by amphiphilic PF127 is attained through a matching of the polymer chemical structure (containing hydrophobic PPO and hydrophilic PEO moieties), and its consequent conformational behavior in solution, with the nanocarbon high aspect ratio one-dimensional morphology. For these samples, regardless of the surface charge (ζ potential), the degree of oxidation, and the nanotube diameter and length, colloidal stability in a 0.9% NaCl solution is attained through (i) the wrapping of PF127 around the nanotubes induced by hydrophobic interactions between the PPO moiety and nonoxidized regions of the graphitic sheets (i.e.. polyaromatic regions with sp2 carbon hybridization) and the consequent exposure of hydrophilic PEO moieties to the medium and (ii) the manifestation of repulsive depletion forces for PF127 concentrations superior to 1.0%. Above this concentration, the CNT colloidal stabilization also has little dependence on the PF127 concentration. The same PF127 was not able to colloidally stabilize graphene oxide (chemically oxidized) through steric-based mechanisms due to the small size of PEO moieties in comparison with the large-sized sheets of GO (lateral size of up to 20 μm), thus preventing a suitable steric repulsion for GO sheets. This aspect also explains the absence of stabilizing depletion forces for the GO-PF127 system, in which there is not a proper dimensional and stereochemical matching between the large (i.e.. GO sheets) and small (i.e.. PF127 micelles) particles present in the liquid. On the other hand, long-chain PEG (MW 35000) was unable to colloidally stabilize CNTs due to the absence of significant short-range interactions (e.g.. hydrophobic) that could result in steric-based mechanisms of stabilization. In addition, the absence of a proper dimensional and stereochemical matching between the long-chain PEG 35000 and the high aspect ratio one-dimensional morphology of CNTs did not lead to the manifestation of stabilizing repulsive depletion forces as well. However, large-sized sheets of GO in the presence of PEG 35000 can be colloidally stabilized through repulsive depletion forces, which strongly depend on the polymer concentration, as shown by the stabilization attained for PEG concentrations from 5.0 wt %. The overlapping of these stabilization mechanisms (steric + depletion) observed for CNTs led to a much higher colloidal stabilization in comparison with that attained for the GO-PEG system. For applications in media with low ionic strengths, electric stabilization attained through nanocarbon oxidation can provide a suitable colloidal stability. Conversely, in the particular context of nanomedicine, in which nanocarbons must behave throughout their application as individualized colloidal entities and not as agglomerates in physiological media (e.g.. 0.9% NaCl, with a high ionic strength), oxidation protocols such as acid treatment (which lead to electric stabilization through negative surface charging) are much less effective than the use of suitable biocompatible polymers such as Pluronic F-127 and long-chain PEG.

The ESIPT mechanisms of alizarin in ethanol solvent and binary solvent of ethanol and water with different proportion have been investigated based on DFT and TDDFT methods. The ground- and excited-state geometric structures, IR vibrational spectra, electronic spectra, frontier MOs, NBO, and the potential energy curves are examined to explore the ESIPT mechanism. The results show that the hydrogen bond is strengthened in the first excited state due to the decrease in hydrogen bond length and the red shift of IR vibrational spectra of group involved in the formation of hydrogen bond, which would facilitate the excited-state intramolecular proton transfer. The calculations of frontier MOs and NBO analysis reveal that the intramolecular hydrogen bond reinforcement is ascribed to the characteristics of intramolecular charge transfer in the excited state. Therefore, the excited-state intramolecular charge transfer is the underlying mechanism of ESIPT, and the ESIPT is the primary isomerization pathway from ALR-E to ALR-K.

Several materials prepared from triazine-containing precursors were explored as active materials in Li half cells. Well-defined materials which exhibit strong triazine character show very low gravimetric capacities even if the triazine units are bridged by conjugated moieties, such as phenylene or 2,2′-bipyridine. This directly contradicts the previously suggested bipolar mechanism in which the triazine is n- or p-doped when cycled. In order to achieve high gravimetric capacities, the well-defined conjugated systems must be synthesized at higher temperatures, thereby destroying the triazine unit and creating an N-containing amorphous carbon material. These materials have high concentrations of localized spins (large numbers of unpaired electrons) that may be involved in the discharge and charge mechanisms. The N-containing amorphous carbon materials are very similar to N-containing porous carbon materials that have been evaluated as supercapacitor materials. , The capacity of the amorphous materials trends loosely with specific surface area and C/N content. However, higher surface area does not always result in a higher capacity, suggesting the mechanism is not purely capacitive. The slight observed rate dependence also suggests a pseudocapacitive behavior involving charge transfer processes. These charge transfer processes could involve the unpaired electrons in the amorphous materials, and indeed, the inactive PTI materials do not contain unpaired electrons. Suggestions for future work to further probe the charge storage mechanisms involve using in situ EPR in order to observe the evolution of the spin concentration as a function of discharging and charging.

dataset_item.question: How does batch equilibration technique influence the sorption behavior of phenanthrene on activated and oxidized black carbon?
dataset_item.answer: The batch equilibration technique significantly influences the sorption behavior of phenanthrene on activated and oxidized black carbon by providing controlled experimental conditions that ensure reproducibility and reliability of the results. Experiments are conducted in sealed glass ampules to prevent contamination and external variability, maintaining a constant temperature of 25 ± 1 °C and an agitation speed of 125 rpm. The solution composition includes 0.01 mol/L CaCl₂, 200 mg/L NaN₃, and 5 mg/L NaHCO₃ at pH 7, ensuring consistent chemical conditions conducive to equilibrium establishment. Sorption isotherms are measured using precise sorbent quantities (0.1–1.23 mg), allowing for accurate analysis of phenanthrene uptake on modified black carbon. Desorption experiments under identical conditions further confirm the reversibility of sorption, demonstrating the reliability of the batch equilibration technique in evaluating the impact of black carbon activation and oxidation on phenanthrene sorption behavior.

It is common for C n mimBF4 RTILs to be contaminated with fluorescent impurities. It has been documented that these contaminants are generally negligible in concentration, do not have a significant effect on the bulk structure of the ionic liquid, and only become apparent with techniques such as fluorescence. , Such contaminants are excited at the 395 nm sample excitation wavelength and emit at 440 nm, meaning that when present they contribute to the experimental fluorescent decays. Because of the very low concentration of both the perylene and the impurities, it is a safe assumption that they will not interact with each other when solvated by ionic liquids. The contributions of the perylene and the contaminants to the fluorescence decays are therefore additive. For this reason, data from reference samples containing only the RTIL/water mixtures with no dissolved probe were also collected. A moving sample stage was used that interchanges the two samples under computer control so that data were collected on both the ionic liquid samples, alternating between those with perylene and those without, keeping all experimental conditions identical over the course of the experiment. The resulting perylene lifetime decay curves attained after subtraction of the reference sample fluorescence decay were single exponentials with time constants of 5.02 ns within experimental error for all RTILs studied. The measured lifetime is consistent with the perylene lifetime in other solvents. This observed single exponential decays with the same lifetimes indicates the reliability of the background subtraction technique for removing the contribution of fluorescent impurities in the RTILs. Because of the absence of fluorescent impurities, Hmim BF4 samples did not require subtraction, and it yielded the same fluorescent lifetime, within error, as the other samples. Furthermore, two different batches of Bmim BF4 from the supplier were used in the Bmim experiments. One batch had fluorescence impurities and required the impurity fluorescence subtraction. No subtraction was performed on the batch without impurities. The results obtained from both batches were the same, clearly demonstrating the validity of the background subtraction method.

Moreover, the polymerization performance in the batch reactor was compared with that in the capillary microreactor. In particular, the specific energy dissipation of the batch processing with high stirring rates (e.g.. 900 rpm) was rather high. In contrast, capillary microreactors could achieve much better control over the polymer properties and largely reduce the reaction time with the reasonable specific energy dissipation, showing its great application potential for free radical polymerization processes.

dataset_item.question: What is the role of DOPG in stabilizing the charge-separated state and enhancing photocurrent generation activity in LH1-RC complexes?
dataset_item.answer: The anionic phospholipid DOPG plays a crucial role in stabilizing the charge-separated state (P+QB−) in light-harvesting-reaction center (LH1-RC) complexes, thereby enhancing photocurrent generation activity. By reducing charge recombination, DOPG increases the yield of charge separation and improves quantum efficiency, achieving a notable 33% under low irradiance conditions. When LH1-RC complexes are incorporated into a DOPG lipid bilayer, they exhibit superior photocurrent activity compared to neutral DOPC bilayers or nonmembrane systems. This enhancement is attributed to DOPG's ability to stabilize the charge-separated state, promote the preferred orientation of LH1-RC complexes on electrodes, and improve electrical contact, leading to a higher fraction of functionally active complexes. Additionally, DOPG facilitates efficient electron release via hydroquinone formation, following Michaelis-Menten kinetics, which further optimizes the performance of biohybrid energy devices. Thus, DOPG serves as a critical effector in the design and development of biohybrid systems for energy generation.

inference_contexts: We evaluated the charge separation yield and photocurrent generation activity of LH1-RC in the absence and presence of phospholipid environments. The analysis using static fluorometry based on the steady-state approximation clearly indicates that this simple method accurately assesses the activity of LH1-RC and that the anionic phospholipid DOPG significantly influences the yield of charge separation by stabilizing the charge-separated state under a low level of irradiation. LH1-RC complexes reconstituted in the DOPG lipid bilayer exhibited more prominent photocurrent generation activity than those in the DOPC lipid bilayer or nonmembrane systems. The overall photocurrent generation reaction can be approximated by the Michaelis-Menten mechanism, which can acceptably characterize the process of charge-separation/recombination and release of electrons as the product in the form of hydroquinone. Through this analysis, the fraction of active LH1-RC and the kinetic parameters of Michaelis-Menten kinetics revealed how efficiently the LH1-RC complex works on the electrode with DOPG. As the membrane matrix, DOPG increases the fraction of functioning LH1-RC complexes on the electrode, resulting from the preferred orientation of LH1-RC and electrical contact with the electrode. In addition, the stabilizing effect of DOPG on the charge-separated state (P+QB -) partially contributes to the highest quantum efficiency of photocurrent generation, 33%, at a low level of irradiance.

In this work, we describe mechanisms of the Pd (II)-controlled disulfide/thiolate interconversion for l-cystine, cystamine, dl-homocystine and 3,3′-dithiodipropionic acid in aqueous solutions. We specifically address the question of different reactivity of homologous disulfides toward Pd2+. We see this different reactivity in different capacities of considered homologous disulfides to stabilize forming S,S′-binuclear complexes, which are believed to be key intermediates toward interconversion products. In case of homocystine and 3,3′-dithiodipropionic acid, formation of the S,S′-binuclear complexes leads to cleavage of the disulfide bond, while we observe formation of the S,N-binuclear and S,N,S′,N′-tetranuclear complexes with the preserved S-S bond for the l-cystine and cystamine ligands. Formation of the S,S′-binuclear complexes increases the d(S-S) bond length by 5%, and the redistribution of charges with Sδ--Sδ- in the original disulfide on Sδ+-Sδ- occurs in the complex. We find that the greater the magnitude of Δδ in S,S′-binuclear complex, the higher the likelihood of disproportionation. Conditions, under which disproportionation takes place, include formation of redox-resistant S,S′-binuclear disulfide complex and the disulfide bond being open for the nucleophilic substitution by water.

In this study, highly purified LH1-RC complexes from a new thermophilic purple sulfur bacterium Alc. tepidum were investigated by spectroscopic and thermodynamic analyses. The Alc. tepidum LH1-RC complex exhibited a LH1 Q y peak at 890 nm, which was slightly red-shifted from that of Alc. vinosum but largely blue-shifted from that of Tch. tepidum. The Q y peaks were linearly correlated with the frequencies for C3-acetyl νC-O Raman bands and slightly blue-shifted upon removal of Ca2+. The results indicate that the hydrogen-bonding interactions between BChl-a and LH1 Trp residues are partly modulated by Ca2+. Based on both ICP-AES and ITC analyses, the number of bound Ca2+ per LH1-RC complex purified from Alc tepidum was determined to be 4-5, which is a quarter of that of Tch. tepidum. The DSC analysis demonstrated that the thermal stability of the LH1-RC complexes was similar between Alc. tepidum and Tch. tepidum in their Ca2+-bound forms but decreased significantly in Tch. tepidum but only moderately in Alc. tepidum upon removal of Ca2+. The thermodynamic parameters evaluated from the ITC analysis indicated that Ca2+-binding to the Alc. tepidum LH1-RC complex is predominantly driven by the largely favorable electrostatic interactions that counteract the unfavorable negative entropy change. In contrast, Ca2+-binding in Tch. tepidum was favorable, both entropically and enthalpically. Based on these findings, we propose that the enhanced thermal stability of the Alc. tepidum LH1-RC complex is in part due to a Ca2+-dependent mechanism, in which the LH1-RC complex is stabilized by the binding of 4-5 Ca2+ per each LH1 complex, but that the location of Ca2+ binding sites and conformational changes around the sites differ significantly from those of Tch. tepidum. Phylogenetic analyses indicated that Alc. tepidum is more closely related to Alc. vinosum than to Tch. tepidum. However, the thermophilic phenotype and presence of Ca2+ in the Alc. tepidum LH1 are properties characteristic of Tch. tepidum but not Alc. vinosum. Thus, it is possible that Alc. tepidum is an evolutionary intermediate between mesophilic and thermophilic chromatia and that Ca2+ is one of the major keys to thermostability of LH1-RC complexes in purple bacteria.

The overlapping of steric (or electrosteric) and depletion mechanisms for colloidal stabilization of oxidized carbon nanotubes (plasma-oxidized SWCNTs and MWCNTs and chemically oxidized MWCNTs) by amphiphilic PF127 is attained through a matching of the polymer chemical structure (containing hydrophobic PPO and hydrophilic PEO moieties), and its consequent conformational behavior in solution, with the nanocarbon high aspect ratio one-dimensional morphology. For these samples, regardless of the surface charge (ζ potential), the degree of oxidation, and the nanotube diameter and length, colloidal stability in a 0.9% NaCl solution is attained through (i) the wrapping of PF127 around the nanotubes induced by hydrophobic interactions between the PPO moiety and nonoxidized regions of the graphitic sheets (i.e.. polyaromatic regions with sp2 carbon hybridization) and the consequent exposure of hydrophilic PEO moieties to the medium and (ii) the manifestation of repulsive depletion forces for PF127 concentrations superior to 1.0%. Above this concentration, the CNT colloidal stabilization also has little dependence on the PF127 concentration. The same PF127 was not able to colloidally stabilize graphene oxide (chemically oxidized) through steric-based mechanisms due to the small size of PEO moieties in comparison with the large-sized sheets of GO (lateral size of up to 20 μm), thus preventing a suitable steric repulsion for GO sheets. This aspect also explains the absence of stabilizing depletion forces for the GO-PF127 system, in which there is not a proper dimensional and stereochemical matching between the large (i.e.. GO sheets) and small (i.e.. PF127 micelles) particles present in the liquid. On the other hand, long-chain PEG (MW 35000) was unable to colloidally stabilize CNTs due to the absence of significant short-range interactions (e.g.. hydrophobic) that could result in steric-based mechanisms of stabilization. In addition, the absence of a proper dimensional and stereochemical matching between the long-chain PEG 35000 and the high aspect ratio one-dimensional morphology of CNTs did not lead to the manifestation of stabilizing repulsive depletion forces as well. However, large-sized sheets of GO in the presence of PEG 35000 can be colloidally stabilized through repulsive depletion forces, which strongly depend on the polymer concentration, as shown by the stabilization attained for PEG concentrations from 5.0 wt %. The overlapping of these stabilization mechanisms (steric + depletion) observed for CNTs led to a much higher colloidal stabilization in comparison with that attained for the GO-PEG system. For applications in media with low ionic strengths, electric stabilization attained through nanocarbon oxidation can provide a suitable colloidal stability. Conversely, in the particular context of nanomedicine, in which nanocarbons must behave throughout their application as individualized colloidal entities and not as agglomerates in physiological media (e.g.. 0.9% NaCl, with a high ionic strength), oxidation protocols such as acid treatment (which lead to electric stabilization through negative surface charging) are much less effective than the use of suitable biocompatible polymers such as Pluronic F-127 and long-chain PEG.

dataset_item.question: How do cation-π interactions between cationic and aromatic collagen-mimetic peptides influence the formation and thermodynamics of AAB-type heterotrimers?
dataset_item.answer: Cation-π interactions between cationic (CR, CK) and aromatic (CF) collagen-mimetic peptides drive the formation of AAB-type heterotrimers through stabilization of C-terminal triple helix folding, following a C-to-N assembly mechanism. The mixing ratios of cationic and aromatic peptides play a crucial role in determining the resulting heterotrimer compositions. CR-CF mixtures exhibit tunable heterotrimer structures based on peptide ratios, while CK-CF mixtures predominantly form (CK)₂(CF)₁ heterotrimers due to the lower stability of (CK)₁(CF)₂. Thermodynamic analysis reveals that entropy is the primary driving force behind the folding process, with cation-π interactions enabling selective and controlled heterotrimer formation. These findings underscore the utility of cation-π interactions for designing synthetic collagen assemblies with tailored structural and thermodynamic properties.

inference_contexts: In the present study, we have designed two cationic CMPs (CR and CK) and one aromatic CMP (CF) and used CD, NMR, and DSC to demonstrate that AAB-type collagen heterotrimers can be induced to form via cation-π interactions on the C-end of a triple helix. The experimental results also provide the evidence that their folding should follow a C → N mechanism. In conclusion, the C-terminal cation-π interactions have been shown an effective force to assist the formation of a pure fold of AAB-type collagen heterotrimer, exhibiting the application potentials of cation-π interactions in preparing collagen heterotrimers for collagen-related studies.
