For the 4:1 mixture, which forms a pair of pyridinium-formate salt capped by three un-ionized formic acid molecules in the asymmetric unit, cooperative enhancement of acidity of formic acid plays a decisive role. Such an unusual influence of polarization for higher stoichiometric mixtures of organic acid-organic base clearly cannot be predicted by just the difference of pK a's between them. In fact, in a very recent report, Steed and co-workers reported salt formation in a 2:1 mixture of formic acid and pyridine under pressure. A molecular picture of the cocrystal → salt transformation shows that the strength of the O-H N H-bond increases with an increase in the number of formic acids and a crossover to the salt form (O-H N → O H-N) occurs for a formic acid to pyridine ratio after 4:1. The proton migration pathway within the 4:1 crystal follows a relay mechanism wherein the proton hops from the donor (acid) to the acceptor (base) assisted cooperatively by the neutral acids. This work indicates that by means of cooperativity the outcome of an acid-base reaction in the solid state can be tuned to exclusively isolate a cocrystal or salt. This should have important consequences in the drug industry, as one can design and predict the API properties of small molecules a priori. Also, from a fundamental aspect, we suggest that the protons in acid-base mixture within crystals can be rather dynamic, and hence, sufficient attention (more so nonequimolar cases) must be paid to aggregation induced structural transformation before classifying them into cocrystals or salts.

In this work, we describe mechanisms of the Pd (II)-controlled disulfide/thiolate interconversion for l-cystine, cystamine, dl-homocystine and 3,3′-dithiodipropionic acid in aqueous solutions. We specifically address the question of different reactivity of homologous disulfides toward Pd2+. We see this different reactivity in different capacities of considered homologous disulfides to stabilize forming S,S′-binuclear complexes, which are believed to be key intermediates toward interconversion products. In case of homocystine and 3,3′-dithiodipropionic acid, formation of the S,S′-binuclear complexes leads to cleavage of the disulfide bond, while we observe formation of the S,N-binuclear and S,N,S′,N′-tetranuclear complexes with the preserved S-S bond for the l-cystine and cystamine ligands. Formation of the S,S′-binuclear complexes increases the d(S-S) bond length by 5%, and the redistribution of charges with Sδ--Sδ- in the original disulfide on Sδ+-Sδ- occurs in the complex. We find that the greater the magnitude of Δδ in S,S′-binuclear complex, the higher the likelihood of disproportionation. Conditions, under which disproportionation takes place, include formation of redox-resistant S,S′-binuclear disulfide complex and the disulfide bond being open for the nucleophilic substitution by water.

In this work, the reaction pathways upon DEA were studied for the potential radiosensitizer SeCNdU. The results indicate that SeCNdU can be considered as a pseudo-halouridine composed of an electron-affinic -SeCN side group and a nucleobase moiety. Eleven dissociation channels were observed within the detection limit of the experiment. The highest ion yield was obtained for (SeU-yl) -, which is a radical and thus highly reactive. A comparable ion yield was observed for the cyano anion. The yields of the other fragment anions are at least 1 order of magnitude smaller. Besides the negatively charged fragments directly obtained in the experiments, neutral counterparts were investigated by calculations. These include radicals such as SeU-yl and molecules such as H2O and HCN. One of the main questions, whether a bond cleavage of the Se-CN bond or the C5-Se bond occurs more efficiently, was solved because the Se-CN bond was far more efficiently cleaved with 5 out of 11 fragmentation pathways and the 2 most intense dissociation channels among them. Cleavage of the C5-Se bond also occurs upon DEA; however, only two channels were observed with low ion yields. Remarkably, all reactions exhibit a 0 eV threshold in the experimental data, which is in full agreement with the calculated thermochemical thresholds. The calculations showed that all DEA channels are exothermic at the present experimental conditions. Few reactions have exothermicities of more than 3 eV. Such behavior also results from the exceptionally high EA of most of fragments released with an excess electron. The anion (SeU-yl)- with the most intense ion yield is formed upon simple cleavage reactions. The formation of CN-, the other abundant anion, is based on simple bond cleavage, while two bonds have to be cleaved and one formed to produce (SeU-yl)-. Most other dissociation processes involve multiple bond cleavages, which are also accompanied by structural rearrangement. The formation of C4N2O2H2CN- represents such a process because the selenium must be cut out of the molecule in order to form a U-yl-CN bond. Moreover, the resonance profiles of C4N2O2H2Se -, C9N2O3H6Se -, and C9N2O5H10Se - showed a very similar structure, suggesting one common electronic state of the TNI.

dataset_item.question: Can nonequilibrium local heating inside a catalyst bed under microwaves explain reaction rate enhancement during dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene over magnetite?
dataset_item.answer: The enhanced reaction rate observed during microwave-assisted dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene over a magnetite catalyst cannot be solely attributed to nonuniform temperature distributions (hot spots) within the catalyst bed. Simulations incorporating temperature gradients demonstrate that while these thermal effects contribute to catalytic activity, they do not fully explain the observed rate enhancement. Notably, at 500°C—where carbon deposition is minimal—microwave irradiation induces additional catalytic effects beyond conventional thermal gradients. This suggests the presence of nonequilibrium local heating mechanisms, which are unique to microwave interactions and significantly influence the reaction kinetics. Thus, microwave-induced nonequilibrium local heating emerges as a key factor driving the enhanced reaction rates during this process.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. **Summary of the Paper's Purpose**  
The paper aims to investigate the impact of microwave-induced nonuniform temperature distributions in a catalyst bed on the reaction rate enhancement for a fixed-bed flow reaction. By employing electromagnetic and heat-transfer simulations, the authors explore the role of temperature gradients and local heating effects (hot spots) in the dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene over a magnetite catalyst. The study reveals that the observed rate enhancement cannot be solely explained by the temperature gradient and suggests the presence of additional nonequilibrium heating effects.

---

### 2. **Classification of Purpose**

dataset_item.true_false_question: Does nonuniform temperature distribution alone explain the reaction rate enhancement during microwave-assisted dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene over magnetite?

inference_contexts: We carried out dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene over a magnetite catalyst under microwaves and evaluated the reaction activity. An accurate evaluation of the reaction activity under microwaves could be performed by considering the temperature distribution in the whole packed bed because the temperature gradient occurred in the packed bed during microwave heating. The simulation methods enable the calculation of theoretical reaction rates originated from the temperature distribution in the whole catalyst bed under microwaves. As a result, microwave enhancement was observed, especially when carbon deposition did not occur in the catalyst bed (500 °C). The result indicates that the rate enhancement under microwaves can not only be attributed to the nonuniform temperature distribution in the catalyst bed. The rate enhancement is possibly due to the generation of nonequilibrium local heating inside the catalyst bed by microwaves.

dataset_item.question: What are the challenges and strategies in improving orbital relaxation effects for core-excited states in configuration interaction singles calculations?
dataset_item.answer:
Improving orbital relaxation effects in configuration interaction singles (CIS) calculations for core-excited states presents significant challenges due to the inability of ground-state Hartree-Fock orbitals to adequately account for the substantial orbital relaxation associated with core excitations. This limitation arises because single-excitation determinants in CIS calculations fail to capture the dynamic electron redistribution following core excitation.

### Challenges:
1. **Inadequate Orbital Relaxation**: Standard CIS calculations rely on ground-state orbitals, which poorly describe the relaxation effects needed for accurate core-excited state predictions.
2. **Rydberg State Placement**: Perturbative corrections like CIS(D) may improve excitation energies but can misplace high-lying Rydberg states.
3. **Correlation Effects**: CIS calculations lack sufficient electron correlation, which is crucial for accurate predictions of core excitation energies.

### Strategies:
1. **Core-Relaxed Reference States**:
   - **Static Exchange (STEX) Method**: Performs an initial Hartree-Fock (HF) calculation on the core-ionized state, ensuring the orbitals reflect core-hole relaxation before applying CIS.
   - **Core-Hole Reference (CHR) CIS**: Uses HF or DFT orbitals optimized for the core-excited state to incorporate relaxation effects directly into the reference orbitals.

2. **Perturbative Corrections**:
   - Methods like CIS(D) and spin-opposite-scaled CIS(D) introduce perturbative corrections to account for orbital relaxation and electron correlation, improving the accuracy of excitation energies.

3. **Advanced Methods**:
   - **Coupled-Cluster Approaches**: Methods such as EOM-CCSD and CVS-CC systematically include both orbital relaxation and electron correlation, providing high accuracy for core-excited states.
   - **CVS-ADC(2)-x**: Core-valence separation (CVS) within the algebraic diagrammatic construction (ADC) framework offers robust accuracy for core excitations by efficiently incorporating relaxation and correlation effects.

### Conclusion:
While the choice of reference state generation (e.g., STEX, CHR CIS) has minor impact for larger molecules, incorporating orbital relaxation effects is essential for reliable predictions of core excitation energies. Advanced methods like CVS-ADC and coupled-cluster techniques are particularly effective for balancing orbital relaxation and electron correlation, addressing the limitations of standard CIS calculations.

These authors focused on the exploitation of different core-excited reference states, all designed to capture orbital relaxation effects at the SCF level. In their core-hole reference (CHR) CIS schemes, they used, for example, restricted Hartree-Fock and Kohn-Sham orbitals, core-excited restricted open-shell Hartree-Fock or Kohn-Sham orbitals, and core-excited unrestricted Hartree-Fock orbitals with the hole in the α-core spin-orbital or with half an electron in each α and β core spin-orbital. The main conclusion of this work is that the inclusion of orbital relaxation effects is crucial to observing a major gain in accuracy, but the details of how the core-excited reference is generated have only a minor influence. For larger molecules, the CVS approximation is (as expected) proven to have only a negligible influence on the results.

A viable pathway to circumvent the problem with the limited orbital relaxation effects is to use a reference state that already takes into account the orbital relaxation due to the core hole. dataset_item.question: What is the relationship between avoided crossing positions and variations in dipole moments for MgLi+?
dataset_item.answer: The relationship between avoided crossing positions and variations in dipole moments for MgLi+ arises from charge transfer processes and changes in the electronic wave function character. Avoided crossings in the potential energy curves correspond to transitions between different electronic configurations, such as ionic (Mg+Li) and covalent (MgLi+) bonding. These transitions induce abrupt shifts in dipole moments, reflecting the redistribution of charge during state interactions. Specifically, both permanent and transition dipole moments exhibit distinct trends with interatomic distance, but show pronounced deviations near avoided crossings. Computational analysis confirms that these variations in dipole moments validate the crossing positions, aligning with spectroscopic data and providing evidence for charge transfer dynamics between Mg+, Li, and MgLi+ species. Thus, the dipole moment behavior serves as a sensitive indicator of electronic structure changes associated with avoided crossings in MgLi+.

dataset_item.question: How does topography-feedback-induced cross-talk influence frequency shift data in simultaneous scanning tunneling microscopy and noncontact atomic force microscopy measurements?
dataset_item.answer:
Topography-feedback-induced cross-talk significantly impacts frequency shift data in simultaneous scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and noncontact atomic force microscopy (NC-AFM) measurements by introducing artifacts that distort the interpretation of chemical interactions. This form of cross-talk arises primarily from the constant-current feedback mechanism in STM, which adjusts the tip height to maintain a constant tunneling current as the tip scans over varying surface topographies. These mechanical adjustments inadvertently alter the tip-sample distance, thereby influencing the measured frequency shift independent of genuine chemical interactions. 

For conductive surfaces, such as the (2√2 × √2)R45° reconstructed oxygen-covered Cu(100) surface at 60K, this effect can dominate over electrical coupling artifacts (e.g., stray capacitance). Controlled experiments and atomic-scale simulations using Cu-CuO and CuO tip models reveal that while true chemical interactions produce distinct force spectroscopy signatures, these can be obscured by topography-feedback-induced artifacts. Advanced techniques like 3D-AFM, which decouple mechanical cross-talk effects, are necessary to accurately interpret frequency shift data and distinguish genuine chemical forces from artifacts introduced by feedback mechanisms.

dataset_item.question: What molecular mechanisms contribute to the exclusion of solvent molecules and anions from interacting with electrode surfaces in concentrated electrolytes?
dataset_item.answer: The exclusion of solvent molecules and anions from direct interaction with electrode surfaces in concentrated electrolytes is driven by molecular reorganization effects and kinetic barriers, as revealed through quantum chemistry calculations and molecular dynamics simulations. Solvent oxidation, coupled with hydrogen transfer (common in carbonates, phosphates, and sulfones), and anion defluorination during reduction are thermodynamically favorable processes. However, these reactions are kinetically hindered due to high reorganization energies, preventing direct interaction with the electrode surface. This exclusion mechanism enhances electrolyte stability by tailoring interphasial structures, thereby widening the electrochemical stability window without relying on passivation layers. The absence of passivation layers preserves electrode accessibility, ensuring optimal electrolyte performance in devices like EDL capacitors and batteries.

dataset_item.question: How do unrestricted and restricted open-shell formalisms compare in computational methods applied to open-shell species derived from gallic acid?
dataset_item.answer:
For open-shell species derived from gallic acid, both unrestricted (U-) and restricted open-shell (RO-) formalisms have been extensively compared using computational methods such as B3LYP, LC-ωPBE, M06-2X, MP2, CCSD, and CCSD(T). Unrestricted methods, while computationally tractable for larger systems, exhibited varying degrees of spin contamination. For instance, unrestricted Hartree-Fock (UHF) calculations showed significant spin contamination with an ⟨S²⟩ value of 1.25, whereas unrestricted DFT methods demonstrated modest contamination, such as an ⟨S²⟩ value of 0.77 for the doublet 5-ArO radical at the B3LYP/aug-cc-pVTZ level. In contrast, restricted open-shell methods avoided excessive spin polarization, offering more reliable and accurate results, particularly for radical species.

Both formalisms were evaluated for key thermodynamic properties such as O-H bond dissociation enthalpies (BDEs) and ionization potentials (IP) of gallic acid and its deprotonated form. Calculations were performed using a range of basis sets, including 6-311++G(df,p) and aug-cc-pVTZ, in both gas-phase and aqueous environments modeled via the IEF-PCM solvation approach. While solvent effects were accounted for, explicit solvation was deemed unnecessary based on prior benchmarks.

Overall, restricted open-shell methods (e.g., RO-CCSD, RO-CCSD(T)) provided more reliable results by minimizing spin contamination, whereas unrestricted methods (e.g., U-B3LYP, U-CCSD) remained useful for computational efficiency, particularly in larger systems. The choice of formalism depends on the balance between computational cost and the accuracy required for studying radical species derived from gallic acid.

dataset_item.question: How does the use of cobalt nanosheet layers as a surface modifier and cobalt source influence the nucleation and growth of ZIF-67 membranes?
dataset_item.answer:
The use of cobalt nanosheet layers (Co-NSL) as both a surface modifier and a cobalt source plays a crucial role in enhancing the nucleation and growth of ZIF-67 membranes. The unique microstructure of Co-NSL, characterized by a high width-to-thickness ratio, ensures maximum contact with the ligand solution, thereby promoting uniform and efficient nucleation. Acting as active sites and a readily available cobalt supply, Co-NSL facilitates the growth of well-cross-linked ZIF-67 crystals, resulting in a thin and stable membrane approximately 3 μm thick.

This approach achieves high hydrogen permeance (~10⁻⁶ mol s⁻¹ m⁻² Pa⁻¹) and an H₂/CO₂ separation factor of ~17, which can be further improved to ~30 through amine modification. The amine modification enhances CO₂ affinity while maintaining membrane stability under varying temperature and pressure conditions. The combination of structural optimization and chemical modification ensures high performance and robustness in separation applications.

dataset_item.question: How does a switched-gain extended state observer improve the control performance of a high-purity distillation column?
dataset_item.answer: A switched-gain extended state observer (ESO) improves the control performance of a high-purity distillation column by dynamically adjusting its gain to achieve fast and accurate disturbance estimation while maintaining robustness against measurement noise. This observer estimates and compensates for both internal plant dynamics and external disturbances using only input-output data, eliminating the need for detailed plant models. By balancing the trade-off between rapid convergence of estimation errors and noise immunity, the switched-gain mechanism enhances the system’s ability to handle nonlinearities, strong coupling between control loops, and external disturbances. Compared to traditional methods like PID, cascade PID, robust control, and direct ADRC, the switched-gain ESO delivers superior disturbance rejection and loop decoupling, resulting in improved control performance in highly nonlinear and complex distillation processes.

dataset_item.question: What are the primary reaction products when nitrogen dioxide interacts with ice surfaces at cryogenic temperatures?
dataset_item.answer:
When nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) interacts with ice surfaces at cryogenic temperatures (100–170 K), it undergoes hydrolysis and forms several reaction products, including nitrous acid (HONO), nitrate (NO₃⁻), hydronium ions (H₃O⁺), and dinitrogen tetroxide (N₂O₄). Below 110 K, the dominant surface species is NO₂ᵟ⁻ (a partially negatively charged NO₂ moiety). As the temperature increases to 110–130 K, NO₂ᵟ⁻ either desorbs as NO₂ gas or reacts with the ice surface to form HONO, NO₃⁻, and H₃O⁺.  

Nitrous acid (HONO) desorbs from the ice surface at 140–160 K. The hydrolysis of NO₂ to HONO occurs efficiently even at low temperatures, with isolated NO₂ molecules being the primary reactants rather than N₂O₄. Studies indicate approximately 40% conversion efficiency to surface-bound HONO and 7% conversion to gaseous HONO. This reaction proceeds with a low energy barrier, highlighting its significance in cold atmospheric environments, such as polar regions, where heterogeneous reactions on ice surfaces play an important role in atmospheric chemistry.

dataset_item.question: What structural features of naphthyl-fused indanone end groups contribute to improved power conversion efficiency in organic solar cells compared to phenyl-fused indanone?
dataset_item.answer: Naphthyl-fused indanone (NINCN) end groups enhance the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of organic solar cells compared to phenyl-fused indanone (FDICTF) by extending π-conjugation, which results in red-shifted optical absorption, higher charge carrier mobility, and more ordered molecular packing. These structural features improve complementary light absorption and strengthen intermolecular interactions between donor and acceptor materials, facilitating efficient charge separation and hole transfer. Additionally, the extended conjugation ensures better donor-acceptor compatibility while maintaining a suitable LUMO energy level. These enhancements lead to higher short-circuit current density (J_sc) and fill factor (FF), with minimal impact on open-circuit voltage (V_oc). Consequently, devices based on NINCN end groups achieve a PCE of 11.2%, outperforming the 10.06% efficiency of devices with phenyl-fused indanone end groups.

dataset_item.question: How does fluorination affect the structural preferences and thermodynamic drivers of partially fluorinated benzene dimers?
dataset_item.answer: Fluorination significantly affects the structural preferences and thermodynamic drivers of partially fluorinated benzene dimers by stabilizing π-stacked configurations through entropic and enthalpic contributions. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that partially fluorinated dimers exhibit contact-pair formation energies ranging between 2.8–3.5 kJ mol⁻¹, with entropy consistently driving π-stacked association and enthalpy further reinforcing this structure, particularly in cases like 1,4-difluorobenzene. In contrast, benzene and hexafluorobenzene avoid π-stacked configurations due to enthalpic destabilization. Additionally, increasing fluorination correlates with reduced water density in the first solvation shell, indicating enhanced hydrophobicity driven by diminished negative electrostatic potential. Thus, partial fluorination optimally balances entropic and enthalpic contributions to stabilize π-stacked geometries, whereas full fluorination or its absence disrupts this equilibrium.

dataset_item.question: How does reduction extent and surface morphology influence oxidation rates in ceria across varying nonstoichiometry levels?
dataset_item.answer: The oxidation rates of ceria are significantly influenced by both reduction extent and surface morphology, exhibiting distinct behaviors across varying nonstoichiometry (δ) levels. At high nonstoichiometry levels (δ > 0.2), oxidation rates decrease substantially, which is linked to a near-order phase change and lattice compression, as evidenced by Raman spectroscopy. These phenomena hinder oxygen transport and reactivity, resulting in slower oxidation. Conversely, at lower nonstoichiometry levels (δ < 0.06), oxidation rates increase linearly with δ in pure ceria. This trend is attributed to defect cluster formation, which enhances bulk transport, and chemical expansion-induced morphological changes. Notably, these effects are less pronounced in gadolinium-doped ceria due to suppressed defect interactions. These findings emphasize the interplay between bulk defect dynamics and surface morphology in governing oxidation kinetics, though further studies are required to disentangle intrinsic reaction mechanisms from secondary effects such as crack propagation and chemical expansion.

dataset_item.answer: X-ray scattering data for sodium sulfide-silicon sulfide glasses are processed using a systematic workflow to extract pair distribution functions (PDFs). High-energy X-ray diffraction patterns are collected using a monochromatic beam (100.305 keV, λ = 0.123607 Å⁻¹) and an area detector at facilities like the Advanced Photon Source. The raw two-dimensional detector images are reduced to one-dimensional scattering data using the FIT2D software. These 1D data undergo corrections for background, Compton scattering, and oblique incidence effects using the PDFgetX2 software. Normalization is performed to account for the average electron density, calculated based on the weighted sum of independent-atom X-ray form factors. The resulting structure factor, *S*(*Q*), is Fourier-transformed to generate the pair distribution function (PDF), which provides insights into local atomic arrangements and helps in analyzing ion conduction mechanisms in glassy solid electrolytes.

dataset_item.question: What is the mechanism underlying selective adsorption of dichlorophen by magnetic Fe3O4 molecularly imprinted polymers compared to adsorption of structurally similar molecules?
dataset_item.answer:
The selective adsorption of dichlorophen by magnetic Fe₃O₄ molecularly imprinted polymers (MMIPs) is driven by the surface imprinting process during synthesis, which creates specific binding sites that are complementary to the molecular structure of dichlorophen. This tailoring of the polymer layer on Fe₃O₄ particles ensures preferential binding of dichlorophen over structurally similar molecules such as 2,4-DCP and 2,6-DCP. The mechanism involves monolayer adsorption and follows pseudo-second-order kinetics, reflecting the chemical affinity and specific interaction between dichlorophen and the imprinted binding sites. 

The enhanced selectivity is a direct result of the use of dichlorophen as the template molecule during synthesis, which ensures that the binding sites closely match its size, shape, and functional groups. Structurally similar molecules, while capable of adsorption to some extent, exhibit lower binding affinity due to less precise structural matching. Furthermore, compounds with higher structural similarity, such as chlorophene, may show greater adsorption than less similar compounds. 

Elevated temperatures improve adsorption performance, and the MMIPs demonstrate stability and reusability, making them effective for trace removal of dichlorophen from water systems. This combination of tailored specificity, adsorption efficiency, and reusability underscores the utility of MMIPs in selective adsorption applications.

dataset_item.question: How does the variational polaron approach account for the localization of exciton states in pigments within light-harvesting systems?
dataset_item.answer: The variational polaron approach accounts for the localization of exciton states in pigments within light-harvesting systems by incorporating temperature effects, energy gaps between pigments, and reorganization energy into its framework. It introduces a renormalized factor \( B \), derived from the variational transformation, as a dynamic criterion for domain assignment. Unlike traditional single-threshold methods, this approach systematically adjusts domain assignments based on \( B \), allowing for the accurate representation of exciton localization across varying parameter regimes. This method effectively captures the interplay between environmental factors and exciton dynamics, providing a robust foundation for refining domain models without relying on empirical thresholds. Validation on photosystem II (PSII) at 77 K demonstrated its ability to determine valid domain models, though potential overestimation of localization effects at higher temperatures (e.g., 300 K) suggests areas for refinement. Overall, the variational polaron approach enhances the understanding of exciton behavior in light-harvesting systems by integrating dynamic localization effects into its domain assignment process.

We demonstrated that B can potentially be a criterion for domain assignment, which includes the possible localization of exciton states by the temperature, energy gap, and reorganization energy. The combined generalized Forster-Redfield approach was successfully applied to study large light harvesting systems, although the best threshold value for domain assignment needs to be determined empirically. dataset_item.question: How does excited-state intramolecular charge transfer influence the hydrogen bond strength and facilitate proton transfer in 1,2-dihydroxyanthraquinone?
dataset_item.answer:
Excited-state intramolecular charge transfer (ICT) in 1,2-dihydroxyanthraquinone (alizarin, ALR) significantly strengthens the intramolecular hydrogen bond by reducing the bond length and inducing red shifts in IR vibrational spectra of the hydrogen-bonded groups. This ICT-driven reinforcement facilitates excited-state intramolecular proton transfer (ESIPT), enabling the isomerization pathway from the enol form to the keto form. Computational analyses, including frontier molecular orbital and natural bond orbital studies, confirm charge redistribution in the excited state, further supporting the strengthening of the hydrogen bond.

However, the presence of water or ethanol-water binary solvents inhibits the ESIPT process. Water forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds with ALR's carbonyl oxygen, weakening the intramolecular hydrogen bond and increasing the energy barrier for proton transfer. As water concentration increases, this attenuation of intramolecular hydrogen bonding aligns with experimentally observed reductions in keto emission intensity, further confirming the inhibitory role of hydration in the ESIPT process.

dataset_item.question: How does the energy decomposition analysis method quantify the interaction energy in host-guest systems?
dataset_item.answer:
The energy decomposition analysis (EDA) method quantifies the interaction energy in host-guest systems by breaking down the total interaction energy (ΔE<sub>int</sub>) into chemically meaningful components: Pauli repulsion (ΔE<sub>Pauli</sub>), electrostatic interaction (ΔV<sub>elstat</sub>), orbital interaction (ΔE<sub>oi</sub>), and dispersion (ΔE<sub>disp</sub>). 

1. **Pauli Repulsion (ΔE<sub>Pauli</sub>)**: Represents the repulsive interactions between occupied orbitals of the host and guest fragments due to the Pauli exclusion principle. This term arises from the overlap of electron densities and prevents the fragments from occupying the same spatial region.

2. **Electrostatic Interaction (ΔV<sub>elstat</sub>)**: Describes the classical Coulombic interactions between the charge distributions of the host and guest. This component can include ion-dipole interactions and other electrostatic contributions, which may be isolated by comparing the guest with a neutral isoelectronic counterpart.

3. **Orbital Interaction (ΔE<sub>oi</sub>)**: Captures charge transfer effects, polarization within fragments, and the interactions between occupied molecular orbitals of one fragment and unoccupied orbitals of the other. This term reflects the covalent bonding contributions to the interaction energy.

4. **Dispersion (ΔE<sub>disp</sub>)**: Accounts for long-range van der Waals forces arising from correlated electron movements in the host and guest fragments. Dispersion is particularly important for non-covalent interactions.

Additionally, the **preparation energy (ΔE<sub>prep</sub>)** is included in the analysis, representing the energy required to deform the individual fragments from their isolated geometries to the geometries they adopt in the host-guest complex. Together, these components contribute to the bond dissociation energy (BDE), which can be validated using dispersion-corrected density functional theory (e.g., BP86-D3/TZ2P) and compared with experimental data.

The EDA method provides a detailed understanding of the physical and chemical contributions to host-guest interactions, linking computational results to measurable properties and enabling the design of systems with tailored interaction profiles.

dataset_item.question: How can surface segregation in Sr-substituted oxides be controlled or engineered to enhance electrocatalyst activity and stability?
dataset_item.answer:
Surface segregation in Sr-substituted oxides can be controlled or engineered to enhance electrocatalyst activity and stability by leveraging a combination of strategies focused on cation distribution, electronic structure optimization, and vacancy management. Specifically, modifying the oxide composition to regulate cation substitution, oxidation states, and vacancy concentrations can suppress the formation of cation-enriched secondary phases and detrimental segregation. Tuning the oxygen p-band center to align closely with the Fermi level, as supported by density functional theory (DFT), has been shown to improve catalytic activity and stability, with potential bifunctionality for oxygen reduction and evolution reactions.

Advanced characterization techniques such as in situ surface X-ray diffraction, coherent Bragg rod analysis (COBRA), and ambient pressure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (APXPS) provide critical insights into the structural and electronic factors governing segregation behavior. Furthermore, heterostructures like (La₁₋ySrᵧ)₂CoO₄±δ/La₁₋ₓSrₓCoO₃₋δ have demonstrated enhanced activity and stability by suppressing segregation and tailoring electronic properties. Substituting Sr with alternative cations (e.g., Ca²⁺, Ba²⁺) can further refine vacancy concentrations and electronic structures to achieve higher performance.

Future work should integrate these design principles with in situ structural and chemical probes to continuously refine the development of stable, high-performance electrocatalysts for energy applications.

dataset_item.question: What mechanisms allow hydrogen-bond networks in enzyme active sites to maintain their functionality despite mutations?
dataset_item.answer: Hydrogen-bond networks in enzyme active sites maintain functionality despite mutations through a combination of electronic and nuclear quantum effects (NQEs) that redistribute electron density and shift proton positions, buffering perturbations caused by mutations. These networks exhibit flexibility due to short oxygen-oxygen distances, which lower the proton transfer energy barrier and enhance proton mobility. NQEs further increase adaptability by enabling dynamic proton behavior, ensuring the network can adjust to structural changes while preserving catalytic activity. Extended hydrogen-bond networks, which include multiple interconnected hydrogen bonds, provide additional robustness by compensating for individual mutations and maintaining large local electric fields critical for catalysis. Experimental observations highlight that single mutations, such as Tyr57Phe or Asp103Leu, result in modest activity reductions due to the network's inherent adaptability. However, multiple mutations that disrupt the network's integrity, such as Tyr57Phe/Asp103Leu combined, lead to significant losses in enzymatic function, emphasizing the importance of the network's structural and quantum properties for enzyme resilience.

dataset_item.question: How does electronic heating influence the electron-phonon coupling and thermal conductivity in stainless steel and γ-Fe under ultrashort laser excitation?
dataset_item.answer: Under ultrashort laser excitation, electronic heating in 316L stainless steel and γ-Fe significantly impacts electron-phonon coupling and thermal conductivity. The excitation shifts d-block electronic states to higher energies, enhancing electronic screening and localization. Electron-phonon coupling exhibits a temperature-dependent behavior: it is initially high at low electronic temperatures, decreases by approximately half at intermediate temperatures, and stabilizes at high temperatures. This trend deviates from the behavior observed in most pure metals. Thermal conductivity increases with rising electronic temperature due to weakened interband transitions, which enhance electronic mobility. While both stainless steel and γ-Fe show similar trends, deviations occur at high temperatures, particularly in free electron density and electron-phonon coupling strength. These findings suggest that γ-Fe can serve as a useful reference for modeling laser-induced nonequilibrium behavior in austenitic steels, aiding the development of hydrodynamic models for femtosecond laser-material interactions. Additionally, the observed similarities between the materials indicate potential generalizability to other austenitic steels.

dataset_item.question: How does the formation of a type II heterojunction between TiO2 and TaOₓNᵧ influence photoelectrochemical performance?
dataset_item.answer:
The formation of a type II heterojunction between TiO₂ and TaOₓNᵧ significantly enhances photoelectrochemical (PEC) performance through multiple synergistic mechanisms. This heterojunction extends TiO₂'s photon absorption into the visible spectrum, reducing the onset potential and improving stability in alkaline electrolytes. The band alignment in the heterojunction creates a built-in electric field that inhibits electron-hole recombination, prolongs photogenerated carrier lifetimes, and promotes efficient charge carrier separation and transport. Additionally, this heterostructure suppresses photogenerated hole accumulation at the semiconductor-electrolyte interface, reducing self-oxidation during photo-irradiation and thereby enhancing long-term stability.

Uniform heterojunction formation, achieved through optimized deposition conditions for TaOₓNᵧ, plays a critical role in maximizing performance gains. Structural engineering, such as the use of an inverse opal (IO) configuration, further improves charge transport pathways and light absorption. These advancements are supported by experimental analyses, including linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), which confirm improved PEC performance through reduced recombination and enhanced charge transfer kinetics.

inference_contexts: In conclusion, we showed that the formation of a type II heterojunction between TiO2 and TaO x N y in an IO structure led to improved PEC performance compared to their standalone counterparts. The uniformity of the heterojunction throughout the IO film is crucial to its PEC performance, and the deposition temperature of TaO x N y plays an important role in achieving this. As a result of this heterostructure formation, the photon absorption of TiO2 is extended into the visible spectrum; an onset potential reduction and improved stability in alkaline electrolytes were achieved for TaO x N y . The appropriate band alignment between TiO2 and TaO x N y creates a large built-in electric field for minority carriers that inhibits electron-hole recombination, extends photogenerated carrier lifetimes, and promotes charge transport, as corroborated by LSV and EIS analyses. Reduction in photogenerated hole accumulation at the SEI and longer photogenerated carrier lifetimes suppress self-oxidation during photo-irradiation, thus improving stability in an alkaline electrolyte.

In summary, we have developed a simple approach to recap CdSe/CdTe HNRs with octanethiol ligands where the capping molecules are added directly to the reaction mixture. While thiols are known to enhance PL and stability of CdTe NCs, they are usually undesirable for CdSe NCs because they introduce hole traps at the surface. Despite latter unfavorable effect of thiols, we have shown that octanethiol ligands on CdSe/CdTe HNRs can maintain fast electron transfer rates across the type II heterojunction and even extend the lifetime of photogenerated electrons by 3 orders of magnitude. These salient characteristics of type II CdSe/CdTe HNRs are easily lost even with a brief air/nonanhydrous solvent exposure for HNRs with native ligands, but thiol recapping allows these features to be maintained under much more severe and extended oxidizing conditions. In addition to the enhanced radiative recombination from the charge separated state and long-term stability along with useful carrier dynamics, thiol recapping also allows photocurrent contribution from the CdTe first exciton transition, which is often difficult to observe due to fast charge trapping caused by surface oxidation of nanocrystalline CdTe. We expect that these improvements from thiol recapping can be extended to practical use in photovoltaics and related applications.

The crystal structure and structural disorder of MgAgSb have been studied by multitemperature high-resolution synchrotron radiation powder X-ray diffraction. α-MgAgSb prepared in this work is in agreement with the nominal stoichiometric ratio at room temperature. Trace impurities of Sb and Ag3Sb appear at elevated temperatures of 400-600 K, and the impurity content increases with temperature. Weak chemical bonds and large atomic disorder are found for α-MgAgSb contributing to the low thermal conductivity of this material. A tendency of increasing structural symmetry with temperature is observed for α-MgAgSb, which may significantly contribute to the temperature evolution of the thermoelectric properties. The high resolution powder data of γ-MgAgSb can be fitted using both type I (with Mg, Ag, and Sb on the 4b, 4c, and 4a sites, respectively) and type II (with Mg, Ag, and Sb on the 4a, 4b, and 4c sites, respectively) half-Heusler crystal structure models. MEM analysis carried out on the extracted factors shows that type II gives a more physically reasonable electron density. The very low thermal conductivity of γ-MgAgSb is attributed to the strong disorder of the cation sublattice with "phonon liquid" feature. The high temperature transport data suggest a semiconducting γ-MgAgSb phase in agreement with theoretical calculation for the type II structure.

In conclusion, we systematically investigated the charge transport at PFIs by combining field-effect electrical and spectroscopic measurements on two polymer/fullerene systems. By using a heterojunction FET structure, we are able to study specifically the interface effects on the transport characteristics of polaronic holes and to correlate the transport property with film morphology, molecular orientation, and spatial arrangement. We have found that fullerene molecules have a tendency to affect the hole transport by inducing deep traps in PDPP-DTT or increasing the energetic disorder, thus weakening the interaction between polymer chains in PTB7. Although our study particularly focused on one semicrystalline system and one amorphous polymer/fullerene system, certain findings are still applicable to other BHJ systems. Our study not only proposed a trade-off between charge transfer (favored by amorphous and intermixing morphology) and charge transport (favored by high crystallinity) at PFIs but also provided insight for further theoretical and experimental studies in molecular design and interface engineering aimed for high-performing PSCs.

Our investigation on the chemical compatibility between V2O5 and AlCl3-[EMIm]Cl ionic liquid electrolytes establishes unambiguously that V2O5 chemically reacts with both Lewis acidic Al2Cl7 - and Lewis neutral AlCl4 - anions. Spectroscopic, electrochemical, and theoretical analyses reveal that the reaction products between V2O5 and Al2Cl7 - are VOCl3 and amorphous Al2O3. Similarly, the reaction products between V2O5 and AlCl4 - are identified as VO2Cl and AlCl3VO3 - with both 4-coordinated and 6-coordinated structures; these soluble products are furthermore electrochemically active, exhibiting reversible redox reactions between V5+ and V2+ oxidation states. It is clear that V2O5 is not a chemically stable positive electrode material for rechargeable Al batteries using chloroaluminate ionic liquid electrolytes, regardless of Lewis acidity. Although an Al-V2O5 cell may appear to have electrochemical performance in terms of capacity and cyclability, researchers must be cautious when identifying the origin of the electrochemical reactions. Our investigation also raises the question of the chemical stability of other Al-ion positive electrode materials in chloroaluminate ionic liquid electrolytes.

dataset_item.question: How does the use of high-selectors in control loops influence the dynamic performance of entrainer-assisted pressure-swing distillation processes for separating minimum-boiling and maximum-boiling azeotropes?
dataset_item.answer:
The use of high-selectors in control loops enhances the dynamic performance of entrainer-assisted pressure-swing distillation (EA-PSD) processes for separating both minimum-boiling and maximum-boiling azeotropes. High-selectors improve process stability by preventing output reductions when key indicators, such as product flow rates, decrease. By selecting product flow rate as the control input instead of feed flow rate, high-selectors offer greater responsiveness to feed flow and composition variations. This excess control minimizes fluctuations in reflux flow rates and stabilizes temperature control near the top of the column during reboiler duty adjustments. 

For methanol/toluene separations, structures such as A-CS3-HSC and B-CS3-HSC demonstrate superior performance when incorporating high-selectors. Similarly, for phenol/cyclohexanone separations, effective configurations like A-CS2-HSC1, A-CS4-HSC2, B-CS2-HSC1, and B-CS4-HSC2 leverage high-selectors to maintain process efficiency. These findings highlight the broader applicability of high-selectors in feedback loops across various distillation processes, ensuring reliable control and dynamic stability under varying operating conditions.

### 1. Summary of the Purpose of the Paper:
The paper aims to improve the dynamic performance of entrainer-assisted pressure-swing distillation (EA-PSD) processes used for separating minimum-boiling and maximum-boiling azeotropes. It introduces new control strategies for managing the recycling or connecting stream and evaluates their performance compared to previous strategies. The study also investigates the application of high-selectors in feedback control loops to enhance process stability and efficiency. A total of 14 control structures are developed and analyzed, offering practical insights for better control of EA-PSD processes.

Here are research questions relevant to the abstract's themes and materials science interests:

1. **Process Optimization**: How can the dynamic performance of EA-PSD processes be improved for separating both minimum-boiling and maximum-boiling azeotropes?
2. **Control Strategies**: What are the advantages and limitations of different control strategies for managing recycling or connecting streams in EA-PSD systems?
3. **System Dynamics**: How does eliminating the proportional relationship between recycling stream flow rate and feed flow rate impact the stability and efficiency of EA-PSD processes?
4. **Feedback Control**: What role do high-selectors in feedback control loops (e.g., reflux flow rate or reboiler duty) play in enhancing the dynamic performance of EA-PSD processes?
5. **Practical Applications**: How can the proposed control structures be applied effectively in industrial settings for separating pressure-insensitive azeotropes?

inference_contexts: In this paper, a variety of control structures are implemented to improve the dynamic performance of EA-PSD processes for separating pressure-insensitive minimum-boiling azeotrope methanol/toluene and maximum-boiling azeotrope phenol/cyclohexanone. The crucial influence of the control mode of the recycling or connecting stream on the controllability of EA-PSD is investigated. The strategy that sets the recycling or connecting stream as flow controlled or level controlled is able to work better than the strategy that sets the recycling or connecting stream flow rate as directly proportional to the feed flow rate. In addition, high-selectors can be applied to the deliberately selected control loops of the reflux flow rate or reboiler duty to further improve the dynamic performance. The input of the ratio multiplier is the output of a high-selector, whose input is deliberately selected to be one of the two product flow rates instead of the feed flow rate, because the selected product flow rate can serve as the indicator for both the feed flow rate and composition changes. The high-selector is used to implement excess control to maintain good results by avoiding decreasing output when the indicator decreases. When manipulating the reboiler duty to control the temperature near the top, the high-selector can also be used to avoid fluctuations when the indicator decreases by maintaining the reflux flow rate unchanged. Overall comparisons and analyses are made for these control structures. Generally, A-CS3-HSC and B-CS3-HSC are the best control structures of EA-PSD for separating the methanol/toluene mixture, and A-CS2-HSC1, A-CS4-HSC2, B-CS2-HSC1, and B-CS4-HSC2 are all the good control structures of EA-PSD for separating the phenol/cyclohexanone mixture. These effective control structures are valuable in practice for the control of EA-PSD for separating both minimum-boiling and maximum-boiling azeotropes. Meanwhile, the analyses on the application of high-selectors are good reference for the control of other distillation processes.

A new separation process is proposed for biobutanol purification from ABE fermentation. Distinctly from the processes widely studied in the literature, this process does not include any extraction unit. Instead, it includes reactive distillation columns to consume water recycling in the process. Thus, butanol-water and ethanol-water azeotropes are broken, and butanol is purified using a conventional distillation column. In addition, ethylene glycol, which is an added-value coproduct for the whole process besides butanol, is obtained as a result of the reaction taking place in reactive distillation columns. Results of the simulation show that the proposed process significantly decreases the TAC (38% against base-case and 27.5% against enhanced heat-integrated processes given in the literature). In addition, dynamic behavior and controllability of the process are studied by designing multiloop SISO control structures. It is illustrated that the proposed control schemes provide robust control against disturbances in feed flow rate and composition.

In this study, robust control strategies are investigated for PHI-PSD for separating the maximum-boiling azeotropes methanol/trimethoxysilane and ethylenediamine/water. First, five new control structures of the HPC → LPC sequence of PHI-PSD for separating the methanol/trimethoxysilane mixture are established and the results show that three of them are robust. Second, the dynamic controllability of the LPC → HPC sequence of PHI-PSD for separating the methanol/trimethoxysilane mixture is investigated for the first time with four robust control structures. Finally, two new robust control structures are proposed for PHI-PSD for separating the ethylenediamine/water mixture. The crucial elements to establish robust control of these processes are that the reboiler duty of the HPC should be manipulated to control the sump level of the HPC, and the bottom flow rate of the HPC should be flow controlled. Meanwhile, the influence of the feedforward control of the ratio of the recycling flow rate or the connecting bottom flow rate to the feed flow rate is investigated for all these processes. The results show that CS4 is the best for the HPC → LPC sequence of PHI-PSD for separating the methanol/trimethoxysilane mixture; CS3 is the best for the LPC → HPC sequence of PHI-PSD for separating the methanol/trimethoxysilane mixture; CS1 is the best for PHI-PSD for separating the ethylenediamine/water mixture. The feedforward control of the ratio of the recycling flow rate or the connecting bottom flow rate to the feed flow rate leads to worse results. In addition, CS4 of the HPC → LPC sequence of PHI-PSD for separating the methanol/trimethoxysilane mixture and CS1 of PHI-PSD for separating the ethylenediamine/water mixture are compared with the robust control structures of the previous studies. All the robust control structures are valuable in practice for the control of PHI-PSD for separating maximum-boiling azeotropes.

A new switching control strategy is proposed for batch processes with time-varying delay and actuator failures satisfying a certain probability. Under this strategy, an iterative learning fault-tolerant control law with different fault probabilities is designed, and a switching condition satisfying the average dwell time (ADT) is given. The proposed switching control strategy ensures that batch processes under different conditions (normal or fault) realize tracking control, reduce operation risks, and achieve the goal of energy conservation and consumption reduction. Finally, taking control of the packing pressure in the injection molding process as an example and comparing with the traditional methods, the comparison results show that the method proposed in this work does ensure that the system has better tracking performance. At present, due to the immature experimental conditions, this method has only been verified in numerical simulation and has not been put into use. In the future, the authors will examine the related issues of the method for future use.

In this study, four different distillation-based configurations employing various combinations of mechanical vapor recompression and self-heat recuperation are proposed, optimized, and compared in terms of their abilities to reduce the energy consumption of a C3 splitter. The two techniques fully eliminate the need for low-pressure steam in the reboiler and reduce the total energy consumption and separation cost. The best configuration employs both mechanical vapor recompression and self-heat recuperation and reduces the annualized separation cost by 20% and the energy consumption by 45%, when compared to the configuration with simple mechanical vapor recompression alone. The modifications proposed in this study for the mechanical vapor recompression system can also reduce the costs and energy consumptions for other energy-intensive distillation processes.

dataset_item.question: How can ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography coupled with electrospray ionization tandem mass spectrometry be optimized for detecting urinary metabolites like IPM3 with high sensitivity and specificity?
dataset_item.answer:
Ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography coupled with electrospray ionization tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-ESI-MS/MS) can be optimized for detecting urinary metabolites like IPM3 with high sensitivity and specificity through the following approach:

**Chromatographic Separation:**
- Use a Waters Acquity UPLC HSS T3 column (100 Å, 1.8 μm, 2.1 mm × 150 mm) paired with a VanGuard precolumn to enhance separation efficiency and reduce column wear.
- Employ a mobile phase gradient consisting of 15 mM ammonium acetate (pH 6.8) and acetonitrile for effective analyte separation.
- Maintain column temperature at 40 °C and sample temperature at 25 °C for optimal chromatographic performance.

**Mass Spectrometer Parameters:**
- Operate in negative ion electrospray ionization (ESI) mode with an optimized voltage of -4000 V.
- Use scheduled multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) for precise quantitation and confirmation.
- Optimize gas flows: curtain gas at 45 psi, CAD gas at 7 psi, GS1 at 55 psi, GS2 at 65 psi.
- Set heater temperature to 650 °C for efficient ionization.

**Sample Preparation and Detection:**
- Dilute samples with a deuterated internal standard (IPM3-d3) at a ratio of 1:10 in ammonium acetate to ensure consistency and accurate quantitation.
- Monitor key transitions: m/z 246 → 117 for quantitation and m/z 246 → 87 for confirmation to improve reliability.
- Establish calibration curves using response ratios against known concentrations to achieve a limit of detection (LOD) of 1.20 ng/mL, ensuring high sensitivity and specificity.

This method integrates robust chromatographic separation, precise mass spectrometry parameters, and reliable sample preparation to maximize the accuracy and reproducibility of urinary IPM3 detection.

inference_contexts: Spot urine samples from NHANES 2015-2016 were analyzed for urinary IPM3 using ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC; I-Classic Acquity, Waters Inc.. Milford, MA) coupled with electrospray ionization tandem mass spectrometry (ESI-MS/MS; Sciex 5500 Triple quad, Sciex, Framingham, MA). A chromatographic separation was achieved using an Acquity UPLC HSS T3, 100 Å, 1.8 μm, 2.1 mm × 150 mm column (Waters Inc.. Milford, MA) with a Waters HSS T3 VanGuard precolumn (Waters Corporation, Milford, MA). The solvents consisted of a gradient of 15 mM ammonium acetate, pH 6.8 (mobile phase A), and acetonitrile (mobile phase B). Column and sample manager temperatures were set to 40 and 25 °C, respectively. The injection volume was 2 μL using a full-loop injection mode. The mass spectrometer was operated in a negative ion ESI-scheduled multiple reaction monitoring mode. The optimized ion source parameters were as follows: ESI voltage, -4000 V (negative mode); CAD gas, 7 psi; curtain gas flow, 45 psi; nebulizing gas (GS1) flow, 55 psi; heating gas (GS2) flow, 65 psi; and heater temperature, 650 °C. UPLC-MS/MS data were acquired using Analyst software (Sciex, Framingham, MA), and the data were processed in MultiQuant 3.0.3 (Sciex, Framingham, MA). Urine specimens were prepared on a robotic liquid handler by diluting urine 1:10 in 15 mM ammonium acetate (pH 6.8) with a deuterated internal standard, IPM3-d3. Sample concentrations were determined based on their relative response ratio (ratio of native analyte to stable isotope-labeled internal standard) against a calibration curve with known standard concentrations. IPM3 was monitored for transitions m/z 246 → 117 (quantitation ion), m/z 246 → 87 (confirmation ion), and m/z 249 → 117 (internal standard). The limit of detection (LOD) was 1.20 ng/mL.

Operation of the Integrated System and Analysis of Sample Data. The integrated system, not drawn to scale, is shown diagrammatically in Figure . The sample was held in a reservoir connected to the PDMS device molded from a silicon master. A continuous system was formed by the PDMS device channel connected to an APS-derivatized transfer capillary that was connected through a liquid junction interface to a microelectrospray needle. Electroosmotic pumping from the sample reservoir to the mass spectrometer inlet was achieved by applying an electric potential (-10 kV) backed with a slight positive pressure (2-3 psi) to the reservoir, while the needle was kept at the electrospray voltage between +1.4 and +1.7 kV at atmospheric pressure. This formed an electric double layer on the positively charged walls of the derivatized transfer capillary resulting in net fluid movement toward the mass spectrometer inlet. A slight pressure was provided behind the system in order to ensure a closed electric circuit through the fluid from sample reservoir to electrospray needle. This pressure did not significantly affect the sample flow rate (data not shown). The microelectrospray needle was positioned in front of an LCQ ion trap mass spectrometer using an in-house-designed x-y-z translation stage. Sample solutions were allowed to pass through the one-channel device and transfer capillary until a stable signal was established at the expected sample's mass-to-charge ratio (m/z). The polymer device was cleaned with ethanol when needed and the device channels and capillary were flushed extensively with CE buffer between sample runs.

Samples were analyzed using an Agilent (Santa Clara, CA) liquid chromatography system and 6460 triple-quadrupole mass spectrometer (LC-MS/MS). For DNAN, an 80:20 methanol/water mixture with 1 mM ammonium acetate (0.25 mL min-1) through a Zorbax C18 column (3 mm × 150 mm, 5 μm) at 35 °C and a 10 min run time was used. For nonlabeled DNAN, the MS/MS transition was 183 > 109 in negative ion electrospray ionization (ESI-) mode. For metabolites, full and product ion scans were typically run with a linear gradient (10 to 90% methanol) over 15 min, with a 10 min hold and a 10 min return to 10% methanol. For positive ion mode (ESI+) analysis, 5 mM formic acid was used with methanol as the organic solvent.

Mass detection of both the target and reference reactants was achieved using a quadrupole mass spectrometer (Extrel MAX-1000) with an electron impact ion source. The mass spectrometer was housed in a vacuum chamber that was pumped by two 6-in. diffusion pumps with liquid nitrogen baffles, and the ultimate pressure of the chamber was less than 1 × 10-8 Torr. The target and reference compounds were ionized by bombardment of electrons with 40 eV of impact energy. Reactant ions were continuously sampled by the mass spectrometer from a two-stage beam-inlet system. The target compounds and reference compounds were then detected by monitoring their molecular ion peaks, i.e.. n-undecane was monitored at m/z = 156, n-dodecane at m/z = 170, and n-nonane, n-decane at m/z = 128, 142, respectively. There was essentially very little interference observed in mass spectral detection between target and reference compounds under our experimental conditions. Beam modulation in the second stage of the inlet system was accomplished by using a 200-Hz tuning fork chopper. Analogue ion signals were directed to a lock-in amplifier (SR510) and the output analogue signals were digitized by an analog to digital converter (Analogue Devices RTI/815) and recorded by a personal computer. The mass spectral signals were found to be linearly proportional to the concentration of the compounds in the flow reactor.

The positive ion distributions are in qualitative agreement with other measurements from the literature on plasmas of pure C2H2 and of C2H2 with Ar or He. We are not aware of anion distributions published for C2H2/He or C2H2/Ar plasmas, and those of the present work are at variance with the negative ion distribution reported in the literature for pure acetylene plasmas, which has a pronounced maximum for C6H-. Given the similitude found in the acetylene chemistry in the two plasmas investigated here, it is not likely that the early polymerization stages can explain possible differences in the structures of dust particles generated in C2H2/He and C2H2/Ar discharges.

dataset_item.question: What mechanisms enable the balance between lubrication and load-bearing in layered hydrogels?
dataset_item.answer: The balance between lubrication and load-bearing in layered hydrogels is achieved through a bioinspired dual-layer structure that synergistically integrates a soft, porous top layer and a robust, antiswelling bottom layer. The top layer absorbs water and swells, enabling exceptional aqueous lubrication and ultralow coefficients of friction (COF ~0.009–0.035) under varying loads (3–20 N). Meanwhile, the bottom layer provides mechanical strength and load-bearing capacity, ensuring durability and stability. This innovative design, created via an alkali-induced network dissociation strategy, allows the hydrogels to maintain low friction (COF < 0.05) even after extended wear cycles (e.g., 50,000 cycles), mimicking the functionality of cartilage. These properties make layered hydrogels highly suitable for applications such as medical devices, including lubrication catheters.
