inference_contexts: Developing bioinspired hydrogel lubrication materials with extraordinary lubrication, load-bearing, and antiwear property is necessary for the preparation of functional lubricious implants or devices. Despite the extensive study focusing on lubrication investigation of hydrogel materials, achieving the balance between lubrication and load-bearing for the current system is commonly difficult because of their poor mechanical property. Inspired by the biochemistry structure of the natural cartilage, herein we report a simple method to prepare a layered hydrogel material by employing a NaOH treatment-induced network dissociation strategy. The top layer of the layered hydrogels is soft and porous, which can adsorb much water for swelling to act as an extraordinary lubrication phase. The bottom layer of the layered hydrogels is robust and antiswelling in water, which can work as a good load-bearing phase. The hard steel balls with a high elastic modulus of ~200 GPa are used as slide pairs against the layered hydrogels under a typical ball-on-disk contact mode to evaluate the lubrication property. Meanwhile, the synergy between the top soft and porous layer, which provides excellent aqueous lubrication, and a high bottom-strength robust layer, which gives a high load-bearing function, is shown to be capable of attaining an ultralow COF of ~0.009 under a 3 N load, a low COF of ~0.016 under a 5 N load, and a COF of ~0.035 even under heavily loaded condition of 20 N (P ave: 3.03 MPa), only by employing low viscosity water as a lubricant. Very surprised, the layered hydrogels with a 5 min NaOH treatment can maintain a low friction state (COF < 0.05) after being subjected to 50 000 reciprocating cycles, indicating their good antiwear property. Especially, our simple method can be used to develop a layered hydrogel lubrication catheter, for which both of its inner and outer surfaces exhibit a slippery feature. The extraordinary lubricious performance of the layered hydrogels and the resulted lubrication tube implies their important potential application in the field of tissue engineering and medical devices.

For biomedical applications, the use of in situ forming hydrogels is preferred over preformed hydrogels since there is no need for surgical interventions as gelation can take place under physiological conditions upon injection. Furthermore, the initial fluidic nature of the precursor solution ensures proper shape adaptation and biological components can be incorporated in the hydrogel by simple mixing with the precursor polymer solution. , Physical cross-links, such as hydrophobic or ionic interactions, can be formed in situ under mild conditions, but the resulting hydrogels generally degrade or dissolve rapidly. Injectable chemically cross-linked hydrogels have been frequently prepared by photocuring polymers functionalized with vinylic groups. Although the presence of photoinitiators and the generated radicals in the polymerization process has been associated with cytotoxicity, frequently good cell compatibility is found for cells encapsulated in this type of hydrogel. , However, important drawbacks of photo-cross-linkable systems include the limited penetration depth of UV radiation and its potentially damaging effects on living tissue. In situ forming hydrogels utilizing covalent cross-linking between polymers with complementary functional groups therefore received much attention in the last two decades. Early examples of chemical cross-linking reactions forming hydrogels include Schiff base formation between aldehydes and amines and the Passerini and Ugi condensation. However, remaining functional groups on polymers may react with functional groups present in biomolecules such as proteins, limiting the application of these hydrogels as in situ forming delivery systems. In this regard, the use of chemoselective, bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies, which do not interfere with biochemical processes or biomolecules, are very appealing. The most investigated chemoselective cross-linking reaction for hydrogels is the Cu (I)-catalyzed Huisgen 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition of terminal alkynes and azides, commonly known as click chemistry. This term was originally coined in 2001 by Sharpless et al. for a number of new regiospecific linking reactions that give high yields and generally require no purification. The first hydrogel cross-linked via click chemistry was described by the group of Hilborn and was based on PVA. Although this category of hydrogels has been mainly used for tissue engineering applications, they have also been applied for the controlled release of therapeutics and different biomolecules, including doxorubicin bovine serum albumin (BSA) and pDNA. Because "classical" alkyne-azide cycloadditions require the use of a copper catalyst, which may cause adverse effects in biomedical applications, the use of strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) is attracting increasing interest. This reaction employs the inherent ring strain of cyclooctyne groups to achieve fast and efficient cross-linking without the need for catalysts or external stimuli such as UV light. Hermann et al. reported on PEG hydrogels for the delivery of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) inhibitors to treat excessive postoperative bone regrowth (resynostosis) after surgical correction of premature fusion of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) in children. Mixing poly [(tetraethylene glycol methacrylate)-co-(azidotetraethylene glycol methacrylate)] with a 4-dibenzocyclooctynol PEG cross-linker resulted in the formation of hydrogels within 30 s, as demonstrated by oscillatory rheology. In vitro release experiments showed that the BMP inhibitor Gremlin1 remained bioactive when it was incorporated in the hydrogels by dissolution in the prepolymer solutions, confirming the bioorthogonal character of the SPAAC cross-linking method. When the prepolymer solutions were injected together with Gremlin1 in a surgically created cranial defect in weanling mice, a hydrogel formed in situ that was able to provide a controlled release of the inhibitor for 14 days. Following this approach, the authors were able to delay, but not completely prevent, postoperative bone regrowth in the cranial defect model. Since the ultimate goal of resynostosis therapy is to slow the postoperative bone growth for a period, but then allow the bone to regrow as the child ages, the reported approach holds promise as treatment after surgical intervention in craniosynostosis. Other emerging bioorthogonal strategies for the preparation of chemically cross-linked hydrogels include thiol-ene/yne reactions, , oxime chemistry, native chemical ligation, , and Diels-Alder cycloadditions. , Table presents a summary of several click chemistry strategies that have been used to form hydrogels, including advantages and disadvantages of each method. Dove and co-workers recently reported on the simultaneous application of thiol-yne and Diels-Alder chemistry to independently create two interpenetrating networks in a one-step procedure (Figure ). A loose network was prepared from norbornene-functionalized chitosan and linear PEG-ditetrazine, while a dense network was constructed by cross-linking 4-arm PEG-tetraalkyne with linear PEG-dithiol. The resulting double network hydrogels displayed a high compressive stress of 15 MPa at 98% compression without fracture or hysteresis upon repeated load. The hydrogels were postfunctionalized with a thiol-containing fluorescent dye and tetrazine-modified biotin via reaction with unreacted alkyne and norbornene groups, respectively. The cross-linking reactions were suggested to be bioorthogonal because of the high viability of human mesenchymal stem cells, which were encapsulated by adding them to the prepolymer solutions prior to hydrogel formation. An extensive recent review concerning bioorthogonal chemistries for hydrogel cross-linking can be found in ref .

Future work must consider each of these phenomena in order to enable high-voltage operation and increase both the energy density and cycle life of sodium layered oxide cathodes. First, the extent of iron migration must be elucidated with advanced characterization techniques, and the migration may be mitigated by substituting other ions for iron or introducing dopants that can act as pillaring ions in the sodium layer. Surface reactivity may then be reduced by modifying the electrolyte or by applying a stable cathode coating. The OP2 phase transition is a more complicated matter. Limiting iron migration is likely to lengthen the duration of the OP2 phase during cycling, which will in principle increase particle cracking, resulting in material isolation and aggravated CEI formation. Pinning ions can limit the OP2 phase transition and avoid cracking concerns, at the expense of capacity. The best approach may be to reduce the volume change of the phase transition, for example, by using dopants in the transition-metal plane with strong oxygen bonding. Regardless, it is evident that there is significant room for improvement both in the understanding and design of sodium layered oxides. Through rational design, the capacity and cycle life of this low-cost material may be improved such that it can compete for large-scale energy storage applications.

In conclusion, supramolecular coordination polymeric hydrogels were obtained from self-assembly of small bis-terpyridine monomer with specific metal salts such as ZnC6H10O6 and Cu (OAc)2. However, other ion salts could not trigger the gelation. DTA can selectively discriminate Zn2+ ions by fluorescence enhancement in blue emission both in solution and gel among test ions. Otherwise, in the presence of Cu (OAc)2, DTA formed injectable, chiral, and electrochemical gels just at room temperature, which showed multistimuli responsive properties including both chemical and physical stimuli such as temperature, thixotropy, light, EDTA, KI, and sodium ascorbate. Therefore, the hydrogelation and corresponding properties such as fluorescence, chirality, and rheology can be modulated just by changing metal salts, which opened a new way for designing hydrogels with multiple needs. Notably, the ditopic ligand was comprised of a π-conjugated system without hydrogen-bonding sites or hydrophilic units, which was a typical paradigm for constructing novel π gelators in water. We believe that these dynamic polymeric gels can be used for biologically relevant materials and soft actuators toward external stimuli in the future.

In summary, we combined ND, XRD, and Raman measurement in concert with density functional theory to carefully investigate the actual stoichiometry and structure of garnet type solid electrolyte Li7La3Zr2O12 with Ta and Al dopants. Our ND and XRD data provide consistent lattice constants and together reveal a slight overstoichiometry in Ta (as compared to the nominal value) and a moderate understoichiometry of Li. Comparing the calculated relative weight of Raman Ta (Zr)-peak with that from the Raman measurement, we also find that the actual Ta content in the samples is slightly higher than the nominal value, and we identify that source of the negative slope of Vegard's law as a strong contraction of the TaO6 octahedra in comparison to the ZrO6 octahedra. The Ta and Li content-deviations do not charge balance each other, however. In combination with our observation that the measured lattice constant is larger than what is expected based on DFT calculations, we suggest that the charge balance is achieved via the presence of O vacancies. These simultaneously create/balance Li vacancies and enlarge the volume of the structure, bringing all observed and calculated quantities into agreement. Finally, we show the microscopic effects of Ta and Al doping on Li channel size in terms of Li1 and Li2 site sizes and the size of the neck that Li must pass through to travel between them. We show that while Ta enlarges all three quantities, Al leaves the site sizes unchanged while enlarging the neck. This provides the possibility of manipulating the Li ion conductivity by codoping with Al and Ta simultaneously to optimize both Li vacancy count and activation barrier.

dataset_item.question: How can kinetic parameters such as reaction orders and apparent activation energy be predicted using microkinetic mechanisms for water-gas shift reactions on nickel catalysts?
dataset_item.answer:
Kinetic parameters, including reaction orders and apparent activation energy, can be predicted using microkinetic mechanisms for the water-gas shift reaction on nickel catalysts by leveraging detailed simulations that account for varying inlet compositions and temperatures. Reaction orders are determined by analyzing the logarithmic dependence of the reaction rate on species mole fraction at constant temperature and pressure, while apparent activation energy is derived from the logarithmic dependence of the reaction rate on temperature at constant pressure and species composition using Arrhenius-based expressions. 

Microkinetic models incorporate mechanistic details of surface reactions, enabling predictions that align with experimental data. For Ni/Al₂O₃-supported catalysts, the model predicts reaction orders close to zero for CO and approximately 0.5 for H₂O, consistent with literature values. Additionally, negligible reaction order for CO₂ and inhibited kinetics for H₂ are observed, validating the mechanistic reliability of the approach. Apparent activation energy is calculated from temperature-dependent variations in reaction rates, further confirming the accuracy of the model in capturing the kinetics of the water-gas shift reaction. By comparing simulation results with experimental trends, the microkinetic mechanism proves to be a powerful tool for predicting and understanding catalytic behavior.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. **Summary of the Paper's Purpose**  
The paper aims to develop and validate a first-principles-based microkinetic model for the water-gas shift (WGS) reaction on nickel (Ni) surfaces. This includes using density functional theory (DFT) to determine binding energies, transition states, and lateral interactions for 19 elementary reaction steps across Ni(111) and Ni(211) surfaces. The model's predictions are validated against experimental data and reveal key mechanistic insights, such as the rate-determining step and dominant reaction pathway. A simplified microkinetic model and a global one-step rate expression are also derived, incorporating a novel thermodynamic-consistent approach for species coverage evaluation.

---

### 2. **Classification of Purpose**  
**<method>**  
The paper emphasizes the development and validation of a **microkinetic modeling methodology** for the WGS reaction using first-principles calculations, rather than solely reporting specific results.

---

### 3. **Research Questions Relevant to the Abstract's Themes and Materials Science Interests**  

1. **Microkinetic Modeling and Reaction Mechanisms**  
   - How can first-principles-based microkinetic modeling be optimized for complex catalytic reactions like WGS?  
   - What is the impact of including lateral adsorbate interactions in microkinetic models on predictive accuracy?  

2. **Catalyst Surface Chemistry**  
   - How do Ni(111) and Ni(211) surfaces differ in terms of binding energies, transition states, and reaction pathways for the WGS reaction?  
   - What is the role of surface geometry in determining the dominant reaction pathway (e.g., carboxyl pathway) and rate-determining steps?  

3. **Validation and Practical Implications**  
   - How well do first-principles-based microkinetic models predict experimental catalytic behavior, such as CO conversion, activation energy, and reaction orders?  
   - Can the novel thermodynamic-consistent approach for species coverage evaluation improve the performance of global rate expressions across varying reaction conditions?  

4. **Simplification and Generalization**  
   - What is the efficacy of sensitivity analysis and principal component analysis in deriving reduced microkinetic models for catalytic reactions?  
   - How can a global one-step rate expression for WGS be generalized to other catalytic systems?  

5. **Computational and Experimental Synergy**  
   - How can DFT-predicted energetics be reconciled with experimental data to enhance the reliability of kinetic models?  
   - Are there limitations in the hierarchical modeling approach that need to be addressed for broader applicability?  

---

This abstract highlights an integrative approach to combining computational and experimental methods for advancing understanding of catalytic processes, with a strong emphasis on method development and validation.

dataset_item.question: What are the observed vibronic progressions and their corresponding vibrational mode assignments in the emission spectra of neptunyl tetrachloride dianion?
dataset_item.answer: The emission spectra of the neptunyl tetrachloride dianion ([NpO₂Cl₄]²⁻) exhibit vibronic progressions corresponding to transitions from the lowest-energy ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) states (IV and V) to the ground (0) or first excited (I) states. The observed origins at 13,265 cm⁻¹ (IV → 0) and 15,402 cm⁻¹ (V → 0) were assigned based on excitation spectra, although IV → I and V → I transitions were not detected. The vibronic structure involves ungerade vibrational modes (ν₂, ν₃, ν₆, ν₈, ν₉, ν₁₀) and the gerade mode ν₁. Time-resolved measurements indicate single-exponential decay for state V, while state IV shows delayed emission, suggesting relaxation from V to IV. Furthermore, vibrational analysis suggests that the unpaired electron occupies a 5fϕ orbital in states I and II, while it occupies a 5fδ orbital in states 0 and III. These observations align with the vibrational mode assignments derived from the energies of the vibrational modes.

dataset_item.question: How are thin films of P3HT prepared and analyzed for changes in electronic properties due to air exposure?
dataset_item.answer:
Thin films of P3HT are prepared in an oxygen-free glovebox to minimize the effects of moisture and oxygen during fabrication. The films are spin-coated from a 1 wt% solution of P3HT in dichlorobenzene onto ITO substrates at a spinning rate of 30 rps and subsequently annealed at 110 °C for 5 minutes to enhance film crystallinity and electronic properties. To investigate the impact of air exposure, selected films are exposed to ambient air for three days, allowing reproducible changes in the density of states (DOS) due to defect formation.

Electrochemical analysis is performed using a microcell setup, which includes a Pt working electrode, Ag/AgCl reference electrode, and Pt counter electrode, with a supporting electrolyte solution of 0.1 M TBAPF6 in acetonitrile. Measurements are conducted using a potentiostat to control the working electrode potential relative to the Ag/AgCl reference electrode, and results are recalculated to the local vacuum level using the Ag/AgCl energy value of 4.66 eV. Energy-resolved electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (ER-EIS) and voltcoulometry (VCM) are employed to map the electronic properties, including HOMO-LUMO levels and defect states within the bandgap. 

A red laser emitting at 670 nm is used to generate excitons in the P3HT films during measurements, enabling further analysis of the electronic properties. Separate anodic and cathodic sweeps are conducted to prevent irreversible degradation of the material and ensure reproducibility in the characterization process.

The purpose of the paper is to investigate the electronic band structure and density of states (DOS) of P3HT, an organic semiconductor, across the full energy range from HOMO to LUMO, including defect states in the band gap. Two electrochemical spectroscopic methods—energy-resolved electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (ER-EIS) and kinetic-sensitive voltcoulometry (VCM)—are applied to map the electronic structure and analyze the influence of air exposure on light-induced polaron states. dataset_item.question: How does functionalization density in high-density polyethylene affect interfacial adhesion with polyethylene terephthalate during coextrusion under varying melt contact times?
dataset_item.answer: Functionalization density in high-density polyethylene (HDPE) plays a critical role in enhancing interfacial adhesion with polyethylene terephthalate (PET) during coextrusion, with adhesion strength and saturation kinetics strongly influenced by maleic anhydride (MA) graft density and melt contact time. Using a miniaturized coextrusion die compatible with a capillary rheometer, studies demonstrated that HDPE functionalized with 1.5 wt% MA grafting achieved a 15-fold increase in interfacial adhesion (measured by G<sub>IC</sub>) after just 4.4 seconds of melt contact time, with saturation occurring at 10 seconds. In contrast, reducing MA grafting density to 0.8 wt% slowed the adhesion kinetics, requiring 22 seconds for saturation. These findings highlight that higher functionalization density accelerates interfacial coupling reactions, enabling stronger adhesion in shorter processing times. The miniaturized die also offers an efficient method for studying interfacial adhesion with minimal material consumption, making it an effective tool for analyzing the effects of functionalization density and processing conditions on polymer compatibility.

dataset_item.question: How can proton relaxation rates measured using NMR techniques be used to determine intermolecular proton distances in drug supramolecule complexes?
dataset_item.answer:
Proton relaxation rates measured using NMR techniques can be utilized to determine intermolecular proton distances in drug-supramolecule complexes by analyzing cross-relaxation rates that arise from dipolar interactions. Bi-selective relaxation experiments, where modulated shaped inversion pulses are used to simultaneously invert specific protons from the drug and the supramolecule (e.g., β-cyclodextrin), allow for the extraction of cross-relaxation rates between these protons. These rates reflect the dipolar contribution to the relaxation process and are directly related to the internuclear distances between the interacting protons.  

Assuming limited internal motion of the drug molecule within the supramolecular cavity, these experimental cross-relaxation rates can be mathematically converted into intermolecular proton distances using established NMR relaxation equations. This method provides valuable insights into the spatial arrangement and insertion mode of the drug within the supramolecule—for example, vertical insertion for paracetamol and horizontal alignment for aspirin—consistent with their functional group polarities.  

The approach is a cost-effective and faster alternative to more complex 2D NMR techniques, while still yielding reliable structural insights. Combining these measurements with computational methods such as density functional theory (DFT) further validates the proposed molecular arrangements and enhances structural interpretations.

### 1. Purpose Summary
The purpose of the paper is to investigate the intermolecular interactions and motional dynamics of paracetamol and aspirin encapsulated within β-cyclodextrin (β-CD) cavities using NMR relaxation measurements. The study demonstrates the use of nonselective, selective, and bi-selective spin-lattice relaxation rates to derive molecular rotational correlation times and cross-relaxation rates, which confirm the formation of inclusion complexes. It also explores the use of these relaxation data to estimate internuclear proton distances in drug-supramolecule complexes, offering a cost-effective alternative to traditional two-dimensional NMR techniques. dataset_item.question: What methods can be used to characterize sticking interactions of proteins in cellular environments?
dataset_item.answer:
Sticking interactions of proteins in cellular environments can be characterized using two primary methods: fluorescence microscopy and in-cell NMR. 

Fluorescence microscopy leverages techniques such as Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET), Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Microscopy (FLIM), Fluorescence Correlation Spectroscopy (FCS), and Fluorescence Recovery After Photobleaching (FRAP) to track labeled proteins and study their diffusion, binding, and stability. These methods are particularly effective for identifying slowdowns in protein dynamics caused by hydrophobic or electrostatic sticking. Fluorescence microscopy is versatile and widely used due to the availability of fluorescent labels, but its reliance on bulky labels can potentially interfere with native protein behavior.

In-cell Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) complements fluorescence microscopy by using isotopically labeled proteins to observe line broadening, which serves as a marker for protein interactions. This technique provides unique insights into conformational dynamics, charge distribution, hydrophobicity, and flexibility, distinguishing between functional and nonspecific interactions. In-cell NMR is particularly valuable for studying subtle destabilization effects and altered protein behavior in vivo compared to in vitro conditions. However, its application in eukaryotic systems may require mutagenesis to reduce strong binding effects and improve resolution.

Together, fluorescence microscopy and in-cell NMR provide complementary approaches for characterizing protein sticking interactions, offering insights into both dynamic behavior and structural changes. These methods highlight the impact of cellular environments on protein stability, diffusion, and functional interactions.

inference_contexts: Fluorescence microscopy is a time-honored technique to study biomolecule dynamics in vivo. The ease of availability of fluorescent labels as well as robust and flexible tagging methods have made fluorescence microscopy the method of choice for studying many different processes in vivo. These include but are not limited to the diffusion, ,, binding, , and stability ,,, of biomolecules. Moreover, the availability of different fluorescence techniques such as FRET, fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM), FCS, , or FRAP can identify different aspects of the tagged biomolecule dynamics. An important outcome of the stickiness of the cytoplasm is the slowdown of biomolecules as they diffuse through the cytoplasm. This can be easily visualized by fluorescently labeling biomolecules and then tracking them as they diffuse through the cytoplasm. Gruebele and Guo measured the diffusion of a GFP-labeled protein, phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK), in both the folded and unfolded states inside cells and saw anomalous diffusion. They also observed that unfolded PGK diffused slower than folded PGK in the cell. It was concluded that this slowdown could not be explained by the larger hydrodynamic radius of the unfolded protein chain alone but required sticking of exposed hydrophobic patches to other cellular constituents.

In-cell spectroscopy has gained considerable momentum in the past decade driven by the need to study biomolecules in their native environment. Whereas in vitro experiments have been indispensable to our understanding of biomolecule structure and function, a large part of the interactome relies on weak interactions that are disrupted in vitro unless a native-like solvation environment can be painstakingly reproduced. In this section, we discuss the two main methods to characterize sticking in vivo: (1) fluorescence microscopy and (2) in-cell NMR.

In most cases, sticking has a negative consequence for the protein stability or function. For example, ProtL, SOD1, and GB1-D40K are destabilized in-cell as compared with buffer. This is evidence that entropic stabilization from crowding can be overcome by destabilization due to sticking. Furthermore, there is also evidence that sticking can lead to the disruption of functional interactions. Oliveberg and coworkers showed that two mammalian proteins, HAH1 and SOD1, diffused freely in mammalian cells but seemed to get stuck in the bacterial cytoplasm (Figure ). A freely diffusing protein can form functional interactions with its partners. A slowdown such as the one observed for SOD1 and HAH1 in E. coli can reduce the sampling of such interactions.

Whereas fluorescence techniques have been extensively diversified for in-cell applications, they are somewhat limited when the conformational dynamics of biomolecules needs to be monitored. Most of these techniques also involve using fluorescent proteins that are bulky and could perturb the tagged biomolecule. In the past decade, in-cell NMR has been developed to complement fluorescence microscopy. ,- Isotopically labeled proteins for in-cell NMR can be both overexpressed and microinjected directly in the cell. In general, NMR line broadening is a signature of the interaction between biomolecules and can be used as such in-cell to characterize both functional and nonspecific interactions. Nonspecific interactions are easy to visualize when exclusively eukaryotic proteins are studied in prokaryotic organisms such as E. coli. In this case, most functional partners for the protein of interest are absent, and only nonspecific interactions occur. In-cell NMR and mutagenesis have been used to predict the role of specific surface charges in nonspecific electrostatic interactions, as explained in section . - , Gierasch, Wang, and Zhuravleva showed that these nonspecific interactions are not modulated by a single variable but are a function of several factors like the overall charge, distribution of hydrophobic patches, and conformational flexibility.

dataset_item.question: How do changes in the chemical structure of polysaccharide derivatives influence their ability to inhibit drug crystallization?
dataset_item.answer: Subtle changes in the chemical structure of polysaccharide derivatives strongly influence their ability to inhibit drug crystallization by altering their hydrophobic-hydrophilic balance and molecular conformation. Effective polysaccharide inhibitors feature hydrophobic groups, such as ethyl functionalities on the backbone, which enhance interactions with drug aggregates, and hydrophilic substituents, such as carboxylate groups, which promote an extended polymer conformation. This extended conformation minimizes intramolecular interactions and maximizes interfacial stabilization with drug nuclei. A combined experimental and computational approach, including molecular dynamics simulations and atomic force microscopy, confirms that this structural balance delays drug crystallization. These insights facilitate the rational design of polysaccharide derivatives for improved drug stabilization and crystallization inhibition.

dataset_item.question: How does the branched molecular architecture of star-like polyacrylamides influence their performance in enhanced oil recovery compared to linear polyacrylamides?
dataset_item.answer: Star-like branched polyacrylamides (SB-PAMs) exhibit superior performance in enhanced oil recovery (EOR) compared to linear polyacrylamides (PAMs) due to their unique molecular architecture. While linear PAMs have higher initial viscosity, they are prone to shear thinning during injection, which limits their effectiveness under harsh reservoir conditions. In contrast, SB-PAMs maintain viscosity under high shear, ensuring consistent performance during oilfield operations. The branched structure of SB-PAMs enhances elasticity and resilience, allowing them to displace trapped oil more efficiently. The entanglement of the polymeric arms creates a pulling effect that extracts residual oil from dead ends, achieving recovery efficiencies of 33–35% of the original oil in place (OOIP)—approximately 3–5 times greater than linear PAMs of slightly higher molecular weight. Furthermore, SB-PAMs demonstrate superior salt tolerance and stability, making them highly effective in reservoirs with challenging conditions. These combined advantages position SB-PAMs as a promising alternative for improving oil recovery rates in EOR applications.

dataset_item.question: What structural and catalytic differences arise from using aluminum acetate or basic aluminum acetate instead of aluminum isopropylate in the synthesis of SAPO-11 for Pt/SAPO-11 catalysts?
dataset_item.answer: Using aluminum acetate or basic aluminum acetate instead of aluminum isopropylate in the synthesis of SAPO-11 for Pt/SAPO-11 catalysts introduces significant structural and catalytic differences. The modified synthesis results in SAPO-11 with a higher proportion of weaker acid sites, which alters the hydroisomerization behavior of the catalyst. These weaker acid sites favor the selective formation of single-branched alkanes while suppressing the formation of multi-branched isomers. This selective behavior enhances the quality of the resulting isoparaffin mixtures, improving their flow properties and making them highly suitable for high-quality renewable diesel fuels and base oil components. Additionally, the Pt/SAPO-11 catalyst derived from aluminum acetate precursors demonstrates superior efficiency in hydroisomerization, offering better control over product selectivity and enabling the production of hydrocarbons with desirable properties.

It has been shown that neither the number of repeats in the protein, nor the presence of a single cysteine residue interfered with the formation of small blue-emitting AuNCs. dataset_item.question: How does sonication time during the synthesis of silicalite-1 influence its textural properties and catalytic performance in hydrodesulfurization reactions?
dataset_item.answer:
Sonication time during the synthesis of silicalite-1 plays a crucial role in determining its textural properties and catalytic performance in hydrodesulfurization (HDS) reactions. A 2-hour sonication period (SILC-2) emerges as the optimal duration, yielding a catalyst support with balanced mesoporosity retention after Ni and Mo metal loading, preserved crystallinity, and enhanced active-phase dispersion. SILC-2 maintains a high percentage of mesoporosity, avoiding the loss of textural stability observed in SILC-4 (4 hours sonication) and outperforming SILC-1 (1 hour sonication) in terms of catalytic efficiency.  

Characterization techniques, such as XRD and H<sub>2</sub>-TPR, reveal that SILC-2 achieves superior dispersion of the active phase, evidenced by a lower reduction temperature and absence of bulk crystalline MoO<sub>3</sub>. NH<sub>3</sub>-TPD and XPS analyses indicate that while longer sonication times increase acidic sites and MoS<sub>2</sub> formation, the balanced porosity and active metal accessibility of SILC-2 yield optimal catalytic activity. Kinetic studies confirm the dominance of the direct desulfurization (DDS) pathway in SILC-2-NM catalysts, attributed to the synergy between textural stability, active-phase acidity, and dispersion.  

Thus, a 2-hour sonication time provides the best compromise between mesoporosity, active-phase properties, and catalytic performance, making it the ideal duration for preparing silicalite-1-supported NiMo catalysts for HDS reactions.

The field of hierarchically porous zeolites in general has seen tremendous growth during the past decades. The main motivation is to reduce the diffusion limitations of molecules that are imposed by the micropores in the conventional zeolites. Many new approaches, herein classified as either the "in situ approach" or "postsynthetic approach", have been developed. Most "bottom-up" strategies involve the use of meso- or macroscale templates, either direct templates, such as the hard template and soft template, or indirect templates, such as inert composite partners and active composite partners. Optimal interactions between the templates and the silicate or aluminosilicate species in the zeolite synthesis gels are essential for the success of the "in situ approach". Different synthesis methods result in different meso- or macroporosity. Thus, in order to realize better catalytic performances in zeolites, efforts should be made to achieve the optimal balance between the introduced mesoporosity, the intrinsic microporosity, and the best control of the amount, location, size distribution, and interconnectivity of the additional pores. In addition, the economic and environmental costs should be considered due to the relatively expensive and irretrievable templates. Although the "in situ approach" without the use of templates has been reported, it is still difficult for a large-scale synthesis due to the time-consuming preparative procedure and the rigid synthesis condition.

The aim of this work is to develop a more efficient methodology to find the optimal pressure and temperature operational conditions to separate carbon dioxide from methane with zeolites. This study is a first approach to set up the method and validate it. With this aim, we use two commercial zeolites, MFI and ITQ-29. This will set the basus for further study in all zeolites reported and for other gas mixtures. From the experimental point of view, doing this in a wide range of materials and conditions is unaffordable in terms of time and cost. In this particular aspect, molecular simulation outperforms experiments, as it allows computing the adsorption behavior in a realistic way in less time and therefore at lower cost. Nevertheless, simulating mixtures at all possible conditions is unaffordable. Another possibility is to use IAST to predict mixtures from pure component isotherms. For this strategy, adsorption isotherms must be calculated for each system of zeolite, gas, and temperature which would also be extremely time-consuming. The right model of ths isotherm should be selected for each combination to apply IAST for the analysis of the mixtures. The data generation and the selection of the optimal model require additional time as well, slowing down the whole process even more. All these arguments motivated us to address the problem from a different perspective, with an approach based on the treatment of the data by applying big data techniques and exploring the options and further possibilities that we can reach with it.

Formally, GGA functionals like BLYP scale as N 3 with system size (with N being the number of electrons), whereas hybrid functionals scale with N 4. To examine this possibility, we present in Table a summary of some of the performance statistics for BLYP-D3-DCP/6-31+G (2d,2p) for the benchmark sets described above and compare these to statistics obtained using B3LYP-D3/6-31+G (2d,2p). We also conducted additional performance assessments of the two methods on the BHPERI, DARC, BSR36, and the RSE43 databases. We use D3 corrections with B3LYP for our comparison because D3 has a computational cost that is negligible relative to that of the underlying DFT method and because D3 corrections (or similar) are required to predict noncovalent interactions that are reasonable. It is worthwhile restating that D3 corrections that were designed for use with B3LYP were also designed for use with nearly complete basis sets. The corrections nevertheless improve the performance of "small basis set" B3LYP, as has been shown in the past, in particular for the treatment of noncovalent interactions.

A >40 times increase in the time constant for oxygen exchange kinetics during ~5 days of aging was found in PCO thin films using the oxygen transmission relaxation method (OTR). The degradation in kinetics was identified to arise from accumulation of a siliceous phase on the PCO film surface. From a systematic examination of impurity sources, Si is likely introduced primarily during the OTR measurement (e.g.. from the quartz tube or furnace insulation) rather than through target purity, processing, or substrate (though these other sources may still have impurities present). Deposition of La oxide or Sm oxide on the aged film surface was found to fully recover oxygen exchange kinetics in aged films and a film intentionally coated with siliceous phase. Surface treatments with other oxides (Nb, Al, Ti, and Zn) were not found to recover oxygen exchange kinetics. La and Sm likely react with Si to form a porous silicate layer allowing gas transfer to the PCO surface, whereas other studied materials are unlikely to form silicates. La oxide was also deposited on aged SrTi0.65Fe0.35O3-δ, prone to degradation via Sr segregation (as opposed to siliceous phases), and no improvement was found, further indicating that La reacts with Si and is not leading to a significant catalytic effect. Finally, La was added to PCO in solid solution, and initial measurements found suppressed aging of redox kinetics.

dataset_item.question: How do vibrational frequencies of amide groups in LM7-2 differ between helical and helix-hinge-helix conformations?
dataset_item.answer: The vibrational frequencies of amide groups in LM7-2 differ between helical and helix-hinge-helix conformations, as determined through Fourier transform analysis of molecular dynamics trajectories. Vibrational spectra were computed in the 1100–1800 cm⁻¹ range by analyzing time-dependent internal coordinates such as C-O and C-N bond lengths, as well as C-N-H angles, over 200 ps trajectories representative of each conformation. These analyses revealed distinct amide band vibrations for the two structural states, with shifts attributed to changes in hydrogen bonding patterns and structural dynamics during hinge formation. The spectral differences serve as markers for identifying conformational transitions, offering insights into the vibrational behavior and dynamics of antimicrobial peptides like LM7-2.
dataset_item.topic:
### Task 1: Summarize the Purpose of the Paper
The paper investigates the structural dynamics and vibrational characteristics of the designed hybrid antimicrobial peptide LM7-2, focusing on its hinge formation near the middle of the peptide during interactions with membranes. Using molecular dynamics simulations and computational vibrational techniques, the study explores how the helix-hinge-helix motif affects vibrational modes sensitive to peptide secondary structure and provides insights into hydrogen bonding mechanisms driving hinge formation. The findings aim to aid spectroscopic interpretation and propose markers for identifying hinge structures in similar peptides.

---

### Task 2: Classify the Purpose
The purpose of the paper emphasizes **"<method>"** because it focuses on developing and applying computational techniques (e.g., molecular dynamics simulations, Fourier transforms, and normal mode analysis) to analyze structural and vibrational properties, as well as providing complementary data for spectroscopic studies.

---

### Task 3: Identify Relevant Research Questions
1. **Structural Dynamics**: What are the key structural changes in LM7-2 that occur during hinge formation, and how does the peptide transition between α-helical and helix-hinge-helix conformations?
2. **Vibrational Behavior**: How do the vibrational frequencies and shapes of amide bands I, II, and III change due to the hinge formation in LM7-2, and can these serve as markers for the helix-hinge-helix motif?
3. **Hydrogen Bonding Mechanisms**: What role do intermolecular hydrogen bonds with water and intramolecular hydrogen bonds within the peptide play in the hinge formation process?
4. **Spectroscopic Implications**: How can high-resolution computational vibrational data complement experimental spectroscopic techniques in identifying hinge structures in antimicrobial peptides?
5. **Peptide-Membrane Interactions**: How does the presence of a hinge in LM7-2 affect its interactions with membrane interfaces, and does this structural feature correlate with antimicrobial activity?

inference_contexts: Applying Fourier transformation (FT) to time-dependent internal coordinates (C-O and C-N bond lengths and C-N-H angles of each amide group in LM7-2) converts the time domain into the frequency domain and provides their vibrational frequencies. To that end, we used the Octave package for fast FT (FFT). As we explain in the Results and Discussion section, LM7-2 experienced helical and helix-hinge-helix conformations. Hence, we applied FFT on C-O and C-N bond lengths and C-N-H angle of all amide groups of LM7-2 for four selected 200 ps time periods in which LM7-2 has either a helical or a helix-hinge-helix conformation. Wavenumbers computed from FFT spanned n/[cNδt] = 0.167-33,400 cm-1 for n = 1 to N = 2 × 105 steps, and c indicates the speed of light. These calculated vibrational spectra over the more narrow range 1100-1800 cm-1 enable us to compare amide band vibrations among these states of LM7-2.

The Gln residue, which is a higher homologue of Asn, with an additional -CH2 group, interacts favorably with TMAO. However, the dimer of Gln is not destabilized, unlike the dimer of the residue Tyr, as the number of TMAO molecules interacting with Gln does not decrease upon dimer formation (Figure S6). The increased stability of Gln dimers in the presence of TMAO might be due to the strong interaction of TMAO with water. The stabilization of compact conformations (folded or aggregated) by TMAO in peptide chains primarily composed of amino acids with amide functional groups in the side chain (Asn and Gln) can also be due to the reduced number of hydrogen bonds between the -C-O group in the amide and water. The premise is that TMAO interacts strongly with water, as a result of which the number of hydrogen bonds between water and the -C-O group decreases and the side chains prefer to form intramolecular hydrogen bonds or hydrogen bonds with other peptide groups, resulting in the stabilization of compact or aggregated protein conformations.

In conclusion, we unravelled and quantified the thermodynamic origin of the phase evolution of the hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite [CH3NH3] PbBr3 by combining high-resolution inelastic neutron scattering with ab initio lattice dynamics. The differences in enthalpy and configurational and vibrational entropy of the phases are all on the same order of magnitude, meaning that each of these factors is important in determining the stable structure as a function of temperature. These contributions are even more significant when one considers the decreased role of the Madelung energy in determining structure in halide perovskites, compared to oxides. We find that a complex interplay between entropy and hydrogen bonding interactions leads to the phase transitions as a function of temperature, a result that seems to be generally applicable for crystalline hybrid materials. These insights can now be used to understand behaviors in related materials and for the design of materials with tunable properties. For instance, it seems that by small substitutions of Pb2+ with Sn2+ or Ge2+, low-frequency modes related to the stereoactive lone pair can be directly manipulated. Likewise, lattice dynamics related to hydrogen bonding strength play an important role and can be manipulated by replacing [CH3NH3]+ with [(NH2)2CH]+. Such attempts, however, also go beyond these considerations; e.g.. the size of the cation must be considered, which in turn can have a significant impact on the crystal chemistry and the symmetry of the molecule can have an impact on configurational entropy. More generally, the methodology applied here demonstrates the power of ab initio lattice dynamics to provide predictions in excellent agreement with experiment. The combination of INS with ab initio calculations provides a blueprint of how to understand lattice vibrations and relate them to macroscopic properties in an accurate, quantitative way, not only in the context of hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites but also similarly for related hybrid materials. For instance, in flexible metal-organic frameworks, a balance between enthalpic dispersion forces and vibrational entropy exists; our methodology paves the way for understanding these on a microscopic level and in turn facilitates the targeted design of such effects.

Polymer collapse driven by positive preferential cosolvent binding has been observed in several previous reports. - ,, Liao et al. have recently shown that TMAO induces the collapse of a hydrophobic elastin-like polypeptide (ELP) below 2 M TMAO concentration. They propose that "TMAO acts as a unique surfactant" that interacts with the chemically heterogeneous surface of the collapsed ELP. Effects of TMAO on ELP-water interactions have however not been considered. In another recent work, the role of polymer hydration in PNIPAM cononsolvency in methanol-water mixtures has been investigated. It could be shown that, at low concentrations, methanol drives polymer collapse by geometrically frustrating the hydrogen bonding between PNIPAM side chain amide protons and water, in agreement with ideas proposed earlier by Graziano and Pica. With a large-scale conformational sampling approach, involving 1600 independent 100 ns long molecular dynamics simulations, Dalgicdir et al. were able to show that methanol reduces the PNIPAM dehydration energy penalty, which opposes PNIPAM collapse in pure water. Although such PNIPAM-water hydrogen bonding interactions are stronger than polymer-water van der Waals interactions, it highlights the role of polymer-water interactions in inducing hydrophobic polymer collapse at low cosolvent concentrations. Interestingly, in the present work, we observe a non-monotonic dependence of the free energy of polymer collapse on the concentration of acetone in water. This observation resembles the cononsolvency phenomenon (mind however that water is not a good solvent for the hydrophobic polymer) and is determined by polymer-water interactions at low acetone concentrations and by polymer-acetone interactions at high acetone concentrations. This example underscores the important role of polymer-water interactions in theoretical models for polymer collapse and cononsolvency. - As for the acetone-water system mentioned above, the results described in this paper show that, above 2 M cosolvent concentration, the hydrophobic collapse-unfolding equilibrium shifts toward unfolded polymer conformations in systems with urea and TMAO, too, driven by favorable polymer-cosolvent van der Waals interactions.

For polymers, natural or otherwise, to produce carbon fiber of a similar quality as PAN, they cannot rely on hydrogen bonding for structural stability or contain a high mass fraction of oxygen, lest they shrink to an unusable extent. A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. Polyalanine-like domains could be incorporated into block copolymers for biomimetic graphite precursors. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

dataset_item.question: Why do twisted tolane derivatives exhibit phosphorescence in glassy media at low temperature while planar ones do not?
dataset_item.answer: Twisted tolane derivatives exhibit phosphorescence in glassy media at low temperatures due to their ability to access a trans-bent minimum in the excited S₁ state (¹¹Aᵤ state) upon photoexcitation. This is facilitated by their initial non-planar geometry, which provides sufficient excess energy to overcome the energy barrier between the planar S₁ minimum (¹¹B₂ᵤ state) and the trans-bent configuration. The trans-bent state enables intersystem crossing (ISC) into the triplet state (¹³B₂ᵤ), leading to phosphorescence. In contrast, planar tolane derivatives lack the initial excess energy required to reach the trans-bent minimum and remain trapped in the planar S₁ state, emitting only fluorescence. The rigidity of the glassy matrix at low temperatures stabilizes the long-lived triplet state, enhancing the phosphorescence observed in twisted derivatives.

inference_contexts: In Figure , the photochemistry of twisted and planar tolane derivatives is summarized. Upon photoexcitation, tolanes planarize in the excited S1 state, and therefore, twisted as well as planar tolane derivatives exhibit very similar fluorescence spectra independent of the twisting angle in the ground-state equilibrium structure. The presence of an energy barrier leading from the planar S1 minimum to the trans-bent minimum was confirmed, which nicely explains the temperature dependence and excitation wavelength dependence of its population. In other words, planar tolanes do not possess sufficient excess energy to overcome the barrier and show normal fluorescence from the planar S1p minimum, which corresponds to the 11B2u state at the planar D 2h symmetric ground-state structure. However, when twisted tolanes are excited, sufficient excess energy is present to overcome the barrier and to also populate the trans-bent minimum of the 11Au state. At low temperature in glassy medium, the lifetime of this population is long enough to allow for ISC into the 13B2u state. This supports the previous suggestion that the 11Au state may act as a precursor for ISC of tolane. In summary, this paper clarifies why only twisted tolane derivatives exhibit phosphorescence while planar ones do not.

The excited states of tolane have been investigated using the ab initio algebraic-diagrammatic construction scheme for the polarization propagator of second order to explain the differences in fluorescence and phophorescence spectra of planar and twisted tolane derivatives. The optical properties of tolane and its derivatives are strongly influenced by the central twisting angle, which determines the relative orientation of the phenyl rings and the degree of π-electron delocalization. Relaxed scans of the lowest excited states have been calculated along this twisting mode but also along the trans-bent motion, which leads to the lowest-energy minimum on the S1 potential energy surface. The trans-bent configuration of tolane is isoelectronic to the azobenzene dication, and the lowest S1 state corresponds to a πn* excitation.

Substitution plays an important role in the evolution of stilbenes. We have recently demonstrated that the phenyl ring substitution results in alteration of the electronic structure of S1 in the vicinity of the Franck-Condon geometries. The present data help one to rationalize the effects of substitution at the central ethylenic sites. Comparison of stiffened stilbenes t4, c4, and t6 with previously studied parent stilbene t0 and c0, stiff stilbenes t5 and c5, and several other substituted stilbenes reveals a dual steric effect of both the stiffening rings and monovalent substituents. On the one hand, bulkier groups and larger stiffening rings destabilize the excited trans and cis conformation due to stronger steric repulsions between the halves of the molecule and thus reduce its lifetime. On the other hand, they hamper pyramidalization of the ethylenic centers in the P state, which is a necessary prerequisite for reaching the ground state through the S1/S0 crossing and hence increases the P lifetime. Those details of the P-state behavior also affect the trans-to-cis photoisomerization yield that requires a separate study. Thus, by combining various substitution motifs in stilbenes, one can tune the photochemical behavior.

The ground and excited states of a series of four aryl boronate esters based on phenyl-1,3,2-benzodioxaboroles (1-4) have been investigated spectroscopically and computationally. Electronic spectroscopy indicates the existence of two excited states, one originating from each aromatic component of the aryl boronate esters. Computations support experimental observations and indicate a general lack of conjugation between the two aromatic π-systems in the ground state of each compound. Substitution of the phenyl component of the boronate esters results in differences in the origins of their S1 and S2 transitions. Most notably, excitation of the 2-(2,6-dimethylphenyl)-1,3,2-benzodioxaborole 3 reveals both a significant red-shift in its observed spectra as well as a rich vibronic progression that is not present in the other three derivatives studied. These differences can be attributed to the nonplanar geometry of the ground-state structure of 3 that results in a nearly flat, double welled potential with minima corresponding to symmetrically equivalent nonplanar conformations. The closely related 2-(ortho-tolyl)-1,3,2-benzodioxaborole 2 also shows significant red-shift of its S1 origin but does not have a similar vibronic progression as it is favored to adopt a planar ground-state conformation.

The energetic reaction routes for the reaction of C4 with atomic O (1D, 3P) were revealed in detail. On the triplet potential energy surface, the O (3P) + C4 reaction undergoes predominantly via the C-O addition/elimination mechanisms in both trans and cis conformational orientations. The N-O addition/elimination and SN1/SN2 displacement mechanisms are less competitive in view of the significant barriers. The nascent products are principally C3F7 and NCO radicals due to the dissociation of the C3F7C (O)N intermediates. On the singlet potential energy surface, the O (1D) + C4 reaction occurs not only via the similar C-O addition/elimination mechanism as the O (3P) + C4 reaction but also via a competitive three-center intramolecular conversion to form the C3F7OCN isomer, leading either C3F7 + NCO or C3F7O + CN. The singlet-triplet intersystem crossing is favorable due to the significant spin-orbital coupling. Master equation calculations were carried out to obtain the temperature- and pressure-dependent rate coefficients and yields for the O (3P) + C4 reaction. It was found that only the NCO + C3F7 product channel is significant. Stabilization of the intermediates is sensitive to the energy transfer parameters, and it could be important at low temperatures and high pressures. The overall rate coefficients are pressure-independent in the range of 1-10 atm. In comparison to the analogous oxidation reactions of nitriles, the O (3P) + C4 reaction does show some interesting structural, energetic, and kinetic features, which provides useful insights into the breakdown diagnostic of the C4/CO2 admixture for dielectric use.

dataset_item.question: What spectroscopic methods are used to analyze carbonyl oximes and their reaction products with amines?
dataset_item.answer: The spectroscopic methods used to analyze carbonyl oximes and their reaction products with amines include Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. FT-IR spectra were recorded using a Thermo Nicolet 6700 FT-IR spectrophotometer in the frequency range of 4000–400 cm⁻¹, employing KBr pellets to identify functional groups and structural changes. NMR spectroscopy was performed using a Varian Mercury plus spectrometer, with ¹H NMR spectra acquired at 400 MHz and ¹³C NMR spectra at 100 MHz. These measurements were conducted in DMSO-d₆ with tetramethylsilane (TMS) as an internal standard, providing detailed structural and electronic information about the reaction intermediates and products. Additionally, elemental analysis (C, H, and N) was performed using a EuroEA 3000 CHNS analyzer to confirm the molecular composition of the compounds. These combined techniques enabled comprehensive characterization of carbonyl oximes and their reaction products, including intermediates like imine oximes and final products such as amido alcohols.

### 1. **Summary of the Purpose of the Paper:**
The purpose of this paper is to investigate the reaction mechanisms and products of carbonyl oximes with amines, focusing on two distinct reaction pathways: (I) the formation of imine oxime and (II) the rearrangement of imine oxime into amido alcohol. The study combines experimental methods (elemental analysis, IR, and NMR spectroscopy) with computational approaches (DFT and dispersion-corrected wB97X-D methods) to understand the thermodynamics, kinetics, and molecular properties of the reactions. Spectroscopic, electrochemical, and theoretical analyses reveal that the reaction products between V2O5 and Al2Cl7 - are VOCl3 and amorphous Al2O3. Similarly, the reaction products between V2O5 and AlCl4 - are identified as VO2Cl and AlCl3VO3 - with both 4-coordinated and 6-coordinated structures; these soluble products are furthermore electrochemically active, exhibiting reversible redox reactions between V5+ and V2+ oxidation states. With respect to characterization, several case studies reveal the peril of over-reliance on a single technique, usually mass spectrometry. Ion silence, ion fragmentation, and reactions with the matrix make the interpretation of mass spectral data more challenging than is often acknowledged. In addition, great care should be taken to faithfully model the isotope patterns and masses of observed mass spectral peaks. We also strongly advise that NMR spectroscopy be routinely employed in nanocluster characterization. The spectral resolution of NMR is unrivaled, and as a result it can provide information on purity and formulation that are hard to collect with any other technique. Indeed, the use of NMR spectroscopy in case studies #1 and #2 would have quickly identified that the nanocluster syntheses were not proceeding as anticipated. XAS is another powerful method of nanocluster characterization, especially in cases where single crystals for X-ray crystallography are not forthcoming. However, as with any technique, it is important to recognize the limitations of XAS, and to use this technique in tandem with other complementary methods. Indeed, this latter point is probably the most important takeaway from this Account, namely, that a wide range of complementary techniques must be employed for nanocluster characterization.

This review introduces the classification of conjugated carbonyl compounds and the properties and mechanism of LIBs and SIBs, and it emphatically discusses the existing problems and improvement methods. Organic carbonyl compounds, as highly promising electrode materials for secondary batteries, have realized their universality in light of their access to metal-free, low-cost, environmentally friendly, flexible advantages. Its conjugated carbonyl systems are one of the most estimable structures that are apt to form enolates during reversible reaction and can be tailored to achieve high electrochemical performance. Coupling n-type materials to other suitable p-type materials is an easy way to form an all-organic battery. The development of full batteries without metals could enable possibilities for large energy-storage applications with high-safety and low-cost.

To date there have not been identified universal parameters of chitosan-titanium dioxide products that are essential to provide their maximal stability. In this case, the chitosan-modified titanium dioxide particles are characterized by improved physicochemical properties in comparison to the base TiO2. The modification of titanium dioxide particles can be a result of the increase in structural packing (cross-linking) of chitosan, which is a consequence of the interactions between the chitosan and titanium dioxide particles. In our opinion, the obtained chitosan-titanium system with the precisely selected compounds ratio is a good candidate for the preparation of new biopolymer mixtures with high potential attractive properties (biocompatibility, biodegradability, and nontoxicity). dataset_item.question: How does the draw ratio influence the crystal index, degree of orientation, and mechanical properties of chitin fibers fabricated using a bottom-up approach?
dataset_item.answer: Increasing the draw ratio from 1.0 to 1.8 during the wet-spinning process of chitin fibers positively influences their structural and mechanical properties. Specifically, the crystal index and degree of orientation exhibit slight improvements due to enhanced alignment of self-aggregated chitin chains. This alignment is stabilized by strong hydrogen bonding, which promotes the formation of densely packed nanofiber bundles. As a result, the tensile strength and Young's modulus of the fibers improve significantly, showcasing enhanced mechanical properties. Furthermore, the fibers retain the native α-chitin characteristics, exhibit biocompatibility with NRVA cells, and demonstrate full biodegradability in soil and in vitro environments, making them suitable for biomedical and environmental applications.

inference_contexts: The chitin fibers with the nanofibril structure were fabricated successfully from the chitin solution via a "bottom-up" approach on a lab-scale wet-spinning machine. In our findings, the chitin molecular chains dissolved in NaOH/urea aqueous solution could self-aggregate easily in a parallel manner to form nanofibers in the phytic acid/Na2SO4 coagulant bath. The dried chitin fibers were composed of nanofibers and displayed excellent tensile strength. With an increase of the draw ratio from 1.0 to 1.8, the crystal index and the degree of orientation increased slightly, whereas the tensile strength and Young's modulus of the chitin fibers enhanced significantly. The strong self-aggregation force between chitin chains and bundles driven by numerous hydrogen bonds sustained the nanofibers and densely aligned structure. Furthermore, the chitin fibers retained the intrinsic characteristics of native α-chitin and displayed good biocompatibility toward NRVA cells by promoting their adhesion and growth. Biodegradation tests demonstrated that the chitin fibers can be completely biodegraded in soil and in vitro. This work provided a new avenue to construct strong chitin fibers with biocompatibility and biodegradability, which is beneficial to both avoiding secondary surgery in clinical use and protecting the environment.

The topic of this Account has been site-selective conjugation of DNA to native proteins, with particular focus on affinity-directed reactions. Whereas these reactions may at first sight seem difficult due to the dual labeling of the DNA strand or the employment of more modified DNA strands, the method offers significant advantages. In addition to the site-selectivity, the noncovalent template effect increases the rate of the reaction dramatically, and only stoichiometric amounts of DNA and protein may be required. With the increasing demand for high-quality DNA-protein conjugates, we believe that these and future methods will provide attractive solutions to the selective preparation of conjugates with native proteins.

This work demonstrates, for the first time, that designed repeat protein scaffolds can be used to synthesize and stabilize gold nanoclusters. dataset_item.question: How do solar radiation and water temperature correlate with attenuation rates of trace organic compounds in river ecosystems?
dataset_item.answer:
Spearman rank correlation analysis was employed to investigate the relationships between attenuation rates (k<sub>att</sub>) of trace organic compounds (TrOCs) and environmental factors such as solar radiation and water temperature, due to the non-linear nature and non-normal distribution of the data (confirmed via Shapiro-Wilk tests). Results demonstrated statistically significant correlations (p < 0.05), suggesting that higher solar radiation and water temperatures generally enhance TrOC attenuation rates through photolysis and biodegradation processes. 

To assess differences in k<sub>att</sub> distributions across varying sampling conditions, non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis tests were conducted, followed by Conover posthoc pairwise comparisons. A two-stage linear step-up p-value correction method was applied to account for multiple comparisons and ensure the reliability of statistical findings. Statistical significance was consistently determined at a 5% threshold.

dataset_item.question: How does alkyl chain length and branching in diglycolamide ligands influence the extraction efficiency and complexation behavior of lanthanide ions?
dataset_item.answer:
The alkyl chain length and branching in diglycolamide (DGA) ligands significantly influence the extraction efficiency and complexation behavior of lanthanide ions. Increasing the alkyl chain length from *n*-pentyl to *n*-dodecyl reduces extraction efficiency and complexation constants, as evidenced by solvent extraction studies and UV-vis titrations for Nd³⁺. In contrast, shorter alkyl chains (methyl to *n*-pentyl) enhance complexation, supported by density functional theory (DFT) calculations showing more favorable Gibbs free energy (ΔG) values.

Branching in the alkyl chains introduces steric hindrance, leading to longer metal-ligand bond lengths and destabilized complexes, as observed with branched derivatives like T2MPrDGA. This steric effect results in less favorable ΔG values for complexation. Luminescence studies confirm the formation of anhydrous Eu³⁺-DGA complexes (EuL₃³⁺) in organic solvents such as *n*-dodecane, indicating high selectivity for trivalent lanthanide ions. Further structural analysis is needed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of selectivity and complex stability.

dataset_item.question: What methods were used to optimize ligand conformations and validate the force-field results for thiolate-protected gold nanoclusters?
dataset_item.answer:
The ligand conformations of thiolate-protected gold nanoclusters were optimized using a force-field (FF) approach with the polymer consistent force field (PCFF) for hydrocarbon ligands and literature-derived parameters for Au-S-C interfacial interactions. Conformational searches involved systematically rotating Au-S, S-C, and C-C bonds by ±120° to explore cis/trans and anti/gauche configurations, followed by geometry minimization using the conjugate-gradient method in LAMMPS. The minimization was performed with a force convergence criterion of 0.02 eV/Å, keeping Au and S atoms fixed while allowing R-group atoms to move.

To validate the FF-derived structures, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were conducted using two independent approaches: (1) Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP) with the PBE functional for electron exchange-correlation, DFT-D3 van der Waals correction, and Γ-point sampling, where only C and H atoms were relaxed; and (2) Turbomole software with the TPSS functional and def2-TZVP basis sets, allowing full atomic relaxation in internal coordinates to avoid periodic boundary effects. Both DFT methods confirmed the stability and reliability of the force-field-optimized ligand conformations.

dataset_item.question: What is the mechanism by which cellulose nanocomposites containing octadecylamine-modified montmorillonite inhibit quorum sensing-regulated processes without affecting bacterial vitality?
dataset_item.answer: Cellulose nanocomposites containing exfoliated octadecylamine-modified montmorillonite (ODA-MMT) inhibit quorum sensing-regulated processes, such as pigment production in *Chromobacterium violaceum* CV026, without compromising bacterial vitality. The mechanism is attributed to the dispersed exfoliated ODA-MMT nanofillers within the cellulose matrix, which interact with N-hexanoyl-L-homoserine lactone, the quorum sensing autoinducer molecule. This interaction likely involves adsorption or disruption of the signaling molecules, thereby interfering with quorum sensing pathways. While the exact molecular mechanism remains under investigation, these nanocomposites selectively target quorum sensing-regulated processes, such as pigment production and biofilm formation, without exhibiting bacterial toxicity. Additionally, their enhanced thermal stability and sustainability make them promising candidates for applications in food packaging, biomedical devices, and antivirulence strategies.

dataset_item.question: How does the protein CarH stabilize the excited electronic state of adenosylcobalamin to prevent the formation of reactive radicals?
dataset_item.answer: CarH stabilizes the excited electronic state of adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl) by restricting the expansion of axial bonds, thereby preventing homolytic cleavage and the formation of reactive 5′-deoxyadenosyl radicals. This stabilization allows CarH to harness the energy of the excited state in a controlled manner, promoting slower and less reactive processes such as triplet-state formation and the production of stable 4′,5′-anhydroadenosine. By optimizing the quantum efficiency and avoiding harmful radical species, CarH achieves precise regulation of excited-state reactivity.

In case of homocystine and 3,3′-dithiodipropionic acid, formation of the S,S′-binuclear complexes leads to cleavage of the disulfide bond, while we observe formation of the S,N-binuclear and S,N,S′,N′-tetranuclear complexes with the preserved S-S bond for the l-cystine and cystamine ligands. Formation of the S,S′-binuclear complexes increases the d(S-S) bond length by 5%, and the redistribution of charges with Sδ--Sδ- in the original disulfide on Sδ+-Sδ- occurs in the complex. We find that the greater the magnitude of Δδ in S,S′-binuclear complex, the higher the likelihood of disproportionation. These vibrational coherences lasted for several picoseconds and appear unperturbed by internal conversion as indicated by the absence of any shift in the node position in the ESA and SE signals along the waiting time, until these coherences completely dephase within a time scale of >10 ps. The slow dephasing of the vibrational wavepacket in the excited state and the invariable node position is a reflection of slow intramolecular vibrational relaxation, which in turn suggests weak coupling of this normal mode to other modes of CV (i.e.. very weak anharmonicity). The system is an ideal example of a weak coupling regime, wherein the excited and ground electronic states interact weakly with each other, and hence coherent nuclear motion generated in the excited state stays there until it dephases completely without facing a reactive internal conversion.
