As presented in this review, the transition-metal-catalyzed addition of C-H bonds to carbonyls, imines, and related polarized π bonds has emerged as a particularly efficient and powerful approach for the construction of an incredibly diverse array of heteroatom-substituted products. Readily available and stable inputs are typically employed, and reactions generally proceed without the production of waste byproducts. Moreover, transition-metal-catalyzed C-H bond additions to polarized π bonds typically occur without of the need for either strong acid or base additives and therefore often proceed with very high functional group compatibility. As additionally presented in this review, many of these C-H bond addition reactions occur within cascade reaction sequences to provide rapid access to a diverse array of different heterocyclic as well as carbocyclic products. Finally, a large variety of different transition-metal catalysts and ancillary ligands have been applied to these transformations. In future work, improvements in catalyst efficiency and selectivity as well as access to an increasing breadth of heteroatom-substituted products can be anticipated.

dataset_item.question: How do variations in catalyst layer thickness and inlet mole fraction of carbon dioxide influence the performance and conversion efficiency of microfluidic flow cell reactors for carbon dioxide electrochemical conversion?
dataset_item.answer:
The performance and conversion efficiency of microfluidic flow cell reactors for carbon dioxide electrochemical conversion are significantly influenced by variations in catalyst layer thickness and inlet mole fraction of carbon dioxide. Sensitivity analyses and Monte Carlo simulations reveal that catalyst properties, particularly charge transfer coefficients, are the most critical parameters affecting reactor performance. The inlet CO₂ mole fraction plays a pivotal role in defining optimal operating ranges, directly impacting reactor efficiency and selectivity. Catalyst layer thickness, while influential, exhibits differing sensitivity rankings under individual and simultaneous parameter variability scenarios. Porosity within the catalyst layer also contributes to reactor performance but is less critical compared to charge transfer coefficients and inlet CO₂ mole fraction.

Machine learning-based regression models have demonstrated high predictive accuracy (over 94%) in forecasting reactor performance, offering a computationally efficient alternative to traditional finite-element methods. These models enable optimized design and control strategies by identifying key parameter dependencies and performance trends. The findings underscore the importance of precise tuning of catalyst properties, inlet CO₂ mole fraction, and structural factors like layer thickness to enhance reactor efficiency and selectivity for CO₂ electrochemical conversion.

inference_contexts: An MCS-based sensitivity analysis was performed in this study on an electrochemical reactor which converts CO2 to CO. A finite-element-based solver was employed to solve the governing equations of the MFC reactor and generate the data set utilized for sensitivity analysis. In addition, reduced regression models of the reactor were developed using the Machine Learning Toolbox of MATLAB. We have studied the effect of a wide range of parameters encompassing the electrochemical, physical, material, operating, and design parameters of the reactor on the cell performance, conversion efficiency, and selectivity of the MFC reactor. Both individual (IND) and simultaneous (SIM) variations of these parameters were undertaken in this body of work. Our investigation revealed similar rankings for the stochastic parameters in the IND and SIM scenarios, with an exception for the catalyst layer thickness. For the entire range of cell potentials considered, we found that the catalyst properties, characterized by the charge transfer coefficients, were the critical parameters influencing the overall performance of the MFC reactor. Following the catalyst properties, the stoichiometric parameters were significant in governing the cell performance, conversion efficiency, and selectivity. In particular, we observed that the inlet mole fraction of CO2 enabled the identified optimal working ranges of the MFC. Additionally, the porosity of the catalyst layer, a physical parameter that determines the available active sites for the electrochemical reaction, also significantly affects the cell performance and conversion efficiency of the MFC reactor. Moreover, we develop reduced regression models using supervised machine learning algorithms to predict the overall cell performance with an accuracy of at least 94% at all cell potentials when compared to the data obtained from MCS. Furthermore, we note that the overall cell performance distribution does not belong to a normal family at all of the cell potentials, even though the stochastic input parameters were distributed normally. Thus, the findings of this study would enable experimentalists to determine the significant parameters and the extent to which they can be varied to obtain optimized reactor performance. The sensitivities of the design parameters discerned in our work may assist manufacturers in setting stricter tolerances to avoid rejection due to poorly performing MFC reactors. The developed regression models may help to design robust control strategies and stack optimization. Finally, the present work can be extended to perform global sensitivity analysis over the entire range of the polarization curve and the wide range of cell lengths and widths, including other electrocatalytic systems that yield more than two products.

Our investigation on the chemical compatibility between V2O5 and AlCl3-[EMIm]Cl ionic liquid electrolytes establishes unambiguously that V2O5 chemically reacts with both Lewis acidic Al2Cl7 - and Lewis neutral AlCl4 - anions. Spectroscopic, electrochemical, and theoretical analyses reveal that the reaction products between V2O5 and Al2Cl7 - are VOCl3 and amorphous Al2O3. Similarly, the reaction products between V2O5 and AlCl4 - are identified as VO2Cl and AlCl3VO3 - with both 4-coordinated and 6-coordinated structures; these soluble products are furthermore electrochemically active, exhibiting reversible redox reactions between V5+ and V2+ oxidation states. It is clear that V2O5 is not a chemically stable positive electrode material for rechargeable Al batteries using chloroaluminate ionic liquid electrolytes, regardless of Lewis acidity. Although an Al-V2O5 cell may appear to have electrochemical performance in terms of capacity and cyclability, researchers must be cautious when identifying the origin of the electrochemical reactions. Understanding how design parameters of targeted drug carriers influence interaction with cells and the subsequent signaling leading to endocytosis is key to inform optimization of drug delivery systems. , Both the size and targeting valency of drug carriers impact cell binding and endocytic uptake. - ,,, However, how these parameters influence receptor-mediated signaling linking binding with internalization is rather obscure. For instance: Is the uptake efficiency correlative with the signaling level? Is this regulated similarly for carriers of different sizes and valencies? Are signaling and uptake events induced independently for each individual carrier or do they depend on cumulative carrier binding to cells? Is the number of receptors engaged by a carrier the factor ruling signaling and uptake, or does this depend on the density of engagement per surface area? Using model submicrometer, micrometer, and supramicrometer carriers targeted to ICAM-1 at varying valencies, we have examined these questions. Our results revealed an intricate interplay between these parameters, where the density of the targeting antibody per carrier surface area (which would determine the density of the receptor cluster on the cell surface) is the main parameter controlling the signaling conducive to endocytosis (Figure ). Larger carriers posed a requirement for stronger signaling, since carrier size impacts the ability of the plasmalemma to efficiently engulf a carrier. It is likely that for endocytic pathways lacking signals that enable sufficient plasmalemma deformability (e.g.. ceramide enrichment shown here for the CAM pathway), size will become restrictive regardless of the targeting density. Each carrier bound on a cell induced signaling based on its antibody-coat density (the density of the clustered receptors, not the absolute number of receptors engaged or the size of the cluster), and rendered endocytosis based on its size and enough buildup of the inducing signal. Each signaling-uptake event was independent for each single carrier bound on a cell, where the total number of carriers bound to the cell, the total surface area occupied by those carriers, and the total number of cell receptors engaged did not exert a major influence. It will be important to examine this regulation for other receptors and pathways in order to extract generic conclusions, and to evaluate how other carrier design parameters (e.g.. smaller sizes, different shape, curvature, carrier type, surface chemistry, etc.) and biological environments (different cell types, presence of flow, pathological alterations, etc.) impact these outcomes. - ,,, Nevertheless, other natural routes associate to signaling common to the CAM pathway, and it is expected that the findings obtained here would broadly apply to the use of said routes for drug delivery applications. For instance, ceramide and/or PKC are key for the formation of lipid domains, vesiculation, cytoskeletal rearrangements, and formation of membrane protrusions observed for phagocytic and macropinocytic pathways, intracellular invasion by certain viral and bacterial pathogens, leukocyte endothelial adhesion and extravasation, and certain events of transcytosis across cellular barriers. - Therefore, these results have shed light on key factors modulating the efficacy of uptake of targeted drug carriers, which shall inform future design of vehicles for intracellular delivery.

In this paper, the effects of the two typical dimensions of the tree-shaped distributor in the rectangular parallel microchannels on the hydrodynamics, flow distribution, and mass-transfer performance of the gas-liquid flow are studied. The results show that the variation of width in the tree-shaped distributor has important influences on the operating range, flow distribution, pressure drop, and mass-transfer coefficient in parallel microchannels. In the halving-width microchannel, the mother bubble in the main channel is long and the length is almost not affected by the breaking up at the bifurcation, resulting in the obvious hydrodynamic feedback, and thus, the operating range in the halving-width microchannel is significantly narrower than that in the constant-width microchannel. Due to the effects of the different ratios of width-depth on bubble generation in the main channel and the hydrodynamic feedback at the outlet, the flow distribution gradually deteriorates in the halving-width microchannel as the ratio of the gas-liquid flow rate increases. However, in the constant-width microchannel, there exists a critical ratio of the gas-liquid flow rate for the most uniform flow distribution. Before this critical value, the flow distribution improves with the increase of the ratio of the gas-liquid flow rate but deteriorates after this critical value. Furthermore, due to the differences in hydrodynamics and flow distribution between the two parallel microchannels with different tree-shaped distributors, the mass-transfer performance is also different. In the halving-width microchannel, the number of gas-liquid units is less, and so the total specific surface area is smaller, and the volumetric mass-transfer coefficient becomes smaller accordingly. However, in the constant-width microchannel, the situation is just the opposite. However, the high mass-transfer coefficient is always accompanied by a high pressure drop. Therefore, the pressure drop in the constant-width microchannel is significantly higher. To comprehensively consider the mass-transfer efficiency and energy consumption, the performance ratio is adopted to evaluate the mass-transfer performance. The results show that the performance ratio of the halving-width microchannel is generally higher than that of the constant-width microchannel, but with the increase of the ratio of the gas-liquid flow rate, the performance ratios of the two microchannels gradually approach each other. The obtained results confirm that designing a tree-shaped distributor of the appropriate width in parallel microchannels is a potentially appealing tool to improve the flow distribution and mass-transfer performance.

The methods used for measuring liquid velocity in the literature include Pavlov tube velocimetry, hot film anemometry (HFA), laser Doppler anemometry (LDA), particle image velocimetry (PIV), and so on. Hills first measured the liquid velocity in the bubble column using a Pavlov tube and obtained the radial distribution of the liquid velocity. Forret et al. used Pavlov tubes to measure the liquid velocity distribution of multiple sections in bubble reactors with different column diameters. Franz et al. investigated the axial, radial, and tangential velocities of the liquid velocity in the bubble reactor using the HFA technology, respectively. The resolution is high, but the contamination of the probe will greatly affect the measurement. Kulkarni et al. used LDA to measure liquid velocity, but this method requires high transparency of the flow field and is not suitable for measuring liquid velocity in reactors with large gas holdups. Among the above-mentioned liquid velocity measurement methods, the Pavlov tube velocity measurement method has been widely used because of the small size of the device, convenient operation, and low cost.

dataset_item.question: How does the oxidation of sulfide groups to sulfones affect drug encapsulation and release behavior of amphiphilic star-shaped block copolymers?
dataset_item.answer: The oxidation of sulfide groups to sulfones in amphiphilic star-shaped block copolymers enhances the polarity of the hydrophobic block, allowing the encapsulation of both hydrophobic and hydrophilic drug molecules. This structural modification enables effective drug retention at physiological pH (e.g., in the bloodstream) and targeted drug release under acidic conditions (e.g., intracellular compartments). For instance, sulfone-modified copolymers achieved a 35 mol% loading capacity for azithromycin, an antimicrobial drug, demonstrating their high drug-loading potential. These copolymers were biocompatible with macrophages, confirming their cytocompatibility, and maintained azithromycin's antibacterial efficacy against *Staphylococcus aureus*. The combination of stimuli-responsive drug release behavior, biocompatibility, and high drug-loading capacity highlights the promise of these oxidized copolymers as versatile and efficient drug delivery systems for biomedical applications.

For polymers, natural or otherwise, to produce carbon fiber of a similar quality as PAN, they cannot rely on hydrogen bonding for structural stability or contain a high mass fraction of oxygen, lest they shrink to an unusable extent. A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. dataset_item.question: What parameters and tools are used for capturing and analyzing surface topography images in the fabrication of metallic nanodot arrays?
dataset_item.answer: Surface topography images of metallic nanodot arrays were acquired using a Digital Instruments Nanoscope IIIA scanning probe microscope in contact mode. Nonconductive silicon nitride cantilevers (Bruker D-NPS) with spring constants ranging from 0.12–0.06 N/m were employed to ensure precise imaging. The images, covering a 10 × 10 μm² area, were captured at scan rates of 2.0–2.5 Hz. For post-acquisition analysis, NanoScope Analysis 1.5 software (Bruker Corp.) was utilized to characterize the morphology of the nanodot arrays. This setup provided reliable and accurate surface topography data essential for the fabrication process.

dataset_item.question: How can orthogonal lipidation pathways such as N-myristoylation and C-cholesterylation be implemented for the scalable synthesis of lipidated proteins with distinct architectures?
dataset_item.answer: Orthogonal lipidation pathways such as N-myristoylation and C-cholesterylation can be implemented for the scalable synthesis of lipidated proteins with distinct architectures by combining bacterial expression systems and post-lysis lipidation reactions. For N-myristoylation, *Escherichia coli* cultures are grown at 37 °C until OD600 reaches 0.8, followed by supplementation with myristic acid at a final concentration of 250 μM prior to induction with IPTG. Protein expression is carried out at 18 °C to optimize yield and folding. For C-cholesterylation, the process involves cell lysis via sonication, clarification of the lysate by centrifugation, and subsequent *in vitro* reaction in a buffer containing bis-Tris (20 mM, pH 7.2), NaCl (137 mM), Triton X-100 (1 mM), TCEP-HCl (5 mM), and EDTA (5 mM), with cholesterol added for lipidation. Negative controls without lipid substrates are included to validate the lipidation specificity. This approach enables the production of lipidated proteins with distinct triblock architectures, allowing controlled hierarchical assembly for hybrid biomaterials, while maintaining scalability and precision in lipid incorporation.

As computational chemistry methods are applied to increasingly larger systems, the question of their efficiency-in particular, with respect to run time-becomes critical. Formally, GGA functionals like BLYP scale as N 3 with system size (with N being the number of electrons), whereas hybrid functionals scale with N 4. Therefore, low-cost corrections such as D3 and DCP that may elevate the performance of BLYP to that of B3LYP or better may be of value. To examine this possibility, we present in Table a summary of some of the performance statistics for BLYP-D3-DCP/6-31+G (2d,2p) for the benchmark sets described above and compare these to statistics obtained using B3LYP-D3/6-31+G (2d,2p). We also conducted additional performance assessments of the two methods on the BHPERI, DARC, BSR36, and the RSE43 databases. We use D3 corrections with B3LYP for our comparison because D3 has a computational cost that is negligible relative to that of the underlying DFT method and because D3 corrections (or similar) are required to predict noncovalent interactions that are reasonable. It is worthwhile restating that D3 corrections that were designed for use with B3LYP were also designed for use with nearly complete basis sets. The corrections nevertheless improve the performance of "small basis set" B3LYP, as has been shown in the past, in particular for the treatment of noncovalent interactions.

Significant progress has been made in material development and understanding of fundamentals of inorganic membrane properties and membrane processes. In spite of the progress and success in commercial applications of inorganic membranes in filtration and hydrocarbon-water separation, the commercialization of inorganic membranes for molecular separation and reaction processes remains a difficult challenge. The key hurdles in commercializing inorganic membrane separators and reactors for process intensification include the high costs and large footprint of membrane units due to moderate permeance, high membrane price, and low membrane module packing density. Most inorganic membranes are not sufficiently stable for industrial applications. Future research and development efforts should be focused on addressing these key hurdles including synthesis of membranes with higher permeance and stability, fabrication of low cost and high packing density membrane substrates, and the development of cost-effective, scalable methods for the synthesis of the separation layer. It is expected that commercial applications of highly permeable water-selective zeolite membrane separation processes will be expanded to membrane reactor coupling reactions with the removal of water from the membrane reactor. Highly stable high siliceous zeolite membranes may also find industrial applications in membrane reactors operated at high pressures.

For polymers, natural or otherwise, to produce carbon fiber of a similar quality as PAN, they cannot rely on hydrogen bonding for structural stability or contain a high mass fraction of oxygen, lest they shrink to an unusable extent. A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. Polyalanine-like domains could be incorporated into block copolymers for biomimetic graphite precursors. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

This work demonstrates, for the first time, that designed repeat protein scaffolds can be used to synthesize and stabilize gold nanoclusters. It has been shown that neither the number of repeats in the protein, nor the presence of a single cysteine residue interfered with the formation of small blue-emitting AuNCs. A possible explanation is the presence of tyrosine residues in the repeat sequence that could adsorb gold ions and therefore stabilize the gold nanoclusters. The synthesis method using NaOH to generate a reducing environment proved to be the most efficient. However, highly basic conditions denature the protein and thus destroy its structure and function. This fact can hamper its use in further applications in which structural and functional properties of the proteins are exploited. Therefore, we developed a new synthesis protocol using milder reducing agents such as ascorbic acid and sodium citrate, increasing the efficiency to obtain the AuNCs when ascorbic acid was employed. Whenever reactions did not include the protein scaffold, the AuNCs generation did not occur, highlighting the key role of the CTPR proteins as stabilizing agents. The optimized conditions for the AuNCs formation include a metal:protein ratio of 5:1 compared to the conditions previously reported for the CTPR stabilization of AuNPs in which larger ratios were used (1000:1 to 20:1) and smaller the ratios yielded smaller nanoparticles, which is in agreement with this report, where nanoclusters are obtained with smaller metal:protein ratios. Most importantly, this method was mild enough to preserve the structure of the protein and thus permitted to take advantage of the specific function of the protein scaffold. Indeed, we demonstrate that neither the synthesis of the nanoclusters, nor the nanoclusters themselves interfered with the protein binding activity. Thus, we obtained a novel bifunctional designed unit that combines the function of the designed CTPR protein scaffold on one hand and the fluorescence emission of AuNCs on the other. Finally, we demonstrate that the fluorescence signal of the protein-stabilized AuNCs is sensitive to the ligand recognition of the specific binding module. This result confirms the potential of this system to develop new sensors. The use of repeat protein scaffolds as biomolecular templates in which stability, size, and function can be tuned at will, ,, that also comprise rational methods for the synthesis of fluorescent nanoclusters preserving the protein functions, leaves a door open for further applications in the field of molecular imaging and sensing.

dataset_item.question: How does the architecture of amphiphilic block copolymers influence the aggregation number and nematic ordering of micelles in selective solvents?
dataset_item.answer:
The architecture of amphiphilic block copolymers plays a critical role in determining micelle aggregation number and nematic ordering in selective solvents. Comb-like copolymers, characterized by flexible backbones and rod-like side chains, form large, spherical micelles with weak nematic ordering due to steric constraints and free energy penalties associated with densely packed corona loops. In contrast, rod-coil diblocks and Y-shaped copolymers form smaller micelles with stronger nematic ordering. This arises from the ability of rod-like blocks to align in antiparallel arrangements, minimizing free energy penalties and enhancing nematic core organization.  

Solvent quality also impacts micelle properties: worsening solvent quality increases aggregation numbers for rod-coil diblocks but decreases them for Y-shaped copolymers, which concurrently exhibit significant enhancements in nematic ordering due to their compact architectures. Comb-like micelles remain stable with weak nematic ordering even under varying solvent conditions, making them suitable for applications requiring robust liquid-crystalline behavior. The ability of rod-coil diblocks and Y-shaped copolymers to adapt aggregation and nematic ordering in response to solvent changes highlights their potential for sensing and tunable material applications.

Pretty abrupt variation of order parameter and aggregation number of the Y-shaped copolymer micelles caused by variation of the solvent quality (temperature), Figures and , might be exploited in a range of sensor applications. In summary, a novel photo- and reduction-responsive monomer composed of coumarin moieties and disulfide linkage was designed and synthesized. The dual-stimuli responsive monomer could be polymerized to form amphiphilic diblock copolymers using a PEO-based macroRAFT agent through RAFT polymerization. The resulting amphiphiles could self-assemble into vesicular nanostructures that naturally inherited the photo- and reduction-responsive characteristics. Upon irradiation the vesicle dispersion with 430 nm light, the coumarin moieties were cleaved with the generation of reactive primary amines that further cross-linked the vesicles through extensive amidation reactions. This process gave rise to a remarkable polarity transition within the bilayer membranes and the release of encapsulated small molecule payloads while retaining the large ones. dataset_item.question: What factors affect phosphorus removal efficiency when using iron or aluminum electrodes under varying hydraulic retention times and current intensities?
dataset_item.answer:
Phosphorus removal efficiency when using iron or aluminum electrodes is influenced by multiple factors, including hydraulic retention time (HRT), current intensity, and mixing conditions. Shorter HRTs generally lead to improved removal rates due to increased interaction between the electrodes and phosphorus, although efficiency may decrease as residual phosphorus levels drop. Current intensity plays a critical role, with higher intensities enhancing phosphorus removal but potentially leading to diminishing returns under low residual phosphorus conditions. Mixing conditions further affect the removal efficiency by ensuring uniform exposure and optimizing reaction kinetics.

Experiments conducted under both batch and continuous flow modes demonstrated similar performance trends for iron and aluminum electrodes, suggesting that operational parameters such as HRT, current intensity, and mixing are more significant than electrode material type in determining efficiency. However, the choice of electrode material may still influence secondary operational factors such as energy consumption and electrode durability. Overall, phosphorus removal efficiency is highly dependent on the interplay between hydraulic loading scenarios and experimental conditions.

Understanding how design parameters of targeted drug carriers influence interaction with cells and the subsequent signaling leading to endocytosis is key to inform optimization of drug delivery systems. , Both the size and targeting valency of drug carriers impact cell binding and endocytic uptake. - ,,, However, how these parameters influence receptor-mediated signaling linking binding with internalization is rather obscure. For instance: Is the uptake efficiency correlative with the signaling level? Is this regulated similarly for carriers of different sizes and valencies? Are signaling and uptake events induced independently for each individual carrier or do they depend on cumulative carrier binding to cells? Is the number of receptors engaged by a carrier the factor ruling signaling and uptake, or does this depend on the density of engagement per surface area? Using model submicrometer, micrometer, and supramicrometer carriers targeted to ICAM-1 at varying valencies, we have examined these questions. Our results revealed an intricate interplay between these parameters, where the density of the targeting antibody per carrier surface area (which would determine the density of the receptor cluster on the cell surface) is the main parameter controlling the signaling conducive to endocytosis (Figure ). Larger carriers posed a requirement for stronger signaling, since carrier size impacts the ability of the plasmalemma to efficiently engulf a carrier. It is likely that for endocytic pathways lacking signals that enable sufficient plasmalemma deformability (e.g.. ceramide enrichment shown here for the CAM pathway), size will become restrictive regardless of the targeting density. Each carrier bound on a cell induced signaling based on its antibody-coat density (the density of the clustered receptors, not the absolute number of receptors engaged or the size of the cluster), and rendered endocytosis based on its size and enough buildup of the inducing signal. Each signaling-uptake event was independent for each single carrier bound on a cell, where the total number of carriers bound to the cell, the total surface area occupied by those carriers, and the total number of cell receptors engaged did not exert a major influence. It will be important to examine this regulation for other receptors and pathways in order to extract generic conclusions, and to evaluate how other carrier design parameters (e.g.. smaller sizes, different shape, curvature, carrier type, surface chemistry, etc.) and biological environments (different cell types, presence of flow, pathological alterations, etc.) impact these outcomes. - ,,, Nevertheless, other natural routes associate to signaling common to the CAM pathway, and it is expected that the findings obtained here would broadly apply to the use of said routes for drug delivery applications. For instance, ceramide and/or PKC are key for the formation of lipid domains, vesiculation, cytoskeletal rearrangements, and formation of membrane protrusions observed for phagocytic and macropinocytic pathways, intracellular invasion by certain viral and bacterial pathogens, leukocyte endothelial adhesion and extravasation, and certain events of transcytosis across cellular barriers. - Therefore, these results have shed light on key factors modulating the efficacy of uptake of targeted drug carriers, which shall inform future design of vehicles for intracellular delivery.

dataset_item.question: What mechanisms drive the formation of oscillatory topographic features in biomorphic sheets composed of barium carbonate and silica?
dataset_item.answer:
The formation of oscillatory topographic features in biomorphic sheets composed of barium carbonate and silica is driven by alternating precipitation cycles of silica and barium carbonate near the crystallization front. These cycles are hypothesized to arise from pH oscillations, which induce periodic deposition and result in height variations that manifest as concentric stripes or patchy patterns with consistent wavelengths. The periodic tilting of nanorods out of the sheet plane is a key feature of these patterns, likely caused by cyclic nucleation and termination processes. This tilting may stem from overcrowding effects and growth limitations imposed by silica deposition, which restrict barium carbonate structures to nanorods rather than larger crystals. 

While the pH oscillation model explains the spatial synchronization of stripes, compositional variation and the independence of wavelength from reactant concentrations suggest a more complex mechanism. A co-crystallization process involving silicate-barium prenucleation clusters may contribute to pattern formation. Additionally, substrate interactions, nanorod growth along the c-axis, and localized symmetry breaking influence sheet morphology and thickness. The role of diffusion dynamics in driving oscillatory behavior requires further investigation to fully understand the underlying mechanisms.

inference_contexts: Our study provides the first direct experimental evidence for oscillatory phenomena during the growth of biomorph sheets. We specifically report the existence of large amplitude height variations that take the shape of nearly concentric stripes or disordered patchy patterns with essentially identical wavelengths. These topographic structures correlate with directional variations in the nanorod alignment tilting them periodically out of the average sheet plane. Our results can be discussed in the context of an earlier proposed mechanism for biomorph growth. This model predicts the alternating precipitation of silica and barium carbonate as a central part of pH oscillations at the expanding sheet front. In each iteration of this cyclic process, the deposition of amorphous silica limits the barium carbonate structures to nanorods, thus preventing them from growing into larger euhedral witherite crystals.

Our results show that the topographic patterns form in the immediate wake of the crystallization front which is in agreement with the pH oscillation model. In addition, the stripes are parallel to the growing front suggesting a spatial synchronization of these oscillations. In this context, one can interpret the patchy patterns as desynchronized states with similar frequency and wavelength that lack long-range, lateral correlation. Interestingly, we occasionally observe line defects in the stripe structures that separate synchronized but phase-shifted band patterns (Figure S3). These patterns might present another dynamic state of the oscillatory system. Despite this supporting evidence for chemical oscillations, there remain open questions and some potential contradictions. Foremost, our data show no compositional variations that would be expected from spatiotemporal changes in the production of barium carbonate and silica. Furthermore, the pattern wavelength shows no appreciable dependence on the reactant concentrations. We also do not observe oscillatory changes in the front speed.

These seeming contradictions might be explainable in terms of more complex mechanistic features. Recent studies have reported the formation of prenucleation clusters during the crystallization of alkaline earth metal carbonates in the presence of polyanionic species. ,- Similar interactions between the silicate oligomers and barium ions can possibly assemble prenucleation clusters during the biomorph crystallization. In this context, the deposition of silica and barium carbonate are not simply coupled by indirect pH changes, but must be considered as a cocrystallization process.

dataset_item.question: How can a parametric drift detection and isolation scheme be designed to detect and isolate batch-to-batch parametric drifts in batch crystallization processes?
dataset_item.answer:
A parametric drift detection and isolation (PDDI) scheme for batch crystallization processes can be designed using a two-stage approach, combining the strengths of preparatory and post-batch stages. 

**Preparatory Stage**: This stage computes drift signatures and threshold values without requiring process measurements. These are derived from drift-free simulations with added noise to account for process variability. The drift signatures represent unique patterns for different types of parametric drifts (e.g., solubility, growth rates), while thresholds are designed to differentiate normal variations from drifts. Additionally, correction parameters are identified to ensure effective drift estimation during operation.

**Post-Batch Stage**: During batch-to-batch operation, residuals are calculated by comparing the absolute differences between drift-free simulation results and actual process measurements obtained both in-batch and post-batch. These residuals are analyzed against the pre-computed thresholds and drift signatures to detect and isolate specific parametric drifts. The magnitude of the drift is estimated using the correction parameters, which enables accurate updates to the batch process model.

**Integration with Model Predictive Control (MPC)**: The updated process model is fed into the MPC system to optimize operational parameters, such as jacket temperatures, for subsequent batches. This ensures corrective adjustments to maintain desired crystal shape distributions under drifting process conditions. Simulations confirm the effectiveness of this approach in improving control over crystal properties, outperforming conventional MPC methods that rely on nominal models.

By leveraging drift signatures, thresholds, and residual-based analysis, this PDDI scheme enables robust detection and isolation of parametric drifts, while ensuring process adaptability through model updates and corrective control strategies.

### 1. **Summary of the Purpose**
The purpose of this paper is to develop and evaluate a parametric drift detection and isolation (PDDI) method for identifying and mitigating batch-to-batch parametric drifts in a batch crystallization process for producing hen egg-white (HEW) lysozyme crystals. The method integrates PDDI with an in-batch model predictive control (MPC) system to improve the production of crystals with desired shape distributions, even in the presence of parametric drifts in solubility, growth rates, mass and energy balances, and nucleation rate. The PDDI method involves a preparatory stage to compute drift signatures and thresholds, and a post-batch stage to monitor residuals and isolate drifts during operation. Its effectiveness is demonstrated via multiscale simulations showing improved process outcomes compared to conventional MPC approaches.

---

### 2. **Classification of Purpose**
The paper emphasizes both "<method>" and "<result>":
- **<method>:** The development of the PDDI system and its integration with MPC.
- **<result>:** The demonstrated effectiveness of the PDDI-enhanced MPC system in achieving desired crystal shape distributions under parametric drift conditions.

If forced to choose one, the emphasis leans more toward **<method>**, as the core contribution is the development and description of the PDDI framework.

---

### 3. **Research Questions**
Based on the abstract's themes and materials science interests, the following research questions are relevant:

1. **Methodological Questions:**
   - How can a PDDI system be effectively designed to detect and isolate parametric drifts in batch crystallization processes?
   - What simulation methods and noise models are most appropriate for computing threshold values and drift signatures in the preparatory stage?
   - How can the PDDI system be integrated with an in-batch MPC framework for real-time and post-batch process adjustments?

2. **Process-Specific Questions:**
   - How do batch-to-batch parametric drifts in solubility, growth rates, and nucleation rates impact the quality and shape distribution of HEW lysozyme crystals?

dataset_item.question: How does the baseplate electronic structure in systems with bacteriochlorophyll a-CsmA influence the localization of trap states and energy transfer dynamics?
dataset_item.answer: The baseplate electronic structure in systems with bacteriochlorophyll a (BChl a)-CsmA significantly influences the localization of trap states and energy transfer dynamics by forming a disordered BChl a-CsmA lattice. This disordered structure promotes the formation of localized low-energy trap states near 818 nm, rather than delocalized excitons across multiple BChl a-CsmA dimers. Excitation energy is transferred to these localized trap states via exciton hopping, with a transfer time of approximately 2.0 ± 0.1 ps. This mechanism results in red-shifted emission near 826 nm in *C. tepidum* and 821 nm in *C. aurantiacus*. The findings challenge earlier models suggesting excitonic coupling across tetramers and instead confirm that the disordered BChl a-CsmA arrangement governs the electronic structure, enabling efficient energy transfer through localized states.

The sulfur and oxygen add a delocalized charge at the center of the chain, which may affect the energy transfer through the molecule. Previously, by comparing butanedithiol to benzenedimethanedithiol, we have shown that delocalized charge at the center of the chain caused localization of the excitonic wavefunction and reduced coupling. Here, enhancement in coupling was measured with the linkers that have delocalized charge at the center, suggesting that the enhancement originates from the additional vibrational modes contributed by the added atoms. The possible ways in which vibrations can assist transport are not straightforward to measure, and therefore it is hard to determine experimentally which mechanism dictates the differences. There are multiple energy gaps (considering the S2 state of the acceptor), and resonance conditions could hold for different parts of an energy band. To investigate the role of vibrations in the mechanism, quantum chemical calculations were done. The results show that there is a good match between the S1-S1 energy gap of the QDs and the vibrations of the molecules that lead to the strongest coupling, in the two different QD sets used. In the dimers, where the energy gap is 773 cm-1, the 5-S linker exhibited the strongest coupling. This linker has a strong vibrational mode around 807 cm-1, which can be characterized by asymmetric C-C and C-S stretching and slight drift of the central S atom along the main molecular axis (see Figure S5A). In films where the energy gap is 1284 cm-1, the strongest coupling was achieved with the linker 5-O. This linker has a strong vibrational mode around 1154 cm-1. Similarly, in the 5-S linker, this mode is characterized by an asymmetric stretching of C-C and C-O bonds and, since the oxygen is lighter than sulfur, the stretch is more pronounced along the main axis of the molecule (see Figure S5B). These vibrations have likely promoted the downhill energy transfer in these samples by vibrational-electronic (vibronic) resonance.

dataset_item.question: How do pseudopotential correlation-consistent polarized valence basis sets impact the accuracy of CCSD (T) geometry optimizations for silver dimers?
dataset_item.answer: Pseudopotential correlation-consistent polarized valence basis sets play a critical role in the accuracy of CCSD(T) geometry optimizations for silver dimers (Ag₂ and Ag₂⁻). Systematic convergence in geometry optimization is achieved at the aug-cc-pVQZ-PP level, which provides reliable predictions for bond lengths at the polarized valence level. Core-valence correlation effects (ΔCV), which are important for further refining geometry accuracy, converge effectively with the smaller cc-pwCVDZ-PP basis set, demonstrating its sufficiency for capturing these corrections. Spin-orbit coupling, while slightly influencing bond lengths (reducing them by approximately 0.001 Å), is negligible and excluded in subsequent calculations due to its minimal impact on structural predictions. These findings underscore the importance of selecting appropriate basis sets, with aug-cc-pVQZ-PP and cc-pwCVDZ-PP ensuring accurate geometry optimizations and core-valence correlation effects for silver clusters.

dataset_item.question: How does stabilization of S,S'-binuclear complexes by homologous disulfides influence disproportionation reactions?
dataset_item.answer: The stabilization of S,S'-binuclear complexes by homologous disulfides significantly influences disproportionation reactions by modifying the structural and electronic properties of the disulfide bond. Formation of S,S'-binuclear complexes leads to elongation of the S-S bond by approximately 5% and redistribution of charges from Sδ--Sδ- in the original disulfide to Sδ+-Sδ- in the complex. This charge redistribution (Δδ) increases the susceptibility of the bond to nucleophilic attack, facilitating disproportionation. Homologous disulfides like homocystine and 3,3′-dithiodipropionic acid stabilize S,S'-binuclear complexes effectively, resulting in cleavage of the disulfide bond and disproportionation. In contrast, ligands such as l-cystine and cystamine preferentially form S,N-binuclear or S,N,S′,N′-tetranuclear complexes, which preserve the S-S bond and suppress disproportionation. Thus, the degree of charge redistribution and the ability of the disulfide to stabilize S,S'-binuclear complexes determine the likelihood of disproportionation under aqueous conditions.

dataset_item.question: How can configurational sampling algorithms based on force fields be utilized to optimize intermolecular energy in molecular clusters?
dataset_item.answer:
Configurational sampling algorithms based on force fields optimize intermolecular energy in molecular clusters by treating molecules as rigid bodies and systematically adjusting their positions and orientations to minimize total interaction energy. These algorithms rely on force fields that model intermolecular interactions, such as Coulomb forces and Lennard-Jones potentials. Coulomb interactions are calculated using atom-centered partial charges, driving the organization of polar molecules, while the Lennard-Jones potential prevents atomic overlap through its repulsive (r⁻¹²) term and accounts for dispersion forces via its attractive (r⁻⁶) term. 

Parameters for these interactions are often sourced from established force fields like CHARMM, which provide predefined values for common molecules. For molecules lacking predefined parameters, quantum chemical methods (e.g., MP2/6-31++G(d,p)) and natural bond orbital (NBO) population analysis can be employed to derive accurate values. This hybrid approach ensures reliable sampling of potential energy surfaces while preventing unintended chemical reactions, making it particularly effective for studying molecular clusters dominated by hydrogen bonding and electrostatic forces, such as those found in atmospheric or biological systems.

inference_contexts: Atmospheric molecular clusters are mostly held together through Coulomb interactions and hydrogen bonds. Since structures of the individual molecules inside of clusters do not change significantly, the molecules can be treated as rigid bodies in the initial step of exploring the potential energy surface (PES). Moreover, the rigid molecule approximation also avoids the possibility of undesired chemical reactions occurring during the PES exploration. Coulomb interactions are the most significant factor for self-organizing polar molecules in clusters. Thus, a configurational sampling algorithm based on force field (FF) methods describing these interactions in terms of atom-centered partial charges can be utilized. Such approaches are indeed part of many existing configurational sampling programs. ,,,

In this work, we use the CHARMM (Chemistry at Harvard MM) FF parameters. , Structures and parameters for those molecules that are not included in the CHARMM parameters can be obtained by optimizing the structures at the MP2/6-31++G (d,p) - level of theory. Partial charges can then be extracted using the natural bond orbital (NBO) population analysis at this level. Missing parameters, such as the Lennard-Jones energy ϵ or distance σ, were taken from similar structures presented in the CHARMM force field database. , This approach is generally sufficient for configurational sampling of atmospheric molecular clusters. When necessary, system-specific FF molecular parameters can also be developed more rigorously, as described in refs and .

In our approach, the orientation and position of all rigid molecules are optimized to minimize the total intermolecular energy. The intermolecular interaction terms of force fields practically always contain a repulsive part, which prevents overlapping of atoms or molecules. A typical example is the Lennard-Jones potential E ij LJ, which is given for atoms i and j with distance rij by E ij LJ ( r ij ) = ϵ ij ( ( σ ij r ij ) 12 - ( σ ij r ij ) 6 ) 1 where ϵ is the energy well depth, and σ is the lowest non-overlapping distance of interacting atoms. (Here, the r ij -12 term corresponds to the repulsive part, and the r ij -6 term corresponds to attractive but rather weak dispersion interactions.) For polar molecules, the formation of different bonding patterns is mainly driven by Coulomb interactions E ij C E ij C ( r ij ) = k e q i q j r ij 2 where k e ≈ 9 × 109 Nm2 C-2, and q represents a (typically atom-centered) partial charge.

By calculating the bond length and IR vibrational spectra of the geometric structure, the intermolecular hydrogen bond in the S1 state was enhanced significantly. The absorption and fluorescence spectra are consistent with the experimental results, which indicate that the calculation methods are valid. dataset_item.question: What precursor solution compositions result in high compositional stability and reproducibility during perovskite synthesis?
dataset_item.answer:
For achieving high compositional stability and reproducibility during perovskite synthesis, a precursor solution composed of methylammonium bromide (MABr) and lead iodide (PbI₂) in dimethylformamide (DMF) with a 1.2:1 molar ratio is highly effective. This formulation yields MAPbI₂Br perovskites that exhibit stable composition and Urbach energy, with minimal dependence on annealing temperature and duration. This stability is attributed to reduced halide segregation and grain boundary defects, making the formulation suitable for large-scale production and efficient device performance.

In contrast, a precursor solution of methylammonium iodide (MAI) and lead bromide (PbBr₂) with a 3:1 molar ratio requires stringent annealing control due to its strong dependence on annealing parameters, making it less reproducible and less viable for scalable production. Similarly, simple mixtures of MAPbI₃ and MAPbBr₃ degrade under prolonged annealing, further limiting their applicability.

The 1.2:1 MABr:PbI₂ precursor composition is recommended for stable perovskite synthesis as it minimizes halide segregation and facilitates reproducibility, though nonradiative recombination remains an area for improvement in optimizing solar cell efficiency.

For polymers, natural or otherwise, to produce carbon fiber of a similar quality as PAN, they cannot rely on hydrogen bonding for structural stability or contain a high mass fraction of oxygen, lest they shrink to an unusable extent. A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. Polyalanine-like domains could be incorporated into block copolymers for biomimetic graphite precursors. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

The overlapping of steric (or electrosteric) and depletion mechanisms for colloidal stabilization of oxidized carbon nanotubes (plasma-oxidized SWCNTs and MWCNTs and chemically oxidized MWCNTs) by amphiphilic PF127 is attained through a matching of the polymer chemical structure (containing hydrophobic PPO and hydrophilic PEO moieties), and its consequent conformational behavior in solution, with the nanocarbon high aspect ratio one-dimensional morphology. For these samples, regardless of the surface charge (ζ potential), the degree of oxidation, and the nanotube diameter and length, colloidal stability in a 0.9% NaCl solution is attained through (i) the wrapping of PF127 around the nanotubes induced by hydrophobic interactions between the PPO moiety and nonoxidized regions of the graphitic sheets (i.e.. polyaromatic regions with sp2 carbon hybridization) and the consequent exposure of hydrophilic PEO moieties to the medium and (ii) the manifestation of repulsive depletion forces for PF127 concentrations superior to 1.0%. Above this concentration, the CNT colloidal stabilization also has little dependence on the PF127 concentration. The same PF127 was not able to colloidally stabilize graphene oxide (chemically oxidized) through steric-based mechanisms due to the small size of PEO moieties in comparison with the large-sized sheets of GO (lateral size of up to 20 μm), thus preventing a suitable steric repulsion for GO sheets. This aspect also explains the absence of stabilizing depletion forces for the GO-PF127 system, in which there is not a proper dimensional and stereochemical matching between the large (i.e.. GO sheets) and small (i.e.. PF127 micelles) particles present in the liquid. On the other hand, long-chain PEG (MW 35000) was unable to colloidally stabilize CNTs due to the absence of significant short-range interactions (e.g.. hydrophobic) that could result in steric-based mechanisms of stabilization. In addition, the absence of a proper dimensional and stereochemical matching between the long-chain PEG 35000 and the high aspect ratio one-dimensional morphology of CNTs did not lead to the manifestation of stabilizing repulsive depletion forces as well. However, large-sized sheets of GO in the presence of PEG 35000 can be colloidally stabilized through repulsive depletion forces, which strongly depend on the polymer concentration, as shown by the stabilization attained for PEG concentrations from 5.0 wt %. The overlapping of these stabilization mechanisms (steric + depletion) observed for CNTs led to a much higher colloidal stabilization in comparison with that attained for the GO-PEG system. For applications in media with low ionic strengths, electric stabilization attained through nanocarbon oxidation can provide a suitable colloidal stability. Conversely, in the particular context of nanomedicine, in which nanocarbons must behave throughout their application as individualized colloidal entities and not as agglomerates in physiological media (e.g.. 0.9% NaCl, with a high ionic strength), oxidation protocols such as acid treatment (which lead to electric stabilization through negative surface charging) are much less effective than the use of suitable biocompatible polymers such as Pluronic F-127 and long-chain PEG.

dataset_item.question: How does the radius of curvature of the ice-water interface change with the degree of supercooling during interactions with Tenebrio molitor antifreeze protein?
dataset_item.answer: The radius of curvature of the ice-water interface decreases with increasing supercooling during interactions with Tenebrio molitor antifreeze protein (TmAFP). Molecular dynamics simulations show that TmAFP inhibits ice growth by promoting the formation of a convex ice-water interface. At lower supercooling (higher temperatures), the radius of curvature is larger, while at higher supercooling (lower temperatures), the radius becomes smaller. This behavior aligns with the Kelvin effect, where greater supercooling sharpens the curvature of the interface, further impeding ice growth. The convex shape induced by local ice growth demonstrates how TmAFP effectively regulates the ice-water interface to inhibit ice propagation.

Attempts have been made to probe how the ice-bound protein inhibits the growth and melting of ice below and above the equilibrium melting temperature, respectively. Our calculations further reveal that above the melting temperature the ice melting is inhibited through the formation of concave ice-water interface. dataset_item.question: How does reaction atmosphere influence cracking severity and pyrolysis oil yield during secondary pyrolysis at different temperatures?
dataset_item.answer:
Reaction atmosphere significantly influences cracking severity and pyrolysis oil yield during secondary pyrolysis, particularly at higher temperatures. At temperatures below 600 °C, the atmosphere has minimal impact on overall vapor composition, and secondary pyrolysis reactions are negligible, as observed experimentally and predicted by the model. However, at temperatures above 600 °C, the choice of atmosphere plays a crucial role. 

Under a nitrogen atmosphere, cracking severity increases, as indicated by the higher CH4/(C2s+C3s) molar ratio, compared to a steam atmosphere. This trend is consistent across both experimental results and computational predictions, although discrepancies exist in the exact temperature at which the effect becomes significant. Steam, in contrast, reduces cracking severity while increasing gas yields (experiment: +1.7 wt%, model: +2.3 wt%) and slightly enhancing organic liquid yields (experiment: +0.8 wt%, model: +0.2 wt%). The computational model accurately predicts these trends but underestimates water formation, highlighting limitations in the kinetic scheme.

Temperature plays a critical role in determining the extent of secondary pyrolysis reactions. At ~500 °C, secondary reactions are negligible, while at 600 °C and higher, significant shifts in product distribution are observed, with steam favoring gas production and nitrogen promoting cracking severity. Overall, while the model captures the directional influence of reaction atmosphere and temperature on product yields and composition, minor discrepancies in quantitative predictions highlight areas for further refinement.

This Account summarizes the recent research work from our group on the design, development, and applications of organocatalytic multiple domino reactions toward the construction of highly functionalized complex structures. A range of triple and quadruple domino reactions catalyzed by a secondary amine organocatalyst have been developed, which provide direct and efficient entry to carbocyclic and heterocyclic scaffolds bearing multiple stereogenic centers with an excellent level of stereocontrol. The salient features of these domino sequences include the use of easily available commercial catalysts and substrates and simple one-pot protocols providing very good domino yields and excellent stereoselectivities under mild reaction conditions. These organocatalytic domino reactions are even combined with other reactions in one-pot reactions to further attain some more diverse scaffolds with increasing molecular complexity. In spite of these exciting results there is still more room for further development of new multiple domino protocols for the asymmetric synthesis of biologically relevant molecular structures. The major limitations found in the development of multiple domino sequences include the limited number of substrate classes activated through the secondary amine catalysts, the lack of generality in the substrate scope, and the high catalyst loading. In future, efforts to design and develop more complex domino reactions leading to the selective products will be the major focus of our group. We envisage that the development of asymmetric multiple domino sequences directed toward specific targets, such as natural products and pharmaceuticals, will make these one-pot processes even more valuable and practical. High-temperature friction, wear, and oxidation behaviors of sodium borate-silicate lubricants have been fully investigated. The tribological performance is affected strongly by both sliding temperature and the composition of the lubricant, particularly borate-silicate ratio. Sodium borate-silicate mixture with the weight ratio of 9:1 (sodium silicate/sodium borate) delivers desirable lubricity and wear prevention at 800 °C. Under isothermal oxidation testing, the flux growth of oxide crystals within the melt was observed at 850 °C and above, which was responsible for the lubrication deterioration at these temperatures. A multilayered functional structure of sodium borosilicate across the tribointerface is developed under friction testing condition at 800 °C, leading to low friction sliding. Self-adaptation of the oxide scale under the infiltration of molten glass results in stable tribological behavior during sliding for up to 600 s exposure. The high-temperature condition provides sufficient energy to trigger the reaction between glass and oxide surfaces, whereas the stressed shearing effect allows surface-to-bulk transport that resulted in the reaction product layer formed in the tribofilm. This study helps advance the understanding of high-temperature tribochemical reactions between molten glass and oxide scale under stressed shearing effect at very high temperature conditions.

dataset_item.question: What is the mechanism of energy transfer between carbon dots, lanthanide complexes, and poly(methyl methacrylate) matrix in the composite material?
dataset_item.answer: The energy transfer mechanism in the carbon dot-lanthanide-poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) composite material involves chemical and physical interactions that immobilize carbon dots and lanthanide complexes within the transparent PMMA matrix. Functionalized carbon dots act as blue light emitters, and upon excitation at 400 nm, they efficiently transfer energy to the lanthanide complexes, resulting in intense white light emission with CIE coordinates (0.31, 0.32) and a quantum efficiency of 16.6%. The PMMA matrix plays a crucial role by enhancing the dispersion of the components, improving thermal stability, and maintaining high optical transparency, which facilitates effective energy transfer and optimized white-light emission.

dataset_item.question: How can computational methods be used to identify new chemical structures capable of undergoing singlet fission?
dataset_item.answer:
Computational methods play a pivotal role in identifying new chemical structures capable of undergoing singlet fission by leveraging advanced theoretical models, electronic structure calculations, and high-throughput screening techniques. These approaches enable the prediction and characterization of electronic states, singlet fission mechanisms, and excited-state dynamics, which are essential for understanding and optimizing singlet fission processes. Key strategies include:

1. **Screening for Candidate Materials:** Computational tools can identify promising singlet fission materials such as carbon nanotubes, covalent organic frameworks (COFs), and other organic/polymeric systems. High-throughput screening methods help expand the catalog of viable compounds by predicting their electronic properties and assessing their potential for singlet fission.

2. **Electronic Structure Analysis:** Ab initio methods, including diabatic and adiabatic state models, are used to quantify fission rates, coupling strengths, and excited-state energies. These calculations help determine the feasibility of singlet fission in candidate materials.

3. **Dynamics Simulations:** Integrating accurate electronic structure methods with dynamics simulations provides insights into condensed-phase behavior, spin decoherence, triplet diffusion, and interfacial charge dissociation—factors critical for singlet fission optimization in solar cell applications.

By combining these computational approaches, researchers can systematically predict, design, and refine materials capable of undergoing singlet fission, paving the way for advancements in energy-efficient technologies such as solar cells.

inference_contexts: Although a large variety of models have been employed so far to compute singlet fission couplings, I am convinced that there is still room for the use of other approaches dedicated to the general study of excitation energy transfer processes to be applied to the study of singlet fission mechanism. The diabatic picture is very useful for the physical characterization of the fission mechanism, but depending on how diabatic (or quasi-diabatic) states are defined and constructed, which is not unique, the computed electronic couplings may vary sensibly. Hence, one should be cautious when interpreting the results, especially in the quantitative assessment of fission rates. On the other hand, the difficulties to compute derivative couplings between eigenstates of model electronic Hamiltonians is one of the main drawbacks of the adiabatic basis, specially in the study of excited state dynamics. I believe that establishing proper connections between adiabatic states and contributions with well-defined physical properties (diabats) can be very powerful in the study of singlet fission at the microscopic level. It is important to highlight that computational studies on the singlet fission dynamics are helping to reinterpret and revisit some of the aspects regarding the fission mechanisms and emphasize the important dynamic nature of it. So far, most of the computational studies on the singlet fission dynamics largely point to the CT-mediated mechanism as the main cause responsible for the fast population of the triplet-pair (1TT) state experimentally measured in singlet fission materials and have attributed a lesser role to the direct S1 to 1TT path. On the other hand, the conclusions extracted from these methodologies are strongly linked to the electronic model employed, in particular the state energies and couplings. Many of such investigations rely on the construction of (simple) effective electronic Hamiltonians within the diabatic framework, which, as discussed above, might hold some fundamental limitations for the study of singlet fission. Hence, integration of accurate electronic structure methods with reliable excited state dynamics approaches is desirable in order to proportionate even more robust results to undercover the intricacies of the singlet fission mechanism.

Polymers are probably one of the less investigated singlet fission materials, specially from a computational point of view. In fact, singlet fission in polymers is less mature than in crystals or molecular dimers, and several fundamental aspects related to the electronic states involved or the fission mechanisms are not well-understood. Hence, I believe that the progress of singlet fission in polymeric systems could benefit from theoretical efforts.

Although electronic states in singlet fission have been characterized to great detail, the expected appearance of new singlet fission compounds will require the application of theoretical models for their study and to perform new calculations to understand the particularities of electronic states and mechanisms for each singlet fission system. Besides, more general aspects should be further investigated at the theoretical level, such is the role of the excimer state or the factors controlling the relationship between coherent and incoherent population of the 1TT state.

Ab initio studies of excited states in solids can be very useful in the theoretical study of singlet fission and can complement the often employed dimer and oligomer approaches. These investigations can potentially provide new and further insights for the comprehension of singlet fission in molecular crystals related to the nature of the excited states in the condensed phases, which cannot be recovered by local dimeric molecular models. Computational studies of singlet fission based on periodic conditions have recently appeared in the singlet fission literature but still are rather scarce. These methods can potentially provide more details related to important phenomena for singlet fission, such as the loss of quantum coherence between fission triplets or the dissipation of excitons mediated by vibronic couplings, which are still not well-understood and require more attention.

The integration of singlet fission in solar cells has been obtained using intermolecular singlet fission materials. The evolution of intramolecular singlet fission in covalent dimers and polymers might help to incorporate these compounds in modular solar cells in the near future. In this sense, theoretical and computational studies will soon be necessary in order to understand and characterize the structural and electronic properties of these systems, in particular those at the interface between singlet fission compounds and the semiconductor. Although not directly involved in the singlet fission process, the good understanding of how the fission triplets diffuse through the system and controlling the key parameters for charge dissociation of triplet excitons at the interface are of great importance for the successful implementation of singlet fission in solar cell devices and need to be further investigated.

dataset_item.question: How do different water management strategies, such as flooded, intermittent irrigation, and rainfed, influence rice cultivation during specific growth stages?
dataset_item.answer:
Different water management strategies significantly influence rice cultivation during specific growth stages by affecting soil conditions, plant development, and grain quality. Five strategies were evaluated: continuous flooding, three intermittent irrigation regimes (3 days flooded followed by 1-, 3-, or 5-day drainage, referred to as Int-F3D1, Int-F3D3, and Int-F3D5), and rainfed conditions relying solely on natural rainfall without irrigation. These treatments were applied for six weeks, spanning three weeks before and three weeks after the heading stage, following an initial flooding period during early growth. 

The study was conducted using replicated field plots to assess the impact of water management on soil redox potential (Eh), pH, and nutrient dynamics, with an emphasis on minimizing arsenic and cadmium accumulation in rice grains. Flooded conditions provided continuous waterlogging, while intermittent irrigation alternated between flooding and drainage to improve aeration. Rainfed conditions, dependent on natural rainfall, resulted in the most variable soil moisture levels. After the six-week experimental period, all plots underwent final drainage prior to harvest to optimize grain maturity. This integrated approach allowed for a comprehensive evaluation of water management strategies during critical growth stages of rice.

dataset_item.question: What are the dominant dissociation pathways for sodiated N-acetylhexosamines under collision-induced dissociation conditions?
dataset_item.answer:
Under collision-induced dissociation (CID) conditions, sodiated N-acetylhexosamines (HexNAcs) primarily dissociate via two dominant pathways: ring-opening followed by dehydration. 

1. **Ring-Opening Mechanism**: This pathway involves the transfer of a hydrogen atom from O1 to O0, leading to cleavage of the C1-O0 bond. The ring-opening mechanism is independent of the anomeric configuration (α or β) of HexNAc monomers.

2. **Dehydration Mechanism**: Following ring-opening, dehydration occurs via a multi-step hydrogen transfer process. First, a hydrogen atom is transferred from C2 to the acetyl oxygen, then from the acetyl oxygen to O3. This results in cleavage of the C3-O3 bond, which is the lowest-energy dissociation pathway. Dehydration leads to the elimination of HDO and is a key feature of CID spectra for HexNAcs.

For HexNAc derivatives that cannot undergo ring-opening, such as those at the nonreducing end of disaccharides, glycosidic bond cleavage (C1-O1) becomes the dominant dissociation pathway. The likelihood of glycosidic bond cleavage is influenced by the anomeric configuration, with β-anomers cleaving more readily than α-anomers. This allows for anomeric configuration determination in such systems.

These insights are critical for advancing structural analysis of oligosaccharides and understanding the behavior of sodiated HexNAcs under CID conditions.

After ring-opening (and the associated loss of the stereo-information of the C1 atom), dehydration, which involves the transfer of the H atom from C2 to the acetyl O atom, followed by the transfer of the same H atom from the acetyl O atom to O3 atom and the cleavage of the C3-O3 bond, has been calculated to feature the lowest barrier. This mechanism for the dehydration following a ring-opening step explains, on one hand, why the elimination of HDO is the dominating reaction in the CID of [D5] GlcNAc. As the C1-O1 cleavage from the β form has a barrier lower than that of the same reaction from the α form, the branching ratio for the glycosidic bond cleavage can be used to determine the anomeric configuration of the glycosidic bond.

dataset_item.question: How does the cross-linking of micellar precursors via sol-gel chemistry coupled with spray-drying improve the stability and drug release properties of hybrid nanomaterials?
dataset_item.answer: The cross-linking of micellar precursors via sol-gel chemistry coupled with spray-drying significantly enhances the stability and drug release properties of hybrid nanomaterials. The sol-gel process creates cross-linked poly(siloxane) domains within the micellar structure, which reinforce the physical stability of the aggregates under unfavorable conditions such as extreme temperature and concentration fluctuations for at least two weeks. This structural reinforcement prevents thermal degradation of the encapsulated drug during the spray-drying process, preserving its integrity and therapeutic efficacy. Furthermore, the hybrid nanomaterials exhibit zero-order drug release kinetics, eliminating the burst release typically observed in conventional polymeric micelles. This enables sustained and controlled drug delivery, making the system highly suitable for applications requiring prolonged and predictable drug release profiles.

dataset_item.question: How can neural networks represent elementary reactions while adhering to physical laws like the law of mass action?
dataset_item.answer:
Neural networks can represent elementary reactions while adhering to physical laws like the law of mass action by utilizing a specialized architecture known as Chemical Reaction Neural Networks (CRNNs). In this framework:

1. **Neuron Representation of Reactions**: Each elementary reaction is modeled as a neuron. Inputs to the neuron are species concentrations expressed in logarithmic scale, ensuring compatibility with the power-law dependence of the law of mass action.

2. **Input Layer**: Reaction orders, such as stoichiometric coefficients of reactants, are represented by the weights in the input layer, while biases encode the logarithmic rate constants. This formulation inherently enforces the law of mass action, as reaction rates are expressed as power-law functions of concentrations.

3. **Output Layer**: The outputs represent the production rates of species, weighted by stoichiometric coefficients of the products, ensuring physical consistency with reaction stoichiometry.

4. **Temperature Dependence**: Temperature-dependent kinetics, such as those governed by the Arrhenius law, are incorporated by modifying the biases with linear functions of temperature. This enables the model to capture the exponential dependence of reaction rates on temperature.

5. **Hidden Layer Structure**: The CRNN architecture includes a hidden layer where each node corresponds to an individual elementary reaction. This design mirrors classical reaction networks and ensures interpretability of the neural network as a digital twin of physical reaction systems.

6. **Training and Sparsity Enforcement**: The CRNN is trained using time-series data of species concentrations, typically through neural ODE frameworks. Sparsity is enforced via weight pruning techniques to eliminate nonphysical contributions, ensuring that only meaningful reactions are retained.

By integrating these elements, CRNNs preserve fundamental chemical principles, including the law of mass action, while enabling data-driven modeling of reaction systems. This approach ensures interpretability, physical consistency, and adaptability to temperature-dependent kinetics.

dataset_item.question: How does methylation of cations influence polymer conformations and phase behavior in poly(ethylene oxide) and imidazolium ionic liquid systems?
dataset_item.answer:
Methylation of cations in imidazolium ionic liquids alters, but does not eliminate, interactions with poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) chains, influencing polymer conformations while having limited impact on phase behavior. Molecular simulations reveal that PEO chains continue to wrap around methylated cations due to modified electrostatic interactions, forming compact motifs such as ringlike structures and crown ether arrangements. These conformational changes result in altered entropy contributions, particularly at lower temperatures, due to the loss of conformational freedom associated with chain wrapping. 

Despite these changes, simulations indicate that methylation does not significantly affect the lower critical solution temperature (LCST) or overall phase separation trends. This discrepancy between simulation results and experimental observations may stem from limitations in the modeled chain lengths, force field approximations, or insufficient sampling of long-range interactions. Advanced techniques, such as deep neural network (DNN) models, have successfully predicted phase diagrams consistent with experimental LCST behavior, highlighting the need for further investigation using more accurate atomistic simulations to reconcile differences and refine understanding of phase behavior in these systems.
