inference_contexts: This Account has summarized recent advances in four innovative strategies for nonconventional water splitting, circumventing many challenges in traditional water electrolysis and showcasing various advantages. In this burgeoning field, many opportunities await further investigation. For instance, most nonprecious bifunctional electrocatalysts for overall water splitting only function well in alkaline (and neutral) electrolytes. Nearly no low-cost electrocatalyst couples have been reported for water electrolysis at low pH. Along with the success in proton-exchange membrane and high conductivity of acidic electrolytes, it is very appealing to conduct water electrolysis under low pH conditions with earth-abundant electrocatalysts. In addition, most nonprecious electrocatalysts will undergo surface (if not bulk) oxidation during OER; hence the real active sites are usually different from those on the original catalysts. How to rationally control and understand such in situ oxidation to yield active sites while still retaining highly conductive bulk composite necessitates further research. The synthetic cost of redox mediators should also be further reduced to be economically attractive for large-scale decoupled water electrolysis. In particular, solubility, stability, and fast electron transfer kinetics of redox mediators are critical factors determining their potential for practical applications. For hybrid water electrolysis, high selectivity for desirable products from those selected organic oxidations should be the primary goal, and the subsequent separation and purification should also be taken into account. As organic electrocatalysis and electrosynthesis is about to witness a renaissance, we are optimistic that integrating many promising organic oxidation reactions (e.g.. oxidative C-C coupling) will burgeon in this field. It is exciting to see recent successes in tandem water electrolysis integrating biological enzymes to yield highly valuable products from inert starting molecules like CO2 and N2. Nevertheless, the long-term stability, scalability, and overall cost of these bioinorganic electrocatalytic systems should be thoroughly analyzed prior to practical implementation. We hope this Account will encourage more efforts into the development of advanced electrocatalysts and the design of novel strategies for H2 production and more importantly organic upgrading under benign conditions.

An overview of the explorations of multimetallic nanomaterials as electrocatalysts has indeed demonstrated a critical role of core-shell/alloy structural evolution under the reaction conditions in the activity and durability. Very often, such evolution could occur under both the post-synthesis processing and the reaction condition evolutions, e.g.. chemical/electrochemical dealloying and adsorbate-induced structural evolution, characteristic of the dynamic nature. While the dynamic process is complex, the ability to gain an insight into the evolution of core-shell and alloy structures is a significant advance. The understanding of the dynamic nature of 3d-TMs in core-shell/alloy evolution in acidic electrolytes remains elusive. The participation of 3d-TMs would greatly enhance the catalytic activity for chemical/electrochemical reactions by introducing lattice strain and ligand/electronic effect. While the perception of "Pt-skin" where 3d-TMs are completely buried under noble metal shells is well supported by high-resolution TEM data of individual NPs, there is increasing evidence for the synergistic participation of 3d-TMs on the catalyst as active sites in the form of a stable alloy structure for the electrochemical reactions. Such active and stable active sites are believed to be originated from the dynamic structure evolution of alloying-dealloying-realloying processes under the operating conditions. Understanding the exact structures of such active sites is important for developing new strategies to control activity and stability while reducing the noble metal content in the catalysts.

One important aspect for the structural evolution for NP/NW catalysts in general is the strong dependence on the chemical environment of the catalysts. In contrast to the above electrocatalysis examples where structural evolution could occur due to the presence of electrolyte at the catalyst interface which facilitates the dissolution of metal ions upon dealloying, the study of the same or similar nanocatalysts under gas-phase reaction conditions offers a different perspective to look at the core-shell structural evolution under reaction conditions. Understanding the dynamic processes of the core-shell/alloy structures under oxidative environments is not only for enhancing the catalytic performance in the gas-phase reaction, but also provides insight for the design of active and stable catalysts. For example, gas-phase hydrocarbon oxidation reactions have traditionally relied on oxygen-activation sites on the peripheral zones of oxide-supported noble metal catalysts. Recently, the initial alloying of NMs and 3d-TMs serves as an intriguing pathway for the design of active surface sites where the NMs provide adsorption site for CO and the surface-oxygenated 3d-TMs offer oxygen-activation sites. The NM/3d-TM alloy NPs undergo surface oxygenation, forming a CHA-type core with 3d-TM-oxygenated shell structure. Further understanding of the role of this type of structural evolution in enhancing activity and durability may lead to a new research frontier for the design of new-generation oxidation catalysts by tuning compositions and morphologies at the atomic scale. ,,, By highlighting the selected examples in connection with the recent advances in the field, this Account serves as a springboard from fundamental understanding of the core-shell and alloy structural dynamics to the broad applications of the nanostructured catalysts and electrocatalysts. There are still many challenging questions remaining to be answered, including how the atomic-scale arrangements of the surface active sites correlate with the nanophase structures of the NPs/NWs during the nanoscale dynamic processes, and how the structural durability of the catalysts in the catalytic processes can be controlled to enable the performance durability of the catalysts. Part of the ongoing investigations involves an in-depth understanding of factors controlling the composition optimization and the realloying under electrochemical and fuel cell operating conditions. Future studies will need to be advanced in several fronts, including the use of surface-sensitive techniques, especially under in situ/operando measurement modes, to probe the surface sites and surface/subsurface species, the design of multicomponent catalysts with nanoscale thermodynamic stability in the reactive environment, and the computational modeling of the atomic mobilities on and in the NPs/NWs in the presence of surface and interfacial species. These advancements will also benefit many areas of the applications of the NP and NW catalysts, especially in the area of energy and environmental sustainability.

Although this Account mainly discusses Sr related migration, other cations such as Ca2+ and Ba2+ are also used for substitution. It is possible to use other cations to tune the oxidation states, vacancy concentration, and oxygen p-band center position with novel electrocatalytic activity and stability. It is also suggested that future work should focus on understanding the mechanism and the functionality of electrocatalysts under reaction conditions. In situ surface techniques are preferred to probe how electrocatalysts work or fail during operational conditions. A combination of studies on atomic and electronic structures can better reveal the underlying structure-property relationships. As mentioned in this Account, there are changes that can be either structurally coherent or incoherent with respect to the catalyst supports. Therefore, complementary methods are needed for achieving comprehensive understanding. The application of in situ surface X-ray diffraction and COBRA for understanding the coherent atomic and chemical changes will be essential for future electrocatalysis studies. These structural probes, together with in situ APXPS for surface chemistry and electronic structure and density functional theory, are providing key insights into electrocatalytic properties and helping to identify suitable activity and stability descriptors for the design of highly efficient oxide electrocatalysts for electrochemical and photoelectrochemical applications.

Chemical composition and surface structure play a critical role in tuning the ORR/OER activity of nonstoichiometric mixed metal oxides, by effecting the nature of the active sites for O2 dissociation and evolution. It is generally found for both high and low temperature electrocatalysis that the B-site terminated surfaces are catalytically more active for ORR/OER than the A-site terminated ones. The A-site composition impacts activity indirectly by effecting the oxygen defect concentration. For high-temperature ORR/OER, it is generally reported that B-site terminated Co containing oxides exhibit the best performance among these oxides due to their promising electronic/ionic conductivity and modest binding strengths of the intermediates. In the case of low-temperature ORR, although Mn, Co, and Ni based oxides have been shown to exhibit good performance, discrepancies still exist regarding the link between activity and B-site composition. In general, low temperature ORR/OER activity trends are convoluted with artifacts from lack of consistent approaches for testing the electrochemical activity of these oxides, due to complexities in electrode composition induced by their low electronic conductivity under these conditions. In addition, the flexibility of the B- and A-site compositions and their various possible combinations in these oxides make the search for optimal OER/ORR oxide electrocatalysts very challenging. Thus, performance descriptors developed based on the correlations between activity and specific oxide properties have been suggested to guide the design of optimal oxides for ORR/OER. While important insights have been reported using activity descriptors that mainly correlate to bulk properties, in order to develop universal descriptors, a direct link between the surface structure and activity is critical.

dataset_item.question: How does the choice of fullerene or nonfullerene acceptors affect the crystallinity and morphology of blends with aggregated polymers such as PffBT4T80-co-3T20-2OD?
dataset_item.answer:
The choice of fullerene or nonfullerene acceptors plays a critical role in determining the crystallinity and morphology of blends with aggregated polymers such as PffBT4T80-co-3T20-2OD. Fullerene acceptors, such as PC71BM, act as antisolvents during film formation, promoting polymer solidification and crystallization. This results in an isotropic, semi-crystalline polymer structure that is conducive to optimal photovoltaic performance. In contrast, nonfullerene acceptors, such as IDTBR, delay polymer crystallization due to structural similarities with the polymer, including shared benzothiadiazole and thiophene units. This delayed crystallization disrupts polymer order and morphology, often leading to reduced device performance in terms of current and fill factor.

The contrasting effects of fullerene and nonfullerene acceptors highlight the importance of selecting polymer:acceptor pairs with complementary crystallinity to achieve favorable morphology. Furthermore, precise control of processing conditions, such as drying time and temperature, is essential to balance aggregation and crystallization dynamics for optimal device performance. By carefully tailoring these factors, researchers can mitigate disruptions caused by nonfullerene acceptors and enhance the photovoltaic efficiency of the blends.

A suite of conjugated polymer semiconductors was studied to determine the role of thermomechanical relaxations on film toughness. The thermomechanical behavior was probed by dynamic mechanical analysis and the film toughness was probed by considering film ductility as a function of temperature. It was found that for most of the polymers considered, a large reduction in film toughness was found that corresponds to secondary thermal relaxations {T β}. The secondary nature, i.e.. local nonsegmental motion, of these thermal relaxations was probed through frequency maps in the DMA and by comparing the polymers with systematic variation to the side-chain and backbone structure. It was found that while the loss in toughness is clearly associated with {T b}, the differences in the molecular structure and packing behavior influence the relative changes in ductility. Furthermore, we observed that a number of polymers retain some ductility below their dominant secondary thermal relaxation temperature. While the origin of this behavior requires further exploration, we propose that crystallites/aggregates in the films allow for energy dissipation through chain slip. It is clear that secondary relaxation behavior driven in part by side-chain characteristics is critical to CP film toughness. Through this observation, the design of the side-chain structures may be used to not only improve the solubility and promote the packing order but also improve the thermal and mechanical stability.

dataset_item.question: How can multicanonical molecular dynamics simulations and umbrella sampling be used to explore binding pathways and estimate free energy landscapes in enzyme-inhibitor systems?
dataset_item.answer:
Multicanonical molecular dynamics (McMD) simulations and umbrella sampling (US), combined with the weighted histogram analysis method (WHAM), are powerful techniques for exploring binding pathways and estimating free energy landscapes in enzyme-inhibitor systems. McMD efficiently samples a wide range of configurations, including intermediate states between bound and unbound conformations, enabling the identification of binding pathways and stable binding configurations. For example, simulations of the inhibitor 3MR binding to β-secretase 1 (BACE) revealed a stable binding configuration partially consistent with experimental X-ray structures.

Umbrella sampling refines the binding pathway by generating a potential of mean force (PMF) profile, which quantifies the free energy changes along the transition between bound and unbound states. The PMF analysis, coupled with WHAM, accurately predicts binding free energy, reproducing experimental data and highlighting key molecular interactions that drive binding affinity. Additionally, canonical molecular dynamics simulations at physiological and elevated temperatures validate the stability of the identified binding configuration and provide further insights into the dynamics of the system.

The combined approach not only elucidates the atomistic interactions governing binding but also addresses challenges such as spatial restraints in large binding pockets. Despite these limitations, the methods successfully predict binding affinity and reveal interaction losses along the dissociation pathway, offering valuable insights for modeling medium-sized inhibitors in enzyme systems with wide binding pockets.

inference_contexts: Starting from the unbound state, we have executed McMD simulations in order to explore the binding pathways of the medium-sized inhibitor 3MR to the wide binding pocket of BACE, followed by US and WHAM to calculate their affinity. The most stable binding configuration was found to partly coincide with the native X-ray structure, as indicated by the FEL and the RMSD values. This is due to the definition of the spatial restraint, which was designed for small ligand binding pockets. The native interactions however were preserved as shown by the high R(native)-value. Canonical MD simulations at 300 and 400 K validated the stability of the obtained binding configuration and showed that additional equilibration can further relax a structure to produce the native structure. We picked representative structures along the dissociation direction λ⃗ from the McMD ensemble in a smoothly connected manner, followed by US simulations and WHAM to accurately predict the standard binding free energy between 3MR and BACE in agreement with the experimental results. The losses of interactions between the molecules along λ⃗ were clearly reflected in the PMF, as they account for most of the change in the binding free energy. The sampled ensemble by the US simulations connected the bound state to the unbound one in a smooth manner, refining the binding pathway while staying true to the McMD ensemble.

We have simulated ultrafast nonadiabatic population relaxation from S2 to S1 using A-FSSH simulations of the dual fluorescent molecule DMABN. Our results are largely consistent with previous theoretical calculations, , though we have gained several new pieces of insight. First, decoherence is found to not play an important role in propagating these dynamics due to the rapid excited-state relaxation and subsequent energetic separation of the first two excited states. Second, we ran simulations of DMABN in the presence of a MECN molecule and found that the ultrafast relaxation was largely unaffected by the solvent, in agreement with time-resolved fluorescence measurements of DMABN in MeCN. Third, we introduced a physically motivated diabatization procedure that is capable of converting the TDDFT excited (adiabatic) states into excited (diabatic) states of La and Lb character (which are diagonal with respect to the rotationally averaged transition dipole operator). Transforming the mixed quantum-classical density matrix into this diabatic representation, the population relaxation from La to Lb was found to be somewhat slower than the adiabatic states and consistent with the decay of the ensemble-averaged transition moment; specifically, our calculations predict a decay in the emission on the order of 15 fs (rather than 11 fs). Fourth and finally, we investigated the dynamics of the diabatization angle for all relaxation events through the CI. We found that 16% of the trajectories that we simulated fully circled the CI clockwise, 18% circled counterclockwise, and the remainder did not circle the CI at all. From these numbers and the fact that the majority of the electronic relaxation occurs within 30 fs according to our TDDFT functional, we hypothesize that if geometric phase effects are important in larger molecules, the 21 atom molecule DMABN will be an ideal test case for higher-level calculations, both for the electronic structure and the nuclear dynamics. It remains an open question as to whether or not we can predict an observable to prove such effects with nonlinear spectroscopy.

With three independent sets of etched AuNRs and two measurement schemes (solution in a cuvette with waveguide spectrometers and sample drop on slides with a Raman microscope), we have come to similar conclusions. Namely, the experimental variations in the main SERS intensity of the adsorbed NBT molecules are quite moderate for nanorods with PRs varied around the laser wavelength of 785 nm within a wide range (650-925 nm). dataset_item.question: How does membrane crowding affect the scaling of rotational diffusion rates with protein size compared to predictions from the Saffman-Delbruck model?
dataset_item.answer:
Membrane crowding significantly impacts the scaling of rotational diffusion rates with protein size, leading to deviations from the Saffman-Delbruck (SD) model. While the SD model predicts \( D_{rot} \sim R^{-2} \) under dilute conditions, even moderately crowded membranes exhibit a stronger scaling of \( D_{rot} \sim R^{-3} \). At biologically relevant levels of crowding, such as in native cellular membranes, the dependency becomes even steeper, indicating a progressive slowdown in rotational diffusion rates for larger proteins.

These deviations arise from specific protein-protein interactions that are not accounted for in the simplified 2D fluid dynamics underlying the SD model. Such interactions become increasingly significant in crowded environments, where steric hindrance, hydrodynamic coupling, and other collective effects dominate. The slower rotational diffusion of larger proteins under these conditions has functional implications, influencing oligomerization kinetics and favoring smaller transmembrane segments, as seen in the prevalence of single-helix receptors like tyrosine kinases. 

Consequently, the SD model is insufficient for accurately estimating protein size or membrane viscosity in native environments. Researchers should account for steeper scaling, such as \( R^{-3} \) or stronger, particularly when interpreting rotational diffusion rates for crowded membranes or setting detection limits for techniques like NMR spectroscopy.

First, we analyzed the translational mobility of polymer crowder coils themselves as a function of the crower concentration. The FCS results showed that the translational mobility of crowder polymer coils decreased in a similar manner as rigid-body-like protein tracers (here, streptavidin) under the same crowding conditions. The translational diffusion on the FCS length scale (a few hundred nanometers) comes almost to rest for all macromolecules when the semidiluted regime is reached, approximately given by the overlap concentration for flexible polymers. Depending on the size of the polymer crowder coils or particles, this concentration is reached between 0.05 and 2.5 mM (from large to small crowders). A residual apparent slow diffusion visible in the FCS data is most probably an artifact caused by photobleaching effects. However, a fast local diffusion process of tracer molecules in the confined space, effectively built up by the polymer mesh, is still possible. According to the Huggins equation describing the bulk viscosity of concentrated polymer solutions, we obtain much higher viscosity values for larger crowding agents as compared to smaller ones at the same w/w% mass concentration. Therefore, we observed in the case of tracer diffusion that concentrated crowder solutions with larger crowding agents exhibit a much stronger deviation from the "macroscopic line" in D 0/D versus η/η0 plots as compared to smaller crowding agents. Furthermore, solutions with several crowder agents exhibit a tracer size-dependence of the diffusion reduction, which indicates a molecular sieving effect. This effect was also observed in the cytoplasm of cells and seems to be a general property of cellular crowding. With respect to absolute diffusion coefficients, we observe a reasonable agreement between measurements in cells and in synthetic crowder solutions for GFP. In fact, a reliable knowledge about ribosome diffusion, but also about the diffusion of smaller molecules under the same crowding conditions, is of specific interest for elucidating the impact of macromolecular crowding on cellular processes, like, for example, the protein biosynthesis. In this respect, molecular sieving effects and the translational mobility of the 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits, the latter important for the 70S ribosome formation, are worth to be studied, for example, in cell-free protein synthesis assays. ,, Finally, we analyzed the impact of crowding on the performance of FRET-based glucose biosensors, equipped with FP derivatives as FRET pair. Although this sensor is designed to respond to ligand binding with a conformational change, it shows also pronounced crowding-induced conformational changes. The latter is challenging, specifically if such sensors are used intracellularily. In summary, we can state that synthetic polymer crowders can mimic already some properties of cellular crowding quite well, but it can be speculated that mixtures of multiple crowder agent components (also with more rigid crowder macromolecules, like double-stranded DNA or proteins) may give even more convincing results.

dataset_item.question: How do simulations of glucose and cellobiose provide insights into solute-solvent interactions and structural characteristics in mixtures containing ethoxy-functionalized ionic liquid and water?
dataset_item.answer:
Simulations of glucose and cellobiose, as model cellulose compounds, provide valuable insights into solute-solvent interactions and structural characteristics in mixtures containing ethoxy-functionalized ionic liquid ([Me-(OEt)3-Et-IM+][OAc-]) and water. Glucose simulations focus on molecular-level interactions, including hydrogen bonding, ring puckering, and omega dihedral distributions, allowing for an isolated analysis of solvation behavior without the influence of neighboring saccharide units. Cellobiose simulations, on the other hand, examine the solvent's impact on glycosidic bond interactions and neighboring saccharide effects, shedding light on solvation around the glycosidic bond and conformational preferences.  

Using advanced molecular dynamics techniques, such as umbrella sampling and metadynamics, these simulations elucidate how the ethoxy-functionalized ionic liquid alters solvation behavior, diffusion, and cellulose structural dynamics. By reducing the complexity inherent in larger cellulose molecules, these studies provide a clearer understanding of the molecular interactions and structural characteristics that make ethoxy-functionalized ionic liquids promising candidates for biomass pretreatment.

dataset_item.question: How do tyrosine-tryptophan dyads contribute to the reduction of free radical yield in peptides after UV photolysis at pH 9?
dataset_item.answer: Tyrosine-tryptophan (YW) dyads in peptides contribute to the reduction of free radical yield after UV photolysis at pH 9 through multiple protective mechanisms. These dyads, typically separated by 6-7 Å, act as effective reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavengers and free radical quenchers. Their protective role is linked to proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) facilitated by hydrogen bonding and aromatic interactions, which accelerate the decay of tryptophan radicals (W*). Additionally, the peptide backbone influences the excited-state dynamics of tryptophan, reducing the likelihood of radical formation. The conformational flexibility of YW dyads further enhances their ability to mitigate oxidative stress, demonstrating a synergistic quenching mechanism that lowers free radical yield.

dataset_item.question: What are the limitations of Peng-Robinson equation of state when modeling energetic materials under high temperatures and pressures?
dataset_item.answer:
The Peng-Robinson equation of state (EOS) is a useful tool for modeling energetic materials like RDX and TNT under high temperatures and pressures, demonstrating reasonable accuracy in predicting properties such as density, bulk modulus, heat capacity, and phase behavior within ~10% of experimental data. However, its applicability is limited due to several factors:

1. **Sparse Experimental Data**: Validation of the EOS is hindered by the lack of reliable experimental data, particularly for critical properties, vapor pressures, high-pressure phase behavior, and melting points. For instance, data for liquid-phase RDX properties (e.g., density and heat capacity) and high-pressure melting points are largely unavailable.

2. **Sample Variability and Impurities**: Scatter in measurements arises from differences in sample preparation (e.g., single crystals vs. pressed materials) and the presence of impurities, making it challenging to achieve consistent results.

3. **Reactive Nature of Energetic Materials**: Energetic materials can undergo decomposition or chemical reactions under extreme conditions, introducing additional uncertainties that are not captured by the Peng-Robinson EOS.

4. **Extension to Higher Pressure Regimes**: While the EOS performs well up to ~500 K and ~2500 bar, its predictive accuracy at higher pressures may require fitting pure-component parameters to unreacted Hugoniot data. This is especially important for extreme conditions where phase behavior and thermodynamic properties are poorly characterized.

5. **Limited Data for Multicomponent Mixtures**: The EOS's ability to model mixtures of energetic materials is restricted due to the scarcity of experimental benchmarks for multicomponent systems.

To address these limitations, further experimental efforts are needed to characterize critical properties, phase behavior, and high-pressure data for both pure substances and mixtures. Improved fitting techniques, including Hugoniot-based adjustments, could extend the EOS's applicability to more extreme conditions.

inference_contexts: The experimental studies discussed in the previous paragraph are necessary to attain a more complete understanding of energetic materials, but the reality of the situation is that it may take decades-if not longer-for them to be completed. Given the data that is currently available, we conclude that the Peng-Robinson equation of state represents a good choice for modeling pure RDX and TNT, in addition to mixtures of these two compounds. One possibility to make the equation of state even more promising is to extend its applicability to higher pressure regimes. One way to do this may be to fit the pure-component parameters a i and b i to unreacted Hugoniot data. The Hugoniot curve describes the relation between the pressure and density discontinuities that exist across shock waves generated in energetic materials. The pressure discontinuities typically lie somewhere between a few kilobars (say, 0.5 GPa) and 20 GPa. By adjusting a i and b i to fit measurements taken along both the Hugoniot and vapor pressure curves, it may be possible to extend the pressure range over which the Peng-Robinson equation of state is applicable.

Finally, we end by pointing out that the equation of state can be used to model a multicomponent mixture of c components if the procedure described for the binary RDX/TNT system is applied to each of the c(c - 1)/2 binary pairs in the multicomponent system. The Peng-Robinson equation of state therefore provides the theoretical framework to model the thermodynamic behavior of energetic materials ranging in complexity from pure components to multiphase, multicomponent mixtures.

Although our results agree well with available data, more experimental measurements are needed to further validate the equation of state and to narrow the uncertainties in the existing data. For example, single crystals can exhibit different properties than pressed materials. Impurities (e.g.. contaminants) may have also been present in some samples. In addition, some of the scatter is undoubtedly due to the reactive nature of energetic materials. The decomposition of these substances is especially prominent at higher temperatures and pressures. Nonetheless, these difficulties must somehow be overcome to obtain the many vital pieces of information that are still currently missing. For example, the critical properties of energetic materials are almost absent in the literature, having been limited to a few theoretical studies ,, only and no experimental measurements. Vapor pressures , have been measured only to temperatures as high as about 480 K, well below the expected values of the critical temperatures (800 K and higher). Vapor pressure data, as well as density and heat capacity data, are still unavailable for liquid RDX. This is also likely true for several other compounds that exist only at high temperatures. More melting temperature measurements at pressures relevant to the Peng-Robinson equation of state are needed. Our melting point results for TNT (Figure ) lie within the experimental uncertainties of Dattelbaum et al.. but we can only compare with two data points from their study, which is oriented toward pressures that are 1 or 2 orders of magnitude greater than those in this study. Moreover, we again note that experimental results for RDX/TNT mixtures are still quite limited. For example, no data exists for the solid-phase curves in the atmospheric-pressure phase diagram of Figure . Combined with these results, we believe that the investigation of chemical reaction of ILs under high pressure is expected to contribute to the development of high-pressure synthesis techniques using ILs.

dataset_item.question: How do ionothermal synthesis methods enable the discovery of new borophosphate materials compared to traditional methods such as solid-state or microwave-assisted synthesis?
dataset_item.answer:
Ionothermal synthesis enables the discovery of new borophosphate materials by leveraging ionic liquids as solvents, which create unique ionic environments conducive to the formation of interrupted, less dense structures, including extra-large microporous frameworks. This method allows access to novel fundamental building units (FBUs) with diverse boron-to-phosphorus (B/P) ratios and dimensionalities, facilitating structural flexibility and connectivity patterns that are not achievable with traditional methods. 

In contrast, solid-state synthesis typically yields condensed structures dominated by P-O-P linkages due to its reliance on high-temperature reactions, while microwave-assisted synthesis prioritizes speed, purity, and selectivity but offers limited structural diversity. Ionothermal synthesis stands out by expanding the range of accessible architectures and enabling the design of functional borophosphates for advanced applications, such as catalysis, ion exchange, and gas storage.

In summary, a strategy for independent shape and doping control of colloidal zinc oxide nanorods was presented. This method utilizes undoped ZnO nanorod seeds as morphological templates for the synthesis of doped nanocrystals and grows a ZnO shell over the nanorods to incorporate surface segregated dopants and overcome kinetic limitations associated with synthesizing oxide nanocrystals at low temperatures. It has been shown that neither the number of repeats in the protein, nor the presence of a single cysteine residue interfered with the formation of small blue-emitting AuNCs. A possible explanation is the presence of tyrosine residues in the repeat sequence that could adsorb gold ions and therefore stabilize the gold nanoclusters. The optimized conditions for the AuNCs formation include a metal:protein ratio of 5:1 compared to the conditions previously reported for the CTPR stabilization of AuNPs in which larger ratios were used (1000:1 to 20:1) and smaller the ratios yielded smaller nanoparticles, which is in agreement with this report, where nanoclusters are obtained with smaller metal:protein ratios. Most importantly, this method was mild enough to preserve the structure of the protein and thus permitted to take advantage of the specific function of the protein scaffold. Indeed, we demonstrate that neither the synthesis of the nanoclusters, nor the nanoclusters themselves interfered with the protein binding activity. Thus, we obtained a novel bifunctional designed unit that combines the function of the designed CTPR protein scaffold on one hand and the fluorescence emission of AuNCs on the other. Finally, we demonstrate that the fluorescence signal of the protein-stabilized AuNCs is sensitive to the ligand recognition of the specific binding module. This result confirms the potential of this system to develop new sensors. The use of repeat protein scaffolds as biomolecular templates in which stability, size, and function can be tuned at will, ,, that also comprise rational methods for the synthesis of fluorescent nanoclusters preserving the protein functions, leaves a door open for further applications in the field of molecular imaging and sensing.

Uranyl compounds have a diverse crystal chemistry. This can be largely attributed to the variety of network forming elements used in the synthesis of uranyl compounds and the complex structures that these network formers often promote. Surprisingly, while the uranyl compounds of many p- and d-block network formers have been studied, there is a dearth of synthetic uranyl titanates. Single crystals of four new uranyl titanates have been grown via the flux growth method using mixed alkali halide fluxes. These compounds contain a range of titanate units including the rare TiO4 tetrahedra and even rarer TiO5 trigonal bipyramids. This rich variety of titanate units combined with the ease of their synthesis via flux growth makes uranyl titanates an exciting class of materials that warrant further exploration.

dataset_item.question: How does reducing polyvinylpyrrolidone concentration in ink formation and applying acetic acid dipping affect copper nanowire-based electrode fabrication?
dataset_item.answer: Reducing the polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) concentration to 0.5 wt% in copper nanowire (Cu NW) ink formulation, combined with a brief acetic acid dipping treatment (1-minute dip followed by 3-minute self-drying), streamlines the fabrication of flexible transparent electrodes while maintaining high performance. The lower PVP concentration enhances nanowire dispersion, reducing the complexity of post-treatment steps, and facilitates the production of ultralong Cu NWs with high aspect ratios (>3200) in just 14 hours, enabling scalable synthesis. The acetic acid dip effectively removes residual PVP without damaging the nanowires, improving surface morphology and electrical properties. The resulting electrodes exhibit excellent metrics, including a sheet resistance of 25 Ω/sq and 90% transmittance at 550 nm, comparable to state-of-the-art electrodes. These electrodes are demonstrated to be suitable for industrial applications, such as self-capacitance touch sensors, due to their high performance and efficient fabrication process.

Increasing the RR from 93% to 99% results in an increase in the (010) structural coherence in the nanowire longitudinal domain by more than a factor of 4. The overlapping of steric (or electrosteric) and depletion mechanisms for colloidal stabilization of oxidized carbon nanotubes (plasma-oxidized SWCNTs and MWCNTs and chemically oxidized MWCNTs) by amphiphilic PF127 is attained through a matching of the polymer chemical structure (containing hydrophobic PPO and hydrophilic PEO moieties), and its consequent conformational behavior in solution, with the nanocarbon high aspect ratio one-dimensional morphology. For these samples, regardless of the surface charge (ζ potential), the degree of oxidation, and the nanotube diameter and length, colloidal stability in a 0.9% NaCl solution is attained through (i) the wrapping of PF127 around the nanotubes induced by hydrophobic interactions between the PPO moiety and nonoxidized regions of the graphitic sheets (i.e.. polyaromatic regions with sp2 carbon hybridization) and the consequent exposure of hydrophilic PEO moieties to the medium and (ii) the manifestation of repulsive depletion forces for PF127 concentrations superior to 1.0%. Above this concentration, the CNT colloidal stabilization also has little dependence on the PF127 concentration. The same PF127 was not able to colloidally stabilize graphene oxide (chemically oxidized) through steric-based mechanisms due to the small size of PEO moieties in comparison with the large-sized sheets of GO (lateral size of up to 20 μm), thus preventing a suitable steric repulsion for GO sheets. This aspect also explains the absence of stabilizing depletion forces for the GO-PF127 system, in which there is not a proper dimensional and stereochemical matching between the large (i.e.. GO sheets) and small (i.e.. PF127 micelles) particles present in the liquid. On the other hand, long-chain PEG (MW 35000) was unable to colloidally stabilize CNTs due to the absence of significant short-range interactions (e.g.. hydrophobic) that could result in steric-based mechanisms of stabilization. In addition, the absence of a proper dimensional and stereochemical matching between the long-chain PEG 35000 and the high aspect ratio one-dimensional morphology of CNTs did not lead to the manifestation of stabilizing repulsive depletion forces as well. However, large-sized sheets of GO in the presence of PEG 35000 can be colloidally stabilized through repulsive depletion forces, which strongly depend on the polymer concentration, as shown by the stabilization attained for PEG concentrations from 5.0 wt %. The overlapping of these stabilization mechanisms (steric + depletion) observed for CNTs led to a much higher colloidal stabilization in comparison with that attained for the GO-PEG system. For applications in media with low ionic strengths, electric stabilization attained through nanocarbon oxidation can provide a suitable colloidal stability. SLA can be undertaken to fabricate an electrode support produced from nonconductive polymers; however, a major issue associated with this fabrication route is that electrode supports must be conductive. , Hence, when SLA is utilized to create electrode supports, an extra step to deposit a conductive layer must be carried out. For example, Ding and co-workers 3D-printed a rectangular-shaped meshed electrode by SLA using a commercial available PlasClear resin for the OER. Because of the fact that the 3D-printed electrode was made from an insulating material, a number of steps were needed in order to achieve a conductive support for the deposition of the active OER catalyst. First, sensitization and activation of the electrode surface was done by alternatively dipping the electrodes, for 5 min each, into two commercially available electroless solutions called "electroless copper solution C", containing 5 wt % HCl and 5 wt % SnCl2, and "electroless copper solution D", consisting of 5 wt % HCl and 5 wt % PdCl2, both additionally with sodium dodecyl sulfate surfactant. Then the electrode was dried in an oven at 60 °C, immersed in 5% H2SO4 for 5 min, and then rinsed with deionized water. The final step to create the conductive layer consisted of immersing the electrode into a commercial electroless solution containing NiCl2, NaPO2H2, C4H4Na2O4, and HF at a temperature of 97 °C for 30 min in order to create a NiP conductive layer. At this point during the study, Ding and co-workers determined that the OER performance of the conductive NiP/PlasClear 3D-printed electrode was 1.53 V vs relative hydrogen electrode (RHE) at the benchmark current density of 10 mA cm-2. This OER performance is already very impressive as a potential of 1.53 V vs RHE is equal to an OER overpotential of 300 mV, which is already rivalling that of the state-of-the-art OER catalysts; RuO2 and IrO2, the best-known OER catalysts, exhibit overpotential values of ca. 300 mV at 10 mA cm-2. ,

dataset_item.question: What factors contribute to the structural diversity observed in uranyl titanates synthesized using flux growth methods?
dataset_item.answer: The structural diversity observed in uranyl titanates synthesized via flux growth methods arises from the flexibility of titanium coordination geometries, including rare TiO<sub>4</sub> tetrahedra and TiO<sub>5</sub> trigonal bipyramids, as well as the adaptability of uranyl polyhedra. These factors enable the formation of complex crystal structures. The use of mixed alkali halide fluxes further facilitates the incorporation of these diverse titanate units, promoting unique structural arrangements and enabling the synthesis of multiple distinct compounds. This versatility underscores the potential of uranyl titanates as a rich class of materials for further exploration and development.

In this paper we have made seminal reflectance infrared observations of uranyl nitrate during the desiccation of the hexahydrate to the trihydrate, possibly even to the dihydrate. Time-resolved infrared reflectance spectroscopy was employed and proved a superior approach to such dehydration studies. We report direct observation of phase transformation from UO2(NO3)2(H2O)6 to UO2(NO3)3(H2O)3 through high resolution reflectance IR measurements and in situ optical microscopy imaging, with absolute confirmation of the phase mixture via XRD. The study confirms previous investigations' findings that with decreasing relative humidity, the UO2(NO3)2(H2O)6 will recrystallize as UNT accompanied by a structural change. The infrared reflectance spectrum can be used as a telltale of the phase state with the hexahydrate having a single reststrahlen reflectance band at 949 cm-1 and the trihydrate a weaker doublet at 966/957 cm-1. There are very significant shifts throughout the 1200-1600 cm-1 region as well and the overall reflectivity increases with the formation of the matte powder. DFT calculations confirm the peak splitting of the uranyl asymmetric stretch mode in UNT that can serve as a signature of UNT during the UNH-UNT transition. The frequencies in the range 1200-1600 cm-1 (largely due to nitrate ligands) show significant normal mode changes which help explain the growth of the peaks at 1286 and 1549 cm-1 and the disappearance of the peaks at 1344 and 1462 cm-1 during the UNH-UNT transition. Further study of the UNH-UNT phase transition, particularly of the shifts for the infrared and Raman frequencies, is clearly warranted.

dataset_item.question: How does the partial molar volume method refine the determination of methylene component volumes in lipids compared to the apparent molar volume method?
dataset_item.answer:
The partial molar volume method refines the determination of methylene component volumes in lipids by calculating the derivative of the total lipid volume with respect to the number of methylenes, allowing the methylene volume to vary with chain length rather than assuming it is constant, as in the apparent molar volume method. This approach is conceptually superior as it adheres to rigorous physical chemistry principles, ensuring volume conservation across all lipid components and accounting for molecular connectivity constraints.

Unlike the apparent molar volume method, which yields a single average methylene volume across chain lengths, the partial molar method captures subtle variations in methylene volume, such as slightly higher values for longer chains, as demonstrated with n-alkanes. Additionally, the partial molar approach reveals temperature-dependent trends, such as increasing methylene volumes with rising temperature and a changing methyl-to-methylene volume ratio. It also resolves inconsistencies in head group volume assumptions, showing a decrease in head group volume with temperature, which contrasts with fixed-ratio approximations used in earlier analyses.

dataset_item.question: How does the coordination of cellulose hydroxyl groups with hydrated zinc cations influence cellulose solubility in zinc chloride hydrates?
dataset_item.answer: Cellulose dissolves in zinc chloride hydrates (ZnCl₂·R·H₂O, R ≈ 3) due to the coordination of its hydroxyl groups with hydrated zinc cations. The primary hydroxyl groups of cellulose directly bind to zinc in the first coordination shell, integrating cellulose into the ionic liquid structure. Secondary interactions occur between the ring hydroxyl groups and higher coordination shells, further stabilizing the dissolved state. This solubility is restricted to a narrow hydration range (approximately 3 ≤ R ≤ 9), as excess water completes both the first and second hydration shells around the zinc cation. When these hydration shells are fully formed, the zinc cations are no longer available for coordination with cellulose hydroxyl groups, leading to precipitation. Additionally, the ionic liquid environment, characterized by its nonpolar nature and hydrogen bond-donating ability, enhances cellulose-zinc interactions, facilitating dissolution.

dataset_item.question: What structural modifications in small molecules and polymers improve electrochemical performance of conjugated carbonyl compounds in rechargeable batteries?
dataset_item.answer:
Structural modifications in small molecules and polymers enhance the electrochemical performance of conjugated carbonyl compounds in rechargeable batteries by addressing challenges such as dissolution, poor conductivity, charge kinetics, and energy density. Key strategies include:  

1. **Molecular Design**:  
   - Increasing conjugation to stabilize redox-active carbonyl groups and improve electronic conductivity.  
   - Incorporating electron-withdrawing groups to raise redox potentials and enhance energy density.  
   - Designing rigid molecular frameworks to reduce dissolution in electrolytes while maintaining structural stability during cycling.  

2. **Polymerization and Composite Formation**:  
   - Polymerizing small molecules into extended networks to improve conductivity and reduce solubility.  
   - Forming composites with conductive additives (e.g., carbon) to address intrinsic conductivity limitations and optimize electrode composition (<40% carbon content).  

3. **Tailored Electrolytes**:  
   - Developing weakly coordinating solvents and compatible electrolytes to minimize dissolution and enhance charge-discharge reversibility.  

4. **Hybrid and Flexible Designs**:  
   - Coupling n-type carbonyl compounds with p-type materials to create all-organic battery systems.  
   - Designing flexible molecular structures to accommodate large ion radii in sodium and potassium-ion batteries, addressing migration kinetics and volumetric energy density.  

5. **Molecular Packing and Interface Control**:  
   - Optimizing molecular packing (tap density) and electrode composition to improve volumetric energy density.  
   - Controlling interfacial properties to facilitate ion transport and enhance charge kinetics.  

6. **Mechanistic Studies and Future Research**:  
   - Conducting detailed studies to clarify charge-discharge mechanisms and establish structure-property relationships for enhanced performance.  
   - Exploring hybrid designs and advanced materials to achieve safer, higher-density, and more stable energy storage solutions.  

These modifications collectively enable the design of high-performance organic electrodes while addressing critical challenges related to conductivity, dissolution, and ion migration.

dataset_item.question: How does SbCl5 concentration influence the formation of oxidized states of propylenedioxythiophene-benzothiadiazole-propylenedioxythiophene molecule?
dataset_item.answer:
The concentration of SbCl5 plays a pivotal role in determining the oxidation pathway and the resulting oxidized states of the propylenedioxythiophene-benzothiadiazole-propylenedioxythiophene (ProDOT-BTD-ProDOT) molecule. At low concentrations, SbCl5 facilitates stoichiometric oxidation, leading to the formation of a radical cation (1e- oxidation state) characterized by cyanine-like electronic configuration and delocalized spin density. However, this radical cation is unstable and can decompose into a monoketone-terminated product due to nucleophilic attack on the oxidized sulfide groups.  

At high SbCl5 concentrations, the oxidation pathway shifts to direct two-electron oxidation via chloronium ion transfer involving SbCl4+, resulting in the formation of a dication with quinoidal character. High-resolution mass spectrometry confirms the presence of a chloride adduct intermediate, supporting the chloronium ion transfer mechanism as distinct from the sequential oxidation observed in electrochemical processes. This highlights that SbCl5 concentration not only dictates whether oxidation proceeds stoichiometrically or via chloronium ion transfer but also enables control over redox states critical for electrochromic applications.  

Thus, SbCl5-mediated chemical oxidation demonstrates unique pathways based on oxidant concentration, offering valuable insights for tailoring oxidation states in redox-active materials.

dataset_item.question: How does rapid thermal annealing at 800 °C under hydrogen and nitrogen atmosphere influence the formation of cobalt silicide layers at the interface of cobalt and silicon?
dataset_item.answer: Rapid thermal annealing at 800 °C for 20 minutes under a hydrogen and nitrogen atmosphere facilitates the formation of a cobalt silicide (CoSi₂) layer at the interface between an evaporated cobalt film and a silicon substrate. This process drives interdiffusion and reaction between cobalt and silicon, resulting in a well-defined crystalline CoSi₂ layer. Excess cobalt that remains unreacted after silicide formation is subsequently removed using a piranha solution, ensuring a clean and controlled interface. This method is significant for applications in advanced semiconductor technologies, such as transistor fabrication, due to its precision in silicide layer formation.

dataset_item.question: How does the oxidation flow reactor minimize the loss of semivolatile and intermediate volatility species during air sampling?
dataset_item.answer: The oxidation flow reactor (OFR) minimizes the loss of semivolatile and intermediate volatility organic compounds (SVOCs and IVOCs) during air sampling through a combination of optimized design features and operational controls. The OFR employs a short, large-diameter inlet (18 inches long, 2 inches in diameter) to reduce surface interactions and particle deposition, which are critical for preserving these "sticky" compounds. This inlet is further equipped with a coarse-grid mesh screen to prevent turbulence and block debris, such as insects, ensuring stable and unobstructed flow conditions. To account for potential diffusional losses and repartitioning effects, the reactor utilizes a lights-off mode, enabling direct comparisons with bypass measurements for accurate quantification. These integrated measures collectively maintain the integrity of SVOCs and IVOCs, facilitating reliable analysis of secondary organic aerosol (SOA) formation.

dataset_item.question: How does calcination temperature influence the fractal indices spectra and their relationship with reaction activity in Cu/ZSM-5 catalysts?
dataset_item.answer:
Calcination temperature plays a critical role in influencing the fractal indices spectra of Cu/ZSM-5 catalysts, which directly correlate with their catalytic activity in phenol oxidation. Higher calcination temperatures lead to increased structural complexity, as demonstrated by changes in interfacial fractal dimensions (\( D_{[BW]} \)) and box-counting fractal dimensions (\( D_{[B+BW]} \)), derived from SEM images and Cu EDS elemental analysis. 

Threshold-dependent analysis reveals that \( D_{[BW]} \) at high thresholds (\( m > 200 \)) and transitions around \( m \approx 40 \) are strongly linked to catalytic performance. Additionally, focal fractal indices (\( D_{ff} \)) in the range of 2.595–2.64 provide further evidence of the relationship between catalyst morphology and reaction activity. Complementary structural insights are obtained from nitrogen adsorption measurements, which highlight surface fractal dimensions. 

These fractal metrics collectively illustrate the impact of calcination temperature on the morphological complexity and catalytic behavior of Cu/ZSM-5 catalysts, emphasizing its importance in optimizing reaction kinetics.

dataset_item.question: What adjustments to the SMTB-Q model parameters could improve alignment with forces and energies calculated using density functional theory?
dataset_item.answer:
To improve alignment of the SMTB-Q model parameters with forces and energies calculated using density functional theory (DFT), the optimization process should incorporate both energy and force data derived from DFT calculations. Specifically, the parameter fitting should target configurations near local minima on the DFT potential energy surface (PES), ensuring that these minima correspond to those in the SMTB-Q model. Incorporating forces into the objective function during parametrization will enhance the model’s ability to capture the gradient of the PES accurately, thereby improving predictive accuracy for atomic interactions.

Additionally, introducing angular-dependent terms to the SMTB-Q model can address deficiencies related to covalent bonding, as these terms are critical for stabilizing configurations and achieving more realistic representations of bonding interactions. This adjustment is particularly important for systems where angular dependencies significantly influence the structural and energetic behavior. 

These refinements will allow the SMTB-Q model to more closely align with DFT results while maintaining computational efficiency, making it well-suited for applications such as generating plausible surface reconstructions (e.g., low-energy ⟨111⟩ steps on rutile (110)) before further refinement via DFT optimization.

Nitrogen monoxide (NO) emissions during the combustion of rapeseed oil methyl ester (ROME) are significantly influenced by variations in spray cone angle and swirl air angle. Optimizing these angles enhances fuel-air mixing, improves combustion efficiency, reduces flame temperature, and suppresses thermal NO formation.

A spray cone angle of 60° was found to yield the lowest NO emissions, reducing them by 6%, 3%, and 10% compared to 30°, 45°, and 90° spray angles, respectively. Similarly, a swirl air angle of 45° demonstrated optimal performance, lowering NO emissions by 13%, 10%, 7%, and 16% compared to swirl air angles of 30°, 37.5°, 52.5°, and 60°, respectively.

The 45° swirl air angle further reduces the divergent angle, increases flame length, lowers exhaust gas temperature, and suppresses thermal NO formation. These conditions improve fuel-air mixing and combustion stability. Additionally, air staging techniques can enhance NO reduction by extending flame length and reducing exhaust gas temperature. During transitional combustion phases, prompt NO dominates, but under optimized conditions, thermal NO formation is minimized.

Thus, the combination of a 60° spray cone angle and a 45° swirl air angle represents the most effective configuration for reducing NO emissions during ROME combustion.

### Task 1: Summary of the Purpose of the Paper
The paper investigates the formation and reduction of nitrogen monoxide (NO) during the combustion of rapeseed oil methyl ester (ROME) in a semi-industrial boiler. It focuses on characterizing NO formation under various operating conditions (e.g., combustion pressure, air swirl angle, spray cone angle) and determining the contributions of thermal and prompt NO. The study further evaluates the potential of air-staging techniques to reduce NO emissions without negatively affecting boiler operation, while also examining the effects of fuel spray patterns and air dynamics on NO reduction.

---

### Task 2: Classification of the Purpose
The purpose of the paper emphasizes **"<result>"**, as the research is primarily focused on analyzing and reporting the observed outcomes related to NO formation and reduction under specific operating conditions, as well as the effectiveness of mitigation techniques.

---

1. What are the dominant factors influencing nitrogen monoxide (NO) formation during the combustion of rapeseed oil methyl ester (ROME) in semi-industrial boilers?
2. How do combustion parameters, such as pressure, excess air, exhaust gas temperature, spray cone angle, and swirl angle, affect the levels of NO emissions?
3. What is the relative contribution of thermal NO and prompt NO to total NO emissions during different combustion phases (e.g., steady-state vs. startup)?
4. Can air-staging techniques effectively reduce NO emissions without compromising boiler efficiency or operation?
5. How do variations in fuel spray patterns and air dynamics influence NO formation and reduction during combustion?
6. What are the optimal burner operating conditions (e.g., swirl angle, spray pattern, combustion pressure) for minimizing NO emissions?
7. How does the post-flame zone environment contribute to the formation of thermal NO, and what strategies can mitigate this effect?

dataset_item.question: What are the effects of integrating thieno [2,3-f] benzofuran segments into benzodithiophene-based donor-acceptor copolymers on microstructure and morphology of bulk heterojunction blend films?
dataset_item.answer: Integrating thieno [2,3-f] benzofuran (TBF) segments into benzodithiophene (BDT)-based donor-acceptor copolymers significantly enhances the microstructure and morphology of bulk heterojunction (BHJ) blend films. The inclusion of TBF segments improves crystallinity and miscibility, promoting ordered molecular packing and maintaining a favorable face-on orientation. This integration reduces single-component self-aggregation, resulting in balanced phase separation that facilitates superior exciton dissociation and minimizes charge recombination. These microstructural enhancements lead to higher power conversion efficiencies (PCEs), with values exceeding 10% in various terpolymer/acceptor systems and reaching over 12% in optimized devices. Additionally, fill factors as high as 76% highlight the improved charge transport and extraction capabilities. The strategy demonstrates universal applicability for achieving high-performance polymer solar cells and shows promise for large-area device fabrication.

dataset_item.question: How do different vehicle electrification scenarios, such as private electric vehicles with controlled charging and shared automated electric vehicles, impact greenhouse gas emissions, peak electricity demand, and total cost of ownership?
dataset_item.answer: Vehicle electrification scenarios significantly impact greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, peak electricity demand, and total cost of ownership (TCO). Private electric vehicles (EVs) with uncontrolled charging reduce GHG emissions by 46% compared to gasoline vehicles. Implementing controlled charging further improves emissions reductions to 49%, decreases peak electricity demand by 53%, and lowers TCO by 38%. Shared automated electric vehicles (SAEVs), which fully manage charging and serve all mobility needs currently addressed by light-duty vehicles, offer even greater benefits. SAEVs reduce GHG emissions by 70%, decrease TCO by 74%, and lower peak electricity demand by 47% compared to private EVs with uncontrolled charging. The widespread adoption of SAEVs could eliminate over 80 GW of peak electricity demand, equivalent to more than half of the current U.S. natural gas combustion turbine capacity. These outcomes depend on the share of trips served by SAEVs and the prevalence of controlled charging among private EVs, emphasizing the importance of strategic adoption and infrastructure planning to maximize environmental and economic benefits.

dataset_item.question: What factors contributed to changes in water withdrawals for oilseed crops between 1995 and 2010?
dataset_item.answer:
Between 1995 and 2010, water withdrawals for oilseed crops increased due to several interconnected factors. A key driver was the 79% expansion in irrigated oilseed acreage, largely influenced by rising commodity prices and growing global demand, particularly from Chinese industries and households. This demand led to increased soybean exports to China, which played a dominant role in driving water use. The proportion of irrigated land also rose significantly, from 37% to 56%, reflecting greater irrigation adoption to meet production needs.

While domestic technological advancements in irrigation efficiency helped mitigate water withdrawals, their impact was overshadowed by external demand factors. Before the 2008 financial crisis, external interrelational effects had a mixed impact, mitigating water use increases in some areas. However, post-crisis, these effects shifted to amplifying water use due to heightened export-driven demand. Domestic final demand contributed minimally to water withdrawal changes during the post-2005 period, as external pressures, particularly exports to China, remained the dominant influence.

dataset_item.question: How do environmental factors such as temperature and water salinity influence the degradation and toxicity of light Louisiana crude oil in marine ecosystems?
dataset_item.answer: Environmental factors such as temperature and water salinity play critical roles in the degradation and toxicity of light Louisiana crude oil in marine ecosystems. The Deepwater Horizon oil spill, which released 507 million liters of oil into the Gulf of Mexico, highlighted these effects. Surface water temperatures (10–33 °C) accelerated microbial degradation and evaporation of volatile compounds, while colder deep-sea temperatures (4 °C) in the aphotic zone slowed degradation, prolonging oil persistence and ecological impacts. Salinity gradients influenced oil dispersion and emulsification, impacting how oil behaved and interacted with marine organisms. Additionally, chemical dispersants, applied both at the surface and subsea during response efforts, enhanced oil dissolution in surface waters but increased toxicity in deep-sea environments. These factors, combined with the spill's large scale—affecting 180,000 km² of surface waters, 2,000 km of shoreline, and leading to the closure of over 20 million hectares of fishing areas—demonstrated the importance of temperature and salinity in determining oil behavior, degradation rates, and toxicity in marine ecosystems.

dataset_item.question: What specific methods were used to synthesize PbSe nanocrystals and ensure their air stability?
dataset_item.answer:
PbSe nanocrystals were synthesized using two distinct methods, each leveraging established protocols. The first method, adapted from Steckel et al., involved preparing a lead precursor by reacting lead acetate trihydrate with oleic acid in 1-octadecene under inert conditions. A selenium precursor, prepared by dissolving selenium powder in diphenylphosphine and trioctylphosphine, was injected into the heated lead precursor solution at 180°C. The reaction was quenched using a methanol/butanol mixture, and the nanocrystals were purified through repeated precipitation and redispersion in toluene. The second method, based on Campos et al., utilized lead oleate as the lead precursor, synthesized separately, and a selenourea precursor (N-cyclohexylpyrrolidine-1-carboselenoamide). The selenourea precursor was injected into the lead oleate solution in hexadecane at 100°C, followed by precipitation and washing steps to purify the nanocrystals.

To ensure air stability, both synthesis methods included a post-synthetic treatment. Excess lead oleate dissolved in toluene was added to the nanocrystal solution, followed by dropwise addition of sodium iodide dissolved in methanol. This treatment created a hybrid ligand shell that improved the nanocrystals' stability under ambient conditions. The ligand density, nanocrystal size, and surface modifications were characterized using FT-IR and NMR spectroscopy, while structural and compositional analyses were performed using TEM, EDX, and XPS.

dataset_item.question: What structural modifications to dihydroxyphthalazine compounds can enhance redox potential, electron transfer rate, and cycling stability for aqueous redox flow batteries?
dataset_item.answer: Structural modifications to dihydroxyphthalazine (DHP) compounds that enhance redox potential, electron transfer rate, and cycling stability for aqueous redox flow batteries include nitrogen incorporation into the quinoid core, targeted functionalization, and computationally guided substitutions. Introducing nitrogen into the quinone base structure increases electron affinity, boosting redox potential by up to 342 mV compared to naphthoquinone and surpassing benzoquinones. Functionalization with methyl or methoxy groups blocks reactive sites, preventing parasitic side reactions such as Michael addition, thereby improving cycling stability while maintaining fast charge transfer kinetics. Computational studies suggest that succinimidyl substitutions further optimize redox potential (>1 V vs. SHE), enhance hydrophilicity for improved solubility, and provide resilience against nucleophilic attacks. These modifications balance high electron affinity, efficient electron transfer, and structural stability, making DHPs sustainable and high-performance catholyte candidates for aqueous redox flow batteries.

dataset_item.question: How does structural uniformity of support materials influence catalytic performance of atomically dispersed noble metals?
dataset_item.answer:
The structural uniformity of support materials plays a critical role in enhancing the catalytic performance of atomically dispersed noble metals by ensuring well-defined and consistent metal-support interactions. Uniform crystalline supports, such as zeolites, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), and covalent organic frameworks (COFs), provide nearly identical bonding sites for the dispersed metal atoms. This homogeneity minimizes heterogeneous bonding environments, leading to optimized reactivity and catalytic activity in reactions like hydrogenation, dehydrogenation, ethylene oligomerization, propane dehydrogenation, and the water-gas shift reaction.  

The uniformity of the support materials simplifies spectroscopic characterization techniques, such as X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF STEM), which can accurately represent unique structures rather than averages of heterogeneous configurations. Additionally, the well-defined nature of these supports enhances the precision of density functional theory (DFT) modeling, enabling deeper insights into catalytic mechanisms and electronic properties. These advancements collectively contribute to superior catalytic performance and a more profound understanding of reaction pathways compared to catalysts supported on heterogeneous materials like metal oxides or carbon.

dataset_item.question: How does Chebyshev decomposition-based quantum master equation compare to hierarchical equations of motion in modeling population dynamics of a dissipative two-site system under different reorganization energies?
dataset_item.answer:
The Chebyshev decomposition-based quantum master equation (QME) and hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) exhibit comparable accuracy in modeling the population dynamics of a dissipative two-site system at low reorganization energies (λ). Both methods predict the transient and long-time dynamics effectively, with good agreement observed for systems with equal and unequal site energies. 

At intermediate λ values (20–100 cm⁻¹), deviations arise due to the second-order perturbative nature of the Chebyshev QME. These deviations are most pronounced in the amplitude and frequency of oscillations, indicating a breakdown of the underlying perturbation theory. Nevertheless, the Chebyshev QME accurately captures the long-time thermal equilibrium, although it approaches this state faster than HEOM, leading to discrepancies in transient dynamics.

At high reorganization energies (λ = 500 cm⁻¹), the Chebyshev QME retains qualitative correctness but reaches equilibrium more quickly than HEOM, with noticeable deviations in the transient dynamics. For systems with unequal site energies, both methods converge to similar equilibrium populations, though small deviations are observed due to the perturbative nature of the Chebyshev approach.

A key advantage of the Chebyshev QME is its ability to handle nonsmooth spectral densities effectively, where HEOM struggles due to its reliance on Lorentzian decompositions. Additionally, the Markovian limit of the Chebyshev QME shows mixed performance: it improves for unequal site energies but underperforms for equal site energies. Ensemble-average wave packet dynamics, while agreeing with HEOM for equal site energies, fail to reproduce the correct thermal equilibrium for biased systems. Overall, the Chebyshev QME offers a computationally efficient alternative to HEOM, particularly in scenarios involving nonsmooth spectral densities, but its accuracy diminishes as λ increases due to its perturbative foundation.

Wave function ansatzes based on linear combinations of moving FWGs guided by the TDVP provide powerful techniques for modeling nonadiabatic dynamics of both isolated and open molecular systems from first principles. We highlighted several features crucial for performance of this set of techniques. First, among possible electronic-state representations, the MCA representation is particularly attractive. It has all the advantages of the diabatic representation and can be directly obtained from electronic structure calculations as the regular adiabatic representation. The only caveat of the MCA use is the nonanalytic parametrization of the wave function. To avoid problems with the system energy conservation, this feature requires using the stationary action version of the TDVP. Second, if individual nuclear Gaussians are propagated classically (or generally independently) the TDVP application to the FWGs' amplitudes does not conserve the system energy. This nonconservation is especially pronounced when several Gaussians interfere in the process of dynamics, and it can be related to basis set incompleteness, which is unavoidable in practice. The only obvious way to conserve the energy is to propagate parameters of individual Gaussians quantum mechanically according to the TDVP in the action formulation. Unfortunately, this makes equations of motion for Gaussian parameters coupled and increases the computational complexity of the overall scheme. Third, to address the increase of the wave function complexity with time, a systematic extension of the number of nuclear FWGs is needed. Rigorous generalizations of two intuitive schemes for nuclear basis set extension (spawning and cloning) have been discussed. The spawning technique can be rooted in perturbative estimates of population flow between electronic states, while the cloning approach uses estimates of the "decoherence strain" acting on FWGs moving on different PESs. Both schemes can be successfully used for either classically propagated FWGs (e.g.. AIMS and MCE) or fully quantum TDVP schemes (e.g.. vMCG). Finally, a straightforward generalization of the TDVP to the Liouville equation in order to use FWGs to simulate a reduced density of an open system encounters two fundamental problems: (1) the total energy of the subsystem in a mixed state is not conserved in the limit of vanishing coupling to the environment, and (2) the subsystem population is not conserved even in the situations when only the energy exchange is allowed. dataset_item.question: How do inkbottle-shaped and slit-like kerogen nanopores influence CO2 and CH4 adsorption capacities and selectivity under varying conditions?
dataset_item.answer:
Inkbottle-shaped and slit-like kerogen nanopores significantly influence CO₂ and CH₄ adsorption capacities and selectivity under varying conditions. CO₂ is preferentially adsorbed over CH₄ due to stronger interactions with kerogen surfaces. Both pore types enhance adsorption capacities, with inkbottle-shaped pores being particularly effective at improving CO₂/CH₄ selectivity. Higher pressures and lower temperatures increase the adsorption of both gases; however, excessive CO₂ injection pressure can reduce selectivity despite increasing CO₂ uptake. The presence of CO₂ also suppresses CH₄ adsorption, highlighting competitive adsorption dynamics.

Confinement effects within nanopores promote dual adsorption mechanisms—micropore filling and monolayer adsorption—driven by the supercritical state of gases and microscale pore geometries. These effects are more pronounced in micropores and small mesopores, enhancing adsorption efficiency. The interplay between pore geometry, pressure, temperature, and gas states underscores the need for optimizing CO₂ injection pressure and geological parameters to balance sequestration goals and enhanced gas recovery in shale reservoirs.

The study employs grand canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulations to explore the effects of temperature, pressure, and pore size on competitive adsorption and confinement effects. dataset_item.question: How does prior experience with rapid water quality tools influence the accuracy of measurements made by citizen scientists?
dataset_item.answer: Prior experience with rapid water quality tools significantly enhances the accuracy of measurements made by citizen scientists, particularly for nitrate and phosphate tests. Experienced and expert users consistently demonstrated higher accuracy in interpreting colorimetric test strips for nitrates (72.2–100%) and phosphates (56.8–87.8%) compared to inexperienced users, who were more prone to overestimating contaminant concentrations. However, accuracy varied by test type—immunochromatographic atrazine strips showed the lowest accuracy overall (14–74.3%), with experienced users performing worst (14%) due to manufacturer defects and challenges in interpretation. All user groups struggled with atrazine measurements, highlighting the impact of tool design on accuracy. Inexperienced users, often younger and less familiar with analytical techniques, showed greater variability in measurements, underscoring the importance of training and preparation of technical materials to improve reliability. These findings emphasize the critical role of user experience, robust tool design, and targeted training in enhancing the accuracy and reliability of citizen science initiatives.

### 1. **Summary of the Paper's Purpose**  
The paper aims to evaluate the accuracy of citizen scientists in using rapid water quality assessment tools to measure agrichemical contamination in water resources. Specifically, it investigates (1) how accurate citizen scientists' observations are compared to laboratory methods, and (2) how prior experience with water quality tools affects the accuracy of their measurements. The study further identifies patterns of error, such as overestimation of contaminant concentrations, and examines differences in tool performance across experience levels. The ultimate goal is to inform the design of more effective citizen science campaigns by accounting for participant background and tool selection.
