inference_contexts: In this work, the reaction pathways upon DEA were studied for the potential radiosensitizer SeCNdU. The results indicate that SeCNdU can be considered as a pseudo-halouridine composed of an electron-affinic -SeCN side group and a nucleobase moiety. Eleven dissociation channels were observed within the detection limit of the experiment. The highest ion yield was obtained for (SeU-yl) -, which is a radical and thus highly reactive. A comparable ion yield was observed for the cyano anion. The yields of the other fragment anions are at least 1 order of magnitude smaller. Besides the negatively charged fragments directly obtained in the experiments, neutral counterparts were investigated by calculations. These include radicals such as SeU-yl and molecules such as H2O and HCN. One of the main questions, whether a bond cleavage of the Se-CN bond or the C5-Se bond occurs more efficiently, was solved because the Se-CN bond was far more efficiently cleaved with 5 out of 11 fragmentation pathways and the 2 most intense dissociation channels among them. Cleavage of the C5-Se bond also occurs upon DEA; however, only two channels were observed with low ion yields. Remarkably, all reactions exhibit a 0 eV threshold in the experimental data, which is in full agreement with the calculated thermochemical thresholds. The calculations showed that all DEA channels are exothermic at the present experimental conditions. Few reactions have exothermicities of more than 3 eV. Such behavior also results from the exceptionally high EA of most of fragments released with an excess electron. The anion (SeU-yl)- with the most intense ion yield is formed upon simple cleavage reactions. The formation of CN-, the other abundant anion, is based on simple bond cleavage, while two bonds have to be cleaved and one formed to produce (SeU-yl)-. Most other dissociation processes involve multiple bond cleavages, which are also accompanied by structural rearrangement. The formation of C4N2O2H2CN- represents such a process because the selenium must be cut out of the molecule in order to form a U-yl-CN bond. Moreover, the resonance profiles of C4N2O2H2Se -, C9N2O3H6Se -, and C9N2O5H10Se - showed a very similar structure, suggesting one common electronic state of the TNI.

In summary, methane is conventionally considered an inert molecule because of its strong C-H bonds, and harsh conditions, especially high temperature, are generally required to activate it and to achieve a high conversion. We managed to make methane react by conducting solar-energy-mediated photochemical reactions with N-haloimides. Similar to conventional organic reactions of functionalized reagents that are conducted in glass vessels, and in contrast to the general features of its industrial route, this methane functionalization reaction proceeds under very mild conditions, circumventing the use of catalysts, high temperature, high methane pressure and reactive reagents. The success of this strategy relies on the in situ generation of reactive N-centered radicals that reacted selectively with methane with a much lower energy barrier upon illuminating the radical precursors with solar light and on the higher oxidation ability of these radicals that led to and/or enhanced the exothermicity of these halogenation reactions. Detailed studies are underway to increase the productivity and to further reduce the cost of this technology by, for example, omitting the use of organic solvents.

In this work, we describe mechanisms of the Pd (II)-controlled disulfide/thiolate interconversion for l-cystine, cystamine, dl-homocystine and 3,3′-dithiodipropionic acid in aqueous solutions. We specifically address the question of different reactivity of homologous disulfides toward Pd2+. We see this different reactivity in different capacities of considered homologous disulfides to stabilize forming S,S′-binuclear complexes, which are believed to be key intermediates toward interconversion products. In case of homocystine and 3,3′-dithiodipropionic acid, formation of the S,S′-binuclear complexes leads to cleavage of the disulfide bond, while we observe formation of the S,N-binuclear and S,N,S′,N′-tetranuclear complexes with the preserved S-S bond for the l-cystine and cystamine ligands. Formation of the S,S′-binuclear complexes increases the d(S-S) bond length by 5%, and the redistribution of charges with Sδ--Sδ- in the original disulfide on Sδ+-Sδ- occurs in the complex. We find that the greater the magnitude of Δδ in S,S′-binuclear complex, the higher the likelihood of disproportionation. Conditions, under which disproportionation takes place, include formation of redox-resistant S,S′-binuclear disulfide complex and the disulfide bond being open for the nucleophilic substitution by water.

The DART ion source associated with time-of-flight mass spectrometry can highlight the role played by a stabilizer such as the Irgafos 168 during the thermal or UV treatment of an industrial polyethylene. The accurate mass measurement results obtained from the analyzed pellets show that under thermal treatment the Irgafos 168 reacts either by decomposing the generated hydroperoxyde or by limiting the formation of peroxide radicals by trapping the oxygen present into the bulk of the polymer. In the absence of Irgafos, the polymer degradation scheme involving homolytic bond cleavage of the polyethylene and a β-scission of its corresponding hydroperoxyde is confirmed by DART-TOF MS analysis. Under UV exposure, the reactivity of the stabilizer toward the treatment appears to be different. This one seems to react not only toward the oxidation mechanism as described above but also toward the UV radiation by an intermolecular breaking that could prevent the in situ formation of the radicals. The description of such behaviors was made possible thanks to the possibility to characterize either the ions of the stabilizer and those of the polymer by DART ionization and exact mass measurement. Also, because of the ability of the DART-TOF MS method used in this study to perform rapid screening of the behavior of polyethylene solid samples, it is reasonable to consider its use to disclose the history of aging of a polymer in a high-throughput analysis context for industrial control.

In this study, we have calculated the homolytic C-H bond cleavage of CH4 over periodic structures of [FeO]2+-ZSM-5, [Cu2(μ-O)]2+-ZSM-5, and [Cu3(μ-O)3]2+-MOR zeolites by using six known meta-GGA functionals combined with the D2 method of the dispersion correction. The reaction involves an adsorption state referred to as reactant complex (RC), a transition state (TS), and a radical intermediate state (RI). For all studied active species, the CH4 adsorption energies calculated by the SCAN-D2 and MS-D2 functionals are found to be slightly stronger than those calculated by the TPSS-D2 and RTPSS-D2 functionals due to their natural abilities to well describe weak interactions. Also, through PDOS analysis, we are able to resolve the dispute on the most favorable electronic structure of the active species where [FeIV-O]2+, [CuII 2(μ-O)]2+, and [CuII 2CuIII(μ-O)2(μ-O )]2+ are found to be the preferred electronic structures.

dataset_item.question: What structural and electronic features of Pt8 enable efficient catalytic reduction of nitrous oxide?
dataset_item.answer:
The Pt<sub>8</sub> cluster enables efficient catalytic reduction of nitrous oxide (N<sub>2</sub>O) through a combination of unique structural and electronic features. Its low-symmetry, anisotropic structure, specifically the triple tetragonal pyramid ground-state isomer, exhibits structural fluxionality that allows dynamic Pt-Pt bond rearrangements during the reaction without destabilization. This fluxionality facilitates multiple regioselective pathways for N<sub>2</sub>O reduction, including significant Pt-Pt bond elongation upon adsorption.

A key feature of the cluster is the presence of a highly reactive tip atom (Pt(8)), which serves as a "hot catalytic site" for spontaneous N<sub>2</sub>O dissociation. Electron transfer from Pt(8) into the antibonding molecular orbital of N<sub>2</sub>O weakens the N-O bond, promoting dissociation via a frustrated bridge transition state with low-energy barriers comparable to rhodium-based catalysts. Hirshfeld analysis confirms that charge donation is critical for N<sub>2</sub>O activation.

Additionally, while the cluster maintains stability during the catalytic process, poisoning effects from successive N<sub>2</sub>O molecules may reduce efficiency over time, highlighting a need for further study to address this limitation.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. **Summary of the Purpose of the Paper:**

The paper investigates the catalytic potential of a low-symmetry Pt8 cluster for the reduction of nitrous oxide (N2O), a harmful pollutant. Using density functional theory (DFT) with relativistic corrections (ZORA), the study identifies multiple regioselective reaction pathways for N2O dissociation and highlights the role of specific structural features, such as fluxionality and tip atoms, in enabling efficient catalysis. The Pt8 cluster is shown to have competitive catalytic performance compared to rhodium clusters, with advantages in preventing poisoning effects and maintaining stability during the reaction process.

---

### 2. **Classification of Purpose:**

The purpose emphasizes **"<result>"**, as the abstract focuses on presenting findings regarding the catalytic performance, reaction mechanisms, and structural advantages of the Pt8 cluster for N2O reduction.

---

### 3. **Research Questions Relevant to the Abstract's Themes:**

- What are the key structural features of the Pt8 cluster that contribute to its catalytic activity for N2O reduction?
- How does the low symmetry of Pt8 influence the regioselectivity and fluxionality of the reaction pathways?
- How do relativistic effects (modeled through ZORA) affect the calculated reaction barriers and catalytic performance of Pt8?
- How does the catalytic performance of Pt8 compare to other sub-nanometric metal clusters, such as rhodium clusters, in terms of efficiency and resistance to poisoning?
- What are the mechanistic details of the formation of the frustrated bridge activated transition state (Pt8-N2O) and its role in spontaneous N2O dissociation?
- Can the fluxionality and multiple reaction pathways observed in Pt8 be generalized to other low-symmetry metal clusters for similar catalytic applications?
- How does the stability of the Pt8 cluster evolve during the catalytic process, and what role do atomic rearrangements play in preserving it?
dataset_item.true_false_question: Does the Pt8 cluster enable efficient catalytic reduction of nitrous oxide primarily through electron transfer from its reactive tip atom into the antibonding molecular orbital of N2O?

inference_contexts: The DFT ZORA relativistic calculations performed in this work allow the characterization of the complex reduction reaction of N2O on the surface of the low-symmetry Pt8 cluster, which presents strong anisotropy. From the various isomeric structures that Pt8 can assume, a triple tetragonal pyramid in a triplet spin state was determined as the ground state and selected in this work to study the reaction with the N2O molecule. We found that multiple reaction pathways are possible for the N2O rupture on this isomer, which are regio selective. Once the N2O molecule is adsorbed on the cluster surface in atop configuration (N-bound), there is a dependence of the reaction barrier on the orientation to which the molecule is rotated to form the bridge. It is not possible to form a bridge between atoms lying on the cluster symmetry plane, including the case between the tip Pt(8) and its neighbor atoms. For this reason precisely, Pt(8) is the hot site for reduction, yielding spontaneous dissociation of N2O from a frustrated bridge transition structure. Moreover, the ability of Pt8 for the transference of charge, mainly via the pivot Pt(8) site, into the antibonding molecular orbital of N2O promotes the reduction. Remarkably, the results reveal a great fluxionality of Pt8, through important rearrangements that the metal cluster performs to adsorb, activate, and finally reduce the N2O molecule. Thus, the considerable lengthening of the bond lengths of the Pt-Pt atoms forming the bridge and the weakening of the metal bonding takes place without compromising the stability of the whole cluster. Fluxionality and multiple reaction pathways appearing on the Pt8 surface make favorable the catalytic reduction of N2O by this cluster with low barrier energies, comparable to those of the more symmetric neutral and charged rhodium clusters: Rh6, Rh6 +, and Rh6 -. The performed Hirshfeld population analysis shows that the transfer of charge from the cluster to N2O weakens its N-O bond, promoting the dissociation. It was confirmed in this work that the Pt8 particle is an efficient catalyst to reduce one N2O molecule. However, it is important to find the reasons why this catalytic activity decreases significantly for the next molecules; we have research in progress that addresses this problem. The fact that experimental techniques as IR-MPD, implemented recently, can be employed to model catalysts of the platinum group metal clusters makes us think that the present study can be verified in the short term.

In contrast to the EA mechanism, the C-H bond cleavage over the [Cu2(μ-O)]2+-MFI and [Cu3(μ-O)3]2+-MOR proceeds through the hydrogen-atom transfer (HAT) mechanism where the β electron from the C-H σ orbital is transferred to the β-LUMO (CuII-O-CuII π* antibonding orbital) of the active species. However, since the [Cu3(μ-O)3]2+ species involves an oxyl (O ), the electron transfer results in a reduction of the O to an oxide (O2-), forming an RI of CuII 2CuIII(μ-O)2(μ-OH) + CH3 that preserves the stability of the Cu2+ centers. On the contrary, [Cu2(μ-O)]2+ species involves only O2-. Thus, when the electron transfer occurs, it would form an RI of CuI-OH-CuII + CH3 that is much less stable than RC due to a reduction of one of the Cu2+ centers to a less stable Cu+. This explains why O is more reactive than O2- and clarifies the critical role of radical character at the active O atom on the reactivity of the active site toward CH4 activation through the HAT mechanism. , In contrast to TS in the EA mechanism, that in the HAT mechanism involves a significant distortion of the CH4 geometry and a partial formation of the O-H bond due to an endothermic nature of the reaction from RC to RI. Observing the energy profiles for [Cu2(μ-O)]2+-MFI and [Cu3(μ-O)3]2+-MOR, we found that only the SCAN-D2 functional predicts an energy trend inconsistent with those calculated by the rest of studied meta-GGA functionals and the B3LYP and PBE-D2 functionals. ,, This discrepancy is attributed to an overestimation imposed by the SCAN-D2 functional on the Cu-O-Cu bond strengths, which causes the β-LUMO acceptor orbital to locate at a lower energy.

Small gas-phase nitrous oxide complexes of coinage metal cations have been studied using infrared spectroscopy in the region of the ligand N-N stretch. Comparison of the experimental spectra with spectral simulations from density functional theory yields clear evidence for isomers containing N-bound and O-bound ligands with the spectral signature of the former blue-shifted from the free N2O frequency by up to 140 cm-1. The trends observed between different metal complexes M+, as well as those with increasing numbers of ligands, are interpreted on the basis of the molecular orbital picture of the binding in which the approaching ligand induces s-d z 2 hybridization of the M+ ion.

We showed the further reduction of the activation energy for the decomposition of formic acid by a water cluster in the previous study. We expect the activation energy for the decomposition of methanediol is also reduced when we include a water cluster in the simulation. The hydrogen bonds in a water cluster make it easy to transfer a proton, leading to the reduction of the activation energy. We study the decomposition of a methanediol catalyzed by water clusters with three and four water molecules. The activation energy is reduced further by 5 kcal/mol and becomes 23 kcal/mol when a water cluster with four water molecules catalyzes the decomposition of a methanediol.

A >40 times increase in the time constant for oxygen exchange kinetics during ~5 days of aging was found in PCO thin films using the oxygen transmission relaxation method (OTR). The degradation in kinetics was identified to arise from accumulation of a siliceous phase on the PCO film surface. From a systematic examination of impurity sources, Si is likely introduced primarily during the OTR measurement (e.g.. from the quartz tube or furnace insulation) rather than through target purity, processing, or substrate (though these other sources may still have impurities present). Deposition of La oxide or Sm oxide on the aged film surface was found to fully recover oxygen exchange kinetics in aged films and a film intentionally coated with siliceous phase. Surface treatments with other oxides (Nb, Al, Ti, and Zn) were not found to recover oxygen exchange kinetics. La and Sm likely react with Si to form a porous silicate layer allowing gas transfer to the PCO surface, whereas other studied materials are unlikely to form silicates. La oxide was also deposited on aged SrTi0.65Fe0.35O3-δ, prone to degradation via Sr segregation (as opposed to siliceous phases), and no improvement was found, further indicating that La reacts with Si and is not leading to a significant catalytic effect. Finally, La was added to PCO in solid solution, and initial measurements found suppressed aging of redox kinetics.

dataset_item.question: What method is used to determine energy landscape and transition-state barriers during reaction path optimization of aluminum oxyhydroxide surfaces?
dataset_item.answer: The energy landscape and transition-state barriers during reaction path optimization of aluminum oxyhydroxide surfaces were determined using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method, as implemented in the USPEX code v10.3. A force convergence criterion of 2 × 10<sup>−3</sup> eV/Å was employed for each image along the reaction path, with optimization carried out using the steepest descent algorithm.

### 1. Purpose of the Paper:
The purpose of this paper is to investigate the radiolytic reactivity of aluminum oxyhydroxide surfaces (specifically boehmite (010) and gibbsite (001)) under γ-irradiation, with a focus on dehydration, rehydration, and proton transfer mechanisms. Using density functional theory (DFT) and nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations, the study aims to provide mechanistic insights into surface hydroxyl reorientation, hydrogen bonding, and defect-driven processes, helping to explain experimental results from vibrational sum frequency generation (VSFG) spectroscopy. This research contributes to understanding the stability and reactivity of these materials, which are critical for processing nuclear wastes.

---

### 2. Classification of Purpose:
**<method>**  
The paper emphasizes the **method** by using computational tools (DFT and NEB calculations) to analyze surface phenomena and provide theoretical insights that complement experimental observations.

---

### 3. Research Questions:
1. How does γ-irradiation affect the dehydration and rehydration mechanisms of boehmite (010) and gibbsite (001) surfaces?
2. What role does the orientation of surface hydroxyls play in controlling the hydrogen bonding network during rehydration?
3. What are the energy barriers and proton transfer mechanisms involved in the rehydration of aluminum oxyhydroxide surfaces, and how do they vary between boehmite and gibbsite?
4. How do surface hydrogen vacancies influence the strength of hydrogen bond interactions and the formation of radiolytic products such as H2 and H2O?
5. What theoretical insights can explain the differences in rehydration behavior observed experimentally for boehmite and gibbsite using VSFG spectroscopy?
6. How can the mechanistic understanding of radiolytic reactivity inform the development of more reliable approaches for processing aluminum oxyhydroxide phases in nuclear waste management?

dataset_item.true_false_question: Is the reaction path optimization of aluminum oxyhydroxide surfaces performed without using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method?

inference_contexts: The determination of the energy landscape and transition-state energy, configuration, and barriers were performed using the climbing image nudged elastic band method (CI-NEB) as implemented in the USPEX code v10.3. , The force convergence criterion for each image on the reaction path was set to 2 × 10-3 eV/Å, and the steepest descendent algorithm was chosen for the reaction path optimization.

The first-principles calculations were carried out using periodic density functional theory, as implemented in the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP). , The exchange-correlation effects were incorporated in the spin-polarized generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the PBE functional. The Kohn-Sham equation was solved iteratively using a plane wave basis set with a cutoff energy of 400 eV to describe the valence electrons, and the electron-ion interactions were described by the projector augmented wave (PAW) , method. For calculations of a gas-phase species, a single k-point was used with a box size of 15 × 15 × 15 Å3, whereas for surface cells, the k-point sampling was performed with a 3 × 3 × 1 Monkhorst-Pack with a SCF convergence criterion of 5 × 10-5 eV. The force threshold for structural optimization was set to 0.05 eV/Å. The energetic profiles along the prescribed reaction pathways were located using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method. The calculated transition states were verified by computing the vibrational frequencies that yield one imaginary frequency [Table S1, Supporting Information (SI)].

Transition states (TS) are searched with the climbing image-nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method with the force on each atom in each image being converged to 0.05 eV/Å. All the transition states are confirmed by ensuring that their vibrational spectra show only one imaginary mode. The vibrational frequencies are calculated by displacing the atoms on both the adsorbate and the first layer of the metal surface using Atomic Simulations Environment (ASE).

The nudged elastic band (NEB) method was used to evaluate the activation energy (ΔE a). The method was applied to a discretized path containing eight images. We calculated the activation energies as the difference between the maximum and the minimum energies of the calculated NEB images. The structures were visualized using the VESTA program.

All calculations were performed at the DFT level within the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP). , The projected augmented wave method (PAW) was used. The electron exchange and correlation energies were calculated using the generalized gradient approximation in the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (GGA-PBE) functional. , The plane wave basis was set up to 400 eV. Spin-polarization calculation was included for iron systems to correctly account for the magnetic properties. Geometry optimization was done when atomic force tolerance becomes smaller than 0.02 eV/Å and the energy difference was lower than 10-4 eV. Bader charge analysis was carried out for discussing charge transfer between the surface and the adsorbed Cu atoms. All transition states were estimated using the climbing-image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method, , and their vibrational frequencies were also calculated.

dataset_item.question: How does Pb doping at the Bi site affect the electronic structure, hole concentration, and power factor of p-type AgBiSe2?
dataset_item.answer: Pb doping at the Bi site in p-type AgBiSe₂ significantly alters the electronic structure, leading to increased hole concentration and enhanced thermoelectric performance. Specifically, Pb substitution raises the hole concentration from ~8.6 × 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ to ~2.1 × 10¹⁹ cm⁻³, which optimizes carrier transport and boosts the power factor. This modification, combined with the intrinsically low thermal conductivity of AgBiSe₂, results in a peak ZT of ~0.5 at 450 K. The enhanced thermoelectric properties demonstrate the effectiveness of defect engineering in overcoming doping limitations in p-type AgBiSe₂. Further increases in hole concentration are expected to yield additional improvements in performance, highlighting the potential for continued optimization.

### 1. **Summary of the Purpose of the Paper**  
The paper aims to address the challenge of achieving ambipolar doping (both n-type and p-type) in thermoelectric materials, which is essential for module design. Specifically, it focuses on overcoming the difficulty of synthesizing p-type AgBiSe2, which has been predicted to have superior thermoelectric performance compared to its n-type counterpart but has not been reliably realized experimentally. Through defect engineering strategies, including suppressing Se vacancies and introducing Pb doping, the study successfully synthesizes p-type AgBiSe2 and optimizes its thermoelectric performance near room temperature.

---

### 2. **Classification of Purpose**  
The purpose of the paper emphasizes **"<result>"**, as the focus is on achieving the experimental realization of p-type AgBiSe2 and demonstrating its thermoelectric performance improvement through defect engineering.

---

### 3. **Relevant Research Questions**  
- How do intrinsic defects, such as Se vacancies, influence the doping type and thermoelectric performance of AgBiSe2?  
- What mechanisms enable the suppression of Se vacancies and their role in stabilizing p-type doping in AgBiSe2?  
- How does Pb doping at the Bi site affect the electronic structure, hole concentration, and power factor of p-type AgBiSe2?  
- What defect engineering strategies can be generalized to improve ambipolar doping and thermoelectric performance in other materials?

dataset_item.question: Can metallic substrates other than gold and silver achieve comparable field enhancement in tip-enhanced Raman scattering for nanoscale chemical imaging?
dataset_item.answer: Yes, metallic substrates beyond gold (Au) and silver (Ag) can achieve comparable field enhancement in tip-enhanced Raman scattering (TERS) for nanoscale chemical imaging. Experimental studies using few-layer WSe₂ on chromium (Cr) and gold substrates, combined with finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations, demonstrate that alternative reflective metals, such as chromium, magnesium (Mg), and aluminum (Al), can support bright TERS signals similar to those achieved with noble metals. These findings expand the range of viable substrates for high-sensitivity TERS, simplifying sample preparation and broadening its applicability across diverse fields, including bioimaging and materials science, where gold and silver substrates may pose limitations.

This theory has fully considered the near-field self-interaction of molecule with the plasmonic nanogap in both the Raman excitation and radiation processes. We have found that the strong plasmonic resonance effect in the plamsonic nanogap would induce multiple elastic scattering of the molecule upon the optical field of the gap mode. Because the molecule has a size comparable with the nanogap distance, this self-interaction effect can strongly modulates the Raman excitation and radiation in both the signal intensity and spatial sensitivity. The self-interaction strength can be large enough to create a "super-hot spot" with a size on the order of nanometer within the plasmonic nanogap. Besides, due to the self-interaction, the molecule-nanogap has become a strongly correlated nanosystem that involves an ultrastrong correlation of Raman signal with the molecule-nanogap physical and geometric configuration, where the molecule polarizability and its lateral and longitudinal position are all key contributing elements. This ultrastrong correlation between the Raman signal intensity and the lateral position of molecule relative to the tip has a direct consequence of ultrahigh lateral spatial resolution of Raman mapping that is much finer than the "hot-spot" size of the passive nanogap plasmonic mode. In short, the subnanometer ultrahigh Raman mapping resolution observed in ref can be attributed to the strong optical coupling of the molecule with its plasmonic nanogap environment via multiple elastic scattering. An optical theory of Raman scattering can well explain the experimental observation, much the same as the conventional optical theory of SERS can well explain and predict Raman signal enhancement in numerous plasmonic nanostructures.

In Figure a, the normal theory predicts a Raman enhancement factor of about 104-105; however, in Figure d, the self-interaction greatly increases the enhancement factor to about 107-108. dataset_item.question: How do the length and composition of elastin-like polypeptide side chains affect the mechanical and swelling properties of protein-based hydrogels at elevated temperatures?
dataset_item.answer: The length and composition of elastin-like polypeptide (ELP) side chains play a crucial role in modulating the mechanical and swelling properties of protein-based hydrogels at elevated temperatures. ELP side chains exhibit thermoresponsive behavior characterized by a lower critical solution temperature (LCST), which drives temperature-dependent micellization and aggregation within the hydrogel network. These processes lead to significant changes in the Young's modulus and swelling ratio of the hydrogels. Longer ELP side chains enhance the aggregation effect, enabling finer control over these properties. When thermoresponsive ELPs, such as Vn-ELPs, are fused with elastomeric proteins like soluble (GR)₄, the resulting copolymers (e.g., Vn-(GR)₄) form hybrid hydrogels with tunable thermoresponsive behavior. By adjusting the length and composition of ELP side chains, these hydrogels can be engineered to exhibit customizable mechanical and swelling characteristics, making them suitable for diverse applications in tissue engineering, drug delivery, and mechanobiology.

dataset_item.question: How does site-directed spin labeling with deuterium-labeled leucine residues contribute to probing secondary structures of amphipathic helical peptides?
dataset_item.answer: Site-directed spin labeling with deuterium-labeled leucine residues enables precise probing of secondary structures in amphipathic helical peptides by combining the specificity of spin labeling with the structural sensitivity of deuterium modulation patterns observed in electron spin echo envelope modulation (ESEEM) spectroscopy. In this method, deuterium-labeled leucine residues are strategically positioned at intervals relative to a spin-labeled cysteine, creating isotopic markers that produce distinct modulation signals in ESEEM spectra. These signals are sensitive to the periodicity of the peptide's helical structure, allowing differentiation between α-helices (3.6-residue repeat) and 310-helices (3.0-residue repeat). The deuterium modulation depth and frequency (~2.3 MHz) reflect the relative spatial arrangement of spin labels and deuterium atoms, providing site-specific insights into secondary structure. This approach is effective at low peptide concentrations and has been validated through complementary techniques such as circular dichroism and EPR spectroscopy in environments favoring distinct helical conformations, such as TFE (α-helix-inducing) and liposomes (310-helix-stabilizing). The combined sensitivity, specificity, and structural resolution make this technique a powerful tool for investigating peptide secondary structures.

dataset_item.question: How does phosphate alter adsorption conformation of humic acids on TiO2 surface at molecular level?
dataset_item.answer: Phosphate alters the adsorption conformation of humic acids (HA) on the TiO₂ surface by competitively binding to TiO₂, reducing HA adsorption and modifying its interfacial interactions. During the adsorption equilibrium phase, phosphate preferentially occupies TiO₂ binding sites, displacing HA, particularly its aromatic or chromophoric fractions, as indicated by reduced UV absorbance at 254 nm. This competitive adsorption diminishes HA’s inhibitory effects on TiO₂ photocatalysis by minimizing electron-hole recombination and enhancing pollutant degradation efficiency. Additionally, pre-mixing TiO₂ with phosphate prior to HA introduction further modifies HA’s adsorption behavior by altering the surface availability of binding sites, which impacts HA's conformation and adsorption density on TiO₂. Overall, phosphate disrupts HA’s surface coverage, altering its molecular-level interactions with TiO₂ and improving photocatalytic activity.

dataset_item.question: How does the fractional occupation of tetrahedral sites by lithium and tin influence the electrochemical performance of hexagonal lithium tin sulfide?
dataset_item.answer: The fractional occupation of tetrahedral sites by lithium and tin in hexagonal Li<sub>4</sub>SnS<sub>4</sub> results in a random distribution of these elements across one of two opposing tetrahedral sites. This unique structural arrangement enhances ionic transport, leading to an ionic conductivity of 1.1 × 10<sup>-4</sup> S cm<sup>-1</sup> at 25 °C, which surpasses that of the orthorhombic phase. Furthermore, the hexagonal phase demonstrates improved chemical stability in humid air compared to Li<sub>3</sub>PS<sub>4</sub> glass-ceramics, making it more suitable for practical applications. The random sharing of tetrahedral sites by lithium and tin optimizes Li-ion mobility while maintaining structural stability, positioning hexagonal Li<sub>4</sub>SnS<sub>4</sub> as a promising solid electrolyte candidate for advanced electrochemical systems.

dataset_item.question: What is the relationship between peptide chain length and the delay in the phase transformation of calcium phosphate during precipitation?
dataset_item.answer: The peptide chain length of negatively charged oligo(l-glutamic acid) peptides significantly influences the delay in the phase transformation of calcium phosphate during precipitation. At low concentrations (0.1 mM), the decamer (10-mer) is the most effective in delaying the transformation of amorphous calcium phosphate (ACP) to crystalline hydroxyapatite (HAP). This effect is achieved by stabilizing the amorphous precursor phase, thereby increasing the induction time for crystallization and reducing the crystal growth rate. Longer peptide chains further enhance this stabilization, ultimately yielding hydroxyapatite with stoichiometry closer to the ideal. The kinetics of calcium and phosphate uptake from the solution are modulated by peptide chain length, and a critical peptide concentration is required to significantly alter the precipitation pathway. Thus, peptide chain length directly governs the kinetics and pathway of calcium phosphate phase transformation, with longer peptides exerting a stronger influence on delaying crystallization and improving product quality.

We have considered two different interface types: sharp interface and more realistic interface that consists of extended chains. Results can be summarized as follows. Highest states in the valence band are delocalized in the crystalline domains for both interface types. Highest states in the amorphous domains are localized on one or two chains, as in the case of single amorphous domain. Amorphous domain presents a barrier for hole transport due to high energetic offset between highest states in the crystalline and in the amorphous domain. This offset is comparable to other reported results in the case of interface that consists of extended chains. dataset_item.question: What are the structural and electronic impacts of beta and gamma boundaries in epitaxially grown molybdenum disulfide bilayers?
dataset_item.answer:
Epitaxially grown molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂) bilayers containing beta (β) and gamma (γ) grain boundaries exhibit significant structural and electronic impacts. Structurally, β boundaries induce localized tensile strain (~1%) while γ boundaries introduce localized compressive strain (~−0.8%) in the pristine layer. These strains arise from suppressed grain boundary distortions and are coupled between layers via van der Waals interactions, resulting in strain transfer to adjacent regions. Additionally, these grain boundaries cause a stacking order change from AA′ to AB alignment across the boundary, further influencing interlayer interactions.

Electronically, both β and γ boundaries introduce mid-gap states, reducing the band gap of the bilayer. This band gap reduction alters the bilayer's conductivity, enabling localized tuning of electronic properties. These effects highlight the potential for precise strain and electronic property engineering in nanoelectronic applications without the need for external strain manipulation.

dataset_item.question: What is the relationship between the dissociation constant of an ion and the binding free energy in the CLC-ec1 transporter binding sites?
dataset_item.answer:
The dissociation constant (\( K_d \)) and binding free energy (\( \Delta G^\circ \)) in the CLC-ec1 transporter binding sites are intrinsically related through the thermodynamic equation \( \Delta G^\circ = RT \ln K_d \), where \( \Delta G^\circ \) is the standard binding free energy, \( R \) is the gas constant, \( T \) is the temperature, and \( K_d \) is expressed in molar units. This equation indicates that a lower \( K_d \) corresponds to a more negative \( \Delta G^\circ \), signifying stronger binding.

For a more detailed analysis, the potential of mean force (PMF) is used to refine the relationship between \( K_d \) and \( \Delta G^\circ \). The PMF quantifies the free energy change as the ion moves from bulk water into the protein binding site, incorporating spatial considerations. This is expressed as \( \Delta w = \Delta \mu_{ex} = RT \ln (K_d V_{bind} / 1660) \), where \( \Delta w \) is the PMF change and \( V_{bind} \) is the accessible ligand volume within the binding site. Corrections for ion motion within the binding site, typically in the range of 3–6 Å radius, further adjust the binding free energy by approximately -1.6 to -0.4 kcal/mol.

For example, at a stabilization length of 6.5 Å in the CLC-ec1 transporter, the average binding free energy for the ion is approximately -5.3 kcal/mol. These values highlight the sensitivity of \( \Delta G^\circ \) to both thermodynamic parameters and spatial constraints, confirming the direct and nuanced relationship between \( K_d \) and binding free energy in the context of the CLC-ec1 transporter binding sites.

The results of the present article demonstrate the usefulness of the droplet technique for investigations of microgels. The single most important result is the evidence of core-shell phase separation in spherical PA-microgels in equilibrium with C12TAB solutions. Earlier the phenomenon has been observed only in macrogels, where the question of equilibrium or not always remains due to the long relaxation times, or as thermodynamically unstable states in microgels undergoing volume phase transition in solutions of large volume. The capacity of the technique to provide new quantitative information is demonstrated by the determined swelling isotherms, showing for the first time how the volume of single PA-microgels depends on the ratio between surfactant and polyelectrolyte charges in the gel. The swelling isotherms resemble those reported earlier for nonspherical macrogels. It is also shown, with PA/cyt c as a demonstrator system, how the combination of droplet experiments and bulk solution experiments can be used to determine both swelling and binding isotherms for systems not displaying a volume phase transition. Comparison between experiments and theoretical model calculations shows that the recently developed gel theory is in semiquantitative agreement with the results for both cyt c and C12TAB, where the compositions of the collapsed homogeneous states at high binding ratios and the high cooperativity of cyt c binding are particularly well captured. The calculations suggest that the latter feature is an effect of polyion-mediated attractions between the protein molecules. Furthermore, comparison with MC simulations of spherical macroions in a model network shows that the gel model is capable of covering a wide range of electrostatic coupling strengths.

Starting from the unbound state, we have executed McMD simulations in order to explore the binding pathways of the medium-sized inhibitor 3MR to the wide binding pocket of BACE, followed by US and WHAM to calculate their affinity. The most stable binding configuration was found to partly coincide with the native X-ray structure, as indicated by the FEL and the RMSD values. This is due to the definition of the spatial restraint, which was designed for small ligand binding pockets. The native interactions however were preserved as shown by the high R(native)-value. Canonical MD simulations at 300 and 400 K validated the stability of the obtained binding configuration and showed that additional equilibration can further relax a structure to produce the native structure. We picked representative structures along the dissociation direction λ⃗ from the McMD ensemble in a smoothly connected manner, followed by US simulations and WHAM to accurately predict the standard binding free energy between 3MR and BACE in agreement with the experimental results. The losses of interactions between the molecules along λ⃗ were clearly reflected in the PMF, as they account for most of the change in the binding free energy. The sampled ensemble by the US simulations connected the bound state to the unbound one in a smooth manner, refining the binding pathway while staying true to the McMD ensemble.

Understanding how design parameters of targeted drug carriers influence interaction with cells and the subsequent signaling leading to endocytosis is key to inform optimization of drug delivery systems. , Both the size and targeting valency of drug carriers impact cell binding and endocytic uptake. - ,,, However, how these parameters influence receptor-mediated signaling linking binding with internalization is rather obscure. For instance: Is the uptake efficiency correlative with the signaling level? Is this regulated similarly for carriers of different sizes and valencies? Are signaling and uptake events induced independently for each individual carrier or do they depend on cumulative carrier binding to cells? Is the number of receptors engaged by a carrier the factor ruling signaling and uptake, or does this depend on the density of engagement per surface area? Using model submicrometer, micrometer, and supramicrometer carriers targeted to ICAM-1 at varying valencies, we have examined these questions. Our results revealed an intricate interplay between these parameters, where the density of the targeting antibody per carrier surface area (which would determine the density of the receptor cluster on the cell surface) is the main parameter controlling the signaling conducive to endocytosis (Figure ). Larger carriers posed a requirement for stronger signaling, since carrier size impacts the ability of the plasmalemma to efficiently engulf a carrier. It is likely that for endocytic pathways lacking signals that enable sufficient plasmalemma deformability (e.g.. ceramide enrichment shown here for the CAM pathway), size will become restrictive regardless of the targeting density. Each carrier bound on a cell induced signaling based on its antibody-coat density (the density of the clustered receptors, not the absolute number of receptors engaged or the size of the cluster), and rendered endocytosis based on its size and enough buildup of the inducing signal. Each signaling-uptake event was independent for each single carrier bound on a cell, where the total number of carriers bound to the cell, the total surface area occupied by those carriers, and the total number of cell receptors engaged did not exert a major influence. It will be important to examine this regulation for other receptors and pathways in order to extract generic conclusions, and to evaluate how other carrier design parameters (e.g.. smaller sizes, different shape, curvature, carrier type, surface chemistry, etc.) and biological environments (different cell types, presence of flow, pathological alterations, etc.) impact these outcomes. - ,,, Nevertheless, other natural routes associate to signaling common to the CAM pathway, and it is expected that the findings obtained here would broadly apply to the use of said routes for drug delivery applications. For instance, ceramide and/or PKC are key for the formation of lipid domains, vesiculation, cytoskeletal rearrangements, and formation of membrane protrusions observed for phagocytic and macropinocytic pathways, intracellular invasion by certain viral and bacterial pathogens, leukocyte endothelial adhesion and extravasation, and certain events of transcytosis across cellular barriers. - Therefore, these results have shed light on key factors modulating the efficacy of uptake of targeted drug carriers, which shall inform future design of vehicles for intracellular delivery.

dataset_item.question: What computational methods and models are used to optimize molecular structures and calculate excitation parameters in donor-acceptor triphenylamine derivatives?
dataset_item.answer:
To optimize molecular structures and calculate excitation parameters in donor-acceptor triphenylamine derivatives, density functional theory (DFT) with the B3LYP functional and 6-31+G(d) basis set is employed for ground-state geometry optimization, ensuring minimal energy and structural stability. Time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) using the CAM-B3LYP functional and the same basis set is utilized to compute excitation properties for the first 15 excited states. Calculations are performed using the Gaussian 09 software package, incorporating solvent effects via the polarizable continuum model (PCM) with tetrahydrofuran (THF) as the solvent.

To analyze intramolecular charge-transfer behavior, charge density difference (CDD) isosurface diagrams and transition density matrix (TDM) heat maps are generated using Multiwfn software. Nonlinear optical properties, such as second hyperpolarizabilities (γ_ijkl) and two-photon absorption (TPA) cross-sections, are also computed to assess electronic and optical responses systematically. These methods collectively enable the optimization and detailed characterization of molecular structures and their electronic excitation behavior.

inference_contexts: DFT is a leading quantum mechanical method for studying the electronic structure of multi-electron systems. , B3LYP - has been one of the most widely used functionals for optimizing the molecular geometric structure ,- in the past 20 years due to its simple form, fast calculation speed, and low dependence on the integral lattice. - In this study, DFT/B3LYP/6-31+G (d) was utilized to optimize the geometric structure of all molecules, and the minimum energy on the molecular potential energy curve was obtained. The absence of imaginary frequency indicates that the energy of this molecular structure is lowest. Time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) is often utilized to calculate parameters about excited states. , Many previous reports have shown that the functional CAM-B3LYP, , a long-range corrected version of the B3LYP functional, can simulate the molecular excitation energy very well. Sometimes the excitation energy is larger (smaller) than the experimental test value, but the deviation is small , and will not affect the order of excitation energies in similar molecular systems. Based on the molecular ground state structure, the relevant parameters of the first 15 excited states of all molecules are calculated by TD-DFT/CAM-B3LYP/6-31+G (d). All the above work is completed using the Gaussian 09 package.

Can DCPs elevate the performance of BLYP to that of B3LYP? This is a question that was posed in the Introduction. As computational chemistry methods are applied to increasingly larger systems, the question of their efficiency-in particular, with respect to run time-becomes critical. Formally, GGA functionals like BLYP scale as N 3 with system size (with N being the number of electrons), whereas hybrid functionals scale with N 4. Therefore, low-cost corrections such as D3 and DCP that may elevate the performance of BLYP to that of B3LYP or better may be of value. To examine this possibility, we present in Table a summary of some of the performance statistics for BLYP-D3-DCP/6-31+G (2d,2p) for the benchmark sets described above and compare these to statistics obtained using B3LYP-D3/6-31+G (2d,2p). We also conducted additional performance assessments of the two methods on the BHPERI, DARC, BSR36, and the RSE43 databases. We use D3 corrections with B3LYP for our comparison because D3 has a computational cost that is negligible relative to that of the underlying DFT method and because D3 corrections (or similar) are required to predict noncovalent interactions that are reasonable. It is worthwhile restating that D3 corrections that were designed for use with B3LYP were also designed for use with nearly complete basis sets. The corrections nevertheless improve the performance of "small basis set" B3LYP, as has been shown in the past, in particular for the treatment of noncovalent interactions.

Using the DFT based B3LYP/6-31++G (d,p) method, we first tried to locate all the possible stationary points in the reaction paths. , All the minima were characterized with no imaginary frequencies. At the same time, all the transition states were characterized with only one imaginary frequency and were confirmed from the analysis of their displacement vectors associated with their imaginary frequencies and from their IRC calculations. It is well-known that most of the DFT methods are deficient in accounting for the dispersive interactions and other long-range interactions. The reason is due to the use of the approximated exchange-correlation (xc) functionals, which are computed empirically and then added to the conventional DFT energies as correction terms. So, we have tried to include the empirical dispersion and long-range interaction corrections by carrying out the calculations again with the wB97xD method (this method uses long-range corrected hybrid density functionals with damped atom-atom dispersion corrections. ), with a basis set like aug-cc-pVTZ, on all the stationary points located in the previously mentioned method (full optimizations for all stationary points). Discussions reported in this work are only limited to the wB97xD method and are sometimes compared with the results from the B3LYP method. All the energetics reported in this work include zero-point energy corrections, unless otherwise mentioned explicitly. As the wB97xD method was providing comparable accurate results like that of the previous reports, computations related to other computationally expensive higher-level energy correction methods were not carried out in this work. In a few cases, we have compared the results from our CCSD (T) calculations with the earlier reported results at various levels of theories and also with results from wB97xD methods reported in this work (CCSD (T)/6-31++G (d,p) energy corrections were carried out on B3LYP/6-31++G (d,p) optimized geometries). - The computational chemistry program Gaussian 09 was used to carry out all these calculations, and the GaussView program was used for visualization purposes.

Our analysis using the DFT and TD-DFT methods employed for some configurations of D/A dimers was complemented by molecular dynamics (MD) calculations. We applied MD to simulate the deposition of DRCN5T/C 60 films formed by solvent evaporation. Those simulations indicated that the face-on and edge-on dimer's configurations that tend to have very negative driving forces (as identified by our DFT and TD-DFT calculations) can be present in a real film. Moreover, we found that the lateral alkyl groups attached to the central thiophene ring of the DRCN5T molecule can behave like tweezers that guide the diffusive movement of C 60 toward the center of the molecule. This effect would favor the formation of dimers with C1-like configurations (that tend to have a negative ΔG). MD simulations also indicated that thermal annealing treatments increase the density and the size of the fullerene cluster in the blend (which is in agreement with the experimental observations).

In this work, we use the CHARMM (Chemistry at Harvard MM) FF parameters. , Structures and parameters for those molecules that are not included in the CHARMM parameters can be obtained by optimizing the structures at the MP2/6-31++G (d,p) - level of theory. Partial charges can then be extracted using the natural bond orbital (NBO) population analysis at this level. Missing parameters, such as the Lennard-Jones energy ϵ or distance σ, were taken from similar structures presented in the CHARMM force field database. , This approach is generally sufficient for configurational sampling of atmospheric molecular clusters. When necessary, system-specific FF molecular parameters can also be developed more rigorously, as described in refs and .

dataset_item.question: How do hybrid orbitals derived from spin-coupled generalized valence bond wave functions differ from traditional sp3, sp2, and sp hybrid orbitals in methane, ethylene, and acetylene?
dataset_item.answer:
Hybrid orbitals derived from spin-coupled generalized valence bond (SCGVB) wave functions differ significantly from traditional sp³, sp², and sp hybrid orbitals in methane (CH₄), ethylene (C₂H₄), and acetylene (C₂H₂). Unlike the predefined spⁿ mixing in traditional models, SCGVB orbitals emerge from quantum mechanical principles, considering factors such as spatial orientation of atomic orbitals, hybridization flexibility, spin contributions, and Pauli repulsion between electron pairs.

SCGVB theory predicts nonstandard hybridization ratios: approximately sp¹.⁵⁸ and sp⁰.⁵⁷ for methane, sp¹.⁰³ and sp⁰.⁵⁷ for ethylene, and sp⁰.²⁹ and sp⁰.⁷⁶ for acetylene. These ratios reveal that SCGVB orbitals are predominantly composed of contributions from carbon’s 2s and 2p atomic orbitals, accounting for 90–98% of the carbon-centered bonding orbitals. Unlike traditional hybridization models, which rely on idealized geometries, SCGVB theory incorporates the effects of Pauli repulsion and electron-pair interactions to determine molecular structure and bonding geometry.

Energetically, SCGVB orbitals offer lower energy configurations compared to traditional hybridization models, with energy decreases ranging from 1.7 to 9.0 kcal/mol. In methane, for example, the tetrahedral geometry arises naturally from four singly occupied orbitals (2s±, 2pₓ, 2pᵧ) without requiring the invocation of high-energy excited atomic states. In acetylene, SCGVB orbitals disrupt the classical triple-bond character, demonstrating reduced orbital overlap and a more complex bonding arrangement.

Thus, SCGVB theory provides a more flexible and quantum-mechanically rigorous framework for understanding molecular bonding, replacing rigid spⁿ hybridization rules with a model that accounts for orbital spatial distribution, hybridization dynamics, and electron-pair repulsion.

### 1. Summary of the Purpose:
The paper aims to analyze the nature of hybrid orbitals derived from spin-coupled generalized valence bond (SCGVB) wave functions and compare them to traditional hybrid orbitals in methane, ethylene, and acetylene. It investigates how modern ab initio valence bond theories deviate from traditional hybridization rules and explores the implications for molecular structure and properties.

### 2. Classification of Purpose:
The purpose emphasizes **"<result>"**, as the paper primarily focuses on the findings regarding how modern valence bond orbitals differ from traditional hybrid orbitals and their implications for molecular structure and properties.

### 3. Relevant Research Questions:
- How do the hybrid orbitals obtained from SCGVB wave functions differ from the traditional sp3, sp2, and sp hybrid orbitals for methane, ethylene, and acetylene?
- What factors in modern valence bond theories contribute to molecular structure and properties if traditional orbital hybridization rules are not followed?
- How do the localized 2s-2p hybrid orbitals in SCGVB wave functions influence the bonding geometry and electron distribution in carbon-centered molecules?
- What computational or experimental methods can be used to further validate the findings of modern valence bond theories in comparison to traditional models?
dataset_item.true_false_question: Do SCGVB-derived hybrid orbitals in methane, ethylene, and acetylene strictly conform to traditional sp³, sp², and sp hybridization geometries?

inference_contexts: Most chemists consider the traditional VB concept of hybrid orbitals-the orthogonal sp3, sp2, and sp hybrid orbitals of the carbon atom-to be one of the basic foundations of chemical theory. These orbitals are used to rationalize the tetravalence of the carbon atom, as well as the structures of methane and many other organic molecules. As we noted, the tetravalence of carbon arises directly from the four singly occupied orbitals (2s z-, 2s z+, 2p x , 2p y ) in the ground state of the carbon atom in the SCGVB theory, which, combined with Pauli repulsion between the bond pairs, leads naturally to the formation of hybrid orbitals in the methane, ethylene, and acetylene molecules. However, the SCGVB hybrid orbitals in these molecules are not the traditional sp n hybrid orbitals. Thus, in the SCGVB theory, we do not have a simple mnemonic-like sp3, sp2, and sp for predicting molecular structure. Rather, the nominal structures of molecules are determined by three factors: (1) the spatial orientation of the atomic orbitals involved in the bonds, (2) the ease with which these atomic orbitals can be hybridized, and (3) Pauli repulsion between the resulting electron pairs. Thus, in the SCGVB theory, the structures of molecules arise in a straightforward manner from the basic principles of quantum mechanics.

The carbon-centered bond orbitals in the SCGVB, SCGVB (PP), and SCGVB (PP/SO) wave functions of CH4, C2H4, and C2H2 are 2s-2p hybrid orbitals that point directly at the atoms to which they are bonded. However, only the orbitals in the SCGVB (PP/SO) wave function are (approximately) sp n hybrid orbitals as predicted by the traditional VB theory. The hybridization ratios for the carbon-centered CH bond orbitals in the SCGVB (PP) and full SCGVB wave functions of CH4, C2H4, and C2H2 differ significantly from sp3, sp2, and sp hybrid orbitals: sp1.58 and sp0.57 (CH4), sp1.03 and sp0.57 (C2H4), and sp0.29 and sp0.76 (C2H2), respectively. This trend also holds true for the CCσ bond orbitals: (sp0.82, sp0.39) for C2H4 and (sp0.29, sp0.37) for C2H2. In all cases, the composition of the carbon-centered bond orbitals is dominated by the carbons 2s and 2p atomic orbital contributions. As measured by P 2s+2p 2, the carbons 2s and 2p atomic orbitals account for 90-98% of the carbon-centered SCGVB orbitals. The C2H2 molecule is somewhat of an anomaly, but, as we have shown previously, the SCGVB wave function of C2H2 has significant contributions from spin functions other than the perfect pairing spin function, i.e.. C2H2 does not have a classical triple bond, which could be the cause of the strange behavior of its SCGVB (PP) wave function.

The SCGVB wave function for the ground state of the carbon atom has four singly occupied orbitals: 2s-, 2s+, 2p x , and 2p y . Although the (2s-, 2s+) lobe orbitals of the carbon atom overlap, they are concentrated in different spatial regions-one lobe is concentrated on one side of the nucleus and the other lobe is concentrated on the other side of the nucleus. , As a result, a strong bond can be formed with the electrons in the (2s-, 2s+) lobe orbitals, as well as the 2p x and 2p y orbitals. This accounts for the tetravalence of the carbon atom-there is no need in the SCGVB theory to invoke the high-energy C (5S) state or a predetermined hybridization ratio. The reason for the tetrahedral structure of methane requires further elaboration. The preceding argument suggests that there might be two different types of CH bonds in methane, two involving the (2p x , 2p y ) orbitals and two involving the (2s-, 2s+) lobe orbitals. As noted by Kutzelnigg, the hybridization of the 2s and 2p orbitals in the first-row atoms is facile. In methane, 2s-2p hybridization in combination with Pauli repulsion between the four bonds leads to the tetrahedral structure of methane. Similar arguments apply to ethylene and acetylene, the difference being that there are π bonds in these molecules that have spatial characteristics that are distinct from those of the σ bonds. Taking this difference into account, Pauli repulsion along with the orbital hybridization found here would predict a nominal bond angle of 120° between the σ bonds in C2H4 and 180° angles between the σ bonds in C2H2.

Figure also depicts that the confidence intervals around the HR using the hybrid uncertainty method are generally much wider at lower PM2.5 concentrations compared to the traditional approach using a standard error that is constant across the full range of the PM2.5 concentration distribution. The increased uncertainty resulting from the hybrid method is shown in Table , where the hybrid uncertainty 95% CIs for the HR reported in Turner et al. include unity at mean annual concentrations below 3.7 μg/m3, indicating more uncertainty at lower concentrations. The PM2.5 concentration at which the hybrid uncertainty intervals first include unity varies by study, depending on the observed mean annual concentration and the standard error. For studies with extremely large sample sizes and/or low mean annual concentrations (e.g.. ref and ), the hybrid 95% CIs never include unity, but are still wider than the standard intervals at concentrations below the respective study means (see Tables S2A-S2C). The increased widths of the CIs also suggest a higher probability that the HRs could be larger at low concentrations. In contrast, the traditional approach to estimating uncertainty assumes a constant standard error and the resulting CIs do not include unity at any concentration in the distribution for any of the cohort studies. Across the PM2.5 concentration distribution, the hybrid uncertainty method results in increasingly larger standard errors at lower concentrations. For example, in Turner et al. the hybrid uncertainty method results in an adjustment to the constant standard error that was 1.32 times larger at 10 μg/m3; 3.18 times larger at 5 μg/m3, and dramatically increased by a factor of 11.19 just above the counterfactual concentration (i.e.. at 2.1 μg/m3; see Table S3).

The dramatic changes in the hybridization ratios of the orbitals from the SCGVB (PP/SO) wave function to the SCGVB (PP) and SCGVB wave functions are accompanied by modest incremental decreases in the energy (1.71 and 0.95 kcal/mol) for CH4 with decreases for C2H4 (1.69 and 4.79 kcal/mol) and C2H2 (1.10 and 9.04 kcal/mol) being far more significant, especially for C2H2. There are also significant decreases in the bond orbital overlaps from the SCGVB (PP/SO) and SCGVB (PP) wave functions, which have similar bond orbital overlaps, to the full SCGVB wave functions, which have much smaller overlaps (acetylene is again an anomaly). The change in the hybridization ratio is evidence of the energetic trade-offs discussed by Shaik et al.. namely, orthogonal orbitals may lead to higher bond orbital overlaps and implying, perhaps, stronger bonds, but this comes at the expense of increasing the contribution of the high-energy 5S (2s2p3) state to the wave function.

dataset_item.question: How does the scaling law of radius of gyration as a function of polypeptide chain length differ between chemically denatured proteins and native proteins?
dataset_item.answer:
The scaling law of the radius of gyration (R_g) as a function of polypeptide chain length (L) differs significantly between chemically denatured proteins and native proteins, reflecting their distinct structural conformations.  

Chemically denatured proteins exhibit a scaling exponent (ν_denatured) of 0.58 ± 0.02, consistent with random coil behavior, where the chains adopt extended conformations. In contrast, native proteins are more compact and folded, with a smaller scaling exponent (ν_native) of 0.45 ± 0.02. This reduced exponent reflects the tighter packing characteristic of the native state.  

Native proteins can be further categorized into monomeric and oligomeric forms. Native monomeric proteins have a scaling exponent of approximately 0.49 ± 0.08, while native oligomeric proteins display an even lower exponent (ν_oligomer = 0.32 ± 0.02). The latter indicates a high degree of compaction, approaching the behavior of collapsed polymers.  

Interestingly, chemically denatured knotted proteins, despite retaining their topological knots, exhibit scaling similar to unknotted denatured proteins (ν_denatured = 0.58 ± 0.02). This suggests that chemically denatured proteins, whether knotted or unknotted, adopt random coil-like conformations without significant compaction.  

These findings highlight the structural variability between chemically denatured and native proteins, with chemically denatured proteins adopting expanded conformations, while native proteins display varying degrees of compaction depending on their monomeric or oligomeric state.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. Summary of the Purpose:
The purpose of the paper is to investigate whether chemically denatured knotted proteins exhibit structural behavior distinct from typical random coils. By employing small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), the study evaluates the scaling law of the radius of gyration (R_g) for chemically denatured proteins, including knotted proteins, and compares them to random coil-like behavior. The findings challenge the assumption that global compaction is necessary for the formation of topological protein knots, showing that loosely knotted polypeptide chains can maintain correct chirality without defined secondary or tertiary structures.

---

### 2. Classification of Purpose:
**<result>**  
The paper emphasizes the results, focusing on the observed behavior of chemically denatured knotted proteins and their implications for understanding the mechanisms of topological knot formation in proteins.

---

### 3. Relevant Research Questions:
1. How do chemically denatured knotted proteins differ structurally from typical random coils in terms of radius of gyration (R_g)?
2. What role, if any, does global compaction play in the formation of topological knots in proteins?
3. Can chemically denatured knotted proteins maintain correct chirality in the absence of secondary or tertiary structures?
4. How does the scaling law of R_g as a function of polypeptide chain length compare between natively folded proteins, chemically denatured proteins, and chemically denatured knotted proteins?
5. What biophysical mechanisms enable chemically denatured knotted proteins to retain their topological properties despite a lack of defined structural features?
dataset_item.true_false_question: Do chemically denatured proteins exhibit a radius of gyration scaling exponent around 0.58, consistent with random coil behavior?

inference_contexts: Note that the SAXS-based scaling exponent for native, monomeric proteins based on SAXS measurements is very similar to the recent finding based on single-molecule fluorescence measurements, which yielded the scaling exponent of native proteins, νnative = 0.46 ± 0.05 (n = 6). In the same study, the authors also determined the scaling exponent for chemically denatured proteins (νdenatured = 0.59 to 0.63, n = 6) that is also consistent with our newly updated scaling exponent based on SAXS measurements for chemically denatured proteins albeit the relatively small sampling size in the single-molecule fluorescence measurements.

A series of SAXS measurements were carried out on the knotted proteins under native and chemically denatured conditions, and the corresponding R g values were extracted using standard Guinier plot analysis (Figure , Table , and Supporting Information Figures S2-S9). The R g values are plotted as a function of L and compared with the reported R g values of unknotted proteins (Figure ). Because many of the knotted proteins are homodimeric, their chemical denaturation processes involve dissociation of dimers into monomers and hence reduce the chain lengths into half of that in their native states, which is taken into consideration in the correlation plot (Figure ). Indeed, significant increases in R g values are observed upon chemical denaturation as a result of unfolding. Compared with the experimentally determined R g values of native unknotted proteins, knotted proteins are generally more compact-their experimental R g values are comparable to or smaller than the nonlinear regression-derived values according to their chain lengths (Figure ). In contrast with our initial expectation that the chemically denatured knotted proteins may exhibit residual structures that can result in significant conformational compactions, our results indicate that the chemically denatured knotted proteins are in fact random coil-like according to their R g values. Some of the denatured states of the knotted proteins are actually larger than the expected values for random-coil proteins. For urea-denatured YibK and YbeA, in particular, which have been shown to maintain their knotted topology in the presence of 8 M urea, their R g values scale with the same chain length dependency as those of the other chemically denatured proteins which are unknotted; that is, they behave like random-coiled chains without significant degree of conformational compaction while being topologically knotted.

We first revisited the scaling law of R g as a function of polypeptide chain length (L) for chemically denatured proteins by updating the reported R g values in the literature (filled pink squares in Figure and Table S1 in the SI). The updated data set gave essentially the same scaling exponent (νdenatured = 0.58 ± 0.02, n = 37) as the previously reported value by Plaxco and coworkers (νdenatured = 0.59 ± 0.02, n = 26); the updated prefactor R 0 of 2.05 ± 0.17 Å is also similar to the previously reported value of 1.95 ± 0.16 Å (Table ). Note that the scaling exponent of chemically denatured proteins is larger than that for IDPs (νIDP = 0.52 ± 0.01, n = 50) reflecting the preferential long-range interactions within some of the IDPs, leading to slightly larger chain dimensions (open cyan circles in Figure ).

We next compiled 226 SAXS-based experimental R g values of folded proteins under native conditions to obtain a scaling law for native proteins (filled green circles in Figure , Table and Tables S2-S4 in the SI). Nonlinear regression of this data set indicated one entry of monomeric proteins and two entries of oligomeric proteins as outliers. These are the peptide subunit 104-363 of V-ATPase (259 residues and R g = 38.8 Å), TcdB, which is a large multidomain protein that adopts an elongated structure (2366 residues and R g = 78 Å), and the subunit H of the A1AO ATP synthase, which also adopts an elongated structure in solution (208 residues and R g = 57 Å). Because native proteins do not necessarily fold into compact and spherical conformations, as evidenced by the aforementioned outliers in the most extreme scenario, the distribution of the R g values as a function of chain length is much more scattered than that of chemically denatured proteins. A scaling exponent of νnative = 0.45 ± 0.02, and the prefactor R 0 of 2.04 ± 0.24 Å was obtained for the complete set of natively folded proteins (Table ). Limiting the analysis to monomeric protein structures results in the same scaling exponent within error (νmonomer = 0.49 ± 0.08, n = 129; Table ). Intriguingly, a separate nonlinear regression for the oligomeric, native proteins yields an even smaller scaling exponent (νoligomer = 0.32 ± 0.02, n = 67; Table ). This is much closer to the expectation for collapsed polymer chains in poor solvents. Nevertheless, the much smaller scaling exponent is accompanied by a much larger prefactor R 0,oligomer = 4.47 ± 0.47 that is more than double the value of its monomeric counterpart. The reason for such a large difference remains to be established.

Having established the scaling relationships of R g versus L for native and chemically denatured proteins, we set out to use SAXS to obtain the R g values of eight topologically knotted proteins, including YibK, YbeA, HP0242, and its tandem repeat HP0242x2, which is the first example of an engineered trefoil-knotted protein, MJ0366, which is the smallest trefoil-knotted protein known to date, human ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolyase, UCH-L1, and -L5 N-terminal domain (UCH-L5 NTD), which are Gordian-knotted protein, and DehI, which contains a Stevedore's knot. These eight topologically knotted proteins cover most of the protein knot types, except for the figure-eight knot, and sizes, with MJ0366 and DehI being the smallest/simplest and the largest/most complex protein knots, respectively. Characterizations of the chemical denaturation processes of YibK, , YbeA, , HP0242, UCH-L1, and MJ0366 have been reported in the literature; we have applied similar spectroscopic strategies to characterize the chemical denaturation of UCH-L5 NTD and DehI to ensure that the SAXS data of chemically denatured knotted proteins are collected under fully chemically denatured conditions according to intrinsic fluorescence, far-UV CD, or NMR spectroscopy (Supporting Information Figure S1). dataset_item.question: How does the presence of an SH OC hydrogen bond influence the geometry and stability of the global minimum conformer of methyl 3-mercaptopropionate?
dataset_item.answer: The global minimum conformer of methyl 3-mercaptopropionate is stabilized by an intramolecular S-H⋯O=C hydrogen bond, which plays a dominant role in its conformational equilibrium. This interaction contributes approximately 6.6 kJ mol⁻¹ to the conformer's stability, as determined through quantum chemical analyses, including QTAIM, NCI, and NBO methods. The hydrogen bond exhibits a bond length of 2.515(4) Å and an angle of 117.4(1)°, as confirmed by both experimental measurements (rotational spectroscopy) and computational studies. This stabilization arises from the favorable electronic redistribution induced by the hydrogen bond, which locks the molecule into its most stable geometry (conformer I), minimizing the impact of methyl group internal rotation and SH tunneling. Furthermore, these findings provide isolated molecular-level insights into sulfur hydrogen bonding, free from external influences such as solvent or crystal packing effects.

The paper investigates the influence of sulfur hydrogen bonding on the conformational equilibrium of methyl 3-mercaptopropionate, using microwave spectroscopy in a supersonic jet expansion.
