The complexes of C4H5N with C6H5OH were investigated using matrix isolation infrared spectroscopy. Quantum chemical calculations using DFT, DFT-GD3, M06, and MP2 levels of theory with aug-cc-pVDZ basis sets predicted three complexes A (O-H π), B (N-H O), and C (N-H π). The uniqueness of this study is that all three complexes were trapped and discerned in the N2 matrix. The complexes were identified from the shifts in the O-H stretching, and N-H stretching and bending modes of C6H5OH and C4H5N, respectively. Computations predicted complex A to be the global minimum structure at all levels of theory having synergistic O-H π and C-H π interactions at the aforementioned level of theory. The energetics and geometries of complexes A, B, and C varied with the levels of theory used to optimize these structures. At B3LYP/aug-cc-pVDZ level of theory, the stabilization energies varied in the order complex A < complex C < complex B, which concur with the Etter's and Legon-Millen first and third rules, respectively. As dispersion correction is applied through empirical or perturbation methods to optimize the geometry of the energy, ordering is altered, complex A < complex B < complex C, showing a deviation from the above rules. At all levels of theory, complex A is the global minimum having both O-H π and C-H π synergistic interactions, but the structure violates the Legon-Millen second rule. Nevertheless, hydrogen bonding is highly directional; the present study on the C4H5N-C6H5OH system is a definitive example where a strong deviation is noticed against generic Legon-Millen rules. The presence of synergistic interactions should thus be responsible for such a divergence.

The ground state rotational spectrum of methyl 3-mercaptopropionate was measured and analyzed in detail using chirped-pulse and cavity-based Fourier transform microwave spectroscopy from 8 to 18 GHz. Rotational transitions belonging to the two most stable conformers (I and II) were successfully assigned in the rotational spectra, and the lines present complex splitting patterns due to the methyl internal rotation and/or SH tunneling motion. The similar experimental V 3 barriers for the two conformers reveal that the electronic distribution of I and II is not strongly affected by their geometrical differences. QTAIM, NCI, and NBO analyses show that conformer I is favored in the conformational equilibrium due to a stable SH O = C IHB, which is estimated to have an energy of about 6.6 kJ mol-1 based on the potential energy at the bond critical point. On the basis of the ground state effective (r 0) and equilibrium (r e) geometries of I, we were able to derive the experimental geometric parameters associated with the sulfur HB, which reveals that the HB distance and angle S-H-O are 2.515(4) Å and 117.4(1)°, respectively. The nonobservation of additional conformers was rationalized based on their conversion pathways to lower energy forms and/or low population in the supersonic jet expansion. The present study provides key experimental data on sulfur HBs at the molecular level in isolation of crystal packing and solvent effects and serves as a benchmark for improved understanding and modeling of these important noncovalent interactions.

XeF6 was prepared and isolated in solid argon and neon matrices. The IR spectra of these deposits revealed significant interactions between the isolated XeF6 monomers and the noble gas host. These interactions are evidenced by significant shifts of the Xe-F stretching modes toward larger wavenumbers going from solid argon to solid neon as well as by extensive matrix-site splitting especially of the e-type modes in solid Ne. In agreement with a previous Ar matrix isolation study the XeF6 bands are very broad and several overlapping bands were observed around 630 cm-1. The influence of the Xe-isotope splitting on these band structures has been investigated by preparing isotopically enriched 129XeF6 and 136XeF6 isotopologues and recording their IR spectra in solid neon. As an internal reference, we have also analyzed matrix-site and Xe-isotope splitting of the corresponding Xe-F and Xe-O stretching modes of XeOF4 in solid neon. The half-width of isotopically enriched XeOF4 bands in solid neon is found to be 0.5-0.7 cm-1, while the width of the isolated Xe-F stretching band of XeF6 at 563.5 cm-1 is 2.4 cm-1. Apart from this unusual band broadening and in contrast to the former Ar matrix isolation study, the IR spectrum of molecular XeF6 in the solid noble gases argon and neon was found to be in complete agreement with the computed vibrational spectrum for the C 3v conformer, while the predicted strong t 1u band of the O h conformer around 590 cm-1 has not been observed. The absence of the O h conformer can probably be attributed to several reasons: (1) The low matrix temperature of about 5 K prevents any isomerization to the O h conformer, whereas interactions with the solid matrix host might also account for an additional stabilization of the low-symmetry C 3v conformer relative to the O h structure. (2) The barrier for the interconversion of the O h conformer into the C 3v minimum is too small to prevent the interconversion of the former into the more stable conformer during the rapid condensation process.

In continuation to our computational study in 2014, in this work, we have confirmed that the mode of action of thiourea moiety in cinchona-thiourea catalyst in the Henry reaction in DMF is via single hydrogen bond formation with the substrate that exploits cooperatively the R3NH+ of protonated quinuclidine moiety of catalyst in the hydrogen bonding with substrate. In the present work, we have dug out the role of catalyst with the trans conformation of the N-H sites of thiourea, which we call conformer (β) of the catalyst, in enantioseletion in more detail. Energy decomposition analysis (EDA) has been performed and frontier molecular orbital interactions are investigated in order to describe the origin of enantioselectivity in this reaction. On the basis of the energy and electronic structure analyses in the case of Henry reaction with cinchona thiourea, the specific conformation of the substrates with respect to the forming C-C bond determines the selection and strength of orbital interaction at the transition states. We found that the conformational preference of the substrates with respect to each other increases the orbital interaction between the substrates in one enantiomer and also the strength of the hydrogen bond between substrates and catalyst pocket. The stabilization of the positive charge developing on the protonated catalyst in the transition state of the S enantiomer is a key factor of the hydrogen bond role. Generally speaking with this work we understand that the origin of enantioselectivity in the Henry reaction with cinchona thiourea in DMF is an orbital interaction and this perhaps hints for design of selectivity in the experiment. The mode of action of typical thiourea catalysts is not always via double hydrogen bond formation but the flexibility of the catalyst molecules permits for a single hydrogen bond with substrate and also allows for simultaneous effective interaction with the environment (solvent). The stronger hydrogen bond formation in S configuration was confirmed utilizing calculated IR spectra of the transition state structures. Our computational studies have provided detailed mechanistic insights into the mode of action of thiourea catalysts that might explain their robustness in various solvent environments.

dataset_item.question: What are the specific energy savings and capital investment reductions achievable with heterogeneous azeotropic dividing-wall column compared to conventional azeotropic distillation sequences?
dataset_item.answer: The heterogeneous azeotropic dividing-wall column (ADWC) offers significant energy savings and capital investment reductions compared to conventional azeotropic distillation sequences, making it an efficient and viable alternative for ethanol dehydration processes. Specifically, the ADWC reduces energy consumption by 21.36% compared to the conventional azeotropic-recovery sequence and by 11.97% relative to the azeotropic-stripper sequence. Additionally, it lowers total annual costs by 18.48% and 18.43%, respectively, compared to these conventional sequences. Beyond energy and cost benefits, the ADWC exhibits comparable dynamic controllability to the azeotropic-recovery sequence and superior controllability to the azeotropic-stripper sequence, further enhancing its practical application and operational reliability.

A ternary extractive distillation process for the separation of the ethyl acetate/isopropanol/water system with a single solvent and mixed solvent and the enhancement of its energy-saving properties was studied. Simulation optimization software was developed and used to simulate the distillation process to improve the optimization rate. The optimal proportion of the mixture solvent was determined by taking into account the minimum TAC as the selection standard. On the basis of the optimal composition of the mixed solvent, an extractive distillation process combining two energy-saving processes based on heat coupling and the use of a heat pump was further explored. The TAC and CO2 emission corresponding to each process was calculated and compared from the perspectives of economy and environment. The results show that the separation process using a mixed solvent shows better economic and environmental performance than the process using a single solvent. The economic and environmental performance of the mixed solvent extractive distillation process combined with partial thermal coupling technology was further improved via reduction of the remixing effect and the good separation performance of the mixed solvent. The extractive distillation process combined with heat pump technology was found to improve the self-heat recovery rate and greatly reduce the energy consumption of the separation process. Therefore, a higher environmental and economic performance was achieved, which can meet the constantly updated clean production requirements of the chemical industry.

dataset_item.question: How does coupling hydrated manganese oxide with permanganate improve the removal efficiency of antibiotic resistance genes compared to other methods?
dataset_item.answer: Coupling hydrated manganese oxide (HMO) with permanganate (KMnO₄) significantly improves the removal efficiency of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) from wastewater treatment plant effluents, achieving a reduction of 2.46–4.23 logs. This method outperforms conventional approaches such as UV disinfection (0.18–1.96 logs), chlorination (0.18–1.96 logs), ozonation (1–2 logs in pure samples), and Fenton-based treatment (approximately 3.78 logs for sulI in effluents). The superior performance of the HMO-KMnO₄ system is attributed to the synergistic mechanisms of oxidation (via KMnO₄) and coagulation (via HMO), which enhance the removal of ARGs, particularly in real wastewater samples. Additionally, this approach circumvents limitations faced by other methods, such as dependency on specific operational conditions (e.g., low pH for Fenton treatment), reduced efficiency in complex wastewater matrices, and higher costs or impractical requirements. By leveraging both chemical and physical removal mechanisms, the coupled system provides a robust and cost-effective solution for mitigating the dissemination of ARGs from wastewater treatment processes.

The present study showed that the aminopolycarboxylic chelating surfactant C12-DTPA can be effectively used in combination with two foaming agents for the removal of extremely toxic metal ions such as Cd2+, Zn2+, and Sr2+ from aqueous solution using the ion flotation technique. It was found that the removal of metal ions from the flotation cell is dependent on their chelation behavior with C12-DTPA and on the foaming properties of the samples, both of which change with the pH of the system. The results indicate that both Zn2+ and Cd2+ can be completely removed at pH 5. However, when the pH is increased to 7 and 9, barely 60% of Zn2+ and Cd2+ can be removed from the solution. On the other hand, at pH 5, no removal of Sr2+ was observed, whereas at a pH of 7-9, ~65% removal was achieved under comparable conditions. For efficient separation of metal ions from water systems, the amount of water transferred to the reject foam must also be considered, which is evaluated by measuring the concentration of metal ions in the collected foam. It was found that the interactions between the foaming agent and chelating surfactant affects the concentration of metal ions in the foam. A higher concentration of DoTAC increased the concentration of Sr2+ in the collected foam, because of the strong interactions between DoTAC and C12-DTPA. A higher concentration of DDAO, on the other hand, increased the removal of metal ions from the bulk, because of better foaming properties of the test solution. The separation efficiency is a measure of both the removal of metal ions from the bulk and the concentration of metal ions in the collected foam, and the foaming agent mixture must be designed accordingly. Taking the above parameters into account, it would be useful to design and optimize a selective ion flotation process in competitive systems for the target metal ions.

dataset_item.question: How does tris pentafluorophenyl boron as an interfacial modification layer improve the efficiency and stability of methylammonium lead iodide perovskite solar cells?
dataset_item.answer:
Tris(pentafluorophenyl)boron (TPFPB) enhances the efficiency and stability of methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3) perovskite solar cells by serving as an interfacial modification layer between the perovskite and the tin oxide (SnO2) electron transport layer. TPFPB improves perovskite film morphology and crystallinity, reduces trap density, and minimizes carrier recombination, leading to better charge extraction. These improvements are facilitated by the formation of weak chemical bonds, such as hydrogen-fluorine (H-F) and nitrogen-boron (N-B), between TPFPB and the respective device materials, which strengthen the interface and reduce interfacial defects.  

As a result, TPFPB treatment increases the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of the solar cells from 16.01% to 18.67%, with enhancements in key performance parameters such as open-circuit voltage (Voc), short-circuit current density (Jsc), and fill factor (FF). Furthermore, TPFPB-treated devices exhibit significantly improved long-term stability and moisture resistance, demonstrating its effectiveness in both efficiency optimization and durability enhancement for high-performance perovskite solar cells.

dataset_item.question: Are topological surface states in bismuth selenide robust under varying oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor conditions?
dataset_item.answer: Topological surface states (TSSs) in bismuth selenide (Bi₂Se₃) are robust under both oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor conditions, as confirmed by first-principles calculations. Oxidized configurations preserve TSSs within the band gap due to the hybridized states formed by interstitial oxygen atoms and substrate atoms remaining far from the Fermi level. These calculations further demonstrate that TSSs persist at the interface between oxidized and non-oxidized Bi₂Se₃ layers, consistent with the topological invariant properties. Importantly, surface oxidation does not break time-reversal symmetry, ensuring the protection of TSSs. Consequently, exposure to air—whether under oxygen-rich or oxygen-poor conditions—has minimal impact on the stability and practical use of Bi₂Se₃ as a topological insulator.

dataset_item.question: What molecular orbital characteristics and geometric factors influence photoinduced reactions in ultranano oxide-supported metal clusters?
dataset_item.answer:
Photoinduced reactions in ultranano oxide-supported metal clusters are governed by molecular orbital (MO) characteristics and geometric factors. The bonding and antibonding nature of MOs, identified through overlap population density of states (OP-DOS) analysis, plays a crucial role in determining the reactive pathways of excited states. Geometric factors, including the arrangement of metal clusters, adsorbates, and the oxide support, further influence these reactions. Explicit modeling of environmental effects, such as oxide supports using ions and point charges, enhances accuracy in capturing key interactions.

Computational protocols, such as time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT), are employed to simulate the evolution of excited states and their corresponding geometric rearrangements. Relaxation of these states reveals correlations between MO characteristics and photochemical processes like ligand detachment, cluster fragmentation, or disaggregation. For example, excited states that weaken bonds between metal atoms and reactive oxygen species often drive these reactions.

Despite the strengths of this approach, challenges remain, including congested potential energy surfaces and limitations in the precision of excited-state descriptions. Hybrid DFT functionals and refined algorithms are proposed to improve computational accuracy and predictive reliability. This integrated methodology offers valuable insights into photoinduced reactivity in ultranano oxide-supported metal clusters, paving the way for advancements in photochemical applications.

The proposed protocol consists in designing a realistic model of the catalytic system, comprising the metal cluster and a shell of adsorbates (either reactants or intermediates or products) and in which the oxide support is described by a small number of explicit, QM-treated ions augmented by a large array of point charges to model the Madelung potential of the environment. The excited states most promising for photochemistry are selected by first inspecting overlap population of density of states (OP-DOS) plots to single out which molecular orbitals (MOs) have a proper bonding or antibonding character which can be expected to produce the desired photochemical process. The orbitals identified via OP-DOS are then searched as components of the excited states as derived from TDDFT simulations at the ground-state equilibrium geometry. Finally, the excited states with the proper MOs as main components are subjected to full geometry relaxation. The computational effort entailed by the present approach is affordable according to current standards, with a typical excited-state optimization requiring about 36 h of elapsed time using 12 cores of a ProLiant DL580 Gen10 HP server equipped with Intel Xeon Gold 6140 CPU @ 2.30 GHz. dataset_item.question: How is conformational entropy of sugar-phosphate backbones calculated using analytical closure solutions?
dataset_item.answer:
Conformational entropy of sugar-phosphate backbones is calculated using analytical closure solutions by combining geometric constraints, steric clash exclusions, and nucleotide correlations along the chain. The process begins with defining RETO coordinates (r, η, θ, ω) and torsion angles (ψ, ν), which specify the internal geometry of the backbone, including bond lengths, bond angles, and ribose ring closure indices (f). These parameters ensure the chain maintains connectivity and adheres to physical constraints.

The analytical closure algorithm enumerates all possible backbone conformations between adjacent nucleotides by solving the closure problem, incorporating steric clash exclusions to discard physically forbidden conformations. The conformational space is discretized into grids for ψ and ν angles, enabling numerical integration to compute the total conformational volume (Ω). To account for correlations between nucleotides, consecutive matrix multiplications are employed, iteratively propagating constraints and conformational possibilities along the chain.

The entropy (S) is derived from the conformational volume as \( S = R \ln \Omega \), where \( R \) is the gas constant. Per-nucleotide entropy is calculated incrementally, allowing the method to capture segment-to-segment coupling and improve accuracy compared to earlier approaches. By combining RETO coordinates, steric clash exclusions, and matrix-based propagation of constraints, this method provides a comprehensive and precise calculation of conformational entropy for sugar-phosphate backbones.

A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. To numerically evaluate the integral for Ω, all possible ribose geometries were first selected by the ribose closure solution and precomputed on a grid of m = 16 ν1 angles spanning its feasibility domain [-ν1 *,+ν1 *] and stored. This is possible because ribose closure solutions are independent of the base configurations (i.e.. they are not functions of RETO). Standard nucleotide geometries were used for both the ribose closure and the closure of the remainder of the main chain. Whereas ribose closure can be precomputed, main-chain closure must be performed explicitly between every pair of nearest-neighbor bases j and j + 1 since the domain for RETO j is large and the functional form for C on it is complex. To do this, each of the two rotation angles ψ′ j and ψ j+1 was discretized on a grid with n = 128 points on its domain [0,2π], and the closure solution C(ψ′ j ,f j ,ν j ;ψ j+1,f j+1,ν j+1RETO j ) was computed on the six-dimensional grid (ψ′ j ,f j ,ν j ;ψ j+1,f j+1,ν j+1) point-by-point producing a (m × 2n) × (m × 2n) matrix. Using a collision distance of 3.2 Å for every pair of non-hydrogen atoms between the two atomic fragments on the two bases, points on the C(ψ j ,f j ,ν j ;ψ j+1,f j+1,ν j+1RETO j ) grid that represented geometries with steric collision(s) involving any pair of atoms between the two fragments were eliminated from C. This calculation was repeated for every backbone segment j between bases j and j + 1, for j from 1 to N - 1. The total conformational volume, Ω, available to the backbone of the entire chain containing N nucleotides was then computed by a discrete approximation of the integral in eq , evaluated as N - 2 consecutive matrix multiplications involving two (m × 2n) × (m × 2n) matrices at a time. With this matrix multiplication approach, the total number of backbone conformations which have been enumerated and screened by Ω is equivalent to (m × 2n) N-1. The conformational entropy over the entire chain is then given by S III/R = ln Ω. The per-nucleotide entropy is defined to be the incremental S III/R when one additional nucleotide is added to the end of the chain.

dataset_item.question: How does sulfur composition in alloyed CdSexS1-x nanoplatelets affect their optical properties, such as excitonic transitions and emission characteristics?
dataset_item.answer:
Increasing sulfur composition in alloyed CdSeₓS₁₋ₓ nanoplatelets (NPLs) leads to a blue shift in excitonic transitions and emission peaks due to the widening of the energy band gap. For instance, raising sulfur content shifts the emission peak from ~513 nm (pure CdSe NPLs) to shorter wavelengths, such as ~488 nm for S/(Se+S) = 0.30, while broadening the full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) of emission features from ~40 meV to ~80–100 meV. This broadening primarily arises from enhanced exciton-phonon coupling, as confirmed by photoluminescence excitation spectroscopy, ruling out inhomogeneous alloying effects. However, higher sulfur concentrations also introduce more surface trap states, reducing photoluminescence quantum yield (PL-QY) to values as low as 10–20%, likely due to lateral size expansion and increased surface defects.

To mitigate these adverse effects, structural modifications such as CdS crown or shell passivation have been employed. Core/crown NPLs enhance PL-QY to ~60% by passivating sidewall trap states, maintaining emission energy, and improving stability. In contrast, core/shell NPLs enable tunable emission over a broader wavelength range (e.g., 560–650 nm) with wider linewidths (~100 meV) due to stronger exciton-phonon coupling, while also reducing optical gain thresholds (e.g., ~53 μJ/cm²) by suppressing reabsorption and Auger recombination. These strategies demonstrate the potential for optimizing optical properties and stability in alloyed CdSeₓS₁₋ₓ nanoplatelets through compositional and structural engineering.

Here the blue-shifting in excitonic features can be explained with the increase of the energy band gap due to the alloying. On the other hand, slight broadening could be attributed to the variation in the composition and/or inhomogeneous alloying of NPLs. However, the similar excitonic transitions observed from the PLE spectra of CdSe x S1-x core NPLs taken at different emission wavelengths has ruled out this possibility and strongly suggested the formation of CdSe x S1-x core NPLs having a homogeneously alloyed crystal structure (Figure S3). Therefore, the broadening of the excitonic features may most likely be due to the enhanced exciton-phonon coupling commonly observed in this material system.

In this study, we prepared CdSe x S1-x alloyed NPLs together with their core/crown and core/shell heterostructures to obtain highly tunable excitonic properties. First, we started with the synthesis of 4 ML thick CdSe x S1-x core NPLs having an additional layer of Cd atoms and used them as a seed for the further synthesis of core/crown and core/shell NPLs. For the synthesis of CdSe x S1-x core NPLs, we modified the recipe of 4 ML thick CdSe core NPLs (see the experimental section for details). By the addition of a certain amount of sulfur precursor after degassing, we succeeded in the formation of a highly uniform CdSe x S1-x alloy, and depending on the amount of injected sulfur precursor, the composition of CdSe x S1-x was tuned in a precisely controlled way. The high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images of CdSe x S1-x alloyed core NPLs with various compositions feature a rectangular shape and uniform size distribution regardless of the sulfur composition (Figure a). While lateral sizes of CdSe x S1-x alloyed core NPLs were observed to be generally increased with increasing the amount of sulfur, their thicknesses were found to be the same with the 4 ML thick CdSe core only NPLs. Also, the elemental composition of CdSe x S1-x alloyed core NPLs is determined by using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (Figure b). It was measured that the elemental composition of sulfur can be increased up to (1 - x) = 0.30 with a 1 mL of sulfur precursor injection. Further increasing the amount of sulfur resulted in the formation of a mixed population of NPLs with excess amounts of colloidal quantum dots so that it is not easy to achieve pure population of CdSe x S1-x alloyed core NPLs with cleaning procedures.

In conclusion, we have reported the synthesis of core/crown and core/shell heterostructures of CdSe x S1-x core-only NPLs together with their resulting excitonic properties, enabling the achievement of highly tunable and low-threshold gain performance. With the synthesis CdSe x S1-x /CdS core/crown NPLs, we demonstrated improved PL-QY, enhanced absorption cross-section, and increased stability without changing the emission spectra of CdSe x S1-x core-only NPLs. On the other hand, with the synthesis of CdSe x S1-x /CdS core/shell NPLs, we realized highly tunable emission for NPLs covering a wide range of the spectrum between 560 and 650 nm, depending on the sulfur composition and shell thickness. Also, we studied the optical gain performances of different heterostructures of CdSe x S1-x alloyed NPLs, offering great advantages including reduced reabsorption and spectrally tunable optical gain range. Considering the emission of CdSe x S1-x based NPLs covering a wide spectral range, we demonstrated highly tunable ASE with low gain thresholds ( ~ 53 μJ/cm2). These findings have shown the importance of the colloidal synthesis of engineered heterostructured NPLs for the achievement of superior excitonic properties and the significant potential for the utilization of NPLs for the next-generation optoelectronic devices including lasers and light-emitting-diodes (LEDs), owing to their profoundly tunable excitonic properties.

Although the emission of the CdSe x S1-x alloyed core NPLs was demonstrated to be shifted to higher energies with increasing sulfur composition, they suffered from the decreased PL-QY ( ~ 10-20%) and the stability issue with respect to the CdSe core only NPLs, which can be explained with the increased surface trap sites owing to their extended lateral size (Figure S1). To achieve better optical properties and enhanced stability without changing the emission behavior of CdSe x S1-x alloyed core NPLs, we synthesized CdSe x S1-x /CdS core/crown NPLs. The formation of CdS crown extension only in the lateral direction and passivation of sidewalls can greatly enhance the PL-QY of NPLs without changing the spectral position of the emission. By using the freshly synthesized CdSe x S1-x alloyed core NPLs as seeds, we prepared core/crown NPLs using a slightly modified recipe (see the experimental section for details). HAADF-STEM images of CdSe x S1-x /CdS core/crown NPLs having different sulfur compositions are shown in Figure a. In comparison to CdSe x S1-x core NPLs, lateral sizes of the core/crown NPLs are found to be increased, while the vertical thicknesses remained the same, suggesting the formation of core/crown heterostructures. It is also important to note that, although we used highly uniform and rectangular-shaped CdSe x S1-x alloyed core NPLs as seeds, the formation of the CdS crown region was nonuniform in the lateral direction, which is typically observed for the CdSe/CdS core/crown NPLs in literature. ,,

dataset_item.question: How does the hexagonal WO3 structure contribute to the resistance of V2O5/HWO catalysts against alkali poisoning during selective catalytic reduction reactions?
dataset_item.answer: The hexagonal WO₃ (HWO) structure significantly enhances the alkali poisoning resistance of V₂O₅/HWO catalysts during selective catalytic reduction (SCR) reactions by utilizing its unique one-dimensional tunnel architecture (~5.4 Å in size). These tunnels, lined with smooth {100}/{1-10} facets, provide energetically favorable pathways (low diffusion barrier: 0.27 eV) for the migration of alkali metal ions, such as K⁺, from the catalyst surface into the tunnel interiors. Once inside, K⁺ ions form stable coordination configurations with the tunnel walls (binding energy: 2.31 eV lower than surface adsorption), effectively isolating them spatially from the catalytically active V₂O₅ sites. This mechanism prevents alkali-induced deactivation and preserves catalytic activity even under challenging conditions involving high alkali concentrations (350 μmol g⁻¹) and SO₂ exposure (1300 mg m⁻³). The resistance is further validated by experimental techniques such as XRD and computational methods like DFT. Unlike conventional V₂O₅/WO₃-TiO₂ catalysts, HWO’s tunnel-based trapping mechanism ensures simultaneous resistance to both alkali and sulfur poisoning, achieving up to 92% NO conversion efficiency in SCR processes.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. Summary of Purpose
The purpose of this paper is to develop and investigate a new catalyst, V2O5 supported on hexagonal WO3 (HWO), that exhibits exceptional resistance to alkali and sulfur poisoning during selective catalytic reduction (SCR) of NOx emissions with NH3. This study addresses the limitations of conventional V2O5/WO3-TiO2 catalysts, which suffer from rapid deactivation under similar conditions. The research explores how the unique structural properties of HWO contribute to improved catalyst performance and provides a strategy for designing SCR catalysts for both stationary and mobile NOx emission control.

---

### 2. Classification of Purpose
The purpose of the paper emphasizes **"<result>"**, as it primarily focuses on demonstrating the performance and resistance of the V2O5/HWO catalyst to alkali and sulfur poisoning, along with its potential applicability in emission control.

---

### 3. Research Questions
Here are relevant research questions inspired by the abstract:

1. What structural properties of hexagonal WO3 (HWO) contribute to the improved resistance of the V2O5/HWO catalyst to alkali and sulfur poisoning during SCR reactions?
2. How does the dispersion of V2O5 on the external surfaces of HWO affect its catalytic activity and resistance to deactivation compared to conventional V2O5/WO3-TiO2 catalysts?
3. What role do the smooth surfaces and size-suitable tunnels of HWO play in facilitating alkali diffusion and trapping?
4. How does the V2O5/HWO catalyst maintain SCR activity under high K+ loading and SO2 concentrations, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
5. Can the V2O5/HWO catalyst be scaled up or optimized for practical applications in controlling NOx emissions from both stationary and mobile sources?

These questions address both fundamental material properties and applied considerations for NOx emission control technologies.
dataset_item.true_false_question: Does the alkali resistance of V₂O₅/HWO catalysts primarily depend on surface adsorption of K⁺ ions rather than their migration into the hexagonal WO₃ tunnels?

inference_contexts: In conclusion, the V2O5/HWO catalysts with the exceptional resistance to alkali and sulfur poisoning were successfully developed to control NO x emissions by the SCR reactions. The V2O5/HWO catalysts are thoroughly characterized by HTREM, EDX mapping, XRD, and SXRD together with the Rietveld refinement analysis. The catalytic tests revealed that the V2O5/HWO catalyst showed the strong resistance to alkali poisoning, and the catalysts with the high K+ loading of 350 μmol g-1 did not decrease the high SCR activity even in the presence of the high-concentration SO2, whereas the conventional V2O5/WO3-TiO2 catalysts almost completely lost SCR activity under the same conditions. The experimental results coupled with theoretical calculations demonstrated that the strong resistance of the V2O5/HWO catalysts to alkali and sulfur poisoning mainly originated from the specific alkali-trapping sites of the HWO. Alkalis accumulated on the catalytically active surface sites of the V2O5/HWO catalysts could spontaneously migrate into the HWO tunnels during the SCR reactions, and arrived at a separate state from the catalytically active sites, thus leading to simultaneous resistance to alkalis and SO2 poisoning. Therefore, the V2O5/HWO catalysts with a hexagonal structure of WO3 are promising candidates for controlling NO x emissions from the stationary source and the mobile source against alkali and sulfur poisoning.

All characterization data above provide the evidence that the V2O5/HWO catalyst has the specific alkali-trapping sites in the HWO tunnels, which can trap the alkali-metal ions and stably fix them in the HWO tunnels under the normal SCR reaction conditions, even if the alkalis are initially accumulated on the catalyst's surfaces such as on the surface of the V2O5. The trapped alkali-metal ions are spatially separated from the catalytically active sites of the V2O5, so the combined deactivation effects of alkali and SO2 are not observed in the SCR reactions. Although conventional V2O5/WO3-TiO2 catalysts show the strong SO2 tolerance, they suffer severe alkali poisoning. Moreover, the V2O5/HWO catalyst gives a high selectivity to N2 and a low oxidation rate of SO2 in the SCR reactions, as shown in Figures S12 and S13 (Supporting Information), respectively. Therefore, the V2O5/HWO catalysts with the exceptional resistance to alkali and SO2 poisoning should have widespread applications in the SCR reactions for controlling NO emissions from both the stationary source and the mobile source.

To investigate the simultaneous resistance of the V2O5/HWO against alkali and sulfur poisoning, the catalysts are first impregnated by K2SO4 at a high loading (350 μmol gcat -1), and after drying at 100 °C, directly tested in the SCR reactions in the presence of high-concentration SO2 (1300 mg m-3). The SCR reactions are initially conducted by a temperature-programmed procedure from 25 to 350 °C, and then the reaction temperature is kept at 350 °C for stable tests. Figure shows the NO conversions (X NO) of the catalysts under isothermal reaction conditions. Obviously, the V2O5/HWO catalyst shows excellent resistance simultaneously against alkali and sulfur poisoning, and under a GHSV of 200 000 h-1, the catalytic activity of the K2SO4-impregnated V2O5/HWO quickly increases and arrives at a steady state with a X NO of 92%. Similarly, at a higher GHSV of 400 000 h-1, the V2O5/HWO catalyst shows such a strong resistance against alkali and sulfur poisoning that alkali and sulfur have almost no influence on its catalytic activity. As expected, the conventional V2O5/WO3-TiO2 catalyst even with a low K+ loading (115 μmol gcat -1) exhibits rather poor alkali resistance and undergoes severe and continuous deactivation with time on stream until complete loss of activity is observed after 4 h. Likewise, the V2O5/HWO catalyst shows the excellent resistance against alkaline earth metals' poisoning such as Ca2+, as shown in Figure S1 in the Supporting Information.

For V2O5-based catalysts, the presence of SO2 might have a negative influence on the alkali resistance of catalysts. , Thus, the effect of SO2 or alkali alone on the V2O5/HWO is also tested in the SCR reactions under two different GHSVs (Figure S2 in the Supporting Information), and still no deactivation is observed over the V2O5/HWO catalyst, regardless of the presence of alkali or SO2 alone or both, indicating no interactions occurring between alkalis and SO2 during the SCR process, unlike the reported results by Liu et al. It is well-known that the V2O5-based catalysts have a strong SO2 tolerance and the weak alkali resistance. ,, Therefore, it is convincing that the strong alkali resistance of the V2O5/HWO originates from the HWO. The SCR reactions over the HWO with and without a loading of K2SO4 (115 μmol gcat -1 of K+) after annealing at 400 °C are also tested and the results are shown in Figure S3 (Supporting Information). The K2SO4 loading does not decrease the catalytic performance, but slightly increases catalytic performance of the HWO. As a matter of fact, the reported WO3-supported/promoted V2O5 catalysts do not have strong alkali resistance, , and thus the strong alkali-resistance of the current V2O5/HWO catalyst should be attributed to the structure of the HWO.

Future work must consider each of these phenomena in order to enable high-voltage operation and increase both the energy density and cycle life of sodium layered oxide cathodes. First, the extent of iron migration must be elucidated with advanced characterization techniques, and the migration may be mitigated by substituting other ions for iron or introducing dopants that can act as pillaring ions in the sodium layer. Surface reactivity may then be reduced by modifying the electrolyte or by applying a stable cathode coating. The OP2 phase transition is a more complicated matter. Limiting iron migration is likely to lengthen the duration of the OP2 phase during cycling, which will in principle increase particle cracking, resulting in material isolation and aggravated CEI formation. Pinning ions can limit the OP2 phase transition and avoid cracking concerns, at the expense of capacity. The best approach may be to reduce the volume change of the phase transition, for example, by using dopants in the transition-metal plane with strong oxygen bonding. Regardless, it is evident that there is significant room for improvement both in the understanding and design of sodium layered oxides. Through rational design, the capacity and cycle life of this low-cost material may be improved such that it can compete for large-scale energy storage applications.

dataset_item.question: What role does overlap fraction ϕr play in predicting wettability and stability of surfaces with reentrant structures?
dataset_item.answer:
The overlap fraction (ϕr) is a critical quantitative parameter for predicting and optimizing both wettability and mechanical stability of surfaces with reentrant structures. It directly influences the Gibbs free energy barrier (G*T) and contact angle hysteresis (CAC), which are key indicators of stability and hydrophobicity, respectively. For paraboloid structures, increasing ϕr leads to a trade-off: stability improves (higher G*T), but hydrophobicity decreases (higher CAC), making simultaneous optimization challenging. In contrast, T-shaped reentrant structures exhibit a more favorable behavior, where increasing ϕr enhances stability without compromising hydrophobicity, as CAC remains constant. This enables the design of surfaces with high superamphiphobicity and stability.

ϕr also plays a vital role in maintaining the Cassie state by influencing structural dimensions and energy barriers. Its incorporation into theoretical models and simulations provides a robust framework for predicting wettability and stability without extensive experimental testing. Validations against experimental data from reported reentrant structures demonstrate strong agreement, confirming ϕr as a reliable design parameter for achieving desired surface properties. By carefully selecting optimal ϕr values, designers can balance wettability and stability, facilitating the creation of advanced functional surfaces tailored for specific applications.

The paper investigates the impact of reentrant surface curvature—a newly proposed factor—on surface wettability and the stability of the Cassie state. It introduces the overlap fraction (ϕr) to quantitatively assess how different reentrant structures affect wettability and mechanical stability. Through theoretical analysis and simulations of specific structures (paraboloid and square T-shaped), the study provides insights into the trade-offs between wettability and mechanical strength. inference_contexts: To explain the influence of the reentrant structures on wettability and stability of the surfaces, the overlap fraction ϕr was introduced in the derivation of the Gibbs free energy of the system, and three novel necessary conditions for the existence of the Cassie state were obtained. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, a novel method that can be used to quantitatively evaluate the influence of different surface structures on the wettability and stability of the Cassie state was presented. In addition, the simulation results and analysis process of two typical structures were demonstrated, which are paraboloid and T-shaped reentrant structures, respectively. For the paraboloid structures, the influence rules of spatial period on CAC and G T * were found to be opposite. The paraboloid structures cannot achieve high hydrophobicity and stability at the same time. In contrast, for the T-shaped reentrant structures, the G T * increases gradually, but the CAC remains constant with the increase of ϕr. To verify the correctness of the theory, three reported reentrant structures were simulated in this study. The simulation results of the apparent contact angles of three structures are almost consistent with the experimental data reported in the literature, and their stability of the Cassie state was also evaluated. The reentrant structures provide us with the possibility to construct the surface with high superamphiphobicity and stability at the same time.

Briefly, the appropriate structural dimension parameter and overlap fraction ϕr should be selected according to the actual needs for wettability and stability in the actual design. The novel theory presented in this study can be very useful for the design of structures of the superamphiphobic surface and avoiding the waste of resources caused by numerous repetitive experiments.

A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

dataset_item.question: How does pressure influence the distribution of tetraphenylethylene derivatives between organic and aqueous phases in multiphase systems?
dataset_item.answer: Pressure significantly influences the distribution of tetraphenylethylene (TPE) derivatives between organic and aqueous phases in multiphase systems by altering the permittivity of water. Increased pressure raises water permittivity, which enhances the partitioning of hydrophobic TPE derivatives (e.g., TPE1H/TPE1-) from the aqueous phase into the organic phase or γ-cyclodextrin cavities, while hydrophilic derivatives (e.g., TPE2H2/TPE22-) predominantly remain in the aqueous phase. This leads to opposing trends in concentration: free TPE1- decreases in the aqueous phase as pressure increases, while TPE22- concentrations rise. The use of pressure as a tunable parameter provides a novel alternative to solvent composition adjustments in multiphase systems, with implications for diverse applications such as chromatography, deep-sea chemical processes, and advanced separation techniques.

### Task 1: Summarize the purpose of the paper
The purpose of the paper is to investigate the pressure-dependent behavior of tetraphenylethylene (TPE) derivatives in multiphase systems consisting of organic and aqueous phases, both in the presence and absence of γ-cyclodextrin (γ-CD). The study explores how pressure influences the distribution ratios of TPE derivatives between phases, their complexation with γ-CD, and the resulting fluorescence properties. The work provides insights into how molecular polarity and water permittivity under high pressure govern these phenomena, offering new perspectives for multiphase partitioning and potential alternatives to conventional extraction methods.

---

### Task 2: Classify the purpose

---

Here are research questions relevant to the themes and materials science interests of the abstract:

1. **Thermodynamics and Pressure Effects**:
   - How does pressure influence the distribution of TPE derivatives between organic and aqueous phases in a multiphase system?
   - What role does water permittivity play in stabilizing polar solutes under high pressure?

dataset_item.true_false_question: Does increased pressure decrease the permittivity of water in multiphase systems involving tetraphenylethylene derivatives?

inference_contexts: The pressure has not been regarded as an important factor in the multiphase partition of compounds. Here, we discuss the results obtained for the multiphase partition of TPE derivatives under hydrostatic pressures. TPE1H/TPE1- and TPE2H2/TPE22- show different P-dependencies in the two-phase partition and γ-CD complexation. This behavior can be interpreted by the permittivity of water. Because this paper presents the first liquid-liquid partition study under hydrostatic pressures, the qualitative discussions based on the reported P-dependence of water permittivity are meaningful. As indicated earlier, the permittivity of water increases with increasing pressure. A hydrophobic molecule escapes from the aqueous phase into the organic phase or the cavity of γ-CD at high pressures, whereas the hydrophilic molecule remains in the aqueous phase. In the present instance, this mechanism leads to two contrasting findings; that is, the concentration of free TPE1- in the aqueous phase decreases but that of TPE2 increases with increasing pressure.

The present study showed that the aminopolycarboxylic chelating surfactant C12-DTPA can be effectively used in combination with two foaming agents for the removal of extremely toxic metal ions such as Cd2+, Zn2+, and Sr2+ from aqueous solution using the ion flotation technique. It was found that the removal of metal ions from the flotation cell is dependent on their chelation behavior with C12-DTPA and on the foaming properties of the samples, both of which change with the pH of the system. The results indicate that both Zn2+ and Cd2+ can be completely removed at pH 5. However, when the pH is increased to 7 and 9, barely 60% of Zn2+ and Cd2+ can be removed from the solution. On the other hand, at pH 5, no removal of Sr2+ was observed, whereas at a pH of 7-9, ~65% removal was achieved under comparable conditions. For efficient separation of metal ions from water systems, the amount of water transferred to the reject foam must also be considered, which is evaluated by measuring the concentration of metal ions in the collected foam. It was found that the interactions between the foaming agent and chelating surfactant affects the concentration of metal ions in the foam. A higher concentration of DoTAC increased the concentration of Sr2+ in the collected foam, because of the strong interactions between DoTAC and C12-DTPA. A higher concentration of DDAO, on the other hand, increased the removal of metal ions from the bulk, because of better foaming properties of the test solution. The separation efficiency is a measure of both the removal of metal ions from the bulk and the concentration of metal ions in the collected foam, and the foaming agent mixture must be designed accordingly. Taking the above parameters into account, it would be useful to design and optimize a selective ion flotation process in competitive systems for the target metal ions.

dataset_item.question: How do DNA strands tethered to nanodiamonds behave in comparison to DNA strands in solution?
dataset_item.answer: DNA strands tethered to nanodiamonds exhibit solution-like behavior, including repetitive hybridization with complementary strands and mobility comparable to DNA in free solution or tethered to proteins. These properties have been confirmed through spin-labeling and electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy studies. The DNA strands are covalently attached to nanodiamonds via copper-free click chemistry, ensuring robust and stable tethering while preserving their dynamic functionality. This attachment method enables the DNA to act as reusable "identity tags" for nanodiamonds, facilitating their use in biosensing platforms and other applications without compromising the natural properties of untethered DNA.

dataset_item.question: What structural properties of designed repeat proteins contribute to the stabilization of fluorescent gold nanoclusters?
dataset_item.answer: The structural properties of designed consensus tetratricopeptide repeat (CTPR) proteins that contribute to the stabilization of fluorescent gold nanoclusters (AuNCs) include the presence of tyrosine residues, which play a critical role in adsorbing gold ions and facilitating AuNC formation. The stabilization process is unaffected by the number of protein repeats or the presence of a single cysteine residue, highlighting the versatility of the protein scaffold. Optimal AuNC formation occurs at a gold-to-protein ratio of 5:1, yielding smaller nanoclusters compared to higher ratios. The use of mild reducing agents, such as ascorbic acid, is crucial for preserving the protein's structure and functional properties during synthesis. This preservation enables the formation of bifunctional hybrid nanostructures that retain both the fluorescence of the AuNCs and the binding activity of the protein. The resulting fluorescence signal is sensitive to ligand recognition, making these nanostructures suitable for developing ligand-sensitive fluorescent sensors.

### 1. Summary of the Paper's Purpose:
The paper investigates the use of designed consensus tetratricopeptide repeat (CTPR) proteins as templates for stabilizing fluorescent gold nanoclusters, with a focus on understanding how the structural and functional properties of the proteins (e.g., number of CTPR units, presence of cysteine residues) influence the fluorescence behavior of the nanoclusters. It also develops synthetic protocols to preserve the structural and functional integrity of the CTPR proteins during the stabilization process. As a proof-of-concept, a CTPR protein with specific binding capabilities is used to create functional hybrid nanostructures, demonstrating their potential application as fluorescence-based sensors for ligand detection.

### 2. Classification of Purpose:

inference_contexts: This work demonstrates, for the first time, that designed repeat protein scaffolds can be used to synthesize and stabilize gold nanoclusters. It has been shown that neither the number of repeats in the protein, nor the presence of a single cysteine residue interfered with the formation of small blue-emitting AuNCs. A possible explanation is the presence of tyrosine residues in the repeat sequence that could adsorb gold ions and therefore stabilize the gold nanoclusters. The synthesis method using NaOH to generate a reducing environment proved to be the most efficient. However, highly basic conditions denature the protein and thus destroy its structure and function. This fact can hamper its use in further applications in which structural and functional properties of the proteins are exploited. Therefore, we developed a new synthesis protocol using milder reducing agents such as ascorbic acid and sodium citrate, increasing the efficiency to obtain the AuNCs when ascorbic acid was employed. Whenever reactions did not include the protein scaffold, the AuNCs generation did not occur, highlighting the key role of the CTPR proteins as stabilizing agents. The optimized conditions for the AuNCs formation include a metal:protein ratio of 5:1 compared to the conditions previously reported for the CTPR stabilization of AuNPs in which larger ratios were used (1000:1 to 20:1) and smaller the ratios yielded smaller nanoparticles, which is in agreement with this report, where nanoclusters are obtained with smaller metal:protein ratios. Most importantly, this method was mild enough to preserve the structure of the protein and thus permitted to take advantage of the specific function of the protein scaffold. Indeed, we demonstrate that neither the synthesis of the nanoclusters, nor the nanoclusters themselves interfered with the protein binding activity. Thus, we obtained a novel bifunctional designed unit that combines the function of the designed CTPR protein scaffold on one hand and the fluorescence emission of AuNCs on the other. Finally, we demonstrate that the fluorescence signal of the protein-stabilized AuNCs is sensitive to the ligand recognition of the specific binding module. This result confirms the potential of this system to develop new sensors. The use of repeat protein scaffolds as biomolecular templates in which stability, size, and function can be tuned at will, ,, that also comprise rational methods for the synthesis of fluorescent nanoclusters preserving the protein functions, leaves a door open for further applications in the field of molecular imaging and sensing.

dataset_item.question: How does the use of nanosized probes improve the functionality and application scope of bioresponsive MRI contrast agents?
dataset_item.answer: The integration of nanosized probes into bioresponsive MRI contrast agents significantly enhances their functionality and broadens their application scope. Nanosized probes amplify signal detection in target tissues, improve biocompatibility, and extend tissue retention time, addressing key challenges such as low sensitivity. Their nanoscale structure facilitates straightforward functionalization, enabling multimodal imaging, targeted tissue accumulation, and improved probe quantification—critical for functional MRI applications. Furthermore, assembling these contrast agents on nanocarriers enhances versatility, allowing noninvasive molecular-level monitoring of dynamic biological processes. These advancements position nanosized probes as indispensable tools for precise and dynamic biochemical imaging.

### 1. **Summary of the Purpose**
The paper focuses on the development and progress of bioresponsive or smart contrast agents (SCAs) for molecular imaging, particularly magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). These SCAs are designed to dynamically monitor biological processes at the molecular and cellular levels by altering MRI signals in response to biochemical changes in their environment. The paper reviews various mechanistic approaches and recent advancements in SCAs, particularly those targeting abundant biological markers like pH, calcium (Ca²⁺), and zinc (Zn²⁺), as well as emerging methods like neurotransmitter tracking. The authors highlight challenges such as low sensitivity and biocompatibility of SCAs in vivo and discuss solutions, including the integration of small SCAs into macromolecular and nanosized probes to enhance MRI signal sensitivity and biocompatibility. The paper emphasizes ongoing efforts to make SCAs more practical for functional imaging and anticipates significant future advancements in probe development and utilization.

### 2. **Purpose Classification**
The purpose of the paper emphasizes **"<result>"** because it focuses on summarizing the progress in the development and application of SCAs, including recent advancements, challenges, and proposed solutions.

### 3. **Relevant Research Questions**
- **Mechanistic Design of SCAs**:
  - What are the most effective molecular mechanisms for designing SCAs that respond to specific biochemical changes (e.g., pH changes, ion concentrations)?
  - How can the sensitivity of SCAs to biochemical changes be improved for enhanced MRI signal detection?

- **Materials Development**:
  - What materials and molecular architectures are best suited for the preparation of biocompatible SCAs with low toxicity and high stability?
  - How can macromolecular and nanosized SCAs be optimized to enhance their tissue retention time and contrast signal generation?

- **Functional Imaging Applications**:
  - How can SCAs be tailored to visualize specific biological processes, such as neurotransmitter flux or ion homeostasis, in vivo?
  - What are the limitations of current SCAs in functional molecular imaging, and how can they be overcome to enable wider in vivo utilization?

- **Challenges and Solutions**:
  - What strategies can address the low sensitivity of MRI when using SCAs, particularly at lower probe concentrations?
  - How does the integration of small SCAs into macromolecular or nanosized systems improve their functionality, and what trade-offs (e.g., toxicity, stability) must be considered?

- **Future Prospects**:
  - What are the emerging trends in SCA development for practical MRI applications, and how might these probes evolve in the next decade?
  - How can advancements in MRI technology itself complement the development of SCAs to achieve better imaging outcomes?

These research questions align with the abstract's themes of improving SCA design, addressing practical challenges, and advancing functional imaging applications.

Till now, many long-lived luminescent probes have been developed for time-resolved bioimaging and biosensing. Among them, lanthanides and transition-metal complexes are the most widely used probes owing to their inherent long luminescence lifetimes. Lanthanides exhibts disdingishable narrow luminescence bands with extremely long lifetimes. The emission wavelengths and lifetimes of transition-metal complexes can be easily tuned by selecting different metal centers and coordinating ligands. They can also be used as energy donors in FRET systems to elongate the fluorescent lifetimes of acceptors. Effort has also been focused on the elongation of fluorescent lifetimes of pure organic dyes and inorganic nanoparticles. The luminescence wavelengths of organic dyes are easily tuned throughout the whole visible region and extending to the NIR region. Nanosized materials can be multiply functionalized by surface modification to meet different requirements. Despite the discussed applications of long-lived luminescent probes, the development of novel luminescent probes for bioimaging and biosensing with high precision and sensitivity is challenging. Current directions of the design of long-lived probes and the development of the time-resolved luminescence imaging techniques include but are not limited to the following: (1) lanthanides and transition-metal complexes contain heavy metal elements, which usually show certain toxicity to cells. Thus, it is necessary to develop novel probes with low toxicity through introduction of biocompatible ligands to lanthanides and transition-metal complexes. Design of long-lived organic dyes and inorganic nanoparticles will provide more choices in the selection of material system for a certain purpose. (2) The focus of probe design will be put on the maximization of the luminescence lifetime response to the analyte to benefit from the time-resolved photoluminescence measurement and imaging. (3) Multiple probes with different luminescence lifetimes can be used simultaneously. They are distinguishable via time-resolved photoluminescence techniques, even if they emit with similar intensity at the same wavelength. (4) Combination of the time-resolved photoluminescence imaging techniques with upconversion dyes that are excitable at the NIR region is an efficient strategy to improve the quality of the images. The low-energy excitation reduces the population of the unwanted excited states and the time-resolved photoluminescence detection further filters off the short-lived noises. Additionally, NIR excitation allows deeper tissue penetration and is suitable for in vivo imaging using live animal models. (5) There are limited examples of long-lived emissive probes used for in vivo time-resolved photoluminescence imaging due to a lack of long-lived NIR emissive probes and imaging techniques. Thus, development of NIR emissive probes with long lifetime and time-resolved photoluminescence techniques that are suitable for live animal models will broaden the scope of time-resolved photoluminescence application in vivo. (6) PLIM using long-lived probes requires longer imaging time. The imaging speed is unacceptable when lanthanides are used, and it needs to be improved. (7) The applications of persistent phosphors are of great usefulness in in vivo bioimaging, since photon acquisition can be performed when external excitation is turned off. The sensitivity is improved and phototoxicity is avoided. (8) Combination of time-resolved detection with modern imaging techniques, such as stimulated emission depletion microscopy, terahertz imaging, and fluorescence anisotropy imaging, will open up new directions in the development of imaging techniques.

dataset_item.question: What are the primary challenges hindering the commercialization of inorganic membranes for molecular separation and reaction processes?
dataset_item.answer: The commercialization of inorganic membranes for molecular separation and reaction processes faces several primary challenges: high capital costs, large system footprints, insufficient membrane stability under industrial conditions, and moderate permeance. These challenges arise from the high cost of membrane materials, low packing density in membrane modules, and current limitations in achieving both high permeability and robust stability required for demanding industrial applications. Addressing these issues requires targeted research and development efforts, including the synthesis of membranes with enhanced permeance and stability, the fabrication of low-cost substrates with higher packing density, and scalable, cost-effective methods for producing separation layers. Progress in these areas could enable broader applications, such as water-selective zeolite membranes in membrane reactors or siliceous zeolite membranes for high-pressure operations.

In spite of the progress and success in commercial applications of inorganic membranes in filtration and hydrocarbon-water separation, the commercialization of inorganic membranes for molecular separation and reaction processes remains a difficult challenge. The key hurdles in commercializing inorganic membrane separators and reactors for process intensification include the high costs and large footprint of membrane units due to moderate permeance, high membrane price, and low membrane module packing density. Most inorganic membranes are not sufficiently stable for industrial applications. Future research and development efforts should be focused on addressing these key hurdles including synthesis of membranes with higher permeance and stability, fabrication of low cost and high packing density membrane substrates, and the development of cost-effective, scalable methods for the synthesis of the separation layer. It is expected that commercial applications of highly permeable water-selective zeolite membrane separation processes will be expanded to membrane reactor coupling reactions with the removal of water from the membrane reactor. Highly stable high siliceous zeolite membranes may also find industrial applications in membrane reactors operated at high pressures.

dataset_item.question: How does acetonitrile as a cosolvent affect the structural and dynamical properties of lithium bis(trifluoromethane)sulfonimide-based electrolytes?
dataset_item.answer:
The addition of acetonitrile (ACN) as a cosolvent significantly influences the structural and dynamical properties of lithium bis(trifluoromethane)sulfonimide (LiTFSI)-based electrolytes, both in normal and water-in-salt (WiSE) formulations. Structurally, ACN reduces the mass density and increases the cohesive energy of the electrolytes, reflecting its role in altering intermolecular interactions. Dynamically, the effects of ACN vary depending on the electrolyte type:

1. **Normal Electrolytes**: ACN systematically reduces species diffusion by approximately half, regardless of its concentration. This reduction is attributed to ACN’s influence on the solvent environment, which likely hinders ionic mobility.

2. **Water-in-Salt Electrolytes (WiSEs)**: In WiSEs, ACN disrupts the strong cation-anion interaction network, weakening electrostatic interactions and reducing ionic pair coordination. This disruption enhances species diffusion, contrasting its effect in normal electrolytes. These structural and dynamical changes align with experimental observations, although discrepancies in capacitance behavior suggest electrode-specific or methodological influences.

Overall, ACN's role as a cosolvent provides a means to tailor electrolyte properties for specific applications, such as supercapacitors, by modulating transport dynamics and interaction networks. Further experimental and simulation studies are recommended to reconcile differences in capacitance trends and optimize electrolyte performance.

dataset_item.question: What role does the dissociative capture of secondary electrons play in the degradation of ionic liquid and crown ether extractant systems under ionizing radiation?
dataset_item.answer:
The dissociative capture of secondary electrons plays a pivotal role in the radiolytic degradation of ionic liquid and crown ether (RTIL/CE) extractant systems under ionizing radiation. This process generates reactive fluoride anions (F⁻) through the radiolysis of fluorinated anions (e.g., BF₄⁻, PF₆⁻) in the ionic liquid. The fluoride anions subsequently react with strontium cations (Sr²⁺) present in radioactive waste, precipitating as insoluble strontium fluoride (SrF₂), which diminishes the extraction efficiency of the system. 

In addition to fluoride precipitation, radiolysis produces fluorine atoms, which chemically modify and degrade the crown ether extractant. This degradation occurs via stable HF formation and radiation-induced macrocycle transformations, leading to irreversible damage to the crown ether structure. While some protective effects arise from hole transfer between crown ether molecules and RTIL anions, the overall degradation is dominated by reactive intermediates, particularly fluoride-driven pathways. These fluoride-related mechanisms highlight the importance of addressing halogenated RTILs' susceptibility to radiolytic damage in the design of more robust extractant systems for radioactive waste reprocessing.

dataset_item.question: How does the localization of DLiPC molecules affect the bicelle-to-vesicle transition in a binary DPPC and DLiPC mixture?
dataset_item.answer:
The localization of DLiPC molecules plays a pivotal role in the bicelle-to-vesicle transition in DPPC/DLiPC mixtures. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that concentrating DLiPC molecules within the bicelle core significantly lowers the critical concentration required for vesicle formation compared to a uniform distribution. While a bulk DLiPC concentration above 0.6 is generally required for spontaneous vesicle formation, localized enrichment in the core reduces this threshold, facilitating the transition.  

Localized DLiPC also governs the spontaneous bending direction of the bicelle, which is critical for successful vesicle formation. This inhomogeneous lipid distribution may result from external factors, such as collapsing bubbles during sonication, and is associated with bimodal vesicle size distributions. Furthermore, controlling the local composition of DLiPC enables precise manipulation of vesicle formation dynamics and bending direction, providing a potential pathway to optimize nanoliposome encapsulation efficiency for drug delivery systems.  

These findings offer molecular-scale insights into the relationship between lipid localization and vesicle formation, presenting opportunities to design advanced lipid-based nanocarriers with improved encapsulation and delivery performance.

dataset_item.question: How are stable and metastable phases of lithium-tin and lithium-antimony intermetallics identified using computational techniques?
dataset_item.answer:
Stable and metastable phases of lithium-tin (Li-Sn) and lithium-antimony (Li-Sb) intermetallics are identified using advanced computational techniques that integrate *ab initio* random structure searching (AIRSS), species swapping, and density functional theory (DFT). 

1. **Structure Generation and Optimization**: 
   - AIRSS is employed to explore the potential energy surface by generating random crystal structures and relaxing them to local minima using DFT. 
   - Species swapping modifies known crystal structures from related systems (e.g., alkali metals combined with group 14 or 15 elements) by substituting lithium and tin or antimony atoms. 
   - Approximately 9000 Li-Sn and 5000 Li-Sb structures are generated and optimized using DFT calculations performed with CASTEP, utilizing gradient-corrected Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functionals, ultrasoft pseudopotentials, and high-accuracy settings for energy cutoffs and k-point spacing.

2. **Thermodynamic Stability Assessment**:
   - Formation energies of the predicted structures are calculated, and a convex hull is constructed to distinguish stable phases (lying on the hull) from metastable phases (above the hull). 
   - Voltage curve calculations for Li-Sn phases further validate thermodynamic properties and potential applications in battery systems.

3. **Mechanical and Dynamical Stability Analysis**:
   - Phonon dispersion calculations are performed to confirm the dynamical stability of predicted structures, ensuring no imaginary frequencies indicative of instability.

4. **Experimental Validation Support**:
   - NMR chemical shielding predictions are conducted to provide insights for experimental characterization and verification of the newly identified phases.

By combining these computational methods, the approach effectively identifies both stable and metastable phases, enabling the discovery of novel intermetallics and providing a robust framework for understanding their properties.

Two plausible dissociative hydrolysis pathways named α-path (inversion) or β-path (retention), depending on the orientation of nucleophilic water and the direction of attack, were considered in this study. The microsolvated model with three or four explicit water molecules is the smallest model capable of minimizing the activation energy for α-path and β-path, respectively. Our results suggest that the α-path is more favorable kinetically than the β-path, where the activation free energies of glycosidic bond dissociation (RDS) are 27.7 and 30.7 kcal mol-1 for the α-path (n = 3) and β-path (n = 4), respectively, whereas the β-path with exergonic formation of β-product (ΔG = -1.7 kcal mol-1) possesses thermodynamic preference over the α-path (ΔG = 4.5 kcal mol-1), where the formation of α-product is endergonic. The thermodynamic preference of the β-path presents theoretical support for the major β-cleavage product observed experimentally after sufficient reaction time. The inversion hydrolysis of analogous cyclo-d4G and dG were also studied using the microsolvated model (n = 3) for a comparison with d4G. The free energy barriers of glycosidic bond dissociation (RDS) for cyclo-d4G (29.1 kcal mol-1) and dG (31.9 kcal mol-1) in contrast to that of d4G (27.7 kcal mol-1) provide a kinetic support for the order of glycosidic bond stability: d4G < cyclo-d4G < dG. The thermodynamic heterolytic dissociation energies of d4G (46.4 kcal mol-1) < cyclo-d4G (49.2 kcal mol-1) < dG (52.7 kcal mol-1) in water present a thermodynamic proof to the order of glycosidic bond stability above. Our kinetic and thermodynamic results together provide exploration for the influence of 6-cyclopropylamino and unsaturated ribose on the glycosidic bond instability of d4G.

In summary, we predict the lightweight alkali-ternary polyhydride by mixing cations of Na and Li in the Na-Li-H system. Structural searches of the Na-Li-H system under high pressure have been investigated using ab initio calculation. Structural stability of Na3LiH12, Na2Li2H12, and NaLi3H12 was confirmed by all positive modes of phonon vibration. The convex hull at 25 GPa indicates that the global minimum of Na2Li2H12, which is the formation pressure of a stable phase, is lower than that of a binary compound system. A thermodynamically stable phase of a lightweight superhydride system was analyzed under high-pressure conditions. Mechanical stability, elasticity, temperature effect, electronic structure, and so forth were also determined. High gravimetric hydrogen capacity prompts us to study H-vacancy occurrence and H2-diffusion in the ternary polyhydride. The high-pressure effect increases the energy barriers of H2 (path-a) and H- diffusion (path-1) because of the effect of highly stimulated stress. The high-pressure effect at 25 GPa gave more suitable conditions for hydrogen storage because of lower energy barriers of the diffusion paths.

Our investigation on the chemical compatibility between V2O5 and AlCl3-[EMIm]Cl ionic liquid electrolytes establishes unambiguously that V2O5 chemically reacts with both Lewis acidic Al2Cl7 - and Lewis neutral AlCl4 - anions. Spectroscopic, electrochemical, and theoretical analyses reveal that the reaction products between V2O5 and Al2Cl7 - are VOCl3 and amorphous Al2O3. Similarly, the reaction products between V2O5 and AlCl4 - are identified as VO2Cl and AlCl3VO3 - with both 4-coordinated and 6-coordinated structures; these soluble products are furthermore electrochemically active, exhibiting reversible redox reactions between V5+ and V2+ oxidation states. It is clear that V2O5 is not a chemically stable positive electrode material for rechargeable Al batteries using chloroaluminate ionic liquid electrolytes, regardless of Lewis acidity. Although an Al-V2O5 cell may appear to have electrochemical performance in terms of capacity and cyclability, researchers must be cautious when identifying the origin of the electrochemical reactions. Our investigation also raises the question of the chemical stability of other Al-ion positive electrode materials in chloroaluminate ionic liquid electrolytes.

dataset_item.question: What is the role of polymer degree of polymerization in plasmid DNA condensation and delivery?
dataset_item.answer: The degree of polymerization (DP) plays a pivotal role in plasmid DNA condensation and intracellular delivery. Longer polymers with higher DP are essential for the efficient condensation, membrane translocation, and nuclear delivery of large plasmid DNA molecules (>4500 base pairs). This contrasts with shorter nucleotide cargos, such as siRNA (<25 base pairs), which require shorter polymers for delivery. Amphiphilic polyhydrazide polymers leverage the hydrazone postpolymerization strategy, enabling precise tuning of polymer length and chemical properties. This strategy optimizes DNA-polyplex formation in a water-soluble and biocompatible manner without the need for additional purification steps. By adjusting the DP, it is possible to identify and tailor polymer motifs for specific nucleotide cargo delivery, enhancing the versatility and efficiency of polymeric scaffolds in gene delivery applications.

inference_contexts: In summary, in this work we have demonstrated the potential of hydrazone postpolymerization strategy to deliver plasmid DNAs inside human cells. The strategy allowed us to quickly extract important conclusions on the importance of the degree of polymerization for plasmid condensation and delivery.
