The minima and saddle points associated with the isomerization of the three strained tricyclic structures, 3-aza-3-ium-dihydrobenzvalene, 3,4-diaza-3-ium-dihydrobenzvalene, and 3,4-diaza-diium-dihydrobenzvalene to their respective cyclic Z,Z-products were studied at the MRMP2/cc-pVTZ//MCSCF (10, 10)/cc-pVDZ level. Single-point calculations were also performed at the QCISD (T)/cc-pVTZ and CCSD (T)/cc-pVTZ levels and using several popular DFT methods. The primary conclusions are as follows. The 3-aza-3-ium-dihydrobenzvalene structure has two unique conrotatory and two unique disrotatory pathways due to Cs symmetry. The activation barriers for the conrotatory pathways range from 52.1 to 54.4 kcal/mol at the MRMP2/cc-pVTZ level, while the disrotatory barriers range from 61.2 to 62.3 kcal/mol at this level. The presence of the secondary ammonium group in the 3-position of the ring caused an increase of over 10 kcal/mol in the conrotatory barriers and an increase of over 7 kcal/mol in the disrotatory barriers of 3-aza-3-ium-dhb compared to dhb. These increases in barrier heights could be due to inductive electron-withdrawing effects. The secondary ammonium had little effect on the π-bond rotation barriers, which ranged from 1.3 to 3.0 kcal/mol at the MRMP2/cc-pVTZ level. This energy range is in agreement with previous calculated results for this class of strained saddle points. The 3,4-diaza-3-ium-dihydrobenzvalene structure has four unique conrotatory and four unique disrotatory pathways due to C 1 symmetry. The activation barriers for the conrotatory pathways range from 50.9 to 55.0 kcal/mol at the MRMP2/cc-pVTZ level, while the disrotatory barriers range from 58.8 to 64.7 kcal/mol at this level. The presence of the secondary ammonium group in the 3-position of the ring caused an increase of 8 kcal/mol in the conrotatory barriers and an increase of 5-11 kcal/mol in the disrotatory barriers of 3,4-diaza-3-ium-dhb compared to dhb. Just as for the 3-aza-3-ium-dhb, the secondary ammonium had little to no effect on the π-bond rotation barriers, which ranged from 0.7 to 3.1 kcal/mol at the MRMP2/cc-pVTZ level. The 3,4-diaza-diium-dihydrobenzvalene structure has only one unique conrotatory and disrotatory pathway due to C 2v symmetry. The activation barriers for the conrotatory pathway, disrotatory, and E,Z to Z,Z-saddle points were 67.2, 70.7, and 1.9 kcal/mol, respectively, at the MRMP2/cc-pVTZ level. The presence of two secondary ammonium groups caused an increase of 24 and 17 kcal/mol for the conrotatory barrier and disrotatory barrier, respectively, relative to the analogous barriers of dhb. Similar to the other two cases there is negligible effect on the trans to cis activation barrier. There was a clear increase in activation barriers with the addition of secondary ammonium groups. The presence of the ammonium groups also tends to draw activation barriers closer in energy. The energy difference between lowest-energy conrotatory and disrotatory barriers were 9.1, 7.4, and 3.7 kcal/mol, respectively, for 3-aza-3-ium-dihydrobenzvalene, 3,4-diaza-3-ium-dihydrobenzvalene, and 3,4-diaza-diium-dihydrobenzvalene. However, considering the energy difference between the least-favorable allowed barrier and most-favorable disallowed barrier, the energy differences were as small as 6.8, 3.3, and 3.7 for 3-aza-3-ium-dihydrobenzvalene, 3,4-diaza-3-ium-dihydrobenzvalene, and 3,4-diaza-diium-dihydrobenzvalene, respectively. Comparisons of ZPE-corrected energies computed using MRMP2 to those obtained using CCSD (T) shows that the higher correlation method is robust enough to overcome the mild multiconfigurational character of the EZ intermediates and the conrotatory saddle points. We found that the disrotatory pathways are quite challenging to describe at the single reference level and that CCSD (T) cannot overcome the deficiencies of the restricted Hartree-Fock reference for these saddle points. However, we find that by using a broken symmetry wave function one can improve the results considerably. The activation barriers computed using the PBEPBE-D3 functional, at the restricted level for the conrotatory pathways and the unrestricted level for the disrotatory pathways, reproduced the MRMP2 values remarkably well.

The ground state rotational spectrum of methyl 3-mercaptopropionate was measured and analyzed in detail using chirped-pulse and cavity-based Fourier transform microwave spectroscopy from 8 to 18 GHz. Rotational transitions belonging to the two most stable conformers (I and II) were successfully assigned in the rotational spectra, and the lines present complex splitting patterns due to the methyl internal rotation and/or SH tunneling motion. The similar experimental V 3 barriers for the two conformers reveal that the electronic distribution of I and II is not strongly affected by their geometrical differences. QTAIM, NCI, and NBO analyses show that conformer I is favored in the conformational equilibrium due to a stable SH O = C IHB, which is estimated to have an energy of about 6.6 kJ mol-1 based on the potential energy at the bond critical point. On the basis of the ground state effective (r 0) and equilibrium (r e) geometries of I, we were able to derive the experimental geometric parameters associated with the sulfur HB, which reveals that the HB distance and angle S-H-O are 2.515(4) Å and 117.4(1)°, respectively. The nonobservation of additional conformers was rationalized based on their conversion pathways to lower energy forms and/or low population in the supersonic jet expansion. The present study provides key experimental data on sulfur HBs at the molecular level in isolation of crystal packing and solvent effects and serves as a benchmark for improved understanding and modeling of these important noncovalent interactions.

dataset_item.question: How does glycan functionalization of collagen hydrogels influence the glycosylation profile of primary neuronal cultures in vitro?
dataset_item.answer: Glycan-functionalized collagen hydrogels, modified with disaccharides such as maltose and lactose, influence the glycosylation profile of primary neuronal cultures in vitro by modulating their glyco-signatures in a monosaccharide-dependent manner. These engineered hydrogels alter key glycosylation patterns, including sialylation and fucosylation, while maintaining cell viability. The coupling of disaccharides to collagen chains demonstrates a functional interplay between the hydrogel matrix and neuronal glycosylation, offering valuable insights into glyco-chemical interactions. This approach highlights the potential of glycan-functionalized biomaterials for neural tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, and opens avenues for the development of advanced 3D cell culture systems by integrating other natural polymers with oligosaccharides.

For biomedical applications, the use of in situ forming hydrogels is preferred over preformed hydrogels since there is no need for surgical interventions as gelation can take place under physiological conditions upon injection. Furthermore, the initial fluidic nature of the precursor solution ensures proper shape adaptation and biological components can be incorporated in the hydrogel by simple mixing with the precursor polymer solution. , Physical cross-links, such as hydrophobic or ionic interactions, can be formed in situ under mild conditions, but the resulting hydrogels generally degrade or dissolve rapidly. Injectable chemically cross-linked hydrogels have been frequently prepared by photocuring polymers functionalized with vinylic groups. Although the presence of photoinitiators and the generated radicals in the polymerization process has been associated with cytotoxicity, frequently good cell compatibility is found for cells encapsulated in this type of hydrogel. , However, important drawbacks of photo-cross-linkable systems include the limited penetration depth of UV radiation and its potentially damaging effects on living tissue. In situ forming hydrogels utilizing covalent cross-linking between polymers with complementary functional groups therefore received much attention in the last two decades. Early examples of chemical cross-linking reactions forming hydrogels include Schiff base formation between aldehydes and amines and the Passerini and Ugi condensation. However, remaining functional groups on polymers may react with functional groups present in biomolecules such as proteins, limiting the application of these hydrogels as in situ forming delivery systems. In this regard, the use of chemoselective, bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies, which do not interfere with biochemical processes or biomolecules, are very appealing. The most investigated chemoselective cross-linking reaction for hydrogels is the Cu (I)-catalyzed Huisgen 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition of terminal alkynes and azides, commonly known as click chemistry. This term was originally coined in 2001 by Sharpless et al. for a number of new regiospecific linking reactions that give high yields and generally require no purification. The first hydrogel cross-linked via click chemistry was described by the group of Hilborn and was based on PVA. Although this category of hydrogels has been mainly used for tissue engineering applications, they have also been applied for the controlled release of therapeutics and different biomolecules, including doxorubicin bovine serum albumin (BSA) and pDNA. Because "classical" alkyne-azide cycloadditions require the use of a copper catalyst, which may cause adverse effects in biomedical applications, the use of strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) is attracting increasing interest. This reaction employs the inherent ring strain of cyclooctyne groups to achieve fast and efficient cross-linking without the need for catalysts or external stimuli such as UV light. Hermann et al. reported on PEG hydrogels for the delivery of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) inhibitors to treat excessive postoperative bone regrowth (resynostosis) after surgical correction of premature fusion of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) in children. Mixing poly [(tetraethylene glycol methacrylate)-co-(azidotetraethylene glycol methacrylate)] with a 4-dibenzocyclooctynol PEG cross-linker resulted in the formation of hydrogels within 30 s, as demonstrated by oscillatory rheology. In vitro release experiments showed that the BMP inhibitor Gremlin1 remained bioactive when it was incorporated in the hydrogels by dissolution in the prepolymer solutions, confirming the bioorthogonal character of the SPAAC cross-linking method. When the prepolymer solutions were injected together with Gremlin1 in a surgically created cranial defect in weanling mice, a hydrogel formed in situ that was able to provide a controlled release of the inhibitor for 14 days. Following this approach, the authors were able to delay, but not completely prevent, postoperative bone regrowth in the cranial defect model. Since the ultimate goal of resynostosis therapy is to slow the postoperative bone growth for a period, but then allow the bone to regrow as the child ages, the reported approach holds promise as treatment after surgical intervention in craniosynostosis. The cross-linking reactions were suggested to be bioorthogonal because of the high viability of human mesenchymal stem cells, which were encapsulated by adding them to the prepolymer solutions prior to hydrogel formation. As a conclusion, the high potential of diphenylborinic acid 2-aminoethyl ester as inducer of regioselective galactofuranosylation of various acceptors was confirmed. Electron-donating groups at primary and anomeric positions significantly increased the Fukui indexes and borinate adducts with high Fukui index on the equatorial oxygen generated the greater amount of orthoester. dataset_item.question: How are emission properties and time-dependent spectral shifts of prodan measured and analyzed using spectroscopic techniques?
dataset_item.answer:
The emission properties and time-dependent spectral shifts of prodan are measured using advanced spectroscopic techniques. Steady-state emission spectra are acquired with a Fluoromax-4 scanning fluorometer (Horiba) at excitation wavelengths of 350 nm and 410 nm, recorded at 1 nm spectral resolution to ensure high accuracy. Time-resolved transient absorption (TA) measurements are conducted using a femtosecond laser setup equipped with a 10 kHz Ti:sapphire regenerative amplifier. A 340 nm pump pulse excites the sample, while white light generated in a sapphire window serves as the probe, achieving an instrument response function of 25 fs for precise temporal resolution.

For analysis, transient absorption spectral maps are fitted to Gaussian functions at various time steps to determine peak maxima. These peak maxima are tracked over time, and the resulting time-dependent spectral shifts are fitted to exponential functions to extract characteristic time constants. Solvent conditions are carefully controlled, with prodan dissolved in spectroscopic-grade solvents, which are dried prior to measurements to ensure consistent polarity and minimize external influences on spectral behavior.

dataset_item.question: How does the presence of secondary ammonium groups affect the activation barriers of conrotatory and disrotatory pathways in aza-dihydrobenzvalene derivatives?
dataset_item.answer:
The presence of secondary ammonium groups significantly increases the activation barriers for both conrotatory and disrotatory isomerization pathways in aza-dihydrobenzvalene derivatives. This increase is attributed to the inductive electron-withdrawing effects of the ammonium groups, which destabilize the transition states.

For 3-aza-3-ium-dihydrobenzvalene, the conrotatory activation barriers rise by over 10 kcal/mol, while the disrotatory barriers increase by over 7 kcal/mol compared to the unsubstituted analog. In 3,4-diaza-3-ium-dihydrobenzvalene, the conrotatory barriers increase by 8 kcal/mol, and disrotatory barriers increase by 5–11 kcal/mol. For 3,4-diaza-diium-dihydrobenzvalene, these effects are amplified further, with conrotatory barriers increasing by 24 kcal/mol and disrotatory barriers by 17 kcal/mol. 

The presence of ammonium groups also narrows the energy gap between conrotatory and disrotatory pathways, reducing the difference from 9.1 kcal/mol in mono-substituted derivatives to 3.7 kcal/mol in di-substituted derivatives. Interestingly, the ammonium groups have minimal impact on π-bond rotation barriers, which only increase by 0.7–3.1 kcal/mol.

These trends are confirmed by computational methods, with MRMP2 and CCSD(T) calculations providing reliable results for conrotatory pathways. However, disrotatory transitions require multireference treatment for accurate modeling due to the increased complexity of their electronic structure.

In summary, secondary ammonium groups raise activation barriers and reduce the energy gap between conrotatory and disrotatory pathways, primarily due to their electron-withdrawing effects, while leaving π-bond rotation barriers largely unaffected.

Single-point calculations were also performed at the QCISD (T)/cc-pVTZ and CCSD (T)/cc-pVTZ levels and using several popular DFT methods. The primary conclusions are as follows. The 3-aza-3-ium-dihydrobenzvalene structure has two unique conrotatory and two unique disrotatory pathways due to Cs symmetry. The activation barriers for the conrotatory pathways range from 52.1 to 54.4 kcal/mol at the MRMP2/cc-pVTZ level, while the disrotatory barriers range from 61.2 to 62.3 kcal/mol at this level. The presence of the secondary ammonium group in the 3-position of the ring caused an increase of over 10 kcal/mol in the conrotatory barriers and an increase of over 7 kcal/mol in the disrotatory barriers of 3-aza-3-ium-dhb compared to dhb. These increases in barrier heights could be due to inductive electron-withdrawing effects. The secondary ammonium had little effect on the π-bond rotation barriers, which ranged from 1.3 to 3.0 kcal/mol at the MRMP2/cc-pVTZ level. This energy range is in agreement with previous calculated results for this class of strained saddle points. The 3,4-diaza-3-ium-dihydrobenzvalene structure has four unique conrotatory and four unique disrotatory pathways due to C 1 symmetry. The activation barriers for the conrotatory pathways range from 50.9 to 55.0 kcal/mol at the MRMP2/cc-pVTZ level, while the disrotatory barriers range from 58.8 to 64.7 kcal/mol at this level. The 3,4-diaza-diium-dihydrobenzvalene structure has only one unique conrotatory and disrotatory pathway due to C 2v symmetry. dataset_item.question: What are the advantages and limitations of bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies for hydrogel formation in therapeutic delivery applications?
dataset_item.answer:
Bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies provide significant advantages for hydrogel formation in therapeutic delivery applications. These strategies enable high coupling efficiency, chemoselectivity, and mild reaction conditions, making them ideal for in situ gelation and incorporation of therapeutic biomolecules under physiological conditions. By minimizing interference with biomolecules and biochemical processes, they ensure compatibility with biological systems while maintaining the bioactivity of incorporated drugs. For example, strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) allows rapid hydrogel formation without requiring cytotoxic catalysts, facilitating controlled drug release, as demonstrated in sustained BMP inhibitor delivery for cranial defect models.

Despite their benefits, bioorthogonal cross-linking methods face limitations, including potential side reactions between reactive polymer groups (e.g., maleimide, thiol) and proteins, which may compromise biomolecule stability, alter protein structure or activity, or trigger immune responses. To address these challenges, strategies such as adjusting pH to reduce functional group reactivity, spatially separating hydrophobic polymerization sites from hydrophilic protein-containing regions, or employing dual-network hydrogels combining orthogonal chemistries (e.g., thiol-yne and Diels-Alder reactions) can be utilized. These approaches enhance mechanical properties, improve biocompatibility, and mitigate undesired interactions. Comprehensive evaluation of biomolecule compatibility under cross-linking conditions remains critical for successful clinical translation.

inference_contexts: For biomedical applications, the use of in situ forming hydrogels is preferred over preformed hydrogels since there is no need for surgical interventions as gelation can take place under physiological conditions upon injection. Furthermore, the initial fluidic nature of the precursor solution ensures proper shape adaptation and biological components can be incorporated in the hydrogel by simple mixing with the precursor polymer solution. , Physical cross-links, such as hydrophobic or ionic interactions, can be formed in situ under mild conditions, but the resulting hydrogels generally degrade or dissolve rapidly. Injectable chemically cross-linked hydrogels have been frequently prepared by photocuring polymers functionalized with vinylic groups. Although the presence of photoinitiators and the generated radicals in the polymerization process has been associated with cytotoxicity, frequently good cell compatibility is found for cells encapsulated in this type of hydrogel. , However, important drawbacks of photo-cross-linkable systems include the limited penetration depth of UV radiation and its potentially damaging effects on living tissue. In situ forming hydrogels utilizing covalent cross-linking between polymers with complementary functional groups therefore received much attention in the last two decades. Early examples of chemical cross-linking reactions forming hydrogels include Schiff base formation between aldehydes and amines and the Passerini and Ugi condensation. However, remaining functional groups on polymers may react with functional groups present in biomolecules such as proteins, limiting the application of these hydrogels as in situ forming delivery systems. In this regard, the use of chemoselective, bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies, which do not interfere with biochemical processes or biomolecules, are very appealing. The most investigated chemoselective cross-linking reaction for hydrogels is the Cu (I)-catalyzed Huisgen 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition of terminal alkynes and azides, commonly known as click chemistry. This term was originally coined in 2001 by Sharpless et al. for a number of new regiospecific linking reactions that give high yields and generally require no purification. The first hydrogel cross-linked via click chemistry was described by the group of Hilborn and was based on PVA. Although this category of hydrogels has been mainly used for tissue engineering applications, they have also been applied for the controlled release of therapeutics and different biomolecules, including doxorubicin bovine serum albumin (BSA) and pDNA. Because "classical" alkyne-azide cycloadditions require the use of a copper catalyst, which may cause adverse effects in biomedical applications, the use of strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) is attracting increasing interest. This reaction employs the inherent ring strain of cyclooctyne groups to achieve fast and efficient cross-linking without the need for catalysts or external stimuli such as UV light. Hermann et al. reported on PEG hydrogels for the delivery of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) inhibitors to treat excessive postoperative bone regrowth (resynostosis) after surgical correction of premature fusion of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) in children. Mixing poly [(tetraethylene glycol methacrylate)-co-(azidotetraethylene glycol methacrylate)] with a 4-dibenzocyclooctynol PEG cross-linker resulted in the formation of hydrogels within 30 s, as demonstrated by oscillatory rheology. In vitro release experiments showed that the BMP inhibitor Gremlin1 remained bioactive when it was incorporated in the hydrogels by dissolution in the prepolymer solutions, confirming the bioorthogonal character of the SPAAC cross-linking method. When the prepolymer solutions were injected together with Gremlin1 in a surgically created cranial defect in weanling mice, a hydrogel formed in situ that was able to provide a controlled release of the inhibitor for 14 days. Following this approach, the authors were able to delay, but not completely prevent, postoperative bone regrowth in the cranial defect model. Since the ultimate goal of resynostosis therapy is to slow the postoperative bone growth for a period, but then allow the bone to regrow as the child ages, the reported approach holds promise as treatment after surgical intervention in craniosynostosis. Dove and co-workers recently reported on the simultaneous application of thiol-yne and Diels-Alder chemistry to independently create two interpenetrating networks in a one-step procedure (Figure ). A loose network was prepared from norbornene-functionalized chitosan and linear PEG-ditetrazine, while a dense network was constructed by cross-linking 4-arm PEG-tetraalkyne with linear PEG-dithiol. The resulting double network hydrogels displayed a high compressive stress of 15 MPa at 98% compression without fracture or hysteresis upon repeated load. The hydrogels were postfunctionalized with a thiol-containing fluorescent dye and tetrazine-modified biotin via reaction with unreacted alkyne and norbornene groups, respectively. The cross-linking reactions were suggested to be bioorthogonal because of the high viability of human mesenchymal stem cells, which were encapsulated by adding them to the prepolymer solutions prior to hydrogel formation. An extensive recent review concerning bioorthogonal chemistries for hydrogel cross-linking can be found in ref .

The above examples show that several bioorthogonal reactions have emerged as innovative and versatile strategies to construct new functional hydrogels due to their high coupling efficiency, chemoselectivity, and mild reaction conditions. Although many of the described cross-linking reactions are believed to be bioorthogonal, caution should still be used when hydrogels are cross-linked in the presence of biomolecules, most notably proteins. The group of Gopferich investigated the compatibility of a number of reactive groups present on polymers, including maleimide and thiol groups, with lysozyme. Hydrogel preparation was simulated by using polymer/lysozyme mixtures and the possible conjugation of polymer chains to lysozyme was determined by SDS-PAGE analysis. Upon incubation with PEG-maleimide or PEG-thiol several protein modifications were indeed detected, which may affect the protein structure, adversely affect its activity and increase the risk of unwanted immune responses. This study indicates that side reactions between biomolecules and polymers, and possible strategies to prevent these, should always be considered when developing new hydrogels for therapeutic delivery and that the stability of each released biomolecule must be carefully evaluated for all cross-linking conditions in question. For example, cross-linking can be performed in slightly acidic solutions below pH 5 in order to decrease the nucleophilicity of amino groups by protonation and reduce their reactivity in Michael-type addition reactions. To protect proteins during radical polymerizations, Censi et al. managed to retain protein activity during photopolymerization of methacrylate groups by separating hydrophobic polymerization sites from more hydrophilic protein-containing areas.

dataset_item.question: How is the apparent activation energy calculated using Friedman's isoconversional method for polymer degradation?
dataset_item.answer: Friedman's isoconversional method is used to calculate the apparent activation energy (Eₐ) for polymer degradation by analyzing the relationship between the conversion rate and temperature. At a fixed degree of conversion (e.g., 5%), the natural logarithm of the conversion rate (ln(dα/dt)) is plotted against the inverse of temperature (1/T). The slope of the resulting straight line is equal to -Eₐ/R, where R is the universal gas constant. By performing this analysis at different heating rates (β) and for multiple conversion intervals, the method provides a model-free determination of Eₐ without assuming a specific reaction mechanism, making it highly versatile for complex degradation processes.

dataset_item.question: How does grafting PNIPAm onto an MC backbone and concurrent cross-linking contribute to thermal hysteresis behavior in PNIPAm-g-MC hydrogel?
dataset_item.answer:
Grafting PNIPAm onto a methylcellulose (MC) backbone and concurrently cross-linking it creates a hydrogel with a thermal hysteresis of 10°C during its volume phase transition. This thermal hysteresis arises from the formation of stable hydrophobic junctions within the MC scaffold, which enhance the difference between the hydrogel's shrinking behavior during heating and its expansion during cooling. These junctions provide structural stability and enable programmable thermal responses.  

When combined with photothermal magnetite nanoparticles (MNPs), the PNIPAm-g-MC hydrogel exhibits light-triggered shrinking and cooling-induced recovery, enabling programmable volume changes and the ability to memorize irradiation history. This unique behavior is demonstrated in applications such as bilayer actuators, which show static bending under light exposure, and in devices inspired by origami, microvalves, and drug delivery systems. The combination of thermal hysteresis and light-responsive properties makes the hydrogel suitable for advanced programmable material applications.

The results of the present article demonstrate the usefulness of the droplet technique for investigations of microgels. The single most important result is the evidence of core-shell phase separation in spherical PA-microgels in equilibrium with C12TAB solutions. Earlier the phenomenon has been observed only in macrogels, where the question of equilibrium or not always remains due to the long relaxation times, or as thermodynamically unstable states in microgels undergoing volume phase transition in solutions of large volume. The capacity of the technique to provide new quantitative information is demonstrated by the determined swelling isotherms, showing for the first time how the volume of single PA-microgels depends on the ratio between surfactant and polyelectrolyte charges in the gel. The swelling isotherms resemble those reported earlier for nonspherical macrogels. It is also shown, with PA/cyt c as a demonstrator system, how the combination of droplet experiments and bulk solution experiments can be used to determine both swelling and binding isotherms for systems not displaying a volume phase transition. Comparison between experiments and theoretical model calculations shows that the recently developed gel theory is in semiquantitative agreement with the results for both cyt c and C12TAB, where the compositions of the collapsed homogeneous states at high binding ratios and the high cooperativity of cyt c binding are particularly well captured. The calculations suggest that the latter feature is an effect of polyion-mediated attractions between the protein molecules. Furthermore, comparison with MC simulations of spherical macroions in a model network shows that the gel model is capable of covering a wide range of electrostatic coupling strengths.

For biomedical applications, the use of in situ forming hydrogels is preferred over preformed hydrogels since there is no need for surgical interventions as gelation can take place under physiological conditions upon injection. Furthermore, the initial fluidic nature of the precursor solution ensures proper shape adaptation and biological components can be incorporated in the hydrogel by simple mixing with the precursor polymer solution. , Physical cross-links, such as hydrophobic or ionic interactions, can be formed in situ under mild conditions, but the resulting hydrogels generally degrade or dissolve rapidly. Injectable chemically cross-linked hydrogels have been frequently prepared by photocuring polymers functionalized with vinylic groups. Although the presence of photoinitiators and the generated radicals in the polymerization process has been associated with cytotoxicity, frequently good cell compatibility is found for cells encapsulated in this type of hydrogel. , However, important drawbacks of photo-cross-linkable systems include the limited penetration depth of UV radiation and its potentially damaging effects on living tissue. In situ forming hydrogels utilizing covalent cross-linking between polymers with complementary functional groups therefore received much attention in the last two decades. Early examples of chemical cross-linking reactions forming hydrogels include Schiff base formation between aldehydes and amines and the Passerini and Ugi condensation. However, remaining functional groups on polymers may react with functional groups present in biomolecules such as proteins, limiting the application of these hydrogels as in situ forming delivery systems. In this regard, the use of chemoselective, bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies, which do not interfere with biochemical processes or biomolecules, are very appealing. The most investigated chemoselective cross-linking reaction for hydrogels is the Cu (I)-catalyzed Huisgen 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition of terminal alkynes and azides, commonly known as click chemistry. This term was originally coined in 2001 by Sharpless et al. for a number of new regiospecific linking reactions that give high yields and generally require no purification. The first hydrogel cross-linked via click chemistry was described by the group of Hilborn and was based on PVA. Although this category of hydrogels has been mainly used for tissue engineering applications, they have also been applied for the controlled release of therapeutics and different biomolecules, including doxorubicin bovine serum albumin (BSA) and pDNA. Because "classical" alkyne-azide cycloadditions require the use of a copper catalyst, which may cause adverse effects in biomedical applications, the use of strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) is attracting increasing interest. This reaction employs the inherent ring strain of cyclooctyne groups to achieve fast and efficient cross-linking without the need for catalysts or external stimuli such as UV light. Hermann et al. reported on PEG hydrogels for the delivery of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) inhibitors to treat excessive postoperative bone regrowth (resynostosis) after surgical correction of premature fusion of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) in children. Mixing poly [(tetraethylene glycol methacrylate)-co-(azidotetraethylene glycol methacrylate)] with a 4-dibenzocyclooctynol PEG cross-linker resulted in the formation of hydrogels within 30 s, as demonstrated by oscillatory rheology. In vitro release experiments showed that the BMP inhibitor Gremlin1 remained bioactive when it was incorporated in the hydrogels by dissolution in the prepolymer solutions, confirming the bioorthogonal character of the SPAAC cross-linking method. When the prepolymer solutions were injected together with Gremlin1 in a surgically created cranial defect in weanling mice, a hydrogel formed in situ that was able to provide a controlled release of the inhibitor for 14 days. Following this approach, the authors were able to delay, but not completely prevent, postoperative bone regrowth in the cranial defect model. Since the ultimate goal of resynostosis therapy is to slow the postoperative bone growth for a period, but then allow the bone to regrow as the child ages, the reported approach holds promise as treatment after surgical intervention in craniosynostosis. Other emerging bioorthogonal strategies for the preparation of chemically cross-linked hydrogels include thiol-ene/yne reactions, , oxime chemistry, native chemical ligation, , and Diels-Alder cycloadditions. , Table presents a summary of several click chemistry strategies that have been used to form hydrogels, including advantages and disadvantages of each method. Dove and co-workers recently reported on the simultaneous application of thiol-yne and Diels-Alder chemistry to independently create two interpenetrating networks in a one-step procedure (Figure ). A loose network was prepared from norbornene-functionalized chitosan and linear PEG-ditetrazine, while a dense network was constructed by cross-linking 4-arm PEG-tetraalkyne with linear PEG-dithiol. The resulting double network hydrogels displayed a high compressive stress of 15 MPa at 98% compression without fracture or hysteresis upon repeated load. The hydrogels were postfunctionalized with a thiol-containing fluorescent dye and tetrazine-modified biotin via reaction with unreacted alkyne and norbornene groups, respectively. The cross-linking reactions were suggested to be bioorthogonal because of the high viability of human mesenchymal stem cells, which were encapsulated by adding them to the prepolymer solutions prior to hydrogel formation. An extensive recent review concerning bioorthogonal chemistries for hydrogel cross-linking can be found in ref .

dataset_item.question: What are the limitations and accuracy challenges associated with thermal imaging in heterogeneous catalytic reactions under microwave heating?
dataset_item.answer:
Thermal imaging in microwave-heated heterogeneous catalytic reactions provides valuable real-time, two-dimensional temperature mapping, with the capability to monitor temperatures up to 1000 °C. However, its accuracy faces significant challenges due to the multiparameter dependence of emissivity. Factors such as the gaseous reaction environment, varying media, object-to-camera distance, microwave field distribution, and the non-uniform emissivity of the catalyst bed can lead to inaccurate temperature measurements. 

These limitations are exacerbated in microwave-heated reactors, where nonhomogeneous heating profiles and localized hot spots are common. Consequently, relying solely on thermal imaging is insufficient for precise temperature monitoring. A dual measurement approach that integrates thermal imaging with at least one contact sensor (e.g., a thermocouple) is essential. This combined methodology enhances reliability by mitigating risks and ensuring accurate temperature readings, as demonstrated in methane dry reforming over a platinum-on-carbon catalyst.

inference_contexts: The thermal camera-thermocouple dual temperature measurement method developed in this work allows for real-time high temperature (300-1000 °C) measurements in MW-heated catalytic reactors. This method was applied for a temperature distribution study in a platinum-on-carbon catalytic bed used for methane dry reforming. For this purpose, a custom-designed microwave cavity was employed to focus the microwave field on the catalyst bed and monitor its temperature in a 2D fashion by means of a thermal camera. The effect of different factors affecting the temperature measurements and emissivity values under microwave heating was investigated. The effects of camera range, the presence of different media and reactant gases in the process domain, object-to-camera distance, heating system, and microwave field distribution were discussed in detail. The multiparameter emissivity dependence in such a complex reaction system does not ensure correct temperature recording by the thermal camera alone; therefore, at least one contact sensor is highly recommended. The developed method successfully detected hot spot generation and provided an explanation for the nonhomogeneous heating profiles during MW processing. Careful handling and continued temperature monitoring with a thermal camera is very helpful to avoid potential risk hazards in MW-heated catalytic reactors.

We carried out dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene over a magnetite catalyst under microwaves and evaluated the reaction activity. An accurate evaluation of the reaction activity under microwaves could be performed by considering the temperature distribution in the whole packed bed because the temperature gradient occurred in the packed bed during microwave heating. The simulation methods enable the calculation of theoretical reaction rates originated from the temperature distribution in the whole catalyst bed under microwaves. As a result, microwave enhancement was observed, especially when carbon deposition did not occur in the catalyst bed (500 °C). The result indicates that the rate enhancement under microwaves can not only be attributed to the nonuniform temperature distribution in the catalyst bed. The rate enhancement is possibly due to the generation of nonequilibrium local heating inside the catalyst bed by microwaves.

We showed how ultrasound reduces dispersion in micropacked-bed reactors by two orders of magnitude. Sonication produces partial fluidization of the bed even at high flow rates, continuously modifying gas channels and reducing liquid dispersion. Direct visualization and RTD experiments confirm that ultrasound can remove common gas channeling phenomena by promoting a dynamically dispersed gas phase flow. A more thorough study under a variety of hydrodynamics conditions is still necessary to assess contributions to mass transfer, the nature of gas-channeling, and the potential for enhancing heterogeneous catalyst reactions. The effects of short ultrasound pulses applied during transient initial bed operation might also present an interesting area of exploration to reduce variation in bed packing and ensure a more uniform packing for longer runtimes. To mitigate any surface damage of the catalyst due to cavitation or friction, more data are essential to quantify the acoustic attenuation in unsaturated porous media and optimize the design of micropacked-bed sonoreactors. The efficient use of ultrasound unlocks new pathways for multiphase reactor design, enabling near-plug-flow operation with enhanced phase homogenization in microscale-packed beds.

High emissivity coatings have the potential to increase the efficiency of high temperature industrial applications by enhancing the heat transfer via radiation. Applications of such coatings are already found in several industries, but others are hesitant to implement it as the longevity of the coating or its impact on the substrate material is yet to be determined. According to the literature, applying high emissivity coatings to the reactor tubes and/or the refractory walls of an industrial steam cracker can increase the furnace efficiency by up to 5% absolute, but the influence of the higher furnace efficiency on the convection section and the transfer line were not determined. Coupled 3D radiant section-1D reactor simulations of the ultra selective conversion U-coil furnace combined with 1D simulations of the convection section and the transfer line exchanger allowed assessment of the effects of applying a high emissivity coating to the reactor coils on the energy balance of the entire unit. The radiant box efficiency increased by 0.7% from 45.7 for uncoated reactors to 46.4% for coated reactors while the firing rate was decreased by 1.73% to maintain the same cracking severity. As the operating conditions for the process side were identical in both cases, the differences in the results for the reactor simulations and the transfer line exchanger were negligible. However, the flue gas flow rate and bridge wall temperature differed due to the changed firing rate. To ensure preheating of the process gas stream to the desired coil inlet temperature, less heat was to be used in the convection section for high pressure steam superheating in the high emissivity case. By eliminating secondary boiler feedwater injection and decreasing the fin size on the second high pressure steam superheater bank, the available duty in the convection section of the high emissivity case was correctly balanced between feed preheating and steam superheating. A total of 18.22% of the fired duty was used to generate high pressure steam in the base case versus 16.95% in the high emissivity case. Overall, the benefits in terms of energy of applying a high emissivity coating to the reactor outer walls are limited, in particular because the emissivity of the uncoated reactor material is already high. A more significant impact is expected when the high emissivity coating is also applied to the refractory walls. Even though the effect on the energy balance is low, a beneficial side effect of the lower average flue gas temperature in the radiant section is reduced formation of thermal NO x and hence lower greenhouse gas emissions.

For polymers, natural or otherwise, to produce carbon fiber of a similar quality as PAN, they cannot rely on hydrogen bonding for structural stability or contain a high mass fraction of oxygen, lest they shrink to an unusable extent. A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. Polyalanine-like domains could be incorporated into block copolymers for biomimetic graphite precursors. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

dataset_item.question: How does the second osmotic virial coefficient vary with temperature and solvent composition in ternary polymer solutions?
dataset_item.answer:
The second osmotic virial coefficient (\( B_2 \)) in ternary polymer solutions exhibits a complex dependence on temperature and solvent composition due to competitive solvation effects and the interplay between miscibility transitions. For a fixed solvent composition, \( B_2 \) vanishes at multiple Θ temperatures (\( T_{\Theta} \)), transitioning between positive (miscible) and negative (immiscible) values. Between two distinct Θ temperatures (\( T_{\Theta}^{(1)} \) and \( T_{\Theta}^{(2)} \)), \( B_2 \) becomes negative, indicating phase separation, while outside this range, it becomes positive, signaling miscibility. This behavior reflects the presence of a closed-loop immiscibility region in the phase diagram.  

Adjusting the solvent composition introduces additional complexity. For an initial solvent composition \( r_o = 5 \), the system exhibits two Θ temperatures. However, reducing the solvent ratio to \( r_o = 0.942 \) results in three Θ temperatures, reflecting combined upper critical solution temperature (UCST) and closed-loop phase behavior. This shift highlights how solvent composition influences miscibility transitions, with \( \Delta T_{\Theta} = T_{\Theta}^{(2)} - T_{\Theta}^{(1)} \) serving as a universal measure of immiscibility. As \( r_o \) decreases, miscibility improves, shrinking the range of immiscibility and reducing the upper critical solution temperature, while the lower critical solution temperature remains nearly constant.  

Overall, \( B_2 \) serves as a direct indicator of phase stability: positive values correspond to miscibility, while negative values signal phase separation. Its variation with temperature and solvent composition reveals the rich and intricate phase behavior of ternary polymer solutions, including the emergence of multiple miscibility transitions and changes in the phase diagram structure.

dataset_item.question: How can genetically encoded photo-cross-linkers be optimized to simultaneously capture promiscuous binding partners and identify interaction interfaces?
dataset_item.answer: Genetically encoded photo-cross-linkers can be optimized by incorporating multifunctional features, such as selenium-based cleavable linkers, which enable simultaneous capture of transient protein interactions and identification of interaction interfaces. These enhancements improve compatibility with advanced proteomic strategies like CAPP-DIGE and IMAPP, facilitating the profiling of native chaperone clients and mapping their binding interfaces under dynamic or stress conditions. This approach is particularly valuable for studying intrinsically disordered and conditionally disordered proteins, which often exhibit promiscuous and transient binding behavior. While challenges remain, such as capturing ultrafast interactions or determining binding affinities, the versatility of selenium-based cleavable linkers and the potential for further functionalization with novel chemical groups promise broader applicability across diverse research areas. Additionally, integrating biocompatible and chemically cleavable tools could extend their utility to other fields requiring precise interaction mapping and transient protein analysis.

dataset_item.question: How can phasor-based analysis quantify contributions of multiple fluorescent components in imaging data?
dataset_item.answer: Phasor-based analysis quantifies contributions of multiple fluorescent components in imaging data by leveraging the geometric properties of phasor plots and the phasor rule of addition. Prior knowledge of the individual components' phasor positions is required, ensuring that these positions are not collinear. Multicomponent analysis becomes feasible if the phasor positions form a polygon, with each fluorescent species at the vertices, and the overall phasor cloud lies within this polygon. The quantitative contributions of each component are determined by projecting the phasor cloud onto axes defined by the polygon geometry. This approach is particularly effective for analyzing up to three components from single-frequency FLIM data, simplifying the separation of overlapping signals such as free NADH, enzyme-bound NADH, and lipid droplets. Unlike non-Euclidean methods, this technique provides a more intuitive and computationally efficient framework for multicomponent fluorescence analysis.

It is common for C n mimBF4 RTILs to be contaminated with fluorescent impurities. It has been documented that these contaminants are generally negligible in concentration, do not have a significant effect on the bulk structure of the ionic liquid, and only become apparent with techniques such as fluorescence. , Such contaminants are excited at the 395 nm sample excitation wavelength and emit at 440 nm, meaning that when present they contribute to the experimental fluorescent decays. Because of the very low concentration of both the perylene and the impurities, it is a safe assumption that they will not interact with each other when solvated by ionic liquids. The contributions of the perylene and the contaminants to the fluorescence decays are therefore additive. For this reason, data from reference samples containing only the RTIL/water mixtures with no dissolved probe were also collected. A moving sample stage was used that interchanges the two samples under computer control so that data were collected on both the ionic liquid samples, alternating between those with perylene and those without, keeping all experimental conditions identical over the course of the experiment. The resulting perylene lifetime decay curves attained after subtraction of the reference sample fluorescence decay were single exponentials with time constants of 5.02 ns within experimental error for all RTILs studied. The measured lifetime is consistent with the perylene lifetime in other solvents. This observed single exponential decays with the same lifetimes indicates the reliability of the background subtraction technique for removing the contribution of fluorescent impurities in the RTILs. Because of the absence of fluorescent impurities, Hmim BF4 samples did not require subtraction, and it yielded the same fluorescent lifetime, within error, as the other samples. Furthermore, two different batches of Bmim BF4 from the supplier were used in the Bmim experiments. One batch had fluorescence impurities and required the impurity fluorescence subtraction. No subtraction was performed on the batch without impurities. The results obtained from both batches were the same, clearly demonstrating the validity of the background subtraction method.

As computational chemistry methods are applied to increasingly larger systems, the question of their efficiency-in particular, with respect to run time-becomes critical. Formally, GGA functionals like BLYP scale as N 3 with system size (with N being the number of electrons), whereas hybrid functionals scale with N 4. Therefore, low-cost corrections such as D3 and DCP that may elevate the performance of BLYP to that of B3LYP or better may be of value. We also conducted additional performance assessments of the two methods on the BHPERI, DARC, BSR36, and the RSE43 databases. We use D3 corrections with B3LYP for our comparison because D3 has a computational cost that is negligible relative to that of the underlying DFT method and because D3 corrections (or similar) are required to predict noncovalent interactions that are reasonable. It is worthwhile restating that D3 corrections that were designed for use with B3LYP were also designed for use with nearly complete basis sets. dataset_item.question: How do preprocessing and postprocessing steps contribute to stiction detection in control valves?
dataset_item.answer: Preprocessing and postprocessing steps are vital for accurate stiction detection in control valves, as they improve data reliability by mitigating issues like noise and external disturbances commonly present in industrial environments. Proper preprocessing ensures signal integrity, enhancing the effectiveness of stiction detection techniques while preventing signal degradation that could lead to misdiagnosis of oscillation causes. Postprocessing further refines the results, ensuring precise detection and interpretation of stiction-related issues. However, careful selection and implementation of these steps are critical, as incorrect preprocessing may compromise data quality and lead to erroneous conclusions. These processes collectively play a key role in achieving reliable and effective stiction detection in industrial applications.

In this work, a parametric drift detection and isolation (PDDI) scheme that consists of a preparatory stage before batch-to-batch operation and a post-batch stage during batch-to-batch operation was proposed for the detection and isolation of batch-to-batch parametric drifts in a batch crystallization process. In the preparatory stage, the threshold values and signatures for each parametric drift are computed without process measurements. Then, during the batch-to-batch operation, this scheme computes residuals by evaluating the absolute value of the difference between the process variables obtained from the drift-free simulation with noise from the time profiles of the states obtained through post-batch (e.g.. number of crystals, average crystal size and shape) as well as in-batch (e.g.. protein solute concentration, temperature in the crystallizer) process measurements. The residuals were compared with thresholds and signatures obtained in the preparatory stage for the detection and isolation of a parametric drift. Subsequently, the magnitude of the batch-to-batch parametric drift is estimated by the PDDI system and it is used to update the parameters of the batch process model which is used in the in-batch model predictive control (MPC) to compute a set of optimal jacket temperatures for the production of crystals with a desired shape distribution in the next batch. dataset_item.question: What are the differences in the electronic origin bands and low-frequency intermolecular modes between para-fluorophenol-cyclopropylamine and para-fluorophenol-ammonia complexes?
dataset_item.answer: The para-fluorophenol-cyclopropylamine (pFP-CPA) complex exhibits a significantly larger spectral red shift (816 cm⁻¹ for the endo conformer) in its S₁←S₀ electronic origin transition compared to the para-fluorophenol-ammonia (pFP-NH₃) complex. This larger red shift is attributed to cyclopropylamine's higher proton affinity and stronger hyperconjugative charge transfer interaction energy compared to ammonia. Additionally, the pFP-CPA complex displays significantly more intense low-frequency intermolecular vibrational modes in its fluorescence excitation spectrum, indicating a greater geometry change upon electronic excitation. This geometry change is further corroborated by the long progression observed in dispersed fluorescence spectra when the intermolecular stretching fundamental is excited. Computational spectral simulations using CAM-B3LYP/6-311++G(2d,2p) calculations and PGOPHER fitting confirm these findings, providing a detailed understanding of the electronic and vibrational differences between the two complexes.

dataset_item.question: How is the uncertainty of carbon emission results in wood utilization scenarios analyzed using probabilistic methods?
dataset_item.answer: The uncertainty of carbon emission results in wood utilization scenarios is analyzed using probabilistic methods, primarily Monte Carlo simulation. This approach involves running 10,000 deterministic computations, where input parameters are sampled from defined probability distributions to capture variability in key variables such as substitution credits and forest carbon sink impacts. The resulting outcomes are expressed as probability distributions and classified using IPCC terminology (e.g., "very likely" for 90-100% probability) to provide clear probabilistic interpretations. To further assess the influence of individual variables on overall uncertainty, sensitivity analysis is conducted using Spearman’s rank correlation (ρ), which quantifies the contribution of each input variable. This comprehensive methodology ensures robust uncertainty quantification and provides a clearer understanding of wood utilization’s climate mitigation potential over a 100-year horizon.

dataset_item.question: What are the crystal structures and stoichiometric compositions of TBPO semiclathrate hydrates in binary and double hydrate systems?
dataset_item.answer:
TBPO semiclathrate hydrates in binary (TBPO-H₂O) and double hydrate (TBPO-H₂O-CH₄) systems crystallize in the orthorhombic structure with the *Pbam* space group. The idealized unit cell composition is 4H·4P·4T·14D·148H₂O, corresponding to a structural stoichiometry of TBPO·34.5H₂O. Analytical measurements yield a stoichiometry of TBPO·(33.6 ± 0.9)H₂O, with deviations attributed to structural defects. 

In the double hydrate system, methane predominantly occupies the small D cages of the TBPO hydrate framework, with a maximum cage occupancy of approximately 85% at 8.5 MPa. The double hydrate retains the same orthorhombic structure and a similar H₂O:TBPO molar ratio as the binary hydrate. Methane storage capacity ranges between 61.6–74.6 mL/g in ~26–30 wt% TBPO solutions, demonstrating superior performance compared to THF and TBAB hydrates by at least 1.5×. Raman spectroscopy confirms selective methane occupancy in the D cages, with no evidence of structural alterations. These properties suggest potential applications in gas separation and thermal energy storage.

dataset_item.question: How does the temperature-responsive behavior of PNIPAAM grafted onto halloysite nanotubes influence properties such as colloidal stability and wettability?
dataset_item.answer: The temperature-responsive behavior of poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAAM) grafted onto halloysite nanotubes significantly impacts both colloidal stability and wettability due to its characteristic coil-to-globule transition at the lower critical solution temperature (LCST). Below the LCST, PNIPAAM remains in a hydrated, coiled state, enhancing colloidal stability through steric hindrance and promoting hydrophilic interactions that increase wettability. Above the LCST, PNIPAAM collapses into a globular state, reducing steric stabilization and making the surface more hydrophobic, which restricts water spreading. This thermoresponsive behavior modulates the Brownian diffusion and electrophoretic mobility of the hybrid nanocarriers, making these properties highly dependent on temperature. Furthermore, the wettability transition enables applications such as controlled drug delivery, where the hydrophilic state below LCST protects the drug, while the hydrophobic state above LCST facilitates its release. The combination of temperature-dependent colloidal stability, wettability, and transport properties makes PNIPAAM-grafted halloysite nanotubes highly suitable for stimuli-responsive applications.

dataset_item.question: What are the relative contributions of food processing, retail, wholesale, and human consumption to avoidable food waste in Norway?
dataset_item.answer: In Norway, human consumption is the largest contributor to avoidable food waste (AFW), generating 92 kt dry matter (DM) per year. This exceeds the combined AFW from food processing (33 kt DM/year), retail (29 kt DM/year), and wholesale (1 kt DM/year). Wholesale plays a negligible role in AFW generation, while food processing and retail contribute significantly. Losses from human consumption represent approximately 10% of total consumer-purchased food, underscoring the critical role of consumer behavior in AFW generation. Addressing waste at the consumption stage would yield the greatest impact in minimizing Norway's avoidable food waste, followed by interventions in food processing and retail.

dataset_item.question: How does planarity in the structure of flavonoid molecules influence their binding affinity toward G4 DNA?
dataset_item.answer:
Planarity in the structure of flavonoid molecules plays a crucial role in their binding affinity toward G4 DNA. Fisetin, a planar flavonoid with a coplanar conformation facilitated by the presence of a C2-C3 double bond in its C-ring, exhibits stronger binding to G4 DNA compared to naringenin, which lacks this double bond and adopts a noncoplanar conformation relative to the ring A/C plane. The planar structure of fisetin enables efficient π-π stacking interactions with the external bases of G4 DNA, while naringenin's noncoplanar conformation hinders such interactions, favoring binding to duplex DNA instead. Furthermore, fisetin forms a greater number of hydrogen bonds with G4 DNA, enhancing its binding affinity.

Spectroscopic and molecular docking studies confirm that fisetin's planar structure facilitates interaction with the hydrophobic environment of G4 DNA, resulting in greater motional restriction, longer fluorescence lifetime, and higher rotational correlation time compared to naringenin. These findings underscore the importance of molecular planarity in selective G4 DNA recognition and provide valuable insights for designing flavonoid-based anticancer agents targeting G4 structures.

Despite possessing quite similar structural backbones, fisetin exhibits preferential interaction with G4 DNA in comparison to the duplex, while the reverse occurs for naringenin. Molecular modeling studies clearly demonstrate that the spatial structures of the flavonoids may cause these differences in the G4 binding. The more coplanar conformation of fisetin may be responsible for the strong binding of this flavonol with the G4. However, due to the absence of a C2-C3 double bond in the C-ring, naringenin adopts a significant noncoplanar conformation relative to the ring A/C plane, resulting in a poor binding with the G4 structure. Interestingly, fisetin forms a greater number of H-bonds with G4 than that of naringenin which may also lead to the higher affinity of fisetin toward G4 than naringenin. The present study elucidates, for the first time, the role of C-ring planarity on the preferential binding of G4 DNA by flavonoids. This study also exemplifies the application of dual emission behavior of flavonoids to probe selective G4 DNA recognition and lays the basis for further applications in this direction. To the best of our knowledge, this may be the first report of two closely similar structured flavonoid molecules showing sharply contrasting selectivity for binding with different DNA structures. These studies may enlighten the understanding of specific interaction of small molecules with DNA structure, helping the drug discovery process.

dataset_item.question: How do ammonia, organotins, and phosphate contribute to growth inhibition of Heterocypris incongruens in sediments?
dataset_item.answer:
Ammonia (NH₃) and organotins, particularly tributyltin (TBT⁺), are the primary contributors to the growth inhibition of *Heterocypris incongruens* in sediments, each exhibiting a toxicity unit (TU) of 0.3. These compounds act as direct inhibitors of growth, with organotins showing strong correlation to toxicity despite their relatively low initial TU contribution. In contrast, phosphate (HPO₄²⁻) has a growth-promoting effect, reducing the toxic impact with a TU of -0.3. 

Speciation calculations indicate that ammonia, organotins, and phosphate collectively account for up to 90% of the observed variance in growth inhibition across various water bodies. Regional differences in toxicity are evident, with sediments in West Flanders demonstrating higher toxic pressure compared to inland areas. The mechanism involves ammonia and organotins exerting toxic effects, while phosphate mitigates their impact by promoting growth. These findings underscore the importance of balancing nutrient levels and controlling toxic compounds in sediment management strategies.

dataset_item.question: How does modularity maximization influence the design and performance of distributed model predictive control in amine gas sweetening plants?
dataset_item.answer: Modularity maximization in distributed model predictive control (DMPC) for amine gas sweetening plants optimizes the decomposition of the plant into subnetworks, typically separating the absorption and regeneration stages. This optimal decomposition results in a control architecture that achieves closed-loop performance comparable to centralized model predictive control (CMPC) while outperforming decentralized and suboptimal distributed MPC strategies. By leveraging modularity, the DMPC framework ensures robust disturbance rejection and noise tolerance, critical for tightly integrated large-scale plants. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of this modular approach makes it highly practical for real-time applications, striking an effective balance between control precision and scalability.

dataset_item.question: How can criteria be developed to select fate and transport models for estimating eutrophication-related impacts in life cycle assessment?
dataset_item.answer:
Criteria for selecting fate and transport (F&T) models for estimating eutrophication-related impacts in life cycle assessment (LCA) can be developed by integrating scientific rigor with practical constraints. The selection process involves identifying candidate models through systematic literature searches, focusing on models published between 2007 and 2017, actively maintained, and widely used—particularly by reputable organizations such as the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). 

Key criteria include:
1. **Model Maintenance and Usage**: Prioritize models that are actively updated, widely applied, and endorsed by recognized agencies (e.g., EPA) to ensure reliability and relevance.
2. **Geographic and Temporal Scope**: Assess the geographic coverage, spatial resolution, and time step of the models to ensure compatibility with the study’s context and objectives.
3. **Representation of Nutrient Dynamics**: Evaluate the model’s ability to accurately represent nutrient loading sources, transport mechanisms, removal processes, and transformation pathways critical to eutrophication modeling.
4. **Accessibility**: Favor publicly available models to facilitate transparency and reproducibility in research.
5. **Practical Constraints**: Consider limitations such as site specificity and challenges in spatial-temporal distribution to balance scientific rigor with feasibility.
6. **Structured Evaluation**: Use a rubric or spreadsheet to systematically assess model suitability based on metadata (e.g., geographic scope, spatial resolution) and nutrient-specific factors (e.g., nitrogen and phosphorus cycling processes).

The goal is to select models that effectively capture nutrient input, transport, removal, and transformation processes while accommodating practical challenges such as resolution limitations and site-specific variability. This ensures the selected models are scientifically robust, contextually relevant, and accessible for eutrophication-related LCA applications.

dataset_item.question: What is the effect of Li and Cl atomic dopants on the band gaps and electronic structure of polythiophene and polypyrrole polymers?
dataset_item.answer:
Li and Cl atomic dopants significantly alter the electronic structure and band gaps of polythiophene (PTh) and polypyrrole (PPy) polymers, as confirmed by density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Lithium acts as an n-type dopant, causing an upward shift in the Fermi level, while chlorine functions as a p-type dopant, resulting in a downward shift in the Fermi level. Both dopants effectively reduce the HOMO-LUMO gap of these polymers, with a pronounced effect observed in polythiophene and its analogs, where sulfur is replaced by oxygen, selenium, or tellurium, and in polypyrrole analogs, where nitrogen is substituted with phosphorus, arsenic, or antimony.

Structural changes in the polymer chains are induced upon doping, facilitating charge transfer between the dopants and the polymers, as supported by Mulliken population analysis. These electronic modifications enhance the tunability of polythiophene and polypyrrole for various electronic device applications, including semiconductors and optoelectronic devices.

dataset_item.question: What is the difference in the excited-state proton transfer mechanism between 2,6-diazaindole clusters containing three and four water molecules?
dataset_item.answer:
The excited-state proton transfer (ESPT) mechanism in 2,6-diazaindole (2,6-DAI) clusters depends on the number of water molecules due to differences in hydrogen bonding configurations and reaction pathways. For the 2,6-DAI (H₂O)₃ cluster, ESPT follows a type A process, while for the 2,6-DAI (H₂O)₄ cluster, ESPT occurs via a type C process. The transition to a type C mechanism in the four-water cluster is driven by the enhanced stability of the proton-transferred (PT) form due to optimized hydrogen bonding interactions. 

Despite the distinct pathways, both clusters exhibit nearly identical energy barriers in the S₁ state, with type A having an energy barrier of 13.16 kcal/mol and type C having an energy barrier of 13.14 kcal/mol. Frontier molecular orbital analysis confirms charge redistribution during ESPT, facilitated by enhanced hydrogen bonding in the excited state. These findings demonstrate that 2,6-DAI can engage in ESPT through either three- or four-water-molecule clusters, following energetically similar but mechanistically distinct pathways.

dataset_item.question: How does the hidden Markov model method compare to the hindered Brownian diffusion method in simulating continuous-wave electron paramagnetic resonance spectra of spin-labeled proteins?
dataset_item.answer:
The hidden Markov model (HMM) method is superior to the hindered Brownian diffusion (HBD) method for simulating continuous-wave electron paramagnetic resonance (CW EPR) spectra of spin-labeled proteins. HMM excels at capturing multi-scale and jump-like transitions between spin-label orientations, making it highly effective for systems with restricted dynamics, such as TOAC-polyalanine, as well as faster, more mobile dynamics observed in R1-labeled proteins. In contrast, HBD relies on a single rotational diffusion tensor and orientational potential energy, which limits its ability to accurately model restricted multisite dynamics and complex motions.

Additionally, HMM offers significant computational advantages, being approximately 50 times faster than HBD for simulating faster dynamics. This efficiency is achieved by avoiding the computational bottleneck associated with interpolative evaluation of the torque term in HBD at each time step. Overall, HMM provides greater flexibility, accuracy, and performance across different spin-label dynamics, making it the preferred method for CW EPR spectral simulations.

dataset_item.question: What are the effects of ultrasound on dispersion and flow behavior in micropacked-bed reactors?
dataset_item.answer: High-power, low-frequency (∼40 kHz) ultrasound significantly enhances dispersion and flow behavior in micropacked-bed reactors by reducing liquid dispersion by two orders of magnitude and promoting near-plug-flow operation. This improvement is achieved through partial fluidization of the packed bed, which dynamically disrupts gas channeling, disperses the gas phase uniformly, and enhances phase homogenization, even at high flow rates. Visualization and residence time distribution experiments confirm these effects, demonstrating the stabilization of flow and reduction of channeling. Additionally, ultrasound continuously modifies gas channels, thereby mitigating liquid dispersion and ensuring more uniform flow. While these findings highlight the potential of ultrasound to improve microscale reactor performance, further studies are needed to optimize reactor design, assess mass transfer contributions, and address potential catalyst damage from cavitation.

dataset_item.question: How does ionic strength influence the twisting period and stability of charged amphiphile nanoribbons?
dataset_item.answer: Ionic strength influences the twisting period and stability of charged amphiphile nanoribbons by modulating electrostatic interactions. At low ionic strengths, reduced electrostatic screening enhances edge charge stabilization, favoring larger twisting periods and promoting helicoid stability. Twisting redistributes charges toward the edges, lowering the system's free energy, making the helicoid shape energetically favorable. However, as ionic strength increases, salt ions screen electrostatic interactions, reducing the electrostatic benefit of twisting and destabilizing the helicoid shape. This leads to shorter twisting periods and flatter ribbons, especially for flexible nanoribbons with high surface charge densities. While molecular chirality can independently drive twisting, electrostatic effects significantly modulate the optimal twisting period, as observed experimentally.

The stabilizing electrostatic free energy for twisting the ribbon and the elastic energetic penalty have similar orders of magnitude. In the case of nanoribbons formed by amphiphile self-assembly, the electrostatic contributions will be relevant for flexible ribbons (thin ribbons with low Young's modulus), large surface charge densities (highly charged amphiphiles), and low ionic strengths (which promote large twisting periods that involve low elastic penalties). Even in the case where the spontaneous twisting of the ribbon results from molecular chirality, electrostatic interactions may be relevant and shift the optimal twisting period. This situation can be recognized in experiments as a dependence of the twisting period on the ionic strength of the solution.

The fact that the helicoid is a minimum free-energy surface in aqueous solution is unexpected if we consider that a one-dimensional string of charges minimizes its energy in the fully stretched conformation. However, twisting the nanoribbon into a helicoid (keeping a constant and homogeneous charge density) results in an increase in its perimeter. We, therefore, ascribe the stability of the helicoid to an increase in the number of charges near the edge, which are more stable than those near the axis. This simple argument successfully explains many of our numerical results, but one should note that there still remain open questions, for example, why the helicoid is the only twisted shape that can be more stable than the flat ribbon and why pairwise-additive electrostatic models fail to capture the effect. In conclusion, the results of this work provide new insights into the role of electrostatics in the shape development of soft materials.

dataset_item.question: How does the use of one-electron pseudopotential calculations combined with advanced computational techniques affect the modeling of the Mg+He van der Waals system?
dataset_item.answer:
The use of one-electron pseudopotential calculations, combined with advanced computational techniques, significantly enhances the modeling of the Mg+He van der Waals system by simplifying the complex problem to a single valence electron while retaining high accuracy. This approach employs semilocal pseudopotentials to describe interactions between the Mg²⁺ core and the valence electron with helium, and high-level CCSD(T) calculations to accurately account for core-core interactions. Large Gaussian basis sets are utilized to improve the precision of the results, while the Tang-Toennies analytical expression refines the potential energy surfaces at intermediate distances. Spin-orbit coupling effects are incorporated using a semiempirical method, leading to energy splitting and minor shifts in equilibrium distances.

The derived potential energy surfaces and spectroscopic constants for the X²Σ⁺ and A²Π states are consistent with prior studies, validating the accuracy of the approach. These results provide a robust foundation for future investigations into Mg+He clusters, helium nanodroplet interactions, and spectral broadening effects in He gas collisions. The combined use of pseudopotential calculations and advanced computational methods ensures a detailed and reliable description of the Mg+He van der Waals system across both ground and excited states.

dataset_item.question: How does the use of HF during synthesis influence the crystallinity and phase formation of zirconium coordination polymers prepared with benzenephosphonate derivatives?
dataset_item.answer: The use of hydrofluoric acid (HF) as a mineralizer during the synthesis of zirconium coordination polymers with benzenephosphonate derivatives promotes crystallinity but results in mixed-phase compounds with unresolved structures. In contrast, fluoride-free synthesis produces poorly crystalline zirconium benzenetriphosphonates (ZrBTP-x) that exhibit superior extraction performance for trivalent lanthanides and tetravalent thorium under highly acidic conditions (>3 M HNO₃). These fluoride-free materials demonstrate fast extraction kinetics, high selectivity for heavy lanthanides, and thermal stability. Upon heating, they form highly crystalline pyrophosphates (AIVP₂O₇), which are suitable for radioactive waste disposal. Therefore, while HF enhances crystallinity, it compromises phase purity and extraction efficiency, making fluoride-free synthesis more advantageous for applications requiring superior extraction performance and selectivity.

dataset_item.question: What is the impact of truncation of C-terminal regions on structural stability and interaction dynamics of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex subunits E2 and E3BP?
dataset_item.answer: Truncation of the C-terminal regions in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex subunits E2 and E3BP significantly destabilizes their structural stability and interaction dynamics. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that while wild-type (WT) E2 and E3BP dimers maintain stable orientations with tightly bound C-terminals embedded in hydrophobic pockets, truncated versions (E2-t8 and E3BP-t7) rapidly lose mutual alignment and detach from these binding pockets. This detachment is accompanied by a sharp reduction in hydrophobic interactions, which play a dominant role in dimer stability and core assembly integrity. The increased distances between C-terminal regions and hydrophobic pockets further underscore the loss of structural cohesion upon truncation. These findings align with experimental observations in other pyruvate dehydrogenase complex species and provide molecular-level evidence for human PDC assembly mechanisms. Preliminary experimental data corroborate these results, demonstrating core disassembly upon truncation. These insights enhance the understanding of human PDC assembly and stability, while informing future designs of artificial multienzyme systems.

The paper aims to develop a model-based understanding of the structure and function of the human pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (hPDC) by utilizing molecular dynamics simulations. Specifically, it focuses on elucidating the assembly mechanisms of hPDC core subunits (E2 and E3BP) and their interactions at the atomistic level. The research highlights the role of hydrophobic interactions in the self-assembly process and explores how structural alterations (e.g., C-terminal truncation) impact these interactions. **<method>**
