inference_contexts: In this study we have presented new homology models of E2 and E3BP monomers of human pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (hPDC) core. We showed that the previous E2-EM model is not stable and not accurate enough. To validate our new models, extensive MD simulations were conducted on E2 and E3BP. For a more quantitative and mechanistic assessment several dynamic and structural properties such as rmsd, rmsf, R g , and secondary structure analysis were carried out. Overall, both models, especially the E2 model, showed very good structural stability and consistency within the extended simulation time in comparison to the low-resolution cryo-EM model (E2-EM). The active site of the new E2 model showed a much higher stability (rmsf = 0.16 nm) than that of E2-EM (rmsf = 0.30 nm). Further the protein interactions and the anchoring effect were studied in dimers of E2 and E3BP where the monomers were oriented as in a 60-meric core to mimic the same interactions. The anchoring effect was observed by simulation of wild-type (WT) and truncated E2 (E2-t8) and E3BP (E3BP-t7) versions. In both WT subunit dimers, the original orientation was well preserved and the C-terminals were tightly bound to the hydrophobic pockets. On the contrary, upon elimination of the C-terminals, within a short simulation time the two monomers lost their mutual orientation in both cases and detached from their binding pockets. The detachment was shown by the distance increase between the C-terminals and the hydrophobic pockets in E2-t8 and E3BP-t7 in comparison to those in WT. Further, a dramatic decrease in the number of hydrophobic interactions in the truncated versions proved a dominant hydrophobic force in the dimers interaction and in the core assembly. This phenomenon is shown for the first time from our simulations at the molecular level for hPDC subunits. The results correlate well with earlier experimental investigations on other PDC species with 20 identical E2 containing trimers; for human PDC however, no experimental proof was reported so far. In our group experimental work is ongoing in this direction, and our preliminary results indicate the disassembly of hPDC for several double truncations, e.g.. E2-t8 and E3BP-t7, for the first time (data not shown).

Above this concentration, the CNT colloidal stabilization also has little dependence on the PF127 concentration. The same PF127 was not able to colloidally stabilize graphene oxide (chemically oxidized) through steric-based mechanisms due to the small size of PEO moieties in comparison with the large-sized sheets of GO (lateral size of up to 20 μm), thus preventing a suitable steric repulsion for GO sheets. This aspect also explains the absence of stabilizing depletion forces for the GO-PF127 system, in which there is not a proper dimensional and stereochemical matching between the large (i.e.. GO sheets) and small (i.e.. PF127 micelles) particles present in the liquid. On the other hand, long-chain PEG (MW 35000) was unable to colloidally stabilize CNTs due to the absence of significant short-range interactions (e.g.. hydrophobic) that could result in steric-based mechanisms of stabilization. In addition, the absence of a proper dimensional and stereochemical matching between the long-chain PEG 35000 and the high aspect ratio one-dimensional morphology of CNTs did not lead to the manifestation of stabilizing repulsive depletion forces as well. However, large-sized sheets of GO in the presence of PEG 35000 can be colloidally stabilized through repulsive depletion forces, which strongly depend on the polymer concentration, as shown by the stabilization attained for PEG concentrations from 5.0 wt %. The computational results are not dependent on whether gas phase- or aqueous-optimized clusters with and without explicit H2O molecules were included with the implicit COSMO SCRF approach. Values derived solely from ZPE contributions are in excellent agreement with the results including all vibrational components, showing that thermal corrections have virtually no effect on ϵ for this reaction. dataset_item.question: What are the advantages of oxidative coupling reactions for bioconjugation in terms of reaction rate, selectivity, and product stability?
dataset_item.answer: Oxidative coupling reactions for bioconjugation offer several advantages that make them highly effective for diverse applications. They exhibit rapid reaction rates, typically completing in 2–20 minutes even at micromolar concentrations, which is ideal for time-sensitive processes like radiolabeling and minimizes biomolecule denaturation. These reactions are minimally affected by steric hindrance, enabling efficient coupling of sterically hindered or full-sized biomolecules. dataset_item.question: What structural differences arise between zirconium oxide prepared by oxidation of zirconium predeposited on copper versus direct deposition of zirconium under oxygen ambient?
dataset_item.answer:
Structural differences between zirconium oxide (ZrO₂) prepared by oxidation of zirconium predeposited on copper versus direct deposition of zirconium under oxygen ambient arise from variations in oxidation pathways, interfacial interactions, and growth modes. 

When zirconium is vapor-deposited on copper at room temperature (300K) followed by oxidation at elevated temperatures (600K), the resulting ZrO₂ forms well-defined, stable islands with larger and more isolated structures. This growth mode is attributed to the controlled oxidation process that minimizes interactions with the underlying copper substrate. Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) confirms the formation of these distinct ZrO₂ islands, while X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) shows the presence of stoichiometric ZrO₂ with fewer oxygen deficiencies.

In contrast, direct deposition of zirconium in an oxygen ambient on preoxidized CuOₓ/Cu(111) at 600K leads to less uniform ZrO₂ structures and stronger interfacial interactions with the CuOₓ support. STM reveals smaller and less isolated islands, while XPS indicates the initial formation of oxygen-deficient ZrOₓ phases, requiring further oxidation to achieve stoichiometric ZrO₂. The differences in structure and composition stem from the direct exposure of zirconium to oxygen during deposition and the influence of the preoxidized copper substrate on the oxidation process.

Overall, the predeposition and subsequent oxidation approach produces more stable and well-defined ZrO₂ structures, while direct deposition under oxygen ambient results in less uniform growth and oxygen-deficient phases due to differing oxidation dynamics and substrate interactions.

dataset_item.question: How does confinement in nanopores affect nanoscale segregation and packing of hydrophobic ionic liquids?
dataset_item.answer: Confinement within nanopores significantly impacts the nanoscale segregation and packing of hydrophobic ionic liquids, such as [C6mim][PF6]. Depending on the ionic liquid-to-precursor ratio, three distinct nanopore morphologies—H2, H3, and H4—are observed. Narrow H2 and H4 nanopores disrupt the intrinsic nanoscale segregation of the ionic liquid due to spatial constraints, while broader H3 nanopores preserve this segregation despite rough surface topography. Within H3 nanopores, the confined ionic liquid exhibits tighter packing, with characteristic lengths reduced to 1.55–1.65 nm compared to the bulk value of 1.71 nm. This enhanced packing is driven by repulsive interactions between the [PF6]⁻ anions and silanol groups on the silica surface. These morphological transitions are governed by the minimization of interfacial energy and the maximization of entropy, which together determine the balance between segregation preservation and packing behavior in confinement.

dataset_item.question: What are the benefits of decomposing probabilistic graphical models into hierarchical structures for process monitoring?
dataset_item.answer: Decomposing probabilistic graphical models into hierarchical structures offers significant benefits for process monitoring by leveraging conditional dependencies among process variables. This hierarchical decomposition enables the efficient representation of the joint probability distribution as a product of conditional densities and low-dimensional densities, simplifying the estimation process. By utilizing nonparametric kernel density estimation, this approach becomes distribution-free, making it particularly effective for handling nonlinear and non-Gaussian systems. Compared to traditional methods like PCA-based contribution plots, hierarchical decomposition improves fault detection and isolation by pinpointing faulty variables with greater accuracy. This capability has been demonstrated in applications such as blast furnace iron-making processes, where it enhances fault localization and process monitoring efficiency.

dataset_item.question: How does the deposition method of sodium fluoride affect the interfacial dipole on organic layers like P3HT and PCBM?
dataset_item.answer: The deposition method of sodium fluoride (NaF) plays a crucial role in determining the interfacial dipole on organic layers like P3HT and PCBM. Sequential depositions, compared to single thick depositions, lead to distinct dipole changes due to variations in interfacial dipole formation and potential water trapping. For NaF/P3HT, the outward-facing dipole component becomes more positive, while for NaF/PCBM, it becomes less positive. These dipole changes are attributed to the electronic structure modifications at the interface, influenced by the deposition method. Thick NaF layers can cause fluorination and damage to the conjugated π states of PCBM, degrading device performance, whereas thin layers enhance charge injection due to favorable dipole effects. Furthermore, the island-like growth mechanism of NaF, similar to LiF, contributes to the interfacial property changes. Understanding these effects is critical for optimizing charge injection and improving the performance of organic photovoltaic devices.

dataset_item.question: How does molecular shape, particularly rigidity of ring structures, influence diffusion rates of hydrocarbons in activated carbon?
dataset_item.answer:
The molecular shape, particularly the rigidity of ring structures, plays a significant role in influencing the diffusion rates of hydrocarbons in activated carbon. Rigid ring structures hinder molecular mobility, resulting in slower diffusion compared to flexible, linear hydrocarbons. Experimental studies using concentration-swing frequency response (CSFR) measurements on C10 hydrocarbons in BPL activated carbon have shown that rigid molecules, such as α-pinene and decalin, diffuse more slowly than flexible molecules like n-decane. This trend was observed across diffusion coefficients ranging from approximately 1 × 10⁻¹² m²/s in the Henry's law regime to higher values at elevated concentrations.

The impact of molecular rigidity on diffusion rates is supported by quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) analysis, which highlights molecular shape factors as key determinants of diffusivity. The absence of size exclusion effects in the porous structure of BPL activated carbon further confirms that molecular rigidity, rather than size, is the dominant factor affecting diffusion. The order of diffusion rates observed—n-decane > limonene > perfluorodecalin > decalin > α-pinene—illustrates how increased ring rigidity reduces mobility within the activated carbon's porous framework. In conclusion, hydrocarbons with rigid ring structures experience slower diffusion due to restricted molecular motion within the pores.

Micropore diffusion was the rate limiting mass transfer mechanism for each adsorbate at various concentrations. Predicted local isotherm slopes from the CSFR experiments agreed well with those calculated from adsorption isotherms for hydrocarbon molecules. The diffusion coefficients were found to be highly concentration dependent, and a Darken analysis was used to predict a lower limit for diffusivity in the Henry's law regime. The lower limit of the diffusivity of C10 hydrocarbons in BPL activated carbon at room temperature is about 1 × 10-12 m2/s, although values can be orders of magnitude faster at higher concentrations. For the molecules studied, the order from fastest to slowest diffusion was n-decane > limonene > perfluorodecalin > decalin > α-pinene. QSAR correlations were performed to relate diffusivity to specific molecular descriptors. Size exclusion based sieving effects were not observed as the wide pore size distribution of BPL activated carbon was larger than any molecular dimensions. However, molecular shape factors based on rigidity of ring structures showed good correlation with diffusivity, with the more rigid molecules diffusing more slowly.

dataset_item.question: How does functionalized graphene improve matrix strength of silicone rubber compared to chemically reduced graphene?
dataset_item.answer: Functionalized graphene (FG) significantly improves the matrix strength of silicone rubber (VMQ) compared to chemically reduced graphene (rGO), due to its stronger compatibility and interactions with the polymer matrix. Rheological tests demonstrate that FG enhances matrix strength by approximately six times, whereas rGO achieves only a two-fold increase. This superior matrix reinforcement by FG prevents cell wall shrinkage during foaming, resulting in VMQ/FG foams with larger cell sizes and lower density—one-third that of VMQ/rGO foams at 1 wt% loading. Additionally, FG-reinforced foams exhibit superior mechanical properties, including higher specific compression strength (1.21 MPa·cm³/g vs. 0.85 MPa·cm³/g for VMQ/rGO), better deformation recovery (2% permanent compression set with full recovery in less than 0.5 hours), and enhanced tensile strength (130%) and elongation at break (140%) compared to VMQ/rGO foams. These properties make FG-reinforced foams highly suitable for demanding high- and low-temperature applications.

dataset_item.question: How can reduced-order modeling improve the efficiency of Bayesian parameter inference for stochastic gene expression models?
dataset_item.answer: Reduced-order modeling enhances the efficiency of Bayesian parameter inference for stochastic gene expression models by simplifying computational complexity and accelerating the sampling process, while maintaining high accuracy in parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification. This is achieved through methods such as adaptive delayed acceptance Metropolis-Hastings (ADAMH) and hybrid extensions, which leverage adaptive tuning of proposal distributions and reduced-order approximations. These approaches reduce computational costs compared to traditional finite state projection (FSP) methods, enabling faster and more scalable inference from single-cell data, including smFISH, time-lapse microscopy, and single-cell sequencing. Numerical tests confirm that reduced-order models preserve precision while delivering substantial speedups, making them particularly effective for analyzing complex stochastic processes in single-cell gene expression studies.

This work extends the current methodology of analyzing CARS spectra by introducing Bayesian inference in the field, enabling uncertainty quantification of spectral features. The statistical inference model is able to produce posterior distributions for physically informative parameters, line shape amplitudes, widths, and locations, for each constituent line shape along with predictive distributions for the estimated resonant Raman signal contained in the CARS measurement spectrum, the error-corrected CARS measurements, and the CARS measurement spectrum, as well as extending currently existing methodology for modeling experimental artifacts present in CARS measurements. The applicability of the methods is demonstrated with experimental CARS spectra of sucrose, fructose, glucose, and adenosine phosphate.

This paper proposes a novel operating performance assessment method for multiphase batch processes based on GPR and Bayesian inference. To take the process dynamics and batch-to-batch uncertainty into account, GPR-based assessment models are established for different phases. Furthermore, from the viewpoint of data distribution, the local influences of production operation on the operating performance of the whole batch are described for each phase. Since the uneven-length characteristic embodies in phases across different batches, the online phase identification results can be a certain interval or a fuzzy interval between two adjacent phases. In the case of a certain interval, only the corresponding assessment model is invoked to evaluate the operating performance. In the case of a fuzzy interval, both of the assessment models corresponding to the adjacent phases are used. The assessment results are adaptively integrated with the Bayesian inference based posterior probabilities as the weights and used to evaluate the operating performance of the batch process, which is very challenging for traditional assessment methods. For the nonoptimal operating performance, the variable contributions are constructed and compared with the upper and lower confidence limits to determine whether it is responsible for the nonoptimality. A case study on the fed-batch penicillin fermentation process is used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. As seen from the simulation results, the proposed online assessment framework is able to give an efficient operating performance assessment for multiphase batch processes. dataset_item.question: How does the length of the alkyl tail on imidazolium cations influence density turnover and nanostructuring in ionic liquid and water binary mixtures?
dataset_item.answer:
The length of the alkyl tail on imidazolium cations plays a crucial role in determining density turnover and nanostructuring in ionic liquid (IL)/water binary mixtures. At lower water concentrations, density increases due to enhanced polar domain structuring involving cation headgroups, anions, and water molecules. This structuring peaks at a specific water mole fraction, which depends on the alkyl tail length. For shorter-tailed cations, such as ethyl-methyl imidazolium ([emim][Ac]), the density turnover occurs at a water mole fraction (Xw) of approximately 0.5, driven by maximal polar domain structuring. As water content increases, further disruption of hydrogen-bonded anion bridges causes density to decline.

For longer-tailed cations, such as butyl-methyl ([bmim][Ac]) and hexyl-methyl imidazolium ([hmim][Ac]), the density turnover is delayed to higher water mole fractions (Xw > 0.7). This delay is attributed to water-induced aggregation of hydrophobic alkyl tails, which enhances nanostructuring even as polar domain correlations weaken. The longer tails provide greater hydrophobicity, promoting tail aggregation and sustaining nanostructuring at higher water concentrations. Thus, alkyl tail length influences the water mole fraction at which density turnover occurs by modulating the balance between polar domain structuring and hydrophobic tail aggregation.

dataset_item.question: How does Fe3+ influence the oxidative dissolution kinetics of arsenopyrite under circumneutral pH conditions?
dataset_item.answer: Ferric iron (Fe³⁺) significantly enhances the oxidative dissolution kinetics of arsenopyrite under circumneutral pH conditions through three interrelated mechanisms: (1) promoting electron transfer from arsenopyrite to oxidants, which accelerates the oxidation process; (2) driving the formation of secondary iron-bearing minerals that modify surface reactivity and further influence dissolution dynamics; and (3) inducing phase transformations that facilitate the release and mobilization of arsenic. These processes collectively intensify arsenic mobilization in redox-dynamic environments, highlighting the critical role of Fe³⁺ in governing arsenopyrite dissolution under these conditions.

dataset_item.question: What are the roles of pore volume and intrinsic pore size in determining iodine adsorption performance in covalent organic frameworks?
dataset_item.answer: Iodine adsorption performance in covalent organic frameworks (COFs) is significantly influenced by both pore volume and intrinsic pore size, which must be carefully regulated to achieve optimal results. Larger pore volumes generally enhance iodine storage capacity, while the intrinsic pore size determines efficient diffusion and full accessibility for iodine molecules. These factors work synergistically—matching the pore size to the molecular dimensions of iodine ensures maximum adsorption efficiency. For example, a COF with a pore volume of 0.84 cm³ g⁻¹ and an intrinsic pore size of 4 nm achieved an impressive iodine uptake of 4.0 g g⁻¹ at 75 °C under ambient pressure. This underscores the importance of balanced design and simultaneous optimization of pore volume and pore size in COFs for high-performance iodine capture.

dataset_item.question: What mechanisms drive the formation of the glassy phase at approximately 1.3 GPa and the partial crystalline phase at higher pressures in 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium iodide?
dataset_item.answer: The formation of the glassy phase at approximately 1.3 GPa in 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium iodide ([C4mim][I]) is driven by pressure-induced structural disordering, where the liquid phase transitions into an amorphous state due to molecular rearrangements. At higher pressures, up to 16.7 GPa, partial crystallization occurs, facilitated by the conformational adaptability of the [C4mim]<sup>+</sup> cation, which modulates molecular packing and enables ordered arrangements. Above 12 GPa, reddish-brown precipitates, likely polyiodide species (I<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> or I<sub>2</sub>), emerge due to pressure-induced concentration effects. High-pressure Raman spectroscopy confirms these transitions, highlighting the interplay between cation conformation, molecular reorganization, and iodide precipitate formation. This sequence of phase transitions suggests potential applications in high-pressure synthesis and dye-sensitized solar cells.

The Tammann-Tait (TT), power-law density scaling (PLDS), and general density scaling (GDS) equations of state (EoS) significantly outperform the Dowson-Higginson (DH) and Zhu and Wen (ZW) equations in predicting lubricant density and volumetric properties across varying pressure and temperature conditions. Experimental data comparisons reveal that TT, PLDS, and GDS achieve average absolute deviations below 0.03%, showcasing exceptional accuracy compared to the higher deviations observed in DH (0.50%) and ZW (0.34%). 

In terms of isothermal compressibility (κₜ) and isobaric thermal expansivity (αₚ), TT, PLDS, and GDS exhibit deviations below 0.40% and 2.1%, respectively, while DH and ZW show much larger deviations ranging from 10% to 19%. These results highlight the limitations of DH and ZW in capturing critical volumetric properties under extreme conditions. Furthermore, TT, PLDS, and GDS demonstrate superior extrapolation capabilities at high pressures (up to 3000 MPa), where DH and ZW fail due to their asymptotic density constraints and simpler formulations.

The accuracy and robustness of TT, PLDS, and GDS make them more suitable for elastohydrodynamic lubrication (EHL) simulations, particularly in applications requiring reliable predictions under extreme pressure and temperature variations. In contrast, the DH and ZW equations are limited by their simplicity and are less effective for accurate modeling under such conditions.

### 1. **Summary of the Purpose of the Paper**
The paper investigates the accuracy and predictive capabilities of various equations of state (EoS) for characterizing elastohydrodynamic lubrication (EHL) contacts. Experimental data on viscosities, speeds of sound, and densities for six lubricants across a wide range of temperatures (278.15 to 398.15 K) and pressures (up to 120 MPa) are reported. The study evaluates the performance of different EoSs in describing experimental data and predicting volumetric properties, such as isothermal compressibility, under extreme pressures (up to 3000 MPa) relevant to EHL conditions. The findings highlight the limitations of widely used EoSs (Dowson-Higginson and Zhu and Wen equations) and propose alternatives that yield more realistic predictions of lubricant behavior under pressure.

---

### 2. **Classification of Purpose**
The purpose of the paper emphasizes **"<method>"**.  
While results are discussed, the core focus is on evaluating, comparing, and refining the predictive methods (EoSs) for characterizing lubricant behavior in EHL systems.

---

### 3. **Relevant Research Questions**
1. What experimental techniques are most effective for accurately measuring viscosities, speeds of sound, and densities of lubricants under varying temperature and pressure conditions?
2. How do different equations of state (EoS) compare in their ability to predict the volumetric properties of lubricants under high-pressure EHL conditions?
3. What are the physical implications of the asymptotic behavior observed in Dowson-Higginson and Zhu and Wen equations when density is plotted against pressure?
4. How can scaling-based EoSs be optimized or adapted to provide more accurate predictions of lubricant properties in extreme-pressure environments?
5. What are the critical volumetric properties (e.g., isothermal compressibility) that influence the performance of lubricants in EHL regimes, and how can these be reliably modeled?
6. What are the limitations of current numerical simulations of EHL lubrication, and how can improved EoSs enhance their accuracy?

inference_contexts: New experimental density data as a function of pressure and temperature were correlated with Tammann-Tait (TT), power-law density scaling (PLDS), and general density scaling (GDS) EoSs, being the average absolute deviations between experimental and correlated data lower than 0.03%. The Dowson-Higginson (DH), Zhu and Wen (ZH), and Jacobson-Vinet (JV) EoSs currently used in numerical simulations of the isothermal EHL lubrication regime predict these densities with high average deviations: 0.50%, 0.34%, and 0.74%, respectively. The sequence we have found at low pressures is the same for isothermal and for isentropic compressibility: PAO6 > G-III > gear oil > motor oil > G-I> G-V. At high pressures, G-V presents higher compressibilities than motor oil and G-I. PAO6 is also the most expansible oil in most experimental p-T conditions. Excellent agreement has been found between the isothermal compressibility and isobaric thermal expansivity, determined from PLDS and GDS EoSs and those values determined from Tammann-Tait equation. Thus, average absolute deviations lower than 0.40% and 2.1% have been found for κ T and α P , respectively. Nevertheless, the α P and κ T values obtained with DH and ZW EoSs present average deviations with those values obtained with the Tammann-Tait correlation, ranging from 17 to 19% and from 10 to 12% for α P and for κ T from 13 to 17% and from 11 to 15%. Due to the fact that the maximum contact pressure in EHL lubrication can reach values up to 3000 MPa, much higher than the pressure interval achieved with oscillating tube densimeters, we have also analyzed the extrapolation ability of five of the above equations. We can conclude that both DH and ZH models underestimates the compressibility at high pressures and temperatures higher than 313 K because of the asymptotic limited density value, whereas GDS EoS seems to provide better extrapolations. That means that DH and ZH equations are unable to perform a satisfactory prediction due to their simplicity. This paper shows the importance to properly take into account the oil compressibility on EHL simulations at very high pressures.

The DFT calculations employed the generalized gradient approximation in the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) flavor of the exchange-correlation functional, supplemented with Grimme's D2 dispersion correction. , All of the electrons, core and valence, were treated explicitly, with the Kohn-Sham orbitals expanded in a 6-31G* basis set. To check for pressure effects and box dilation, we also performed whole-box volume optimization for selected configurations, imposing a pressure of 1 bar. For the strict [BMIM] [I] form without added iodine (consisting of 832 atoms), the volume was 5.47% smaller than the experimental value, without any substantial change in the configuration. The importance of the dispersion correction can be judged by an overestimation of the volume by 16.7% when only PBE was used. A similar behavior of functionals for IL crystals had already been reported for a family of related systems. The volume underestimation of the dispersion-corrected PBE should be partially compensated by thermal expansion because experimental data corresponds to a temperature of 93 K, whereas calculations were performed at T = 0 K. When optimizing the volume with the inclusion of the iodine molecule, the volume increased by less than 2%. In any case, this cell relaxation did not change the configurations appreciably and left the I- I3 - arrangements practically intact. On the basis of this analysis, we are confident that the crystal-phase density is reasonable for the current purposes and not too different from that of the (viscous) liquid state of [BMIM] [I].

dataset_item.question: What are the limitations and challenges associated with using the kinetic method to estimate thermodynamic values for ion-bound dimers?
dataset_item.answer: The kinetic method (KM) for estimating thermodynamic values of ion-bound dimers has several limitations and challenges. One key issue is that the method assumes relative product intensities from dimer dissociation directly reflect thermodynamic differences, initially neglecting entropic effects. While extended KM approaches attempt to account for entropy, differences in reference system entropies are often still ignored, introducing inaccuracies. Another significant limitation is the ill-defined, non-Maxwellian temperature during evaluation, which contributes to uncertainties in the accuracy of the results. Additionally, the KM provides only relative thermodynamic values, making its reliability highly dependent on the accuracy of the reference data used for calibration. Errors in reference values can propagate into the results, and experimental uncertainties are often overlooked, potentially overstating the precision and reliability of the method. Despite these challenges, the KM remains a valuable tool for relative comparisons, especially in situations where more definitive thermodynamic data are unavailable.

A kinetic model has been developed for the acetic acid esterification with methanol catalyzed by the gel-type polystyrene-based resin Lewatit K1221. The thermodynamic activities appearing in the kinetic model have been determined in two ways and compared. Namely, a thermodynamic model based on the FH solution theory in which the selective sorption and swelling behavior of the resin is explicitly described, has been compared to the simple NRTL model in which equality between the thermodynamic activities in the bulk liquid and polymer liquid phases are implicitly assumed to be equal. Because in the latter model the phase partitioning is not taken into account, the polymer liquid-phase activities are systematically overestimated and, consequently, the pre-exponential factor of the kinetic rate coefficient and the adsorption coefficients are estimated at slightly lower values, albeit within the confidence intervals. Moreover, remarkably, the confidence intervals of the parameter estimates appear to be more narrow if the polymer liquid phase activities are explicitly accounted for. In general, it seems that for the development of a kinetic model to describe a single data set, that is, one resin catalyzing a reaction in a single solvent, both thermodynamic models perform similarly. Hence, one could argue that, for such case studies, the effort of the additional experimentation and analysis required to explicitly account for the phase equilibrium is not worth the benefit. However, if multiple data sets acquired using significantly different resin catalysts or in various solvents have to be reconciled employing a kinetic model, it is expected that the shortcomings of a simplified description of the thermodynamics using models, such as NRTL, will come to the surface. Moreover, when aiming at a more detailed understanding of the kinetics and an improved predictive capability of the model, it is worthwhile, if not to say recommended, to explore the phase equilibria in detail.

The method is versatile for testing the majority of bacterial pathogens and it does not require any special equipment. , Moreover, it is simple and practical and well-standardized. In conclusion, we unravelled and quantified the thermodynamic origin of the phase evolution of the hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite [CH3NH3] PbBr3 by combining high-resolution inelastic neutron scattering with ab initio lattice dynamics. The differences in enthalpy and configurational and vibrational entropy of the phases are all on the same order of magnitude, meaning that each of these factors is important in determining the stable structure as a function of temperature. These contributions are even more significant when one considers the decreased role of the Madelung energy in determining structure in halide perovskites, compared to oxides. We find that a complex interplay between entropy and hydrogen bonding interactions leads to the phase transitions as a function of temperature, a result that seems to be generally applicable for crystalline hybrid materials. These insights can now be used to understand behaviors in related materials and for the design of materials with tunable properties. For instance, it seems that by small substitutions of Pb2+ with Sn2+ or Ge2+, low-frequency modes related to the stereoactive lone pair can be directly manipulated. Likewise, lattice dynamics related to hydrogen bonding strength play an important role and can be manipulated by replacing [CH3NH3]+ with [(NH2)2CH]+. Such attempts, however, also go beyond these considerations; e.g.. the size of the cation must be considered, which in turn can have a significant impact on the crystal chemistry and the symmetry of the molecule can have an impact on configurational entropy. More generally, the methodology applied here demonstrates the power of ab initio lattice dynamics to provide predictions in excellent agreement with experiment. The combination of INS with ab initio calculations provides a blueprint of how to understand lattice vibrations and relate them to macroscopic properties in an accurate, quantitative way, not only in the context of hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites but also similarly for related hybrid materials. For instance, in flexible metal-organic frameworks, a balance between enthalpic dispersion forces and vibrational entropy exists; our methodology paves the way for understanding these on a microscopic level and in turn facilitates the targeted design of such effects.

dataset_item.question: How do variations in current density influence the generation of hydrogen peroxide and the subsequent degradation of trace organic contaminants?
dataset_item.answer:
Variations in current density significantly influence the generation of hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) and the subsequent degradation of trace organic contaminants in advanced oxidation processes. Experiments conducted with cathodic current densities ranging from 0 to 30 A m⁻² demonstrated that higher current densities enhance H₂O₂ production, which directly improves contaminant degradation efficiency. The applied charge density (ρₚ), calculated based on current density, electrode area, and hydraulic residence time, plays a critical role in determining the system's oxidative performance. Testing under varying hydraulic residence times (1.5–5.0 minutes) and flow rates (35–120 L d⁻¹) revealed consistent H₂O₂ generation and effective degradation of trace organic contaminants initially amended at concentrations of 10 μg L⁻¹.

Notably, H₂O₂ production remained stable even under oxygen-depleted conditions (e.g., N₂-sparged water), indicating that dissolved oxygen concentration did not limit performance. Long-term testing at an intermediate current density of 15 A m⁻² confirmed the scalability and reliability of this electrochemical method for water treatment. The integration of H₂O₂ generation with a UV reactor further enhanced contaminant degradation across various water matrices, showcasing the system's versatility and potential for real-world applications.

dataset_item.question: How does the geometric descriptor eta improve the characterization of ion-water pair interaction energies in bromide hydration?
dataset_item.answer: The geometric descriptor η enhances the characterization of ion-water pair interaction energies in bromide hydration by providing a precise and continuous measure of the linear interaction between bromide ions and water molecules. Unlike traditional radial distribution models that rely on arbitrary geometric cutoffs, η integrates multiple geometric parameters, including lone pair arrangements, into a single function. This approach enables a nuanced distinction between tightly bound (strongly interacting) and loosely bound (weakly interacting) water molecules within the bromide’s first hydration shell. Ab initio calculations demonstrate a strong correlation between η and ion-water interaction energies, making it a reliable indicator of hydrogen bond formation and solvation dynamics. Furthermore, η reveals a tetrahedral hydration geometry for bromide, resolving ambiguities in previous experimental and computational studies while offering deeper insights into hydration structure and energetics.

### 1. Purpose of the Paper:
The paper aims to provide a refined understanding of bromide hydration in aqueous solution by unveiling a tetrahedral hydration structure using ab initio molecular dynamics. The study introduces a new geometric descriptor to characterize ion-water interactions, allowing for a more nuanced division of the first hydration shell into tight and loose subregions. This approach enhances the understanding of the role of lone pairs and hydrogen bonding in the solvation of weakly hydrated anions, improving upon previous radial models.

### 2. Classification of Purpose:

- How does the newly proposed geometric descriptor improve the characterization of ion-water pair interaction energies compared to traditional radial models?
- What implications does the tight versus loose first hydration shell distinction have for understanding solvation processes in highly disordered systems?

inference_contexts: Finally, in this work we introduced a geometrical descriptor, η, that can effectively describe a linear interaction between two species. Ab initio calculations have proven a neat correlation between ion-water pair interactions energies and the η descriptor. Furthermore, it has been shown that η is able to distinguish which water molecules form strong interactions with the bromide ion, and which do not. Beside the capability to discern between tight and loose water molecules, we believe that η can be used to determine the presence of an hydrogen bond between two species. It is known that the hydrogen bond energy is not a physical observable and hence can only be estimated and not measured. A huge effort has been made in the literature to develop hydrogen bond definitions based on energetic, geometric or wave function approaches. - The simplest approach to identify hydrogen bonds from MD trajectories or Monte Carlo simulations is the use of geometrical criteria. However, any of these criteria will have some arbitrariness and will be approximate. A complete geometrical description of the configuration taken by two hydrogen bonded species would require several parameters (e.g.. six parameters of the water dimer). For the sake of simplicity, only a subset of these parameters is usually chosen to define an hydrogen bond, and hence it is important to select the most significant ones. The significativity of the three geometric parameters chosen in this work (r LP-H, α, and β) is testified by the strong correlations between them that have been found. Furthermore, the use of sharp cutoffs on several geometric parameters can be a crude approximation in the description of properties that are instead continuous. A more desirable approach is the application of a cutoff on a function depending on all of the geometric parameters, as this would be a continuous extension of multiple cutoffs. In this framework, η has shown the further quality of having a strong correlation with the ion-water pair interaction energy, which is the most relevant quantity in defining an interaction. Thus, we suggest that the η function is a valid descriptor for the purpose of determining whether two species are hydrogen bonded or not.

The excess partial molar energy of ion in water was analyzed through spatial decomposition. This thermodynamic quantity describes an overall response of the energetics upon insertion of the solute and is formulated as an integral over the whole space of local quantities representing the solute-solvent (ion-water) and solvent-solvent (water-water) interactions. The averaged interactions of a water molecule with the ion and with the other water molecules were then computed as functions of the distance from the ion, and it was observed that the ion-water interaction is favorable (negative) over the whole distance and that the water-water interaction is unfavorable (positive) relative to the interaction in the bulk. Actually, when the water molecule is located beyond the contact distance with solute, the variations of the ion-water and water-water interactions with the ion-water distance were found to compensate against each other; the solute's influence on the total interaction of a water molecule is short-ranged due to the compensation.

Bearing in mind the results presented, we come to several important conclusions in the topic of halide hydration. The first result is that the bromide ion has a tetrahedral solvation geometry in aqueous solution. Although bromide aqueous solutions are indeed disordered systems, they are not as disordered as depicted thus far. They do possess a tight first hydration shell, forming a short-lived complex with a defined tetrahedral geometry, composed by water molecules strongly interacting with the ion via hydrogen bonds. The remaining water molecules contributing to the g(r) first peaks (loose hydration shell) are unstructured water molecules penetrating into the first shell region from the bulk, and they are only mildly perturbed by the electrostatic charge of the ion. dataset_item.question: How do environmental conditions, such as relative humidity, influence the scattering properties of secondary organic aerosol derived from cis-3-hexenol?
dataset_item.answer: Relative humidity (RH) plays a crucial role in influencing the scattering properties of secondary organic aerosol (SOA) derived from cis-3-hexenol (HXL). Experimental investigations conducted at varying RH levels, specifically 10% and 70%, demonstrated that increasing RH enhances light scattering by the SOA particles. This enhancement is quantified using the scattering enhancement coefficient \( f(RH) \), which is calculated by comparing the mass scattering coefficient (MSC) at elevated RH to that under dry conditions (10% RH). The transition from dry to humid conditions resulted in a measurable increase in MSC, indicating that water uptake by the particles amplifies their scattering efficiency due to increased hygroscopicity. These findings highlight the critical role of environmental humidity in modulating the optical properties and radiative impact of HXL-derived SOA. Notably, this effect was specific to HXL-derived SOA and was not observed for SOA derived from cis-3-hexenyl acetate (CHA), which was only tested under dry conditions. Overall, changes in RH significantly alter the scattering behavior of HXL-derived SOA, underscoring the importance of considering environmental conditions in studies of aerosol optical properties.

dataset_item.question: How can the Kriging model predict values of an unknown function based on sampled points?
dataset_item.answer:
The Kriging model predicts values of an unknown function by representing it as the sum of a global trend (μ(x)) and a local deviation (ε(x)). The global trend captures the overall behavior of the function, while the local deviation models spatial correlations between sampled points.

The prediction at an unknown point \( y(x) \) is computed using the formula:
\[
y(x) = \mu(x) + r^T R^{-1} (F - \mu),
\]
where:
- \( \mu(x) \): The global trend of the function.
- \( r \): The correlation vector between the target point \( x \) and sampled points.
- \( R \): The correlation matrix of sampled points, which quantifies spatial relationships.
- \( F \): The vector of sampled function values.

Correlations between points are modeled using a Gaussian random function, where the strength of correlation decreases with distance. Typically, an exponential decay function or other correlation functions (e.g., squared exponential) are used, governed by a distance-based parameter \( \theta \).

The model parameters (\( \theta \), \( \sigma^2 \), \( \mu \)) are optimized using techniques such as maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to ensure accurate predictions. Optimization algorithms, like gradient-based methods or evolutionary algorithms (e.g., NSGA-II), are often employed for this purpose.

In addition to providing predictions, the Kriging model quantifies uncertainty at the target point using the mean square error \( s^2(x) \). This uncertainty depends on the spatial distribution of sampled points and their correlation strength, offering insights into the reliability of the prediction.

Thus, the Kriging model achieves high predictive accuracy by leveraging both global trends and localized deviations, with correlations between sampled points playing a central role in determining the weights for interpolation.

dataset_item.question: How can deep learning techniques be adapted to handle limited or noisy molecular datasets in drug discovery?
dataset_item.answer: Deep learning techniques can be adapted to handle limited or noisy molecular datasets in drug discovery by employing a multifaceted approach that combines improved data curation, collaboration with experimentalists, and leveraging advanced AI-driven methods. Robust data curation strategies are essential to filter unreliable data, detect errors, and ensure consistency across both publicly available databases such as PubChem and ChEMBL, as well as proprietary datasets. Collaborative efforts between model developers and experimentalists can enhance the quality of data generation and archiving practices, fostering a more standardized and reliable foundation for predictive modeling. Additionally, automated error detection and exclusion systems, powered by AI, can further mitigate the impact of noisy or inconsistent data. While deep learning holds great promise in addressing challenges like multi-parameter optimization, it should be viewed as a valuable tool that complements traditional methods, rather than a standalone solution. As the field evolves, ongoing refinement of data practices and modeling techniques will be key to maximizing the potential of deep learning in drug discovery.

dataset_item.question: How does substituting alkyl side chains with alkylthio side chains affect π-π stacking distance and intermolecular interactions in donor molecules?
dataset_item.answer: Substituting alkyl side chains with alkylthio side chains in donor molecules slightly decreases intermolecular interactions and increases the π-π stacking distance. This effect is attributed to a larger dihedral angle between the thieno[3,2-b]thiophene (TT) and benzo[1,2-b:4,5-b′]dithiophene (BDT) units in the alkylthio-substituted molecules. The increased dihedral angle reduces molecular packing efficiency, weakening intermolecular interactions and leading to less optimal π-π stacking. Consequently, alkylthio-substituted molecules exhibit slightly poorer absorption and device performance compared to their alkyl-substituted counterparts, despite maintaining high power conversion efficiencies (>8%) and fill factors (>0.70). These findings underscore the delicate balance required in side-chain modifications to optimize intermolecular interactions, molecular packing, and photovoltaic performance.

dataset_item.question: How can oxidation-reduction potential measurements determine the end point of enzymatic oxidation reactions catalyzed by horseradish peroxidase for orange II?
dataset_item.answer: Oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) measurements provide an accurate and real-time method to determine the end point of enzymatic oxidation reactions catalyzed by horseradish peroxidase (HRP) for Orange II (OII). During fed-batch reactions, the ORP signal reaches a maximum value, corresponding to the critical time (t<sub>C</sub>) when decolorization is complete and substrate oxidation ceases. This critical point is further validated by the first derivative of ORP over time, which identifies t<sub>C</sub> with high precision. Continuous ORP monitoring offers a more reliable and consistent endpoint determination compared to absorbance measurements, which are intermittent and less sensitive to real-time changes. The approach has been experimentally verified with OII and extended to other substrates, such as phenol and bisphenol A, demonstrating broader applicability.

dataset_item.question: How does concentration affect the optical density and path length used in spectroscopic measurements of methylene blue monomers and dimers?
dataset_item.answer: In spectroscopic measurements of methylene blue (MB) monomers and dimers, concentration plays a critical role in determining the optical density (OD) and path length to ensure accurate data without artifacts or distortions. For monomer-dominant samples (~2 × 10⁻⁵ M), a 1 mm path length cuvette yields an OD of approximately 0.15, which is suitable for reliable analysis. For dimer-dominant samples (~7 × 10⁻⁴ M), the higher concentration requires a reduced path length of 0.1 mm to achieve an OD in the range of 0.25–0.29, minimizing signal distortion and inner filter effects. Additionally, fluorescence measurements necessitate maintaining OD ≤ 0.05 when using a standard 1 cm cuvette to prevent inner filter effects and ensure accurate fluorescence readings. These adjustments in path length and OD thresholds across varying concentrations ensure optimal spectroscopic measurements for both monomers and dimers.

dataset_item.question: What molecular mechanisms contribute to the reduction of friction on superhydrophilic surfaces with specific charge patterns?
dataset_item.answer:
The reduction of friction on superhydrophilic surfaces with specific charge patterns arises from the formation of an ordered water monolayer at the interface. This structured water layer is induced by strategic charge patterning, which aligns water molecules into an organized configuration. The ordered monolayer exhibits a low friction coefficient with the bulk water above it, significantly reducing the overall surface friction. The mechanism involves two key contributions: the friction coefficient between the surface and the first water layer (λsolid/liquid), and the friction coefficient between the ordered monolayer and the subsequent water layers (λ1,2). 

Experimental observations on materials such as TiO2, sapphire, and mica confirm the presence of such ordered water structures, demonstrating the versatility of this mechanism. Importantly, superhydrophilic surfaces achieve friction levels comparable to hydrophobic surfaces while maintaining biocompatibility, as evidenced in applications like TiO2-coated intravascular stents. These findings challenge the conventional assumption that hydrophilic surfaces inherently exhibit high friction and highlight the potential for manipulating interfacial water structure to optimize frictional properties across diverse applications.

### 1. **Summary of the Purpose**  
The purpose of this paper is to investigate and demonstrate, through molecular dynamics simulations, how superhydrophilic surfaces with specific charge patterns can achieve reduced friction comparable to hydrophobic surfaces. This is particularly significant for applications in biomedical and engineering fields, such as intravascular stent coatings, where low friction and superhydrophilic properties are critical for nonfouling and biocompatibility. The study identifies the formation of an ordered water monolayer on superhydrophilic surfaces with appropriate charge patterns as the key mechanism behind the observed friction reduction.

This friction reduction is attributed to the existence of the ordered water structures on the superhydrophilic surface with appropriate charge patterns, and the friction between this ordered water monolayer and the water molecules above is small. We also highlight the importance of combining the friction coefficient λsolid/liquid between the surface and the first water layer and the friction coefficient λ1,2 between the first water layer and the water layers above, which jointly determine the surface friction coefficient λsurface. This highlights the role of water molecules themselves, which are usually neglected, in determining the solid/water interfacial frictions. Our work provides a new way to reduce surface friction by introducing ordered water on the superhydrophilic surfaces. In practice, room temperature ordered water exists on a variety of materials surfaces, including the sapphire, titania (TiO2), talc, hydroxylated SiO2 and Al2O3, the Pt(100), and mica. We believe that the results in this study will prompt more extensively experiments and may be of great help for designing superhydrophilic materials requiring low surface friction and other possible engineering fields. Very recently, it has been also found that the similar phenomenon of "ordered water that does not completely wet water" exists on the TiO2 surface at room temperature, which may indicate that the friction reduction on the superhydrophilic surface indeed exists but is still unrevealed before.

dataset_item.question: What methodologies were used to measure emissions from Euro 6 diesel and gasoline vehicles under various driving cycles?
dataset_item.answer: Emissions from Euro 6 diesel and gasoline vehicles were measured using a chassis dynamometer at the Transport and Environment Laboratory of the French Institute of Science and Technology for Transport, Development, and Networks (IFSTTAR). Exhaust gases were collected at the tailpipe outlet and diluted with filtered air using a constant volume sampler (CVS). Pollutants were analyzed using online gas and particulate analyzers for real-time measurements, along with offline analysis through filters and cartridges for additional insights. Testing was conducted over five driving cycles—NEDC, WLTC, Artemis urban, road, and motorway—to simulate diverse real-world driving conditions. To ensure reliability, each driving cycle was repeated two to six times, except for NEDC, which was measured only once per vehicle. Standardized commercial low-sulfur fuels (EN 590 for diesel, EN 228 for gasoline) with sulfur content below 10 ppm were used to minimize variability due to fuel composition.

dataset_item.question: How do variations in pH and ionic composition of solutions affect the mobility of biflagellate and encysted zoospores in porous media?
dataset_item.answer:
Variations in pH and ionic composition of solutions significantly influence the mobility of *Phytophthora capsici* zoospores in porous media by modifying physicochemical interactions such as electrostatic attraction, electrical double layer compression, and adhesion to surfaces. Experiments using saturated sand columns demonstrated that biflagellate zoospores exhibit higher mobility compared to encysted zoospores, with transport being notably affected by solution pH, cation type, ionic strength, and the presence of iron oxide coatings on sand grains.  

At pH 4.0, zoospore retention is enhanced compared to neutral pH (7.7), likely due to increased electrostatic attraction between the zoospores and iron-oxide-coated sand (IOCS). Divalent cations (Ca²⁺ in CaCl₂ solutions) further reduce mobility by compressing electrical double layers, promoting adhesion to sand surfaces. In contrast, NaCl solutions exhibit lower retention due to weaker ionic interactions. Breakthrough curve data reveal reduced effluent recovery at low pH and high ionic strength, corroborated by SEM analysis, which shows greater zoospore attachment under these conditions.  

Additionally, grain size and iron oxide coatings influence zoospore transport, with finer, iron-oxide-coated sand retaining more zoospores due to increased surface area and enhanced electrostatic interactions. Encysted zoospores, due to their altered surface properties, are more susceptible to deposition and retention compared to biflagellate zoospores under these conditions.  

Overall, solution pH, ionic composition, and porous media characteristics collectively determine the deposition rate coefficient, retention efficiency, and mobility of zoospores in porous media.

dataset_item.question: How can mixed integer nonlinear programming models be implemented to optimize biomass-to-liquid production processes?
dataset_item.answer:
Mixed integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) models optimize biomass-to-liquid (BtL) production processes by formulating a superstructure framework that represents interconnected processing blocks for thermochemical conversion, upgrading, and separation. Input specifications—including feedstocks, intermediate components, catalyst ratios, cost parameters, and technology constraints—are derived from literature and rigorous simulations and encoded in matrix form. Mass balance equations, thermodynamic relationships, and binary and fractional variables define the existence of unit operations and enable flexible process integration scenarios.

The MINLP algorithm is implemented using advanced computational platforms, such as GAMS, to efficiently solve the optimization problem. Economic calculations encompass capital costs, operating labor costs, energy consumption, waste disposal, and raw material expenses, with the objective function minimizing the total cost of manufacturing (TCOM) while maximizing productivity. Product profile constraints ensure adherence to quality and composition standards, while the superstructure enables simultaneous optimization of multiple process flowsheets, outperforming conventional single-process methods.

Once optimal solutions are identified, they undergo rigorous validation through detailed simulations to verify performance metrics, including TCOM, product profiles, and productivity. This approach provides a systematic and robust framework for identifying cost-effective and high-performing BtL production pathways under given technical and economic constraints.

dataset_item.question: How does the SiO2 to Al2O3 ratio in ZSM-5 influence the catalytic oxidation activity and nitrogen gas selectivity of CuO on ZSM-5 catalysts?
dataset_item.answer: Lowering the SiO₂/Al₂O₃ ratio in ZSM-5 significantly enhances the catalytic oxidation activity and nitrogen gas (N₂) selectivity of CuO/ZSM-5 catalysts during diethylamine oxidation. Specifically, reducing the ratio from 360 to 18 increases surface acidity and improves the dispersion of CuO species, leading to a synergistic interaction between highly dispersed CuO and acidic sites. This interaction promotes diethylamine activation and selective N₂ formation, resulting in improved catalytic efficiency. The 6CuO/ZSM-5-18 catalyst demonstrates superior performance, achieving the widest temperature window (160 °C) for high N₂ selectivity. The enhanced catalytic activity and selectivity are attributed to increased surface acidity and the cooperative catalysis between the CuO active species and acid sites, as evidenced by a greater low-temperature reduction peak area and optimized oxidation dynamics.

dataset_item.question: How does using N,N-dimethyl formamide in the aqueous phase and triphenyl phosphate in the organic phase during interfacial polymerization affect water flux and the polyamide layer morphology in thin-film composite forward osmosis membranes?
dataset_item.answer: The use of N,N-dimethyl formamide (DMF) in the aqueous phase and triphenyl phosphate (TPP) in the organic phase during interfacial polymerization significantly enhances the performance of thin-film composite forward osmosis (TFC-FO) membranes. Specifically, incorporating 10 wt/v% DMF and 0.25 wt/v% TPP leads to a substantial increase in water flux, achieving 21.2 LMH in FO mode and 44.1 LMH in PRO mode at 25 °C using a 2 M sodium chloride draw solution—nearly double that of membranes prepared without cosolvents. This dual-cosolvent strategy promotes increased polyamide (PA) polymer formation, resulting in a thicker, multilayered PA structure with a complex morphology. The enhanced PA layer provides improved water transport properties while maintaining selectivity, contributing to superior membrane performance in forward osmosis applications.

dataset_item.question: What are the correlations between resistance to triclosan or benzalkonium chloride and clinically relevant antibiotics?
dataset_item.answer:
Resistance to triclosan (TCS) and benzalkonium chloride (BC) demonstrates significant positive correlations with resistance to clinically relevant antibiotics, raising concerns about potential cross-resistance and multidrug resistance (MDR) development. Positive correlations were observed between TCS and BC resistance and antibiotics such as nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim, ampicillin, chloramphenicol, azithromycin, and amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. Specifically, TCS-resistant isolates showed nearly universal resistance to ampicillin, along with strong correlations to nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim, and chloramphenicol. BC resistance was more strongly associated with azithromycin and amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. These findings suggest potential overlapping resistance mechanisms or colocation of resistance genes, such as on plasmids.

Additionally, a significant negative correlation was identified between tetracycline and colistin resistance. Restricting the analysis to TCS-resistant isolates yielded similar patterns, underscoring the robustness of the observed correlations. The findings emphasize the potential role of antiseptic overuse in driving MDR in bacterial populations and highlight the need for further research to elucidate underlying mechanisms.

dataset_item.question: Why is electronic conductance in AB-stacked bilayer graphene insensitive to the position of monolayer nanoribbon leads?
dataset_item.answer: The electronic conductance in AB-stacked bilayer graphene is insensitive to the position of monolayer nanoribbon leads due to the spatial localization of low-energy edge states (E < 0.3 eV). These edge states, which arise from the moiré pattern at the flake edges, are confined to AB-stacked regions far from the boundaries of the flake and the nanoribbon lead contacts. As a result, the conductance in the low-energy regime is dominated by these localized states and remains largely unaffected by the configuration or position of the leads. In contrast, at higher energies (E > 0.3 eV), delocalized states contribute to transport, leading to conductance that is more sensitive to the lead positions. Thus, the interplay between the spatial localization of edge states and the energy-dependent transport behavior explains the insensitivity of conductance to lead placement in the low-energy regime.

dataset_item.question: What mechanism enables TPEPA to emit strong far-red or near-infrared fluorescence in aqueous media?
dataset_item.answer: TPEPA emits strong far-red or near-infrared fluorescence in aqueous media due to the restriction of its intramolecular motion following a bio-orthogonal click reaction with azide-labeled bacterial surface markers (e.g., Kdo-N3 for Gram-negative and d-Ala-N3 for Gram-positive bacteria). This reaction locks the molecular structure, suppressing non-radiative decay pathways and significantly enhancing fluorescence emission. Additionally, TPEPA generates singlet oxygen under light irradiation, providing dual functionality as a selective imaging probe and a phototherapeutic agent for targeted bacterial ablation. Its high biocompatibility, rapid response, and ability to selectively bind bacterial markers make it suitable for clinical diagnosis and treatment of bacterial infections.

dataset_item.question: How can heterodimeric coiled coil cross-linking mechanisms be used to design protein-based hydrogels with tunable dynamic properties and multiple energy dissipation modes?
dataset_item.answer: Heterodimeric coiled coil cross-linking mechanisms, such as CCE/CCK complexes, offer a powerful strategy for designing protein-based hydrogels with tunable dynamic properties and multiple energy dissipation modes. These mechanisms leverage the temperature-dependent association and dissociation of CCE/CCK complexes, allowing the hydrogel to exhibit broad and dual dissipation modes. Dynamic properties can be further tailored by adjusting protein concentration and stoichiometric ratios of CCE- and CCK-containing elastomeric proteins, enabling precise control over the hydrogel's mechanical response. Additionally, these hydrogels feature shear-thinning behavior and rapid self-healing due to the fast kinetics of the cross-linkers, making them ideal for applications such as injectable biomaterials. The combination of tunable network structures, dynamic mechanical properties, and versatile energy dissipation modes establishes a robust framework for designing advanced hydrogels with tailored functionality for biomedical and other specialized applications.

The engineered Vn-(GR)4 protein polymers showed much improved solubility in aqueous media over Vn-ELP polymers and displayed temperature-dependent micellization. The Young's modulus and swelling ratio of the resultant hydrogels showed temperature-dependent changes, which are resulting from the temperature-dependent aggregation of the Vn-ELP side chains in the hydrogel network. The biomaterials possess extremely high stretchability and their breaking strain can reach 1200%. During the stretching-contraction process, the covalently cross-linked polyprotein framework is able to stabilize the hydrogel system, whereas noncovalent interactions enable BSA protein sliding along the alginate chains to achieve high elasticity, accompanied by reversible protein unfolding and refolding. Furthermore, the macroscopic expansion-contraction phenomenon of the hydrogels may help to improve our understanding of the muscle movement, where the dynamic process can be well controlled and directly visualized. Notably, the addition of Ca2+ plays a pivotal role in triggering the contraction process, which is similar to that in natural muscles. Therefore, the protein-based hydrogels have unique advantages of both the structure and function in mimicking natural muscles: polyprotein frameworks can act as the elastic spring titin via protein folding-unfolding and also achieve tunable sliding facilitated by alginate due to their reversible noncovalent interactions resembling the sliding of myofilaments, whereas the folding-unfolding-induced conformational change of protein and Ca2+ regulation can function as natural systems to guarantee the whole movement behavior. In addition to superior stiffness, stretchability, and recoverability, excellent biocompatibility endows the hydrogels with promising applications in bionanomaterials and tissue engineering.

For biomedical applications, the use of in situ forming hydrogels is preferred over preformed hydrogels since there is no need for surgical interventions as gelation can take place under physiological conditions upon injection. Furthermore, the initial fluidic nature of the precursor solution ensures proper shape adaptation and biological components can be incorporated in the hydrogel by simple mixing with the precursor polymer solution. , Physical cross-links, such as hydrophobic or ionic interactions, can be formed in situ under mild conditions, but the resulting hydrogels generally degrade or dissolve rapidly. Injectable chemically cross-linked hydrogels have been frequently prepared by photocuring polymers functionalized with vinylic groups. Although the presence of photoinitiators and the generated radicals in the polymerization process has been associated with cytotoxicity, frequently good cell compatibility is found for cells encapsulated in this type of hydrogel. , However, important drawbacks of photo-cross-linkable systems include the limited penetration depth of UV radiation and its potentially damaging effects on living tissue. In situ forming hydrogels utilizing covalent cross-linking between polymers with complementary functional groups therefore received much attention in the last two decades. Early examples of chemical cross-linking reactions forming hydrogels include Schiff base formation between aldehydes and amines and the Passerini and Ugi condensation. However, remaining functional groups on polymers may react with functional groups present in biomolecules such as proteins, limiting the application of these hydrogels as in situ forming delivery systems. In this regard, the use of chemoselective, bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies, which do not interfere with biochemical processes or biomolecules, are very appealing. The most investigated chemoselective cross-linking reaction for hydrogels is the Cu (I)-catalyzed Huisgen 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition of terminal alkynes and azides, commonly known as click chemistry. This term was originally coined in 2001 by Sharpless et al. for a number of new regiospecific linking reactions that give high yields and generally require no purification. The first hydrogel cross-linked via click chemistry was described by the group of Hilborn and was based on PVA. Although this category of hydrogels has been mainly used for tissue engineering applications, they have also been applied for the controlled release of therapeutics and different biomolecules, including doxorubicin bovine serum albumin (BSA) and pDNA. Because "classical" alkyne-azide cycloadditions require the use of a copper catalyst, which may cause adverse effects in biomedical applications, the use of strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) is attracting increasing interest. This reaction employs the inherent ring strain of cyclooctyne groups to achieve fast and efficient cross-linking without the need for catalysts or external stimuli such as UV light. dataset_item.question: How does spin polarization influence calculations of magnetic properties of metals in density functional theory simulations?
dataset_item.answer: Spin polarization plays a crucial role in accurately calculating the magnetic properties of metals in density functional theory (DFT) simulations. By explicitly accounting for the electronic spin states, spin polarization enables the representation of exchange interactions between unpaired electrons, which are essential for describing magnetic moments, magnetization, and exchange coupling. Incorporating spin polarization in DFT calculations, typically using functionals like GGA-PBE, refines predictions of electronic structure and energetics in magnetic metals. Advanced computational setups, such as those involving the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) with projector augmented wave potentials, ensure precision through high energy cutoffs, dense Brillouin zone sampling, and strict convergence criteria for electronic and ionic relaxations. This approach provides a robust framework for understanding and predicting the magnetic behavior of metallic systems.

dataset_item.question: How do rainfall patterns and seasonal variability influence mercury deposition in tropical forests?
dataset_item.answer:
Rainfall patterns and seasonal variability play a critical role in mercury (Hg) deposition in tropical forests, primarily through precipitation volume and atmospheric scavenging dynamics. In the Luquillo Mountains of Puerto Rico, annual wet mercury deposition ranged from 26.4–29.5 μg m⁻², significantly exceeding U.S. monitoring sites due to high annual rainfall (2732–2978 mm) and moderate mercury concentrations in precipitation (8.9–10.8 ng L⁻¹). Seasonal variability revealed peak mercury deposition during summer, driven by tropical waves and convective storms, which produce elevated rainfall and higher mercury concentrations. Conversely, the winter dry season (December–May), dominated by trade-wind orographic precipitation, exhibited lower mercury concentrations and minimal deposition. 

Atmospheric processes such as cloud scavenging of gaseous oxidized mercury (GOM) and particulate-bound mercury play a pivotal role, especially during summer when easterly air masses gain elevation, enhancing mercury deposition through convective rainfall. Despite low measured GOM concentrations (<10 pg m⁻³), tropical forests function as mercury deposition hotspots due to the interplay of high rainfall and atmospheric dynamics. Rainfall measurements, potentially underestimated by up to 40% due to windy conditions, suggest actual mercury fluxes may be higher. Minimal rainout effects (decreasing mercury concentration with increasing rainfall) were observed, indicating that precipitation-driven scavenging processes are a dominant factor in mercury deposition rather than elevated atmospheric mercury concentrations.

dataset_item.question: Which sampling method demonstrates the highest efficiency in collecting reactive gaseous mercury under varying humidity conditions?
dataset_item.answer: The KCl-coated denuder sampling method demonstrates the highest efficiency in collecting reactive gaseous mercury (RGM) under varying humidity conditions. Laboratory and field experiments consistently show that the KCl-coated denuder outperforms alternative methods such as cation-exchange membranes, nylon membranes, mist chambers, activated carbon traps, and solid-phase amalgamation techniques. This method exhibits superior collection efficiency across a wide range of humidity levels, minimizing measurement artifacts and ensuring accurate quantification of RGM. Its consistent performance and reliability make it the preferred choice for atmospheric studies, supporting its adoption as a standardized approach for RGM measurement.

dataset_item.question: Which density functional exchange-correlation functionals exhibit the highest accuracy for transition metal reaction barrier heights based on evaluations against benchmark energies?
dataset_item.answer: The density functional exchange-correlation functionals ωB97M-V, ωB97X-V, and SCAN0 exhibit the highest accuracy for transition metal reaction barrier heights based on evaluations against benchmark DLPNO-CCSD(T)/CBSW1 energies in the MOBH35 database. These functionals demonstrate minimal deviation from benchmark values and achieve accuracy comparable to high-level coupled-cluster methods for transition metal systems. While double-hybrid functionals such as B2K-PLYP and revDOD-PBEP86-D4 offer slightly improved accuracy, their substantially higher computational cost makes them less practical for routine applications. Overall, ωB97M-V, ωB97X-V, and SCAN0 provide an optimal balance between accuracy and computational efficiency for modeling transition metal reaction barriers.
