Alternatively, one could calculate energies using either the B2K-PLYP or revDOD-PBEP86-D4 double hybrid functional, whose slightly improved accuracy is counterbalanced by their significantly increased computational cost. It is interesting to note that these functionals have similar accuracies for the MOBH35 database as coupled-cluster methods. The use of the results presented here should be beneficial to any future mechanistic studies involving transition metal complexes.

Overall, the SCAN-D2 and MS-D2 functionals are as good as the hybrid B3LYP functional for reasonably predicting an energy trend of the CH4 activation over the [FeO]2+-MFI. In contrast, the TPSS-D2, RTPSS-D2, and MS-D2 functionals are best for treating the CH4 activation over the [Cu2(μ-O)]2+-MFI and [Cu3(μ-O)3]2+-MOR, as they predict an activation barrier consistent with the experimental value and an energy trend consistent with the logic of reaction mechanisms described above.

To summarize, with the 6-31+G (2d,2p) basis sets, BLYP-D3-DCP generally outperforms B3LYP-D3 in the prediction of binding energies of noncovalently bonded complexes and in the prediction of bond dissociation enthalpies for simple organic systems. With respect to the prediction of barrier heights for pericyclic and Diels-Alder reactions, BLYP-D3-DCP displays more uniform performance than does B3LYP-D3 but does not always outperform it: B3LYP-D3 displays better performance than BLYP-D3-DCP for the BSR36 and RSE43 databases. Collectively, these results suggest that BLYP-D3-DCP has some promise to perform at a level that is superior to an unadorned GGA functional. We remind the reader that entries in the GMTKN30 subdatabased that are listed in Table were not part of the fitting set for the DCPs presented herein. It is likely that inclusion of barrier heights and other data into the DCP fitting would improve their performance more generally; however, the outcome of such an effort depends strongly on the underlying performance of the density-functional method. It is clear from the data presented herein that corrections to DFT-based methods, whether they be D3 or DCP corrections, tend to act in the same direction. For example, the D3 corrections will always increase BEs and BDEs and reduce barrier heights for reasons described above. Therefore, we suggest that the D3 and DCP corrections may be most effective if combined with a DFT method that behaves in a consistent manner with respect to all binding properties of interest (e.g.. consistently underbinding). At this time we are not aware of a DFT-based method that display consistent behavior in this connection.

Can DCPs elevate the performance of BLYP to that of B3LYP? This is a question that was posed in the Introduction. As computational chemistry methods are applied to increasingly larger systems, the question of their efficiency-in particular, with respect to run time-becomes critical. Formally, GGA functionals like BLYP scale as N 3 with system size (with N being the number of electrons), whereas hybrid functionals scale with N 4. Therefore, low-cost corrections such as D3 and DCP that may elevate the performance of BLYP to that of B3LYP or better may be of value. To examine this possibility, we present in Table a summary of some of the performance statistics for BLYP-D3-DCP/6-31+G (2d,2p) for the benchmark sets described above and compare these to statistics obtained using B3LYP-D3/6-31+G (2d,2p). We also conducted additional performance assessments of the two methods on the BHPERI, DARC, BSR36, and the RSE43 databases. We use D3 corrections with B3LYP for our comparison because D3 has a computational cost that is negligible relative to that of the underlying DFT method and because D3 corrections (or similar) are required to predict noncovalent interactions that are reasonable. It is worthwhile restating that D3 corrections that were designed for use with B3LYP were also designed for use with nearly complete basis sets. The corrections nevertheless improve the performance of "small basis set" B3LYP, as has been shown in the past, in particular for the treatment of noncovalent interactions.

Using the DFT based B3LYP/6-31++G (d,p) method, we first tried to locate all the possible stationary points in the reaction paths. , All the minima were characterized with no imaginary frequencies. At the same time, all the transition states were characterized with only one imaginary frequency and were confirmed from the analysis of their displacement vectors associated with their imaginary frequencies and from their IRC calculations. It is well-known that most of the DFT methods are deficient in accounting for the dispersive interactions and other long-range interactions. The reason is due to the use of the approximated exchange-correlation (xc) functionals, which are computed empirically and then added to the conventional DFT energies as correction terms. So, we have tried to include the empirical dispersion and long-range interaction corrections by carrying out the calculations again with the wB97xD method (this method uses long-range corrected hybrid density functionals with damped atom-atom dispersion corrections. ), with a basis set like aug-cc-pVTZ, on all the stationary points located in the previously mentioned method (full optimizations for all stationary points). Discussions reported in this work are only limited to the wB97xD method and are sometimes compared with the results from the B3LYP method. All the energetics reported in this work include zero-point energy corrections, unless otherwise mentioned explicitly. As the wB97xD method was providing comparable accurate results like that of the previous reports, computations related to other computationally expensive higher-level energy correction methods were not carried out in this work. In a few cases, we have compared the results from our CCSD (T) calculations with the earlier reported results at various levels of theories and also with results from wB97xD methods reported in this work (CCSD (T)/6-31++G (d,p) energy corrections were carried out on B3LYP/6-31++G (d,p) optimized geometries). - The computational chemistry program Gaussian 09 was used to carry out all these calculations, and the GaussView program was used for visualization purposes.

dataset_item.question: What are the mechanisms by which the kinked structure imide monomer and 3-ethynylaniline end groups improve the properties of liquid crystalline poly(esterimide)s?
dataset_item.answer: The improved properties of liquid crystalline poly(esterimide)s (LCPEIs) are attributed to the synergistic effects of the kinked imide monomer and the 3-ethynylaniline (3-EA) end groups. The kinked structure of the imide monomer disrupts chain symmetry and regularity, lowering the melting temperature (Tm) and enhancing solubility. Simultaneously, the 3-ethynylaniline end groups reduce the molecular weight, further decreasing Tm and melt viscosity (η*), thereby improving processability. The high imide content promotes stronger π-π interactions between polymer chains, while the curing process introduces chain extension and cross-linking, significantly increasing the glass transition temperature (Tg) to 225 °C and improving thermal stability. These combined effects yield LCPEIs with a balanced profile of high-temperature resistance, ease of processing, and enhanced solubility.

### Task 1: Summarize the purpose of the paper
The purpose of the paper is to develop a new solution polymerization method for synthesizing thermosetting all-aromatic liquid crystalline poly(esterimide)s (LCPEIs) at medium-low temperatures (below 120 °C). This method aims to address two significant challenges: improving the processability and achieving high thermal resistance of LCPEIs. The study also explores the synthesis and characterization of two new LCPEIs terminated with 3-ethynylaniline (3-EA), compares their properties with control samples, and investigates the mechanisms behind their enhanced performance.

---

2. **Structure-Property Relationships**: How do the 3-ethynylaniline (3-EA) end groups influence the thermal, mechanical, and processing properties of LCPEIs compared to control samples without these end groups?
3. **Thermal Performance**: What mechanisms contribute to the high glass transition temperature (Tg) and storage modulus of the cured LCPEIs?

inference_contexts: Novel thermosetting all-aromatic LCPEIs containing kinked structure imide monomer and reactive end groups were synthesized via a new direct esterification solution polymerization at medium-low temperature (120 °C). The new strategy not only completely overcomes the bottleneck problems of the high-temperature traditional melt polycondensation and solution polymerization (imidization) but also endows LCPEIs with super comprehensive performances, including high T g, low T m, low η*, and good solubility, compared to traditional LC polyesters. The mechanism behind includes two aspects. On the one hand, the kinked structure of IM monomer suppresses the symmetry and regularity of the main chain, which is beneficial to obtain low T m and good solubility; on the other hand, the introduction of reactive end groups (3-EA) reduces the molecular weight of the polymer main chain, leading to low T m and η*. In addition, a stronger π-π interaction occurs between the molecular chains for LCPEIs with high content of IM as well as the chain extension and cross-linking reaction during cure procedure, endowing Cured-LCPEI-2 with higher T g (225 °C) and good processability.

This paper presents an extensive investigation of the structure and thermal properties of α-CD inclusion complexes built from alkyl grafted polysaccharides, with various lengths of alkyl chains. In all preparations, the inclusion complexes formed crystals with a platelet shape with nanometric thickness and high aspect ratio. All crystals contain at equilibrium water molecules in their structures with a proportion increasing with ambient RH and showing specific thermal stability. All humid platelets exhibit identical XRD patterns, which belong to the "generic" channel-type structure. The humid samples have a monoclinic symmetry, and their unit cell volume is around 4500 Å3. According to Harata and Kawano, the symmetry corresponds to the head-to-tail packing mode of α-CD molecules, with the molecular axis inclined against the column axis. The platelets also contain the backbones of the polymer chains. SEM FEG images show that the platelets are composed of successive thin layers where the α-CD-rich inclusions and polysaccharide backbone could alternate. None of the crystalline structures reported so far in the literature of α-CD inclusions shows such structures. Upon dehydration, platelets keep their crystalline structure with a decrease of the unit cell volume. Solubility and melting temperatures of platelets differ from those of pure crystals of α-CDs. The platelets in aqueous solutions are remarkably stable against temperature and show a cooperative melting temperature above 100 °C, for the palmitoyl grafted polysaccharides, depending on the polymer backbone. One can envisage new drug delivery applications of platelets in relation with their specific structure. The crystalline platelets are susceptible to disintegrate by interacting with other molecules of their environment following a mechanism specific to these autoassemblies.

A series of six PBI derivatives bearing one or two voluminous substituents at 1 or 1,7-bay positions show similar absorption bands and intense emission with fluorescence quantum yields close to unity in dichloromethane solution. In contrast, the absorption and emission characteristics differ significantly for mono- and disubstituted compounds in the solid state according to our investigations of annealed thin films, oriented microcrystals on surfaces, as well as neat PBI powders. Thus, absorption bands provide evidence of short-range π-π interactions and long-range exciton coupling for those derivatives bearing less bulky substituents, while for those derivatives bearing the most bulky substituents, monomer-like absorption bands are observed. Similar insights are obtained from fluorescence spectroscopy where even stronger interactions attributable to excimer states are observed. The most sensitive quantity is, however, the fluorescence quantum yield, which varies between only 4% for the least-shielded dyes and 64% (82%) for the most shielded dyes within this series of solid-state emitter materials. These optical properties are attributable to the propensity of the different bay substituents to shield the chromophore's π-system in the solid state and thereby to isolate the chromophore and to prohibit any kind of π-π interactions between the PBI units. As the volume of the phenoxy substituents increases, the closest distance between the centroids of the chromophores' π-systems is enlarged to >15 Å, i.e.. beyond the length of the PBI π-scaffold of about 12 Å, thereby raising the fluorescence quantum yields in the solid state up to 60 and 64% (82%) for compounds bearing the most bulky 2,4,6-tris (4-tert-butylphenyl)-phenoxy (3c) and 2,4,6-tris (3,5-di-tert-butylphenyl)-phenoxy (3d) substituents. We thus could establish valuable packing structure-optical property relationships for this class of strongly emissive solid-state materials based on phenoxy-(1,7-bay-) substituted perylene bisimide dyes. A comparison to other studies performed for PBIs bearing bulky substituents at the imide position suggests that the here-explored bay functionalization is superior to the more common functionalization of the imide groups.

Azobenzene derivatives have been extensively employed as the photochromic moiety; however, the exploration of other photochromic groups has not been paid adequate attention. Therefore, there is a large scope to play with other photochromic groups in the development of light driven liquid crystalline materials. Similarly, rod-shaped LCs have been the focus of research, it is high time to extend the studies to discotic and bent-core liquid crystalline materials, especially in the context of polymer networks and elastomers. Like photoresponsive cholesteric LCs, other chiral LC phases such as ferroelectric LCs and blue phases deserve more systematic investigations. Supramolecular photoresponsive liquid crystalline materials have been less enquired of, even though they seem to furnish exciting functional attributes. Nanoparticle-doped light-driven LCs could evolve as an independent enterprise. Moreover, the design, synthesis, and study of photoresponsive liquid crystalline nanoparticles whose properties could be reversibly tuned by the action of light through dynamic assembly and disassembly may open up a new direction in the area of nanomaterials research. The prospects for the utilization of upconversion nanoparticles and anisotropic nanorods seem bright. Toward this end, chemists are bound to play a critical role in the design and synthesis of engineered photoaddressable liquid crystalline materials with a gamut of intriguing phenomena and properties which could attract other stake holders into this interdisciplinary vibrant frontier.

Our investigation on the chemical compatibility between V2O5 and AlCl3-[EMIm]Cl ionic liquid electrolytes establishes unambiguously that V2O5 chemically reacts with both Lewis acidic Al2Cl7 - and Lewis neutral AlCl4 - anions. Spectroscopic, electrochemical, and theoretical analyses reveal that the reaction products between V2O5 and Al2Cl7 - are VOCl3 and amorphous Al2O3. Similarly, the reaction products between V2O5 and AlCl4 - are identified as VO2Cl and AlCl3VO3 - with both 4-coordinated and 6-coordinated structures; these soluble products are furthermore electrochemically active, exhibiting reversible redox reactions between V5+ and V2+ oxidation states. It is clear that V2O5 is not a chemically stable positive electrode material for rechargeable Al batteries using chloroaluminate ionic liquid electrolytes, regardless of Lewis acidity. Although an Al-V2O5 cell may appear to have electrochemical performance in terms of capacity and cyclability, researchers must be cautious when identifying the origin of the electrochemical reactions. Our investigation also raises the question of the chemical stability of other Al-ion positive electrode materials in chloroaluminate ionic liquid electrolytes.

dataset_item.question: How does the bottom-up stock accounting method estimate metal stocks in urban environments?
dataset_item.answer:
The bottom-up stock accounting method estimates metal stocks in urban environments by calculating the total metal content across various product categories. For each product *i* containing metal *j* at time *t*, the method multiplies the product quantity (*P<sub>i,j</sub>(t)*) by its metal intensity (*m<sub>i,j</sub>(t)*) and aggregates these values across all products and metals. 

When direct data is unavailable, proxies are employed; for example, the metal content per power unit of agricultural machinery is used to estimate the metal content in industrial machinery, adjusting for total power capacity differences. For nonresidential buildings, metal stocks are determined by calculating the total floor area, which is derived from population data and per capita floor area estimates. Historical construction data is accumulated over time to account for building stock growth.

This method addresses data limitations by leveraging reasonable assumptions and proxies while ensuring comprehensive quantification of metal stocks across diverse urban infrastructure and product categories.

The present study showed that the aminopolycarboxylic chelating surfactant C12-DTPA can be effectively used in combination with two foaming agents for the removal of extremely toxic metal ions such as Cd2+, Zn2+, and Sr2+ from aqueous solution using the ion flotation technique. It was found that the removal of metal ions from the flotation cell is dependent on their chelation behavior with C12-DTPA and on the foaming properties of the samples, both of which change with the pH of the system. The results indicate that both Zn2+ and Cd2+ can be completely removed at pH 5. However, when the pH is increased to 7 and 9, barely 60% of Zn2+ and Cd2+ can be removed from the solution. On the other hand, at pH 5, no removal of Sr2+ was observed, whereas at a pH of 7-9, ~65% removal was achieved under comparable conditions. For efficient separation of metal ions from water systems, the amount of water transferred to the reject foam must also be considered, which is evaluated by measuring the concentration of metal ions in the collected foam. It was found that the interactions between the foaming agent and chelating surfactant affects the concentration of metal ions in the foam. A higher concentration of DoTAC increased the concentration of Sr2+ in the collected foam, because of the strong interactions between DoTAC and C12-DTPA. A higher concentration of DDAO, on the other hand, increased the removal of metal ions from the bulk, because of better foaming properties of the test solution. The separation efficiency is a measure of both the removal of metal ions from the bulk and the concentration of metal ions in the collected foam, and the foaming agent mixture must be designed accordingly. Taking the above parameters into account, it would be useful to design and optimize a selective ion flotation process in competitive systems for the target metal ions.

Combined analysis of 4-CP decomposition rates, pH and leached metal content in the homogeneous phase over the Fenton-like heterogeneous catalysts FeO x /TiO2 and CuFe2O4 indicates subppm levels of Fe and Cu ions dissolved from the solid phases are sufficient to explain the observed 4-CP degradation rates. 4-CP reaction rates were affected by time-dependent metal leaching, which is caused by pH variations associated with acidic 4-CP decomposition products. Buffering solutions at pH 7.4 suppressed metal leaching from 1 wt % FeO x /TiO2 and thereby 4-CP degradation. Dissolution of Cu from CuFe2O4 is much less affected at the same pH and 4-CP degradation catalyzed by dissolved Cu (and some Fe) remained significant. The Fenton-like FeO x /TiO2 and CuFe2O4 systems thus appear to be homogeneous rather than heterogeneous. We conclude that the development of heterogeneous Fenton-like water treatment processes requires careful monitoring of aqueous metal content with analytical sensitivity below ppm concentrations and control experiments. We believe that the conclusions arrived at in this paper may well be applicable for other Fenton-like systems, and are not necessarily limited to Cu and Fe systems. What our work certainly highlights is the fact that monitoring metal content in the solid phase by gravimetry, X-ray fluorescence, electron microscopy and other conventional analytical means is unlikely to be sensitive enough to detect the low metal losses due to leaching.

Metals that are atomically dispersed and bonded to surfaces of solids have reactivities and catalytic properties that are markedly different from those of conventional supported metal catalysts, which consist of clusters or nanoparticles on the supports. Metals that are atomically dispersed on supports such as metal oxides are positively charged and have reactivities determined by the charge and the ligands bonded to the metals, which include the support. Understanding of these materials is emerging rapidly from characterization by complementary methods that prominently include XAS, IR spectroscopy, theory, and, most significantly, atomic-resolution imaging by AC HAADF STEM and iDPC.

dataset_item.question: What is the role of vanadium (III) systems in the methanol dehydrogenation process?
dataset_item.answer: Vanadium (III) systems play a pivotal role in methanol dehydrogenation by providing thermodynamically favorable sites for methanol adsorption and dissociation. These systems enable the formation of stable fivefold coordinate methoxy intermediates, which lack vanadyl (V=O) groups, distinguishing their mechanism from vanadium (V) species. The absence of vanadyl groups facilitates the stabilization of the transition state, promoting a reaction pathway that produces hydrogen and formaldehyde with energies below the reference energy. Additionally, hydride intermediates, while less kinetically favorable, may contribute to catalytic activity. Overall, reduced vanadium (III) systems are more effective than oxidized vanadium (V) species for methanol oxidation, as they provide a more favorable energetic pathway for the process.

inference_contexts: The present theoretical work adds a new insight into the gas-phase mechanisms of the dehydrogenation of CH3OH to be compared with supported reduced vanadium oxides. The results show that the methanol adsorption on V (III) systems sites is thermodynamically favorable, while methanol dissociation gives rise to stable fivefold coordinate V (III) methoxy intermediates. The most likely intermediate does not contain vanadyl V-O groups. As result, the role of the catalyst is first to dissociate the CH3OH molecule and second to improve the gas-phase mechanism by stabilizing the transition state. In fact, one of the reaction pathways (Path B2) to obtain H2 and CH2O is found to proceed below the reference energy. The CH3OH adsorption process may also bring about the formation of hydride intermediates; although kinetically less favorable, they may present an interesting catalytic activity. The overall methanol oxidation process is found to be more favorable over V (III) than on V (V) species.

For polymers, natural or otherwise, to produce carbon fiber of a similar quality as PAN, they cannot rely on hydrogen bonding for structural stability or contain a high mass fraction of oxygen, lest they shrink to an unusable extent. A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. Polyalanine-like domains could be incorporated into block copolymers for biomimetic graphite precursors. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

In this work, we describe mechanisms of the Pd (II)-controlled disulfide/thiolate interconversion for l-cystine, cystamine, dl-homocystine and 3,3′-dithiodipropionic acid in aqueous solutions. We specifically address the question of different reactivity of homologous disulfides toward Pd2+. We see this different reactivity in different capacities of considered homologous disulfides to stabilize forming S,S′-binuclear complexes, which are believed to be key intermediates toward interconversion products. In case of homocystine and 3,3′-dithiodipropionic acid, formation of the S,S′-binuclear complexes leads to cleavage of the disulfide bond, while we observe formation of the S,N-binuclear and S,N,S′,N′-tetranuclear complexes with the preserved S-S bond for the l-cystine and cystamine ligands. Formation of the S,S′-binuclear complexes increases the d(S-S) bond length by 5%, and the redistribution of charges with Sδ--Sδ- in the original disulfide on Sδ+-Sδ- occurs in the complex. We find that the greater the magnitude of Δδ in S,S′-binuclear complex, the higher the likelihood of disproportionation. Conditions, under which disproportionation takes place, include formation of redox-resistant S,S′-binuclear disulfide complex and the disulfide bond being open for the nucleophilic substitution by water.

The exploration of site-specific strategies presented herein aims to provide the community with alternative strategies, particularly for applications that require a desired protein orientation on the nanotube surface. These applications include optical monitoring of protein activity and charge transfer mechanisms to the nanotube surface. The two approaches demonstrated in this work focus on site-specific conjugation to either an ssDNA wrapping or PM linker via covalent thiol-maleimide "click" chemistry with the protein. dataset_item.question: How do variations in bed porosity and space time influence yield, concentration, and productivity during continuous esterification of oleic acid and 2-ethylhexanol using Candida antarctica lipase immobilized on STY-DVB-M?
dataset_item.answer:
Variations in bed porosity and space time significantly influence the yield, concentration, and productivity of 2-ethylhexyl oleate during continuous esterification of oleic acid and 2-ethylhexanol using *Candida antarctica* lipase immobilized on STY-DVB-M. Optimal production conditions were achieved with a bed porosity of 0.892 and a space time of 12 hours, resulting in high productivity and satisfactory yields. Increased bed porosity (ranging from 0.866 to 0.916) enhanced mixing and mass transfer, as evidenced by an increase in the mass transfer coefficient from 8.989 × 10⁻⁶ m s⁻¹ to 1.497 × 10⁻⁵ m s⁻¹. 

A validated mathematical model (R² = 0.991) accurately predicted reactor performance, estimating a maximum reaction rate of 4.683 kmol m⁻³ min⁻¹ under optimal conditions. Additionally, the immobilized lipase demonstrated robust operational stability, retaining 85% of its initial activity after 16 days of continuous operation, with a calculated half-life of 1714 hours. Consistent yields (ranging from 0.65 to 0.77 mmol g⁻¹ L⁻¹) highlight the industrial potential of this process. These findings underscore the importance of optimizing bed porosity and space time to maximize mass transfer, reaction efficiency, and enzyme stability.

dataset_item.question: How does Rh decoration affect the morphology of WO3 nanorods and contribute to gas sensing performance?
dataset_item.answer: Rhodium (Rh) decoration significantly impacts the morphology of tungsten trioxide (WO3) nanorods by inducing retarded surface diffusion and trapping effects at heterojunctions. These morphological alterations lead to improved heterojunction formation, which plays a critical role in enhancing gas sensing performance. Additionally, Rh decoration introduces electronic and chemical sensitization effects, creating synergistic interactions that amplify the sensor's response to volatile organic compounds, particularly acetone. The unique combination of morphological changes and sensitization effects optimizes the nanostructure design, contributing to high sensitivity and selectivity in gas sensing applications. This advancement highlights the promising potential of Rh-decorated WO3 nanorods in next-generation gas sensor technology.

dataset_item.question: What role does withdrawal speed play in determining band density and nematic alignment of silica helices during evaporation-induced assembly?
dataset_item.answer: The withdrawal speed plays a crucial role in determining both band density and nematic alignment of silica helices during evaporation-induced assembly. Slow withdrawal speeds (evaporative transport mode) lead to the formation of dense, thick, periodic bands oriented perpendicular to the withdrawal direction. Within these bands, nematic alignment is achieved due to capillary contraction forces that align the helices parallel to the contact line. In contrast, faster withdrawal speeds (advection mode) produce less dense bands aligned parallel to the withdrawal direction. Here, shear forces dominate, aligning the helices perpendicular to the contact line while maintaining nematic order. These alignment mechanisms and structural properties—such as pitch, width, and inter-band spacing—are quantitatively described by a capillary hydrodynamic model that correlates withdrawal speed with the organizational features of the silica helices.

dataset_item.question: How does the oxidizing or reducing nature of plasma reactant affect the oxidation state of manganese in deposited thin films?
dataset_item.answer:
The oxidizing or reducing nature of plasma reactants plays a pivotal role in determining the oxidation state of manganese in deposited thin films during atomic layer deposition (ALD). Using Mn(thd)₃ as a precursor, plasma-activated gases facilitate film growth by providing reactive species that enable oxidation or reduction, whereas non-plasma-activated gases fail to initiate deposition due to the stable nature of the precursor. 

The oxidation state of manganese in the deposited films depends on the reactivity and nature of the plasma reactants. Strongly oxidizing plasmas, such as O₂*, lead to the formation of MnO₂ (Mn⁴⁺), while reducing plasmas like H₂* and NH₃* result in MnO (Mn²⁺). Intermediate conditions, such as H₂O*, yield mixed-valence Mn₃O₄ (Mn²⁺/Mn³⁺). These phases are confirmed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), which provides detailed insights into the chemical composition and oxidation states.

Additionally, characterization techniques such as X-ray diffraction (XRD) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) reveal the crystallinity and morphology of the films, while electrochemical testing using cyclic voltammetry and galvanostatic charge/discharge demonstrates their suitability for applications like lithium-ion batteries. For example, MnO₂ serves as an excellent cathode material, while MnO functions effectively as an anode. This plasma-dependent tunability in manganese oxide phases allows for precise control over film properties to meet specific functional requirements.

In summary, the nature of plasma reactants—oxidizing or reducing—not only determines the manganese oxidation state but also enables targeted synthesis of thin films for advanced applications.

dataset_item.question: How do high concentrations of NaCl and CaCl2 affect the adsorption of chitosan-graft-polyacrylamide chains on silica and alumina surfaces of kaolinite?
dataset_item.answer: High concentrations of NaCl and CaCl₂ inhibit the adsorption of chitosan-graft-polyacrylamide (chi-g-PAM) chains on both silica and alumina surfaces of kaolinite. This inhibition occurs due to changes in polymer conformation and surface charge properties, as well as weakened bridging interactions between chi-g-PAM and kaolinite surfaces, as demonstrated by QCM-D measurements and confirmed through SFA force analysis. These effects align with DLVO theory, which explains the disruption of polymer adsorption and interparticle bridging under high salinity conditions. Consequently, the reduced adsorption leads to diminished flocculation performance, as evidenced by lower initial settling rates and improved supernatant turbidity in saline solutions. Overall, high salinity impairs the polymer's ability to form effective flocculating networks, weakening its interaction with kaolinite surfaces.

dataset_item.question: What are general microstructural design guidelines for optimizing cycling life and rate capability in tin-based anode materials for sodium-ion batteries?
dataset_item.answer:
To optimize cycling life and rate capability in tin-based anode materials for sodium-ion batteries, microstructural design should focus on accommodating the large volume changes during sodiation, mitigating mechanical degradation, and enhancing electrochemical performance. Key strategies include:

1. **Nanostructuring:** Utilize nanoscale tin materials to buffer stress and reduce mechanical strain caused by sodiation-induced volume changes. Nanostructures also enhance ion and electron transport, improving rate capability.

2. **Composite Formation:** Incorporate tin into conductive matrices, such as carbon-based materials, to enhance electrical conductivity, stabilize the electrode structure, and maintain electrical contact during cycling.

3. **Porous Architectures:** Design controlled porosity to facilitate efficient ion diffusion and accommodate volume expansion without compromising structural integrity.

4. **Tailored Architectures:** Develop architectures that balance active material utilization with structural stability. This includes managing incomplete alloying reactions and metastable phase transformations to improve cycling stability.

5. **Surface Coatings:** Apply conductive coatings or protective layers to tin-based materials to buffer mechanical stress, improve electron transport, and enhance the stability of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI).

By integrating these strategies, tin-based anodes can achieve improved cycling life, enhanced rate capability, and greater resistance to sodiation-induced stresses.

dataset_item.question: What are the specific mechanisms responsible for capacity fade in O3-type layered oxide cathodes during high-voltage cycling?
dataset_item.answer:
Capacity fade in O3-type layered oxide cathodes during high-voltage cycling (>4 V) is caused by three interconnected mechanisms:

1. **Iron Migration and Phase Transition Loss**: Irreversible migration of iron into the sodium layer impedes Na⁺ diffusion and destabilizes the thermodynamic stability of the cathode. This eliminates the high-voltage P3-to-OP2 phase transition, which is critical for maintaining capacity. Iron migration occurs rapidly during early cycles but becomes self-limiting over time due to ionic repulsion and reduced availability of migration sites.

2. **Cathode-Electrolyte Interphase (CEI) Formation**: Electrolyte decomposition at high voltages forms a resistive surface layer, known as the CEI, on the cathode. This layer increases impedance and reduces the efficiency of sodium ion transport, contributing to capacity loss.

3. **Structural Degradation**: Repeated high-voltage cycling induces structural damage from phase transitions and volume changes. This degradation compromises the integrity of the cathode material, further exacerbating capacity fade.

Early cycles exhibit rapid capacity loss due to severe iron migration and phase transition destabilization. Later cycles show a more linear fade dominated by CEI growth and slower structural degradation. Mitigation strategies include doping to suppress iron migration, optimizing electrolyte composition to stabilize the CEI, and tuning cathode materials to minimize structural changes during cycling.

dataset_item.question: How do feed solution characteristics, such as the presence of surfactants, organics, or oils, influence membrane wetting in membrane distillation systems?
dataset_item.answer:
Feed solution characteristics, such as the presence of surfactants, organics, or oils, significantly influence membrane wetting in membrane distillation (MD) systems. These contaminants reduce the surface tension of feedwater, increasing the wetting propensity of hydrophobic membranes and compromising their performance. Severe wetting can result in reduced vapor flux and contamination of the permeate.

Pretreatment methods, including filtration, flocculation, coagulation, dissolved air flotation, oxidation, biological treatment, or photocatalysis, can effectively remove these contaminants and mitigate wetting. Advanced membrane technologies, such as superhydrophobic, omniphobic, or Janus membranes (featuring hydrophilic/hydrophobic layers), provide enhanced resistance to wetting due to their higher contact angles and lower surface energies. These membranes are particularly effective in handling challenging feed solutions containing oils, organics, or surfactants.

If wetting does occur, restoring membrane performance may require interventions such as backwashing with water, air, or chemical agents, as simple drying or water flushing may be insufficient. Combining robust pretreatment strategies with advanced membrane designs ensures optimal MD system performance in the presence of challenging feed solutions.

dataset_item.question: What advancements have been achieved in the use of halogen bonding for the design of functional materials over time?
dataset_item.answer: Halogen bonding (XB) has evolved significantly over time, transitioning from a tool primarily used for crystal engineering to a sophisticated and versatile strategy for designing functional materials. This progression spans a wide range of material classes, including liquid crystals, polymers, micelles, gels, and two-dimensional systems at nanoscale and microscale levels. By leveraging XB, researchers have been able to create self-assembled materials with emergent properties that are absent in their individual components, enabling tailored functionalities and increasingly complex hierarchical structures. These advancements demonstrate halogen bonding's scalability and maturity as a powerful tool for innovative material design, offering new possibilities for applications in soft and functional materials.

In conclusion, we unravelled and quantified the thermodynamic origin of the phase evolution of the hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite [CH3NH3] PbBr3 by combining high-resolution inelastic neutron scattering with ab initio lattice dynamics. The differences in enthalpy and configurational and vibrational entropy of the phases are all on the same order of magnitude, meaning that each of these factors is important in determining the stable structure as a function of temperature. These contributions are even more significant when one considers the decreased role of the Madelung energy in determining structure in halide perovskites, compared to oxides. We find that a complex interplay between entropy and hydrogen bonding interactions leads to the phase transitions as a function of temperature, a result that seems to be generally applicable for crystalline hybrid materials. These insights can now be used to understand behaviors in related materials and for the design of materials with tunable properties. For instance, it seems that by small substitutions of Pb2+ with Sn2+ or Ge2+, low-frequency modes related to the stereoactive lone pair can be directly manipulated. Likewise, lattice dynamics related to hydrogen bonding strength play an important role and can be manipulated by replacing [CH3NH3]+ with [(NH2)2CH]+. Such attempts, however, also go beyond these considerations; e.g.. the size of the cation must be considered, which in turn can have a significant impact on the crystal chemistry and the symmetry of the molecule can have an impact on configurational entropy. More generally, the methodology applied here demonstrates the power of ab initio lattice dynamics to provide predictions in excellent agreement with experiment. The combination of INS with ab initio calculations provides a blueprint of how to understand lattice vibrations and relate them to macroscopic properties in an accurate, quantitative way, not only in the context of hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites but also similarly for related hybrid materials. For instance, in flexible metal-organic frameworks, a balance between enthalpic dispersion forces and vibrational entropy exists; our methodology paves the way for understanding these on a microscopic level and in turn facilitates the targeted design of such effects.

The cgff tool computes a corresponding contribution to each force projection, b D ref, from the reference potential, i.e.. using F I ref in the place of f I in eq . The cgff tool then optimizes the remaining terms in U R to match the remainder of each force projection, δb D = b D - b D ref. In particular, if Coulombic or other long-ranged potentials are defined as reference potentials, then the cgff tool will determine the short-ranged potentials that, when combined with the specified long-ranged potentials, provide an optimal approximation to the many-body PMF.

dataset_item.question: What are the advantages of equilibrium molecular dynamics over non-equilibrium molecular dynamics for predicting thermal conductivity in complex materials?
dataset_item.answer: Equilibrium molecular dynamics (EMD) offers significant advantages over non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD) for predicting thermal conductivity in complex materials. One key benefit is its reduced sensitivity to finite-size effects, enabling converged thermal conductivity values with fewer simulation cells, which makes EMD computationally more efficient. This is particularly advantageous for intricate systems like covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and their nanocomposites, where phonon interactions and vibrational matching are critical for thermal transport. EMD leverages the Green-Kubo formalism, which calculates thermal conductivity by integrating the heat current autocorrelation function over time. Unlike NEMD, EMD avoids the artificial thermal gradients imposed during simulations, which can distort results in anisotropic or nanostructured materials. Consequently, EMD provides a more accurate and robust approach for studying the thermal conductivity of complex materials, ensuring reliable predictions even in systems with intricate molecular architectures.

dataset_item.question: What is the effect of tensile and compressive strain on hydrogen evolution reaction catalytic activity of h-B2O monolayer?
dataset_item.answer: The h-B2O monolayer demonstrates excellent hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) catalytic activity, with the B site identified as the most active. The pristine monolayer exhibits a near-optimal Gibbs free energy of hydrogen adsorption (ΔG<sub>H*</sub>) of -0.07 eV, comparable to platinum (-0.09 eV), indicating favorable catalytic performance. Tensile strain (0–2%) further enhances HER activity by pushing ΔG<sub>H*</sub> closer to 0 eV, particularly at low hydrogen coverage, thereby improving reaction kinetics. In contrast, compressive strain strengthens hydrogen bonding to the monolayer, resulting in more negative ΔG<sub>H*</sub> values, which negatively impacts HER catalytic activity. Importantly, the h-B2O monolayer maintains robust performance even at high hydrogen coverage (ΔG<sub>H*</sub> = -0.03 eV at θ = 5/9). Electronic structure analysis reveals metallic behavior, while reaction kinetics suggest a Heyrovsky-dominated Volmer-Heyrovsky mechanism. These findings underscore the strain-dependent tunability of h-B2O as a promising metal-free HER catalyst.

dataset_item.question: How does the design of tree-shaped distributors with halving-width branches and constant-width branches affect flow distribution, mass transfer coefficient, and pressure drop in parallel microchannels?
dataset_item.answer:
The design of tree-shaped distributors with halving-width branches (Tree-1) and constant-width branches (Tree-2) plays a critical role in influencing flow distribution, mass transfer coefficient, and pressure drop in parallel microchannels.

**Flow Distribution:**  
Tree-1 exhibits a narrower operating range and deteriorating flow distribution as the gas-liquid flow rate ratio increases. This is primarily due to hydrodynamic feedback effects and the presence of long mother bubbles that are less influenced by bifurcation. On the other hand, Tree-2 achieves more uniform flow distribution at a critical gas-liquid flow rate ratio, but this advantage diminishes beyond the critical point due to bubble generation and outlet hydrodynamics.

**Mass Transfer Coefficient:**  
Tree-2 generally exhibits higher mass transfer coefficients due to its greater specific surface area and the presence of more gas-liquid interaction units. However, this enhancement comes at the cost of increased energy consumption and higher pressure drops. Tree-1 provides fewer gas-liquid units and consequently lower mass transfer coefficients but achieves better energy efficiency.

**Pressure Drop:**  
Tree-2 designs suffer from higher pressure drops due to the increased interaction between gas and liquid phases, while Tree-1 designs maintain lower pressure drops. This makes Tree-1 favorable in scenarios where energy efficiency is prioritized.

**Performance Ratio:**  
Considering the balance between efficiency and energy consumption, Tree-1 designs typically demonstrate a higher overall performance ratio, favoring applications where minimizing pressure drop is crucial. However, as the gas-liquid flow rate ratio increases, the performance ratios of Tree-1 and Tree-2 converge, reducing the advantage of Tree-1 designs.

**Conclusion:**  
Tree-1 designs are ideal for applications prioritizing energy efficiency and lower pressure drops, whereas Tree-2 designs are better suited for scenarios requiring higher mass transfer rates despite increased energy consumption. The choice between the two depends on the specific operational requirements and trade-offs between flow distribution, mass transfer, and pressure drop.

inference_contexts: In this paper, the effects of the two typical dimensions of the tree-shaped distributor in the rectangular parallel microchannels on the hydrodynamics, flow distribution, and mass-transfer performance of the gas-liquid flow are studied. The results show that the variation of width in the tree-shaped distributor has important influences on the operating range, flow distribution, pressure drop, and mass-transfer coefficient in parallel microchannels. In the halving-width microchannel, the mother bubble in the main channel is long and the length is almost not affected by the breaking up at the bifurcation, resulting in the obvious hydrodynamic feedback, and thus, the operating range in the halving-width microchannel is significantly narrower than that in the constant-width microchannel. Due to the effects of the different ratios of width-depth on bubble generation in the main channel and the hydrodynamic feedback at the outlet, the flow distribution gradually deteriorates in the halving-width microchannel as the ratio of the gas-liquid flow rate increases. However, in the constant-width microchannel, there exists a critical ratio of the gas-liquid flow rate for the most uniform flow distribution. Before this critical value, the flow distribution improves with the increase of the ratio of the gas-liquid flow rate but deteriorates after this critical value. Furthermore, due to the differences in hydrodynamics and flow distribution between the two parallel microchannels with different tree-shaped distributors, the mass-transfer performance is also different. In the halving-width microchannel, the number of gas-liquid units is less, and so the total specific surface area is smaller, and the volumetric mass-transfer coefficient becomes smaller accordingly. However, in the constant-width microchannel, the situation is just the opposite. However, the high mass-transfer coefficient is always accompanied by a high pressure drop. Therefore, the pressure drop in the constant-width microchannel is significantly higher. To comprehensively consider the mass-transfer efficiency and energy consumption, the performance ratio is adopted to evaluate the mass-transfer performance. The results show that the performance ratio of the halving-width microchannel is generally higher than that of the constant-width microchannel, but with the increase of the ratio of the gas-liquid flow rate, the performance ratios of the two microchannels gradually approach each other. The obtained results confirm that designing a tree-shaped distributor of the appropriate width in parallel microchannels is a potentially appealing tool to improve the flow distribution and mass-transfer performance.

dataset_item.question: How does translational jump diffusion contribute to molecular transport in supercooled water?
dataset_item.answer:
Translational jump diffusion plays a critical role in molecular transport in supercooled water, particularly at lower temperatures. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the jump diffusion coefficient (\( D_{\text{Jump}} \)) increasingly contributes to the total diffusion coefficient as temperature decreases, while the residual diffusion coefficient (\( D_{\text{Res}} \)) remains strongly coupled to viscosity. This mechanism leads to the breakdown of the Stokes-Einstein equation, as \( D_{\text{Jump}} \) drives the decoupling of self-diffusion from viscosity.

The findings highlight translational jump diffusion as a key mechanism for molecular transport in supercooled water, providing insights into the diffusion-viscosity relationship in complex systems. Importantly, no abrupt changes in diffusion or viscosity were observed near the Widom line at ambient pressure, suggesting the need for pressure-dependent studies to further explore critical behavior near the liquid-liquid critical point.

The paper aims to investigate the decoupling of viscosity from translational self-diffusion in supercooled water, which challenges the Stokes-Einstein equation. Through molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, the study provides direct quantitative evidence that translational jump diffusion plays a critical role in this decoupling phenomenon. By isolating the contribution of jump diffusion, the researchers uncover a residual diffusion coefficient that remains strongly coupled to viscosity, thereby clarifying molecular transport mechanisms in supercooled water.

4. How does the residual diffusion coefficient relate to viscosity in the supercooled regime?

By making use of a recently developed approach to minimize artifacts in FCS studies mainly caused by refractive index mismatch in additive enriched aqueous solutions, we were able to obtain reliable diffusion coefficients of biological tracer molecules in synthetic polymer crowder solutions at concentrations up to 25 w/w%, in a systematic study with six different macromolecular tracer molecules and seven different crowding agents. First, we analyzed the translational mobility of polymer crowder coils themselves as a function of the crower concentration. The FCS results showed that the translational mobility of crowder polymer coils decreased in a similar manner as rigid-body-like protein tracers (here, streptavidin) under the same crowding conditions. The translational diffusion on the FCS length scale (a few hundred nanometers) comes almost to rest for all macromolecules when the semidiluted regime is reached, approximately given by the overlap concentration for flexible polymers. Depending on the size of the polymer crowder coils or particles, this concentration is reached between 0.05 and 2.5 mM (from large to small crowders). A residual apparent slow diffusion visible in the FCS data is most probably an artifact caused by photobleaching effects. However, a fast local diffusion process of tracer molecules in the confined space, effectively built up by the polymer mesh, is still possible. According to the Huggins equation describing the bulk viscosity of concentrated polymer solutions, we obtain much higher viscosity values for larger crowding agents as compared to smaller ones at the same w/w% mass concentration. Therefore, we observed in the case of tracer diffusion that concentrated crowder solutions with larger crowding agents exhibit a much stronger deviation from the "macroscopic line" in D 0/D versus η/η0 plots as compared to smaller crowding agents. A direct look on the reduction of diffusion coefficients as a function of the crowder volume fraction revealed that PEG crowders cause the most pronounced reduction of the tracer diffusion. Furthermore, solutions with several crowder agents exhibit a tracer size-dependence of the diffusion reduction, which indicates a molecular sieving effect. This effect was also observed in the cytoplasm of cells and seems to be a general property of cellular crowding. With respect to absolute diffusion coefficients, we observe a reasonable agreement between measurements in cells and in synthetic crowder solutions for GFP. In the case of very slow diffusion, for example, for ribosomes in highly crowded environments, FCS measurements fail to deliver diffusion coefficients below ~1 μm2/s with the required accuracy. A more appropriate approach to study slow diffusion of biological macromolecules in crowded environments is given by single-particle tracking methods. In fact, a reliable knowledge about ribosome diffusion, but also about the diffusion of smaller molecules under the same crowding conditions, is of specific interest for elucidating the impact of macromolecular crowding on cellular processes, like, for example, the protein biosynthesis. In this respect, molecular sieving effects and the translational mobility of the 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits, the latter important for the 70S ribosome formation, are worth to be studied, for example, in cell-free protein synthesis assays. ,, Finally, we analyzed the impact of crowding on the performance of FRET-based glucose biosensors, equipped with FP derivatives as FRET pair. In the case investigated here, glucose binding as well as the presence of macromolecular crowders lead to a structural compaction of the sensor construct, which both alter the FRET ratio. dataset_item.question: How does temperature affect the crystallization of monoclinic alpha-phase and orthorhombic gamma-phase in propylene ethylene random copolymers during flow-induced conditions?
dataset_item.answer:
Temperature plays a critical role in the flow-induced crystallization behavior of monoclinic α-phase and orthorhombic γ-phase in propylene-ethylene random copolymers. At 132°C, the application of shear stress leads to the formation of both α-phase and γ-phase crystals, with the α-phase forming first due to its lower nucleation barrier and faster kinetics. The γ-phase appears later, facilitated by nucleation on {010}α surfaces. 

At 142°C, which is closer to the nominal melting temperature, shear stress induces crystallization exclusively in the α-phase. Although nucleation sites for the γ-phase are generated during shear, the higher temperature suppresses the growth of γ-phase crystals due to slower kinetics and reduced stability of this phase. To crystallize the γ-phase at 142°C, subsequent cooling is required to lower the temperature and enable its growth. 

These findings highlight that shear stress accelerates the crystallization of both phases, but elevated temperatures favor the formation of the α-phase by limiting the growth of the γ-phase. The results emphasize the interplay between temperature, shear flow, and phase selection in the crystallization process.

dataset_item.question: How does nanocrystal size affect electrocatalytic activity and stability of Pd3Pb catalysts during ethanol oxidation in alkaline media?
dataset_item.answer:
The electrocatalytic activity and stability of Pd₃Pb nanocrystals during ethanol oxidation in alkaline media are strongly influenced by nanocrystal size. Larger nanocrystals (10 nm) initially exhibit higher current densities due to their greater active surface area, but smaller nanocrystals (6–10 nm) demonstrate superior electrocatalytic activity after extended cycling. This improved performance of smaller nanocrystals is attributed to their enhanced reactivation efficiency during in-situ electrochemical cycling, which effectively removes poisoning intermediates. 

All nanocrystal sizes experience rapid current decay within the first 500 seconds of operation due to surface poisoning by strongly adsorbed intermediates. However, simple cycling processes can restore catalytic activity without disassembling the cell, with smaller nanocrystals showing a greater ability to recover performance. Prolonged cycling also induces elemental redistribution within the nanocrystals, driven by the differing oxygen affinities of palladium and lead, as well as electrochemical oxidation/reduction processes, further influencing catalytic activity and stability. 

Overall, smaller Pd₃Pb nanocrystals offer improved long-term electrocatalytic performance and stability compared to larger nanocrystals, making them more effective for ethanol oxidation in alkaline media.

The use of oxides is a promising alternative to replace precious metals as cost-effective and highly active electrocatalysts. Although oxides exhibit a wide range of physical, chemical, and electrochemical properties, there are still many issues associated with their electrochemical activity and stability. Substituted cations with different oxidation states can modify the catalysts' electrochemical activity, but the change in oxide composition during electrochemical reactions may result in cation segregation and enrichment that could cause stability issues. By reviewing efforts on understanding cation distribution in different oxides using various surface techniques, it is realized that proper control or engineering of the surface segregation could lead to improved activity and stability, as perhaps shown in the case of (La1-y Sr y )2CoO4±δ/La1-x Sr x CoO3-δ and (La1-y Sr y )2CoO4±δ/La1-x Sr x Co0.2Fe0.8O3-δ heterostructures. Following the guidance from this descriptor for perovskites, it is optimal to design oxide electrocatalysts with an electronic structure such that the O p-band can approach as close as possible to the Fermi level while maintaining stability, thus improving electrocatalyst activity and perhaps even leading to bifunctionality for both the ORR and OER.

Although this Account mainly discusses Sr related migration, other cations such as Ca2+ and Ba2+ are also used for substitution. It is possible to use other cations to tune the oxidation states, vacancy concentration, and oxygen p-band center position with novel electrocatalytic activity and stability. It is also suggested that future work should focus on understanding the mechanism and the functionality of electrocatalysts under reaction conditions. In situ surface techniques are preferred to probe how electrocatalysts work or fail during operational conditions. A combination of studies on atomic and electronic structures can better reveal the underlying structure-property relationships. As mentioned in this Account, there are changes that can be either structurally coherent or incoherent with respect to the catalyst supports. Therefore, complementary methods are needed for achieving comprehensive understanding. The application of in situ surface X-ray diffraction and COBRA for understanding the coherent atomic and chemical changes will be essential for future electrocatalysis studies. These structural probes, together with in situ APXPS for surface chemistry and electronic structure and density functional theory, are providing key insights into electrocatalytic properties and helping to identify suitable activity and stability descriptors for the design of highly efficient oxide electrocatalysts for electrochemical and photoelectrochemical applications.

dataset_item.question: How does acetyl protection influence the polymerization process and the structure of poly(9,10-phenanthrene quinone)?
dataset_item.answer:
Acetyl protection plays a critical role in the polymerization process of poly(9,10-phenanthrene quinone) (PFQ) by enabling an indirect synthesis route. This protection prevents the oxidation of the Ni(COD)₂ coupling reagent, which is unstable at voltages above 2.14–2.54 V vs. Li/Li⁺. By circumventing the voltage limitations of direct polymerization, acetyl protection allows for the synthesis of higher voltage polymers like PFQ, preserving the quinone redox activity essential for high energy density applications.  

The resulting PFQ polymer exhibits an average discharge potential of 2.54 V, which is 400 mV higher than its anthraquinone analog, highlighting its suitability for advanced electrode materials. Furthermore, the polymer demonstrates structural stability and insolubility in organic solvents. When composited with reduced graphene oxide (21 wt%), PFQ achieves a capacity of 153 mAh/g with 91% retention over 500 cycles. This performance is attributed to improved porosity and enhanced redox utilization, making it a promising candidate for high-energy-density applications.

Finally, the rate capability testing of PFQ/rGO showed comparable properties to those of better known PAQS and PAQ polymers.

The extent to which the catalyst alters this landscape will, of course, be dependent on the details of the catalyst. This result highlights an important catalyst design consideration, however. If the catalyst's ligand behaves akin to the hydroxyl radical considered here, without bias toward CP formation, then removal of the hydronium ion would be favorable. Even a small remnant electrostatic attraction could alter this behavior, however.

dataset_item.question: How do electron-donor and electron-withdrawing substituents influence interaction energy, intramolecular distances, and electron density in peri-substituted naphthalene systems with chalcogen atoms?
dataset_item.answer:
Electron-donor and electron-withdrawing substituents significantly influence chalcogen interactions in peri-substituted naphthalene systems. Electron-withdrawing groups (e.g., F, CN) enhance interaction energy, making it more negative, and shorten intramolecular distances (O···Y, where Y = O, S, Se) due to stronger σ-hole interactions. This is accompanied by increased electron density at the bond critical point (BCP) and higher second-order perturbation energy, as evidenced by natural bond orbital (NBO) analysis. Conversely, electron-donor substituents weaken the interaction, resulting in less negative interaction energy and longer intramolecular distances.

Substitutions directly on the chalcogen atom (OX groups) have a stronger impact on chalcogen bonding compared to substitutions on the naphthalene ring. Ring substitutions, particularly at ortho/para positions, introduce competing dispersion effects that weaken binding energy but still reduce intramolecular distances, especially in sulfur and selenium derivatives. Electron density maps confirm these trends, showing greater density redistribution with electron-withdrawing substituents. Overall, σ-hole interactions dominate the bonding mechanism, with ring modifications acting as secondary modulators of chalcogen bond strength.

dataset_item.question: What methodological approach was used to quantify uncertainty in hazard ratios for long-term exposure to fine particulate matter across varying concentrations?
dataset_item.answer:
The methodological approach to quantify uncertainty in hazard ratios (HRs) for long-term exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) involved analyzing data from six cohort studies with diverse geographic and demographic profiles. A novel hybrid uncertainty method was developed to address the limitations of traditional approaches that assume constant standard error across concentrations. 

This method utilized study-specific hypothetical PM2.5 concentration distributions, generated by varying the mean concentration in 0.1 μg/m³ increments below observed levels, while maintaining defined standard deviation values. The variance of these distributions was used to calculate standard errors around HRs for each concentration. Wider confidence intervals were observed at lower PM2.5 concentrations, reflecting increased uncertainty where observational data is sparse. 

The hybrid approach demonstrated that uncertainty grows exponentially as concentrations decrease below observed levels, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) including unity (indicating higher uncertainty) at low PM2.5 concentrations, such as below 3.7 μg/m³ in one study. This contrasts with traditional methods, which assume uniform uncertainty regardless of concentration. Additionally, population attributable fraction (PAF) analyses confirmed heightened uncertainty under hypothetical low-concentration scenarios, emphasizing the need for caution when extrapolating HR estimates beyond observed exposure ranges.

This paper proposes a novel operating performance assessment method for multiphase batch processes based on GPR and Bayesian inference. To take the process dynamics and batch-to-batch uncertainty into account, GPR-based assessment models are established for different phases. Since the uneven-length characteristic embodies in phases across different batches, the online phase identification results can be a certain interval or a fuzzy interval between two adjacent phases. In the case of a certain interval, only the corresponding assessment model is invoked to evaluate the operating performance. In the case of a fuzzy interval, both of the assessment models corresponding to the adjacent phases are used. The assessment results are adaptively integrated with the Bayesian inference based posterior probabilities as the weights and used to evaluate the operating performance of the batch process, which is very challenging for traditional assessment methods. A case study on the fed-batch penicillin fermentation process is used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. As seen from the simulation results, the proposed online assessment framework is able to give an efficient operating performance assessment for multiphase batch processes. Furthermore, the responsible process variable identified by the variable contributions is consistent with the actual situation, which provides a valuable reference for operators and managers to make further production adjustment.

dataset_item.question: How does Gibbs free energy influence ionic mobility and conductivity in ultrathin films of FAA3 and PPO ionomers with different anionic forms?
dataset_item.answer: Gibbs free energy of hydration plays a critical role in determining ionic mobility and conductivity in ultrathin films of FAA3 and PPO ionomers with different anionic forms. This thermodynamic parameter governs the interaction energy between anions and water molecules, which directly influences ionic transport. Fluoride anions exhibit the strongest water affinity (most negative Gibbs free energy), resulting in higher ionic mobility and conductivity at low hydration levels (λ) compared to bromide and bicarbonate forms. FAA3 thin films demonstrate enhanced conductivity relative to membranes due to reduced tortuosity from aligned structures, while PPO films in bromide form experience suppressed conductivity due to ion clustering. Notably, fluoride forms of both ionomers achieve comparable conductivity at equal hydration levels, underscoring the dominant role of hydration thermodynamics. These findings are specific to SiO₂ substrates and may vary with other support materials.

dataset_item.question: How do variations in hydrophobic monomer carbon length and chain type influence the antimicrobial and hemolytic activities of amphiphilic copolymers?
dataset_item.answer:
Variations in hydrophobic monomer carbon length and chain type significantly influence the antimicrobial and hemolytic activities of amphiphilic copolymers. Increasing carbon length enhances hydrophobicity, which generally improves antimicrobial activity by promoting membrane disruption, but also raises hemolytic activity due to increased compatibility with mammalian cell membranes. Shorter carbon lengths (5–9 carbons) and moderate hydrophobicity (C log P between 0 and 2) strike a balance between strong antimicrobial effects and reduced hemolysis.  

Chain type, including cyclic, aromatic, linear, or branched structures, plays a critical role in structural compatibility with microbial membranes and biocompatibility. Linear and branched chains typically reduce hemolysis by limiting excessive hydrophobic interactions, while cyclic and aromatic chains can disrupt this balance, leading to either enhanced antimicrobial activity or increased toxicity. Optimal performance is achieved through a careful balance of hydrophobicity, cationic charge density, and structural compatibility, making the hydrophobicity index (C log P) a valuable pre-screening tool for identifying effective and safe amphiphilic copolymers.

dataset_item.question: What are the thermochemical properties of CaO and CaCO3 that make them suitable for energy storage applications in calcium looping processes?
dataset_item.answer: Calcium oxide (CaO) and calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) are ideal for energy storage in calcium looping (CaL) due to their favorable thermochemical properties. The reversible calcination (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, endothermic) and carbonation (CaO + CO₂ → CaCO₃, exothermic) reactions enable efficient energy storage and release at high temperatures (up to 830°C). During calcination, solar energy drives the decomposition of CaCO₃ into CaO and CO₂, storing energy in chemical form. These products can be stored at ambient temperature with negligible heat loss, ensuring long-term seasonal storage potential. Upon demand, the exothermic carbonation reaction releases heat at high temperatures suitable for power generation, offering high energy density (3.2 GJ/m³). Compared to molten salt systems, CaL operates at higher temperatures, avoids risks of solidification, and achieves efficient integration with concentrated solar power (CSP). Our investigation on the chemical compatibility between V2O5 and AlCl3-[EMIm]Cl ionic liquid electrolytes establishes unambiguously that V2O5 chemically reacts with both Lewis acidic Al2Cl7 - and Lewis neutral AlCl4 - anions. Spectroscopic, electrochemical, and theoretical analyses reveal that the reaction products between V2O5 and Al2Cl7 - are VOCl3 and amorphous Al2O3. Similarly, the reaction products between V2O5 and AlCl4 - are identified as VO2Cl and AlCl3VO3 - with both 4-coordinated and 6-coordinated structures; these soluble products are furthermore electrochemically active, exhibiting reversible redox reactions between V5+ and V2+ oxidation states. Transesterification of cyclic carbonates with CaO catalyst involves a reversible catalytic reaction that occurs in both the homogeneous and heterogeneous phases because of the significant activity of the sparingly soluble CaO in the reaction medium. In this work, kinetic modeling of the homogeneous-heterogeneous-catalytic transesterification is reported for the first time. Homogeneous-reaction kinetics were studied using the range of limiting CaO solubility in methanol. The intrinsic activation energy for the homogeneous reaction is 82.4 kJ/mol, which is greater than that for the heterogeneous reaction (56.8 kJ/mol). Microkinetic models based on reported reaction mechanisms were proposed for both the homogeneous- and heterogeneous-CaO-catalyzed transesterifications. The excellent match between the simulated reaction data and the experimental ones indicate that the proposed mechanisms represent the transesterification reaction reasonably well. Although more rigorous analysis and characterization are needed to provide strong support for the proposed mechanisms, the present work nevertheless provides valuable insights into the reaction mechanism and intrinsic kinetics on a molecular level.

This Account summarizes the recent research work from our group on the design, development, and applications of organocatalytic multiple domino reactions toward the construction of highly functionalized complex structures. A range of triple and quadruple domino reactions catalyzed by a secondary amine organocatalyst have been developed, which provide direct and efficient entry to carbocyclic and heterocyclic scaffolds bearing multiple stereogenic centers with an excellent level of stereocontrol. The salient features of these domino sequences include the use of easily available commercial catalysts and substrates and simple one-pot protocols providing very good domino yields and excellent stereoselectivities under mild reaction conditions. These organocatalytic domino reactions are even combined with other reactions in one-pot reactions to further attain some more diverse scaffolds with increasing molecular complexity. In spite of these exciting results there is still more room for further development of new multiple domino protocols for the asymmetric synthesis of biologically relevant molecular structures. The major limitations found in the development of multiple domino sequences include the limited number of substrate classes activated through the secondary amine catalysts, the lack of generality in the substrate scope, and the high catalyst loading. In future, efforts to design and develop more complex domino reactions leading to the selective products will be the major focus of our group. We envisage that the development of asymmetric multiple domino sequences directed toward specific targets, such as natural products and pharmaceuticals, will make these one-pot processes even more valuable and practical. General rules of thumb for efficient secondary amine-catalyzed domino reactions are given in Scheme .

In pursuit of an efficient and reversible storage medium for the clean energy carrier H2, an extensive DFT study on the structural and hydrogen storage properties of BC3 and BN sheets is performed by means of DFT calculations. In their pristine form, neither of the monolayers can adsorb H2 sufficiently strongly; however, adsorption of small iron clusters, Fe n (n = 1-3), on these monolayers resulted in stable functionalized monolayers which could adsorb H2 effectively. It is observed that the binding energies of Fe n are higher on BC3 than on the BN sheet. Because of the difference of electronegativities, the monolayers there is charge transfer from the Fe clusters to the sheets to give the Fe clusters a partial positive charge. These cations polarize the H2 molecules that are brought into their vicinities and then bind them with electrostatic and van der Waals interactions. The well-known underestimation of H2 adsorption energies caused by the GGA functional has treated by the application of van der Waals corrections to obtain more reliable values. It is revealed that both functionalized systems adsorb H2 with average adsorption energies suitable for practical H2 storage applications although desorption from the BN systems is generally more difficult. Thus, Fe n -BC3 and Fe n -BN could be promising choices as reversible H2 storage materials.

dataset_item.question: How does the combination of aromatic alcohol and aliphatic alcohol as a mixed ring-opening reagent affect the hydroxyl value and mechanical properties of bio-based polyols?
dataset_item.answer: The combination of aromatic alcohol and aliphatic alcohol as a mixed ring-opening reagent significantly enhances the hydroxyl value and mechanical properties of bio-based polyols. This novel approach increases hydroxyl group density, leading to improved compression strength and a more uniform cell structure in derived polyurethane foams. These foams exhibit superior dimensional stability, higher glass transition temperatures, and lower thermal conductivity compared to those made from conventional petroleum-based polyols. The synergistic effects of the aromatic-aliphatic alcohol blend during ring-opening contribute to the enhanced structural integrity, mechanical performance, and thermal properties of the resulting materials.

dataset_item.question: How is fluorescence anisotropy measured in solutions containing perylene and ionic liquids using time-correlated single photon counting?
dataset_item.answer:
Fluorescence anisotropy in solutions containing perylene and ionic liquids is measured using time-correlated single photon counting (TCSPC). The excitation source is a Ti:sapphire oscillator producing ~100 fs laser pulses at 790 nm, which are frequency-doubled in a barium borate crystal to 395 nm for perylene excitation. The polarization of the excitation beam is controlled using a half-wave plate, and the emitted fluorescence at 440 nm is collected and frequency-resolved using a monochromator. Single photons are detected with a multichannel plate detector, providing precise temporal resolution.

To ensure reliable measurements, the instrument response function is calibrated using malachite green under identical experimental conditions, yielding an approximate response time of 85 ps. Background fluorescence contributions from impurities in the ionic liquids are accounted for by measuring reference samples without perylene and subtracting their signals from the perylene-containing samples. This subtraction method isolates perylene's fluorescence, yielding single-exponential decay curves with a consistent lifetime of 5.02 ns, which confirms the reliability of the anisotropy measurements. The technique enables accurate analysis of perylene's reorientational dynamics in ionic liquid solutions.
