inference_contexts: It is common for C n mimBF4 RTILs to be contaminated with fluorescent impurities. It has been documented that these contaminants are generally negligible in concentration, do not have a significant effect on the bulk structure of the ionic liquid, and only become apparent with techniques such as fluorescence. , Such contaminants are excited at the 395 nm sample excitation wavelength and emit at 440 nm, meaning that when present they contribute to the experimental fluorescent decays. Because of the very low concentration of both the perylene and the impurities, it is a safe assumption that they will not interact with each other when solvated by ionic liquids. The contributions of the perylene and the contaminants to the fluorescence decays are therefore additive. For this reason, data from reference samples containing only the RTIL/water mixtures with no dissolved probe were also collected. A moving sample stage was used that interchanges the two samples under computer control so that data were collected on both the ionic liquid samples, alternating between those with perylene and those without, keeping all experimental conditions identical over the course of the experiment. The resulting perylene lifetime decay curves attained after subtraction of the reference sample fluorescence decay were single exponentials with time constants of 5.02 ns within experimental error for all RTILs studied. The measured lifetime is consistent with the perylene lifetime in other solvents. This observed single exponential decays with the same lifetimes indicates the reliability of the background subtraction technique for removing the contribution of fluorescent impurities in the RTILs. Because of the absence of fluorescent impurities, Hmim BF4 samples did not require subtraction, and it yielded the same fluorescent lifetime, within error, as the other samples. Furthermore, two different batches of Bmim BF4 from the supplier were used in the Bmim experiments. One batch had fluorescence impurities and required the impurity fluorescence subtraction. No subtraction was performed on the batch without impurities. The results obtained from both batches were the same, clearly demonstrating the validity of the background subtraction method.

The laser repetition rate was kept at 5 MHz, and excitation peak power was ~70 mW. The instrument response function (IRF) was ~220 ps. The decay analyses were performed by using F 900 software from Edinburgh Instruments. The time-resolved anisotropy was constructed using the expression, r(t) = [I ∥(t) - GI ⊥(t)]/[I ∥ + 2GI ⊥(t)], where G is the ratio between the fluorescence intensity at parallel (I ∥(t)) and perpendicular (I ⊥(t)) polarizations of the emission with respect to the excitation beam. The value of G was measured at a gating window, in which the fluorescence is almost completely depolarized (tail-matching technique). dataset_item.question: How does encapsulation in IRMOF-74-VI affect thermal stability and structural dynamics of cutinase compared to its native state?
dataset_item.answer: Encapsulation of cutinase within IRMOF-74-VI markedly enhances its thermal stability and structural dynamics compared to its native state. Molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that the encapsulated enzyme retains a larger fraction of its secondary structure and exhibits reduced thermal fluctuations even at extreme temperatures, such as 500 K, where the free enzyme denatures. This stabilization arises from hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and salt bridges between the MOF's mesoporous pore walls and the enzyme's surface residues, particularly arginine. These interactions create a protective microenvironment that restricts excessive thermal motion and prevents denaturation. Importantly, the tailored pore size and hydrophobic linkers of IRMOF-74-VI provide an optimal balance of interaction strength to stabilize cutinase without metal ion involvement. These findings highlight the potential of MOFs with engineered structural properties to stabilize large biomolecules under extreme conditions.

inference_contexts: The structural dynamics and properties of the cutinase enzyme encapsulated in IRMOF-74-VI were investigated by MD simulations at five different temperatures. Upon encapsulation, cutinase@IRMOF-74-VI exhibited a higher structural stability with smaller thermal fluctuations at elevated temperatures. During 50 ns of the MD simulations, cutinase retained a larger portion of its secondary structure even at temperatures reaching 500 K, whereas free cutinase had already denatured. The surface activity of the encapsulated cutinase was mostly hydrophobic. IRMOF-74-VI's pore walls consisted of hydrophobic linkers that interacted with the hydrophobic amino acid residues of cutinase. Most of the interactions identified originated from the Arg residues at the surface of the protein. The interactions created by Arg were mostly hydrophobic, i.e.. H-bonding and salt bridges. It is important to note that there was no evidence of metal ion involvement from IRMOF-74-VI in regard to stabilizing the protein structure. IRMOF-74-VI showed that it could provide a suitable environment for protecting cutinase, which led to an improvement in the stability of the enzyme with an optimum range of interaction strengths that prevented enzyme denaturation at extreme temperatures. This indicates that the selective encapsulation of large biomolecules, such as enzymes, can be achieved using mesoporous MOFs with suitable pore sizes, appropriate internal pore environments, and proper organic linker utilizations. More atomic-level investigations of different biomolecules are needed with different MOFs in order to unravel the otherwise unknown behaviors or interactions that occur when targeting potential biocomposites. Such information will significantly contribute to the properly informed utilization of these porous materials for biological applications.

For polymers, natural or otherwise, to produce carbon fiber of a similar quality as PAN, they cannot rely on hydrogen bonding for structural stability or contain a high mass fraction of oxygen, lest they shrink to an unusable extent. A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. Polyalanine-like domains could be incorporated into block copolymers for biomimetic graphite precursors. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

The present study showed that the aminopolycarboxylic chelating surfactant C12-DTPA can be effectively used in combination with two foaming agents for the removal of extremely toxic metal ions such as Cd2+, Zn2+, and Sr2+ from aqueous solution using the ion flotation technique. It was found that the removal of metal ions from the flotation cell is dependent on their chelation behavior with C12-DTPA and on the foaming properties of the samples, both of which change with the pH of the system. The results indicate that both Zn2+ and Cd2+ can be completely removed at pH 5. However, when the pH is increased to 7 and 9, barely 60% of Zn2+ and Cd2+ can be removed from the solution. On the other hand, at pH 5, no removal of Sr2+ was observed, whereas at a pH of 7-9, ~65% removal was achieved under comparable conditions. For efficient separation of metal ions from water systems, the amount of water transferred to the reject foam must also be considered, which is evaluated by measuring the concentration of metal ions in the collected foam. It was found that the interactions between the foaming agent and chelating surfactant affects the concentration of metal ions in the foam. A higher concentration of DoTAC increased the concentration of Sr2+ in the collected foam, because of the strong interactions between DoTAC and C12-DTPA. A higher concentration of DDAO, on the other hand, increased the removal of metal ions from the bulk, because of better foaming properties of the test solution. The separation efficiency is a measure of both the removal of metal ions from the bulk and the concentration of metal ions in the collected foam, and the foaming agent mixture must be designed accordingly. Taking the above parameters into account, it would be useful to design and optimize a selective ion flotation process in competitive systems for the target metal ions.

The overlapping of steric (or electrosteric) and depletion mechanisms for colloidal stabilization of oxidized carbon nanotubes (plasma-oxidized SWCNTs and MWCNTs and chemically oxidized MWCNTs) by amphiphilic PF127 is attained through a matching of the polymer chemical structure (containing hydrophobic PPO and hydrophilic PEO moieties), and its consequent conformational behavior in solution, with the nanocarbon high aspect ratio one-dimensional morphology. For these samples, regardless of the surface charge (ζ potential), the degree of oxidation, and the nanotube diameter and length, colloidal stability in a 0.9% NaCl solution is attained through (i) the wrapping of PF127 around the nanotubes induced by hydrophobic interactions between the PPO moiety and nonoxidized regions of the graphitic sheets (i.e.. polyaromatic regions with sp2 carbon hybridization) and the consequent exposure of hydrophilic PEO moieties to the medium and (ii) the manifestation of repulsive depletion forces for PF127 concentrations superior to 1.0%. Above this concentration, the CNT colloidal stabilization also has little dependence on the PF127 concentration. The same PF127 was not able to colloidally stabilize graphene oxide (chemically oxidized) through steric-based mechanisms due to the small size of PEO moieties in comparison with the large-sized sheets of GO (lateral size of up to 20 μm), thus preventing a suitable steric repulsion for GO sheets. This aspect also explains the absence of stabilizing depletion forces for the GO-PF127 system, in which there is not a proper dimensional and stereochemical matching between the large (i.e.. GO sheets) and small (i.e.. PF127 micelles) particles present in the liquid. On the other hand, long-chain PEG (MW 35000) was unable to colloidally stabilize CNTs due to the absence of significant short-range interactions (e.g.. hydrophobic) that could result in steric-based mechanisms of stabilization. In addition, the absence of a proper dimensional and stereochemical matching between the long-chain PEG 35000 and the high aspect ratio one-dimensional morphology of CNTs did not lead to the manifestation of stabilizing repulsive depletion forces as well. However, large-sized sheets of GO in the presence of PEG 35000 can be colloidally stabilized through repulsive depletion forces, which strongly depend on the polymer concentration, as shown by the stabilization attained for PEG concentrations from 5.0 wt %. The overlapping of these stabilization mechanisms (steric + depletion) observed for CNTs led to a much higher colloidal stabilization in comparison with that attained for the GO-PEG system. For applications in media with low ionic strengths, electric stabilization attained through nanocarbon oxidation can provide a suitable colloidal stability. Conversely, in the particular context of nanomedicine, in which nanocarbons must behave throughout their application as individualized colloidal entities and not as agglomerates in physiological media (e.g.. 0.9% NaCl, with a high ionic strength), oxidation protocols such as acid treatment (which lead to electric stabilization through negative surface charging) are much less effective than the use of suitable biocompatible polymers such as Pluronic F-127 and long-chain PEG.

dataset_item.question: What advancements in catalysts and reaction conditions have contributed to the increased versatility and adoption of palladium-catalyzed N-arylation reactions?
dataset_item.answer: Recent advancements in palladium-catalyzed N-arylation reactions have been driven by innovations in catalyst design, including the development of highly active and selective palladium precatalysts and optimized ligands that enhance reaction efficiency and selectivity. Simplified and user-friendly reaction conditions, such as milder temperatures, broader solvent compatibility, and operational simplicity, have further increased the versatility and accessibility of these reactions. These improvements have enabled reliable C-N bond formation across diverse nitrogen-based coupling partners, facilitating applications in the synthesis of heterocycles, medicinal compounds, natural products, organic materials, and catalysts. The widespread availability of modern palladium precatalysts has accelerated adoption in both academic and industrial settings. Despite significant progress, challenges such as scalability and sustainability continue to motivate further refinement of these methods.

A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. Polyalanine-like domains could be incorporated into block copolymers for biomimetic graphite precursors. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

dataset_item.question: How does the morphology of Pt-Cu frame and shell thickness influence the catalytic performance and recyclability of Pt-Cu frame@HKUST-1 structures?
dataset_item.answer:
The morphology of the Pt-Cu frame and the shell thickness of HKUST-1 play crucial roles in determining the catalytic performance and recyclability of Pt-Cu frame@HKUST-1 structures. Using microwave irradiation, the Pt-Cu frame morphology is tailored by varying glycine concentration, while the HKUST-1 shell thickness is adjusted by tuning crystallization time. Among the synthesized structures, the octahedral Pt-Cu frame exhibits superior catalytic activity for 1-hexene hydrogenation, achieving a turnover number (TON) of 1004 and turnover frequency (TOF) of 2008 h⁻¹, attributed to its abundant exposed active sites and enriched hydrogen environment.

The HKUST-1 shell provides a protective layer that preserves the size and dispersion of the Pt-Cu core, enhancing recyclability by enabling the catalyst to be reused for at least four cycles with minimal activity loss. Additionally, the core-shell architecture facilitates size-selective olefin hydrogenation, showcasing its multifunctional catalytic potential. These combined features highlight the importance of precise control over core morphology and shell thickness in optimizing both catalytic efficiency and durability.

The paper focuses on developing a controllable and efficient method to synthesize metal nanoparticle (NP)-metal organic framework (MOF) composites with unique nanostructures. Specifically, it reports the successful synthesis of Pt-Cu alloy core-shell structures integrated with HKUST-1 MOF using microwave irradiation in a short timeframe (30 minutes). In summary, based on the first-principles calculations, we have systematically investigated the ground structural property, electronic property, and photocatalytic performance of the h-B2O monolayer. Besides, the effects of hydrogen coverages and strains-driven on the HER catalytic activity has been studied. First, we confirmed that the B site of the h-B2O monolayer is a highly active site for HER compared with other possible active sites on the h-B2O monolayer and the B/O defective model. The calculated Gibbs free energy (ΔG H*) of the pristine h-B2O monolayer is -0.07 eV with the adsorbed hydrogen, which is more favorable compared with the Pt catalyst (-0.09 eV). The predicted catalytic activity of the h-B2O monolayer is quite robust with increasing hydrogen ratio, in which ΔG H* is -0.03 eV at the coverage θ = 5/9, revealing that the h-B2O monolayer is quite suitable for HER catalysis even with high coverage. Additionally, we found that the tensile strains (0-2%) have a positive effect on the HER activity of the h-B2O monolayer, resulting in ΔG* being close to 0 eV at low hydrogen coverage. However, the applied compressive strain could strengthen the bonding of hydrogen with the h-B2O monolayer, leading to lower values of ΔG*. After analyzing the DOS, we found that the hydrogen-absorbed h-B2O monolayer retains the metallic property, while increasing the hydrogen coverage drives the Fermi level move toward the lower energy level. Moreover, the reaction kinetics suggest that the HER mechanism of the h-B2O monolayer should follow the Heyrovsky-dominated Volmer-Heyrovsky reaction.

To summarize, we have developed an LDH precursor technique to fabricate a novel NiRu bimetal structure confined by a weak crystalline Ni (Al) O x matrix, Ru/Ni/Ni (Al) O x , with raised catalytic property in selective hydrogenation of DMT to DMCD. The Ru/Ni/Ni (Al) O x catalyst not only showed excellent catalytic activity and selectivity but also exhibited good stability. XRD and SEM confirmed the structure and morphology of the LDH precursor. Cs-corrected HADDF-STEM, HRTEM, and other supplementary characterization techniques demonstrated the initial microstructure evolution of the NiAlRu-LDH precursor unto the NiRu-based catalysts with a unique structure. In addition, low-temperature N2 adsorption-desorption experiments show that compared with those samples at different reduced temperatures, Ru/Ni/Ni (Al) O x formed by reduction temperature 350 °C has a higher surface area, total pore volume, and pore size. This work indicates the effect of Ru for Ni on the preparation process and catalytic properties. And the catalytic reaction data directly show the relationship between the catalytic structure and the performance of catalysts.

(2) Synergistic effects through in situ formation of Co/Fe oxide/hydroxides further enhance the electrocatalytic activity of Co-Fe-S@PB NBs. A series of FeTPA/TiO2 catalysts were prepared and exhibited excellent catalytic performance on the acylation of m-xylene with benzoyl chloride. Meanwhile, these catalysts were characterized by FT-IR, XRD, BET, NH3-TPD, and Py-IR. It was obviously found that 30% FeTPA/TiO2 exhibited better catalytic performance than other catalysts, which was attributed to its larger surface area and micropore volume. dataset_item.question: What is the relationship between ultramicropore volume, nitrogen content, and CO2 adsorption efficiency in porphyrin-based triazine polymers and their carbonized derivatives?
dataset_item.answer:
The relationship between ultramicropore volume, nitrogen content, and CO2 adsorption efficiency in porphyrin-based triazine polymers and their carbonized derivatives is characterized by a synergistic enhancement of adsorption performance. Ultramicropore volume serves as a critical structural parameter, providing the necessary pore size for effective CO2 capture, while nitrogen doping enhances chemical interactions with CO2 molecules.

The polymer HTP2b exhibited an ultramicropore volume of 17% and a CO2 uptake of 173 mg/g, demonstrating good adsorption efficiency and high CO2/N2 selectivity (IAST: 59.35). Upon carbonization with KOH activation at 600°C, its derivative, HTP2b-K600, achieved a significantly higher ultramicropore volume of 62% and nitrogen content of 2.64%, resulting in an improved CO2 uptake of 282 mg/g. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing both ultramicropore volume and nitrogen content for enhanced CO2 adsorption performance. Furthermore, increasing the carbonization temperature was shown to improve surface area and pore volume, underscoring the role of ultramicropores and nitrogen doping in maximizing CO2 capture efficiency.

In summary, higher ultramicropore volume facilitates physical adsorption, while nitrogen doping enhances chemical affinity, making both factors critical for optimizing CO2 adsorption in porphyrin-based triazine polymers and their carbonized derivatives.

### 1. **Summary of the Purpose of the Paper:**
The paper aims to address the challenge of fabricating nitrogen-containing porous organic polymers and their derived porous carbons for efficient CO2 capture. It introduces a simple synthetic strategy using porphyrin-based triazine polymers constructed through one-pot Scholl coupling and Friedel-Crafts reactions. The study evaluates the CO2 capture performance of the polymers and their KOH-activated carbonized derivatives, highlighting the importance of ultramicropore volume and nitrogen content as critical factors for improving CO2 adsorption.

---

### 2. **Classification of Purpose:**

### 3. **Research Questions Relevant to the Abstract:**

- How do the structural and chemical properties of the polymers influence their CO2 capture performance?
- What is the relationship between ultramicropore volume (pore size < 1.2 nm), nitrogen content, and CO2 adsorption efficiency?

inference_contexts: A series of the porphyrin-based triazine polymers was easily fabricated from two N-containing monomers TPP and CC by adjusting the two competitive chemical reactions, namely, Scholl coupling and Friedel-Crafts reaction. The resultant polymer HTP2b had notable V ultra (17%), CO2 uptake (173 mg/g), and CO2/N2 selectivity (IAST: 59.35). After KOH-activated carbonization, the S BET, S micro, V total, and V micro increased greatly, and the S BET (1004-3238 m2/g), V total (0.54-1.76 cm3/g), and V micro (0.41-1.02 cm3/g) increased as the carbonization temperature increased. HTP2b-K600 manifested preferable V ultra (62%, d < 1.2 nm) and N content (2.64%), indicative of its outstanding CO2 uptake (282 mg/g). The N-doped porous carbons had excellent CO2/N2 selectivity (IAST: 25.3), remarkable thermal stability, and recyclability performance. In summary, the fabricated porphyrin-based triazine polymers and derived porous carbons are promising sorbents for CO2 capture and the synthesis strategy based on the one-pot simple reaction is effective for synthesis of some other N-containing polymers and derived porous carbons.

Moreover, the obtained NOCKs exhibited high CO2 capacity (6.77 mmol g-1 at 0 °C and 4.46 mmol g-1 at 25 °C), high dynamic adsorption performance, and excellent regenerability. A large computational data set of polymers and related materials has been mined to unravel trends and hidden chemistry in their dielectric constants and band gaps. By understanding the role of specific atoms and coordination environments, certain "design rules" were developed for optimizing polymers for dielectric (and related) applications. Some of the main conclusions are listed as follows: Organic polymers containing a majority of 4-fold C atoms bonded to H atoms show very large band gaps but low electronic dielectric constants and almost negligible ionic dielectric constants. Organic polymers containing S atoms bonded to 3-fold C atoms show very high electronic dielectric constants and low band gaps. In organic polymers, O and N atoms lead to slightly higher ionic dielectric constants (compared to polymers with only C and H atoms) via bonds with C while maintaining large band gaps. Organometallic polymers far outperform pure organics in terms of simultaneously enhancing the dielectric constant and the band gap. The metal atom, the metal concentration, and its coordination chemistry are the important factors that control the polymer's dielectric constant. 6-fold Sn, Zn, Cd, and Pb atoms bonded with O or F lead to the highest ionic dielectric constants observed in this work, with band gaps in the moderate to high regions. For many of these polymers, modest metal fractions (by volume) of 2-5% were sufficient to obtain dielectric constants greater than 10. The same metal atoms in a 4-fold coordination, meanwhile, led to lower dielectric constants between 3 and 5, highlighting the significance of a higher coordination number.

The DFT calculations in this study show that the formation of inner- and outer-sphere DMA-iron (oxyhydr) oxide complexes are thermodynamically favorable, but that the activation barrier for bidentate formation from monodentate is significantly higher than that for the arsenate system. The calculations reported herein include dispersion corrections which, to our knowledge, were not included in any previous theoretical studies of arsenicals adsorption on metal oxide clusters. Also, extending the model iron (oxyhydr) oxide surface to include four Fe centers produces geometries for DMA complexes that do not over-relax and are in good agreement with experimental bond distances. However, no significant difference in the bidentate complex was obtained when modeling with two or four Fe model surfaces. The Mulliken charge distribution analysis revealed that electrostatic attraction may also play a role in the formation of monodentate complexes (in the transition from an outer-sphere complex), but the same is not observed in the formation of outer-sphere or bidentate complexes.

Several materials prepared from triazine-containing precursors were explored as active materials in Li half cells. Well-defined materials which exhibit strong triazine character show very low gravimetric capacities even if the triazine units are bridged by conjugated moieties, such as phenylene or 2,2′-bipyridine. This directly contradicts the previously suggested bipolar mechanism in which the triazine is n- or p-doped when cycled. In order to achieve high gravimetric capacities, the well-defined conjugated systems must be synthesized at higher temperatures, thereby destroying the triazine unit and creating an N-containing amorphous carbon material. These materials have high concentrations of localized spins (large numbers of unpaired electrons) that may be involved in the discharge and charge mechanisms. The N-containing amorphous carbon materials are very similar to N-containing porous carbon materials that have been evaluated as supercapacitor materials. , The capacity of the amorphous materials trends loosely with specific surface area and C/N content. However, higher surface area does not always result in a higher capacity, suggesting the mechanism is not purely capacitive. The slight observed rate dependence also suggests a pseudocapacitive behavior involving charge transfer processes. These charge transfer processes could involve the unpaired electrons in the amorphous materials, and indeed, the inactive PTI materials do not contain unpaired electrons. Suggestions for future work to further probe the charge storage mechanisms involve using in situ EPR in order to observe the evolution of the spin concentration as a function of discharging and charging.

dataset_item.question: How does the ionic conductivity of sodium-based Na7P3X11 compounds compare to other known sodium-ion solid-state conductors?
dataset_item.answer: The sodium-based Na7P3X11 (X = O, S, Se) compounds exhibit exceptionally high ionic conductivity at room temperature, outperforming other known sodium-ion solid-state conductors. Derived from the Li7P3S11 structure, these materials are predicted by first-principles calculations to be highly promising candidates for next-generation solid-state electrolytes. Their superior ionic conductivity positions them as potential alternatives for advanced sodium-ion batteries. However, further experimental validation is required to confirm their performance and address synthesis challenges, ensuring their practical application in energy storage technologies.

Different series of substitutions on peri-1,8-substituted naphthalene derivatives have been performed to explore how the chalcogen interactions between the O and Y atoms (Y = O, S, and Se) can be modulated. Using our previous experience, we have directly substituted the H atoms of the OH and YH groups by electron-donor (CH3) and electron-withdrawing (F, CN) groups. It is observed that the inclusion of an electron-withdrawing group in the electron acceptor site increases the interaction energy becoming more negative as the polarizability of the atom increases. This is in agreement with an interaction through the σ-hole, and it is also corroborated by a shortening of the intramolecular O Y distances andan increase of the electron density at the BCP and of the second-order perturbation energy E(2) provided by the NBO analysis.

In this study, the humidity-dependent ion conductivity and water content for thin films of different ionic forms of two different alkaline exchange ionomers (AEIs)-FAA3 and PPO ionomer on SiO2 substrate-are reported. This is the first study to report conductivity data for ultrathin films of AEIs and to correlate it to water content. From the computed Gibbs free energy of hydration for ionomer thin films, it is revealed that the fluoride form has highest affinity to water, followed by bromide and bicarbonate forms. From the Gibbs free energy, water content, and conductivity data analyses, it is found that at low λs, ionic conductivity is strongly dependent on ionic mobility which is governed by the energy of interaction (Gibbs free energy) between anion and water molecules. At similar λ, owing to the alignment of FAA3 ionomer thin films, the tortuosity of thin films is much lower than the tortuosity of the membrane; thus, the conductivity of all the ion forms of FAA3 thin films is much greater than the corresponding form of membranes. In addition, the water content and conductivity relationship for fluoride and bromide forms of FAA3 and PPO were compared. At similar λ, fluoride forms of PPO show similar conductivity to FAA3 thin films. The conductivity of the bromide form of PPO is more suppressed than tht of FAA3, which is attributed to the aggravated clustering in PPO. Note that this work reports AEI thin-film property on SiO2 substrate which is not a catalyst support in the fuel cell and electrolyzers. It is known that substrate-polymer interactions can induce structural changes manifesting in substrate-dependent properties of polymers. Accordingly, any extrapolation of the results from the present study to ionomer films on different substrates must be done with caution. A separate future study needs to be conducted on polymer films on a versatile substrate such as carbon.

Our investigation on the chemical compatibility between V2O5 and AlCl3-[EMIm]Cl ionic liquid electrolytes establishes unambiguously that V2O5 chemically reacts with both Lewis acidic Al2Cl7 - and Lewis neutral AlCl4 - anions. Spectroscopic, electrochemical, and theoretical analyses reveal that the reaction products between V2O5 and Al2Cl7 - are VOCl3 and amorphous Al2O3. Similarly, the reaction products between V2O5 and AlCl4 - are identified as VO2Cl and AlCl3VO3 - with both 4-coordinated and 6-coordinated structures; these soluble products are furthermore electrochemically active, exhibiting reversible redox reactions between V5+ and V2+ oxidation states. It is clear that V2O5 is not a chemically stable positive electrode material for rechargeable Al batteries using chloroaluminate ionic liquid electrolytes, regardless of Lewis acidity. Although an Al-V2O5 cell may appear to have electrochemical performance in terms of capacity and cyclability, researchers must be cautious when identifying the origin of the electrochemical reactions. Our investigation also raises the question of the chemical stability of other Al-ion positive electrode materials in chloroaluminate ionic liquid electrolytes.

We have presented the first study of a lithium ion-doped IL incorporated into a MOF and investigated its phase behavior and ionic conductivity. Moreover, for the first time, we have studied the dynamics of lithium ions inside the micropores of the MOF in terms of the self-diffusion coefficient of the lithium ions. XRPD measurements suggest that the (EMI0.8Li0.2) TFSA is incorporated into the micropores of ZIF-8. 19F solid-state NMR measurements show that the motion of the TFSA- anions was gradually suppressed inside the micropores by lowering the temperature, which indicates the absence of the apparent freezing transition. In contrast, the motion of the Li+ cations showed a steeper decrease than that for the TFSA- anions below 193 K. This is explained by the phase transition of the Li+ cations with other ions or the inner surface of ZIF-8 into a solid phase inside the micropores. This explanation is consistent with the results of the DSC measurements, in which the endothermic heat flow was obtained at the onset temperature of 200 K. The ionic conductivity of the (EMI0.8Li0.2) TFSA inside the micropores was 2 orders of magnitude lower than that of the bulk (EMI0.8Li0.2) TFSA. This result suggests that the ionic conductivity is drastically enhanced by the conductive paths for the ions, which are strongly connected with increasing concentrations of the guest ions. The activation energy for the self-diffusion coefficient of lithium ions in ELT@Z 100 is comparable with that in ELT-bulk. This result suggests that Li+ cations can diffuse with low activation energy through the micropores because of the exchange of the solvating TFSA- anions, similarly to the Grotthuss mechanism. The lithium ion-doped IL@MOF system provides a novel ion conductor to study the conductive mechanism of lithium ions.

dataset_item.question: How do centralized and decentralized strategies for organic waste treatment differ in terms of economic performance, electricity generation, and greenhouse gas emissions?
dataset_item.answer: Centralized and decentralized organic waste treatment strategies each offer distinct advantages across economic performance, electricity generation, and greenhouse gas emissions. Centralized systems excel in economic performance and chemical production due to economies of scale and higher energy efficiency, despite requiring higher initial investment costs. These systems also benefit from improved biomass utilization, which partially offsets transportation-related greenhouse gas emissions from long-distance biomass transport. However, decentralized systems are more cost-effective for electricity generation, as they involve lower investment costs and minimize transportation emissions due to localized operations. While centralized strategies generate higher greenhouse gas emissions from logistics, their overall energy efficiency mitigates these impacts. Both approaches significantly contribute to job creation, with over 22,000 new jobs generated across the bioenergy supply chain. A hybrid model integrating centralized and decentralized elements could optimize the balance between economic performance, electricity generation, and environmental sustainability.

### 1. **Summary of the Purpose**  
The paper aims to evaluate the impacts of decentralized and centralized supply chain strategies in the context of bio-based waste management. Specifically, it formulates a multi-echelon structure and uses a mixed-integer linear programming model to optimize the supply chain strategy. The study integrates economic, social, and environmental aspects to minimize system costs, reduce negative impacts of transportation and production, and adapt to dynamic demands. The ultimate goal is to determine the most robust supply chain strategy for optimal biomass feedstock utilization.

---

### 2. **Classification of Purpose**  
The purpose of the paper emphasizes **"<result>"**, as it focuses on determining the outcomes of different supply chain strategies (centralized vs. decentralized) and identifies the most effective approach based on the study's findings.

---

### 3. **Relevant Research Questions**  
1. How do decentralized and centralized supply chain strategies differ in their impacts on bio-based waste management?  
2. What are the key factors influencing the optimal utilization of biomass feedstocks in a multi-echelon supply chain structure?  
3. How can supply chain models be optimized to balance economic, social, and environmental objectives in bio-based waste management?  
4. What are the trade-offs between investment and operating costs in centralized vs. decentralized supply chain strategies?  
5. How does the centralized model enable the production of a broader portfolio of bio-based products despite its higher costs?  
6. What role does dynamic demand play in the optimization of bio-based supply chain strategies?  
7. How does the mixed-integer linear programming model using generalized disjunctive programming improve decision-making for supply chain integration?
dataset_item.true_false_question: Does a centralized organic waste treatment strategy minimize greenhouse gas emissions more effectively than decentralized systems purely due to lower transportation emissions?

inference_contexts: Considering the emissions from transportation, the main driver for the generation of greenhouse gas emissions is the transportation of the waste to treatment facilities. Centralization increases the shipment of biomass feedstock from supply locations to treatment facilities over longer distances. However, since centralization benefits from high capacities and economies of scale, such as an increase in biomass utilization and energy efficiency and a decrease in the production cost, it can compensate for its transportation expenses and emissions. Investment in renewable energy sources is also associated with the formation of jobs and employment opportunities, regional development, and the creation of a new source of income for the local communities, in addition to enhancing the market reliability of bioenergy industries and energy security. The results indicated that opening centralized and decentralized biomass treatment plants generated more than 22,000 new jobs in all stages of the bioenergy supply chain.

The results showed that the centralized model for the deployment of organic waste treatment and upgrading facilities is the superior strategy in terms of economic performance and production of all types of chemicals, although it involves higher investment costs. However, the centralized approach had a lower capacity for electricity generation compared to the decentralized strategy. Therefore, the centralized approach is less efficient in terms of producing electricity than the decentralized model. This implies that the production of chemicals is the main driver of the profitability of the centralized network for the treatment of organic waste. In case the generation of electricity is the primary goal, a decentralized scheme should be taken into consideration since it generates a higher amount of power, involving a noticeably lower investment cost. However, its economic performance is more inferior to the centralized model.

A further study with more focus on incentive policies for the deployment of a bio-based waste treatment system is recommended. Moreover, a hybrid strategy combining centralized and decentralized supply chain models will need to be explored to assess its potentials for the design of optimal supply chain networks, considering the treatment and valorization of organic waste. In addition, the sensitivity analysis of the principal process parameters toward the design of a resilient network needs to be carried out. Another possible area of future research would be to investigate the strategic decision-making process on the location of the facilities in the target region to decide which centralized or decentralized scheme would be more beneficial.

In this research, mathematical models are developed to determine the optimal supply chains for the treatment and valorization of organic waste. Two strategies for the deployment of processing facilities are studied, including a centralized approach, in which all stages of the organic waste treatment are integrated into the same location, and a decentralized strategy, where different stages of the biomass processing are distributed across diverse areas allowing multiple exchanges of products between various locations. The proposed supply chain models are built based on the sustainable development objectives in which the economic, environmental, and social aspects are considered concurrently. The economic component of the model calculates the total cost of the network and net profit. Environmental impacts on industrial operations and transportation are considered and analyzed by measuring their effects on the ecosystems. Finally, the impact of the geographical location of facilities on the creation of employment opportunities for the local population and the improvement of the regional human development index of each region are analyzed to assess the social impact of the deployment of the bio-based waste treatment facilities.

This work was aimed at the plant-wide control of an amine gas sweetening plant. The plant comprises two gas absorption columns in which the sour gases are absorbed from natural gas, two solvent regeneration columns, and two heat exchangers. DMPC was implemented on this network for the start up of the plant with and without disturbances and measurement noise. The optimal architecture for DMPC was obtained from a modularity maximization algorithm which separates the two stages of absorption and regeneration as different subnetworks. The performance of DMPC on the optimal decomposition was compared with that of a fully centralized MPC architecture, a decentralized MPC architecture, and distributed MPC on the suboptimal decomposition obtained from the modularity maximization algorithm. The closed-loop performance of DMPC implemented on the optimal decomposition was found to be comparable to that of CMPC and superior to the other architectures for all the control problems considered. The computation time for solving the optimization problem was also reasonably low (larger than only the decentralized MPC architecture) for DMPC based on the optimal decomposition. This work, thus, demonstrates a promising path for designing practically implementable model based controllers for large-scale tightly integrated plants. Future research will address the state estimation problem, further improvement and validation of the model based on plant data, and the real-time implementation of the proposed control structure.

dataset_item.question: How do molecular aggregations in chlorobenzene solutions of PTB7 and PTB7-Th vary with concentration and temperature?
dataset_item.answer: Molecular aggregations in chlorobenzene solutions of PTB7 and PTB7-Th exhibit distinct concentration- and temperature-dependent behavior. Both copolymers form H-aggregates in concentrated solutions and films, which are disrupted by dilution or heating. PTB7-Th demonstrates more pronounced variations in photoluminescence (PL) peak intensity and spectral shifts compared to PTB7, indicating a greater susceptibility of its aggregates to dissociation. This behavior is attributed to the enhanced chain coplanarity and thiophene-modified structure of PTB7-Th, which results in a red-shifted optical transition and lower band gap relative to PTB7. These structural differences lead to PTB7-Th aggregates being more readily disrupted in solution, as revealed by absorbance and PL spectra.

inference_contexts: A comparative study of the optical properties and the molecular aggregation of the two copolymers PTB7 and PTB7-Th is presented. By spectroscopic ellipsometry, it has been shown that the differences of the chemical structure between these two copolymers induces a change in the morphology and the optical properties. By replacing the oxygen atom in the BDT side chains of the PTB7 by a thiophene unit, the optical transitions in the imaginary part of the dielectric function of PTB7-Th are red-shifted, resulting in a lower bad gap due to an enhancement of chains coplanarity. In order to go further in the comparison and the understanding, we have presented a detailed analysis of absorbance and PL spectra of the two copolymers in chlorobenzene solutions. We have shown that it is possible to resolve the solution morphology and its changes by following the evolution of the intensity of the 0-0 and 0-1 peaks. Concentration and temperature dependent absorbance and PL spectra show that diluting and heating the chlorobenzene solutions of the aggregates can break the aggregates. We observe that the variations of the PL peak intensity and the spectral shift are more pronounced in the PTB7-Th than in the PTB7. Moreover, the PL spectra analysis shows that the emission of the film and of the concentrated solution arises from H-aggregates and that these H-aggregates are more easily broken in the PTB7-Th solution than in the PTB7 one. This study contributes to the understanding of the photophysics of two well-known copolymers in organic photovoltaics and permits correlation of the morphological change in the optical properties.

The protonated DAT moieties function as hydrogen-donors and interact with triphosphates of ATP via multiple hydrogen-bonding and electrostatic interactions. Without ATP, the DAT-containing block copolymer self-assembled into spherical micelles in a thermodynamically steady state at pH higher than its pK a. By binding with ATP fuel, the polymeric micelles disrupted into the aggregates of ATP/polymer hybrid complexes spontaneously. Once the energy stored in ATP was consumed through enzymatic hydrolysis, the aggregates of hybrid complexes underwent an automatous fusion to the initial PDAT micelles. Transient self-assembly cycles were established by ATP fuel and phosphatase. The temporal change in the assembly structure was controlled by the ATP binding and hydrolysis energy, and the cyclical transition of polymeric micelles to hybrid complexes driven by the continuous supply of ATP fuel. The good biocompatibility of this DAT-containing polymer make it a promising candidate for biological applications. Taking advantage of the molecular recognition of DAT-containing polymer via versatile nonconvalent interactions, we expect this study will provide a new strategy to construct active biomimetic assemblies for imitating cellular and organellar activities and applying in therapeutics.

dataset_item.question: What is the influence of Lewis acidic strength and textural properties on the catalytic performance of iron-modified tungstophosphoric acid supported on titania in the acylation of m-xylene?
dataset_item.answer: The catalytic performance of iron-modified tungstophosphoric acid supported on titania (FeTPA/TiO₂) in the acylation of *m*-xylene with benzoyl chloride is significantly influenced by both Lewis acidic strength and textural properties. A 30% FeTPA/TiO₂ catalyst demonstrated optimal activity, attributed to its enhanced Lewis acidity, larger surface area, and increased micropore volume, which together improve reactant accessibility and activation. The strong Lewis acidity promotes the activation of benzoyl chloride, facilitating the acylation reaction. Textural properties, such as high surface area and micropore volume, further contribute to efficient catalytic performance by increasing the active sites available for the reaction. However, calcination temperatures above 573 K lead to the decomposition of the active component, adversely affecting performance. Under optimized reaction conditions—including controlled temperature, catalyst dosage, and reactant ratio—a high yield of 95.1% of 2,4-dimethylbenzophenone was achieved. This highlights the critical balance between acidity and porosity in achieving superior catalytic efficiency.

inference_contexts: A series of FeTPA/TiO2 catalysts were prepared and exhibited excellent catalytic performance on the acylation of m-xylene with benzoyl chloride. Meanwhile, these catalysts were characterized by FT-IR, XRD, BET, NH3-TPD, and Py-IR. It was obviously found that 30% FeTPA/TiO2 exhibited better catalytic performance than other catalysts, which was attributed to its larger surface area and micropore volume. Moreover, the increase of Lewis acidic strength could also efficiently enhance the catalytic activity. Furthermore, the influence of catalyst calcination temperature was studied, and it was observed that the active component started to decompose when catalyst calcination temperature was beyond 573 K. Then, the reaction parameters, including reaction temperature, catalyst dose, and molar ratio of m-xylene to benzoyl chloride, were optimized, and a 95.1% yield of 2,4-dimethylbenzophenone was obtained under optimal conditions. Finally, the kinetics of the benzoylation of m-xylene over 30% FeTPA/TiO2 was established.

One important aspect for the structural evolution for NP/NW catalysts in general is the strong dependence on the chemical environment of the catalysts. In contrast to the above electrocatalysis examples where structural evolution could occur due to the presence of electrolyte at the catalyst interface which facilitates the dissolution of metal ions upon dealloying, the study of the same or similar nanocatalysts under gas-phase reaction conditions offers a different perspective to look at the core-shell structural evolution under reaction conditions. Understanding the dynamic processes of the core-shell/alloy structures under oxidative environments is not only for enhancing the catalytic performance in the gas-phase reaction, but also provides insight for the design of active and stable catalysts. For example, gas-phase hydrocarbon oxidation reactions have traditionally relied on oxygen-activation sites on the peripheral zones of oxide-supported noble metal catalysts. Recently, the initial alloying of NMs and 3d-TMs serves as an intriguing pathway for the design of active surface sites where the NMs provide adsorption site for CO and the surface-oxygenated 3d-TMs offer oxygen-activation sites. The NM/3d-TM alloy NPs undergo surface oxygenation, forming a CHA-type core with 3d-TM-oxygenated shell structure. Further understanding of the role of this type of structural evolution in enhancing activity and durability may lead to a new research frontier for the design of new-generation oxidation catalysts by tuning compositions and morphologies at the atomic scale. ,,, By highlighting the selected examples in connection with the recent advances in the field, this Account serves as a springboard from fundamental understanding of the core-shell and alloy structural dynamics to the broad applications of the nanostructured catalysts and electrocatalysts. There are still many challenging questions remaining to be answered, including how the atomic-scale arrangements of the surface active sites correlate with the nanophase structures of the NPs/NWs during the nanoscale dynamic processes, and how the structural durability of the catalysts in the catalytic processes can be controlled to enable the performance durability of the catalysts. Part of the ongoing investigations involves an in-depth understanding of factors controlling the composition optimization and the realloying under electrochemical and fuel cell operating conditions. Future studies will need to be advanced in several fronts, including the use of surface-sensitive techniques, especially under in situ/operando measurement modes, to probe the surface sites and surface/subsurface species, the design of multicomponent catalysts with nanoscale thermodynamic stability in the reactive environment, and the computational modeling of the atomic mobilities on and in the NPs/NWs in the presence of surface and interfacial species. These advancements will also benefit many areas of the applications of the NP and NW catalysts, especially in the area of energy and environmental sustainability.

Can DCPs elevate the performance of BLYP to that of B3LYP? This is a question that was posed in the Introduction. As computational chemistry methods are applied to increasingly larger systems, the question of their efficiency-in particular, with respect to run time-becomes critical. Formally, GGA functionals like BLYP scale as N 3 with system size (with N being the number of electrons), whereas hybrid functionals scale with N 4. Therefore, low-cost corrections such as D3 and DCP that may elevate the performance of BLYP to that of B3LYP or better may be of value. To examine this possibility, we present in Table a summary of some of the performance statistics for BLYP-D3-DCP/6-31+G (2d,2p) for the benchmark sets described above and compare these to statistics obtained using B3LYP-D3/6-31+G (2d,2p). We also conducted additional performance assessments of the two methods on the BHPERI, DARC, BSR36, and the RSE43 databases. We use D3 corrections with B3LYP for our comparison because D3 has a computational cost that is negligible relative to that of the underlying DFT method and because D3 corrections (or similar) are required to predict noncovalent interactions that are reasonable. It is worthwhile restating that D3 corrections that were designed for use with B3LYP were also designed for use with nearly complete basis sets. The corrections nevertheless improve the performance of "small basis set" B3LYP, as has been shown in the past, in particular for the treatment of noncovalent interactions.

A novel titanosilicate with MWW structure was synthesized by a sequential treatment of ERB-1 with deboronation and atom-planting method to develop an epoxide catalyst. The XRD patterns and N2 sorption isotherm curves demonstrate that the fundamental morphology of MWW structure and order stacking layers are retained intact during the sequential treatment. The FTIR and DRIFT characteristic results reveal that the silanol hydroxyl nests generated by deboronation process are further consumed by the dehydrochlorination of TiCl4 during the atom-planting treatment. At the same time, the titanium species are incorporated into the framework of MWW structure. The EDS, UV-vis, and UVRRS characterization results reveal that the amount and coordination states of the incorporated Ti species can be controlled by the atom-planting treatment time and temperature. The incorporated Ti species treated at 573 K by atom-planting are coexisted in T d and Oh coordination, and those treated at 773 K are mainly T d coordination Ti species, all these samples contain small amounts of TiO2. The epoxidation performance of the incorporated different Ti species in the MWW micropore zeolite structure were investigated through the liquid-phase epoxidation of 1-hexene with H2O2 and epoxidation of cyclohexene with tert-butyl hydroperoxide to compare the efficiency of Ti species in the hydrophilic and hydrophobic system. The catalytic results show the samples with both the T d and Oh coordination Ti species can catalyze the 1-hexene epoxidation with H2O2 and epoxidation of cyclohexene with TBHP. Moreover, the framework T d-coordinated titanium species are more efficient for epoxidation than extra-framework Oh Ti species. The Ti-containing deboronated ERB-1 of MWW structure samples show superior epoxidation catalytic performance on bulky molecules than the TS-1. Moreover, the reactant conversion increases with the increase of the incorporated titanium amount for both 1-hexene and cyclohexene epoxidation. After acid treatment, a portion of the Ti species in the samples can be leached, and the conversion also decreases. The reusability experiment results indicate that the implanted Ti species by atom-planting are stable in Ti-D-ERB-1.

dataset_item.question: How can potency and selectivity of protein tyrosine phosphatase inhibitors be improved?
dataset_item.answer: The potency and selectivity of protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) inhibitors can be improved by adopting a multi-faceted approach that leverages both active site targeting and interactions with unique peripheral binding pockets. Anchoring inhibitors to the PTP active site with non-hydrolyzable pTyr mimetics ensures strong and specific binding, while incorporating secondary binding elements enhances selectivity by discriminating against off-target phosphatases. Employing bivalent ligand strategies and fragment-based optimization of pTyr mimetics further refines binding affinity and pharmacological properties. This approach addresses challenges of bioavailability and selectivity, yielding inhibitors with high potency, selectivity, and favorable pharmacokinetics. The efficacy of these optimized inhibitors has been demonstrated in vivo across animal models of diseases such as cancer, diabetes/obesity, autoimmune disorders, and tuberculosis, validating PTPs as viable therapeutic targets.

### Task 1: **Summary of the Paper's Purpose**  
The paper aims to address the challenges in targeting protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPs) for therapeutic intervention, overcoming concerns about their "undruggable" nature due to issues of inhibitor selectivity and bioavailability. The authors propose a novel approach using bivalent ligands and nonhydrolyzable pTyr mimetics to develop potent, selective, and bioactive PTP inhibitors. The study demonstrates the feasibility of these inhibitors in animal models for diseases such as cancer, diabetes/obesity, autoimmune disorders, and tuberculosis, with the ultimate goal of advancing PTP-based drug discovery and therapeutic applications.

---

### Task 2: **Classification of Purpose**  
The paper's emphasis is on **"<result>"**, as the focus is on demonstrating the feasibility and efficacy of the proposed PTP inhibitors, as well as providing experimental results that validate their potency, selectivity, and bioactivity.

---

### Task 3: **Relevant Research Questions**  
1. **Biological Function and Mechanisms**:  
   - How does aberrant tyrosine phosphorylation contribute to the etiology of specific diseases such as cancer or autoimmune disorders?  
   - What unique peripheral pockets exist near the PTP active site, and how can they be exploited for selective inhibition?  

2. **Drug Design and Selectivity**:  
   - What molecular strategies can be employed to enhance the selectivity of PTP inhibitors among closely related family members?  
   - How do bivalent ligands interact with both the PTP active site and peripheral pockets to achieve increased potency and selectivity?  

3. **Bioavailability and Cell Permeability**:  
   - What structural characteristics enable nonhydrolyzable pTyr mimetics to penetrate cell membranes efficiently while maintaining binding affinity?  
   - Can the polar properties of pTyr mimetics be optimized further to enhance bioavailability without compromising inhibitor activity?  

4. **Therapeutic Applications and Validation**:  
   - How effective are PTP inhibitors in vivo in treating specific diseases such as diabetes/obesity or tuberculosis?  
   - What experimental models can be used to validate the efficacy and safety of PTP inhibitors for clinical use?  

5. **Drug Discovery and Broader Impacts**:  
   - How can the findings of this study dispel concerns about the druggability of PTPs and encourage further exploration of PTP-based drug development?  
   - What are the implications of well-characterized PTP inhibitors for functional interrogation of disease biology and therapeutic innovation?  

These questions align with the themes of the abstract and contribute to advancing materials science knowledge in the context of biomolecular interactions and therapeutic design.
dataset_item.true_false_question: Can the potency and selectivity of protein tyrosine phosphatase inhibitors be improved by solely targeting the active site with non-hydrolyzable pTyr mimetics?

inference_contexts: The PTPs comprise a large family of signaling enzymes that are key regulators of cellular signaling. There is ample evidence that alteration of PTP expression, misregulation, and mutation lead to disease manifestations. These connections have made targeting of PTPs attractive as a novel therapeutic strategy. However, the PTPs have historically been widely dismissed as "undruggable" and so they remain a largely underexploited resource for therapeutic intervention. Major obstacles to successful PTP-based drug discovery are target validation and attaining inhibitor selectivity and bioavilability. Our work demonstrate that PTP inhibitor potency and selectivity can be addressed by targeting both the active site and unique peripheral binding pockets. Using appropriate pTyr mimetic to anchor the inhibitor to PTP active site, the success of this approach relies on the introduction of secondary binding elements to enhance on-target potency and impart selectivity against off-target phosphatases. Our work also establish that it is feasible to acquire PTP inhibitors that are sufficiently polar to bind the active site and yet still possess favorable pharmacological properties. By taking a fragment-based approach with a number of nonhydrolyzable pTyr mimetics, we have obtained PTP inhibitors with high potency and selectivity as well as excellent in vivo efficacy in animal models of oncology, diabetes/obesity, autoimmunity, and tuberculosis. Well-characterized, potent, selective, and bioactive inhibitors are essential tools for functional interrogation of PTPs in disease biology and target validation. They will also play a critical role in illuminating the druggability of this underexplored target class and provide the groundwork for new therapies for the treatment of human diseases.

dataset_item.question: How does sodium ion concentration affect the desorption of ciprofloxacin from pyrogenic carbonaceous materials?
dataset_item.answer: Increasing sodium ion concentration significantly enhances the desorption of ciprofloxacin (CIP) from pyrogenic carbonaceous materials (PCMs). Experimental results demonstrate that raising sodium ion concentration from 0.01 mol/L to 0.45 mol/L, a level that mimics the ionic strength of river estuary conditions, promotes CIP release over multiple desorption cycles. This phenomenon is attributed to the weakening of cation-π interactions—a primary sorption mechanism for CIP on PCMs—caused by competitive displacement of CIP by sodium ions in solution. The effect of sodium ions was consistently observed across four consecutive desorption cycles, indicating the robustness of this interaction under varying conditions.

dataset_item.question: How do molecule-molecule and substrate-molecule interactions influence the structure and stability of croconic acid networks on Au(111) and Ag(111)?
dataset_item.answer: Croconic acid (CA) forms distinct self-assembled networks on Au(111) and Ag(111) due to differences in molecule-molecule and substrate-molecule interactions. On Au(111), the network structure is dominated by intermolecular hydrogen bonding, resulting in a synthetic nonpolar Kagome lattice with minimal influence from the substrate. This configuration is energetically favorable, though polar variants are plausible due to small energy differences comparable to crystalline CA. Conversely, on Ag(111), the network is strongly influenced by substrate-molecule interactions, leading to the formation of a chiral honeycomb structure. The stability of this network arises from strong carbonyl oxygen-silver interactions, epitaxial matching, and enhanced overlap between adsorbate and surface wave functions. Additionally, the Ag(111) substrate provides a chemically equivalent environment for each CA molecule, which, along with entropy effects and finite temperature contributions, stabilizes the high-symmetry honeycomb network despite it not being the lowest energy configuration predicted by DFT. Overall, the interplay between optimized intermolecular interactions on Au(111) and specific adsorbate-substrate electronic interactions on Ag(111) drives the distinct structural and stability differences observed.

dataset_item.question: What are the spectroscopic signatures and timescales associated with bimolecular excited-state proton transfer between hydroxy-trifluoromethyl-coumarin and methylimidazole in deuterated chloroform?
dataset_item.answer:
The bimolecular excited-state proton transfer (ESPT) between hydroxy-trifluoromethyl-coumarin (CouOH) and methylimidazole (MI) in deuterated chloroform occurs with a time constant of approximately 1 picosecond, as determined by ultrafast transient infrared (TRIR) and transient absorption (TA) spectroscopies. The reaction proceeds exclusively through pre-hydrogen-bonded CouOH-MI complexes, which have an equilibrium constant of 300 M⁻¹, and does not involve diffusion-controlled processes or excited-state tautomerization under the studied conditions (≤8 mM MI).  

Spectroscopic signatures of the ESPT include vibrational markers of the CouO⁻*···HMI⁺ photoproduct detected via TRIR measurements, and subsequent rearrangement into a π-stacked exciplex observed in TA spectroscopy. The study confirms that the reaction is limited to direct proton transfer within pre-associated pairs, ruling out multibody tautomerization or diffusion-limited mechanisms.  

These findings highlight the ultrafast nature of ESPT and provide insight into the dynamics and structural evolution of the reaction intermediates.

dataset_item.question: What are the spectroscopic advantages of lipid tether WK3SH in minimizing spectral interference during SEIRA analysis of membrane proteins?
dataset_item.answer: The lipid tether WK3SH offers significant spectroscopic advantages in minimizing spectral interference during surface-enhanced infrared absorption (SEIRA) analysis of membrane proteins. By reducing the contribution of overlapping IR bands from the lipid bilayer, WK3SH enables unobstructed observation of key processes such as the catalytic generation of transmembrane proton gradients and redox-active ubiquinone dynamics. This design enhances the ability to monitor pH changes in the submembrane reservoir and facilitates detailed spectroscopic analysis of bioenergetic processes, such as those involving membrane proteins like ubiquinol oxidase. Overall, WK3SH optimizes SEIRA measurements by isolating protein-specific signals and minimizing background interference, improving the clarity and precision of data.

dataset_item.question: How does the type of noble-gas matrix affect the reaction pathways and product distribution during photoreaction of O3-trimethylamine complexes?
dataset_item.answer:
The type of noble-gas matrix profoundly impacts the reaction pathways and product distribution during the photoreaction of O3-trimethylamine (TMA) complexes. In a neon (Ne) matrix, visible-light irradiation at wavelengths ≥ 800 nm predominantly yields trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO), while higher-energy light at 455 nm also produces dimethylaminomethanol (DMAM). The Ne matrix facilitates gas-phase-like reaction mechanisms, allowing TMAO formation through collision between O (³P) and TMA, followed by rapid relaxation to the ground state. DMAM forms either via recombination of radical intermediates (OH and CH₂N(CH₃)₂) within the matrix cage or relaxation on the triplet surface.

In contrast, an argon (Ar) matrix significantly alters the reaction dynamics due to heavy-atom effects, which suppress TMAO production and favor DMAM as the dominant product. Additionally, DMAM exists as stable G+G⁻ and TG conformers within the Ar matrix, with low isomerization barriers (<4 kJ mol⁻¹), preventing other conformers from persisting. The matrix environment thus dictates the reaction selectivity and product distribution, highlighting the critical role of noble-gas matrices in modulating photochemical pathways.

dataset_item.question: What is the mechanism by which La oxide deposition recovers oxygen exchange kinetics in PCO films affected by Si impurities?
dataset_item.answer: Lanthanum oxide (La₂O₃) deposition restores oxygen exchange kinetics in silicon-contaminated Pr₀.₁Ce₀.₉O₂-δ (PCO) films through a reaction with silicon impurities to form a porous La-silicate layer. This silicate layer prevents the silicon-related phase from blocking oxygen exchange sites while ensuring gas accessibility to the PCO surface, thus recovering the oxygen exchange rate. The mechanism is selective to La and Sm oxides, which are capable of forming reactive silicates, unlike other tested oxides such as Nb, Al, Ti, and Zn, which do not exhibit this behavior. Additionally, the recovery effect is specific to Si-induced degradation, as La oxide shows no improvement in materials affected by other mechanisms, such as Sr segregation in SrTi₀.₆₅Fe₀.₃₅O₃-δ. Incorporating La into PCO as a solid solution further demonstrates long-term stability by mitigating Si-related aging and maintaining oxygen exchange functionality.

### Task 1: Summarize the Purpose of the Paper
The paper investigates the impact of Si impurities on oxygen exchange kinetics in Pr₀.₁Ce₀.₉O₂-δ (PCO), a mixed ionic-electronic conductor used in solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) electrodes. Using a novel optical transmission relaxation (OTR) technique, the study demonstrates how Si impurities degrade surface oxygen exchange kinetics by forming a blocking layer. The authors show that this degradation can be mitigated by depositing a La oxide film, which reacts with Si to form a porous La- and Si-containing layer, thereby recovering oxygen exchange performance. Surface treatments with other oxides (Nb, Al, Ti, and Zn) were not found to recover oxygen exchange kinetics. La oxide was also deposited on aged SrTi0.65Fe0.35O3-δ, prone to degradation via Sr segregation (as opposed to siliceous phases), and no improvement was found, further indicating that La reacts with Si and is not leading to a significant catalytic effect. dataset_item.question: How do sequential bleach cleaning and ventilation practices influence indoor volatile organic compound mixing ratios and secondary organic aerosol formation?
dataset_item.answer:
Sequential bleach cleaning practices significantly influence indoor volatile organic compound (VOC) mixing ratios and secondary organic aerosol (SOA) formation. Experiments conducted in controlled environments, such as test houses, revealed that repeated bleach mopping throughout the day increases the concentrations of chlorinated VOCs, nitrogenated VOCs, and secondary pollutants like cyanogen chloride (ClCN) and isocyanic acid (HNCO). These reactions are further amplified when terpenes from prior cooking or cleaning activities interact with bleach, contributing to the formation of volatile chlorinated organic acids and submicrometer particulate organic mass concentrations.

Ventilation practices, such as opening doors and windows after cleaning events, temporarily reduce pollutant levels by diluting the indoor air. However, repeated bleach applications sustain high concentrations of harmful compounds, demonstrating that these chemical reactions occur independently of light exposure. Measurements using advanced analytical tools like time-of-flight chemical ionization mass spectrometry and gas chromatography provide insights into the complex interactions between cleaning chemicals and indoor air quality. While ventilation mitigates short-term risks, the persistent formation of SOAs and toxic VOCs highlights the need for caution when using bleach for sequential cleaning indoors.

dataset_item.question: How do thermodynamic efficiencies and controllability features compare between dividing-wall distillation columns with upper and lower partitions and conventional distillation columns?
dataset_item.answer: Dividing-wall distillation columns (DWCs) with upper (DWCU) and lower (DWCL) partitions demonstrate significantly higher thermodynamic efficiencies compared to conventional distillation columns and the Petlyuk system. Exergy analyses and simulations reveal that DWCU achieves the highest thermodynamic efficiency, as it allows all components to be vaporized simultaneously at moderate reflux ratios, minimizing energy consumption. In contrast, DWCL offers improved controllability due to the inclusion of additional reboilers, which provide more operational flexibility. Conventional distillation columns, while less energy-efficient, outperform DWCs in terms of controllability due to their simpler configuration and more straightforward operation. Thus, DWCs present a trade-off between energy efficiency and controllability, with DWCU optimized for thermodynamic performance and DWCL better suited for operational flexibility.

dataset_item.question: How does substituting Te with Se affect the solid solubility of Pb and thermal conductivity in Ge0.55Pb0.45Te-based alloys?
dataset_item.answer: Substituting tellurium (Te) with selenium (Se) in Ge₀.₅₅Pb₀.₄₅Te-based alloys significantly enhances the solid solubility of lead (Pb) within the GeTe-based phase, effectively suppressing PbTe precipitation. This increased solubility strengthens phonon scattering through intensive alloy scattering, leading to a substantial reduction in lattice thermal conductivity. Record-low thermal conductivity values of 0.67 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ at room temperature and 0.45 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 723 K were achieved in Ge₀.₅₅Pb₀.₄₅Te₀.₅Se₀.₅ alloys. Importantly, this substitution maintains the power factor, enabling an optimized thermoelectric performance. A peak ZT value of 1.55 at 723 K was achieved with 50% selenium substitution, representing a significant improvement over the selenium-free counterpart.

dataset_item.question: How do functional groups in phenylalanine and acid ligands influence passivation of surface defects in methylammonium lead bromide perovskite nanocrystals?
dataset_item.answer:
Functional groups in phenylalanine (Phe)—including the aromatic benzene ring, amine group, and carboxylic acid group—play a critical role in passivating surface defects in methylammonium lead bromide (MAPbBr₃) perovskite nanocrystals (PNCs). These groups mediate the solution pH and surface hydrophobicity, facilitating interactions with charged or electron-deficient surface defects. Acid ligands such as oleic acid (OA) and methylphosphoric acid (MPA) influence the behavior and configuration of phenylalanine, enhancing its passivation efficiency by modulating acid-base equilibrium and functional group accessibility. 

A multiligand approach combining phenylalanine with complementary ligands such as (3-aminopropyl) triethoxysilane (APTES) and OA or MPA establishes a balanced acid-base environment, enabling functional groups with electron lone pairs or charges to neutralize surface defects effectively. This synergistic strategy not only improves defect passivation but also enhances photoluminescence and long-term stability of the nanocrystals. The approach is generalizable to other ligand systems with tailored functional groups, providing a versatile framework for optimizing perovskite nanocrystal performance.

dataset_item.question: How do open-shell singlet and triplet configurations influence inversion paths compared to closed-shell singlet configurations for phosphorus trihalides?
dataset_item.answer:
The inversion paths of phosphorus trihalides (PF₃, PCl₃, PBr₃, PI₃) are significantly influenced by open-shell singlet and triplet configurations, which provide lower-energy pathways compared to closed-shell singlet configurations. For PF₃, PCl₃, and PBr₃, the inversion predominantly proceeds via a D₃h transition state involving open-shell singlet diradical configurations, which are energetically preferred over the closed-shell singlet pathway. PI₃, however, follows a distinct mechanism: its lowest-energy inversion path connects two closed-shell singlet geometries via an intermediate open-shell singlet configuration. Additionally, triplet D₃h local minima are observed for PCl₃, PBr₃, and PI₃, further lowering energy barriers and influencing the inversion mechanism.

The inversion mechanism is driven by electron promotion from lone pairs to the LUMO, which stabilizes open-shell configurations. These findings underscore the importance of considering multiple spin states, diradical character, and unpaired electron numbers in understanding inversion processes, challenging the traditional assumption that closed-shell singlets dominate such reactions.

We investigated reaction paths for the inversion of PZ3 (Z = F, Cl, Br, I) molecules. These paths were determined using both DFT and WFT; the WFT calculations employ the XMS-CASPT2 method for singlet states and the PT2 method for triplet states, where the DFT calculations employ the M06 functional for all the states. DFT and WFT give similar results for the calculated relative energies and geometries of various stationary points (pyramidal equilibrium structure, planar D 3h transition structure or hilltop, and planar C 2v transition structure) along the paths, with a few exceptions. The path that goes via the C 2v transition structure was found to be the minimum-energy singlet path, which is already known in the literature (although occasionally forgotten). Higher-energy paths via the D 3h structure can occur via the closed-shell singlet structure or the open-shell singlet structure, and the one involving the open-shell singlet electronic configuration is more favorable for PF3, PCl3, and PBr3. Besides the singlet D 3h structures, a triplet D 3h local minimum for PCl3, PBr3, and PI3 is also found that is lower in energy than the two D 3h singlet structures.

The inversion of PZ3 species illustrates how complicated bonding changes can be even for seemingly simple, textbook-type processes, and the present investigation especially brings forward the previously unrecognized participation of open-shell species (triplets and hyper-open-shell singlet diradicals) during the inversion. This raises the possibility that other species commonly investigated with the assumption that they are closed-shell singlets are actually better described as open-shell singlets.

In the closed-shell D 3h structure of PF3, PCl3, and PBr3 the promotion of one of the lone pair electrons to the LUMO lowers the energy of the structure. This electron transfer leads to the D 3h open-shell singlet and an ordinary open-shell triplet state. Therefore, to understand the complete picture of the inversion mechanism, all possible spin states and numbers of unpaired electrons need to be considered.
