inference_contexts: We have performed a time-resolved photoluminescence study of magnetic polaron formation and compared it to the evolution of PL circular polarization, in II-VI magnetic quantum dots with type-II band alignment in the presence of an external magnetic field B. A direct comparison of our measurements with a similar nonmagnetic sample has allowed us to exclude extrinsic effects and establish a significant difference in our findings as compared to the better studied epitaxial type-I quantum dots. - ,,,, We have observed significant time dependence of interband photoluminescence. The transition energies undergo a large red-shift, and a sizable circular polarization develops. The two circularly polarized photoluminescence components, which are degenerate at B = 0, exhibit a small energy difference of several millielectronvolts for all time delays when B ≠ 0. Interestingly, we have found that the magnetic polaron formation time is shorter than the polarization time scale τP. We have proposed a theoretical model to interpret these results. An important extension of the present work will be the investigation of magnetic quantum dots with double hole occupancy. Theoretical calculations indicate that these may exhibit several interesting effects: reentrant magnetic polaron formation, closed-shell magnetism, and spin-Wigner molecules.

Figure presents the sorption kinetic results, showing the time dependencies of [54Mn (II)]aq in experiments 1 and 2, and that of [Mn (II)]aq in experiment 3. The results of experiment 1 demonstrate a slow, continuous decline of [54Mn (II)]aq with no evidence to suggest that the partitioning of 54Mn reaches equilibrium in the 3 month time frame of the experiment. This kinetic pattern is mirrored by the dynamics of 54Mn partitioning in experiment 2, where 54Mn initially is present only in the 54MnO2(s) solid. This system exhibits a gradual increase in [54Mn (II)]aq as the 54MnO2(s) substrate reacts with aqueous Mn (II), with no evidence to suggest that isotope equilibrium has been reached after 3 months. The kinetic trajectories of the [54Mn (II)]aq levels of experiments 1 and 2 appear to track toward a similar level, suggesting that the solid-liquid partitioning of 54Mn isotopes slowly approaches the same end point in both systems. The slow dynamics of 54Mn equilibration in these systems contrast with the rapid attainment of the macroscopic Mn (II) sorption equilibrium in experiment 3, where Mn (II)aq levels stabilize within the first week at ~660 μM (Figure ). The repartitioning of 54Mn isotopes in experiments 1 and 2 is therefore not associated with net Mn (II) sorption or desorption but is driven by Mn atom exchange between the mineral solid and aqueous Mn (II). Results from the control experiments show no release of 54Mn (II)aq from the 54MnO2(s) substrate in the absence of Mn (II) or during reaction with Zn (II) and Ni (II) (Figure S1). This indicates that the appearance of aqueous 54Mn (II) in experiment 2 is not due to 54Mn (II)-Mn (II) cation exchange at the 54MnO2(s) surface. Instead, it is attributed to the interfacial redox reactions between Mn (II) and 54MnO2(s) discussed further below.

It is understood that the specificities of the electronic material are crucial in determining the relaxation mechanism of electronic spins, but the physical picture of spin decoherence (or relaxation) is still far from complete. The spin disentangling between the two fission triplets (i.e.. quantum decoherence) remains largely unexplored. Experimentally, spin coherence of fission triplets has been investigated by means of the oscillations observed in the delayed fluorescence of crystal tetracene and through magneto photoluminescence experiments. On the other hand, there is a lack of theoretical works tackling this phenomenon. The theoretical characterization of spin decoherence between the two fission triplets requires the time-evolution modeling of entangled triplet pairs in a bath of electronic and atomic spins (i.e.. the triplet excitons interacting with the environment) (electronic material), which opens coherence deactivation paths not possible in a closed quantum system. Hence, it is necessary to consider open quantum system approaches able to model the spin interaction of triplet excitons with the electronic material (i.e.. the electronic bath or environment). Adaptation of the methods typically used for decoherence of electronic spins in the frame of spintronics , or quantum computing - to the case of singlet fission would help to understand the origins of the rather long coherence times and the parameters controlling it.

Here, we present the first investigation of photoinduced spin dynamics in CFO. Ultrafast XUV-RA measurements show the element-specific oxidation and spin-state dynamics in this material on the femtosecond time scale. Spectral analysis demonstrates that photoexcitation of CFO at 400 nm excites a metal-to-metal charge transfer transition that drives intersystem crossing from HS Co2+ to LS Co3+ via a CTIST mechanism. This process occurs with a time constant of 405 ± 29 fs and unity quantum efficiency. SCO in this material is enabled by the presence of an intervalence charge transfer transition. We hypothesize that this intervalence transition, which is unique to CFO compared to Co3O4, is facilitated by the stronger metal-metal coupling in the predominately inverse spinel structure of CFO. This observation indicates that other magnetic materials in this class of ferrimagnetic inverse spinel ferrites are also expected to support efficient photoinduced SCO.

The time is right to harness the exquisite design of colloidal QDs as platforms for quantum information science. With precise control over composition and structure and the advantages of quantum confinement to engineer the spatial distribution, energy, and interactions between charge and spin states, a variety of photon and spin qubits can be realized. Their small size presents opportunities for device integration and complex assembly, while the availability of large-scale production indicates their viability for commercial applications. Looking toward this aspiration, we highlight a few areas where the community is already exploring QDs as quantum optical materials and key directions for future research that can facilitate the realization of robust, optically addressable qubits. Single-photon emission: A QD's discrete, core electron and hole states constitute the prerequisite two-level electronic structure for single-photon emission. Single-QD spectroscopies have reported single-photon excitonic emission for various colloidal QD sizes, shapes, and compositions, including observations of spherical II-VI and cubic metal-halide perovskite QDs with near-perfect single-photon purity. An important difference in these two materials systems is the role of the QD surface. In archetypical II-VI QDs, surface electronic states create non-radiative pathways for recombination via traps and Auger autoionization; however, the problem can be solved using well-established growth methods for core-shell QD heterostructures. By engineering the composition and thickness of the shell, guided by wave function engineering to reduce the overlap of carriers, this approach has nearly eliminated the Auger process and the associated PL intermittency, for low excitation intensities. For metal-halide perovskite QDs, in contrast, surface states are electronically shallow and ineffective recombination pathways in core-only QDs. Studies of these example QDs are uncovering the design rules for bright single-photon emitters, i.e.. the role of the core and surface on the electronic structure that governs the brightness and optical coherence of single-photon emission, described in more detail next. These design rules are guiding the development of color-tunable, single-photon emitters in the ultraviolet, visible, and infrared spectrum from the broader colloidal QD library for the wide range of quantum information science applications. The most studied examples are Cd-based II-VI QDs and Pb-based metal-halide perovskite QDs. Demonstrations of single-photon emission from Cd- and Pb-free compositions, such as InP-ZnSe core-shell QDs, are important in particular for life-science applications. Unlike the water solubility of metal-halide perovskites, protocols for ligand engineering of core-shell II-VI, III-V, IV-VI, and I-III-VI2 QDs are well established and have allowed their use as compatible, fluorescent probes for biological imaging, labeling, and tracking. , Optical coherence: For the purpose of generating indistinguishable single photons, the two examples of II-VI core-shell QDs and metal-halide perovskite QDs provide an interesting comparison. The shorter exciton lifetime, even at room temperature, of metal-halide perovskite QDs advantageously makes for brighter emission than that for spherical II-VI QDs. At cryogenic temperatures, these systems show similar ZPL line widths and comparable optical coherence times, T 2 ~ 100 ps. However, the fine structure in the lowest-energy state creates a 100-fold disparity in their radiative lifetimes, T 1. Spherical II-VI QDs have an optically forbidden, low-energy, dark excitonic state and thus a relatively long T 1 > 10 ns. In contrast, CsPbBr3 QDs have low-energy optically bright states and much faster radiative lifetimes of T 1 ~ 210 ps, closer to T 2. In II-VI QDs, dephasing is dominated by phonon-assisted, spin-flip transitions between bright and dark states within the fine structure manifold. For applications that require longer T 2, and thus longer T 1, engineering the electronic fine structure by tailoring the size, crystal structure, shape, composition, and internal structure can alter the energy separation and order of bright and dark states in the fine structure, promising a route to exploit the sophistication of QD design and to explore the manipulation of optical coherence times. In metal-halide perovskite QDs, ligands at the QD surface have been suggested as a possible source of phonon dephasing. To create indistinguishable photons and to limit coupling to phonons and prevent electronic fluctuations that cause noise, the architecture of core-shell QD heterostructures may provide a route to remove the interactions with vibrational modes of the ligands and to electrostatically shield states delocalized across or in defect states within the QD core. Oscillator strength: Excitonic QD states have large optical dipole moments of ~50 D, as the oscillator strength of bulk semiconductors is concentrated in the QD core. The large optical dipole moment naturally leads to a large coupling strength with photonic structures, e.g.. making it easier to achieve strong coupling with an optical cavity. For QDs hosting defects and dopants, the oscillator strength of the defect transitions depends on their electronic structure. Defects with ground and excited states composed of sp orbitals with dipole-allowed transitions generally have dipole moments comparable to single molecules at ~1-10 D, whereas transitions arising from d or f orbitals from TM and RM dopants, respectively, generally have much smaller optical dipole moments of 0.001-0.1 D, consistent with their longer optical lifetimes. These considerations raise the possibility of intentionally coupling the strong optical absorption or emission properties of the host QD to the spin or optical properties of a defect in the core, which may have a weaker intrinsic oscillator strength. Charge or energy transfer between the QD and defect states could be used, for example, to improve the optical excitation or readout efficiency of defects utilized as spin qubits or sensors. Spin coherence: The spin coherence times of excitonic states in QDs are generally short, ~100 ps. However, QDs can serve as wide-band-gap hosts for QPDs, with low spin-orbit coupling and dilute nuclear spin concentrations that protect the defects' spin coherence. The exploration of defects and dopants as spin qubits in colloidal QDs is still in early stages. However, a great deal is known about defect complexes and TM and RE dopants in the bulk analogues of many classic colloidal QD materials. QDs may provide a convenient platform to probe and identify defects and dopants at the individual level, since they can be spatially isolated in individual QDs even at relatively high (i.e.. ~100 ppm) impurity levels. Several pioneering studies have already shown the ability to use exchange coupling between spin levels of TM dopants such as Mn2+ with QD excitonic states for spin initialization and readout. This effect is especially promising for interfacing with QPDs that have internal transitions which are weak or energetically removed from bands that are useful for telecommunications or biological sensing. Adaptation of these approaches, through collaborations between experts in theory, synthesis, and quantum measurements, can likely provide a versatile set of new spin qubit architectures. Spin-photon interfaces: Ultimately, many of the most exciting future applications in quantum information science-including long-distance quantum communication and scalable, distributed quantum computing-will be enabled by robust, efficient quantum interfaces between long-lived, controllable quantum registers (e.g.. spin states) and coherent photonic channels. A spin-photon interface is the essence of a quantum repeater, which facilitates the distribution and control of entanglement over arbitrary distances. The realization of spin-photon interfaces demands control over optical coherence, spin coherence, and efficient conditional interactions between the spin and photonic degrees of freedom. Practical applications will likely require integration with optical cavities and integrated photonic devices to control the flow of photons between spatially separated nodes. For all of the reasons listed earlier, colloidal QDs are promising platforms for building quantum repeaters and other systems based on spin-photon interfaces. In particular, they feature strong, tunable optical properties, are ideal hosts for spin qubits, and can be reproducibly synthesized and integrated with photonic structures. Research in pursuit of this goal can focus on the identification of stable spin qubits with long coherence times (this will likely include individual nuclear spins coupled to an optically addressable electron-spin qubit) along with optimization of optical coherence and spin-dependent transitions that can be used to transfer quantum information from spins to photons and vice versa. Scalable fabrication: One of the clear advantages of colloidal QDs is their scalable synthesis and assembly. QD inks are being commercially produced at the tens of tons scale per year for display technologies. In research, nanomanipulation, colloidal assembly, and optical printing techniques are enabling the deterministic assembly of individual particles with tens of nanometers precision, setting the stage for the integration of QD emitters in optical cavities and device architectures, created by metallic, dielectric, and magnetic materials via fabrication and multiparticle assembly, to control the behavior of exciton, charge, and spin states at will. Akin to colloidal crystallization, self-assembly of QD superlattices enables single-nanometer precision in interparticle spacing and the organization of single-particle and multiparticle assemblies, a platform commensurate with the definition of arrays that entangle quantum coherent spin states.

dataset_item.question: How does interlayer slipping in layered covalent organic frameworks influence methane adsorption capacity and CO2 to CH4 selectivity?
dataset_item.answer: Interlayer slipping in layered covalent organic frameworks (COFs) significantly enhances methane (CH4) adsorption capacity and CO2:CH4 selectivity by increasing surface area and optimizing the spatial distribution of adsorption sites. Slipping distances between 10–15 Å are particularly effective, yielding methane delivery capacities of 109–141 cm³ (STP) cm⁻³ in specific configurations. This structural modification also improves CO2:CH4 selectivity due to the stronger CO2 binding energy, which is 1.2–2.0 times higher than CH4. While functionalization of COFs has minimal impact on methane uptake, it tends to reduce CO2:CH4 selectivity. These findings establish interlayer slipping as a promising design parameter for enhancing both methane storage and gas separation performance in COFs. Further investigation into dynamic structural effects and long-term stability is needed to fully optimize these materials for practical applications.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. Summary of the Paper's Purpose:
The purpose of this paper is to investigate how structural modifications—specifically slipping and chemical functionalization—affect methane adsorption and methane-carbon dioxide separation properties in layered covalent organic frameworks (COFs). Through grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations, the authors explore the impact of these modifications on methane uptake, CO2:CH4 selectivity, and delivery capacity. They also analyze molecular-level mechanisms such as binding energy, heat of adsorption, pore characteristics, and energy landscapes to understand the underlying adsorption behavior and identify design principles for enhancing methane storage performance.

---

### 2. Classification of Purpose:
**<result>**  
The paper primarily emphasizes the results of methane adsorption and separation properties in COFs under various structural modifications, as well as the molecular-level insights derived from these findings.

---

### 3. Research Questions:
Here are some potential research questions based on the abstract's themes and materials science interests:

1. How does structural slipping in layered COFs influence methane adsorption capacity and CO2:CH4 selectivity?
2. What role does chemical functionalization play in modifying the adsorption properties of COFs for methane storage and gas separation?
3. How do molecular interactions, such as CH4-CH4 binding and proximity of adsorption sites, contribute to the heat of adsorption and methane delivery capacity in COFs?
4. What specific pore characteristics and energy landscapes are most favorable for optimizing methane uptake in COFs?
5. Can COFs be systematically designed to exhibit increasing heat of adsorption profiles with pressure, and how does this correlate with improved methane delivery capacity?
6. What are the trade-offs between maximizing methane uptake and maintaining high CO2:CH4 selectivity in functionalized and structurally altered COFs?

These questions aim to extend the understanding of how structural and chemical modifications affect adsorption performance and provide a basis for designing more efficient nanoporous materials for methane storage and separation applications.

inference_contexts: In this work, we have analyzed the effect of interlayer slipping and functionalization on methane adsorption and CO2:CH4 separation performance of layered COFs. We considered various slipped structures of TpPa1, TpBD, and PI-COFs and functionalized COFs of TpPa1 and TpBD series. Our key findings are summarized as follows: We found that the slipping enhances the CH4 adsorption uptake significantly, while functionalization showed only a slight variation in the CH4 uptake compared to the nonfunctionalized eclipsed (AA) COF structures. Slipping results in an increase in adsorption uptake in both nonfunctionalized and functionalized COFs. The CH4 adsorption uptake in COFs is mainly governed by surface area, -Q st, and spatial distribution of adsorption sites. The higher slipping results in higher surface area and hence higher CH4 uptake in slipped structures with slipping distance between 10-15 Å. We found high CH4 delivery capacity of 109 (and 141) cm3 (STP) cm-3 in the 60-AB structure of TpPa1 (and TpBD) COF at 35 (and 65) bar. In 60-AB COF structures, the higher CH4 delivery capacity was observed compared to other slipped structures due to increasing profile of total -Q st with the pressure (and loading). Our analysis showed that the profile of total -Q st can be increasing in porous material when the CH4 adsorption sites are located within 4-6 Å of each other. The COFs showed around 1.2-2.0 times higher CO2 binding energy compared to CH4 molecule, indicating the potential of COFs for CO2:CH4 separation. We found that slipping improves the CO2:CH4 selectivity of layered COFs, while functionalization decreases the selectivity values.

In this work, heterocycles comprising S, O, and N were first screened through comparing the binding energies from ab initio calculations, in order to find heterocycles with great CO2 affinities. Three kinds of heterocycles, including thiophene, furan, and triazole, were chosen for further studies. The SAPT energy decompositions indicated that dispersion force and electrostatic interactions made contributions to CO2 adsorption simultaneously in "heaping" conformations. However, in "coplane" conformations, the electrostatic interaction played a more dominant role than dispersion force. From the results of GCMC simulations, it was observed that the incorporations of heterocycles to organic linkers can significantly enhance CO2 adsorption in MOF materials. Among the MOFs grafted by univariate heterocycles, triazole@UiO-67 shows the best performance in the CO2 adsorption process and the volumetric uptake amount is over 4 times higher than that of the original UiO-67 at 298 K and 100 kPa. This improvement can be mainly attributed to the profoundly enhanced electrostatic interactions by grafting triazoles, which is in agreement with the analysis of SAPT interaction energy decompositions. The incorporations of multivariate heterocycles show even larger improvement on the CO2 uptake amount in MOFs. The volumetric CO2 uptake amount in oxazole@UiO-67 is nearly 5 times higher than that in the parent UiO-67 at 298 K and 100 kPa. In UiO-67, CO2 molecules preferred to be adsorbed at the corners around the metal cluster. Comparatively, in oxazole@UiO-67, CO2 molecules were adsorbed at not only the corners around the metal cluster, but also the site surrounded by oxazoles. Besides, it is found that the extension of MOF organic linkers can significantly enhance the delivery amount which is important in practical applications.

Although the literature showcases multiple protein functionalization strategies that preserve SWCNT fluorescence, ,,- most common strategies rely on nonspecific adsorption or bioconjugation. The exploration of site-specific strategies presented herein aims to provide the community with alternative strategies, particularly for applications that require a desired protein orientation on the nanotube surface. These applications include optical monitoring of protein activity and charge transfer mechanisms to the nanotube surface. The two approaches demonstrated in this work focus on site-specific conjugation to either an ssDNA wrapping or PM linker via covalent thiol-maleimide "click" chemistry with the protein. While both strategies were demonstrated using cysteine-based bioconjugation, they can be extended to immobilize proteins via unnatural amino acids, such as p-azido-l-phenylalanine, as done in other studies. The biorthogonal chemistry enabled by such artificial residues are especially beneficial to proteins that are otherwise not amenable to site-specific conjugation strategies based on cysteine.

As the applications of αAAs at the frontiers of molecular science continue to evolve, chemists must address developing demand for more efficient synthetic methods as well as new αAAs with novel structures and functions. Complementary to the established methods of de novo synthesis of αAAs or limited transformations of side chain functional groups, we sought to develop a more straightforward and versatile means to access new αAAs via the selective functionalization of side chain sp3 C-H bonds of existing αAA precursors. For several years, we have systematically investigated the applications of Pd-catalyzed auxiliary-directed C-H functionalization for αAAs synthesis. Our strategies encompass two types of amide-linked auxiliary groups attached on either the N or C terminus of αAA substrates. These auxiliary types exhibit complementary regio- and stereoselectivity in side chain C-H functionalization reactions proceeding through palladacycle intermediates. N-linked PA-directed C-H functionalization reactions can transform αAA substrates at the distal γ and δ positions to generate more complex αAA products. In contrast, C-linked AQ-directed C-H functionalization reactions are uniquely suited to transform αAA substrates at the proximal β position. With the ability to selectively functionalize previously unreachable side chain sp3 C-H bonds, readily available αAA precursors can now be used for broader applications in organic synthesis. Many previously underutilized αAAs such as Val, Thr, and Abu may now be viewed as valuable chiral "C-H" synthons that can be readily functionalized at methyl and methylene positions to give αAA products difficult to access by other means.

Regardless of the coating degree, CH4-poor fuel mixtures have shown resistance to the inhibiting effect of CO2 even at low temperature, while a significant shift of the ignition pressure at higher values has been detected for CH4-rich fuel mixtures. Hence, a novel light-off strategy has been proposed: if syngas and CH4 come from different sources (such as in IGCC plants), the catalytic combustor can be ignited with a syngas-rich fuel, and after ignition, syngas can be partially substituted with CH4, quite independently of the partial pressure of CO2. dataset_item.question: What is the effect of π stacking on the inversion barriers of corannulene, sumanene, and dibenzo [a,g] corannulene when adsorbed on graphene or intercalated in bilayer graphene?
dataset_item.answer: π stacking interactions with graphene significantly reduce the inversion barriers of corannulene, sumanene, and dibenzo[a,g]corannulene compared to their gas-phase behavior. Density functional theory calculations reveal that adsorption on monolayer graphene reduces the inversion barrier of corannulene by at least 50%, with similar reductions observed for sumanene and dibenzo[a,g]corannulene. Intercalation in bilayer graphene further lowers these barriers—corannulene's inversion barrier decreases to below 3.5 kcal/mol, while dibenzo[a,g]corannulene adopts an almost planar structure, with its bowl depth reduced from 0.83 Å in the gas phase to nearly zero. These findings underscore the strong influence of π stacking on the inversion dynamics of buckybowls, highlighting graphene-based systems as promising molecular receptors for facilitating bowl inversion processes.

### 1. Summary of the Purpose:
The paper investigates the inversion behavior of bowl-shaped molecules (corannulene, sumanene, and dibenzo [a,g] corannulene) when adsorbed onto graphene or intercalated in bilayer graphene. Using computational methods, the study demonstrates that nonbonded interactions with graphene significantly reduce the inversion barriers of these molecules compared to their behavior in the gas phase. The findings aim to provide insights into how graphene-based systems can influence molecular inversion dynamics, which may aid in the design of molecular receptors for catalyzing buckybowl inversion.

inference_contexts: By means of dispersion-corrected density functional theory, we have studied how the inversion barriers of corannulene, sumanene, and dibenzo [a,g] corannulene are affected when they are adsorbed on monolayer graphene or intercalated in bilayer graphene. The results obtained with the M06-L, M06-2X, TPPS-D3, TPSS-D3BJ, B3LYP-D3, and B3LYP-D3BJ methods indicated that π stacking reduces the inversion barrier of corannulene by at least a 50% with respect to the gas phase. Similar trends were found for adsorbed sumanene and dibenzo [a,g] corannulene. In the same line, the intercalation inside bilayer graphene makes the inversion barrier of corannulene to be smaller than 3.5 kcal/mol. For sumanene and dibenzo [a,g] corannulene the results followed the same trend and significant reductions of the inversion barrier were observed. In the particular case of dibenzo [a,g] corannulene intercalated in bilayer graphene, the bowl depth of the molecule (0.83 Å gas phase) is almost zero, displaying an almost planar structure. Finally, in Table we present our best estimations for the inversion barriers for the three curved conjugated systems studied when they are adsorbed and intercalated inside bilayer graphene. These results clearly indicate the strong effect of π stacking on the inversion barriers. For this reason we expect that receptors like ExCage6+ would have a stronger effect on the inversion barriers of buckybowls than ExBox4+. Such studies are under investigation at our laboratory.

We observed the reactivity differences between bilayer graphene with two identified stacking modes by reacting it with 4-NBD diazonium salts. The 4-NBD grafting reaction on tBLG was found to be almost 5 times more reactive than that on AB-stacking graphene. We attribute this reactivity difference to variations in the electron distribution and DOS between these two stacking modes. In addition, the reaction rate of the two stacking modes of graphene can be fitted as an exponential growth model along with a kinetics-dominated effect. These results provide a positive way to control the electronic properties and tune the bandgap of graphene bilayers. The methodology presented herein will provide a method to control the electronic structure of bilayer graphene.

Using the DFT based B3LYP/6-31++G (d,p) method, we first tried to locate all the possible stationary points in the reaction paths. , All the minima were characterized with no imaginary frequencies. At the same time, all the transition states were characterized with only one imaginary frequency and were confirmed from the analysis of their displacement vectors associated with their imaginary frequencies and from their IRC calculations. It is well-known that most of the DFT methods are deficient in accounting for the dispersive interactions and other long-range interactions. The reason is due to the use of the approximated exchange-correlation (xc) functionals, which are computed empirically and then added to the conventional DFT energies as correction terms. So, we have tried to include the empirical dispersion and long-range interaction corrections by carrying out the calculations again with the wB97xD method (this method uses long-range corrected hybrid density functionals with damped atom-atom dispersion corrections. ), with a basis set like aug-cc-pVTZ, on all the stationary points located in the previously mentioned method (full optimizations for all stationary points). Discussions reported in this work are only limited to the wB97xD method and are sometimes compared with the results from the B3LYP method. All the energetics reported in this work include zero-point energy corrections, unless otherwise mentioned explicitly. As the wB97xD method was providing comparable accurate results like that of the previous reports, computations related to other computationally expensive higher-level energy correction methods were not carried out in this work. In a few cases, we have compared the results from our CCSD (T) calculations with the earlier reported results at various levels of theories and also with results from wB97xD methods reported in this work (CCSD (T)/6-31++G (d,p) energy corrections were carried out on B3LYP/6-31++G (d,p) optimized geometries). - The computational chemistry program Gaussian 09 was used to carry out all these calculations, and the GaussView program was used for visualization purposes.

dataset_item.question: How is binding free energy calculated for receptor-binding domain and ACE2 complexes using molecular mechanics Poisson-Boltzmann surface area methodology?
dataset_item.answer:
Binding free energy between the receptor-binding domain (RBD) and ACE2 complexes is calculated using the molecular mechanics Poisson-Boltzmann surface area (MMPBSA) methodology. This approach combines contributions from molecular mechanical energy changes, solvation free energy, and entropy (typically neglected due to its minimal impact).  

1. **Molecular Mechanical Energy (ΔE_MM)**:  
   - Includes covalent, electrostatic, and van der Waals interactions.  

2. **Solvation Free Energy (ΔG_solv)**:  
   - **Polar Solvation Energy**: Computed using Poisson-Boltzmann calculations with dielectric constants of 80 for the solvent and 2 for the solute.  
   - **Nonpolar Solvation Energy**: Estimated based on the solvent-accessible surface area (SASA).  

3. **Snapshots from Molecular Dynamics Simulations**:  
   - Snapshots are extracted from the final phase of molecular dynamics simulations (e.g., the last 200-400 ns) to ensure convergence and stability of the binding free energy calculations.  

4. **Neglecting Entropy**:  
   - Entropic contributions (-TΔS) are considered negligible based on prior studies and are typically excluded from the final calculation.  

The total binding free energy (ΔG_bind) is obtained by summing ΔE_MM and ΔG_solv. This methodology provides a reliable estimate of the binding interaction between RBD and ACE2.

Understanding how design parameters of targeted drug carriers influence interaction with cells and the subsequent signaling leading to endocytosis is key to inform optimization of drug delivery systems. , Both the size and targeting valency of drug carriers impact cell binding and endocytic uptake. - ,,, However, how these parameters influence receptor-mediated signaling linking binding with internalization is rather obscure. For instance: Is the uptake efficiency correlative with the signaling level? Is this regulated similarly for carriers of different sizes and valencies? Are signaling and uptake events induced independently for each individual carrier or do they depend on cumulative carrier binding to cells? Is the number of receptors engaged by a carrier the factor ruling signaling and uptake, or does this depend on the density of engagement per surface area? Using model submicrometer, micrometer, and supramicrometer carriers targeted to ICAM-1 at varying valencies, we have examined these questions. Our results revealed an intricate interplay between these parameters, where the density of the targeting antibody per carrier surface area (which would determine the density of the receptor cluster on the cell surface) is the main parameter controlling the signaling conducive to endocytosis (Figure ). Larger carriers posed a requirement for stronger signaling, since carrier size impacts the ability of the plasmalemma to efficiently engulf a carrier. It is likely that for endocytic pathways lacking signals that enable sufficient plasmalemma deformability (e.g.. ceramide enrichment shown here for the CAM pathway), size will become restrictive regardless of the targeting density. Each carrier bound on a cell induced signaling based on its antibody-coat density (the density of the clustered receptors, not the absolute number of receptors engaged or the size of the cluster), and rendered endocytosis based on its size and enough buildup of the inducing signal. Each signaling-uptake event was independent for each single carrier bound on a cell, where the total number of carriers bound to the cell, the total surface area occupied by those carriers, and the total number of cell receptors engaged did not exert a major influence. It will be important to examine this regulation for other receptors and pathways in order to extract generic conclusions, and to evaluate how other carrier design parameters (e.g.. smaller sizes, different shape, curvature, carrier type, surface chemistry, etc.) and biological environments (different cell types, presence of flow, pathological alterations, etc.) impact these outcomes. - ,,, Nevertheless, other natural routes associate to signaling common to the CAM pathway, and it is expected that the findings obtained here would broadly apply to the use of said routes for drug delivery applications. For instance, ceramide and/or PKC are key for the formation of lipid domains, vesiculation, cytoskeletal rearrangements, and formation of membrane protrusions observed for phagocytic and macropinocytic pathways, intracellular invasion by certain viral and bacterial pathogens, leukocyte endothelial adhesion and extravasation, and certain events of transcytosis across cellular barriers. - Therefore, these results have shed light on key factors modulating the efficacy of uptake of targeted drug carriers, which shall inform future design of vehicles for intracellular delivery.

Several materials prepared from triazine-containing precursors were explored as active materials in Li half cells. Well-defined materials which exhibit strong triazine character show very low gravimetric capacities even if the triazine units are bridged by conjugated moieties, such as phenylene or 2,2′-bipyridine. This directly contradicts the previously suggested bipolar mechanism in which the triazine is n- or p-doped when cycled. In order to achieve high gravimetric capacities, the well-defined conjugated systems must be synthesized at higher temperatures, thereby destroying the triazine unit and creating an N-containing amorphous carbon material. These materials have high concentrations of localized spins (large numbers of unpaired electrons) that may be involved in the discharge and charge mechanisms. The N-containing amorphous carbon materials are very similar to N-containing porous carbon materials that have been evaluated as supercapacitor materials. , The capacity of the amorphous materials trends loosely with specific surface area and C/N content. However, higher surface area does not always result in a higher capacity, suggesting the mechanism is not purely capacitive. The slight observed rate dependence also suggests a pseudocapacitive behavior involving charge transfer processes. These charge transfer processes could involve the unpaired electrons in the amorphous materials, and indeed, the inactive PTI materials do not contain unpaired electrons. Suggestions for future work to further probe the charge storage mechanisms involve using in situ EPR in order to observe the evolution of the spin concentration as a function of discharging and charging.

dataset_item.question: How does Ru catalyze the reduction of Ni ions during the preparation of bimetallic catalysts?
dataset_item.answer: Ruthenium (Ru) catalyzes the reduction of nickel (Ni²⁺) ions during the preparation of bimetallic catalysts through hydrogen spillover. In this process, metallic Ru (Ru⁰) facilitates the dissociation of hydrogen molecules into activated hydrogen species and promotes their transfer to adjacent Ni²⁺ ions, enabling their reduction at lower temperatures. This mechanism is supported by H₂-TPR analysis, which demonstrates the role of Ru in enhancing the reduction process. The reduction leads to the formation of Ni nanoparticles with smaller particle sizes, confined within a weakly crystalline Ni(Al)Ox matrix. This confinement enhances the surface area and pore volume of the catalyst, contributing to improved catalytic activity and selectivity, particularly in the hydrogenation of dimethyl terephthalate (DMT). The synergistic interaction between Ru and Ni is fundamental to the efficient preparation and high performance of the bimetallic catalyst. Optimal reduction temperatures, such as 350 °C, further refine the catalyst’s microstructure and properties.

dataset_item.question: How does the molar ratio of hydrophobic catecholic groups and ionizable amine groups affect micelle formation and antimicrobial properties in cationic random copolymers?
dataset_item.answer: The molar ratio of hydrophobic catecholic groups to ionizable amine groups plays a critical role in determining micelle formation and antimicrobial properties in cationic random copolymers. A 70/30 molar ratio optimally balances hydrophobic and cationic characteristics, facilitating self-assembly into flower-like micelle structures. This formation is driven by stacking interactions among catecholic groups, which create a robust hydrophobic core while preserving sufficient cationic charge density. The resulting amphiphilic balance minimizes intermolecular polymer chain aggregation and enhances interaction with bacterial membranes, yielding superior antimicrobial efficacy with the lowest minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). Experimental techniques such as molecular dynamics simulations, dynamic light scattering, and electrical conductivity measurements confirm micelle formation and validate the structure-performance relationship across different copolymer compositions. Thus, the 70/30 ratio emerges as the ideal configuration for achieving enhanced antimicrobial properties and effective micelle assembly.

dataset_item.question: What mechanisms allow carbon monoxide to mitigate the inhibitory effects of carbon dioxide during methane combustion over perovskite-coated monoliths?
dataset_item.answer: Carbon monoxide mitigates the inhibitory effects of carbon dioxide during methane combustion over perovskite-coated monoliths through several synergistic mechanisms. First, CO exhibits higher reactivity on LaMnO3 perovskite surfaces compared to CH4, allowing it to outcompete CO2 for adsorption sites, thereby reducing CO2 surface coverage. Second, the combustion of CO generates heat, elevating the catalyst's surface temperature, which further displaces adsorbed CO2 and enhances reaction kinetics. Third, CO combustion requires significantly less oxygen than CH4, alleviating the oxygen availability limitations caused by CO2 adsorption. This combination of effects is particularly beneficial in CH4-poor fuel mixtures, where CO's dominance stabilizes ignition even at lower temperatures. Additionally, partially coated "core-shell" monoliths improve performance by optimizing the balance between catalytic and homogeneous combustion, with coating parameters tailored to fuel composition, CO2 concentration, and reactor size. Employing a syngas-rich ignition strategy further enhances combustion stability in high-CO2 environments, ensuring efficient operation under challenging conditions.

dataset_item.question: How does the size of ethylene oxide block in sodium lauryl ether sulfate influence the hydrodynamic radius and ζ-potential of polyelectrolyte-surfactant complexes formed with linear polyDADMAC and branched polyethylenimine?
dataset_item.answer:
The size of the ethylene oxide (EO) block in sodium lauryl ether sulfate (SLES) influences the hydrodynamic radius and ζ-potential of polyelectrolyte-surfactant complexes (PESCs) differently depending on the polycation structure. 

For linear polyDADMAC, a stiff polycation, the EO block size does not affect the hydrodynamic radius. These complexes remain submicron-sized below charge stoichiometry and precipitate into macroscopic particles near stoichiometry. The ζ-potential of polyDADMAC-based PESCs remains highly positive across a wide range of stoichiometry ratios and decreases sharply near charge stoichiometry, sometimes retaining a positive charge.

For branched polyethylenimine (PEI), a flexible polycation, the EO block size significantly influences the hydrodynamic radius. Larger EO blocks result in unstable, aggregating complexes with increased hydrodynamic radii at lower surfactant concentrations. The ζ-potential of PEI-based PESCs decreases more gradually compared to polyDADMAC-based complexes, with larger EO blocks causing a more pronounced reduction in positive charge. Additionally, larger EO blocks lower the critical micelle concentration/critical aggregation concentration (CMC/CAC) ratio, suggesting hindered surfactant incorporation into the PESC structures.

dataset_item.question: How do injection temperature and Bi to S precursor ratios influence the morphology of Bi2S3 nanocrystals?
dataset_item.answer:
The morphology of Bi₂S₃ nanocrystals is significantly influenced by injection temperature and Bi/S precursor ratios during hot injection synthesis. Higher injection temperatures and optimized Bi/S ratios promote the formation of elongated nanorods with increased aspect ratios (e.g., 1, 3, and 5), while lower temperatures favor the synthesis of spherical nanodots (approximately 3 nm diameter). The transition from nanodots to nanorods correlates with increased crystallinity and aspect ratio, resulting in a redshift of the band gap from 2.02 eV (nanodots) to 1.82 eV (7 nm nanorods), due to quantum confinement effects. 

Photoluminescence (PL) intensity improves with higher crystallinity and aspect ratio, but surface defects, such as sulfur vacancies, influence the electronic structure by shifting the valence band maximum (VBM) to lower energies, as confirmed by XPS and UPS analysis. These defects arise from crystal imperfections in nanodots and sulfur vacancies in nanorods. Regardless of the synthesis conditions, all nanocrystals maintain a pure orthorhombic phase.

dataset_item.question: How does a mixed-integer nonlinear programming model improve the optimization of separation vessel design?
dataset_item.answer: A mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) model enhances the optimization of separation vessel design by automating the least-cost design process, eliminating the need for direct designer intervention, and providing more accurate results compared to heuristic or linear models. The model captures nonlinear relationships, such as the dependence of drag coefficient on Reynolds number, ensuring precise calculations. By incorporating discrete standard values for pipe and plate dimensions, it avoids rounding errors that can arise from continuous variables. Additionally, the MINLP framework evaluates both optimistic and conservative vessel height estimations, allowing for a thorough exploration of design criteria. It also assesses the impact of key design parameters, including the inclusion of demisters, which improves separation efficiency. This holistic approach reduces capital costs, minimizes engineering effort, and delivers reliable, cost-effective vessel designs.

dataset_item.question: What is the reproducibility of MIL-88B-type MOF crystallites in terms of pore characteristics and BET surface area across multiple synthesis and characterization attempts?
dataset_item.answer: The reproducibility of MIL-88B-type MOF crystallites in terms of pore characteristics and BET surface area was assessed through five independent syntheses, with each crystallite undergoing five separate characterization analyses. The reported data include average values for BET surface area, ultramicropore, micropore, upper mesopore, mesopore, and total pore volumes, along with their corresponding standard deviations to quantify variability. Fractions of microporosity and mesoporosity were determined by calculating the ratio of micropore and mesopore volumes to total pore volume using the NLDFT method. Results demonstrated high reproducibility, with consistent BET surface area and stable pore characteristics across all synthesis and characterization attempts, confirming reliable structural control and robust synthetic methodology for MIL-88B-type MOFs.

However, the number of acid sites decreased with the Al-extraction from the framework. Other methods like the delamination approach lead to the exposure of a larger fraction of the highly acidic zeolite surface for adsorption and catalysis. Nevertheless, it can be applied only to a small range of zeolites. Besides, the high surfactant content and the alkalinity used for the delamination process result in the partial dissolution of the zeolite framework. Zeolite recrystallization through the initial desilication/depolymerization and the following reassembling process in the presence of conventional surfactants gives high yield and relatively low environmental damage when compared with the demetallization, delamination, and the "in situ approach". For example, the FCC catalysts using mesoporous zeolite Y prepared by zeolite recrystallization were scaled up and successfully utilized in North American refineries. dataset_item.question: How does charge density influence the swelling behavior and deformation resistance of cellulose-based gel beads under osmotic stress?
dataset_item.answer:
Charge density plays a crucial role in influencing the swelling behavior and deformation resistance of cellulose-based gel beads under osmotic stress. Gel beads with higher charge densities, such as 600 μeq/g, demonstrate enhanced resistance to contraction compared to beads with lower charge densities (30 and 300 μeq/g). This increased resistance is attributed to the higher swelling pressure generated within the network, which increases linearly with charge density as long as the cellulose network remains within its linear elastic regime. Experimental deswelling data shows that deformation resistance (Πdef) is the dominant factor preventing collapse at cellulose volume fractions of 2–15%, while mixing entropy (Πmix) becomes more significant at higher cellulose contents (>35%). At very low volume fractions (<2%), ionic contributions (Πion) play a notable role, though nonionic polymer-water interactions are the primary factor governing water retention and swelling behavior in cellulose-rich networks. 

Additionally, the elastic features of the cellulose network are independent of charge density, as deformation resistance values collapse onto a single curve when analyzed across different charge densities. The swelling behavior aligns well with predictions from theoretical models such as Wall and Flory-Huggins, with χ values ranging from 0.55 to 0.70, further highlighting the interplay of charge density and polymer-water interactions in governing the mechanical and osmotic response of the gel beads.

These data were then used in classical gel swelling theories to calculate the distribution of the osmotic pressure between Πmix, Πion, and Πdef. The results showed that gel beads with a higher charge density, 600 μeq/g, were, as expected, able to withstand the contraction to a greater extent than the lower charged beads at 30 and 300 μeq/g. The calculated Πdef values also collapsed on a single curve, indicating that the elastic features of the cellulose network were independent of charge density. When the three factors Πmix, Πion, and Πdef were quantified using an interaction parameter of 0.55, it was found that at volume fractions between 2% and 15% Πdef was dominating in hindering the cellulose network to collapse and, as a consequence, retaining the water. We performed an in situ X-ray scattering experiment to reveal the behavior of the FL-MoS2 flakes during the Langmuir film formation. Relying on the evaluation of the width of the pole figure profile and surface pressure during the compression, five principal stages of the Langmuir film formation were identified. During stage I, the MoS2 flakes are randomly distributed and the film compression does not lead to an increase in the surface pressure. No tilting of MoS2 flakes affecting the pole figure width was observed. Stage II is associated with a slight increase in the surface pressure, elastic modulus, and width of the tilt angle distribution of the FL-MoS2 flakes. During this stage, the FL-MoS2 flakes agglomerate into islands and start to collide, forming a continuous (closed) layer at the end of this stage. At stage III, the surface pressure and elastic modulus increase rapidly with further compression. A significant broadening of the distribution of the flake tilts is observed as the increasing surface pressure forces the flakes to flip up and slide onto each other. During stage IV, the surface pressure reaches the critical pressure Πc for the monolayer collapse. A maximum in the elastic modulus and the saturation of the broadening in the flake tilt distribution are observed, and the formation of a second layer relaxing the accumulated stress starts. Subsequently, at stage V, the increase in the surface pressure is slowed-down, the elastic modulus drops rapidly, and the flake tilt distribution evolution is reversed, becoming narrower.

dataset_item.question: How are the off-diagonal coupling terms in the Empirical Valence Bond Hamiltonian defined in terms of energy gaps?
dataset_item.answer:
The off-diagonal coupling terms \( C_{mk} \) in the Empirical Valence Bond (EVB) Hamiltonian are defined as functions of the energy gap \( \varepsilon_{mk} \), which represents the difference in configurational energy between two chemical states \( m \) and \( k \). Mathematically, \( \varepsilon_{mk} = E_c^{(m)} - E_c^{(k)} \), where \( E_c^{(m)} \) and \( E_c^{(k)} \) are the configurational energies of states \( m \) and \( k \), respectively. The coupling terms are expressed as \( C_{mk} = C_{mk}(\varepsilon_{mk}) \), emphasizing their dependence on the energy gap rather than spatial coordinates.

To ensure the Hermitian property of the Hamiltonian, the coupling terms satisfy \( C_{mk} = C_{km} \), and they are real-valued by construction. This dependence on energy gaps is crucial for enabling the calculation of forces and stress tensors in EVB simulations, which are necessary for molecular dynamics under conditions such as NPT ensembles.

The derivatives of \( C_{mk} \) with respect to atomic coordinates are given by:
\[
\frac{dC_{mk}}{dR_{J\alpha}} = C'_{mk} \left( F_{J\alpha}^{(k)} - F_{J\alpha}^{(m)} \right),
\]
where \( C'_{mk} = \frac{dC_{mk}}{d\varepsilon_{mk}} \), and \( F_{J\alpha}^{(m)} \) and \( F_{J\alpha}^{(k)} \) are the force components for particle \( J \) in states \( m \) and \( k \), respectively. This formulation allows for the computation of forces and stress tensors, facilitating advanced simulations of chemical and physical systems.

The historically eldest quantum theoretical method is Valence Bond (VB) theory, which was used by Heitler and London in their pioneering study in 1927. It was the prevailing approach for some decades, which is mainly due to the strong support by Pauling. The advent of computers and the development of numerical algorithms and codes showed that Molecular Orbital (MO) theory is far better suited for quantum chemical calculations, basically rendering VB methods obsolete for numerical studies. Wave function based MO methods clearly became the dominant approaches for quantum chemical calculations during the 1970s. They were gradually replaced in the past two decades by Density Functional Theory (DFT), which is presently, in numerous different variations, the most important tool for quantum chemical studies of larger molecules. Examination of the basis of the Kohn-Sham (KS) DFT calculations reveals that they are essentially parametrized variants of the MO method, which is the reason that some authors call them Density Functional Approximation (DFA). We will use the more common term DFT for this method. Because of the close resemblance of the fundamental equations in wave function based MO and KS-DFT calculations, we describe the two methods first before we introduce the basis of VB calculations. The latter has lost its relevance not only because of its computational drawback as already mentioned but also because the apparent advance for the interpretation of chemical bonding in terms of the electron-pair model of Lewis has been lost with the development of the Natural Bond Orbital (NBO) method by Weinhold introduced below. -

Our investigation also raises the question of the chemical stability of other Al-ion positive electrode materials in chloroaluminate ionic liquid electrolytes.

The improved coupling achieved when sulfur or oxygen replaces a carbon atom in pentanedithiol alkyl chain may arise either from the differences in the electronic structure of the molecule or from the differences in the vibrational modes. The sulfur and oxygen add a delocalized charge at the center of the chain, which may affect the energy transfer through the molecule. Previously, by comparing butanedithiol to benzenedimethanedithiol, we have shown that delocalized charge at the center of the chain caused localization of the excitonic wavefunction and reduced coupling. Here, enhancement in coupling was measured with the linkers that have delocalized charge at the center, suggesting that the enhancement originates from the additional vibrational modes contributed by the added atoms. The possible ways in which vibrations can assist transport are not straightforward to measure, and therefore it is hard to determine experimentally which mechanism dictates the differences. There are multiple energy gaps (considering the S2 state of the acceptor), and resonance conditions could hold for different parts of an energy band. To investigate the role of vibrations in the mechanism, quantum chemical calculations were done. The results show that there is a good match between the S1-S1 energy gap of the QDs and the vibrations of the molecules that lead to the strongest coupling, in the two different QD sets used. In the dimers, where the energy gap is 773 cm-1, the 5-S linker exhibited the strongest coupling. This linker has a strong vibrational mode around 807 cm-1, which can be characterized by asymmetric C-C and C-S stretching and slight drift of the central S atom along the main molecular axis (see Figure S5A). In films where the energy gap is 1284 cm-1, the strongest coupling was achieved with the linker 5-O. This linker has a strong vibrational mode around 1154 cm-1. Similarly, in the 5-S linker, this mode is characterized by an asymmetric stretching of C-C and C-O bonds and, since the oxygen is lighter than sulfur, the stretch is more pronounced along the main axis of the molecule (see Figure S5B). These vibrations have likely promoted the downhill energy transfer in these samples by vibrational-electronic (vibronic) resonance.

dataset_item.question: How does the temperature of heat treatment influence the porous structure and nitrogen content of activated carbon fibers?
dataset_item.answer:
The temperature of heat treatment plays a critical role in determining the porous structure and nitrogen content of activated carbon fibers (ACFs). Higher temperatures during the one-step carbonization/activation process using potassium carbonate result in ACFs with enhanced BET surface area (ranging from 919 to 1625 m²/g) and increased ultramicropore volume (~0.3 cm³/g), which are essential for CO₂ adsorption performance. However, higher temperatures also lead to a reduction in nitrogen content (1.23–2.76 wt%) due to thermal decomposition of nitrogen-containing functional groups.

At an optimal heat treatment temperature of 800 °C, the ACFs exhibit a well-balanced structure, characterized by dominant ultramicropores that facilitate CO₂ uptake (5.0 mmol/g at 25 °C and 1 bar). The synergy between the porous structure and residual nitrogen functionalities enhances low-pressure adsorption (0.15 bar), making the material suitable for CO₂ capture applications. Therefore, heat treatment temperature directly tunes the porosity and nitrogen retention, balancing structural and chemical properties for targeted adsorption performance.

For polymers, natural or otherwise, to produce carbon fiber of a similar quality as PAN, they cannot rely on hydrogen bonding for structural stability or contain a high mass fraction of oxygen, lest they shrink to an unusable extent. A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. Polyalanine-like domains could be incorporated into block copolymers for biomimetic graphite precursors. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

dataset_item.question: Does the recrystallization of water sorbed into poly methacrylates and poly acrylates depend on a diffusion mechanism or a reorientation mechanism?
dataset_item.answer: The recrystallization of water sorbed into poly(meth)acrylates and polyacrylates is governed by a diffusion mechanism rather than a reorientation mechanism. This conclusion is supported by experimental observations using variable-temperature mid-infrared (VT-MIR) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. VT-MIR spectra reveal a positive correlation between the recrystallization temperature (T<sub>rc</sub>) and the glass-transition temperature (T<sub>g</sub>) for polymers such as PMEA, PTHFA, and PMA, indicating that polymer mobility plays a key role in the process. MD simulations further confirm that at temperatures above T<sub>rc</sub>, water molecules detach from the carbonyl oxygens of the polymer matrix, enabling the formation of water clusters that subsequently recrystallize. Additionally, the gradual change in the ice peak in VT-MIR spectra as a function of temperature reinforces the diffusion-controlled nature of the process. In PMMA, recrystallization is absent because its diffusion temperature approaches or exceeds water's melting point, preventing the necessary molecular mobility for recrystallization. These findings collectively establish diffusion as the dominant mechanism driving water recrystallization in poly(meth)acrylates.

dataset_item.question: How does the incorporation of Pd2+ ions into CuS nanocrystals influence the structure and stability of near-infrared localized surface plasmon resonances?
dataset_item.answer: The incorporation of Pd²⁺ ions into CuS nanocrystals, facilitated by an electron donor such as ascorbic acid, induces structural amorphization by disrupting the S-S layers in the covellite phase. This process results in the formation of a core-shell heterostructure, consisting of a crystalline CuS core and an amorphous CuPdₓS shell. The amorphization enhances the environmental stability of the nanocrystals, particularly their near-infrared localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) properties, which remain preserved even under oxidative conditions, such as exposure to iodine. The core-shell morphology effectively protects the plasmonic response from degradation while maintaining the nanocrystals' optical tunability and structural integrity. This design highlights the synergistic role of Pd²⁺ ions and ascorbic acid in stabilizing the LSPR properties and improving resistance to oxidative stress.

The paper investigates the design, synthesis, and stabilization of a semiconductor-based core-shell heterostructure with tunable localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) properties. By embedding a plasmonic CuS core in an amorphous CuPdₓS shell, the authors demonstrate enhanced environmental stability of the plasmonic response under oxidative conditions. The study integrates experimental synthesis, structural characterization, density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and theoretical optical simulations to understand and optimize the LSPR properties of these heterostructures.

dataset_item.question: How does O2-plasma treatment enhance optical contrast for detecting structural features of CVD-grown graphene on copper substrates?
dataset_item.answer: O₂-plasma treatment enhances optical contrast for detecting structural features of CVD-grown graphene on copper substrates by introducing defects into the graphene layers and promoting localized oxidation of the underlying copper. The plasma-induced defects modulate copper oxide formation beneath graphene, with thicker graphene layers exhibiting greater defect density and oxidation contrast. This results in a grayscale contrast increment of approximately 23.4% per graphene layer, enabling clear visualization of structural features such as wrinkles, grain boundaries, and layer thickness variations. The method is rapid, scalable (suitable for meter-scale samples using atmospheric plasma), and does not require complex instrumentation, making it an efficient approach for large-area quality assessment of graphene.

dataset_item.question: How does the effective charge method improve the accuracy of intermolecular electrostatic interaction modeling in Brownian dynamics simulations?
dataset_item.answer:
The effective charge method improves the accuracy of intermolecular electrostatic interaction modeling in Brownian dynamics (BD) simulations by addressing the two-cavity problem inherent in low-dielectric protein regions immersed in a high-dielectric solvent. This method replaces standard partial atomic charges with precomputed, rescaled effective charges that approximate the true external electrostatic potential of each protein. These effective charges are positioned identically to standard charges, preserving molecular architecture and charge distribution, but their magnitudes are adjusted using a linear regression algorithm to better fit the electrostatic field surrounding the proteins.

By precomputing these effective charges, the method avoids the computationally expensive iterative solutions of the Poisson-Boltzmann equation during simulations, while still accurately capturing the influence of low-dielectric protein cavities on intermolecular forces and torques. Additionally, the effective charge method refines the electrostatic modeling by fitting the electrostatic potential within a 10 Å surface layer around the proteins, ensuring improved representation of intermolecular interactions compared to traditional approaches, such as multipole approximations. Although this method is unsuitable for modeling intramolecular interactions, it significantly enhances the precision of force and torque calculations in BD simulations. For example, rescaled net effective charges for proteins like native cyt b5r (-16.6e) and cyt b5 (-18.7e) demonstrate the method's ability to reproduce realistic electrostatic interactions in a homogeneous dielectric environment.

inference_contexts: To take full account of the dielectric inhomogeneity and salt concentration necessitates: (a) use of effective charges (rescaled) to include the effect of two low dielectric protein cavities; and (b) inclusion of electrostatic desolvation. Each of these enhancements is discussed below. In studies where BD simulations are performed on two proteins, i.e.. two low dielectric macromolecules in a high dielectric aqueous electrolyte, the finite-difference PB method has been widely used to compute the intermolecular forces. To rigorously treat the effect of two low dielectric cavities would require iterating a PB equation at every time step, since the mutual configuration of the two low-dielectric cavity regions is changing at every time step. However, as BD simulations require as many as a million trajectories each with tens of thousands of time steps, performing a PB calculation at each and every BD step would be prohibitive.

This shortcoming has been overcome by adopting the "effective charge method" developed by Gabdoulline and Wade which addresses the two-cavity problem. In this method effective charges are precomputed to replace the standard partial atomic charges. Rescaled effective charges are derived such that when the protein charge distributions are placed into a homogeneous solvent dielectric they accurately approximate the same fields around them that the standard charges do when placed inside a low dielectric cavity immersed in a high dielectric medium. A molecule's effective charges are determined by fitting to its "true" external electrostatic potential. The fitting region is adjustable, and taken here to be a 10 Å layer (skin) around the protein's surface. Effective charges are positioned at the same location as the standard partial atomic charges in all our work. In such a way they model the architecture and charge distribution of the molecule much more accurately than a multipole representation of the molecule. This effective charges method is not suitable for describing the intramolecular interactions, though it accurately describes the intermolecular electrostatic interactions. dataset_item.question: How does the polarization and intensity of an assisting beam affect the inscription and manipulation of holograms in azo dye doped polymers?
dataset_item.answer: The polarization and intensity of an assisting beam play a crucial role in the inscription and manipulation of holograms in azo dye-doped polymers. These parameters can either enhance or completely erase holographic gratings by influencing molecular orientation and diffraction efficiency in the photosensitive material. The mechanism relies on photoassisted diffraction, where the assisting beam modulates the light-induced molecular reorientation to control holographic storage and manipulation. This precise control has significant potential for applications in all-optical signal processing. Future research aims to optimize this process by improving photosensitive materials to achieve higher diffraction efficiency and more effective manipulation of holograms.

The present study reveals the impact that stacking orientation can have on the donor-acceptor interface in organic solar cells. dataset_item.question: What role does vinylidene anion play in ionic polymerization of acetylene in cold plasmas?
dataset_item.answer: The vinylidene anion (H₂CC⁻) plays a pivotal role as the primary initiator of anionic polymerization in the ionic polymerization of acetylene in cold plasmas. This conclusion, supported by mass spectrometry measurements and kinetic modeling of C₂H₂/He and C₂H₂/Ar discharges, addresses the observed dominance of even-carbon C₂ₙH₂⁻ ions in steady-state ion distributions. Unlike traditional models that assume the ethinide anion (C₂H⁻) as the initiator, the vinylidene anion-driven mechanism explains the monotonic decline in peak intensity with increasing anion mass and accounts for 60–75% of the negative charge in the plasma. The consistency of this mechanism across different carrier gases (He and Ar) further underscores the robustness of the vinylidene anion’s role, demonstrating that acetylene’s plasma chemistry remains largely unaffected by the choice of rare gases. Additionally, while polyyne chain structures dominate the polymerization, increasing hydrogen content in larger ions suggests deviations from purely linear growth, highlighting the complexity of the polymerization process.

dataset_item.question: How does the NRTL-SAC model perform in predicting partition coefficients of naringin and other polyphenols during liquid-liquid extraction?
dataset_item.answer:
The NRTL-SAC model demonstrates strong predictive accuracy for liquid-liquid partition coefficients of most polyphenols, such as naringenin, trans-resveratrol, and p-coumaric acid, with predictions closely matching experimental data, even in mixed solvent systems. However, the model's performance for naringin is notably less accurate, with predictions significantly deviating from experimental values—often overestimating partition coefficients by up to 56% average relative error when parameters are derived from solid-liquid equilibrium (SLE) data. This discrepancy likely arises from naringin's complex hydration behavior, variable hydration states, or amorphous nature, which are not fully captured by the SLE-based parameterization. 

To address this limitation, regressing naringin's molecular descriptors using liquid-liquid extraction (LLE) data instead of SLE data substantially improves prediction accuracy, reducing the error to 40%. This highlights the importance of using relevant experimental data for parameterization when modeling compounds with intricate solvation behavior. Additionally, the NRTL-SAC model's ability to predict partition behavior in mixed solvent systems, such as heptane-isobutyl acetate, makes it a valuable tool for optimizing extraction conditions, particularly for hydrophobic polyphenols. While effective for most polyphenols, careful attention to data sources and molecular characteristics is essential for improving predictions for compounds like naringin.

dataset_item.question: How does peptide functionalization of polycaprolactone nanofibers influence human pluripotent stem cell proliferation, pluripotency maintenance, and osteogenic differentiation?
dataset_item.answer: Peptide functionalization of polycaprolactone (PCL) nanofibers enhances human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) proliferation and pluripotency maintenance in defined media, such as mTeSR1, while promoting osteogenic differentiation without requiring embryoid body formation or Matrigel coating. The functionalized nanofibers provide a chemically defined and xeno-free scaffold, reducing contamination risks associated with animal-derived proteins and ensuring a safer platform for hPSC-based applications. This modification improves cellular morphology, alkaline phosphatase activity, and osteogenesis-related gene expression, as confirmed by gene analysis, immunofluorescence, and enzymatic assays. By supporting hPSC osteogenic differentiation in vitro, peptide-functionalized PCL nanofibers offer a promising, safe, and effective alternative for bone tissue engineering.

dataset_item.question: How are first-order rate coefficients for silylene monitored and calculated during the reaction with 2,5-dihydrofuran?
dataset_item.answer:
The first-order rate coefficients (\(k_{obs}\)) for the reaction of silylene (SiH₂) with 2,5-dihydrofuran (2,5-DHF) are determined using real-time laser absorption spectroscopy following the photolysis of phenylsilane (PhSiH₃) at 193 nm to generate SiH₂. A Coherent 699-21 single-mode dye laser, tuned to the \( \tilde{A}^1B_1 \leftarrow \tilde{X}^1A_1 \) vibronic transition at 17,259.50 cm⁻¹, is employed to monitor SiH₂ concentrations. The laser beam is multipassed 36 times through a quartz reaction vessel, creating an effective optical path length of 1.5 m. The transmitted light signal is measured using a dual photodiode/differential amplifier system and stored in a transient recorder.

Signal decays are averaged over 5–15 photolysis laser shots to improve signal-to-noise ratio and are analyzed using nonlinear least-squares fitting of the exponential decay traces, yielding \(k_{obs}\). Experimental conditions include gas mixtures containing controlled pressures of PhSiH₃ (1.4–5.3 mTorr), 2,5-DHF (0–450 mTorr), and SF₆ (total pressure 1–100 Torr) to ensure precise kinetic measurements. Rigorous purification and gas chromatography (GC) analysis are employed to minimize impurities and ensure the accuracy of the results.

dataset_item.question: How can a matrix-based spatial approach be developed to analyze water use impacts in agricultural systems?
dataset_item.answer: A matrix-based spatial approach for analyzing water use impacts in agricultural systems can be developed by integrating spatially explicit data into process-based life cycle assessment (LCA) methodologies. This involves defining the agricultural system under study, collecting key input data—such as crop types, water usage patterns, geographic characteristics, and water scarcity indices—and structuring this information into matrices that capture spatial variability and regional dynamics. Geographic information system (GIS) data can be linked to the matrix framework to enable spatially explicit tracking of agricultural activities, including feed production, transport, livestock operations, and crop cultivation. By incorporating location-specific variability and uncertainty, the approach facilitates quantification of water stress impacts at multiple production stages (e.g., milk processing or crop cultivation). This spatially resolved framework enhances the precision of water use impact assessments compared to traditional non-spatial LCA methods and enables targeted analysis of regional water scarcity effects, supporting more sustainable agricultural water management practices.

dataset_item.question: How does the pore structure of polymeric scaffolds influence cell adhesion and proliferation in tissue engineering applications?
dataset_item.answer: The pore structure of polymeric scaffolds plays a critical role in enhancing cell adhesion and proliferation in tissue engineering applications. Porous scaffolds outperform nonporous ones due to their increased surface area and the presence of small pores, which act as mechanical anchoring points for cells, facilitating attachment and growth. This improved cell-material interaction makes porous scaffolds particularly suitable for applications such as skin, bone, cardiac, liver, and neural tissue regeneration. Polycaprolactone (PCL) is a widely used biomaterial for scaffold fabrication due to its biocompatibility, toughness, and processability. However, its slow degradation rate can be tailored by blending it with faster-degrading biopolymers to meet specific application needs. Advanced fabrication techniques, such as 4D bioprinting, further optimize scaffold design to achieve desired pore structures and properties, enabling improved tissue regeneration outcomes.
