inference_contexts: The overall pair-separation results are consistent with established studies of radiolytic processes in condensed-phase water, and the present analysis unravels the source of this trend. Of course, ion solvation serves as the obvious driving force for many textbook chemical processes, such as ion-pair separation. For the hydronium half of the oxidized-water species, such a result is intuitive. The other half of this process-solvation of the hydroxyl radical and the radical's competition for the ion-was not a priori obvious. The results of this study clearly show that (1) ion solvation outcompetes the ion-radical effect to drive contact-pair separation, and (2) this solvation, through second- or third-shell effects, is strong enough to drive continued pair separation in large clusters and, likely, condensed-phase water.

This result is also encouraging for renewable energy processes involving the oxidation of water for solar fuels. The (first) oxidation has now been shown to lead to separation of the newly formed H3O+ unit, which must then migrate across a proton-exchange membrane. The present analysis suggests that initial migration away from a putative hydroxyl ligand and out of the first solvation shell is electronically favorable. Motion thereafter is only slightly downhill, although preliminary molecular dynamics simulations (not presented here) suggest that rapid Grotthuss diffusion - of the hydronium ion subsequently occurs. The extent to which the catalyst alters this landscape will, of course, be dependent on the details of the catalyst. This result highlights an important catalyst design consideration, however. The first oxidation of the surrounding water must occur with sufficient efficiency and with sufficient movement of the removed electron away from the oxidized water molecule that the hydronium unit bears no remnant attraction to the catalyst core. If the catalyst's ligand behaves akin to the hydroxyl radical considered here, without bias toward CP formation, then removal of the hydronium ion would be favorable. Even a small remnant electrostatic attraction could alter this behavior, however.

The preceding series of analyses has shown that the unique hydronium-hydroxyl contact pair, which has previously been studied extensively, must be a low-population species in the presence of sufficient solvation. Solvation of the ion and radical subunits serves as a subtle-yet-steady driving force for full separation of this pair. The magnitude of the driving force is large enough to cause separation at chemically relevant temperatures. It was also shown to be competitive with ZPE and thermal effects in certain cluster regimes, however, which highlights the need for added temperature control in cluster spectroscopy experiments. Nonetheless, in the largest cluster studied in this work, (H2O)+ 21, the ion and radical exhibited a clear propensity to stabilize at opposite edges of the cluster.

According to this formalism, the electronic wave function of the system, Ψ⟩, is represented by a linear combination of valence bond states φ i ⟩ that describe all possible molecular configurations of the hydronium ion. 1 Ψ ⟩ = ∑ i N EVB c i φ i ⟩ where N EVB is the total number of EVB states and c i is the expansion coefficient associated with the ith EVB state. In practice, at each step of the simulation the valence bond configurations are generated by identifying first the "pivot hydronium", which corresponds to the valence bond state with the largest value of c i . All water molecules located in the first three solvation shells of the pivot hydronium are also allowed to form hydronium ions, resulting in additional valence bond states φ i with different topologies for both the hydronium ion and the surrounding hydrogen bond network. The effect of confinement on proton transport can be counterintuitive because of two possible effects. The dynamics of water and ions slow down with increasing confinement, ,,, and in the absence of the Grotthuss transport mechanism, one would expect similar trends to hold for proton transport. In addition, slower water dynamics can diminish Grotthuss transport rates because this mechanism depends on reorganization of water solvation structures. ,, It is also possible for confinement to alter the hydrogen bond networks in a manner that is advantageous for proton hopping. Previous studies of proton transport in carbon nanotubes and other hydrophobic pores - , have shown that single water wire networks in small-diameter pores may exhibit very high Grotthuss proton transport rates. Thus, both the confinement-mediated structure and dynamics of water networks near hydronium ions can affect proton transport in different ways, and the resulting quantitative enhancement/reduction in dynamics may be specific to the microscopic properties of the system.

dataset_item.question: What is the effect of adding graphene to the casting solution on the pore size distribution, water contact angle, and water entry pressure of poly(vinylidene fluoride)/graphene membranes?
dataset_item.answer: The incorporation of graphene (GE) into the poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) casting solution significantly impacts membrane properties, leading to a refined pore size distribution with the largest mean pore size observed at 0.5 wt% GE. The addition of graphene enhances membrane hydrophobicity, as evidenced by increased water contact angles (CAs) and water entry pressures (WEPs). These improvements result in complete water repellency, enabling the membranes to perform effectively during prolonged oil/water separation processes. Membranes containing 0.5 wt% GE exhibit optimal performance, combining high separation efficiency, durability, and reusability across multiple cycles without degradation, demonstrating their suitability for practical applications.

In this study, we have investigated the macroscopic swelling of and accompanying free-volume changes in TO-CNF films. While these films swell according to expectation when subjected to 90% RH water vapor, swelling is reduced when the film drying temperature is increased. This observation is attributed to higher film density, as verified by SEM and suggesting enhanced hornification. In marked contrast, the total free volume of fully dried films is not affected by the drying temperature even though the pore size decreases and the pore number density increases with increasing drying temperature. Suspension sonication prior to casting serves to increase the free-volume pore size due to a combination of disruption and size reduction of the TO-CNF fibrils. Subjecting TO-CNF films to various RH levels reveals free-volume pore filling at low levels ( < 33% RH). As the RH is increased, free-volume pores expand. At RH levels beyond ~53%, water likely creates new free-volume pores and behaves as free water inside the film, thereby eliciting a free-water PALS signal. This conclusion is supported by comparing PALS spectra with free-volume intensity and lifetime calculations. Lastly, swollen films that are subjected to redrying exhibit slight free-volume pore size hysteresis. dataset_item.question: How do emission centers and traps in Ca8BaCe(PO4)7:Mn2+ influence its temperature sensitivity and potential applications?
dataset_item.answer:
The emission centers (Ce³⁺ and Mn²⁺) and traps in Ca₈BaCe(PO₄)₇:Mn²⁺ play a crucial role in determining its temperature sensitivity and potential applications. The material exhibits temperature-dependent emissions, with the blue emission of Ce³⁺ demonstrating lower thermal stability and the red emission of Mn²⁺ maintaining excellent stability up to 573 K. This difference enables ratiometric thermometry, achieving maximum relative sensitivities of 2.17% K⁻¹ (intensity-based) and 5.14% K⁻¹ (lifetime-based), making it highly suitable for noncontact optical thermometry.

Furthermore, the incorporation of Eu²⁺ ions introduces a temperature-dependent emission color shift, transitioning from yellow to deep red under UV light irradiation. This programmable color change enhances the material’s functionality for dynamic anticounterfeiting applications. By leveraging the interplay of emission centers and traps, Ca₈BaCe(PO₄)₇:Mn²⁺ demonstrates versatile applications in precise temperature sensing and security technologies, combining high thermal stability, tunable emissions, and visual temperature indicators.

dataset_item.question: How does the S0 → S3 excitation contribute to light-harvesting efficiency in meso-β-substituted porphyrin dyes?
dataset_item.answer: The S0 → S3 excitation in meso-β-substituted porphyrin dyes significantly enhances light-harvesting efficiency by introducing an additional absorption band in the 500–600 nm range. This absorption arises from intramolecular charge transfer between donor and acceptor subunits, which improves charge separation and reduces recombination. The coplanar and steric structure of the dyes further minimizes charge recombination, while acetylene-conjugated linkers enhance electronic coupling with TiO2, facilitating efficient charge injection. The broad visible-light absorption with higher oscillator strength, combined with optimized HOMO-LUMO electron density distributions, makes meso-β-substituted dyes like m-βet and m-βac superior to meso- or β-disubstituted analogs for dye-sensitized solar cell applications.

Till now, many long-lived luminescent probes have been developed for time-resolved bioimaging and biosensing. Among them, lanthanides and transition-metal complexes are the most widely used probes owing to their inherent long luminescence lifetimes. Lanthanides exhibts disdingishable narrow luminescence bands with extremely long lifetimes. The emission wavelengths and lifetimes of transition-metal complexes can be easily tuned by selecting different metal centers and coordinating ligands. They can also be used as energy donors in FRET systems to elongate the fluorescent lifetimes of acceptors. Effort has also been focused on the elongation of fluorescent lifetimes of pure organic dyes and inorganic nanoparticles. The luminescence wavelengths of organic dyes are easily tuned throughout the whole visible region and extending to the NIR region. Nanosized materials can be multiply functionalized by surface modification to meet different requirements. Despite the discussed applications of long-lived luminescent probes, the development of novel luminescent probes for bioimaging and biosensing with high precision and sensitivity is challenging. Current directions of the design of long-lived probes and the development of the time-resolved luminescence imaging techniques include but are not limited to the following: (1) lanthanides and transition-metal complexes contain heavy metal elements, which usually show certain toxicity to cells. Thus, it is necessary to develop novel probes with low toxicity through introduction of biocompatible ligands to lanthanides and transition-metal complexes. Design of long-lived organic dyes and inorganic nanoparticles will provide more choices in the selection of material system for a certain purpose. (2) The focus of probe design will be put on the maximization of the luminescence lifetime response to the analyte to benefit from the time-resolved photoluminescence measurement and imaging. (3) Multiple probes with different luminescence lifetimes can be used simultaneously. They are distinguishable via time-resolved photoluminescence techniques, even if they emit with similar intensity at the same wavelength. (4) Combination of the time-resolved photoluminescence imaging techniques with upconversion dyes that are excitable at the NIR region is an efficient strategy to improve the quality of the images. The low-energy excitation reduces the population of the unwanted excited states and the time-resolved photoluminescence detection further filters off the short-lived noises. Additionally, NIR excitation allows deeper tissue penetration and is suitable for in vivo imaging using live animal models. (5) There are limited examples of long-lived emissive probes used for in vivo time-resolved photoluminescence imaging due to a lack of long-lived NIR emissive probes and imaging techniques. Thus, development of NIR emissive probes with long lifetime and time-resolved photoluminescence techniques that are suitable for live animal models will broaden the scope of time-resolved photoluminescence application in vivo. (6) PLIM using long-lived probes requires longer imaging time. The imaging speed is unacceptable when lanthanides are used, and it needs to be improved. (7) The applications of persistent phosphors are of great usefulness in in vivo bioimaging, since photon acquisition can be performed when external excitation is turned off. The sensitivity is improved and phototoxicity is avoided. (8) Combination of time-resolved detection with modern imaging techniques, such as stimulated emission depletion microscopy, terahertz imaging, and fluorescence anisotropy imaging, will open up new directions in the development of imaging techniques.

dataset_item.question: How does the hydration state, such as anhydrate and trihydrate phases, influence proton conductivity and structural properties in copper-based two-dimensional metal-organic frameworks?
dataset_item.answer: The hydration state plays a critical role in determining proton conductivity and structural properties in copper-based two-dimensional metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). The trihydrate phase (1·3H₂O) contains ordered water molecules that form well-defined hydrogen-bonded chains, enabling efficient proton-conducting pathways along the crystallographic [100] direction. This results in highly anisotropic conductivity, with the conductivity along [100] being approximately two orders of magnitude higher than along the [010] direction (σ[100]/σ[010] ≈ 100). The trihydrate phase achieves a remarkable proton conductivity of 1.43 × 10⁻³ S cm⁻¹ at 80 °C and 95% relative humidity, alongside excellent structural stability under humid conditions. In contrast, the anhydrate phase lacks these ordered water molecules and proton-conducting pathways, leading to significantly lower proton conductivity and differing structural properties. The reversible transformation between the anhydrate and trihydrate phases, driven by humidity and temperature, highlights the adaptability of the MOF structure and the pivotal role of water in facilitating proton transport and maintaining structural integrity.

dataset_item.question: What role does conformational polymorphism play in enabling cyclic peptides to penetrate lipid bilayers?
dataset_item.answer: Conformational polymorphism plays a critical role in enabling cyclic peptides to penetrate lipid bilayers by allowing them to dynamically adapt their structures to the varying environments within the membrane. This structural flexibility facilitates their movement through the bilayer, enhancing membrane permeability. Studies using molecular dynamics simulations and NMR experiments have demonstrated that this adaptability is essential for efficient translocation across lipid membranes. Understanding and leveraging conformational polymorphism is vital for designing cyclic peptides with improved oral bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy.

The ability of cyclic peptides to target protein surfaces and protein-protein interaction interfaces makes them an attractive drug modality. Capturing the solution structure of a cyclic peptide is a crucial step toward any quantitative understanding of its properties. However, cyclic peptides tend to adopt multiple conformations in solution and such a feature makes it difficult to characterize their solution structures using traditional means such as NMR spectroscopy. This review shows that MD simulations with enhanced sampling techniques are capable of characterizing the solution structures of cyclic peptides and providing a rationale for their sequence-structure-activity relationships.

This Review has covered cyclic peptides of 3-21 amino acid residues, with variations in the nature of the cyclization linkage (end-to-end, side chain-to-end, many different covalent linkers not just disulfide), the size of macrocycles formed (12- to 47-membered rings), and the number of macrocycles present within the structure (monocyclic, bicyclic, multicyclic). The primary structure of the cyclic peptides has been varied to reduce proteolytic degradation (through adding N- or C-capping groups, positioning of the cyclization constraint) and modulate structure and affinity, cell permeability, and function (incorporation of d-amino acids, Pro and Gly residues, non-natural amino acids, non-peptidic and lipidic components, and different cyclization constraints). The secondary structure of cyclic peptide components has been modulated (through intramolecular hydrogen, electrostatic and covalent bonds; cyclization constraints; other molecular constraints such as heterocycles or derivatives of amino acids) to increase rigidity and favor well-defined secondary structural motifs within the macrocycle. Some of these secondary structures (e.g.. amphipathic β-sheets, helices, loops) were induced by binding to the protein, and they mimic protein conformations found at interfacial hot spots in proteins.

dataset_item.question: What are the mechanisms by which fungal spores rupture under elevated relative humidity conditions?
dataset_item.answer:
Fungal spores rupture under elevated relative humidity (RH) conditions primarily due to hygroscopic swelling and internal pressure buildup resulting from water vapor uptake. Prolonged exposure to high RH levels (up to 98–99% for durations of 0.5–10 hours) weakens the structural integrity of the spore walls, leading to their rupture and the release of submicrometer fragments. Environmental scanning electron microscope (ESEM) observations reveal that repeated hydration-dehydration cycles exacerbate swelling stresses, ultimately causing spore wall failure.  

The released fragments exhibit hygroscopic growth, influencing atmospheric processes such as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) activity. Elemental and compositional analyses using techniques like EDX, EELS, and STXM confirm that these fragments retain both organic and inorganic components. Morphological studies conducted under dry conditions characterize the fragments’ structure, while dynamic hydration experiments at RH levels up to 96% provide insights into their growth behavior. Size distribution data from scanning mobility particle sizer (SMPS) measurements link spore rupturing events to nanoparticle release in regions like the Amazon basin, highlighting their role in atmospheric particle dynamics.

dataset_item.question: How do density functional theory methods optimize geometries and predict nuclear magnetic resonance parameters for phosphole derivatives?
dataset_item.answer:
Density functional theory (DFT) methods are highly effective for optimizing geometries and predicting nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) parameters of phosphole derivatives. Geometry optimization is typically performed using hybrid functionals such as B3LYP and basis sets like 6-311G(d,p), ensuring accurate refinement of crystallographic data and inversion barriers consistent with experimental values. Alternative functionals, including ωB97X-D, BLYP, τ-HCTH, PBE1PBE, and BHandH, and basis sets like 6-31G(2d), cc-pVDZ, aug-cc-pVTZ-J, and Huz-IIIsu3-J, can also be employed depending on the computational requirements.

NMR parameters, including magnetic shieldings (σ), chemical shifts (δ), spin-spin coupling constants (J), and hyperfine coupling constants (ΔAₛₒ), are calculated using gauge-including atomic orbital (GIAO) methods. Chemical shifts for ³¹P and ¹³C are typically referenced to PH₃ and benzene, respectively. Solvent effects are incorporated using the polarized continuum model (PCM), ensuring better alignment with experimental conditions. Nonbonded electron interactions and contributions are analyzed through natural bond orbital (NBO) methods to further refine electronic structure predictions.

To improve computational accuracy and reduce variations in NMR parameters, statistical techniques such as response surface methods and Counter’s graphs are employed. These methods help minimize discrepancies in hyperfine coupling constants, spin-spin coupling constants, and chemical shifts, making DFT-based approaches reliable for NMR-based quantum applications in phosphole derivative research.

dataset_item.question: Which coupled-cluster methods most accurately reproduce potential energy curves and spectroscopic data for beryllium dimer?
dataset_item.answer:
The most accurate coupled-cluster methods for reproducing potential energy curves and spectroscopic data of the beryllium dimer are the CC(P;Q)-based approaches, specifically **CC(t;3)** and **CC(q;4)**. These methods correct active-space CCSDt and CCSDTq calculations for missing higher-order excitations, incorporating relaxed lower-order cluster amplitudes in the presence of dominant higher-order contributions. This enables them to achieve near CCSDT and CCSDTQ-level accuracy at a reduced computational cost.

Compared to traditional coupled-cluster methods like CCSD(T), CCSD(TQ), and even the high-performance CR-CC(2,3) and CR-CC(2,4), CC(t;3) and CC(q;4) consistently outperform by more faithfully reproducing binding energies, equilibrium bond lengths, and vibrational spectra. Notably, when combined with augmented correlation-consistent basis sets of triple- and quadruple-ζ quality and complete basis set (CBS) extrapolation, **CC(q;4)** delivers results that closely match experimental data, including binding energies within a few cm⁻¹, equilibrium bond lengths within ~0.01 Å, and vibrational spectra within ~4 cm⁻¹. It also successfully predicts the weakly bound *v* = 11 vibrational state near dissociation.

The CC(P;Q)-based methods excel due to their ability to incorporate dynamic correlation effects and higher-order excitations, making them particularly effective for weakly bound systems such as the beryllium dimer. Their superior performance highlights their role as the most reliable computational tools for studying the complex electronic structure and spectroscopic properties of this challenging system.

dataset_item.question: How do formic acid and water differ in their ability to catalyze sulfur trioxide hydrolysis to form sulfuric acid?
dataset_item.answer:
Formic acid (FA) is more effective than water (H₂O) in catalyzing sulfur trioxide (SO₃) hydrolysis to form sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄). Collision simulations indicate that the prereactive SO₃-H₂O-FA complex forms more readily and persists longer than the SO₃-H₂O-H₂O complex. This higher stability and frequency of formation result in faster sulfuric acid production in FA-catalyzed reactions. FA promotes reaction rates by imparting collisional energy that excites internal molecular motions, helping to overcome potential energy barriers more effectively than water.  

While water exhibits greater rotational flexibility and orients itself more easily into favorable positions near SO₃, it forms fewer stable hydrogen-bonded prereactive complexes, limiting its catalytic efficiency. Despite water's abundance in the atmosphere, FA's catalytic properties suggest it may play a significant role in accelerating sulfuric acid formation, particularly in the upper atmosphere where FA concentrations are non-negligible.

dataset_item.question: What strategies can be implemented to optimize phosphorus use while minimizing its negative environmental and ecological consequences?
dataset_item.answer:
To optimize phosphorus use while minimizing its negative environmental and ecological consequences, a multifaceted approach is essential:

1. **Enhancing Agricultural Efficiency**: Improve agricultural practices to maximize phosphorus use efficiency in food production systems. This includes precision farming techniques, soil testing, and crop-specific fertilizer application to minimize waste and overuse.

2. **Policy Interventions**: Implement regulatory measures to discourage excessive application of phosphorus fertilizers, incentivize sustainable farming practices, and promote awareness of phosphorus-related environmental risks.

3. **Phosphorus Recovery Technologies**: Develop and adopt innovative technologies to recover and recycle phosphorus from waste streams such as manure, sewage sludge, and food waste. These technologies help close the phosphorus cycle and reduce dependency on finite phosphate rock reserves.

4. **Dietary Shifts**: Encourage sustainable dietary patterns that emphasize reduced consumption of animal-derived foods, as livestock farming is a major contributor to phosphorus inefficiencies and environmental pollution.

5. **Education and Collaboration**: Promote education and collaboration among stakeholders, including farmers, policymakers, scientists, and consumers, to ensure widespread adoption of sustainable phosphorus management practices.

By integrating these strategies, short-term ecological risks such as eutrophication can be mitigated, while addressing long-term challenges related to food security and the global phosphorus cycle.

dataset_item.question: How do bonding preferences such as Ge-Se, Sb-Se, Se-Se, and M-M vary with composition in Ge20SbxSe80-x glasses, and how do they conform to the chemically ordered network model?
dataset_item.answer: In Ge<sub>20</sub>Sb<sub>x</sub>Se<sub>80-x</sub> glasses, bonding preferences generally conform to the chemically ordered network model (CONM), with Ge-Se and Sb-Se bonds being dominant. Se-Se bonds are absent in Se-poor compositions, while M-M (M = Ge, Sb) bonds are avoided in Se-rich compositions. A slight deviation from chemical order is observed near stoichiometric compositions. Compared to analogous systems such as Ge-As-Se and Ge-As-Te, replacing As with Sb and Se with Te enhances chemical ordering. Notably, Se-rich Ge-Sb-Se glasses lack M-M bonds, unlike Se-rich Ge-As-Se glasses, which exhibit Ge-Ge and As-As bonds. Similarly, Te-rich Ge-As-Te glasses avoid Ge-Ge and Ge-As bonds but contain As-As bonds, further demonstrating strengthened chemical ordering in the Ge-Sb-Se system.

dataset_item.question: What is the impact of structural defects on the selectivity of propane and propylene adsorption in Zr-fumarate-MOF?
dataset_item.answer: Structural defects in Zr-fumarate-MOF, particularly missing-cluster defects where 1/8 of zirconium clusters are absent, significantly impact the adsorption selectivity for propane and propylene. These defects reverse the material's typical preference from propylene to propane, as demonstrated by experimental isotherms, mixture coadsorption simulations, and breakthrough experiments. While missing-linker defects have minimal influence on equilibrium adsorption behavior, missing-cluster defects not only alter selectivity but also enhance adsorption kinetics due to phonon-assisted diffusion when pore apertures align with adsorbate sizes. Although the separation factor remains low for large-scale industrial applications, this defect-induced selectivity shift showcases the potential of defect engineering in metal-organic frameworks to fine-tune separation performance. This insight could enable the recovery of valuable propylene from raffinate streams, making it a promising approach for adsorption-based separation processes.

dataset_item.question: What are the transcriptomic responses of Dehalococcoides mccartyi strain 195 to arsenite and arsenate exposure?
dataset_item.answer:
*Dehalococcoides mccartyi* strain 195 exhibits distinct yet overlapping transcriptomic responses to arsenite (As(III)) and arsenate (As(V)) exposure. Arsenite exposure (10 μM) resulted in the downregulation of 52 transcripts and upregulation of 278 transcripts, while arsenate exposure (100 μM) caused the downregulation of 33 transcripts and upregulation of 332 transcripts. A shared response to both arsenite and arsenate included upregulation of 236 genes and downregulation of 13 genes, suggesting general stress adaptation or partial reduction of arsenate to arsenite.

Key upregulated genes under both conditions included those involved in stress responses, DNA repair, translation, nucleotide metabolism, and biosynthesis pathways such as folate and arginine. Specific responses to arsenite included upregulation of valine, leucine, and isoleucine biosynthesis pathways, while arsenate exposure uniquely upregulated genes associated with phosphate metabolism (e.g., kinases, phosphatases) and potassium transporters, reflecting arsenate's interference with phosphate pathways.

The *arsR* transcriptional regulator and *arsM* methyltransferase were upregulated under both conditions, though no methylated arsenic was detected. Conversely, arsenate reductase (*arsC*) and arsenite transporter genes did not show differential expression. The reductive dehalogenase gene *tceA*, responsible for TCE dechlorination, was unaffected by arsenic exposure.

Arsenic exposure also impacted aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, with differential abundance of aminoacyl-tRNA species. For instance, glutamyl-tRNA increased under arsenate exposure, while arginyl-tRNA decreased under both stressors. This suggests arsenic's disruption of sulfur-dependent enzymes and its broader impact on protein synthesis.

Overall, these transcriptomic responses highlight both specific and shared mechanisms by which *D. mccartyi* strain 195 adapts to arsenite and arsenate stress, emphasizing its resilience to toxic environmental conditions.

dataset_item.question: How do pH and PFOA concentration influence the adsorption efficiency of capsules in water?
dataset_item.answer:
The adsorption efficiency of amine-functionalized graphene oxide/silicate capsules for PFOA removal from water is influenced by both pH and PFOA concentration due to their impact on capsule-PFOA interactions. Experiments were conducted by adding a known volume of capsules to aqueous PFOA solutions of varying concentrations (0.1–10 mg/L) and pH (adjusted using HCl or NaOH to achieve values between 3 and 10). After hand-shaking for one minute, adsorption was allowed to occur for up to 3 days, with PFOA concentrations measured using HPLC, including analysis of capsule contents after mechanical breakage.

At lower pH levels (pH 3–5), protonation of the amine-functionalized capsules enhances electrostatic attraction to negatively charged PFOA molecules, significantly improving adsorption efficiency. Higher PFOA concentrations initially increase adsorption due to greater molecular availability, but saturation occurs as capsule binding sites become occupied. Kinetic studies demonstrated rapid adsorption within minutes, with equilibrium typically reached within hours. Optimal conditions for adsorption were observed at pH 3–5 and moderate PFOA concentrations, achieving over 90% removal efficiency. Additionally, the capsules maintained structural integrity during mechanical extraction, demonstrating robustness across varying conditions.

The present study showed that the aminopolycarboxylic chelating surfactant C12-DTPA can be effectively used in combination with two foaming agents for the removal of extremely toxic metal ions such as Cd2+, Zn2+, and Sr2+ from aqueous solution using the ion flotation technique. It was found that the removal of metal ions from the flotation cell is dependent on their chelation behavior with C12-DTPA and on the foaming properties of the samples, both of which change with the pH of the system. The results indicate that both Zn2+ and Cd2+ can be completely removed at pH 5. However, when the pH is increased to 7 and 9, barely 60% of Zn2+ and Cd2+ can be removed from the solution. On the other hand, at pH 5, no removal of Sr2+ was observed, whereas at a pH of 7-9, ~65% removal was achieved under comparable conditions. For efficient separation of metal ions from water systems, the amount of water transferred to the reject foam must also be considered, which is evaluated by measuring the concentration of metal ions in the collected foam. It was found that the interactions between the foaming agent and chelating surfactant affects the concentration of metal ions in the foam. A higher concentration of DoTAC increased the concentration of Sr2+ in the collected foam, because of the strong interactions between DoTAC and C12-DTPA. A higher concentration of DDAO, on the other hand, increased the removal of metal ions from the bulk, because of better foaming properties of the test solution. The separation efficiency is a measure of both the removal of metal ions from the bulk and the concentration of metal ions in the collected foam, and the foaming agent mixture must be designed accordingly. Taking the above parameters into account, it would be useful to design and optimize a selective ion flotation process in competitive systems for the target metal ions.

dataset_item.question: What are the potential applications of filamentous phage in materials science, biomedicine, and molecular targeting?
dataset_item.answer:
Filamentous phage demonstrates exceptional versatility in materials science, biomedicine, and molecular targeting due to its genetically modifiable structure and ability to display peptides. Key applications include synthesizing organic-inorganic nanohybrids, directing stem cell differentiation, promoting tissue regeneration, developing biomaterials for disease treatment, and generating bioanalytical methods for disease diagnosis. In materials science, phage-based supramolecular chemistry enables the creation of novel hybrid materials, while in biomedicine, its biomimetic properties contribute to precision medicine and tissue engineering. Molecular targeting benefits from its ability to identify cell-specific peptides, offering advancements in diagnostics and therapeutics. 

While filamentous phage is considered safe for in vitro use due to its nontoxicity to mammalian cells, further research is essential to address challenges related to immune responses and potential risks associated with in vivo applications. These efforts are critical for the clinical translation of phage-based technologies. The integration of filamentous phage with conventional fields represents an emerging frontier, paving the way for innovations in materials science, biomedicine, and molecular targeting.

dataset_item.question: Why do amorphous materials with limited triazine functionality exhibit higher charge storage capacities compared to those with persistent triazine units?
dataset_item.answer: Amorphous materials with limited triazine functionality exhibit higher charge storage capacities compared to those with persistent triazine units due to the destruction of triazine structures during high-temperature synthesis, which transforms the material into nitrogen-containing amorphous carbon. This process generates a high concentration of unpaired electrons and localized spins within the disordered structure, enabling pseudocapacitive charge transfer mechanisms. Unlike well-defined triazine-rich materials, which lack unpaired electrons and exhibit low gravimetric capacities, the amorphous materials leverage these electronic features to enhance charge storage. While surface area and C/N ratios contribute to the overall capacity, the primary mechanism is not purely capacitive. Evidence such as slight rate dependence and cases where higher surface area does not necessarily increase capacity further supports the pseudocapacitive behavior. These findings challenge prior assumptions that intact triazine doping drives charge storage and highlight the critical role of unpaired electrons in disordered, amorphous carbon structures.

inference_contexts: Several materials prepared from triazine-containing precursors were explored as active materials in Li half cells. Well-defined materials which exhibit strong triazine character show very low gravimetric capacities even if the triazine units are bridged by conjugated moieties, such as phenylene or 2,2′-bipyridine. This directly contradicts the previously suggested bipolar mechanism in which the triazine is n- or p-doped when cycled. In order to achieve high gravimetric capacities, the well-defined conjugated systems must be synthesized at higher temperatures, thereby destroying the triazine unit and creating an N-containing amorphous carbon material. These materials have high concentrations of localized spins (large numbers of unpaired electrons) that may be involved in the discharge and charge mechanisms. The N-containing amorphous carbon materials are very similar to N-containing porous carbon materials that have been evaluated as supercapacitor materials. , The capacity of the amorphous materials trends loosely with specific surface area and C/N content. However, higher surface area does not always result in a higher capacity, suggesting the mechanism is not purely capacitive. The slight observed rate dependence also suggests a pseudocapacitive behavior involving charge transfer processes. These charge transfer processes could involve the unpaired electrons in the amorphous materials, and indeed, the inactive PTI materials do not contain unpaired electrons. Suggestions for future work to further probe the charge storage mechanisms involve using in situ EPR in order to observe the evolution of the spin concentration as a function of discharging and charging.

dataset_item.question: How does the application of harmonic restraints to a proton indicator influence water recruitment into hydrophobic carbon nanotubes?
dataset_item.answer: The application of harmonic restraints to a proton indicator near the entrance of a hydrophobic carbon nanotube promotes water recruitment into the pore by creating a favorable solvation environment for the proton. The restrained proton, which is delocalized and naturally prefers a high-dielectric medium, is prevented from moving away from the interface between the nanotube and bulk solvent. This restraint draws water molecules into the hydrophobic pore to stabilize the proton, as the solvated proton relies on water molecules to form its solvation shell. This recruitment mechanism not only facilitates the establishment of water wires, which are crucial for proton transport, but also provides insights into how confined hydrophobic systems can sustain water-mediated proton translocation.

dataset_item.question: How can reduced-complexity models improve the analysis of PM2.5-related health impacts compared to conventional chemical transport models?
dataset_item.answer: Reduced-complexity models (RCMs), such as the Intervention Model for Air Pollution (InMAP), enhance the analysis of PM2.5-related health impacts by enabling high-resolution simulations and efficient sensitivity analyses that are computationally prohibitive with conventional chemical transport models (CTMs). While CTMs offer detailed atmospheric chemistry and physics representations, their resource-intensive nature limits their scalability and flexibility for extensive studies. RCMs simplify atmospheric chemistry and meteorology but retain key spatially varying parameters derived from CTMs, allowing for fine-scale grid resolutions (as small as 1 km). This granularity is crucial for evaluating environmental justice concerns, such as race- and income-disaggregated health impact assessments, and quantifying disparities in PM2.5 exposure across regions. Additionally, the lower computational requirements of RCMs facilitate Monte Carlo analyses, longer-duration studies, and efficient evaluation of source-receptor relationships. By balancing computational efficiency with spatial detail, RCMs provide a practical and powerful tool for addressing inequities in PM2.5 exposure and health outcomes.

dataset_item.question: How can a feedforward open-loop control strategy be designed to improve the efficiency of single-tank activated sludge systems for small-scale industrial wastewater treatment?
dataset_item.answer:
A feedforward open-loop control strategy can enhance the efficiency of single-tank activated sludge systems for small-scale industrial wastewater treatment by simultaneously regulating oxygen supply rates and external soluble carbon addition. This approach ensures compliance with effluent chemical oxygen demand (COD) and total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN) limits under varying influent load conditions, particularly for challenging scenarios such as low-COD, high-TKN influent. 

The strategy optimizes the dosing of oxygen and carbon by tuning specific weighting parameters (e.g., α₁, α₂, βCOD, βTKN, γ₁, γ₂) to achieve a balance between effluent quality and operational costs. By addressing influent imbalances, it sustains heterotrophic bacterial growth and enhances nitrogen removal, surpassing traditional oxygen-only control methods. Additionally, the system enables dynamic adjustment of control parameters to minimize resource consumption while maintaining treatment effectiveness. Case studies confirm the method’s ability to improve effluent quality, reduce costs, and adapt to diverse influent conditions.

dataset_item.question: What role do specific salt bridges such as Lys-Glu, Lys-Asp, and Heme-Lys play in the aggregation of deoxygenated sickle cell hemoglobin?
dataset_item.answer: Specific salt bridges, such as Lys-Glu, Lys-Asp, and Heme-Lys, play a pivotal role in the aggregation of deoxygenated sickle cell hemoglobin (deoxy-HbS) by stabilizing HbS aggregates through favorable electrostatic interactions. These salt bridges help overcome electrostatic repulsion and contribute to the balance of attractive and repulsive forces, which, together with van der Waals interactions, dominate the aggregation process. Molecular dynamics simulations have demonstrated that these interactions significantly lower the binding free energy (~ -14 kcal/mol), underscoring their importance in the stabilization of HbS aggregates. However, competing repulsive forces involving the same residues highlight the complexity of the aggregation mechanism. Targeting these salt bridges with antisickling drugs—such as those containing carboxylate or ammonium groups—represents a promising therapeutic strategy to disrupt HbS aggregation and mitigate sickle cell disease progression.

dataset_item.question: How are intra- and intermolecular diradical characters defined in rectangular-shaped tetraradical systems?
dataset_item.answer:
In rectangular-shaped tetraradical systems, intra- and intermolecular diradical characters (y<sub>intra</sub> and y<sub>inter</sub>) are analytical measures of bond weaknesses caused by intramolecular and intermolecular interactions, respectively. These parameters are defined based on a two-site diradical model and are expressed as:

\[
y_{intra} \equiv 1 - \frac{4t_{intra}/U_{OS}}{\sqrt{1 + 16(t_{intra}/U_{OS})^2}}
\]

\[
y_{inter} \equiv 1 - \frac{4t_{inter}/U_{OS}}{\sqrt{1 + 16(t_{inter}/U_{OS})^2}}
\]

Here:
- \( t_{intra} \) and \( t_{inter} \) represent the transfer integrals for intramolecular and intermolecular interactions, respectively.
- \( U_{OS} \) is the on-site Coulomb repulsion, which quantifies electron-electron repulsion within a single site.

These diradical characters provide a localized description of electronic structure, offering insights into the bond weaknesses due to intra- and intermolecular interactions. Unlike conventional global diradical parameters (e.g., \( y_0 \) or \( y_1 \)), \( y_{intra} \) and \( y_{inter} \) enable a more nuanced analysis of two-dimensional tetraradical systems, particularly in understanding electronic coupling and stability in such systems.

dataset_item.question: How does the anharmonic version of the third-generation Multistate Empirical Valence Bond method improve the simulation of proton dynamics in aqueous environments?
dataset_item.answer: The anharmonic third-generation Multistate Empirical Valence Bond (aMS-EVB3) method improves the simulation of proton dynamics in aqueous environments by providing a more accurate representation of both structural and dynamic properties of the excess proton, aligning closely with experimental observations. This improvement stems from its ability to treat the excess proton as delocalized across multiple water molecules, represented by a dynamically updated linear combination of valence bond states. By refining the description of hydronium ion configurations and hydrogen bond networks within the first three solvation shells, the method enhances the modeling of proton reorientation dynamics and corrects the underestimation of proton diffusion seen in earlier MS-EVB versions. These advancements enable a more realistic depiction of proton transport mechanisms, making the aMS-EVB3 method particularly valuable for studying complex systems such as hydrated materials or confined environments.

dataset_item.question: What evidence supports the existence of nitrogen-bound and oxygen-bound ligands in complexes involving coinage metal cations and nitrous oxide?
dataset_item.answer: The existence of nitrogen-bound (N-bound) and oxygen-bound (O-bound) nitrous oxide (N₂O) ligands in complexes with coinage metal cations (Cu, Ag, Au) is supported by infrared spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT) simulations. Infrared spectroscopic analysis in the N-N stretch region reveals distinct spectral signatures for these isomers. The N-bound isomer exhibits a blue shift in the N-N stretching frequency, up to 140 cm⁻¹ higher than free N₂O. This shift is attributed to the interaction between the metal cation and the nitrogen atom of N₂O. DFT calculations confirm these observations and provide insight into the binding mechanisms, revealing that metal ion s-d<sub>z²</sub> hybridization induced by ligand binding governs the observed spectral trends across different metals and ligand numbers. The coexistence of N-bound and O-bound ligands highlights the potential for isomer-selective infrared-driven chemistry in catalytic applications.

dataset_item.question: How do pH conditions and foaming agent interactions influence the removal efficiency of cadmium, zinc, and strontium ions in ion flotation using C12-DTPA?
dataset_item.answer:
The removal efficiency of cadmium (Cd²⁺), zinc (Zn²⁺), and strontium (Sr²⁺) ions in ion flotation using C12-DTPA is significantly influenced by pH conditions and the choice of foaming agents. At pH 5, cadmium and zinc are fully removed (100% efficiency) due to optimal chelation with C12-DTPA, while strontium removal is negligible. As the pH increases to 7–9, the removal efficiency of cadmium and zinc decreases to approximately 60%, likely due to reduced chelation stability, whereas strontium removal improves to about 65%, benefiting from stronger interactions at higher pH.

The foaming agent selection further impacts the removal process. DoTAC enhances the concentration of strontium ions in the foam, attributed to strong interactions with C12-DTPA, while DDAO improves overall metal ion removal from the bulk solution due to superior foaming properties. To design an effective ion flotation process, it is essential to optimize pH conditions and foaming agent concentrations based on the target metal ions. Balancing chelation stability at varying pH levels and leveraging specific foaming agent properties ensures maximum separation efficiency and effective purification.

dataset_item.question: How do salts influence conformational changes in ionic coaggregates of polylysine and polyglutamic acid during freezing?
dataset_item.answer: Salts, such as NaBr, influence conformational changes in ionic coaggregates of polylysine (PLL) and polyglutamic acid (PLGA) during freezing by disrupting salt bridges between the charged lysine and glutamic acid side chains. This disruption destabilizes electrostatic interactions within the polypeptide aggregates, triggering a reversible transition from β-sheet-rich structures to disordered conformations. Spectroscopic analysis, particularly in the amide I′ band, reveals this β-sheet-to-disorder transition during freezing, which reverses upon thawing. The phenomenon underscores the critical role of salts in modulating polypeptide structure under freezing conditions.

dataset_item.question: How does laser flash photolysis coupled with time-resolved laser-induced fluorescence enable the detection of peroxy radicals and their photodissociation products?
dataset_item.answer:
Laser flash photolysis (LFP) coupled with time-resolved laser-induced fluorescence (LIF) enables the detection of peroxy radicals (RO₂) and their photodissociation products through a precisely timed two-laser system. The first laser initiates the photolysis process, generating peroxy radicals at time-zero. A second laser, fired shortly before the LIF probe laser (typically 100–200 ns), dissociates the RO₂ radicals into detectable fragments such as OH or CH₃O. The LIF probe laser then excites these fragments at specific wavelengths (e.g., 282 nm for OH, 298.5 nm for CH₃O), producing fluorescence signals that are collected using filters and photomultipliers.

This short delay between the photolysis and probe lasers ensures minimal interference from secondary reactions, allowing accurate quantification of the original peroxy radical concentration. The experimental setup involves overlapping laser beams in a reaction cell, fluorescence detection perpendicular to the laser plane, and precise synchronization of laser firing and data acquisition. Additionally, temperature control and calibrated gas flow systems maintain stable experimental conditions, enabling detailed kinetic and thermodynamic analysis of RO₂ radicals and their reactions.

dataset_item.question: What transient structural configurations emerge within amyloid beta peptide dimers and how do these configurations contribute to polymerization into beta-sheet structures?
dataset_item.answer: Amyloid beta (Aβ1-40) peptide dimers exhibit highly disordered equilibrium ensembles characterized by diverse secondary structures and dynamic tertiary/quaternary contacts. Among these configurations, transient β-hairpin structures persist from the monomeric state and are consistent with experimental observations of oligomers. These β-hairpins may serve as nucleation seeds for polymerization into parallel or antiparallel β-sheet structures, which are characteristic of amyloid fibrils. However, significant structural rearrangements are required to achieve the highly ordered fibrillar conformations observed in mature amyloid aggregates. Detailed atomistic simulations also highlight N-terminal behavior, offering insights into how pathogenic and protective mutations may influence the early stages of polymerization and Alzheimer's disease progression.

dataset_item.question: What are the activation energies for the hydrolysis reaction and the decomposition reaction of Cu₂OCl₂ into CuCl₂ and CuO?
dataset_item.answer: The activation energy for the hydrolysis reaction of Cu₂OCl₂ is 44.8 kJ/mol, while the activation energy for its decomposition into CuCl₂ and CuO is 20 kJ/mol. Optimal conditions for the hydrolysis reaction include a temperature range of 300–325 °C, a steam mole fraction of at least 0.5, and a reaction time of 20–40 minutes. These conditions are critical for maximizing product yield and minimizing side reactions, which are important for the efficiency of the Cu-Cl thermochemical cycle.

In this study, we measured the yields of 2-ketones formed from the OH radical-initiated reactions of the C6-C13 2-methyl-1-alkenes in the presence of NO x , and combined these with results from previous studies to calculate the branching ratios for decomposition and isomerization of the β-hydroxyalkoxy radicals from which they are formed. The slight differences are due to a lowering of the activation energy for decomposition by the added alkyl groups, , but overall it is clear that decomposition and isomerization are both important pathways in all cases. On the other hand, the SARs predict nearly complete decomposition. As the carbon number of the 2-methyl-1-alkene decreases from C9 to C6, the ratio of the branching ratios (equal to the ratio of the rate constants) for decomposition and isomerization increases from 0.96 for the C9-C13 plateau to 1.5, 3.4, and 37 for C8, C7, and C6, respectively. This is likely due at least in part to decreasing rates of isomerization (caused by increasing strength of the C-H bond involved in the 1,5-H-shift reaction), but prompt decomposition (caused by chemical activation) may also play a role. If the first of these is the dominant cause, and the rate constant for decomposition is assumed to be constant at the C9-C13 plateau value, then the rate constants for isomerization are 3.9, 2.5, 1.1, and 0.1 (× 106 s-1) for the C9 to C6 β-hydroxyalkoxy radicals. dataset_item.question: How does energy input in catalytic methane combustors affect methane conversion and nitrous oxide formation in cocurrent and counter-current modes?
dataset_item.answer:
In catalytic methane combustors, higher energy input enhances methane conversion efficiency while influencing nitrous oxide (N₂O) formation differently in cocurrent and counter-current modes. Complete methane conversion is achieved over a broad range of flow velocities (5.1–57.3 m/s) in both modes without nitric oxide (NO) formation. However, N₂O is detected at the combustor outlet, with concentrations significantly lower in counter-current mode due to its higher energy input compared to cocurrent mode.  

Counter-current operation offers superior methane conversion and reduced N₂O formation, but requires careful thermal management to prevent flashbacks caused by reaction zone delocalization. Cocurrent mode, while achieving transiently higher methane conversion in reformers, demands substantially more energy input (approximately three times at ~1000 °C) to maintain comparable performance. This underscores the critical role of energy input and flow configuration in optimizing conversion efficiency and minimizing byproduct formation.

dataset_item.question: What are the differences in methanol dehydrogenation pathways between Pt terraces and Pt/Al2O3 interfacial sites?
dataset_item.answer:
Methanol dehydrogenation pathways differ significantly between Pt terraces and Pt/Al2O3 interfacial sites due to variations in bond cleavage sequences, intermediate stability, and interactions with the Al2O3 support. 

At Pt terraces, the dehydrogenation process begins with C-H bond cleavage, forming hydroxymethyl (CH2OH*), followed by subsequent C-H cleavage to yield formaldehyde-like intermediates, before the O-H bond is broken. These intermediates interact minimally with the Al2O3 support, and CO* formed at the final step preferentially adsorbs onto Pt.

In contrast, at Pt/Al2O3 interfacial sites, methanol binds strongly due to favorable interactions with Lewis acid sites on Al2O3. The initial step involves O-H bond cleavage, producing methoxy (CH3O*), which remains stabilized by an O-Al bond. Sequential C-H cleavages then occur, retaining the O-Al bond until CO* is formed. CO* formation requires breaking the O-Al bond, which involves overcoming a higher kinetic barrier. Throughout this pathway, intermediates at interfacial sites exhibit stronger interactions with the support compared to those on Pt terraces.

Additionally, these vapor-phase pathways may differ in aqueous environments, where water can influence reaction energetics and site competition, potentially altering the relative activity of Pt terraces and interfacial sites.

With the exception of CO*, species with incompletely saturated methyl groups and broken O-H bonds (CH2O*, CHO*) bind to the Al2O3 support via their O atoms and the Pt4 cluster via their C atoms. dataset_item.question: How do different 3D-printing techniques influence the fabrication of electrodes for water splitting applications?
dataset_item.answer:
Different 3D-printing techniques significantly influence the fabrication of electrodes for water splitting applications by determining material compatibility, structural precision, and post-processing requirements. 

Fused deposition modeling (FDM) enables the use of thermoplastic polymers such as PLA or ABS for electrode fabrication. However, these materials are inherently non-conductive, necessitating post-printing treatments, such as embedding conductive additives (e.g., graphene) or surface modifications, to enhance conductivity and catalytic activity. 

Stereolithography (SLA) offers high-resolution printing with non-conductive polymer resins, which allows for precise structural designs. These electrodes require additional steps, such as the deposition of conductive layers (e.g., nickel-phosphorus coatings) and catalytic materials, to achieve electrochemical functionality for water splitting.

Selective laser melting (SLM) directly produces conductive metal electrodes, such as stainless steel, eliminating the need for conductivity-enhancing treatments. However, the printed metals are typically not catalytically active for water splitting reactions. Post-processing steps, including the deposition of active catalysts, are essential to improve performance for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER).

In all cases, further modifications, such as surface structuring, catalyst deposition, or coating, are critical for optimizing electrode activity and ensuring efficient water splitting performance. The choice of 3D-printing technique depends on the desired material properties, structural complexity, and functional requirements of the electrode.

This likely stems from the fact that SLM electrodes require no additional treatments to make conductive electrodes, unlike FDM and SLM. Such steps can include altering the structure of the electrode support itself to facilitate water splitting or performing postprinting modifications, such as electrodeposition or atomic layer deposition (ALD), to deposit active OER or HER catalysts onto the electrode to improve the activity. Both of these routes will be discussed in the following sections.

Nanographite-nanocellulose suspensions exhibit highly shear-thinning behavior. This property is utilized by passing the suspensions through a slot-die and the fluidized suspension thus obtained can be applied onto a flexible substrate to produce conductive coatings in a continuous process. CMC addition lowers the yield stress and helps in pumping the suspensions easily. In addition, CMC improves the water retention of the suspension, resulting in improved coatability and runnability. GrCNF suspensions were coated utilizing a slot-die in a continuous process onto graphite foil, kraft paper, and paperboard to produce flexible electrodes for energy devices. The electrodes thus produced are highly porous with porosities close to 80 and 90% for coatings with and without CMC, respectively. Calendering causes an 80% reduction in sheet resistances and electrode thicknesses. Sheet resistance and resistivity as low as 1 Ω sq-1 and 12 μΩ m, respectively, were obtained for electrodes coated on a paper substrate. Electrodes with CMC show higher resistances, while calendering and creasing had no effect on their electrical properties. Finally, metal-free aqueous-electrolyte SCs were fabricated from electrodes coated on GF and KP, and a maximum specific capacitance of 63 F g-1 was achieved. Although the electrical properties are lower than for other devices demonstrated in the literature, given the low-cost materials and high-throughput processes used to produce the electrodes, the performance is justified, especially for low-cost devices.

Additionally, mechanistic investigations of the pentairon complex clarified the intrinsic features of the multinuclear catalytic system, which are totally different from those of conventional mononuclear-metal-complex-based catalysts. In the catalysis promoted by the mononuclear complexes, the accumulation of charge and the chemical conversion of the substrate coordinated to the catalytically active metal center proceed in a stepwise manner (Figure a). In contrast, in multinuclear catalysts, the multinuclear core can function as a redox pool and accumulate the charges required for the catalysis to reach the catalytically active state. Subsequently, the catalyst in the active state reacts with the substrate, which initiates the transfer of electrons to the substrate and rearrangement of covalent bonds in the substrate to afford the products (Figure b). In other words, the multiply accumulated charge can instantly be injected into the substrate to trigger the subsequent conversion reaction without the formation of any intermediates.

As already mentioned in this Review, there are various 3D-printing techniques that can be implemented to create 3D-printed electrode supports for water splitting applications (Table ). In addition, within each of these techniques there are a number of precursor materials that can be utilized. Hence, the material from which the electrode needs to be made dictates the 3D-printing technique used. For example, if one wants to fabricate an electrode from thermoplastic materials including polylactic acid (PLA), acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), and polyurethane, FDM would be the 3D-printing technique of choice. , Various groups have produced electrodes for the OER and HER through FDM 3D printing. Foster and co-workers were the first group to create graphene/PLA electrodes for the HER with a commercial filament called "Black Magic" using FDM. Unfortunately, because of conductivity issues with the commercial filament, the as-printed graphene/PLA electrode exhibited poor HER activity. To achieve better conductivity and hence a more conventional electrode support for water splitting, postfabrication modifications to these graphene/PLA electrodes are needed. In section of this Review, we will discuss how the post 3D-printing modifications performed on these graphene/PLA electrode affect the resulting water splitting capabilities. ,,

SLA can be undertaken to fabricate an electrode support produced from nonconductive polymers; however, a major issue associated with this fabrication route is that electrode supports must be conductive. , Hence, when SLA is utilized to create electrode supports, an extra step to deposit a conductive layer must be carried out. For example, Ding and co-workers 3D-printed a rectangular-shaped meshed electrode by SLA using a commercial available PlasClear resin for the OER. Because of the fact that the 3D-printed electrode was made from an insulating material, a number of steps were needed in order to achieve a conductive support for the deposition of the active OER catalyst. First, sensitization and activation of the electrode surface was done by alternatively dipping the electrodes, for 5 min each, into two commercially available electroless solutions called "electroless copper solution C", containing 5 wt % HCl and 5 wt % SnCl2, and "electroless copper solution D", consisting of 5 wt % HCl and 5 wt % PdCl2, both additionally with sodium dodecyl sulfate surfactant. Then the electrode was dried in an oven at 60 °C, immersed in 5% H2SO4 for 5 min, and then rinsed with deionized water. The final step to create the conductive layer consisted of immersing the electrode into a commercial electroless solution containing NiCl2, NaPO2H2, C4H4Na2O4, and HF at a temperature of 97 °C for 30 min in order to create a NiP conductive layer. At this point during the study, Ding and co-workers determined that the OER performance of the conductive NiP/PlasClear 3D-printed electrode was 1.53 V vs relative hydrogen electrode (RHE) at the benchmark current density of 10 mA cm-2. This OER performance is already very impressive as a potential of 1.53 V vs RHE is equal to an OER overpotential of 300 mV, which is already rivalling that of the state-of-the-art OER catalysts; RuO2 and IrO2, the best-known OER catalysts, exhibit overpotential values of ca. 300 mV at 10 mA cm-2. ,

dataset_item.question: How does molecular water influence ethanol decomposition kinetics on Cu(111) and enhance acetaldehyde production?
dataset_item.answer: Molecular water significantly influences ethanol decomposition kinetics on Cu(111) by catalyzing double hydrogen exchange reactions. These reactions involve the concerted transfer of hydrogen atoms, which lower activation barriers compared to sequential steps, thereby enabling a pathway-switching mechanism. This mechanism redirects reactive flux toward acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) production, enhancing its yield. Specifically, water facilitates two key transformations: the conversion of CH₃CHOH to CH₃CH₂O and CH₃COH to CH₃CHO via H-atom transfers. Computational studies reveal that even a small water coverage of 0.05 monolayers (ML) can increase acetaldehyde production by a factor of 2.4. Beyond accelerating individual steps, water modulates the global reaction network, making it a tunable parameter for improving selectivity and optimizing ethanol decomposition pathways.

The paper aims to investigate the ethanol decomposition mechanism on a Cu(111) surface using first-principles calculations, with a particular focus on how the selectivity for acetaldehyde production can be enhanced by introducing molecular water into the reaction network. By modeling a novel water-mediated pathway-switching mechanism involving double hydrogen exchange reactions, the study evaluates the impact of water on ethanol decomposition and acetaldehyde yield. The authors employ advanced computational techniques, including density functional theory (DFT), transition-state theory (TST), and the sum over histories representation (SOHR), to calculate reaction rates and describe the chemical pathways. The results show that water catalysis significantly increases acetaldehyde production, aligning well with experimental observations.

dataset_item.question: How does the incorporation of poly(ε-caprolactone)-b-polystyrene diblock copolymer affect the damping temperature range, glass transition temperature, and tensile properties of epoxy thermosets?
dataset_item.answer: Incorporating poly(ε-caprolactone)-b-polystyrene (PCL-PS) diblock copolymer into epoxy thermosets significantly enhances their thermal and mechanical properties. At 40 wt% PCL-PS, the glass transition temperature (Tg) decreases from 171.66°C to 107.84°C, while the damping temperature range (tan δ > 0.2) broadens from 28.02°C to 52.95°C. This broadening is attributed to nanoscale gradient plasticization caused by the spherical nanostructures with gradient coronas formed by the copolymer. Additionally, the incorporation of PCL-PS improves the tensile properties of the epoxy thermosets, demonstrating the copolymer's dual role in enhancing damping performance and mechanical reinforcement.

Spherical nanostructures were constructed in epoxy thermosets through controlling the lengths of each block in the synthesis of PCL-PS diblock copolymer. Together with PCL/EP and PCL/PS/EP composites, the damping mechanism of epoxy thermosets containing PCL-PS diblock copolymer were systematically discussed through DSC and DMA. Because of the gradient coronas structure around the nanostructures and the plasticization of PCL subchains, gradient plasticizing effect at nanometer scale was formed. Dynamic mechanical analysis shown that when the content of PCL-PS was 40 wt %, the glass transition temperature were decreased from 171.66 to 107.84 °C, whereas the damping temperature range (tan δ > 0.2) of the composites were broaden from 28.02 to 52.95 °C. Dissipative particle dynamics simulation has been performed on model systems of nanorod and diblock copolymer composite to understand the dynamics, structure, and morphology of self-assembled bundles of nanorods in gyroid phase. The nanorods are given preferential enthalpic interaction with minority component B of diblock copolymer by increasing repulsion with majority component C, so that nanorods tend to self-assemble and settle inside the confined contours of minority component B, aiming to explore the relative size and shape of the self-assembled bundles under confining locations within the matrix. The dynamics of self-assembly of nanorods is found to be fast and independent of phase separation of diblock copolymer. We have observed that nanorods self-assemble to form bundles of different sizes and shapes (spherical and elongated) depending on the relative flexibility of the nanorods and the nanorod-block copolymer interactions. In the case of flexible nanorods, both spherical and elongated bundles have been observed to form within matrix. Less flexible nanorods form elongated bundles for all cases of nanorod-major component repulsive interaction (a AC). The size of the bundles increases from flexible to rigid nanorod. Thus, gyroid phase formed by diblock copolymer can be used as a potential material to prepare templates to get nanorod arrays of different size and shapes depending on the nanorod flexibility and nanorod-copolymer interactions. In this study, we have doped nanorods by 2 wt %. In future, doping with higher amount of nanorods, the morphology and structure of nanorod arrays can be explored. We expect the outcomes of this study will help to fabricate templates for potential applications.

In summary, we developed a solution for inherent curing issues of rubbers, which combined a green-curing strategy for the epoxy-functionalized rubber and a high-efficiency recycling method for the end-of-life rubbers. The epoxy-functionalized SBR (SBR-GMA) with different epoxy group contents was synthesized through emulsion polymerization. The epoxy group and bio-based dicarboxylic acid served as a cross-linking site and cross-linking agent, respectively, resulting in a cross-linking network containing ester linkages. The SBR-GMA rubbers can be cross-linked effectively by various dicarboxylic acids without additional additives. Additionally, this curing system shows excellent scorch safety. With the increase in the acidity of dicarboxylic acids, the cross-linking rate and cross-linking efficiency of SBR-GMA/CB composites increase. The mechanical properties of rubber composites with the green cross-linking system can be tuned over a wide range in practical applications. Specifically, the SBR-GMA/CB composites with only a small amount of SA as a cross-linking agent can achieve excellent cross-linking and mechanical properties. By increasing the SA and epoxy group contents in SBR-GMA, the cross-linking density and modulus can be improved, while the elongation at break is reduced. Furthermore, due to the incorporation of ester linkages into the cross-linking structure, a rubber recycling method is provided by the selective cleavage of ester linkages. Most importantly, this recycling strategy for high-efficiency recycling of rubbers is facile and cost-effective. A triazine-based compound TN, and a phosphonate-based compound TP were also synthesized as controls. It was found that the charring effect of TNTP on DGEBA epoxy resin might be caused by phosphonate units rather than triazine moiety, and there was a synergistic effect on charring between phosphonate and triazine groups. TNTP modified thermosets exhibited not only the enhancement effect on char formation but also excellent flame retardancy compared with its TN and TP counterparts. The LOI value of TNTP-3/DGEBA/DDS was 32.4%, while that of TN-3/DGEBA/DDS was 29.0%, and TP-3/DGEBA/DDS was 31.8%. The flammability rating of TNTP/DGEBA/DDS could reach UL-94 V-0 rating with only 1.0 wt % phosphorus content, while that of TP/DGEBA/DDS could just reach UL-94 V-1 rating with 1.5 wt % phosphorus content, and TN/DGEBA/DDS was no rating. Besides, EP/P-ATA materials achieved excellent mechanical properties due to more hydrogen bonding. Furthermore, the EP-2.5% and EP-5.0% thermosets can still maintain the transmittance more than 90% of neat EP. As a consequence, the P-ATA exhibited a great prospect in fire-safe EP with high mechanical properties and transparency.

dataset_item.question: What mechanisms contribute to improved photocatalytic activity in RGO/g-C3N4/BiVO4 heterostructures during tetracycline hydrochloride degradation?
dataset_item.answer: The improved photocatalytic activity in RGO/g-C3N4/BiVO4 heterostructures during tetracycline hydrochloride degradation is primarily attributed to the RGO-promoted Z-scheme charge-carrier transfer mechanism. RGO acts as an efficient electron mediator, facilitating enhanced charge separation and reducing recombination of photoinduced carriers. This mechanism preserves the strong redox potentials of the heterostructure, enabling effective degradation of organic pollutants under visible-light irradiation. The ternary heterostructure exhibits a degradation rate 1.13–1.41 times higher than binary composites (RGO/g-C3N4, g-C3N4/BiVO4, and RGO/BiVO4), showcasing superior photocatalytic performance. Additionally, the composite demonstrates good stability during the degradation process, confirming its potential for long-term applications in organic pollutant remediation.

dataset_item.question: Why does Al2O3 coating fail to stabilize oxidation states of near-surface nickel cations in Ni-rich layered oxide cathode materials?
dataset_item.answer: The Al₂O₃ coating fails to stabilize the oxidation states of near-surface nickel cations in Ni-rich layered oxide cathode materials due to the inherent instability of surface Ni species during oxidation. X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and STEM-EELS analyses reveal that even with a uniform ~3 nm Al₂O₃ layer, near-surface nickel cannot achieve oxidation states comparable to bulk nickel. This suggests that the instability arises from structural or electronic factors, such as weakened metal-oxygen bonding or reduced bonding covalency in the near-surface region, rather than insufficient surface protection. The coating alone is unable to address these intrinsic challenges. Effective stabilization may require alternative strategies, including modifying the near-surface composition, enhancing bonding covalency, or applying advanced coatings or treatments tailored to improve high-voltage stability.

inference_contexts: The intention of the work presented herein was to establish a model system that would enable the study of electrochemically active Niδ+ species, located in the near-surface regions of NMC-type oxides, using hard X-ray techniques. This system provides a platform for studies aimed at testing, in working cells, the efficacy of various mitigation strategies such as additives, coatings, dopants, and high-voltage electrolyte formulations in stabilizing reactive surface species. XAS and STEM-EELS results have shown that electrochemically active Ni2+ cations were successfully doped into layered R3m configurations of a Ni-free parent material. By controlling postannealing conditions, STEM-EELS confirmed that active Ni2+ could be preferentially concentrated toward the surface of particles resulting in a larger fraction of the subsequent hard X-ray XAS signal originating from the surface as opposed to bulk Niδ+. High-temperature annealing resulted in a distribution of active nickel deeper into the bulk of the parent material. XAS data revealed an inability of near-surface Ni to achieve high states of oxidation relative to Ni in the bulk. A preliminary investigation into the efficacy of ALD coatings revealed that for electrodes coated with a uniform ~3 nm layer of Al2O3, surface Niδ+ species were not able to oxidize more than in uncoated electrodes. This result implies an inherent instability related to Ni oxidation in the near-surface regions of charged cathodes, which is not stabilized by the use of Al2O3. Therefore, modifications to the composition and/or structure of the near-surface regions of Ni-rich cathodes, which result in changes to metal-oxygen bonding (e.g.. covalency), perhaps combined with more advanced surface-treatment materials and methods, represent a better strategy for enabling "high-voltage" stability, specifically above the limit of inherent cathode-oxygen instabilities for a given composition.

Future work must consider each of these phenomena in order to enable high-voltage operation and increase both the energy density and cycle life of sodium layered oxide cathodes. First, the extent of iron migration must be elucidated with advanced characterization techniques, and the migration may be mitigated by substituting other ions for iron or introducing dopants that can act as pillaring ions in the sodium layer. Surface reactivity may then be reduced by modifying the electrolyte or by applying a stable cathode coating. The OP2 phase transition is a more complicated matter. Limiting iron migration is likely to lengthen the duration of the OP2 phase during cycling, which will in principle increase particle cracking, resulting in material isolation and aggravated CEI formation. Pinning ions can limit the OP2 phase transition and avoid cracking concerns, at the expense of capacity. The best approach may be to reduce the volume change of the phase transition, for example, by using dopants in the transition-metal plane with strong oxygen bonding. Regardless, it is evident that there is significant room for improvement both in the understanding and design of sodium layered oxides. Through rational design, the capacity and cycle life of this low-cost material may be improved such that it can compete for large-scale energy storage applications.
