Interestingly, taurine was detected not only in the control group (SI, Table S2) but also in the low-dose group after 14 days (SI, Table S1), which may suggest the existence of adaptive metabolic pathways in fish in response to exposure to lower BaP's level in the surrounding environment. The lack of the osmolytes in the high-dose group may be indicative of an imbalance in osmoregulation, which confirms previous findings. ,

Apart from the observed disturbances in the tissue components involved in muscle metabolism and osmotic regulation, additional unique and untypical compounds were captured by SPME probes. For example, the formation of arachidonoyl serinol, a metabolite of endocannabinoid (2-arachidonoyl glycerol), was observed in the high-dose group after day 1 and day 14 of the experiment (SI, Table S1 and Table S2). The exclusive presence of this unique compound in the high-dose group may indicate that higher doses of BaP (10 ng/L) can significantly impact the endocannabinoid system, which can also be used to distinguish this group from the other two. In contrast, 2′,3′- cyclic CMP and glucose-6-phosphate, which are crucial intermediates of multiple biochemical pathways, were present exclusively in the control group. Additionally, the end products of nicotinamide metabolism, N1-methyl-4-pyridone-5-carboxamide (4PY) and N1-methyl-2-pyridone-5-carboxamide (2PY), were initially only detected in the control group; however, after 14 days, they were also detected in the low-dose group. The low-dose group's metabolomic pattern underwent significant changes over the duration of the experiment and ultimately came to resemble that of the control group after 14 days. This change may imply the presence of adaptive mechanisms developed by the fish over time exposed to low concentrations of BaP. Conversely, the control group's metabolic profile remained relatively constant, although some differences in metabolite composition were observed, possibly related to the growth and development processes.

In prey, both Δ199Hg and δ202Hg values generally decrease with increasing depth (Figure a, SI Figure S1). Slopes of Δ199Hg/δ202Hg in muscle tissue of prey species in the EPO (1.50 ± 0.02 SE) and WPO (1.77 ± 0.06 SE) are shallower than experimentally determined slopes of photodemethylation in lab studies (2.43 ± 0.10 SE) and for muscle tissue in pelagic fish from the CPO (2.64 ± 0.24 SE) , (Figure a). The highest Δ199Hg and δ202Hg values are found in surface foraging fish, including flying fish (Exocoetidae spp.) in the WPO and Pacific mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the EPO (Figure a and SI Figure S1). The Δ199Hg values of flying fish ( ~ 5‰) observed in the central Pacific Ocean (CPO) are higher than those in surface fish in the EPO and WPO ( < 3‰) (Figure a).

The presence of BaP and its active metabolites in fish muscles affected several metabolic pathways mainly related to energy metabolism and osmotic regulation. As previously reported, the metabolism of amino acids is tightly regulated within the cells and is susceptible to alterations caused by environmental pollutants. ,, Indeed, the application of in vivo SPME revealed distinct differences in amino acid composition between the three groups, which indicates that the metabolism of these endogenous compounds is highly sensitive to BaP (Table ). In the control group, several amino acids were extracted using SPME probes, including proline and its derivative -5-oxoprolinate, as well as proline dipeptides. Moreover, an intermediate of proline metabolism, l-4-hydroxyglutamate semialdehyde, was also detected in the control group of fish. In contrast, the muscle tissue of the fish that had been at 10 ng/L of BaP for 14 days only showed the presence of free tryptophan and proline (SI, Table S1), with the level of the latter found to be 10 times higher than the level of free proline in the control group. In vivo SPME sampling also revealed differences in lipid metabolism in analyzed groups of fish. Among the detected lipids, two crucial intermediates in the β-oxidation of fatty acids, carnitine and its estrified form, acylcarnitine, were present only in the control group. In the low- and high-dose groups, only the presence of carnitine was detected, which suggests that BaP causes disturbances in lipid metabolism within the muscle cells. Moreover, several specific metabolites that are active in fatty acid transformation, such as l-2-aminoethyl seryl phosphate (l-serine phosphoethanolamine), which participates in glycerophosholipid metabolism, were detected only in the low- and high-dosage groups. The observed changes in the metabolism of lipids and amino acids are indicative of BaP's strong impact on energy metabolism, which is consistent with previous observations. ,

Untargeted metabolomics can be used to provide insight into the toxic activity of environmental pollutants in organisms, as they can enable exposome compounds to be detected and potential biomarkers of altered tissue metabolism to be characterized. , In the current study, the structural annotation of molecular features detected in in vivo SPME extracts revealed changes in the composition of endogenous compounds among three groups of fish (i.e.. control group, low-dose group, and high-dose group). After 1 day of the experiment, 277 features (peaks appeared in all samples within group) were detected in the control group, with masses ranging between 102 and 878 m/z (Figure a); after 14 days of the experiment, the number of detected features increased to 325, with a range of molecular masses between 104 and 928 m/z (Figure a). This increase in detected features could be related to the development and growing processes in juvenile rainbow trout. Conversely, analysis of the high-dose group revealed a lower number of detected molecular features and lower range of molecular masses than the control group. The high-dose group had 99 detected features after 1 day of the experiment, with masses ranging from 102 to 628 m/z, and 112 detected features after 14 days of the experiment, with masses ranging from 102 to 540 m/z (Figures c and c). This difference may be attributable to the altered fish's metabolism caused by higher doses of BaP. Interestingly, the low-dose group initially had 82 detected molecular features (masses ranged from 109 to 695 m/z) (Figure b), which was similar to the results obtained for the high-dose group. However, in the low-dose group, after 14 days the number of molecular features increased to 380 with masses ranged from 104 to 901 m/z (Figure b). This change may suggest the presence of an adaptive mechanisms in the metabolism that is responding to low pollutant levels in the surrounding environment.

dataset_item.question: What are the differences in thermal relaxation rates and activation energies of naphthopyran molecules in anisotropic versus isotropic phases of mesogenic solvents?
dataset_item.answer:
Naphthopyran molecules exhibit distinct thermal relaxation rates and activation energies in anisotropic versus isotropic phases of mesogenic solvents. In anisotropic phases, such as the ordered liquid crystal hosts 5CB and 8CB, relaxation rates are significantly slower (0.039 s⁻¹ and 0.014 s⁻¹, respectively) compared to the isotropic phase of toluene (0.18 s⁻¹). This difference arises due to the higher viscosity and restricted molecular motion in the ordered phases, as well as anisotropic guest-host interactions that affect the ring-closure dynamics. 

Activation energies for the thermal relaxation process are also higher in anisotropic phases, reflecting the greater energy barriers required for solvent reorganization during the ring-closure process. These barriers are influenced by the structured environment and reduced free volume in the ordered phases, which contrast with the more disordered and less restrictive environment in isotropic solvents. The temperature dependence of relaxation rates follows Arrhenius behavior, further demonstrating the sensitivity of naphthopyran dynamics to solvent order and viscosity.

These findings have important implications for designing photoresponsive materials and using naphthopyran derivatives as probes for local order in liquid crystal systems.

### 1. Summary of the Purpose of the Paper:
The purpose of the paper is to investigate the thermal relaxation behavior of naphthopyran photoproducts in guest-host liquid crystal (LC) mixtures, specifically focusing on how temperature and excitation conditions influence relaxation rates in anisotropic (ordered) and isotropic (disordered) states of mesogenic solvents. The study aims to understand how the organization of the liquid crystal host environment affects the activation energy and relaxation dynamics of the guest naphthopyran species.

### 2. Classification of Purpose:
**<result>**  
The paper emphasizes experimental results, as it reports findings related to thermal relaxation behavior, temperature dependence, and activation energy differences in the ordered and disordered phases of liquid crystal solvents.

### 3. Relevant Research Questions:
1. What are the specific mechanisms driving the thermal relaxation of naphthopyran photoproducts in liquid crystal environments?
2. How does the molecular organization of the host liquid crystal matrix influence the activation energy and relaxation dynamics of guest molecules?
3. What are the differences in thermal relaxation rates between anisotropic (ordered) and isotropic (disordered) phases of mesogenic solvents?
4. How can guest-host interactions in naphthopyran-containing LC systems be optimized to enhance phase transition control or material properties?
5. Can the findings on activation energy and phase-dependent relaxation be generalized to other guest-host liquid crystal systems or photochemical species?
6. What potential applications can arise from understanding the mutual interactions between naphthopyran derivatives and liquid crystal hosts?

inference_contexts: Guest-host LC systems containing naphthopyrans are known to undergo an increase in order when exposed to UV light, resulting from the conformational change from the closed form to the open form of the guest molecules. After removal of the UV excitation, the photoinduced population of the open form reverts to the closed form. Here we have investigated the kinetics of the thermal relaxation of the naphthopyran derivative G1. The decay rate is host dependent and increases with temperature. At room temperature, the decay rate was 0.18 s-1 in toluene, 0.039 s-1 in 5CB, and 0.014 s-1 in 8CB. The temperature dependence followed an Arrhenius behavior within each phase of the guest-host LC systems. Larger activation energies are observed in the ordered phases of the 5CB and 8CB hosts than in their isotropic phase. In addition, relaxation rates were larger in a nonmesogenic solvent than in mesogenic ones. The results indicate that the ring-closure process of the class of naphthopyran molecules studied here is very sensitive to the nature of the environment, including the amount of local order and the viscosity. The observed trend in activation entropy suggests that the change in geometry from the open form to the transition state requires a larger reorganization of the solvent molecules in ordered solvents than in an isotropic environment. This could be due to a change in the free volume or of the solvation sphere around the naphthopyran molecules in a liquid crystalline environment as a result of the anisotropic nature of the guest-host intermolecular interactions.

In summary, we have demonstrated an extensive application of 1H NMR relaxation to examine the 1:1 host-guest inclusion complex of β-CD with two orally active drugs in aqueous media, and reported their stoichiometry and binding constant. In the 1:1 drug-β-CD complex, both paracetamol and aspirin behave similarly, exhibiting an intermediate motional dynamics and giving rise to R 1 ns/R 1 se very close to the theoretically expected value of 1.05. To emphasize the use of NMR relaxation measurements for supramolecular inclusion complexes the following points might be highlighted: NMR relaxation measurement allows the assessment of intermolecular interactions between a drug and supramolecule present in solution. Measurement of nonselective and selective relaxation rate ratio for the free drugs indicates activation of any other relaxation mechanism other than IDD and XDD dipolar interactions for the free drugs. The molecular rotational correlation time of the free drug can be evaluated from the selective relaxation rate by considering the extreme narrowing limit (ωH 2τc 2 ≪ 1). Significant change in the molecular rotational correlation time (τc) extracted from the nonselective and selective relaxation rate ratio in the case of the drug in the presence of β-CD confirms encapsulation. Measurement of bi-selective relaxation rates employing modulated shaped inversion pulses for the simultaneous inversion of a drug proton and a β-CD proton allows extraction of the cross-relaxation rate of the drug proton. The cross-relaxation rate thus measured represents the contribution toward overall drug proton relaxation due to dipolar interaction with the β-CD proton after encapsulation. The cross-relaxation rates can further be converted into intermolecular proton distances between the drug and β-CD to estimate a mode of insertion of the test molecule. However, it should be mentioned here that experimental cross-relaxation rates can be directly converted into internuclear distances provided there is no internal motion. Hence, in the present case, limited internal motion of the drug molecules within the cavity has been assumed. Further, it would be advisable to measure the internuclear distances of these intermediate-sized inclusion complexes at a lower external magnetic field strength, ca. 200 MHz. Results of the DFT calculations performed further reinforce our predictions of the host-guest geometry presented here. Paracetamol enters the cavity through vertical insertion whereas aspirin chooses a horizontal mode, which is in agreement with the order of polarity of the different functional groups present as substituents, for example, amide > acid > alcohol > carbonyl. Finally, it may be concluded that 1D 1H NMR relaxation experiments offer a much faster and cost-effective method compared to that of 2D ROESY experiments to analyze drug-supramolecule complexes.

Tactic movement enables MNMs to be intelligent. In this Account, we first elucidated the intelligent responses of tactic MNMs using two models. One is that local vector fields, including chemical gradients, gravity, flows, and magnetic fields existing in systems make the overall alignment of asymmetric MNMs via an aligning torque M, directing the MNMs to swim toward or away from the sources. The other is that isotropic MNMs may produce directional propulsion forces independent of Brownian rotations. Then a variety of tactic MNMs based on them were introduced. In chemical gradients of fuels and chemicals that can regulate motor-fuel reactions, asymmetrically built MNMs achieve directed motion and chemotaxis by aligning themselves under M resulting from asymmetric distributions of products. Phototactic MNMs can be built through both light-induced self-alignment of anisotropic MNMs and directed propulsion of isotropic MNMs. MNMs with asymmetric morphology when exposed to fluid flows may suppress Brownian motion and exhibit rheotactic motion. For eccentric particle MNMs, the asymmetric distribution of mass or catalytic component results in M that allows the MNMs to align and exhibit negative gravitactic motions. Magnetotactic MNMs that are built by asymmetrically introducing magnetic components into MNMs will migrate toward the magnetic source. These tactic MNMs have been demonstrated to self-navigate to target locations and are useful for active drug delivery, microsurgeries, environmental remediation, and dynamic separation of active and passive particles.

dataset_item.question: How does pH influence the uptake and translocation of carbamazepine and lamotrigine in hydroponic plant systems?
dataset_item.answer:
The influence of pH on the uptake and translocation of carbamazepine (CBZ) and lamotrigine (LTG) in hydroponic plant systems was investigated using cucumber plants exposed to hydroponic solutions maintained at pH 4.5 and 7.5. Specific buffering agents were used to stabilize pH: MES for pH 4.5 and HEPES for pH 7.5. Additionally, nutrient composition was adjusted, with ammonium nitrate and calcium chloride substituted for calcium nitrate in the low pH treatment to ensure stability.  

Experimental results demonstrated that pH significantly impacts the pharmacokinetics of CBZ and LTG in plants. At pH 7.5, uptake and translocation followed typical patterns, while at pH 4.5, changes in protonation states and membrane permeability altered uptake dynamics. Reduced translocation to shoots at lower pH was attributed to increased retention of the drugs in roots, likely due to ion trapping mechanisms. These findings underscore the critical role of environmental pH in regulating pharmaceutical uptake, solute speciation, and root-shoot partitioning within hydroponic plant systems.

This "proof of concept" study aimed to provide real world data about human exposure to xenobiotics through ingestion of crops irrigated with reclaimed wastewater. Carbamazepine was chosen as a model compound for environmentally persistent xenobiotics. Carbamazepine is ubiquitous in reclaimed wastewater and is known to be taken up by crops; thus it is not surprising that carbamazepine and its metabolites were detected in all reclaimed wastewater-irrigated crops (Figure ). Statistically significant differences in the fresh weight concentrations of carbamazepine in the produce from the three different sources were found for cucumbers (p = 0.004), lettuce (p = 0.036), parsley (p = 0.004), peppers (p = 0.036), and tomato (p = 0.007), whereas for carrots the difference showed borderline significance (p = 0.054). The highest carbamazepine levels were detected in leafy vegetables, especially lettuce and parsley. In most cases the parent compound was detected at higher levels than the metabolites EP-CBZ or DiOH-CBZ. However, carbamazepine made up less than 50% of the total carbamazepine species in the produce, similar to previous findings , suggesting significant metabolism of carbamazepine by plants. The ratio of carbamazepine to metabolites appeared to be lower in fruits as compared to vegetables (SI Figure S2). With the exception of parsley and coriander, none of the fresh water-irrigated produce contained carbamazepine and/or its metabolites at quantifiable levels (Figure ). The supermarket-purchased produce (unknown source of irrigation) exhibited quantifiable levels of carbamazepine and its metabolites in four of the seven analyzed items. Lettuce exhibited significantly lower concentrations than observed in produce irrigated with reclaimed wastewater, and carbamazepine was not detected in peppers, coriander, or parsley. For cucumbers, carrots, and tomatoes the observed concentration of carbamazepine was similar in the supermarket-purchased produce and the produce irrigated with reclaimed wastewater. This suggests that some of the produce supplied by the supermarket on the day of sampling had originated from growers using reclaimed wastewater.

The median urinary levels of carbamazepine, EP-CBZ and DiOH-CBZ during the whole experiment are shown in Figure (urine concentrations for each study subject are presented in SI Figure S3). The concentration of DiOH-CBZ was highest among the metabolites in all urine samples, an order of magnitude higher than that of the parent compound, carbamazepine, or the EP-CBZ metabolite (Figure ) as expected from previous work. , EP-CBZ is quickly metabolized in the liver to DiOH-CBZ via epoxy hydrolase. The dominance of DiOH-CBZ in urine corresponds to reports on carbamazepine metabolism in people taking therapeutic doses. In our experiment the origin of some of the excreted metabolites might have been from direct exposure to these compounds, as they were present in the ingested produce (Figure , SI Figure S2), and not merely due to metabolism of carbamazepine. Interestingly, the conjugated form of carbamazepine (carbamazepine N-glucuronide) was undetected in the urine samples following consumption of produce irrigated with reclaimed wastewater. In contrast, in patients chronically receiving carbamazepine in therapeutic doses the metabolite profile includes carbamazepine N-glucuronide as one of the most abundant metabolites of carbamazepine excrete in the urine. , Uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase is responsible for the N-glucuronidation in the liver. Our findings of an altered metabolic profile may be due to the lack of autoinduction of enzymatic activity at very low exposures, or due to the actual ingestion of metabolites in produce.

dataset_item.question: How do donor and acceptor spatial orientations influence the driving force for electron transfer in organic photovoltaic devices?
dataset_item.answer: The spatial orientation between donor (D) and acceptor (A) molecules plays a pivotal role in determining the driving force for electron transfer (ΔG) in organic photovoltaic (OPV) devices. Face-on configurations, where the acceptor molecule (e.g., C60) is positioned near the central donor group (e.g., the A-D-A structure in DRCNnT), promote hybridization between the donor's highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the acceptor's lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO). This hybridization lowers the energy of the charge transfer state (CT1), resulting in a favorable negative ΔG. In edge-on configurations, ΔG becomes negative when the acceptor aligns near the donor's positive partial charges, enhancing the dipole moment of the complex and inducing a downward shift in the acceptor's LUMO energy. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that these favorable spatial orientations, guided by the donor molecule's lateral alkyl groups, are likely to form in real OPV films. Importantly, a more negative average ΔG across various configurations correlates strongly with higher power conversion efficiency (PCE), making ΔG a valuable screening criterion for optimizing donor-acceptor combinations. Thus, precise control of donor-acceptor spatial alignment is essential for improving OPV device performance.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. **Summary of the Purpose**  
The purpose of the paper is to investigate how the molecular orientation between donor and acceptor molecules in organic photovoltaic devices (OPVs) affects the driving force for electron transfer (ΔG), which is critical for overcoming exciton binding energy and improving device efficiency. By combining density functional theory (DFT), time-dependent DFT, and molecular dynamics simulations, the study identifies specific donor/acceptor configurations that result in favorable ΔG values. It further explores how molecular features, such as lateral alkyl groups, influence the formation of these configurations during film deposition, ultimately linking molecular orientation to OPV performance.

---

### 2. **Purpose Classification**  
The purpose emphasizes **"<result>"** because the study focuses on identifying configurations that optimize ΔG and correlating these findings with OPV performance, highlighting the implications of these results for device efficiency.

---

### 3. **Research Questions**  
Here are some research questions relevant to the themes and materials science interests in the abstract:

- How does the molecular orientation between donor and acceptor species affect the driving force for electron transfer (ΔG) in OPVs?  
- What are the specific donor/acceptor configurations that maximize the negative ΔG value, favoring exciton dissociation?  
- How do molecular features, such as lateral alkyl groups, influence the self-assembly and orientation of donor/acceptor pairs during film deposition?  
- What role does hybridization between the molecular orbitals of donor and acceptor molecules play in stabilizing the lowest charge transfer state (CT1)?  
- How does the electrostatic potential induced by dipole moments in specific configurations impact ΔG?  
- Can molecular dynamics simulations predict the prevalence of optimal donor/acceptor configurations in thin-film OPV materials?  
- What is the correlation between ΔG values (averaged over D/A configurations) and the experimental performance of OPV devices?  
- How can the design of donor molecules be fine-tuned to promote favorable orientations (e.g., face-on dimers) and improve OPV efficiency?

These questions address the interplay between molecular orientation, electronic properties, and device performance, aligning with key materials science interests in optimizing organic photovoltaic materials.

inference_contexts: We have developed several alternating electron accepting polymers with weak acceptor-strong acceptor (WA-SA) combination. The SA moiety is necessary for the efficient electron transfer as an acceptor. The most promising polymer is PQP, which exhibited a PCE of 3.52% when coupled with plasmonic effect. The improved device performance was achieved only when 1-chloronaphthalene was used as a cosolvent, which helps to organize polymer films with favored face-on polymer chain assembly and phase separation between donor and acceptor. Despite similar backbone structures between PQP and PFP, PQP devices showed much better photovoltaic performance. Through the fluorescence quenching experiment, we revealed the PQP has the better binding affinity with a PTB7-Th donor polymer, resulting in better electron accepting characteristic. These results suggest that the proper internal polarization of acceptor polymers, similar to what we observed in our PTB series of donor polymers, and the face-on orientation in an active layer is highly important to optimize the photovoltaic properties in all-polymer solar cells. Although lengthy synthesis is used in obtaining some of the polymers, the insight gained will guide our further development of better electron accepting materials.

It is common in the literature to associate a higher Δμge of the donor with a better photovoltaic performance of the OPV. Yet our results indicate that even when the donor is a centrosymmetric molecule so that Δμge ≈ 0, the best performance is obtained when ΔG tends to be more negative. Indeed we found a correlation between the magnitude of the driving force averaged over all tested dimer's configurations (ΔG ) and the measured power conversion efficiency (higher PCEs are observed when the ΔG is more negative). Here is important to mention that low CT1 energies can make ΔG more negative, but in some systems, it can also produce trapping states that are detrimental to the charge separation. - Hence a detailed description of the importance of the magnitude of the CT1 energy for charge separation needs a more sophisticated analysis involving, for example, Marcus theory to calculate the charge transfer rates. ,- Yet our results suggest that the calculation of ΔG for the dimer can be a sound and preliminary criterion to test possible combinations of donor and acceptor materials for photovoltaic applications even before they are actuality tested in the laboratory. Our results demonstrate the importance of the microscopy structure of the D/A dimer to define ΔG. It is clear then that a fine-tuning of the donor and acceptor relative spatial orientation can be a valuable strategy to improve the OPV efficiency.

A favorable driving force for charge generation is obtained when ΔG < 0. For some configurations of the D/A dimer, ΔG is near or greater than zero, which hinders the electron transfer from the donor to the acceptor. For the face-on orientation, ΔG < 0 occurs when C 60 is near the central group of the A-D-A molecules. This configuration favors the hybridization between the HOMO of the donor and the LUMO of the acceptor which decreases the energy of the CT1 state. Considering the edge-on orientation, negative values of ΔG are obtained when the C 60 is aligned close to the positive partial charges of the donor's molecule. In this case, the magnitude of the complex's dipole moment increases. The electrostatic potential energy associated with this dipole moment induces a downward shift of the acceptor's LUMO, which decreases the energy of the CT1 state so that ΔG < 0.

In this work, we find that different positions of the C 60 relative to the donor DRCNnT molecule can induce large variations in the complex's dipole moment, the energy of the charge transfer states, and the driving force for electron transfer.

We have used a small-molecule azomethine (TPA-TBT-TPA) as an electron donor in a standard bulk heterojunction solar cell configuration. The best devices were obtained using a high (1:5) donor to acceptor (PCBM) ratio and a film thickness of ~70 nm. PCE's of 2.17% could be achieved, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the highest reported efficiency for an azomethine-based organic photovoltaic reported to date. We found that the PCE is limited by a nongeminate charge recombination process, which we attribute to low hole mobilities. Transient absorption measurements showed that the excitons exhibit a very short lifetime (120 ps). dataset_item.question: How are vibrational couplings between nitrate ester groups in pentaerythritol tetranitrate calculated using transition dipole coupling models?
dataset_item.answer:
Vibrational couplings between nitrate ester groups in pentaerythritol tetranitrate (PETN) are calculated using a transition dipole coupling (TDC) model, which treats each nitrate ester group as a point dipole. The coupling constant \( \beta_{ij} \) between local vibrational modes \( i \) and \( j \) is calculated using the equation:

\[
\beta_{ij} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \left[ \frac{\vec{\mu}_i \cdot \vec{\mu}_j}{r_{ij}^3} - \frac{3(\vec{\mu}_i \cdot \vec{r}_{ij})(\vec{\mu}_j \cdot \vec{r}_{ij})}{r_{ij}^5} \right]
\]

Here:
- \( \vec{\mu}_i \) and \( \vec{\mu}_j \) are the transition dipole moments of groups \( i \) and \( j \), respectively.
- \( \vec{r}_{ij} \) is the separation vector between the groups.
- \( r_{ij} \) is the magnitude of \( \vec{r}_{ij} \).
- \( \varepsilon_0 \) is the permittivity of free space.

The transition dipole moments \( \vec{\mu}_i \) are derived from density functional theory (DFT) calculations using the B3LYP functional with the 6-31G(d,p) basis set on an isolated PETN molecule. The model assumes uniform dipole orientations relative to the N-O bond axis for all nitrate ester groups.

The crystal structure of PETN is used to determine the relative positions and distances between nitrate ester groups. These inter-group distances and dipole orientations are used to compute coupling constants \( \beta_{ij} \), which populate a one-exciton Hamiltonian matrix. The Hamiltonian is then diagonalized to obtain normal-mode frequencies and eigenvectors. These results are subsequently used to simulate the linear FTIR spectrum of PETN.

This approach provides insight into the vibrational interactions between nitrate ester groups and enables accurate modeling of the spectral features observed in experiments.

dataset_item.question: What are the major oxidation products and the stability of intermediates formed during methimazole oxidation by chlorite and chlorine dioxide?
dataset_item.answer: Methimazole (MMI) oxidation by chlorite and chlorine dioxide leads to desulfurization, with sulfate and N-methylimidazole as the final oxidation products. The major intermediate observed is sulfonic acid, which forms prior to complete sulfate generation. Sulfenic and sulfinic acids are likely intermediates in the reaction pathway, but they are highly unstable and rapidly oxidize further, preventing significant accumulation or observation in analytical methods like ESI-MS. Negligible formation of S-oxide occurs during chlorite-mediated oxidation. Experimental evidence using excess MMI with aqueous bromine supports the transient presence of sulfenic and sulfinic acids, confirming their role as fleeting intermediates in the reaction.

dataset_item.question: How does shape morphology influence the surface-enhanced Raman scattering intensity of gold nanorods?
dataset_item.answer: The shape morphology of gold nanorods (AuNRs) plays a dominant role in influencing their surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) intensity, often surpassing the importance of plasmon resonance tuning. Experimental studies demonstrate that reshaping AuNRs from cigarlike to dumbbell morphologies can enhance SERS response by up to fivefold, highlighting the critical impact of morphology optimization. While electromagnetic theory predicts strong SERS intensity variations with plasmon resonance shifts, experimental results show only moderate changes across a wide plasmon resonance range (650–925 nm). Instead, AuNR morphology emerges as the key factor, as structural changes significantly alter the localized electromagnetic fields responsible for SERS enhancement. Additionally, the background signal in SERS spectra has been found to correlate with AuNR photoluminescence and elastic light scattering, providing further insights into the interplay between shape and optical properties. These findings suggest that optimizing nanorod shape morphology, rather than strictly aligning plasmon resonance with the excitation wavelength, is the most effective strategy for maximizing SERS performance.

The gold rod was rotated and translated slowly to provide a fresh surface for each ablation pulse. The resulting supersonic expansion was probed 10 cm downstream from the nozzle by a xenon chloride excimer-pumped dye laser (Lambda Physik COMPex 102 and Lumonics Hyperdye 300) operating over the 470-680 nm range. Spectral acquisition required the use of several different laser dyes and the concatenated spectrum was not normalized to the laser power. Laser-induced fluorescence was imaged by adaptive optics and detected using a 0.67 m monochromator (McPherson 207) with 1 mm slit widths and equipped with a water-cooled, intensified CCD array (Andor iStar). Excitation scans were recorded by simultaneously scanning both the laser and monochromator to maintain a constant wavenumber offset (Stokes shift). Low resolution dispersed fluorescence spectra were simultaneously collected during excitation scans. This two-dimensional spectral acquisition made it possible to distinguish fluorescence arising from the gold dimer, Au2, which has transitions throughout the wavelength range of interest. - For recording higher resolution dispersed fluorescence spectra, the slits were narrowed to 0.25 mm, and the excitation laser was fixed at the wavelength of a particular band in the excitation spectrum. Radiative lifetimes were measured by tuning the laser wavelength to be in resonance with a particular feature of the excitation spectra and recording the DF spectrum at variable time delays from the pulsed laser. Typically, the detection gate for the CCD was set to a large value (2 μs) and the time delay from the laser excitation stepped in 50 ns increments to produce a series of DF spectra. The resulting DF spectra were integrated over the appropriate wavelength region to give the relative fluorescence intensity at a given delay from the laser excitation. dataset_item.question: How does the binding energy and disorder in charge-transfer state energies influence the temperature dependence of the Langevin reduction factor?
dataset_item.answer:
The temperature dependence of the Langevin reduction factor is predominantly governed by two factors: the binding energy of electron-hole pairs within charge-transfer (CT) states and the energetic disorder in the distribution of CT-state energies. These factors influence the recombination dynamics through a two-step interface process, where CT states act as intermediaries. As temperature increases, the reduction factor decreases qualitatively, even when charge carrier mobilities are assumed to be temperature-independent. This behavior arises because higher temperatures reduce the binding energy's impact and allow for greater thermal activation of CT states, while energetic disorder further modulates recombination pathways.

For accurate quantitative predictions, it is crucial to account for the specific temperature dependence of charge carrier mobilities and the degree of disorder in CT-state energies. Experimental observations suggest that up to approximately 150 K, the reduction factor aligns with the CT-state equilibrium model, after which it converges with predictions from continuum models. The extended CT-state equilibrium model successfully reproduces realistic device characteristics, demonstrating that reduced Langevin recombination originates from the dynamic behavior of CT states and their interaction with disorder and temperature.

Thus, while the model qualitatively explains the reduction in the Langevin factor with increasing temperature, precise predictions require detailed knowledge of temperature-dependent mobilities and the extent of energetic disorder in CT states.

For example, it will be important to decouple intrinsic reaction rates from any changes in subtle morphology during reduction (i.e.. expansion, crack propagation). In addition, the inherent thermal instability of LEDC suggests that, in order to develop lithium ion batteries with long life, electrolyte formulations should be used which limit the presence of EC reduction products on the anode surface. Alternative solvents or additives which generate initial reduction products with superior stability but comparable or better lithium ion conductivity would be preferable.

dataset_item.question: How do persistent free radicals in nitrogen-doped biochar influence Cr (VI) reduction and Cr (III) generation during quenching tests?
dataset_item.answer: Persistent free radicals (PFRs) in nitrogen-doped biochar (BC) play a critical role in Cr(VI) reduction and Cr(III) generation by acting as electron donors and mediating redox processes. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy was utilized to quantify PFR concentrations in biochar before and after reactions with Cr(VI), confirming their presence and activity. Quenching tests using hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) and methanol as competitive electron scavengers demonstrated the direct involvement of PFRs in electron transfer processes, while benzoquinone (BQ) helped probe the limited role of superoxide radicals (O₂⁻) in these transformations. Pre-extraction experiments using organic solvents effectively removed PFRs from biochar, significantly reducing Cr(VI) reduction and Cr(III) generation, further validating the essential role of PFRs in the redox mechanism.

dataset_item.question: What mechanisms enable ditopic ligands containing π-conjugated systems to selectively recognize Zn²⁺ ions and form fluorescent hydrogels?
dataset_item.answer: Ditopic ligands containing π-conjugated systems selectively recognize Zn²⁺ ions through metal-ligand coordination interactions, which induce fluorescence enhancement in the blue emission range in both solution and gel states. This selective recognition arises from the ability of Zn²⁺ to promote supramolecular polymerization, enabling the formation of fluorescent hydrogels with ordered structures. Unlike other metal salts, Zn²⁺ ions uniquely trigger gelation, while Cu²⁺ ions lead to the formation of stimuli-responsive hydrogels with distinct properties, such as chirality and electrochemical activity. The absence of hydrogen-bonding or hydrophilic groups in the ligand emphasizes the importance of π-conjugation and metal coordination in driving self-assembly processes. This mechanism demonstrates the versatility of ditopic ligands in designing multifunctional hydrogels with tunable fluorescence, rheology, and responsiveness to various stimuli.

dataset_item.question: How can the actuation force be determined for a droplet moving on an inclined plane under an electric field?
dataset_item.answer:
The actuation force for a droplet moving on an inclined plane under an electric field can be determined using an energy minimization principle and a capacitive network model. The system consists of a droplet modeled as a perfect conductor bridging two electrodes separated by a dielectric layer. When a voltage \( V \) is applied to the front electrode and the rear electrode is grounded, a capacitive network is formed, and the droplet's position determines the distribution of capacitances.

The actuation force arises from the tendency of the system to minimize the stored electrostatic energy. This force is mathematically derived as the spatial derivative of the stored energy with respect to the droplet’s displacement:

\[
F_{\text{act}} = \frac{dE}{dx} = \frac{1}{2} \frac{C_2 - C_1}{C_1 + C_2} \frac{dC_1}{dx} V^2,
\]

where:
- \( C_1 \) and \( C_2 \) are the capacitances associated with the droplet's contact areas over the front and rear electrodes, respectively,
- \( \frac{dC_1}{dx} \) represents the rate of capacitance change with respect to the droplet’s displacement,
- \( V \) is the applied voltage.

The capacitances \( C_1 \) and \( C_2 \) are calculated using parallel-plate approximations based on the geometry of the droplet, which is modeled as a non-deformable spherical cap. The geometry of the droplet and its displacement influence \( \frac{dC_1}{dx} \), making it a key parameter in determining the actuation force.

In addition to the actuation force, opposing forces such as viscous drag, contact line friction, gravity, and contact angle hysteresis must be considered to analyze the net motion of the droplet. These forces act to resist the droplet's movement and influence its dynamics on the inclined plane.

Thus, the actuation force is determined by the electrostatic energy gradient, while the net motion of the droplet is the result of the interplay between this actuation force and the opposing forces.

dataset_item.question: How does the serum half-life extension of sfGFP conjugated with human serum albumin compare to sfGFP conjugated with polyethylene glycol?
dataset_item.answer:
The serum half-life of superfolder green fluorescent protein (sfGFP) conjugated with human serum albumin (HSA) is comparable to that of sfGFP conjugated with polyethylene glycol (PEG). In mice, sfGFP-HSA exhibited a serum half-life of 13.5 hours, while sfGFP-PEG20 and sfGFP-PEG30 exhibited serum half-lives of 11.0 hours and 14.3 hours, respectively. These values represent substantial increases compared to the unmodified sfGFP, which has a serum half-life of only 1.5 hours (9.0-, 7.3-, and 9.5-fold increases for sfGFP-HSA, sfGFP-PEG20, and sfGFP-PEG30, respectively). 

Both conjugation strategies enhance serum half-life without compromising sfGFP fluorescence. HSA offers additional advantages, including lower immunogenicity and better biodegradability compared to PEG. However, potential immune responses due to HSA denaturation during conjugation warrant further investigation. These findings highlight HSA as a promising alternative to PEG for extending the serum half-life of sfGFP.

dataset_item.question: What are the factors that influence the efficiency of enzymatic cascade reactions in nanocompartments?
dataset_item.answer:
The efficiency of enzymatic cascade reactions in nanocompartments is influenced by several interrelated factors:

1. **Diffusion of Intermediates**: The rate at which substrates and reaction intermediates pass through the membrane pores of nanocompartments significantly affects reaction efficiency. Membrane permeability must be optimized to ensure sufficient molecular transport while maintaining compartmental integrity.

2. **Encounter Probability**: The likelihood that reaction intermediates from one compartment successfully encounter and enter subsequent nanocompartments containing the next enzyme in the cascade is critical. This is influenced by spatial organization and the proximity of enzyme-containing nanocompartments.

3. **Protective Role vs. Transport Efficiency**: Nanocompartments provide essential protection for encapsulated enzymes, particularly in complex biological environments such as serum and cellular conditions. However, this shielding effect must be balanced against the need for effective molecular transport between compartments to sustain reaction flow.

4. **Spatial Distribution of Compartments**: Optimizing the spatial arrangement of nanocompartments can enhance the efficiency of cascade reactions by reducing the diffusion distance and increasing the likelihood of productive encounters between intermediates and subsequent enzymes.

By carefully balancing these factors—membrane permeability, spatial organization, and the protective nature of nanocompartments—reaction efficiency can be optimized for applications such as therapeutic interventions and biochemical engineering.

dataset_item.question: How does the concentration of gamma-butyroselenolactone affect the cross-link density and swelling degree of diselenide-containing hydrogels?
dataset_item.answer: The concentration of gamma-butyroselenolactone plays a critical role in determining the cross-link density and swelling degree of diselenide-containing hydrogels. Increasing the concentration of gamma-butyroselenolactone during synthesis raises the diselenide content, leading to a higher cross-link density. This results in reduced swelling of the hydrogels due to the tighter network structure that limits water absorption. Conversely, lower concentrations yield a less cross-linked network, allowing for greater swelling. Additionally, these hydrogels exhibit tunable mechanical properties, strong skin adhesion, and the ability to dissolve on-demand via oxidation or reduction, making them ideal for applications such as burn wound dressings. Their light responsiveness and biocompatibility further enhance their suitability for medical uses.

dataset_item.question: How do structural parameters such as fiber thickness and channel size of ZIF-8 monoliths affect adsorption capacity and breakthrough behavior for biobutanol?
dataset_item.answer: The structural parameters of ZIF-8 monoliths, such as fiber thickness and channel size, play a critical role in determining their adsorption capacity and breakthrough behavior for biobutanol. Monoliths with smaller fiber thicknesses (e.g., 250 μm) exhibit broader breakthrough profiles due to inhomogeneous gas velocity distribution near the inlet, as revealed by computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. This uneven distribution is likely caused by restricted side channel sizes. However, fully unobstructed side channels in smaller monoliths can promote uniform gas flow, improving overall distribution within the structure. Both small and large fiber monoliths retain the high equilibrium adsorption capacity, hydrophobicity, and selectivity characteristic of ZIF-8, ensuring effective biobutanol recovery. Importantly, thermal regeneration completely restores adsorption capacity, demonstrating the robustness and reusability of the material. These findings underscore the importance of optimizing fiber thickness and channel size to enhance both adsorption efficiency and flow dynamics in biobutanol recovery applications.

For polymers, natural or otherwise, to produce carbon fiber of a similar quality as PAN, they cannot rely on hydrogen bonding for structural stability or contain a high mass fraction of oxygen, lest they shrink to an unusable extent. A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. Polyalanine-like domains could be incorporated into block copolymers for biomimetic graphite precursors. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

dataset_item.question: How do molecular structure and degree of polymerization of carboxylic acid-side-chain polyacrylates influence cellular association and intracellular processing?
dataset_item.answer: The molecular structure and degree of polymerization (DP) of carboxylic acid-side-chain polyacrylates play a crucial role in influencing cellular association and intracellular processing. N-propionyl substitution consistently leads to higher cellular association compared to N-acetylation, and increasing the side-chain DP further enhances cellular uptake within the N-propionyl group. Intracellular trafficking of these polymers is primarily determined by the labeling dye: Cy5-modified polymers preferentially localize to mitochondria, while sulfoCy5-labeled polymers predominantly colocalize with lysosomes. These findings underscore the importance of tuning polymer side-chain chemistry, DP, and dye selection to strategically control cellular interactions and achieve organelle-specific targeting for potential applications in drug delivery and biomaterials design.

dataset_item.question: How does the thickness of PDA coating influence the pitch of chiral nematic liquid crystal phases formed by CNC@PDA rods?
dataset_item.answer: Increasing the thickness of the polydopamine (PDA) coating on cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) in core-shell CNC@PDA hybrid nanorods systematically increases the pitch of the resulting chiral nematic liquid crystal (CLC) phase. This occurs because thicker PDA coatings weaken the chiral interactions between the hybrid rods by masking the molecular-level or geometrical chirality of the CNC core, which are key drivers of the chiral nematic phase formation. The PDA layer directly modulates these chiral interactions, independent of surface charge or electrostatic double-layer effects. As a result, thicker coatings reduce the helical twisting power of the rods, leading to a less tightly twisted CLC structure with a longer pitch.

### 1. **Summary of the Purpose of the Paper**  
The paper explores how nanoscale conformal coatings of non-chiral polymeric materials, specifically polydopamine (PDA), affect the chiral nematic liquid crystal (CLC) behavior of cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs). The researchers developed core-shell CNC@PDA hybrid nanorods with varying PDA coating thicknesses to investigate their liquid crystal phase behavior. They observed that increasing the PDA coating thickness reduces the chiral interactions between CNC rods, resulting in larger CLC pitches. dataset_item.question: How do pendant group modifications influence bioactive release and thermal properties in biodegradable polymers with sugar alcohol backbones?
dataset_item.answer:
Pendant group modifications in biodegradable polymers with sugar alcohol backbones play a crucial role in influencing bioactive release and thermal properties. These modifications enable controlled bioactive release through hydrolytic degradation, while maintaining cytocompatibility and bioactive efficacy. For instance, polymers with high bioactive loading (e.g., ~70% ibuprofen) have demonstrated sustained release profiles, reducing burst release effects. Key factors such as the number of pendant groups, their stereochemistry, and the hydrophobicity of the polymer backbone can be adjusted to tailor release rates and thermal behavior.

Increasing the number of pendant groups per repeat unit allows for enhanced bioactive loading and provides the flexibility to incorporate additional bioactives, synergistic agents, or targeting moieties for precise delivery. Stereochemical adjustments and hydrophobicity modifications further enable fine-tuning of polymer properties, addressing challenges like low bioactive loading and undesired release patterns. Moreover, these pendant group modifications facilitate the design of polymers with versatile thermal properties, supporting applications in drug delivery and biodegradable material development.

This approach offers a robust platform for creating customizable polymers with optimized bioactive release profiles and material characteristics, addressing specific therapeutic and functional requirements.

Although the presence of photoinitiators and the generated radicals in the polymerization process has been associated with cytotoxicity, frequently good cell compatibility is found for cells encapsulated in this type of hydrogel. , However, important drawbacks of photo-cross-linkable systems include the limited penetration depth of UV radiation and its potentially damaging effects on living tissue. Early examples of chemical cross-linking reactions forming hydrogels include Schiff base formation between aldehydes and amines and the Passerini and Ugi condensation. The most investigated chemoselective cross-linking reaction for hydrogels is the Cu (I)-catalyzed Huisgen 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition of terminal alkynes and azides, commonly known as click chemistry. This term was originally coined in 2001 by Sharpless et al. for a number of new regiospecific linking reactions that give high yields and generally require no purification. The first hydrogel cross-linked via click chemistry was described by the group of Hilborn and was based on PVA. Although this category of hydrogels has been mainly used for tissue engineering applications, they have also been applied for the controlled release of therapeutics and different biomolecules, including doxorubicin bovine serum albumin (BSA) and pDNA. Because "classical" alkyne-azide cycloadditions require the use of a copper catalyst, which may cause adverse effects in biomedical applications, the use of strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) is attracting increasing interest. dataset_item.question: How do higher ethanol-to-acetate substrate ratios affect the thermodynamic favorability and ATP yield during n-caprylate production?
dataset_item.answer:
Higher ethanol-to-acetate substrate ratios enhance both the thermodynamic favorability and ATP yield during n-caprylate production. Thermodynamic modeling demonstrates that at elevated ethanol-to-acetate ratios (e.g., 16.5 and 7.01 mol/mol), the Gibbs free energy of n-caprylate formation becomes significantly more negative than the energy required for ATP synthesis, making the reaction both feasible and energetically favorable. This improved thermodynamic environment supports higher ATP yields and increased specificity for n-caprylate production, as evidenced by model predictions showing n-caprylate specificity of 82% and 64% at these higher ratios. Conversely, lower ethanol-to-acetate ratios (e.g., 3.11 mol/mol) lead to mixed-product formation (n-butyrate, n-caproate, and n-caprylate), while ratios below 1.4 mol/mol render n-caprylate production thermodynamically unfavorable. Experimental results corroborate these predictions, showing reduced n-caprylate yields at lower substrate ratios. 

Although the thermodynamic model provides valuable insights, it assumes uniform substrate distribution and fixed ATP requirements, which may oversimplify real-world bioreactor conditions. Factors such as spatial variations in substrate concentrations, adaptive microbial ATP production mechanisms, and product toxicity are not fully accounted for, potentially influencing microbial performance and n-caprylate yield in practical applications.

Indeed, we observed high n-caprylate-to-n-caproate product ratios of 5.9 and 2.0 g COD g COD-1 (4.3 and 1.5 mol mol-1) and n-caprylate specificities of 82% and 64% for our bioreactor during periods 2 and 3, respectively (Table S1).

During period 4 at an ethanol-to-acetate substrate ratio of 6.7 g COD g COD-1 (4.5 mol mol-1) (Table ), the ethanol-to-acetate liquor ratio declined to 3.11 (Table S3). At this ratio that was observed by the microbiome, the model predicted that formation of only n-caprylate was not thermodynamically feasible, but formation of a mixture of n-butyrate, n-caproate, and n-caprylate was (ΔG rxn > ΔG req for scenarios 2 and 3, but not scenario 1 in Figure S2). This mixed product spectrum was experimentally verified (Figure and Table S1). At the lowest ethanol-to-acetate substrate ratios that we maintained during the main period (i.e.. 3.6, 2.9, and 1.8 during periods 5, 6, and 7, respectively, Table ), the ethanol-to-acetate liquor ratios were also correspondingly low (i.e.. 1.4, 1.0, and 0.6, respectively, Table S3). At these liquor ratios none of the scenarios that we tested were thermodynamically feasible (Figure S2), ruling out considerable amounts of n-caprylate production from our thermodynamic model. However, we did observe lower n-caprylate production during periods 5 and 6 with specificities of 25.7% and 23.7%, respectively, but did not observe any n-caprylate production during period 7 (Figure and Table S1). These experimental specificities for periods 5 to 6 were, indeed, lower than the alleged specificity for our third scenario (i.e.. 1.5 mol of n-butyrate, 1.5 mol of n-caproate, and 0.625 mol of n-caprylate), which would have translated into a 35.3% n-caprylate specificity based on COD, and which was not possible according to our model (Figure S2).

Even though the predictions of our model are in agreement with the bioreactor performance, real care should be taken in using the model because of our oversimplifications and assumptions. First, we assumed that the effluent ethanol and acetate concentrations represented a uniform concentration in the bioreactor experienced by the microbiome. In fact, we saw different microbiome compositions at two different sampling locations in our bioreactor across the study period (discussed later in the text), which suggests that the substrate composition (i.e.. ethanol-to-acetate liquor ratio may have varied throughout the bioreactor height. Second, we developed a formula for the moles of ATP produced by our model assuming that the Rnf complex (ferredoxin-NAD oxidoreductase complex) found in C. kluyveri was being used to establish a proton gradient across the cell membrane and drive ATP production. Wang et al. have reported that under low ethanol and acetate concentrations ( ~ 1 mM), and therefore correspondingly lower reaction Gibbs free energies, C. kluyveri can adjust the activity of two enzymes (an electron bifurcating Nfn complex and a NADP+dependent β-hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase) to decrease its ATP production requirements. Our current model does not account for this potential shift in ATP production (and lower associated Gibbs free energy requirements) in considering the thermodynamic feasibility of n-caprylate production. Third, our model was based on the reported metabolism of C. kluyveri, which may not represent the actual situation for our reactor microbiome. Fourth, this model was designed for a system with product extraction (e.g.. our bioreactor) where n-caprylate is continuously being removed from the bioreactor broth. Our model does not account for the effect of product toxicity on n-caprylate production, and therefore cannot be directly applied to batch systems without product extraction.

dataset_item.question: What mechanisms lead to stable water droplets forming on specific FCC metals with (100) crystal surfaces?
dataset_item.answer:
Stable water droplets form on specific FCC metals with (100) crystal surfaces, such as palladium, platinum, and aluminum, due to the formation of rhombic ordered water monolayers. These monolayers arise from the favorable geometric match between the atomic arrangement of the metal surface and the structure of water molecules. This alignment reduces hydrogen bonding between the ordered monolayer and subsequent layers of water, preventing complete wetting and enabling droplet formation. This phenomenon is not observed on the (100) surfaces of metals such as nickel, copper, gold, silver, and lead, nor on any (110) or (111) surfaces of FCC metals, as these surfaces lack the required atomic spacing to support rhombic ordering of water molecules.

The rhombic ordered water monolayers also reduce surface friction, offering potential applications in anti-icing and friction-reduction technologies. However, oxidation of metal surfaces may obscure experimental detection of these effects, highlighting the need for precise experimental conditions to study this phenomenon. Additionally, the apparent contact angles observed on these surfaces may reflect wetting of the adsorbed water monolayer rather than the underlying metal surface.

### 1. Purpose Summary:
The purpose of the paper is to investigate the microscopic wetting behaviors of various metal surfaces at room temperature using molecular dynamics simulations. The study examines the influence of lattice constants and crystal faces on wetting behavior and reveals the formation of stable water droplets on certain metal surfaces due to ordered water monolayers. These findings provide insights into the correlation between metal surface structure and wetting behavior, with potential applications in surface friction reduction, anti-icing materials, and nonfouling materials.

---

### 2. Classification of Purpose:
The paper emphasizes **"<result>"**, as it focuses on uncovering specific wetting behaviors and their dependence on material properties, as well as discussing their implications for potential applications.

---

### 3. Research Questions:
Based on the abstract, the following research questions are relevant:

1. How do lattice constants and crystal faces influence the wetting behavior of metal surfaces at the microscopic level?
2. What mechanisms lead to the formation of stable water droplets on certain metal surfaces, and how do ordered water monolayers contribute to this phenomenon?
3. Why do some metal surfaces exhibit a complete wetting behavior while others form water droplets at room temperature?
4. What is the role of rhombic ordered water layers in reducing hydrogen bond formation between the water monolayer and overlying water molecules?
5. How can the observed wetting behaviors be leveraged to design materials with tailored surface properties, such as reduced friction, anti-icing capabilities, or nonfouling characteristics?

inference_contexts: In summary, we have studied the nanoscale wetting behaviors of water molecules on some FCC metals. We have found that both the lattice constants and crystal surfaces greatly affect the wettability of FCC metals. Particularly, stable water droplets on water monolayers are found on crystal surface (100) of the metals Pd, Pt, and Al. The key to the water droplet on the water monolayer is the appropriate matching between the surface atoms arrangement and water molecules, which results in the rhombic ordered water monolayers. The ordered water structures reduce the number of hydrogen bond formed between the monolayers and other water molecules. In contrast, no water droplet can be found on other metal surfaces (Ni, Cu, Au, Ag, Pb) with (100) crystal surface and all of those metal surfaces with (110) and (111) crystal faces due to the lack of ordered water. Our work provides a better understanding of the wettability of some FCC metals and helps to expand our understanding of hydrophobicity and hydrophilicity and the "molecular-scale hydrophilicity" we proposed. Particularly, more attentions should be paid when the macroscopic surface contact angles on some specific solid surfaces with ordered water are measured in the experiments, where the apparent contact angles may reflect the wetting degree of adsorbed water, rather than the wetting degree of solid surfaces. We note that the metal surfaces are easily to be oxidized, which may affect the surface constituent and atomic arrangements. This may account of the fact that there is still lack of the direct experimental evidence of the room temperature "ordered water monolayer that does not completely wet water" on the mental surfaces. In applications, we have found that the ordered water monolayer that does not completely wet water can reduce the surface frictions at the hydrophilic surfaces. It should be noted that the work by Ho et al. presented direct slip length on the hydrophilic surfaces, which also shows the friction reduction at hydrophilic surfaces.

Contrary to the general viewpoint that friction on hydrophilic or superhydrophilic surfaces is always high, we show that the friction on the superhydrophilic surface with appropriate charge patterns can be evidently reduced, which is similar to that of a rather hydrophobic surface with a contact angle of a water droplet of ~44°. This friction reduction is attributed to the existence of the ordered water structures on the superhydrophilic surface with appropriate charge patterns, and the friction between this ordered water monolayer and the water molecules above is small. We also highlight the importance of combining the friction coefficient λsolid/liquid between the surface and the first water layer and the friction coefficient λ1,2 between the first water layer and the water layers above, which jointly determine the surface friction coefficient λsurface. This highlights the role of water molecules themselves, which are usually neglected, in determining the solid/water interfacial frictions. Our work provides a new way to reduce surface friction by introducing ordered water on the superhydrophilic surfaces. In practice, room temperature ordered water exists on a variety of materials surfaces, including the sapphire, titania (TiO2), talc, hydroxylated SiO2 and Al2O3, the Pt(100), and mica. We believe that the results in this study will prompt more extensively experiments and may be of great help for designing superhydrophilic materials requiring low surface friction and other possible engineering fields. We noted that the TiO2 is used as the coatings of the biomedical intravascular stents. Very recently, it has been also found that the similar phenomenon of "ordered water that does not completely wet water" exists on the TiO2 surface at room temperature, which may indicate that the friction reduction on the superhydrophilic surface indeed exists but is still unrevealed before.

Solid-state monolayers of a series of ester surfactants were locally heated with an IR-laser, while the texture of the film was followed under a microscope. All the compounds investigated showed a peculiar behavior: in the presence of an appropriate thermal gradient, all monolayers yielded to a kinetically excited liquid that flowed to the hot laser's spot. These observations tally with the fact that compression isotherms of the same compounds, measured at different temperatures, reveal negative pyrobaric coefficients. Structurally related fatty acids and alcohols, behave in the opposite way: their monolayers show a positive pbc and simply melt under the laser's hot spot. We conclude that the difference between esters and the other molecules is due to the lack of influence, in the former case, of hydration water at high molecular packing. Ester monolayers seem to be decoupled from water, i.e.. there is no hydration water around the polar moieties as is the case for alcohols and fatty acids. Water only provides the interface where the molecules are confined.

This review is mainly focused on the two-component, polymeric materials formed from fullerenes and transition metals, frequently through electrochemical deposition. The information about transition metal complexes of fullerenes and the interactions between transition metals surfaces and monolayers of fullerenes gives a strong background for the description of the process of polymeric phase formation and properties of the polymeric materials. These systems can be considered both as conducting polymers and as metal-fullerene frameworks that are similar to metal-organic frameworks in which organic linkers are replaced with fullerene cages. These materials bridge a gap between conducting polymers and MOFs. Thus far, most of the studies of two-component, polymeric materials have been devoted to the exploration of their electrochemical properties, which are related to research on more conventional conducting polymers. Studies related to metal-organic-fullerene frameworks are much less advanced. In part, progress here has been hampered by the difficulty in preparation of suitably functionalized fullerenes that can coordinate metals complexes in a suitable way to form polymers. Introduction of organic linkers into transition metal-fullerene frameworks may lead to a number of structures with novel material architectures and unique and tunable properties. Recent work of the Saito group has opened this large research area.

dataset_item.question: How does subsurface doping of palladium with boron influence bond strengths and catalytic activity?
dataset_item.answer: Subsurface doping of palladium with boron simultaneously weakens palladium-phosphorus (Pd-P) and palladium-hydrogen (Pd-H) bond strengths, leading to enhanced catalytic activity. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations predict that this bond weakening optimizes the binding energy of intermediates, such as HPO(OH), which correlates with improved hypophosphite oxidation and reduced hydride formation. Experimental validation using boron-doped palladium (Pd-B) catalysts, including Pd₅.₃B/C, confirms reduced reaction barriers and superior faradaic and energy efficiencies in hypophosphite fuel cells. The simultaneous weakening of Pd-P and Pd-H bonds is identified as the key factor driving improved catalytic performance for hydrogen-containing liquid fuels, enabling efficient operation of direct hypophosphite fuel cells.

dataset_item.question: What are the advantages of using DC-sliced velocity-mapped ion imaging in resolving product speeds and identifying sources of NO+ in mixed gas expansions?
dataset_item.answer: DC-sliced velocity-mapped ion imaging (VMII) offers significant advantages in resolving product speeds and identifying NO+ sources in mixed gas expansions by combining superior speed and angular resolution. This technique simultaneously detects both the velocity and direction of photoproducts, enabling precise differentiation of NO+ ions from various precursors such as NO, NO₂, HONO, and N₂O₃. By analyzing the radial and angular components of ion images, DC-sliced VMII can effectively discriminate between overlapping dissociation pathways and parent molecules, providing detailed insights into complex photodissociation dynamics. Unlike traditional Doppler-resolved laser-induced fluorescence (LIF), which relies on linewidths for separation, DC-sliced VMII integrates quantum-state selectivity with velocity mapping, surpassing LIF in resolving fast dissociation processes like the photodissociation of N₂O₃ at 355 nm. This capability was instrumental in isolating N₂O₃ photodissociation products for the first gas-phase study of this reaction, demonstrating its utility in advancing photodissociation research.

The methods used for measuring liquid velocity in the literature include Pavlov tube velocimetry, hot film anemometry (HFA), laser Doppler anemometry (LDA), particle image velocimetry (PIV), and so on. Hills first measured the liquid velocity in the bubble column using a Pavlov tube and obtained the radial distribution of the liquid velocity. Forret et al. used Pavlov tubes to measure the liquid velocity distribution of multiple sections in bubble reactors with different column diameters. Franz et al. investigated the axial, radial, and tangential velocities of the liquid velocity in the bubble reactor using the HFA technology, respectively. The resolution is high, but the contamination of the probe will greatly affect the measurement. Kulkarni et al. used LDA to measure liquid velocity, but this method requires high transparency of the flow field and is not suitable for measuring liquid velocity in reactors with large gas holdups. Among the above-mentioned liquid velocity measurement methods, the Pavlov tube velocity measurement method has been widely used because of the small size of the device, convenient operation, and low cost.

A crossed-beam apparatus capable of determining absolute reactive cross sections with varying collision energies can be used to determine energy dependent rate coefficients, k(E), and hence k(T) for very low T following appropriate averaging. However, in practice it is very difficult to generate absolute reactive cross sections to implement this method. The use of Laval nozzles for low temperature studies of chemical kinetics, both for neutral and for charged species, has been reviewed extensively, and the CRESU (Cinetique de Reaction en Ecoulement Supersonique Uniforme) method is described only briefly. As shown in Figure , a Laval nozzle has a converging-diverging shape, and if designed correctly generates a collimated supersonic flow of known and uniform temperature and density for an extended distance from the nozzle. Although a Laval nozzle with a continuous flow of gas can reach extremely low temperatures (the current record being 6 K), the volumetric flow rates and the size of the pumps are enormous. It is very difficult to entrain a sufficient amount of a reagent with a low vapor pressure (usually at ~0.1-1% of the total flow), and more recently pulsed Laval nozzles have been developed, capable of generating pulsed flows of 10-20 ms in duration down to ~22 K, which use much less gas and employ standard sized pumps. In order to characterize the uniform flow from the Laval nozzle flow, a pitot tube is placed in the flow and the impact pressure is measured with a differential pressure transducer. The impact pressure is related via the Rayleigh equation to the Mach number of the flow, which in turn can be used to calculate the temperature and density of the flow for the particular bath gas used. dataset_item.question: How does water accessibility to the active site influence the enzymatic hydrolysis of fluorinated phospholipid analogues?
dataset_item.answer: Water accessibility to the active site plays a critical role in the enzymatic hydrolysis of fluorinated phospholipid analogues. In the bulk phase, water influx remains high, ensuring efficient hydrolysis. However, interfacial adsorption of enzyme-substrate complexes can reduce water accessibility, which is influenced by the substrate's chemical topology. Fluorinated analogues, such as HF-ProAEL and F2-ProAEL, exhibit lower reaction barriers compared to non-fluorinated counterparts, resulting in faster hydrolysis rates. This makes them promising candidates for applications like liposomal vesicles, where controlled degradation and PLA2-triggered drug release can be achieved while preserving desirable physicochemical properties.

dataset_item.question: How does the superoxide radical generated by copper-activated oxygen contribute to the degradation of soybean oil?
dataset_item.answer: The superoxide radical generated by copper-activated oxygen plays a critical role in the oxidative degradation of soybean oil. Experimental analyses using NMR, GPC, and chemical scavengers reveal that superoxide radicals initiate polymerization reactions, leading to increased molecular weight and accelerating the oil's aging process. This degradation is driven by oxidative processes, which are further catalyzed by dissolved copper (II) cations. The role of superoxide radicals in this breakdown is underscored by the complete inhibition of degradation when benzoquinone is used to scavenge these radicals. Additionally, other antioxidants, such as 2,6-dibutyl-4-methylphenol, can trap secondary reactive oxygen species, further enhancing the oil's oxidative stability. These findings highlight the importance of reactive oxygen species in oil degradation and suggest antioxidant strategies to mitigate oxidative damage and prolong the shelf life of soybean oil.

dataset_item.question: How are quasi-bound states of F CH4 complex computed without employing absorbing potentials?
dataset_item.answer:
Quasi-bound states of the F-CH4 complex are computed using the multiconfigurational time-dependent Hartree (MCTDH) method and its multilayer extension (ml-MCTDH), without employing absorbing potentials or other techniques typically used to handle resonance states. The calculation leverages the high barrier toward dissociation into HF + CH3 products, which effectively confines the wavepacket during imaginary time propagation, allowing resonance states to be treated as if they were bound. 

Eigenstates are obtained through block relaxation of state-averaged MCTDH wave functions propagated in imaginary time. Correlation discrete variable representation (CDVR) and harmonic oscillator DVRs are employed for potential energy evaluations, while specialized coordinate treatments, such as cot-DVR for angular singularities (Θ), ensure accurate representation of the system's dynamics. Extensive basis set optimizations and layering schemes are used to capture the complex interactions and long-lived resonance states. These resonance states exhibit lifetimes that exceed the timescale of the numerical simulation, enabling their eigenenergies to be computed without explicit consideration of decay dynamics.

dataset_item.question: How does microbial reduction of Fe(III) in biotite and chlorite affect the reactivity of Tc(VII), U(VI), and Np(V)?
dataset_item.answer: Microbial reduction of Fe(III) in biotite and chlorite significantly enhances the reactivity and immobilization of Tc(VII), U(VI), and Np(V), with the efficiency of removal modulated by aqueous carbonate concentrations. For Tc(VII), microbially reduced biotite and chlorite exhibit extensive removal, achieving 86–89% by the experimental end point, while unaltered minerals show negligible reactivity. Np(V) demonstrates rapid scavenging, dropping below detection limits (< 4 × 10⁻¹¹ M) within 24 hours in systems with reduced minerals, highlighting the strong reductive scavenging effect. U(VI) reactivity is more sensitive to carbonate conditions: under low carbonate concentrations, microbially reduced minerals achieve near-complete U(VI) removal within 14 days, whereas high carbonate conditions hinder removal due to uranyl-carbonate complexation, limiting removal efficiency to 37% with chlorite. These findings underscore the role of microbial Fe(III) reduction in promoting radionuclide immobilization, with carbonate concentrations acting as a critical control on reactivity.
