inference_contexts: Here, we present the first investigation of photoinduced spin dynamics in CFO. Ultrafast XUV-RA measurements show the element-specific oxidation and spin-state dynamics in this material on the femtosecond time scale. Spectral analysis demonstrates that photoexcitation of CFO at 400 nm excites a metal-to-metal charge transfer transition that drives intersystem crossing from HS Co2+ to LS Co3+ via a CTIST mechanism. This process occurs with a time constant of 405 ± 29 fs and unity quantum efficiency. SCO in this material is enabled by the presence of an intervalence charge transfer transition. We hypothesize that this intervalence transition, which is unique to CFO compared to Co3O4, is facilitated by the stronger metal-metal coupling in the predominately inverse spinel structure of CFO. This observation indicates that other magnetic materials in this class of ferrimagnetic inverse spinel ferrites are also expected to support efficient photoinduced SCO.

Several materials prepared from triazine-containing precursors were explored as active materials in Li half cells. Well-defined materials which exhibit strong triazine character show very low gravimetric capacities even if the triazine units are bridged by conjugated moieties, such as phenylene or 2,2′-bipyridine. This directly contradicts the previously suggested bipolar mechanism in which the triazine is n- or p-doped when cycled. In order to achieve high gravimetric capacities, the well-defined conjugated systems must be synthesized at higher temperatures, thereby destroying the triazine unit and creating an N-containing amorphous carbon material. These materials have high concentrations of localized spins (large numbers of unpaired electrons) that may be involved in the discharge and charge mechanisms. The N-containing amorphous carbon materials are very similar to N-containing porous carbon materials that have been evaluated as supercapacitor materials. , The capacity of the amorphous materials trends loosely with specific surface area and C/N content. However, higher surface area does not always result in a higher capacity, suggesting the mechanism is not purely capacitive. The slight observed rate dependence also suggests a pseudocapacitive behavior involving charge transfer processes. These charge transfer processes could involve the unpaired electrons in the amorphous materials, and indeed, the inactive PTI materials do not contain unpaired electrons. Suggestions for future work to further probe the charge storage mechanisms involve using in situ EPR in order to observe the evolution of the spin concentration as a function of discharging and charging.

This Account brings to a close the most recent chapter of a collaborative investigation of photoinduced charge transfer in DNA begun over 20 years ago. In addition to the studies of hole transport described herein, we have extended the methods developed to charge transfer in less-common DNA structures such as diblock and triblock purines, , locked nucleic acids (LNAs), 3-way-junctions, G-quadruplexes, and i-motifs. The synergy of molecular design, structure, dynamics, and theory has led to our current state of understanding of DNA charge separation. We and others have applied similar methods to the study of electron transport in DNA. , Future work will focus on a number of new research directions that have become apparent from the work carried out thus far. These involve the need to develop a deeper understanding of the structural and electronic changes within the DNA duplex that accompany charge generation and transport as well as how to take advantage of charge and spin motion within the DNA duplex to develop new device structures. For example, we expect that substituted guanine derivatives such as EG may be particularly effective in tracking and controlling hole transport in such systems. In addition, our observation of photogenerated entangled multispin states within DNA makes it possible to take advantage of spin dynamics to manipulate quantum information at a molecular level and to create DNA structures that may form the basis of quantum circuitry.

Heterogenous charge transfer has continued to be a critical area of advancement in science because of the increase in demand of society on technology that predicates itself off interfacial charge movement. The role of heterogenous charge transfer in modern conveniences such as smart phones to energy infrastructure cannot be under-represented. This importance on understanding heterogenous charge transfer has set the stage for this work and has shown both a novel and nuanced approach to modulate the kinetics of mesoscale heterogenous charge transfer. This was accomplished through the functionalizing semiconducting QDs with redox noninnocent (RNI) ligands as hole acceptors. Through nonstandard application of these RNI ligands, controlled modulation of the charge transfer dynamics has been achieved on mesoscale materials. Moreover, this study has illuminated an intriguing band gap dependence on the photoluminescent recombination lifetimes, which can be observed across both deposited substrates of ITO and ZnO. While interesting, further work is needed in terms of characterizing the complex charge transfer dynamics as well as the effect of other RNI type ligands through tuning of the band gap.

The finding that the lifetime of the S2 state is much shorter than previously estimated and the suggestion that the decay of the resulting S x state is significantly slowed by solvent friction have significant implications in understanding the mechanism of excitation energy transfer from peridinin to Chl a in PCP. On the basis of fluorescence excitation experiments, the overall energy transfer efficiency from peridinin to Chl a after optical preparation of the S2 state is found to be ~90%, of which 25% is thought to occur nearly instantaneously between the peridinin S2 state to the Chl a Q x state; the remaining 75% of the energy transfer yield is currently thought to involve energy transfer from the S1/ICT state to Q y with a 3 ps time constant. , The present results suggest, in contrast, that it may actually be the S x state that serves as the excitation energy donor to either of the Chl a excited states. The average structure of peridinin in PCP is somewhat compressed along the conjugated polyene and bent prior to the allene moiety. The result is a partial inversion of the bond-length alternation pattern compared to that in the planar, all-trans ground state, as obtained as a energy minimum in electronic structure calculations. It is proposed that this distortion results in a strong mixing of the S2 and S1 states and a large enhancement of the energy transfer yield to the Chl a acceptor. , We suggest that the ground-state conformation favored in PCP results in an S x -like conformation immediately upon optical preparation of the S2 state. This conformation would be expected to relax further along torsional or out-of-plane coordinates in the protein to assume an even larger ICT character and a larger Forster transition-dipole-transition-dipole coupling to the Chl a acceptor. dataset_item.question: What is the preparation process for CaAlSiN3:Eu2+ phosphors synthesized via carbothermal reduction?
dataset_item.answer: CaAlSiN<sub>3</sub>:Eu<sup>2+</sup> phosphors were synthesized via carbothermal reduction using calcium hydride (CaH<sub>2</sub>), aluminum nitride (AlN), silicon nitride (Si<sub>3</sub>N<sub>4</sub>), europium oxide (Eu<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>), and graphite powder. The raw materials were weighed according to the nominal composition of Ca<sub>0.90</sub>AlSiN<sub>3</sub>:0.10Eu<sup>2+</sup>, with a carbon-to-oxygen (C/O) mole ratio of 1.20. The mixture was finely ground using an agate mortar and then heated in a horizontal tube furnace at 1550 °C for 6 hours under a nitrogen/hydrogen gas atmosphere (8% H<sub>2</sub>) flowing at 400 mL/min. After firing, the phosphor sample, which contained residual carbon, was finely ground again to remove carbon residues, yielding the final product designated as CaAlSiN<sub>3</sub>:Eu<sup>2+</sup>/C.

For polymers, natural or otherwise, to produce carbon fiber of a similar quality as PAN, they cannot rely on hydrogen bonding for structural stability or contain a high mass fraction of oxygen, lest they shrink to an unusable extent. A direct pathway, without significant molecular rearrangement or combustion, to form graphite from existing crystals in the polymer is useful in maintaining alignment, as observed with PAN. Given high enough temperatures, the graphite crystals in PAN can grow by accumulating amorphous parts of the polymer, while maintaining sufficient amorphous carbon to keep the fibers intact. One common strategy to create graphitic fibers is to include cyclic or aromatic structures into a precursor fiber, but this often leaves no mechanism for the fusion of separate polymer chains, likely limiting the overall extent of graphitization. Polyalanine-like domains could be incorporated into block copolymers for biomimetic graphite precursors. However, careful attention must be paid to the graphitization mechanisms of the other blocks with intentional design to maximize the bonding between neighboring polymer chains and the eventual formation of graphite aligned along the fiber.

Understanding how design parameters of targeted drug carriers influence interaction with cells and the subsequent signaling leading to endocytosis is key to inform optimization of drug delivery systems. , Both the size and targeting valency of drug carriers impact cell binding and endocytic uptake. - ,,, However, how these parameters influence receptor-mediated signaling linking binding with internalization is rather obscure. For instance: Is the uptake efficiency correlative with the signaling level? Is this regulated similarly for carriers of different sizes and valencies? Are signaling and uptake events induced independently for each individual carrier or do they depend on cumulative carrier binding to cells? Is the number of receptors engaged by a carrier the factor ruling signaling and uptake, or does this depend on the density of engagement per surface area? Using model submicrometer, micrometer, and supramicrometer carriers targeted to ICAM-1 at varying valencies, we have examined these questions. Our results revealed an intricate interplay between these parameters, where the density of the targeting antibody per carrier surface area (which would determine the density of the receptor cluster on the cell surface) is the main parameter controlling the signaling conducive to endocytosis (Figure ). Larger carriers posed a requirement for stronger signaling, since carrier size impacts the ability of the plasmalemma to efficiently engulf a carrier. It is likely that for endocytic pathways lacking signals that enable sufficient plasmalemma deformability (e.g.. ceramide enrichment shown here for the CAM pathway), size will become restrictive regardless of the targeting density. Each carrier bound on a cell induced signaling based on its antibody-coat density (the density of the clustered receptors, not the absolute number of receptors engaged or the size of the cluster), and rendered endocytosis based on its size and enough buildup of the inducing signal. Each signaling-uptake event was independent for each single carrier bound on a cell, where the total number of carriers bound to the cell, the total surface area occupied by those carriers, and the total number of cell receptors engaged did not exert a major influence. It will be important to examine this regulation for other receptors and pathways in order to extract generic conclusions, and to evaluate how other carrier design parameters (e.g.. smaller sizes, different shape, curvature, carrier type, surface chemistry, etc.) and biological environments (different cell types, presence of flow, pathological alterations, etc.) impact these outcomes. - ,,, Nevertheless, other natural routes associate to signaling common to the CAM pathway, and it is expected that the findings obtained here would broadly apply to the use of said routes for drug delivery applications. For instance, ceramide and/or PKC are key for the formation of lipid domains, vesiculation, cytoskeletal rearrangements, and formation of membrane protrusions observed for phagocytic and macropinocytic pathways, intracellular invasion by certain viral and bacterial pathogens, leukocyte endothelial adhesion and extravasation, and certain events of transcytosis across cellular barriers. - Therefore, these results have shed light on key factors modulating the efficacy of uptake of targeted drug carriers, which shall inform future design of vehicles for intracellular delivery.

dataset_item.question: What are the thermal decomposition products and temperature ranges of components in the solid electrolyte interphase formed on silicon electrodes during thermogravimetric analysis?
dataset_item.answer: The thermal decomposition products of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formed on silicon electrodes during thermogravimetric analysis include lithium ethylene dicarbonate (LEDC), which decomposes into lithium alkyl carbonate (RCO₂Li) and lithium carbonate (Li₂CO₃). LEDC decomposition occurs at lower temperatures and contributes to increasing SEI complexity during cycling due to repeated volume changes and interactions with reactive components like LiPF₆ salt and lithiated silicon surfaces. Additionally, LiₓPOₓFₓ decomposes around 300 °C, while the polyimide binder decomposes at higher temperatures, approximately 550 °C. The decomposition of SEI components spans a broad temperature range, generally between 25 °C and 900 °C. To enhance battery longevity, electrolyte formulations should minimize ethylene carbonate (EC) reduction products and favor solvents or additives that form more thermally stable SEI components.

inference_contexts: TGA has been employed to investigate the thermal decomposition behavior of the SEI deposited on the silicon electrode. The large surface area and repeated volume change upon cycling of silicon nanoparticles lead to continuous electrolyte reduction generating a sufficient quantity of SEI for TGA analysis. The polyimide binder, which thermally decomposes over 500 °C, was employed to avoid overlap of the thermal decomposition of the SEI components and the binder. Thermal decomposition temperatures of the SEI were evaluated by scanning the temperature from 25 to 900 °C in N2 atmosphere. The solid residue was characterized at various stages of thermal decomposition by XPS and IR. The independently prepared reduction product of EC, LEDC, thermally decomposes to generate RCO2Li and Li2CO3. The SEI deposited on the silicon electrode contains DTG peaks consistent with the decomposition of LEDC, RCO2Li and Li2CO3, but also includes peaks characteristic of Li x PO y F z around 300 °C and the polyimide binder around 550 °C. TGA analysis obtained at various stages of cycling suggests that the LEDC on the silicon electrode thermally decomposes during cycling accumulating the thermal decomposition products in the SEI on the electrode surface. The thermal decomposition could be accelerated during prolonged cycling or storage due to the low decomposition temperature of LEDC, repeated volume change causing damages on SEI (that is, LEDC), reactivity of the LiPF6 salt, or the surface reactivity of the lithiated silicon electrode. While the dominant component of the initial SEI is LEDC, from the reduction of EC, along with LiF and Li x PF y O z from the reduction of LiPF6, the thermal decomposition of LEDC during cycling increases the complexity of the SEI. In addition, the inherent thermal instability of LEDC suggests that, in order to develop lithium ion batteries with long life, electrolyte formulations should be used which limit the presence of EC reduction products on the anode surface. Alternative solvents or additives which generate initial reduction products with superior stability but comparable or better lithium ion conductivity would be preferable.

In summary, the interfacial reaction process, dynamic morphology changes, and chemomechanical effects of the interphase between LATP and lithium metal are systematically investigated through ss-NMR, XRD, and in situ TEM. These results suggest the (electro) chemical transformation at the interface and the interphase is mainly composed of the Li3Al0.3Ti1.7(PO4)3 phase. This (electro) chemical transformation process leads to a significant enhancement of electronic conductivity and ignites continuous side reactions at the interface. High electron conductivity of the side reaction products can also induce the direct growth of lithium metal in/-passing through the interphase and accelerate the chemical and mechanical degradation of the electrolyte. What is worse is that the formation of the new phase and coupled mechanical stress will finally break up the electrolyte and its connection with the electrode, leading to a large internal resistance of solid-state batteries. An artificial layer with robust chemical and flexible properties is imperative to avoid the formation of an ion/electron mixed interfacial conductor and alleviate the corresponding mechanical stress. dataset_item.question: How do agitation methods such as magnetic stirring and ultrasonication influence salt crystallization and properties in a supersaturated NaCl solution after cooling by a solid hollow fiber cooling crystallization system?
dataset_item.answer:
Agitation methods such as magnetic stirring and ultrasonication significantly influence salt crystallization and crystal properties in a supersaturated NaCl solution cooled by a solid hollow fiber cooling crystallization (SHFCC) system. Magnetic stirring at 500 rpm and ultrasonication were compared to a control group without agitation to evaluate their effects on nucleation, crystal growth, and overall crystallization efficiency. 

The optimized process involved a 27.25% NaCl feed solution cooled from 80°C to 18°C using the SHFCC system. Magnetic stirring was performed using a multiposition magnetic stirrer, providing controlled and uniform agitation that enhanced nucleation rates, crystal growth, and yield. Ultrasonication, conducted in a water bath at room temperature, promoted nucleation but produced less uniform crystals compared to magnetic stirring. Both agitation methods outperformed static conditions, where quiescent settling led to slower nucleation and irregular crystal morphology.

After cooling and agitation, salt crystals were collected by filtration, dried overnight, and characterized to evaluate size, uniformity, and crystallization efficiency. Magnetic stirring demonstrated superior performance, yielding higher-quality crystals with greater uniformity and improved crystallization outcomes. These findings confirm that controlled agitation, particularly magnetic stirring, plays a critical role in optimizing salt crystallization processes in supersaturated solutions cooled by the SHFCC system.

dataset_item.question: What challenges arise when determining relative infrared intensities of electronic states from difference time-resolved infrared spectra?
dataset_item.answer: Determining relative infrared intensities of electronic states from difference time-resolved infrared (TRIR) spectra presents several challenges, primarily due to the overlap of spectral features from the ground and excited states within the same frequency region. This overlap can lead to partial or complete cancellation of signals in the difference spectrum, complicating the extraction of accurate excited-state intensities. To address this, ground-state intensities are typically determined from static Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectra, which provide a reliable baseline. Excited-state intensities, however, can only be estimated when spectral overlap is minimal, as demonstrated in systems like [Re(X)(CO)₃(α-diimine)] and rhenium bipyridine complexes. Additionally, difference spectra must account for fully relaxed triplet-state signals, requiring careful selection of time delays to avoid artifacts from dynamic relaxation processes. This approach ensures more accurate characterization of the relative intensities despite inherent challenges.

dataset_item.question: What is the role of multiconformer transition state theory in calculating reaction rate coefficients for unimolecular reactions?
dataset_item.answer:
Multiconformer transition state theory (MC-TST) enhances the accuracy of calculating reaction rate coefficients for unimolecular reactions by systematically accounting for multiple conformations of reactants and transition states. It computes the rate coefficient as a weighted sum of the partition functions of all relevant conformers, with weights determined by their relative energies through exponential scaling. This approach ensures the contribution of each conformer is properly incorporated, capturing the complexity of molecular configurations.

MC-TST also incorporates quantum mechanical tunneling corrections, which are particularly significant for reactions involving hydrogen shifts. The method employs a hierarchical computational strategy: low-level conformer sampling identifies the most relevant configurations, while high-level optimizations (e.g., B3LYP, ωB97X-D, CCSD(T)-F12a) refine energy barriers and partition functions for precise rate calculations. This systematic approach excludes negligible reactions and yields rate coefficients that closely match experimental values, often within a factor of 5. MC-TST has proven effective for modeling complex atmospheric reactions, such as peroxy radical rearrangements in the ozonolysis of limonene.

dataset_item.question: How does the nitrile group's extended π-system influence valence transitions and absorption features near ionization limits in 3-methoxyacrylonitrile?
dataset_item.answer: The extended π-system of the nitrile group in 3-methoxyacrylonitrile (3MAN) significantly influences its absorption features and valence transitions near the ionization limit. This π-system enhances broad valence transitions below the ionization limit, with contributions from π-system excitations and potential σσ* transitions above 8 eV, similar to acrylonitrile. Unlike methylvinylether, observable Rydberg series are absent, primarily due to substantial geometry changes between the neutral and cationic forms of 3MAN, including a 60° rotation of the methyl group. These changes result in poor Franck-Condon overlap and low oscillator strengths for Rydberg states. Furthermore, the absorption features arise from overlapping transitions with mixed electronic configurations, influenced by molecular geometry. Additionally, vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) irradiation triggers a photochemical process producing carbon monoxide, indicative of complex multistep reactivity.

dataset_item.question: What does the correlation between 207Pb isotropic shift and mean Pb-I distance reveal about the local structural features of two-dimensional halide perovskites?
dataset_item.answer: The correlation between the **207Pb isotropic chemical shift** and **mean Pb-I bond distance** reveals a linear relationship that provides valuable insights into the local structural features of two-dimensional halide perovskites. This predictive relationship highlights how variations in Pb-I bond lengths directly influence the electronic environment around Pb, as detected by solid-state NMR. It enables differentiation between **3D-like "inner" Pb sites** and **surface-like "outer" Pb sites**, reflecting distinct bonding environments within the layered perovskite structure. These findings are instrumental in characterizing organic-inorganic interactions, local structural distortions, and their impact on optoelectronic properties. Furthermore, this methodology can be extended to study material degradation, phase transitions, and bonding environments in related lead halide systems, offering a powerful tool for understanding and optimizing the structure-property relationships in these materials.

The paper aims to demonstrate the use of solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, specifically 1H and 207Pb NMR techniques, as a noninvasive and complementary method to probe the local structural features of two-dimensional (2D) organic-inorganic hybrid halide perovskites. The study focuses on understanding the Pb-I bonding within the perovskite layers and the organic-inorganic interactions between the spacer molecules and the perovskite layer, using the 2D Ruddlesden-Popper phase BA₂MAₙ₋₁PbₙI₃ₙ₊₁ (n = 1–4) as a model system. dataset_item.question: How do active species such as h+ and O2⁻ influence the graft polymerization process of acrylic acid onto polyvinylidene fluoride membranes?
dataset_item.answer: Active species such as h⁺ and O₂⁻, generated by Bi₂O₃ under UV illumination, significantly enhance the graft polymerization process of acrylic acid (AA) onto polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. These oxidizing species promote chain-growth polymerization, resulting in a grafting ratio over five times higher compared to non-catalyzed membranes. This increase in grafting improves membrane hydrophilicity, reducing the water contact angle from 98.8° (pristine PVDF) to 40.4°, and enhances performance metrics such as retention efficiency (85.89% vs. 31.29% for pure PVDF). Additionally, the grafted layer demonstrates exceptional stability, maintaining performance after rigorous testing, and enables self-cleaning via visible-light-driven contaminant degradation. These combined effects make the modified PVDF membranes highly effective for applications such as organic dye removal and other advanced filtration processes.

dataset_item.question: How does irradiation with visible light at 430 nm affect vesicular nanostructures formed by amphiphilic diblock copolymers synthesized from coumarin-based disulfide-containing monomers?
dataset_item.answer: Irradiation with visible light at 430 nm cleaves the coumarin moieties in amphiphilic diblock copolymers synthesized from coumarin-based disulfide-containing monomers, generating reactive primary amines. These amines trigger extensive amidation reactions, leading to traceless cross-linking of the vesicular nanostructures. The cross-linking induces a polarity transition in the bilayer membranes, resulting in the selective release of small encapsulated molecules while retaining larger ones. Subsequent exposure to glutathione (GSH) disassembles the cross-linked vesicles by reducing the disulfide bonds, enabling the release of the remaining large-molecule payloads. This dual-stimuli response mechanism allows for sequential, spatiotemporally controlled release, making the system ideal for synergistic drug delivery applications requiring precise dosing of therapeutics.

The paper aims to develop and investigate dual-stimuli responsive polymersomes based on diblock copolymers synthesized via RAFT polymerization. These polymersomes are designed to respond to visible light and glutathione (GSH) stimuli, enabling sequential, spatiotemporally controlled release of encapsulated payloads. The study demonstrates that light-triggered traceless cross-linking of the polymersome membranes selectively releases small molecules while retaining large ones, and further structural disintegration by GSH leads to the release of larger payloads. This functionality holds potential for applications in synergistic drug delivery and programmed therapeutic release.

The dual-stimuli responsive monomer could be polymerized to form amphiphilic diblock copolymers using a PEO-based macroRAFT agent through RAFT polymerization. The resulting amphiphiles could self-assemble into vesicular nanostructures that naturally inherited the photo- and reduction-responsive characteristics. This process gave rise to a remarkable polarity transition within the bilayer membranes and the release of encapsulated small molecule payloads while retaining the large ones. Moreover, the cross-linked vesicles could be further disassembled upon incubation with GSH, resulting in the release of large molecule encapsulants. We expect these dual-stimuli responsive vesicles could be of important use in the treatment of diseases where distinct therapeutic agents should be concomitantly administrated and sequentially dosed.

In this work, the reaction pathways upon DEA were studied for the potential radiosensitizer SeCNdU. The results indicate that SeCNdU can be considered as a pseudo-halouridine composed of an electron-affinic -SeCN side group and a nucleobase moiety. Eleven dissociation channels were observed within the detection limit of the experiment. The highest ion yield was obtained for (SeU-yl) -, which is a radical and thus highly reactive. A comparable ion yield was observed for the cyano anion. The yields of the other fragment anions are at least 1 order of magnitude smaller. Besides the negatively charged fragments directly obtained in the experiments, neutral counterparts were investigated by calculations. These include radicals such as SeU-yl and molecules such as H2O and HCN. One of the main questions, whether a bond cleavage of the Se-CN bond or the C5-Se bond occurs more efficiently, was solved because the Se-CN bond was far more efficiently cleaved with 5 out of 11 fragmentation pathways and the 2 most intense dissociation channels among them. Cleavage of the C5-Se bond also occurs upon DEA; however, only two channels were observed with low ion yields. Remarkably, all reactions exhibit a 0 eV threshold in the experimental data, which is in full agreement with the calculated thermochemical thresholds. The calculations showed that all DEA channels are exothermic at the present experimental conditions. Few reactions have exothermicities of more than 3 eV. Such behavior also results from the exceptionally high EA of most of fragments released with an excess electron. The anion (SeU-yl)- with the most intense ion yield is formed upon simple cleavage reactions. The formation of CN-, the other abundant anion, is based on simple bond cleavage, while two bonds have to be cleaved and one formed to produce (SeU-yl)-. Most other dissociation processes involve multiple bond cleavages, which are also accompanied by structural rearrangement. The formation of C4N2O2H2CN- represents such a process because the selenium must be cut out of the molecule in order to form a U-yl-CN bond. Moreover, the resonance profiles of C4N2O2H2Se -, C9N2O3H6Se -, and C9N2O5H10Se - showed a very similar structure, suggesting one common electronic state of the TNI.

dataset_item.question: What are the physicochemical properties of bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide-based ionic liquids and their impact on phase equilibrium in binary and ternary systems with 2-phenylethanol and water?
dataset_item.answer:
Bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide-based ionic liquids (ILs) exhibit unique physicochemical properties, including density, dynamic viscosity, and surface tension, which significantly influence phase equilibrium in binary and ternary systems. These ILs demonstrate complete miscibility with 2-phenylethanol (PEA) and immiscibility with water, making them promising candidates for PEA extraction from aqueous solutions. 

Four newly synthesized ILs ([HMMOR][FSI], [OiQuin][FSI], [BMPYR][FSI], and [N2228][FSI]) were characterized, with [HMMOR][FSI] showing the highest selectivity and extraction capacity among them. However, its performance was lower compared to benchmark ILs such as [N2228][NTf2] and [C8iQuin][NTf2] reported in prior studies. Ternary systems of {IL + PEA + water} at 308.15 K and 101 kPa exhibited Treybal's Type II phase behavior, characterized by high selectivity and solute distribution ratios, indicating the potential of these ILs for efficient extraction processes.

The NRTL model successfully correlated experimental binary and ternary liquid-liquid equilibrium data, while COSMO-RS provided reliable predictions for extraction behavior, further validating these tools for designing IL-based separation systems. These findings highlight the potential of bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide-based ILs as effective entrainers for PEA separation from aqueous mixtures, with applications in industrial extraction processes.

dataset_item.question: How does weak anharmonicity influence the vibrational coherence and dephasing of a wavepacket in the excited state of cresyl violet?
dataset_item.answer: Weak anharmonicity in cresyl violet influences the vibrational coherence and dephasing of the wavepacket in the excited state by enabling prolonged vibrational coherence and slow dephasing. This weak anharmonicity minimizes mode-mode coupling and intramolecular vibrational relaxation, allowing the wavepacket to retain coherence for several picoseconds before completely dephasing over a time scale exceeding 10 picoseconds. The constant nodal positions observed in transient absorption and stimulated emission signals confirm the absence of significant perturbations from reactive internal conversion or strong vibrational coupling. This coherence and slow natural dephasing within the excited state highlight the weak coupling between vibrational modes, ensuring that the wavepacket dephases naturally before transitioning to the ground state via Fermi's golden rule.

dataset_item.question: How does the acid to metal molar ratio influence the yield of cyclohexylbenzene in benzene hydroalkylation using palladium-based catalysts?
dataset_item.answer: The acid-to-metal molar ratio plays a critical role in determining the yield of cyclohexylbenzene (CHB) during benzene hydroalkylation over palladium-based catalysts, specifically Pd/Hβ zeolite. The optimal acid-to-metal molar ratio is 22.4 μmol H+ per μmol of exposed palladium, achieving a maximum CHB yield of 32.8%. This ratio ensures a balanced interaction between acid and metal sites, which is essential for both benzene conversion and alkylation efficiency. Weak and Lewis acid sites primarily facilitate benzene conversion, while strong and Brønsted acid sites are key drivers for the alkylation step. Furthermore, the catalyst synthesis method—using a methanol-mediated weakly capping growth approach—enhances catalyst stability and performance compared to traditional methods, making it promising for industrial applications.

dataset_item.question: How does the Al to Na concentration ratio in CuO-doped Na2O-Al2O3-SiO2 glass influence the reduction of Cu ions and the formation of metallic Cu?
dataset_item.answer:
The Al to Na concentration ratio in CuO-doped Na₂O-Al₂O₃-SiO₂ glass plays a critical role in the reduction of Cu ions and the formation of metallic Cu. This ratio influences the structural network and coordination environment within the glass matrix, thereby affecting hydrogen diffusion, Cu²⁺ reduction mechanisms, and metallic Cu precipitation.

Higher Al/Na ratios, achieved by increasing Al₂O₃ content, promote Cu²⁺ reduction by introducing [AlO₄]⁻ tetrahedra into the glass structure, which create non-bridging oxygen sites. These sites facilitate hydrogen interaction and enhance diffusion through the glass network, accelerating the reduction process. Analytical techniques such as NMR and FT-IR confirm that higher Al content increases hydrogen penetration and OH bond formation, enabling more uniform precipitation of metallic Cu throughout the glass matrix.

Conversely, lower Al/Na ratios (higher Na⁺ content) result in fewer reactive sites and slower hydrogen mobility, thereby hindering the reduction of Cu ions. In such compositions, metallic Cu tends to form localized clusters rather than uniform distributions.

Experimental observations using melt-quenching synthesis with varying Al₂O₃ content (0, 10, 15, and 20 mol%) while maintaining 70 mol% SiO₂ and balancing Na₂O content demonstrate this behavior. Glasses doped with 1 wt% CuO and exposed to hydrogen atmospheres consistently show distinct redox behavior based on the Al/Na ratio, with higher Al content favoring efficient reduction and uniform metallic Cu formation.

dataset_item.question: How does phosphate-to-hydroxyl substitution influence the crystal structure and defect chemistry of lithium iron phosphate cathodes?
dataset_item.answer:
Phosphate-to-hydroxyl substitution in lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO₄) cathodes under hydrothermal synthesis leads to the formation of hydrotriphylite solid solutions with the general formula Li₁₋ₓFe₁₊ₓ(PO₄)₁₋ᵧ(OH)₄ᵧ. This substitution significantly alters the crystal structure and defect chemistry through charge compensation mechanisms, primarily involving a reduced lithium-to-iron ratio and increased iron occupancy within lithium diffusion channels, reaching up to 12%. These changes disrupt charge balance and introduce noncentrosymmetric distortions due to lithium displacement and shortened Li-O bonds, which increase lithium diffusion activation barriers and hinder electrochemical performance.

The substitution also lowers the antiferromagnetic ordering temperature, serving as an indicator of hydroxyl incorporation. Furthermore, it introduces off-stoichiometry and anion defects, highlighting the active role of the polyanion sublattice in defect chemistry—a notable departure from prior assumptions of its inertness. The extent of these structural and defect changes is heavily influenced by hydrothermal synthesis conditions, with precursor and reducing agent concentrations playing critical roles in determining defect concentration and the degree of substitution. Overall, phosphate-to-hydroxyl substitution has profound implications for the material’s structural integrity, lithium-ion transport properties, and electrochemical functionality.

dataset_item.question: How does the hydrolysis precipitation method influence the dispersion and interaction of copper and zinc species with silica support in the synthesis of CuZn-SiO2 catalysts?
dataset_item.answer: The hydrolysis precipitation (HP) method significantly enhances the dispersion of copper and zinc species on the silica support in CuZn-SiO₂ catalysts. By promoting strong interactions between copper and zinc oxide, the HP method inhibits the formation of copper phyllosilicate, which would otherwise reduce the surface area of active Cu⁺ sites. Instead, it facilitates the formation of Cu-ZnOₓ species, which are highly catalytically active and contribute to a higher density of Cu⁺ sites. Additionally, optimizing the zinc-to-copper ratio further improves the generation of Cu-ZnOₓ species, enhancing the catalytic activity. These improvements result in superior performance in methyl acetate hydrogenation, with the HP-synthesized Cu₉Zn₁-SiO₂ catalyst achieving a space-time yield (STY) of 1.024 gEtOH gcat⁻¹ h⁻¹, compared to 0.775 gEtOH gcat⁻¹ h⁻¹ for traditional coprecipitated catalysts. The enhanced metal-support interactions and tailored Zn/Cu ratio collectively contribute to the improved catalytic efficiency.

dataset_item.question: How does functionalized graphene improve the mechanical and thermal properties of bone cement nanohybrids?
dataset_item.answer: Functionalized graphene, particularly amine-functionalized graphene (AG), significantly enhances the mechanical and thermal properties of bone cement nanohybrids, making them highly suitable for orthopedic applications. The incorporation of AG increases the thermal stability of the nanohybrids by 37 °C compared to pure bone cement, while also improving stiffness and toughness. The functionalization reduces the mixing and curing temperature to body temperature, preventing cell necrosis during implantation. Furthermore, AG moderates the polymerization rate, ensuring better control over the curing process. These properties contribute to improved bioactivity, osteointegration, and in vivo bone healing, as evidenced by enhanced cell viability, adhesion, and accelerated bone regeneration within 20 days. Overall, AG-modified bone cement nanohybrids represent a superior material for applications requiring durability, biocompatibility, and effective integration with surrounding bone tissue.

For biomedical applications, the use of in situ forming hydrogels is preferred over preformed hydrogels since there is no need for surgical interventions as gelation can take place under physiological conditions upon injection. Furthermore, the initial fluidic nature of the precursor solution ensures proper shape adaptation and biological components can be incorporated in the hydrogel by simple mixing with the precursor polymer solution. , Physical cross-links, such as hydrophobic or ionic interactions, can be formed in situ under mild conditions, but the resulting hydrogels generally degrade or dissolve rapidly. Injectable chemically cross-linked hydrogels have been frequently prepared by photocuring polymers functionalized with vinylic groups. Although the presence of photoinitiators and the generated radicals in the polymerization process has been associated with cytotoxicity, frequently good cell compatibility is found for cells encapsulated in this type of hydrogel. , However, important drawbacks of photo-cross-linkable systems include the limited penetration depth of UV radiation and its potentially damaging effects on living tissue. In situ forming hydrogels utilizing covalent cross-linking between polymers with complementary functional groups therefore received much attention in the last two decades. Early examples of chemical cross-linking reactions forming hydrogels include Schiff base formation between aldehydes and amines and the Passerini and Ugi condensation. However, remaining functional groups on polymers may react with functional groups present in biomolecules such as proteins, limiting the application of these hydrogels as in situ forming delivery systems. In this regard, the use of chemoselective, bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies, which do not interfere with biochemical processes or biomolecules, are very appealing. The most investigated chemoselective cross-linking reaction for hydrogels is the Cu (I)-catalyzed Huisgen 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition of terminal alkynes and azides, commonly known as click chemistry. This term was originally coined in 2001 by Sharpless et al. for a number of new regiospecific linking reactions that give high yields and generally require no purification. The first hydrogel cross-linked via click chemistry was described by the group of Hilborn and was based on PVA. Although this category of hydrogels has been mainly used for tissue engineering applications, they have also been applied for the controlled release of therapeutics and different biomolecules, including doxorubicin bovine serum albumin (BSA) and pDNA. Because "classical" alkyne-azide cycloadditions require the use of a copper catalyst, which may cause adverse effects in biomedical applications, the use of strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) is attracting increasing interest. This reaction employs the inherent ring strain of cyclooctyne groups to achieve fast and efficient cross-linking without the need for catalysts or external stimuli such as UV light. Following this approach, the authors were able to delay, but not completely prevent, postoperative bone regrowth in the cranial defect model. Since the ultimate goal of resynostosis therapy is to slow the postoperative bone growth for a period, but then allow the bone to regrow as the child ages, the reported approach holds promise as treatment after surgical intervention in craniosynostosis. dataset_item.question: What computational methods and parameters were used to optimize atomic structures and calculate mechanical properties in Eu-doped NaAlSiO4 systems?
dataset_item.answer:
The atomic structures of Eu-doped NaAlSiO4 systems were optimized using periodic density functional theory (DFT) within the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). The Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional was employed, incorporating a Hubbard U correction of 2.5 eV for Eu 4f electrons. Electron interactions were described using the projector augmented wave (PAW) method, explicitly treating the valence electrons for Eu, Na, Al, Si, and O. A plane-wave cutoff energy of 530 eV was applied.

Geometry optimization convergence criteria were set to 10⁻⁶ eV for total energy and 0.01 eV/Å for atomic forces. K-point grids were tailored based on the Eu doping concentration: a 2 × 2 × 2 grid was used for L-NASO:0.083Eu²⁺ and N-NASO:0.143Eu²⁺, while a denser 4 × 4 × 2 grid was used for L-NASO:0.333Eu²⁺.

Mechanical properties were calculated using the stress-strain method to determine elastic constants, while elastic moduli were derived using Voigt-Reuss-Hill approximations. The Debye temperature was computed using the quasiharmonic model.

dataset_item.question: How does NH4NO3 formation and decomposition contribute to N2O formation over Cu(OH)+ and other sites at low temperatures during NH3-SCR?
dataset_item.answer:
At low temperatures during NH₃-SCR, N₂O formation is predominantly driven by the formation and decomposition of NH₄NO₃. NH₄NO₃ forms on Cu(OH)⁺ sites under both NH₃ + NO₂ and NH₃ + NO + O₂ conditions due to the oxidative capability of Cu(OH)⁺, which facilitates the conversion of NO to NO₂ and nitrites to nitrates. Additionally, smaller amounts of NH₄NO₃ can form on Cu²⁺ and Brønsted acid sites via NO₂ disproportionation under NH₃ + NO₂ conditions. The decomposition of NH₄NO₃ is a critical step leading to N₂O formation at these temperatures.

Higher NO₂/NOₓ ratios enhance NH₄NO₃ formation, which increases the potential for N₂O generation. However, the yield of N₂O depends on the decomposition rate of NH₄NO₃, which becomes significant at sufficiently elevated temperatures. At higher temperatures, N₂O formation transitions to alternative pathways such as NSNO species and the Eley-Rideal mechanism, which are distinct from NH₄NO₃ decomposition.

dataset_item.question: How does the incorporation of sulfonated groups affect the glass transition temperature and oxygen transmission rate of poly(hexamethylene isophthalamide)?
dataset_item.answer:
The incorporation of sulfonated groups into poly(hexamethylene isophthalamide) (PA6I), typically through the use of 5-sulfoisophthalic acid sodium salt (5-SIPA), increases the glass transition temperature (Tg). This increase is attributed to the formation of intermolecular ionic crosslinks, which restrict chain mobility and enhance the rigidity of the polymer. As a result, the material exhibits improved thermal properties. 

Additionally, the oxygen transmission rate (OTR) decreases with higher sulfonation levels due to the enhanced barrier properties provided by the ionic interactions, which reduce the free volume available for gas diffusion. At sulfonation levels of 10 mol% or more, the polymer becomes water-soluble, expanding its potential applications in waterborne coatings, adhesives, and other solutions-based processes. Compositions with 15 mol% 5-SIPA can form thin, adherent layers suitable for polar substrates, while lower sulfonation levels (up to 10 mol%) retain melt processability, making them suitable for barrier films or as adhesion modifiers in extrusion processes. Furthermore, the OTR reduction is particularly notable at 50% relative humidity, highlighting the polymer's performance under typical environmental conditions.

dataset_item.question: What mechanisms lead to the formation of molecular complexes during photodissociation of CH3CONHOH in an Ar matrix?
dataset_item.answer:
Photodissociation of CH₃CONHOH (AHA) in an Ar matrix proceeds via two simultaneous pathways: isomerization (1Z to 1E) and bond cleavage. This process leads to the formation of four molecular complexes: CH₃OH···HNCO, H₂O···CH₃NCO, H₂O···CH₃CNO, and CO···CH₃NHOH. The first three complexes arise from N-O bond fission, while the fourth is formed via C-N bond cleavage. Subsequent reactions between the photodissociation products facilitate the formation of these complexes.

Computational analysis using MP2 methods revealed multiple stable configurations for each complex, corresponding to global and local energy minima. Experimental matrix isolation spectroscopy confirmed the presence of these configurations, demonstrating selective generation of the complexes during photodissociation. This study highlights the ability of matrix photolysis to produce molecular complexes that are difficult to synthesize via conventional methods.

The paper investigates the photochemical reactions and resulting coproducts formed during the irradiation of CH3CONHOH/Ar (AHA/Ar) matrices with Xe lamp and 225 nm OPO radiation. We see this different reactivity in different capacities of considered homologous disulfides to stabilize forming S,S′-binuclear complexes, which are believed to be key intermediates toward interconversion products. In case of homocystine and 3,3′-dithiodipropionic acid, formation of the S,S′-binuclear complexes leads to cleavage of the disulfide bond, while we observe formation of the S,N-binuclear and S,N,S′,N′-tetranuclear complexes with the preserved S-S bond for the l-cystine and cystamine ligands. Formation of the S,S′-binuclear complexes increases the d(S-S) bond length by 5%, and the redistribution of charges with Sδ--Sδ- in the original disulfide on Sδ+-Sδ- occurs in the complex. We find that the greater the magnitude of Δδ in S,S′-binuclear complex, the higher the likelihood of disproportionation. Eleven dissociation channels were observed within the detection limit of the experiment. The highest ion yield was obtained for (SeU-yl) -, which is a radical and thus highly reactive. A comparable ion yield was observed for the cyano anion. The yields of the other fragment anions are at least 1 order of magnitude smaller. These include radicals such as SeU-yl and molecules such as H2O and HCN. One of the main questions, whether a bond cleavage of the Se-CN bond or the C5-Se bond occurs more efficiently, was solved because the Se-CN bond was far more efficiently cleaved with 5 out of 11 fragmentation pathways and the 2 most intense dissociation channels among them. Cleavage of the C5-Se bond also occurs upon DEA; however, only two channels were observed with low ion yields. Remarkably, all reactions exhibit a 0 eV threshold in the experimental data, which is in full agreement with the calculated thermochemical thresholds. The calculations showed that all DEA channels are exothermic at the present experimental conditions. Few reactions have exothermicities of more than 3 eV. Such behavior also results from the exceptionally high EA of most of fragments released with an excess electron. The anion (SeU-yl)- with the most intense ion yield is formed upon simple cleavage reactions. The formation of CN-, the other abundant anion, is based on simple bond cleavage, while two bonds have to be cleaved and one formed to produce (SeU-yl)-. dataset_item.question: How does the gas/liquid volume ratio influence methane concentration in the residual gas phase during one-stage hydrate formation with tert-butyl peroxy-2-ethylhexanoate?
dataset_item.answer: The gas/liquid volume ratio plays a critical role in determining methane concentration in the residual gas phase during one-stage hydrate formation with tert-butyl peroxy-2-ethylhexanoate (TBPO). Decreasing the gas/liquid volume ratio enhances methane enrichment in the residual gas phase. Using a 26 wt% TBPO aqueous solution at 287 K and 2 MPa, the highest methane concentration of 89.6% was achieved at an initial gas/liquid volume ratio of 2.23, compared to an initial concentration of 67.0%. Additionally, further pressure recovery during hydrate formation increased methane concentration to 93.3%, indicating that both lower gas/liquid ratios and controlled pressurization conditions optimize methane retention in the residual gas phase.

dataset_item.question: How does the grafting-to approach contribute to the synthesis of biomimetic proteoglycans with a bottlebrush architecture?
dataset_item.answer: The grafting-to approach contributes to the synthesis of biomimetic proteoglycans with a bottlebrush architecture by coupling glycosaminoglycan (GAG) chains directly onto a synthetic polymer core through reactions involving primary amine groups on the GAGs. This method preserves the native chemical structure of the GAGs by avoiding the need for additional functionalization of their disaccharide units, which is often required in other synthesis strategies. Furthermore, it allows precise control over key structural parameters, including the type of GAG chains, bristle density, and polymer core length, enabling the replication of various proteoglycan architectures. The resulting biomimetic proteoglycans exhibit a three-dimensional bottlebrush structure and water retention properties akin to natural proteoglycans, making them particularly suitable for applications in tissue repair and regenerative medicine.

dataset_item.question: How is the uptake coefficient of butanol on mineral dust calculated using first-order kinetics?
dataset_item.answer:
The uptake coefficient (\( \gamma \)) of butanol on mineral dust is calculated using first-order kinetics based on the decay of gas-phase butanol concentration over time. The first-order rate constant (\( k_{obs} \)) is determined using the logarithmic relationship between the initial (\( C(0) \)) and time-dependent (\( C(t) \)) butanol concentrations: \( k_{obs} = -\frac{1}{t} \ln \frac{C(t)}{C(0)} \).

Once \( k_{obs} \) is obtained, the uptake coefficient (\( \gamma \)) is calculated using the formula:  
\[
\gamma = \frac{4 k_{obs} \langle v \rangle V}{S_{surf}}
\]
where:  
- \( \langle v \rangle \) is the average molecular velocity of butanol,  
- \( V \) is the reactor volume, and  
- \( S_{surf} \) is the exposed surface area of the mineral dust.

For a cylindrical flow tube, the geometric uptake coefficient (\( \gamma_{geo} \)) is derived using the tube radius (\( r \)):  
\[
\gamma_{geo} = \frac{2 r k_{obs}}{\langle v \rangle}
\]

These calculations typically assume steady-state butanol concentrations after 10 minutes of surface exposure.

Understanding how design parameters of targeted drug carriers influence interaction with cells and the subsequent signaling leading to endocytosis is key to inform optimization of drug delivery systems. , Both the size and targeting valency of drug carriers impact cell binding and endocytic uptake. - ,,, However, how these parameters influence receptor-mediated signaling linking binding with internalization is rather obscure. For instance: Is the uptake efficiency correlative with the signaling level? Is this regulated similarly for carriers of different sizes and valencies? Are signaling and uptake events induced independently for each individual carrier or do they depend on cumulative carrier binding to cells? Is the number of receptors engaged by a carrier the factor ruling signaling and uptake, or does this depend on the density of engagement per surface area? Using model submicrometer, micrometer, and supramicrometer carriers targeted to ICAM-1 at varying valencies, we have examined these questions. Our results revealed an intricate interplay between these parameters, where the density of the targeting antibody per carrier surface area (which would determine the density of the receptor cluster on the cell surface) is the main parameter controlling the signaling conducive to endocytosis (Figure ). Larger carriers posed a requirement for stronger signaling, since carrier size impacts the ability of the plasmalemma to efficiently engulf a carrier. It is likely that for endocytic pathways lacking signals that enable sufficient plasmalemma deformability (e.g.. ceramide enrichment shown here for the CAM pathway), size will become restrictive regardless of the targeting density. Each carrier bound on a cell induced signaling based on its antibody-coat density (the density of the clustered receptors, not the absolute number of receptors engaged or the size of the cluster), and rendered endocytosis based on its size and enough buildup of the inducing signal. Each signaling-uptake event was independent for each single carrier bound on a cell, where the total number of carriers bound to the cell, the total surface area occupied by those carriers, and the total number of cell receptors engaged did not exert a major influence. It will be important to examine this regulation for other receptors and pathways in order to extract generic conclusions, and to evaluate how other carrier design parameters (e.g.. smaller sizes, different shape, curvature, carrier type, surface chemistry, etc.) and biological environments (different cell types, presence of flow, pathological alterations, etc.) impact these outcomes. - ,,, Nevertheless, other natural routes associate to signaling common to the CAM pathway, and it is expected that the findings obtained here would broadly apply to the use of said routes for drug delivery applications. For instance, ceramide and/or PKC are key for the formation of lipid domains, vesiculation, cytoskeletal rearrangements, and formation of membrane protrusions observed for phagocytic and macropinocytic pathways, intracellular invasion by certain viral and bacterial pathogens, leukocyte endothelial adhesion and extravasation, and certain events of transcytosis across cellular barriers. - Therefore, these results have shed light on key factors modulating the efficacy of uptake of targeted drug carriers, which shall inform future design of vehicles for intracellular delivery.

dataset_item.question: What role do analytical techniques like scanning electrochemical microscopy and cyclic voltammetry play in characterizing self-assembled monolayers?
dataset_item.answer: Analytical techniques like scanning electrochemical microscopy (SECM) and cyclic voltammetry (CV) play a critical role in characterizing self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) by probing their electrochemical behavior, spatial properties, and surface interactions. Cyclic voltammetry is employed to study reductive desorption of SAMs, revealing their stability and electrochemical responses under varying conditions such as pH, applied voltage, and interactions with charged redox centers. It provides insights into charge transfer dynamics and SAM integrity. Scanning electrochemical microscopy complements this by offering spatially resolved electrochemical imaging, enabling the identification of local reactivity, defect sites, and charge-dependent interactions. SECM also investigates tip-to-substrate interactions in the presence of redox mediators, facilitating precise mapping of functionalized regions and defect-related properties. Together, these techniques provide a comprehensive evaluation of SAM electrochemical functionality and structural properties.

Several materials prepared from triazine-containing precursors were explored as active materials in Li half cells. Well-defined materials which exhibit strong triazine character show very low gravimetric capacities even if the triazine units are bridged by conjugated moieties, such as phenylene or 2,2′-bipyridine. This directly contradicts the previously suggested bipolar mechanism in which the triazine is n- or p-doped when cycled. In order to achieve high gravimetric capacities, the well-defined conjugated systems must be synthesized at higher temperatures, thereby destroying the triazine unit and creating an N-containing amorphous carbon material. These materials have high concentrations of localized spins (large numbers of unpaired electrons) that may be involved in the discharge and charge mechanisms. The N-containing amorphous carbon materials are very similar to N-containing porous carbon materials that have been evaluated as supercapacitor materials. , The capacity of the amorphous materials trends loosely with specific surface area and C/N content. However, higher surface area does not always result in a higher capacity, suggesting the mechanism is not purely capacitive. The slight observed rate dependence also suggests a pseudocapacitive behavior involving charge transfer processes. These charge transfer processes could involve the unpaired electrons in the amorphous materials, and indeed, the inactive PTI materials do not contain unpaired electrons. Suggestions for future work to further probe the charge storage mechanisms involve using in situ EPR in order to observe the evolution of the spin concentration as a function of discharging and charging.

Samples were collected at predetermined times and stored at -20 °C in amber vials prior to analysis by liquid chromatography with triple quadrupole tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) or high-performance liquid chromatography with UV absorbance detection. Dark controls were included to account for other reactions, including the hydrolysis and direct reaction of EBS with reactive species quenchers, scavengers, and sensitizers. All experiments were conducted at room temperature (i.e.. 22 ± 1 °C).

Fourteen years after C&B93, Yao et al. studied the effect on the pH measurements of impurities in the mCP indicators. The most important impurities are compounds perturbing the absorbance properties of the dye. Common impurities result in an negative bias for measured pH that ranges from -0.003 to -0.02 pH units, with the bias being larger at high pH values. This magnitude depends on the manufacturer (i.e.. the type and quantity of impurities), but even varies from batch to batch of a single manufacturer. Initially Yao et al. proposed an equation to empirically correct the effect of impurities based on calibrations against the Kodak indicator used by C&B93. Nevertheless, the equation was only suitable for pH measurements obtained with indicator from the manufacturer Sigma-Aldrich. Given the range of manufacturers, the approach has recently evolved toward removing the impurities with high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) or flash chromatography to produce purified mCP (PUR mCP). The optical properties of PUR versus unpurified mCP (UNPUR mCP) were evaluated, and Liu et al. proposed a new PUR mCP parametrization. This parametrization has been independently validated by several laboratories , and even extended to wider temperature and salinity ranges, for fresh, estuarine and seawater or even more extreme conditions, including seawater near the freezing point and brines with extreme salinity values.

A merry-go-round photoreactor system was employed and equipped with a medium pressure mercury lamp (Heraeus Noblelight model TQ 718, operated at 500 W) and a 0.15 M sodium nitrate filter solution that minimizes direct phototransformation reactions. The experimental setup was described in detail previously. Aliquots of ozonated DOM solutions and blanks were supplemented either with only the target compounds (i.e.. SMX, SD, and TMP) or additionally with the excited triplet state sensitizer CBBP and diluted to yield final concentrations of 0.19 mmolC L-1 = 2.3 mgC L-1 for DOMs, 5 μM for target compounds, and 50 μM for CBBP. The solution pH was adjusted to 7.0 by addition of phosphoric acid (11.5 mM final buffer concentration) prior to irradiation. This pH was chosen to match the pH used in EDC measurements. A 20 mL sample of each solution was filled into capped quartz-glass tubes and irradiated for 5 min (all CBBP-target compound combinations), 100 min (DOMs-TMP), or 225 min (DOMs-SMX/SD). These irradiation times were determined on the basis of preliminary kinetic irradiation experiments. During irradiation, six aliquots of 400 μL each were withdrawn at equidistant time intervals and analyzed, either immediately or stored at 4 °C, by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Details on HPLC equipment and the methods employed to quantify the concentration of the target compounds (SMX, SD, and TMP) are available elsewhere. , To confirm that t-BuOH had no effect on the phototransformation kinetics of the target compounds, we conducted control irradiation experiments with DOM solutions that were ozonated in the absence of t-BuOH but were subsequently amended with 5 mM t-BuOH prior to the irradiations.

dataset_item.question: What are the differences in method requirements for passive sampling in regulatory frameworks across the United States, OSPAR, and the European Union?
dataset_item.answer:
The regulatory frameworks in the United States, OSPAR, and the European Union exhibit distinct approaches to passive sampling method requirements. 

In the United States, passive sampling adoption is limited for compliance monitoring under the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES), which prioritizes total effluent concentrations. Ambient water monitoring, on the other hand, lacks federal standardization and relies on state-level practices guided by EPA recommendations, such as the Consolidated Assessment and Listing Methodology (CALM). This flexible, innovation-driven approach encourages new technologies but lacks consistency in sampler selection, deployment, and data reporting.

OSPAR similarly supports innovation in monitoring technologies and mandates the use of documented and validated methods with quality assurance protocols. However, OSPAR does not enforce quantitative performance criteria for passive sampling methods, instead requiring comparisons against background assessment concentrations (BACs) derived from long-term monitoring data.

The European Union enforces the most rigid framework under the Water Framework Directive (WFD), requiring legally binding, standardized methods for compliance monitoring. These methods must meet strict performance criteria, including measurement uncertainty ≤50% at environmental quality standard (EQS) levels and a limit of quantification (LOQ) ≤30% of the EQS. Methods must also comply with EN/ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation. While this ensures high reliability and comparability, the stringent requirements hinder the rapid adoption of passive sampling methods.

Across all regions, standardization gaps in passive sampling methodologies, particularly in sampler selection, deployment protocols, and data reporting, limit broader regulatory acceptance. The U.S. and OSPAR emphasize flexibility and innovation, while the EU prioritizes precision and legal compliance.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. Summary of the Paper's Purpose
The paper reviews compliance monitoring requirements for nonpolar organic compounds across major regulatory frameworks (EU, US, and the Oslo-Paris Convention) and evaluates whether passive sampling methods can meet these requirements. It assesses the strengths and weaknesses of passive sampling for water, sediments, and biota, highlights scientific inconsistencies in regulatory definitions, identifies areas requiring quality control improvements, and outlines research priorities to address gaps in bioaccumulation prediction and standardization. The ultimate aim is to advance the adoption of passive sampling as the best available technology for chemical monitoring of nonpolar organic compounds.

---

### 2. Classification of Purpose
The paper emphasizes **"<method>"** because its primary focus is on evaluating the suitability, limitations, and potential improvements of passive sampling methods for compliance monitoring.

---

### 3. Research Questions
Here are relevant research questions based on the abstract:

1. **Method Development and Validation**:
   - How can standardized methods for passive sampling be developed to improve data quality and ensure consistent application across regulatory frameworks?
   - What laboratory performance studies are necessary to validate passive sampling techniques for nonpolar organic compounds?

2. **Regulatory Compatibility**:
   - How can passive sampling results be aligned with existing regulatory definitions, such as the EU's quality standards, which are based on total concentrations in water?
   - Are there scientifically valid alternatives to the current regulatory definitions that better reflect the behavior of nonpolar compounds?

3. **Bioaccumulation Prediction**:
   - What are the mechanisms driving bioaccumulation in higher trophic levels, and how can passive sampling methods be adapted to predict these processes more accurately?

4. **Application in Environmental Monitoring**:
   - What strategies can be implemented to encourage the adoption of passive sampling methods by commercial laboratories and environmental monitoring agencies?
   - What are the key knowledge gaps that need to be addressed to make passive sampling the standard for monitoring nonpolar organic compounds?

5. **Environmental Impact Assessment**:
   - How does the use of passive sampling contribute to understanding the long-term environmental impact of nonpolar organic compounds in marine ecosystems?

These research questions align with the paper's themes and the broader interests of materials science, particularly in relation to analytical techniques and environmental monitoring applications.
dataset_item.true_false_question: Does the European Union prioritize flexibility over precision and legal compliance in passive sampling method requirements?

inference_contexts: To promote adoption of passive sampling into the implementation of compliance monitoring regulations, there is a critical need to get beyond passive sampling as a purely scientific endeavor and begin to standardize PSD type selection, deployment, chemical analysis, and data reporting. For example, in the United States, the lack of standardized methods has impeded greater acceptance of passive sampling in regulations. The following discussion reviews the progress made with passive sampling with regard to use in water, sediments, and biota. The discussion also emphasizes the areas in which passive sampling needs more work before standardizing can be successfully initiated.

Differences in the monitoring approaches between the U.S. and OSPAR on one hand, and the EU on the other, will likely affect the further application of passive sampling in a regulatory context. In the U.S. context, States, U.S. EPA, and the research community cooperate in the CALM approach, to generate monitoring data that are best fit for a given purpose. Also OSPAR promotes the use of new technologies to amend existing methods for chemical monitoring. By contrast, monitoring in the EU is strongly regulated in legally binding directives that define EU-wide EQSs and specify method requirements for compliance checking with these EQSs.

Method requirements for the application of PSDs in chemical monitoring of nonpolar compounds in a regulatory context are fulfilled to varying degrees (Table ). Detailed guidelines for the use of PSDs are available for silicone sheet samplers and semipermeable membrane devices. ,, ASTM International developed a standard method for SPME of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in pore waters. Several interlaboratory studies that demonstrate method consistency are available, and are discussed below. A proficiency testing scheme organized by QUASIMEME is operational (www.quasimeme.org). Certified reference materials (CRMs) are presently not available, but CRM preparation for passive sampling could be easier than for batch water sampling. Data quality can be assessed from repeated analysis of CRMs (when available) or reference materials prepared by laboratories in-house, similar to current practice for the analysis of sediment and biota samples. Although Table is focused on passive sampling in water, it can be envisioned that similar requirements exist for passive sampling in sediments.

In the U.S.. acceptable chemical analysis methods for compliance monitoring of effluents under the NPDES are listed in the Code of Federal Regulations, title 40, part 136, but a permitting authority may specify the use of alternative methods. Passive sampling may not be the first method of choice for this type of compliance monitoring, because discharge permits are defined as TMDLs (i.e.. concentrations in total effluent, multiplied by the daily effluent discharge volume). By contrast, method requirements for ambient water monitoring by the States are essentially unregulated by federal law, but instead result from the interaction between the U.S. EPA and a given State's department of environmental quality on how to assess water quality in relation to the WQC, using the best available practices. The Consolidated Assessment and Listing Methodology (CALM) aims to continuously improve the quality of ambient water monitoring, using chemical, biological, and toxicological data, among others.

In the U.S. context, ambient WQC for the protection of aquatic life against nonpolar compounds are based on toxicity tests with low organic carbon concentrations in the test water, and hence are essentially based on C free, albeit implicitly. WQC for the protection of human health are derived from chemical uptake by consumption (drinking water, fish/shellfish). Concentrations in fish/shellfish that are considered to be sufficiently protective are converted to aqueous concentrations using (preferably field derived) BAFs that are based on C free. However, for use in WQC development, to be consistent with water quality monitoring data, these BAFs are converted back to values based on the total concentration. , Thus, human health WQC cannot be directly compared with passive sampling results. Consequently, while regulators in the U.S. recognize the importance of C free, the actual water quality monitoring regulations do not yet use this parameter. OSPAR also aims to define water standards on a C free basis. Quality standards in the EU are commonly defined as C total, but EU regulations allow the use of standards for other matrices if these offer an equal level of protection. Generic suspended particulate matter (SPM) contents of 15 mg L-1 (fresh waters) and 3 mg L-1 (marine waters) are recommended to convert between C free, C total and concentrations in SPM. ,, An ISO standard for the deployment, retrieval, and analysis of passive samplers is available, but guidance that is specific to particular sampler types and contaminant groups (e.g.. polychlorinated biphenyls - PCBs, PAHs, polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins/furans - PCDD/Fs) may have to be added in the future. This ISO standard also includes quality control measures to assess recoveries, precision, and method detection limits. Guidance for the selection, validation (QA/QC) and deployment of PSDs for contaminated sediments is also available.

dataset_item.question: How do Soxhlet extraction and grinding compare in terms of process efficiency, impurity removal, and recovery yields during the synthesis of 2-hydroxydodecyl starch ethers?
dataset_item.answer: Soxhlet extraction and grinding are two purification methods compared in the synthesis of 2-hydroxydodecyl starch ethers, each with distinct advantages and limitations. Soxhlet extraction offers a simpler and more automated process but requires longer processing times and achieves a lower recovery yield of 63%. Grinding, on the other hand, is faster, provides significantly higher recovery yields of 85%, and better aligns with industrial scalability due to compatibility with existing equipment for crude product grinding and soluble byproduct extraction. Both methods yield similar substitution degrees (MS ~1.1) and allow for solvent recycling, supporting sustainable practices. Grinding also demonstrates superior impurity removal, effectively isolating previously unidentified byproducts like bis(2-hydroxydodecyl) oxide. Overall, grinding is deemed more efficient and practical for large-scale applications, while Soxhlet extraction may be more suitable for smaller-scale or automated laboratory processes.

The hydrometallurgical purification of MG-Si by leaching with HF in the presence of H2O2 as an oxidizing agent was investigated under different conditions of leaching temperature, particle size, lixiviant composition, and leaching duration. After introduction of H2O2 into HF lixiviant, the extraction capacity for metallic impurities can be significantly enhanced, especially for Cu, with extraction efficiency increasing from 23.98% to 92.88% when leaching MG-Si in 2 mol L-1 HF and 2 mol L-1 H2O2. Accordingly, when leaching temperature is increased above 55 °C, the extraction efficiency for Cu decreases dramatically. The leaching yields of impurities will increase with decrease in particle size, but taking grinding cost into consideration, particle size fraction of 74-154 μm will be suitable for SOG-Si production. In addition, the phenomenon of cracking effect by the lixiviant will be more obvious with increasing particle size of silicon, which is beneficial for impurity removal. It is found that the silicon purity increases from 99.74% to more than 99.96% after only 0.25 h of leaching by 1 mol L-1 HF and 2 mol L-1 H2O2 with particle size of 74-154 μm. After a prolonged leaching duration, 99.99% pure silicon can be achieved. An obvious increase in purity of silicon cannot be found with increasing HF concentration. According to the microstructural evolution of MG-Si after etching with different lixiviants, sensitivity sequences of precipitates to HF, alone and associated with H2O2, can be obtained. In addition, the influences of two complexing agents (oxalic acid and acetic acid) on the impurity extraction by HF and H2O2 are moderated. Different types of MG-Si from different origins may be responsible for that. After Raman analysis, it is reasonable that etching silicon starts with the first oxidizing reaction by H2O2 and then dissolving by HF. Like Si-Si bonds, some Si-F and Si-O bonds can also be found on silicon surface after acid etching with HF and H2O2 etchant.

The present study showed that the aminopolycarboxylic chelating surfactant C12-DTPA can be effectively used in combination with two foaming agents for the removal of extremely toxic metal ions such as Cd2+, Zn2+, and Sr2+ from aqueous solution using the ion flotation technique. It was found that the removal of metal ions from the flotation cell is dependent on their chelation behavior with C12-DTPA and on the foaming properties of the samples, both of which change with the pH of the system. The results indicate that both Zn2+ and Cd2+ can be completely removed at pH 5. However, when the pH is increased to 7 and 9, barely 60% of Zn2+ and Cd2+ can be removed from the solution. On the other hand, at pH 5, no removal of Sr2+ was observed, whereas at a pH of 7-9, ~65% removal was achieved under comparable conditions. For efficient separation of metal ions from water systems, the amount of water transferred to the reject foam must also be considered, which is evaluated by measuring the concentration of metal ions in the collected foam. It was found that the interactions between the foaming agent and chelating surfactant affects the concentration of metal ions in the foam. A higher concentration of DoTAC increased the concentration of Sr2+ in the collected foam, because of the strong interactions between DoTAC and C12-DTPA. A higher concentration of DDAO, on the other hand, increased the removal of metal ions from the bulk, because of better foaming properties of the test solution. The separation efficiency is a measure of both the removal of metal ions from the bulk and the concentration of metal ions in the collected foam, and the foaming agent mixture must be designed accordingly. Taking the above parameters into account, it would be useful to design and optimize a selective ion flotation process in competitive systems for the target metal ions.
